# THE INSTITUTIONS
## OF HARMONY
### BY MASTER GIOSEFFO ZARLINO OF CHIOGGIA;

->In which; beyond those matters pertaining<-
->TO MUSIC;<-
->One finds explained many passages<-
->of Poets, Historians, and Philosophers;<-

->*As may be clearly seen upon reading them.*<-

->When God grants, envy has no power.<-
<note>original Greek: "Θεοῦ διδόντος, οὐδὲν ἰσχύει φθόνος."</note>
->And when He grants not, labor has no power.<-
<note>original Greek: "Καὶ μὴ διδόντος, οὐδὲν ἰσχύει πόνος." This couplet emphasizes divine grace over human effort or spite.</note>

->The Privilege of the Most Illustrious Lordship of Venice<-
->October 16, 1557, in the Senate.<-

THAT it be granted to Master Gioseffo Zarlino of Chioggia <note>Chioggia is a coastal town near Venice; Zarlino is often identified by his birthplace</note>, that no one other than he, or those authorized by him, may print in this our city, nor in any place of our Lordship, nor sell within it if printed elsewhere, the work titled *Harmonic Institutions* <note>original: "Istitutioni harmoniche"</note>, whether in Latin or the vernacular <note>Italian</note>, composed by him, for the space of the next ten years, under all the penalties contained in his petition; being obliged to observe everything that is decreed in the matter of Printing.

->Giuseppe Tramezzino<-
->Ducal Notary<-

<insert>
J. B. Pory
Sept. 15, 1851
</insert>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page begins the formal dedication of the work. The catchword "li infe-" from the previous page likely refers to the beginning of the text or a preceding section not included here.</meta>

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## AND MOST REVEREND LORD, LORD
## VINCENZO DIEDO
### PATRIARCA OF VENICE.

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'S' containing a landscape scene with foliage and a building in the background.</image-desc>

**S**enior wise men of ancient times were of the common opinion that all things, through the desire they have to return to their origin, are naturally inclined toward their own proper function and toward achieving their perfection. Wherefore, since Science <note>The author uses "Science" in the classical sense of *Scientia*, meaning organized knowledge or certain understanding.</note> is the perfection of the Intellect, and Understanding and Knowing are the proper functions of Man—through which he comes to be joined to his Creator—it follows that everyone is naturally drawn to the knowledge of things. Nor does one ever tire or weary of investigating their causes and wishing to understand the high secrets of Nature. Nor do I think that the hope of acquiring knowledge of many things alone drives him to this, but even the knowledge of a single thing; because in knowing it, he understands that he is journeying toward perfection. He judges that in surpassing all others in this, it is a thing worthy of much praise and honor. Therefore, I believe that because men love to hold the first place in any faculty, adding one thing one day and another the next, the Sciences and the Arts have grown in such a way that it is almost impossible to see from which side anything new could be added to them. 

And although it could be said that each of these has enjoyed this good fortune—perhaps because of the profit that men derive from them—nevertheless, until now it seems to me, if I am not mistaken, that Music has been little favored by fortune. For although many authors are found who have written many things on the Science and the Art <note>The "Science" refers to the mathematical theory of music, while the "Art" refers to the practical application and composition.</note>, nonetheless, a man reading them cannot acquire that knowledge which he desires; because truly they have not sufficiently touched upon, nor shown, any of those things which are of great importance. 

Wherefore I, who from my tender years have always had a natural inclination toward Music, having already consumed a good part of my life in the pursuit of its knowledge, and having noticed this state of affairs, wished to try if I could in some way bring those things pertaining to Theory and Practice back toward their perfection, to do something pleasing for all those who delight in such a faculty. And although I knew that this was too heavy a burden for me, I nevertheless thought that even if I were not to bring them to their ultimate degree of perfection, at least I might perhaps have been able to set the matter on such a path that I would be the cause of giving courage to some noble spirit to pass even further. For which reason, having proposed such a goal for myself, and having in these past years written the present INSTITUTIONS, which—

<summary>In this dedication to the Patriarch of Venice, Gioseffo Zarlino argues that music has lagged behind other sciences in its development and explains his motivation for writing a comprehensive treatise on musical theory and practice.</summary>
<keywords>Vincenzo Diedo, Patriarch of Venice, music theory, musical practice, perfection of the intellect, history of science, Gioseffo Zarlino, Istitutioni Harmoniche</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal dedication of Gioseffo Zarlino’s work to a high-ranking ecclesiastical figure, likely the Patriarch of Venice, following the initial salutations of the previous page.</meta>

...they teach those things pertaining to one and the other of the aforementioned parts; spurred by my friends, who judged that they could be useful to students, it seemed right to me to bring them to light, dedicating them to Your Illustrious and Most Reverend Lordship. And in doing this, I was moved primarily to show, in some part, how much I remain obligated to the kindnesses shown to me by you. Furthermore, I did so because if by chance there were anyone of such a malignant spirit that—having no respect for the fact that I do this with the intention of helping others—he should be moved to blame these labors of mine, he would at least be constrained to have regard for the Illustrious name of that Lord to whom they have been dedicated. Added to this is the fact that your singular prudence, justice, religion, and kindness—qualities in you known and praised by all—have given birth in me to an incredible reverence and devotion, and I had no other way nor means to demonstrate it.

Nor can one truly have doubt concerning the singular virtues of Your Illustrious and Most Reverend Lordship, since clear testimony has been given by this most wise Senate; which, through many experiences, having known how prudent you were in the governments of the Republic, both in the city and abroad in the administrations of Verona and Udine; and finally, while you were holding office in Padua, the death of the Most Reverend Contarino <note>Gasparo Contarini (1483–1542), a Venetian noble and cardinal</note> having occurred, the Senate, judging you worthy of such honor, elected you Patriarch of Venice. And although attained honors most often tend to change the minds and habits of men, nevertheless, even though you have reached such an honored rank, the goodness of your soul has not changed or diminished in the slightest; rather, it has increased by a great deal. This can be clearly seen: for as soon as you had attained such dignity, you turned yourself first to adorning the Church, and then, with very great expense, to repairing the Palace, which was already beginning to fall into ruin. 

But just as you continually do not cease to renovate and adorn the material church, so from day to day (which is a most evident sign of religion and charity) you do not stop sustaining and relieving the spiritual one, continually offering aid to the poor—not only to those of your own city, but also to foreigners, and to those who, departing from infidelity, come to Christianity. And like a vigilant shepherd, and diligent farmer and guardian of the Vineyard of the Lord <note>A common biblical metaphor for the Church or the faithful</note>, you attend to providing that your flock be not harmed by wolves, and that from this Vineyard the bad branches be removed, or otherwise managed in such a way that they become fruitful. All these things truly bear most clear witness to the world of your rare virtues, which have moved me to dedicate these labors of mine to you, such as they may be. And if the gift is small, look at least upon the respect of my soul toward you, which is infinitely great.

->Of Your Illustrious and Most Reverend Lordship<-
->The most affectionate servant,<-
->Gioseffo Zarlino.<-

<summary>In this dedication, the music theorist Gioseffo Zarlino presents his work to the Patriarch of Venice, praising the prelate's administrative history in Verona, Udine, and Padua, as well as his charitable works and church renovations.</summary>
<keywords>Gioseffo Zarlino, Patriarch of Venice, Gasparo Contarini, Verona, Udine, Padua, patronage, Counter-Reformation, church architecture, charity</keywords>

## TO THE READERS.

IF I see, my most kind Readers, that these labors of mine are truly dear to you, I will strive to give you, as soon as it can be done, these same *Institutions* written in the Latin language, along with the **Harmonic DEMONSTRATIONS** *mentioned in several places in this Work*, and *some other things besides*; to which I have not yet (as they say) put the finishing touch. In the meantime, read with a happy and sincere heart that which I have labored over for many years to benefit you. And if you find anything that does not fully satisfy you, remember that I am a man; and I do not think, as that good old Terentian <note>original: "Terentiano" — Refers to the Roman playwright Terence and his famous line: "I am a man; I consider nothing human foreign to me."</note> used to say, that anything belonging to man is foreign to me. I wish to add that it could very well be that I have erred in some thing, since we are all subject to such a law. And that this is true, you may now recognize; for with all the diligence used in printing, it has not been possible to prevent several errors from occurring on a few pages of some books (though not in all); which you will cheerfully correct before you begin to read. In doing so, you will show how kind you are in forgiving those that might be (if you find any) of some importance and cannot be understood except by the intellect. The first Number is that of the Page of the Work, and the second is that of the Line.

<header>TO THE READERS</header>

<note>The following text is mirrored on the original page due to ink bleed-through from the reverse side; it is transcribed here in standard reading order for clarity.</note>

IF I see my unfortunate labors—which, resulting from a very long and grave infirmity, are brought forth to my detriment and that of anyone who reads them—presented in this manner after two lustra <term>lustra: periods of five years each; ten years in total</term> of the same, which by the supreme value of **RATIONAL DIAGNOSTICS** deserved much greater applause than my meager talent will give them: yet I am certain that no one can blame me for lack of diligence. Indeed, these works were for the most part composed by me under the tyranny of said infirmity, which has made me realize (if I did not know it already) that the Soul of man, as long as it lives joined with the Body, can almost never perform excellently unless health concurs, for health and life are like a continuous Harmony. Since some changes have been made in these Treatises, or the sequence of their order partially altered, I have thought it well to give you this brief enlightenment. This is to remove all confusion and to make clear the labor of those who committed themselves to reducing them to the form in which they now appear combined, serving for a clearer understanding of certain points misunderstood—or better to say, poorly explained—in the second volume of the Press <note>original: "Prelo" — likely referring to the specific printing house or a volume title associated with the printing process</note>. May it all be for the glory of God and the benefit of one's Neighbor.

Regarding the sheets of the *Principles*, etc., many things have been added and corrected with great accuracy that remained imperfect and flawed in the London and Leiden editions in quarto and duodecimo <term>quarto and duodecimo: common book sizes of the 17th century</term>, especially in the section on Pores, and on the pith of Silk <note>Refers to Malpighi's pioneering microscopic studies of silkworms</note>, and in the chapter on Bones. Likewise, another piece of writing has been added that treats the Bones at p. 32, and the response to an objection made regarding the same at p. 51. In the *Treatise on the Uterus*, the Annotations—which in other editions were confused—have been put in order at p. 101 and p. 110, and another unpublished note on said Treatise has been added at p. 117; a letter written to a Physician of Bologna regarding the same Treatise has also been provided at p. 120. In the second volume of the Press, the order has also been changed because the responses given to Giara <note>Domenico Giara: A contemporary critic who engaged in academic disputes with Malpighi</note>—which the Author never intended as standalone pieces but were composed in defense of the *Treatise on the Heart and Lungs*—might be seen more clearly. The order was changed to place the said *Treatise on the Heart* before those responses at p. 121 of the same volume, and after it was placed the *Treatise on the Structure of the Glands* at p. 136, after which follow the responses to said Giara until the end of the book. Read it according to this scheme at the pages we shall note here below: at p. 121, Heart first; at p. 136, Glands second; at p. 147, first response to Giara; at p. 154, second; at p. 165, third; at p. 174, fourth; at p. 182, fifth; at p. 191, sixth; at p. 200, seventh; at p. 210, eighth; at p. 219, ninth; at p. 230, tenth: and with the tenth, the *Discourse of the Press* ends at p. 244, followed by the other works until the end of the Volume, which are distinguished in the Index. The Annotations made upon the *Discourse of the Press*, which in other editions are placed in confusion at the end of the *Principles*, are here placed in their proper locations; for their understanding, see the note at p. 14. In the *Response to Giara*, p. 132, the numbers of the Annotations have been placed so that they correspond to the Discourses, as seen at pages 121 and 136, where the same numbers are found. Similarly, the order has been changed for the Discourses titled *Whether the Cook or the Physician Makes the Flesh*; specifically, that which the Physician says has been placed first, and then that which the Cook says, so that the response may be more clearly understood; see p. 153. In the second Volume, regarding those works which are not in the English editions, nor even in the catalogs of the first and second volumes from Bologna found in the book's Index, the same accuracy has been observed. This applies not only to placing the sheets in their proper place and according to the order of him who composed them, but also in correcting many errors that had slipped in during transcription, especially in that writing on the *Observations of Man*, p. 18, and in that on *Calculi* <term>calculi: stones, such as kidney or gallstones</term>, p. 35, so as to regulate and direct it.

# THE FIRST PART
## Of the Harmonic Institutions
### BY MASTER GIOSEFFO ZARLINO
### FROM CHIOGGIA.
#### *Preface.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring a stylized letter within a rectangular frame filled with intricate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc> MANY times, reflecting within myself and turning over in my mind the various things that the supreme God, through His kindness, has granted to mortals, I have clearly understood that among the most marvelous is His having conceded them the particular grace of using an articulate voice <term>articulate voice: human speech composed of distinct, meaningful sounds, as opposed to the simple cries of animals</term>. By this means alone, man is fit above all other animals to be able to express all those thoughts he has conceived within his soul. And there is no doubt that through speech it is openly manifested how unlike he is to the beasts, and how much he is their superior. And I believe it can truly be said that such a gift has been of the greatest utility to the human race. For nothing else but speech induced and drew men—who in the beginning were scattered in the woods and on the mountains, living a life much like wild animals—to bring themselves to dwell and live together in company, as is required by the nature of man, and to build cities and castles; and, united by the virtue of good order, to preserve themselves; and by dealing with one another, to offer help in every need.

Having gathered and joined in neighborliness in this way, it was then discovered day by day through experience how great was the power of speech, even if it was crude. Wherefore some men of elevated intellect began to put into use certain ornate and delightful manners of speaking, with beautiful and illustrious sentiments, striving to surpass other men in that very thing in which men remain superior to other animals. Nor being satisfied with this, they attempted to go even further, seeking always to rise to a higher degree of perfection. And having for this purpose added Harmony to speech, they began to investigate various Rhythms and diverse Meters, which, when accompanied by harmony, offer the greatest delight to our soul.

Having thus discovered (among many others) a manner of composition which they called Hymns, they also discovered the Heroic, Tragic, Comic, and Dithyrambic <term>Dithyrambic: a passionate, rhythmic choral song or poem, originally ancient Greek hymns to Dionysus</term> poems. With number, speech, and harmony, they could use these to sing praises and render glory to the Gods; and with these—according as it pleased them—they could more easily and with greater force restrain unbridled souls, and with greater delight move the wills and appetites of men, leading them back to a tranquil and civilized life. Having successfully achieved this, they acquired such authority among the people that they were held and honored much more than others. And those who reached such great knowledge were, without any distinction, named Musicians, Poets, and Sages.

But since Music was then understood as a supreme and singular doctrine, Musicians were held in great esteem, and an inestimable reverence was shown to them. Yet, whether it has been due to the malice of the times or the negligence of men who have placed little value not only on Music but on other studies as well, from that supreme height in which it was placed, it has fallen to the lowest depths. Where it was once shown incredible honor, it was later deemed so vile and abject, and so little valued, that it is hardly recognized for what it is even by learned men. And this seems to me to have happened because no part or vestige remains of that venerable gravity which it used to possess in ancient times. Wherefore everyone has felt permitted to tear it apart and treat it most poorly in many unworthy ways. Nevertheless, the excellent God—to whom it is pleasing that His infinite power, wisdom, and goodness be magnified and manifested by men with hymns accompanied by graceful and sweet accents—not appearing to tolerate any longer that this art, which serves His worship, be held in contempt; and which here below gives us a hint of what sweetness there may be in the songs of the Angels who stand in heaven praising His majesty; He has granted to us—

<meta>catchword: grace (original: "gratia")</meta>

Zarlino laments the contemporary decline of music from its ancient status as a supreme science and hints at a divinely inspired restoration of the art.</summary>

# Preface

...the grace to bring forth in our times Adrian Willaert <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562) was a Flemish composer who became the chapel master at St. Mark's Basilica in Venice; Zarlino was his student.</note>, truly one of the rarest intellects who has ever practiced **practical music** <term>practical music: the actual performance and composition of music, as opposed to theoretical study</term>. Acting like a new Pythagoras <term>Pythagoras: an ancient Greek philosopher who, according to legend, discovered that musical intervals could be expressed as mathematical ratios</term> by examining minutely everything that can occur within it, and finding infinite errors, he has begun to remove them and to restore music toward that honor and dignity which it once held, and which it reasonably ought to have. He has shown a reasonable method for composing every musical melody <term>cantilena: a song or vocal melody</term> in an elegant manner, and in his own compositions, he has given a most clear example of this. 

Now, because I have understood that there are many—some out of curiosity and others truly out of a desire to learn—who wish for someone to set out to show the way of composing music with a beautiful, learned, and elegant order, I have taken the trouble to write the present **INSTITUTIONS** <note>original: "ISTITVTIONI"</note>. I have gathered various matters from the good ancients and discovered new things myself to see if I might perhaps be fit to satisfy, in some part, such a desire and the obligation that a man has to be useful to other men. 

But seeing that, just as for one who wishes to be a good painter and acquire great fame in painting, it is not enough to use colors beautifully if he does not know how to give a solid reason for the work he has done; so to him who desires to have the name of a true Musician, it is not enough, nor does it bring much praise, to have joined consonances together if he does not know how to give an account of such a union. Therefore, I have set myself to treat together those things which belong to both the practice and the theory <term>speculatiua: the "speculative" or theoretical branch of music focused on mathematical laws</term> of this science, so that those who love to be numbered among good Musicians may, by accurately reading our work, give a reason for their compositions. 

And although I know that treating this subject carries many difficulties, nonetheless I have good hope that by discussing it with as much brevity as possible, I will show it to be clear and very easy, revealing such secrets of it that everyone may perhaps remain largely satisfied. But so that one may have a clear understanding of this our treatise, it has seemed right to me to divide it into several parts, in such a way as to show the things that must be presupposed before coming to the teaching of the said science. 

And because to establish the order of sounds contained in Music, one requires **harmonic intervals** <term>harmonic intervals: the distance in pitch between two sounds that create a harmony</term>, both regarding their invention and their placement, and the differences that occur between the discovered sounds; I shall therefore first discuss their principles. For we say we truly know things only when we know their principles. Dividing the work, then, into four parts:

*   In the first, we will discuss Numbers, Proportions, and their operations, leaving nothing out, however small, that belongs to the Musician.
*   In the second, we will speak of Sounds, showing how each of their intervals necessary for harmony is accommodated to its proportion, and the division of the **Monochord** <term>Monochord: a scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used since antiquity to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</term> in every species of harmony in all genres. Then, having shown the true intervals that can be used in musical concerts, we will show how they are accommodated in artificial instruments; furthermore, how one can build an instrument that contains every kind of harmony.
*   In the third, we will consider how, and with what beautiful order, the **consonances** and **dissonances** <term>consonances and dissonances: sounds that are perceived as stable and pleasant (consonant) versus those that create tension or harshness (dissonant)</term> should be placed in compositions of two voices, and how they are adapted for more voices.
*   In the fourth and last, we will treat the **Modes** <note>The "Modes" or "Tones" were the precursors to the modern system of major and minor keys.</note>—otherwise called **Tones** by practical musicians—and their differences; and we will say how the harmonies should be suited to the words, and the words accommodated beneath the **musical figures** <term>figure cantabili: the visual notes or symbols in a score representing specific pitches and durations to be sung</term>.

Thus, without any doubt, he who has well learned all these things may worthily be placed among the number of perfect and honored Musicians. But before we enter into treating what we have proposed above, I judge that it can only be a pleasure and satisfaction to recount a few things: such as the origin and certainty of Music, its praises, the purpose for which it should be learned, its utility, how we should use it, and other similar matters.

# OF THE ORIGIN AND
## certainty of Music.

### CHAPTER ONE.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a pastoral scene with figures and trees within a square border.</image-desc>

*ALTHOUGH God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Iddio Ottimo Massimo," a phrase echoing the Latin "Deo Optimo Maximo," used here to bridge Classical philosophy and Christian theology</note>, through His infinite goodness has granted to man the state of being along with the stones, the state of growth along with the trees, and the state of feeling in common with the other animals; nevertheless, because He willed that His omnipotence be known through the excellence of His creation, He endowed man with intellect—a quality that makes him only slightly less than the Angels. And so that man might know his beginning and his end to be above, He created him with his face turned toward heaven, where the seat of God resides. This was so that he would not fix his love upon base and earthly things, but would lift his intellect to contemplate higher and celestial things, penetrating hidden and divine matters by means of the things that exist and are understood through the five senses.* And although two senses alone might have been sufficient for existence, He added three more for the sake of well-being. For if through **touch** one knows hard and rough things from soft and smooth ones; and through **taste** the difference is made between sweet and bitter foods and other flavors; and through both one feels the diversity of cold and heat, of the hard and the soft, and of the heavy and the light—things which would truly suffice for our existence—it still remains that **seeing**, **hearing**, and **smelling** are necessary for our well-being. Through these, man comes to refuse what is bad and choose what is good. Among these, whoever wishes to examine their virtues well will undoubtedly find **sight**, considered by itself, to be of greater utility to our bodies and consequently more necessary than the others. But it will then be clearly recognized that **hearing** is much more necessary and better, considering it incidentally, in things that belong to the intellect. This is because although more differences in things are known through the sense of sight—since it extends further than hearing—nevertheless, hearing extends further in the acquisition of the Sciences and intellectual judgment, and brings much greater benefit. From this it follows that hearing is truly both more necessary and better than the other senses, even though all five are called instruments of the intellect. This is because everything we see, hear, touch, taste, and smell is offered to the intellect by means of the senses and the "common sense" <note>The "common sense" (*senso commune*) was a concept in Aristotelian psychology referring to a faculty that binds the inputs of the five individual senses into a single perception</note>; nor can the intellect have knowledge of anything except through one of these five, it being true that all our knowledge has its origin in them. From hearing, then, as the most necessary of the other senses, the science of **Music** had its origin. Its nobility can easily be demonstrated by its antiquity; for (as Moses, Josephus, and Berosus the Chaldean <note>Berosus was a Hellenistic-era Babylonian writer; Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian</note> say) before the universal flood, it was found at the sound of hammers by **Jubal** of the lineage of Cain. But having been lost afterwards due to the occurring flood, it was found anew by **Mercury**. For (as Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> maintains) he was the first who observed the course of the stars, the harmony of song, and the proportions of numbers. And he also says that Mercury was the inventor of the **Lyre** with three strings—an opinion also held by Lucian; although Lactantius, in his book on *False Religion* <note>original: "Falsa religione," referring to the "Divine Institutes" by the early Christian author Lactantius</note>, attributes the invention of the Lyre to Apollo, and Pliny wishes the inventor of Music to have been Amphion. But be that as it may, Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on music were standard textbooks for a millennium</note>, following the opinion of Macrobius and departing from Diodorus, maintains that **Pythagoras** was the one who rediscovered the ratio of musical proportions from the sound of hammers. For as he was passing by a blacksmith's shop, where they were striking a piece of glowing iron on the anvil with various hammers, there reached his ears a certain order of sounds that moved his hearing with delight. Having stopped for a moment, he began to investigate from where such an effect proceeded. Thinking at first that it might proceed from the unequal strength of the men, he had those who were striking exchange hammers. But seeing no sound different from the first, he judged (as was the truth) that the diversity of the weight of the hammers was the cause. For this reason, having had each one weighed separately, he found among the numbers of the weights the ratios of the **consonances** <term>consonance: a combination of notes that sounds pleasant and stable to the ear</term> and of the **harmonies**. These he then industriously increased in this way: having made strings of sheep gut of equal thickness, and attaching to them the same weights as the hammers, he found the same consonances—all the more resonant since strings by their nature yield...

It recounts various mythological origins of music, concluding with the famous story of Pythagoras discovering musical ratios by listening to blacksmiths' hammers.</summary>

the sound most pleasing to the ear. This harmony continued for some space of time, and later his successors—who already knew its foundations were placed in specific and determined numbers—testing it more subtly, little by little reduced it to such a state that they gave it the name of a perfect and certain science. And by removing the false and demonstrating the true harmonies <note>original: "concenti"</note> with most evident and infallible numerical reasons, they set down very clear rules in writing. We see this has happened openly in all other sciences, for the first inventors of them (as Aristotle clearly demonstrates) never had perfect knowledge; rather, with that little light many shadows of error were mixed, which, once removed by those who recognized them, allowed truth to succeed in their place. This is just as Aristotle himself did regarding the principles of Natural Philosophy: by adducing various opinions of the ancient philosophers, he approved the good and true ones, rejected the false, clarified the obscure and misunderstood, and, adding his own opinion and authority, demonstrated and taught the true science of Natural Philosophy.

Thus, regarding our science of Music, posterity—by showing the errors of those past and adding their own authority—made it so clear and certain that they numbered it among and made it part of the mathematical sciences. This was for no other reason than for its certainty: for music, together with the other mathematical disciplines, surpasses the other sciences in certainty and holds the first rank of truth. This is known from its very name, since "mathematics" is derived from *mathēma* <note>original: μαθημα</note>, a Greek word which in Latin signifies Discipline, and in our Italian tongue implies Science or Wisdom. This (as Boethius says) is nothing other than an intelligence, or to put it more clearly, a capacity for the truth of things that exist and are by their nature unchangeable. The mathematical sciences make a particular profession of this truth, given that they consider things which by their nature have true being.

In this, they are quite different from certain other sciences which, being founded upon the opinions of various men, have no firmness in themselves; whereas the mathematical sciences, having the senses <note>original: "sentimenti," here referring to sensory perception</note> as their proof, come to possess every certainty. For mathematicians are of the same mind regarding essential matters, nor do they consent to anything other than what can be perceived by the senses. And so great is the certainty of these sciences that by means of numbers one knows infallibly the rotation of the heavens, the conjunctions of the planets, the phases of the Moon, its eclipses and those of the Sun, and infinite other most beautiful secrets, without there being any discord among them. It remains, then, that Music is both noble and most certain, being part of the mathematical sciences.

## On the praises of Music. Chap. 2.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' containing an illustration of a landscape with buildings and foliage.</image-desc>ALTHOUGH its praises are clearly manifest through its origin and certainty, nevertheless, when I consider that nothing is found which does not have the greatest harmony with it, I cannot pass over it entirely in silence. And even though that which has been written by so many excellent philosophers ought to be enough, I nonetheless do not wish to remain behind in my duty to discuss a few things. For even if I do not speak of all the praises that befit it, I will at least touch upon a very small portion of the most notable and excellent ones, and I shall do so with as much brevity as possible.

How much Music has been celebrated and held as a sacred thing is made clear by the ancient writings of the Philosophers, and especially those of the Pythagoreans. They held the opinion that the World was composed musically, and that the heavens in their turning were the cause of harmony, and that our Soul was formed with the same proportions <note>original: "ragione"</note>, and is awakened and its virtues almost brought to life by songs and sounds. Consequently, it was written by some of them that Music holds the principality among the liberal arts, and by some it was called *enkyklopaidia* <note>original: εγκυκλοπαιδεία</note>, from *kyklos* <note>original: κύκλος</note>, a Greek word meaning Circle, and *paideia* <note>original: παιδεία</note>, meaning Discipline—as if to say, the circle of the sciences.

This is because Music, as Plato says, embraces all disciplines, as can be known by discourse. If we begin with **Grammar**, the first among the seven liberal arts, we will find what we have said to be true, since a great harmony is heard in the adaptation and proportioned order of words; if the Grammarian departs from this, he makes a most unpleasant sound reach the ears. For one can hardly listen to or read that prose or verse which is deprived of a polished, beautiful, ornate, sonorous, and elegant order. In **Dialectic**, whoever well considers and examines the proportion of Syllogisms will see, with wonderful concord and great pleasure to the hearing, that truth is shown to be very far from falsehood. The **Orator** then, using musical accents at the proper times in his speech, provides marvelous delight to the listeners, which the great orator Demosthenes knew perfectly; for being three times asked what was the principal part in an Orator, three times he answered:

Part.

[re]plied that delivery <note>original: "pronuntia"</note> was worth more than anything else. Gaius Gracchus, a man of supreme eloquence, also recognized this (as Cicero and Valerius Maximus demonstrate): for whenever he had to speak before the people, he kept behind him a most perfect musician servant, who secretly, by playing an ivory flute, gave him the measure—that is, the voice or the tone for speaking—in such a way that whenever he saw him becoming too high-pitched, he would draw him back, and seeing him too low, he would urge him on. But then, one clearly sees that poetry is so closely joined with music that whoever would wish to separate it from the latter would remain like a body separated from its soul. This point is confirmed by Plato in the *Gorgias*, saying that if anyone took away the harmony <note>original: "concento"</note> and the meter <note>original: "numero," referring to rhythmic number or poetic meter</note> along with the measure from all poetry, there would be no difference between it and domestic or popular speech. And so one sees that the poets have used the greatest diligence and marvelous artifice in accommodating words into verses and arranging the poetic feet according to the suitability of the speech; just as Virgil observed throughout his poem. For in all three styles of his speech, he accommodates the proper sonority of the verse with such artifice that it truly seems as if, through the sound of the words, he places the very things he is treating before one's eyes. Thus, where he speaks of love, one sees he has artfully chosen words that are smooth, sweet, pleasing, and highly grateful to the ear; and where it was necessary for him to sing of a feat of arms, to describe a naval battle, a storm at sea, or similar things involving bloodshed, anger, disdain, sorrow of the soul, and every hateful thing, he made a choice of words that are hard, harsh, and unpleasant, so that in hearing and pronouncing them, they bring terror.

To give some examples of this, in showing the poverty of the hut of Meliboeus, he shortens the word for "cottages" <note>original: "Tuguri"</note> by one letter, as if showing the actual effect through it; just as he also did when he wanted to manifest the grief of that Nymph who was forced to abandon the graceful sight of her shepherd. In that verse:

> *And a long "farewell, O beautiful one, farewell," (he said) to Iolas,* <note>original: "Et longum formoſe vale, vale (inquit) Iola"</note>

by making the verse be interrupted, as if by weeping and sighs, he makes that syllable long which he had previously placed as short. Then, wanting to show how fast Time is, he demonstrates it with a verse composed of many dactyls—which are poetic feet suited to speed and to showing such an effect—saying:

> *But meanwhile it flees, irreparable time flees.* <note>original: "Sed fugit interea fugit irreparabile tempus"</note>

I will omit for now how, wanting to show the Carthaginians as always enemies and contrary to the Romans, in describing the site of Carthage, he deliberately placed after the word that which should have been placed before, and said:

> *Opposite Italy.* <note>original: "Italiam contra"</note>

And wanting to demonstrate with what silence the city of Ilium <note>Troy</note> was assaulted by the Greeks, he shows it with a verse composed of many spondees—which are feet by their nature suited to slowness and to things weak or idle—saying:

> *They invade the city buried in sleep and wine;* <note>original: "Inuadunt vrbem ſomno, vinoque ſepultam"</note>

and infinite others, which would be too long to recount in this place, and of which his work is full. It will suffice now as a final conclusion to say that poetry would be without any grace if it were not given by harmoniously placed words. Besides this, I will set aside the discussion of how much similarity and union Music has with *Arithmetic* and *Geometry*; and I will say only that if the Architect did not have knowledge of *Music* (as Vitruvius well demonstrates), he would not know how to correctly balance machines, nor how to place the acoustic vessels in theaters, nor how to arrange buildings well and musically. *Astronomy*, likewise, if it were not aided by harmonic foundations, would not know good and evil influences. Indeed, I will say more: if the *Astronomer* did not know the concordance of the seven planets, and when one joins with another, or one opposes another, he would never predict future things. *Philosophy* as well, which has as its own purpose the reasoning out of things produced by nature and possible to be produced—does she not confess that everything depends on the first motor and is ordered with such admirable order that a silent harmony results in the universe? Behold how, primarily, heavy things hold the low place, light things the high <note>original: "soprano"</note>, and those of less weight, according to their nature, possess the middle place. And proceeding further, the Philosophers affirm that the Heavens, in revolving, make harmony; which, even if we do not hear it, may happen either because of their rapid revolution, or because of the great distance, or for some other cause hidden from us. *Medicine* cannot stay far from this: for if the physician has no knowledge of *Music*, how will he know how to proportion hot things with cold in his medicines according to their degrees? And how can he have excellent knowledge of pulses? Which the most learned Herophilus arranged according to the order of musical numbers. And to climb higher, our *Theology*, placing the angelic spirits in heaven, divides them into nine Choirs and three Hierarchies, as Dionysius the Areopagite writes. These are continually present at the [sight]...

presence of the Divine majesty, and they do not cease to sing Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts, as is written in Isaiah. And not only these, but the four Animals as well, who are described by Saint John in the book of his Revelations, stand before the throne of God and sing the same song. Then the twenty-four elders stand before the immaculate Lamb, and with the sound of Harps <note>original: "cetere," referring to the cittern or ancient lyre-like instruments</note> and most high voices they sing to the most high God a new song, which is also sung by the voices of the harpists playing upon their harps before the four animals and twenty-four elders. Divine Scripture is full of these and other almost infinite examples relevant to our purpose, which we shall pass over for the sake of brevity; it suffices only to say, as the supreme praise of Music, that without making any mention of any other science, it alone—according to the testimony of the sacred books—is found in Paradise, and is there most nobly practiced. And just as in the celestial court, which is called the Church Triumphant <note>The "Church Triumphant" refers to the spirits of the saved in heaven, who have already won their spiritual battle</note>, so in our earthly one, which is called the Militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians on earth still "fighting" the battle of faith</note>, the Creator is praised and thanked with nothing other than Music. But let us now set aside higher matters and return to those things produced by nature for the ornament of the world, for we shall see that everything is full of musical harmonies. The Sea primarily has the Sirens, who, if it is permitted to give credit to writers, make themselves heard by sailors in such a way that, often overcome by their harmony and overtaken by sleep, the sailors lose that which is dearest to all living things above all else. In the Air and on the Earth together are the birds, which also delight and recreate with their harmonies not only weary minds full of troublesome thoughts, but bodies as well; for the traveler, often tired from a long journey, refreshes his spirit, rests his body, and forgets his past labors through the sweet harmony of the woodland songs of birds of so many various kinds that it would be impossible to recount them. The Rivers and Springs, likewise fashioned by nature, are accustomed to give pleasing delight to whoever finds themselves near them, and very often invite them to refresh themselves by accompanying their rustic song with their own clamorous harmonies.

<margin>They change</margin>
The most learned Virgil expressed all these things in a few words when he said that at the song of Silenus, not only the Fauns and other wild beasts, but even the hard Oaks danced—the former leaping, and the latter often moving with rhythmic motions. This denotes to us that not only sensible things, but even those lacking sense, are almost captured and overcome by musical harmonies, and are turned from hard and harsh into gentle and pleasing. But if so much harmony is found in celestial and terrestrial things—or to put it better, if the world was composed by the Creator full of so much harmony—why should we believe Man to be deprived of it? And if the Soul of the World (as some maintain) is nothing other than Harmony, could it be that our soul is not the cause of every harmony within us, and is not harmonically joined with the body? This is especially so given that God created man in the likeness of the greater World, called by the Greeks <term>κόσμος</term> <note>kosmos</note>, that is, "ornament" or "adorned"; and being made in that likeness but of smaller quantity, in distinction from the former he is called <term>μικρόκόσμος</term> <note>mikrokosmos</note>, that is, "little world." Certainly, it is not reasonable [to think otherwise]. Hence Aristotle, wishing to show the musical composition of man, said very well that the vegetative part has the same relationship to the sensitive part, and the sensitive to the intellectual, as a three-sided figure has to a four-sided one. It is a certain thing, then, that nothing good is found that does not have a musical disposition; and Music truly, besides gladdening the soul, also leads man to the contemplation of celestial things; and it has such a property that it makes perfect everything to which it is added. Those men are truly happy and blessed who are endowed with it, as the Holy Prophet affirms, saying: "Blessed is the people that knows jubilation" <note>A reference to Psalm 89:15 (or 88:16 in the Vulgate)</note>. By this authority, Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, a Catholic doctor, explaining Psalm 65, was moved to say that Music is necessary to the Christian man, since beatitude is found in the science of it. Thus, for this reason, I have the boldness to say that those who have no knowledge of this science are to be numbered among the ignorant. In ancient times, as Isidore says, it was no less a shame not to know Music than not to know letters. Therefore, it is no wonder if Hesiod, a most famous and ancient poet, as Pausanias relates, was excluded from the contest as one who had never learned to play the Cithara, nor to accompany his song with its sound. So too Themistocles, as Cicero <note>original: "Tullio," referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> relates, by refusing to play the Lyre at a banquet, was deemed less learned and less wise. On the contrary, we read that Linus and Orpheus were held in great esteem among the ancients, both being sons of the Gods; for with their sweet song (as it is said) they not only softened human spirits, but even the wild beasts and birds. And what is more marvelous to say, they moved stones from their proper places and held back the course of rivers. And this very thing the learned Horace attributes to Amphion, saying:

He cites classical and biblical authorities to prove that music is essential for spiritual well-being and that ignorance of it was historically considered a mark of a lack of education.</summary>

# Part.
<meta>catchword: To which</meta>

->It is said that Amphion, the founder of the Theban citadel, could move stones with the sound of his lyre <note>original: "testudinis," literally "tortoise-shell," referring to the ancient construction of the lyre</note> and, with sweet persuasion, lead them wherever he wished.<-

From these examples, perhaps, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed the universe was governed by mathematical and musical ratios</note> learned to soften fierce spirits with musical sounds; and likewise Asclepiades, who many times in this way quieted discord born among the people, and with the sound of the trumpet restored hearing to the deaf. Similarly, Damon the Pythagorean, through song, brought certain youths addicted to wine and lust back to a temperate and honest life. And therefore those spoke well who affirmed that Music was a certain law and rule of modesty. And I say that Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> discovered certain musical Modes <note>The "Modes" were ancient scales or melodic patterns believed to trigger specific emotional responses</note> to quiet perturbed spirits. Therefore, Diogenes the Cynic rightly and wisely mocked the musicians of his time who, while having the strings of their lyres in harmony, had souls that were undisciplined and discordant, being abandoned by the harmony of good character. 

And if we must lend faith to history, what we have said should seem as almost nothing: for it is a much greater thing to have the power to heal the sick than to correct the lives of unrestrained youths. We read this of Xenocrates, who with the sound of organs <note>likely referring to ancient pipe instruments or the hydraulic organ</note> restored the insane to their former health; and of Thales of Crete, who with the sound of the Lyre drove away the plague. And we see today that marvelous things are performed by way of Music: for so great is the power of sounds and dances against the poison of Tarantulas <note>Large spiders; it was believed their bite caused "tarantism," a state of hysteria</note> that in a very short time it heals those who have been bitten by them, as is seen every day by experience in Puglia, a land most abundant in such animals. 

But without further secular testimony, do we not have in Holy Scripture that the prophet David quieted the evil spirit of Saul with the sound of his Lyre? And for this reason, I believe that this royal Prophet ordered that songs and harmonic sounds be used in the Temple of God, knowing that they were suited to gladden spirits and to lead men to the contemplation of heavenly things. The Prophets as well (as Ambrose says regarding Psalm 118) wanting to prophesy, would ask that someone skilled in sound begin to play, so that, invited by that sweetness, spiritual grace might be infused into them. Thus Elisha would not prophesy to the King of Israel what he should do to obtain water so that the armies would not die of thirst until a musician was first brought into his presence to sing; and as he sang, Elisha was inspired by the divine Spirit and predicted everything. 

But let us move further, for examples are not lacking. Timothy (as the Great Basil narrates along with many others) incited King Alexander to battle with Music, and when he was so incited, revoked the call with that same music. Aristotle narrates in the book on the nature of animals that stags are captured by the song of hunters and the shepherd’s pipe, and they take much delight in song; this is confirmed by Pliny in his natural history. And so as not to extend myself further on this, I will only say that I know some who have seen stags stop their flight and stand still to listen to the sound of the Lira and the Lute; and likewise one sees every day birds overcome and deceived by harmony, most often remaining caught by the bird-catcher. Pliny also narrates that Music saved Arion from death, who, throwing himself into the sea, was carried by a dolphin to the shore of the island of Taenarum. 

But let us now leave aside many other examples that we could bring forth, and let us speak a little of the good Socrates, the teacher of Plato, who, though already old and full of wisdom, wished to learn to play the lyre. And old Chiron, among the first arts that he taught to Achilles in his tender age, was Music; he wished that his bloody hands, before they were stained with Trojan blood, should play the Lyre. Plato and Aristotle do not allow that a well-educated man should be without Music; rather, they persuade us with many reasons that such a science must be learned. They show the power of Music to be very great, and therefore they wish that effort be given to it from childhood: since it is sufficient to induce in us a new and good habit, and a character that guides and leads us to virtue and makes the soul more capable of happiness. 

Even the most severe Lycurgus, King of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, among his most severe laws, praised and highly approved of Music; for he knew very well that it was very necessary to man and of the greatest benefit in matters of war. Thus, their armies (as Valerius narrates) never used to go into battle unless they were first well-warmed and encouraged by the sound of pipes. This custom is still observed in our times; for of two armies, one would not attack the enemy unless invited by the sound of Trumpets and Drums, or by some other sort of musical instruments. And although, besides those narrated, infinite other examples are not lacking by which one could even more greatly know the dignity and excellence of Music; nevertheless, so as not to go on longer, we shall leave them, what has been discussed until now being sufficient.

# For what purpose Music should be learned. Chapter 3.

<margin>M</margin>
Because it was said above that a well-educated man should not be without Music, and since he must learn it, before we pass any further, I want us to see what goal he should set for himself. There have been various opinions regarding this; having seen these, we will also see the utility that comes from Music and in what manner we should use it. Starting then from the first point, I say there have been some who held the opinion that Music should be learned to give solace and delight to the hearing, for no other reason than to make this sense perfect—just as sight becomes perfect when it looks with delight and pleasure upon a beautiful and proportioned thing. But in truth, it should not be learned for this purpose, because that is a matter for the common folk and the laborers <note>original: "meccanici," referring to those who work with their hands or in "low" trades, contrasted with the liberal arts of the nobility</note>. Such things have no part of virtue in them (even though they possess a certain delight by calming the soul) and are for coarse men who seek nothing but to satisfy the senses, attending to this goal alone. 

Others then desired that it be learned for no other purpose than to be placed among the liberal arts <note>the *artes liberales*, the traditional curriculum for a free-born person, including Grammar, Logic, Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy</note>, in which only the nobility practiced; and because it disposes the soul toward virtue and regulates its passions by accustoming it to rejoice and to grieve virtuously. This disposes one toward good character, no differently than Gymnastics <note>physical training or "Ginnastica" in the classical sense of balanced bodily development</note> does for the body in creating a good disposition and habit. They also learned it to be able, through such means, to arrive at the contemplation of various sorts of harmony, since through Music the intellect knows the nature of musical consonances. 

And although this goal has an element of the honorable, it is not yet enough. For he who learns Music does not learn it only to acquire perfection of the intellect, but to be able—when he ceases from the cares and business of both body and soul (that is, when he is at leisure and away from daily occupations)—to pass the time and entertain himself virtuously. Thus, living rightly and commendably far from laziness, he might by such means become prudent and then move on to doing better and more praiseworthy things. This goal is not only worthy of praise and honorable, but it is the true goal; for Music was not discovered or ordained for any other purpose than that which we have shown above, just as the Philosopher <note>A standard Renaissance reference to Aristotle</note> reveals in his *Politics*, citing and recounting many authorities from Homer. 

Wherefore the ancients rightly placed it in the order of those entertainments that serve free men and among the praiseworthy disciplines—not among the necessary ones, such as Arithmetic, nor even among the useful ones, like those intended only for the acquisition of external goods (such as money and the needs of the family). Nor is it like those that serve the health and strength of the body, like Gymnastics, which is an art belonging to things that help make the body healthy and strong—such as wrestling, throwing the spear, and other things belonging to the exercise of war. Music should therefore be learned not as a necessity, but as something liberal and honorable, so that by its means we may arrive at a good and virtuous habit that leads us in the way of good character. It makes us walk toward other sciences that are more useful and necessary, and makes us pass the time virtuously; and this should be the primary, or ultimate intention, however we wish to call it. But in what way it has the power to induce new habits of character and move the soul to various passions, we shall discuss in another place.

# Of the utility had from Music, and of the study we should put into it, and in what way to use it. Chapter 4.

Great truly is the utility taken from Music when we use it temperately. For it is a manifest thing that not only man, who is capable of reason, but also many of the other animals who lack it, clearly take delight and pleasure in it. Since every living thing delights and rejoices in the proportion and temperament of things, and such qualities are found in harmonies, it follows immediately that pleasure and delight are common to all living beings. And it is truly a reasonable thing; since nature consists in such proportion and temperament, every like thing delights in its like and desires it. Of this, infants barely born give very clear evidence; taken by the sweetness of the singing voices of their nurses, they not only grow quiet after long crying but become cheerful, also making <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the catchword "spesse" (often) on the next page</note>

often [making] some festive gestures. And Music is so natural to us, and joined to us in such a way, that we see everyone wanting to give some judgment of it in a certain manner, even if imperfectly. For this reason, one could say that he who takes no delight in Music is not composed with harmony; because (as we have said) if every delight and pleasure is born from similarity, it is necessary that he who has no pleasure in harmony somehow lacks it within himself and is ignorant of it. And if one wishes to examine the matter well, he will find such a person to be of the lowest intellect and without a spark of judgment; and it could be said that nature had failed him, not having formed his organs proportionately. This is because that part which is in the middle of the brain, and is closest to the ear, when it is proportionately composed, serves in a certain way the judgment of harmony—by which a man, as if by something similar to himself, is captured and overcome, and takes great pleasure in it. But if it happens that he is deprived of such proportion, he takes much less delight in it than anyone else; and he is as fit for speculative and ingenious things as an **Ass is for the Lyre** <note>original: "Aſino alla Lira," a classical proverb (Asinus ad lyram) used to describe someone who is tone-deaf or incapable of understanding art and wisdom</note>. 

And if we wish to follow the opinion of the Astrologers in this, we shall say that at his birth **Mercury** was his enemy, just as he is favorable to those who not only delight in harmony, but do not disdain—for the alleviation of their labors—to sing and play themselves, recreating the spirit and regaining their lost strength. And thus nature has well-ordered that, having joined the body and the Soul together within us by means of the spirit (as the **Platonists** <note>followers of the philosopher Plato, who believed in the harmony between the physical body and the immortal soul</note> maintain), she has provided opportune remedies for each of them when they are weak and infirm. For the languid and infirm Body is healed by the remedies offered by Medicine; and the afflicted and weak Spirit by the airy spirits, and by sounds and songs, which are its proportionate remedies. The Soul then, imprisoned in this corporeal jail, is consoled by way of the high and divine mysteries of sacred Theology. 

Such benefit, then, does Music bring us, and more; for by driving away the boredom that comes from labor, it makes us cheerful, and it doubles and preserves that cheerfulness. We see Soldiers go to attack the enemy much more fiercely, incited by the sound of Trumpets and Drums; and not only they, but the Horses as well move with great impetus. This excites the soul, moves the affections, mitigates and quiets fury, makes time pass virtuously, and has the power to generate in us a habit of good character—especially when it is used in the proper ways and with temperance. For since the proper office of Music is to delight, we must use it not dishonestly, but honestly, so that what happens to those who drink Wine immoderately does not happen to us. Those people, once heated, harm themselves, and by performing a thousand follies, move whoever sees them to laughter—not because the nature of Wine is so malicious that it would work such an effect in a man when drunk temperately, but it appears so to him who drinks it greedily. Indeed, all things are good when they are used temperately for that end for which they were discovered and ordained; but when they are used intemperately, and not according to their proper end, they are harmful and pernicious. 

In this way, we can hold this as true: that not only natural things, but every art and every science can be good or bad according to how they are used. I say they are good when they are directed to that end for which they were ordained, and bad when they distance themselves from that end. Therefore, man having been born for things much more excellent than Singing, or playing the Lyre, or other sorts of instruments merely to satisfy the sense of hearing, he misuses his nature and deviates from his proper goal if he cares little for giving food to the intellect, which always desires to know and understand new things. 

A man should not, therefore, only learn the art of Music and withdraw from other sciences, abandoning his true goal—for that would be great folly. Rather, he should learn it for that end for which it was ordained. Nor should he spend his time only on it, but he should accompany it with the study of **speculation** <note>the theoretical or philosophical study of principles, as opposed to mere practical performance</note>, so that, aided by this, he may come to a greater knowledge of the things that belong to its use. Through this use, he can put into practice what he has investigated through long speculative study. For when accompanied in such a way, it brings benefit to every science and every art, as we have seen at other times. And if he did otherwise, such a thing would not be of much utility to him, nor of much glory; rather, it would be attributed to him as a vice. This is because exercising oneself continually in it without any other study induces sleepiness and laziness, and renders the souls soft and effeminate. Recognizing this, the ancients desired that the study of Music be joined to **Gymnastics** <note>original: "Ginnaštica"; in the classical sense, this referred to the balanced physical training of the body to complement the training of the mind</note>. They did not want one to be practiced without the other; and they did this so that by giving oneself too much to Music, the soul would not become lowly; and by giving effort only to Gymnastics, the souls would not become beyond measure fierce, cruel, and inhuman. But by these two exercises joined together, they were rendered human, modest, and temperate. And in doing this they were moved by reason, which clearly...

...clearly it can be seen that those who, in their youth, have abandoned the study of more important things and have given themselves solely to consorting with actors and parasites—constantly frequenting schools of games, dances, and leaps, playing the Lyre and the Lute, and singing songs that are less than decent—are soft, effeminate, and without any good character. For Music used in such a way renders the minds of the young ill-composed, as Ovid well demonstrated by saying:

> *Zithers, songs, and lyres enervate the soul,* <note>original: "Eneruant animos citharæ, cantusque lyræque," from Ovid's *Remedia Amoris*.</note>
> *As do the voice and arms moving to their own rhythms.* <note>original: "Et vox, & numeris brachia mota ſuis."</note>

As do the voice and arms moving to their own rhythms. Nor do they speak of anything else but such things; nor are any but indecent words heard coming from their filthy mouths. On the contrary, there are some who, through such study, become not only soft and effeminate, but also troublesome, unpleasant, proud, stubborn, and inhumane. Thus, seeing themselves arrived at a certain level, and considering themselves excellent above all others, they boast, exalt, and praise themselves; by reviling others to appear full of wisdom and judgment, they carry themselves with the greatest reputation and pride in the world. Never, except with a great persistence of prayers and with praises far greater than they deserve, can they be persuaded to show even a little of their knowledge. For this reason, the saying of Horace regarding all these "Tigelli" <note>Tigellius was a famous Sardinian singer in Rome, mentioned by Horace as a type of the temperamental musician.</note> is verified, which says:

> *This is a vice common to all singers: among friends,* <note>original: "Omnibus hoc vitium est cantoribus, inter amicos," from Horace's *Satires*.</note>
> *they can never bring themselves to sing when asked,*
> *but when unasked, they never stop.*

It would have been better if their fathers had instead had them taught some other trade, however lowly, for perhaps then they would not have fallen into such errors and would have acquired better manners. I have wanted to say all this so that those who wish to make a profession of the art of Music may fall in love with the science and devote themselves to the study of the <term>speculative</term> <note>The theoretical or mathematical study of music, as opposed to mere practical performance.</note>; for I do not doubt that by joining these things together, they will become virtuous, honest, and well-mannered. In this way, they will come to imitate the ancients, who (as has been said) accompanied Music with Gymnastics; for thus Music will be powerful enough to lead everyone onto the straight path of good character. Nor should anyone believe that what I have said about the art of Music was intended to disparage it, or those who practice it in such a manner—a thought that has never entered my mind. Rather, I have said it so that, when joined in such a way with other honorable sciences full of severity, we may defend it from the wandering and idle ruffianism of tricksters and restore it to its true place. Thus, it should not serve those who are devoted only to pleasures, but be for the use of students of good sciences and those who follow virtue, living decorously and civilly.

## What Music is in General, and its Division. Chapter 5.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring floral motifs and scrolls.</image-desc>

WE SHALL therefore begin such an honest and honorable study by first seeing what Music is, and then how many kinds are found, assigning to each kind its own definition. This we shall do so as not to deviate from the good order held by the ancients, who maintained that every discussion of any matter conducted reasonably must begin with a definition, so that what is to be disputed may be understood. Therefore, speaking generally, I say that Music is nothing other than Harmony; and we could say that it is that "strife and friendship" proposed by <term>Empedocles</term> <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who believed the universe was governed by the opposing forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note>, from which he claimed all things were generated—that is, a "discordant concord," which is to say, a concord of various things that can be joined together. But because this word "Music" has various meanings, and reason dictates that anything carrying many meanings must first be divided before being defined (especially when wishing to clarify every part of it), we shall first divide it by saying: Music is of two kinds, <term>Animastica</term> <note>From the Latin "anima" (soul/breath); refers here to the "animate" or vital harmony found within living organisms.</note> and <term>Organica</term> <note>Instrumental music, from the Greek "organon" (tool/instrument).</note>. One is the harmony that arises from the composition of various things joined together in one body, even if they are discrepant among themselves—such as the mixture of the four Elements or other qualities in a living body. The other is harmony that can arise from various instruments. And this we shall again divide into two, for there are two kinds of instruments: <term>Natural</term> and <term>Artificial</term>. The natural ones are those parts that concur in the formation of voices, such as the Throat, the Palate, the Tongue, the Lips, the Teeth, and finally the Lungs, formed by nature. When these parts are moved by the Will, and from their movement sound is born, and from sound Speech, there is then born Modulation, or Singing.

<summary>The author warns against the moral corruption caused by superficial music and argues that music must be studied as a theoretical science to foster virtue. He then defines Music as harmony—a "discordant concord"—and begins categorizing it into Animate (bodily/spiritual) and Instrumental (natural and artificial) forms.</summary>

# Part II

And so, through the movement of the body, the logic of sound, and words suited to song, harmony is made perfect, and the music called **Harmonic** or **Natural** is born. Artificial instruments are human inventions and derive from Art; they form **Artificial Music**, which is that harmony arising from such instruments. This is produced in three ways: it either arises from instruments that return a blown sound, whether natural or artificial, such as **Organs, Pipes, Trumpets**, and the like; or from stringed instruments where breath is not required, such as **Citterns, Lyres, Lutes, Harpsichords, Dulcimers**, and the like, which are struck by fingers or quills, or played with bows. Finally, it arises from percussion instruments, such as **Drums, Cymbals, Kettledrums, Bells**, and other similar things made of hollow wood and animal skins stretched over them, or of metal, when they are struck by any object whatsoever. Thus, Artificial music is found in three sorts: **By Wind, By Strings**, and **By Percussion**. Natural music is of four sorts: **Plain, Measured, Rhythmic**, and **Metric**; although these four can also be attributed to Artificial music for reasons we shall state elsewhere. Of **Soul-music** <note>original: "Animastica", referring to the music of the spirit or soul.</note>, we shall likewise make two parts, placing the **Worldly** <note>original: "Mondana", or cosmic music—the "music of the spheres."</note> in the first and the **Human** in the second, as appears in the division set out below.

And although some have made a distinction between the music that arises from wind instruments, naming it **Organic**, and that which arises from strings without breath, calling it **Rhythmic**; nevertheless, I have chosen to call both indifferently **Artificial**. First: because it is of little importance to name them in one way rather than another; and then to preserve the meaning of the word **Organ** <note>original: "Organo", used here in the classical sense of a tool or instrument.</note>, from which comes this name **Organic**, which universally encompasses all sorts of artificial instruments. Furthermore, this avoids ambiguity: for in saying "Rhythmic," one might understand not only that harmony which arises from artificial stringed instruments, but also that which results from well-composed prose. # First Book

## Of Worldly Music. Chapter 6.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'R' containing ornate foliate patterns and scrolls.</image-desc>

RESUMING then our discussion of **Soul-music** <note>original: "Musica animastica," music pertaining to the spiritual or cosmic soul.</note>, we shall say that it is of two kinds: *Worldly* and *Human*. **Worldly Music** is that harmony which is perceived not only in the things seen and known in the heavens, but is also understood in the binding of the Elements and the variety of the seasons. I say "seen and known in the heavens" regarding the Rotation, the Distances, and the Parts of the celestial spheres; and from the Aspects, the Nature, and the Position of the seven planets, which are the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. For it was the opinion of many ancient Philosophers, and most especially of Pythagoras, that the rotation of such a great machine with such swift movement could not pass without sending forth some sound. This opinion, although rejected by Aristotle, is nonetheless favored by Cicero in the sixth book of *The Republic*, where the elder Scipio Africanus responds to the younger, who had asked him: *What is this sound, so great and so sweet, that fills my ears?* He says: *This is that sound which, joined by unequal intervals—yet distinct through partitioned proportion—is made by the pushing and moving of these circles; which, by tempering the high sounds with the low, equally creates various harmonies. For such great movements cannot be made in silence, and Nature dictates that the extremes sound deep on one side and high on the other.* For this reason, that highest course of the starry heaven, whose rotation is swiftest, moves with a high and louder sound, while this lunar and lowest sphere moves with a very deep sound. Cicero says this, following the opinion of Plato, who, to show that harmony is born from such rotation, imagined that a Siren sits atop each sphere. For "Siren" means nothing other than "Singer to God." And likewise, Hesiod in his *Theogony*, hinting at this same thing, called the eighth Muse <term>Urania</term> <note>original: "ουρανία"</note>, who is assigned to the eighth sphere, from <term>Ouranos</term> <note>original: "ουρανός"</note>, the name by which the Greeks call the Heaven. And to show that the Ninth sphere was the one that gave birth to the great and concordant unity of sounds, he named her <term>Calliope</term> <note>original: "καλλιόπη"</note>, which means "of the Finest Voice," wishing to show by this the harmony that results from all those other spheres; as is seen hinted at by the Poet when he said:

> *I pray to you, O Calliope, breathe upon me as I sing;* <note>original Latin: "Vos o Calliope precor aspirate canenti;" from Virgil's Aeneid.</note> *invoking Calliope alone among the many as the principal one, and as she by whose will alone all others move and turn.*

And the ancients held this opinion as so true that in their sacrifices they used Musical instruments and sang certain Hymns composed of sonorous verses, which contained two parts: one they named <term>Strophe</term> <note>original: "στροφή," meaning a turn.</note> and the other <term>Antistrophe</term> <note>original: "ἀντιστροφή," meaning a counter-turn.</note>. This was to show the various turns made by the celestial spheres; for by the one they understood the motion made by the sphere of the fixed stars from East to West, and by the other the various movements made by the other spheres of the planets proceeding in the opposite direction, from West to East. And with such instruments they also accompanied the bodies of their dead to the grave, for they were of the opinion that after death, souls returned to the origin of musical sweetness—that is, to heaven. The ancient Hebrews observed such a custom at the death of their kin, of which we have very clear testimony in the Gospel, where the raising of the daughter of the ruler of the Synagogue is described; there, musical instruments were present, and our Lord commanded the players to play no more. And they did this (as Ambrose says) to observe the custom of their ancestors, who in such a way invited those present to weep with them. Many also held the opinion that in this life every soul was conquered by Music; and that even though it was enclosed in the bodily prison, by remembering and being conscious of the Music of heaven, it might forget every hard and tedious labor. But if this should seem strange to us, we have the testimony of Holy Scripture regarding the harmony of heaven, where the Lord speaks to Job, saying: *Who shall tell the reasons or voices of the Heavens? And who shall make their harmony sleep?* <note>A paraphrase of Job 38:37.</note> And if I were asked why such a great and sweet sound is not heard by us, I could answer nothing else but what Cicero says in the place cited above: That our ears, filled with such great harmony, are deaf; just as happens, for example, to the inhabitants of those places where the Nile falls headlong from very high mountains, called the <term>Catadupa</term> <note>The cataracts of the Nile.</note>, who lack the sense of hearing due to the greatness of the roar. Or perhaps, just as our eye cannot fix its gaze upon the light of the Sun, our own light being overcome by its rays, so our ears cannot grasp the sweetness of the celestial harmony because of its excellence and greatness. But every reason persuades us to believe, at the very least, that the world is composed with harmony;
