Part.

...[of] another, it is called a **Relational Number** <note>original: "numero Relato"; a number defined by its relationship to another, such as in a ratio or proportion.</note>; and the **Musician** <note>In the Renaissance, a "Musician" was primarily a theorist who understood the mathematical laws of harmony, rather than just a performer.</note> uses such numbers in his speculations. In the same way, within **Continuous Quantity** <note>Quantity that can be divided infinitely, like a line or a physical object, as opposed to "Discrete Quantity" like whole numbers.</note> (also called Magnitude), there are some things that are perpetually at rest—such as the Earth, a Line, a Surface, a Triangle, a Square, and every mathematical body—and others that are in continuous motion, such as the celestial bodies. The first are treated in **Geometry**; the second, which are always turning, are the profession of **Astronomy**. Thus, from the diversity of things considered in different ways, the variety of sciences and the diversity of their **Subjects** are born. Just as the **Arithmetician** primarily considers Number, so Number is the Subject of his science. And because Musicians, wishing to find the underlying ratios of every musical interval, use sounding bodies and the Relational Number to understand the distances found between sound and sound, and between voice and voice—and to know how much one differs from the other in low and high pitch—they join these two parts together (Number and Sound). Creating a composite, they say that the **Subject of Music** is **Sonorous Number** <note>original: "Numero sonoro"</note>. And although **Avicenna** <note>A famous 11th-century Persian philosopher and physician whose works were central to European university education.</note> says that its Subject is **Tones** and **Times**, nevertheless, considering the matter in itself, we will find it all to be one and the same; that is, Times refer to Number, and Tones refer to Sound.

### What Sonorous Number is. Chap. 19.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'H' depicting a figure standing in a landscape with hills and a classical building in the background.</image-desc>
WE MUST therefore know that some, wishing to provide information about this number, have said that **Sonorous Number** is nothing other than the number of parts of a **Sounding Body** <note>original: "Corpo sonoro"</note>, such as a string. By taking on the properties of discrete quantity, the string makes us certain of the quantity of sound it produces. This description, though it might seem good to some, nevertheless, in my judgment, seems truncated and imperfect. This is because **Voices**—which are the primary consideration of the Musician and are not far removed from Sonorous Number since they have proportion among themselves—would not fall under such a description. This is because voices originate from animate and human bodies (that is, from Man). It is only reasonable that all things considered in a science—even if they are not considered on their own, but rather in relation to the Subject—should be reduced to that Subject; just as it is reasonable that a definition should agree with the thing being defined. And although man is a body, this is not enough: it is also required that he be "sonorous." Thus, he must have three conditions: first, that he be smooth; second, that he be hard; and finally, that he be wide. I do not know how all these conditions can be found in him. But let us suppose that man has all these conditions; even so, one could not have knowledge of the quantity of voices by way of the man himself, because the parts where they are born are not subject to the senses in such a way that one can have any determined measure of them. But if someone were to say that Voices are applied to the sounds born from strings, and that in this way one comes to have the ratio of their proportions, and by this same means they are reduced under the said description—this person would be speaking improperly. Sounds are applied to voices so that we may have a true and determined ratio of them, and not the other way around. It seems to me, therefore, that it would be better to say that **Sonorous Number** is **Number related to voices and sounds**. This is found artificially in a sounding body, such as a string, which, by receiving the ratio of a certain number in its parts, makes us certain of the quantity of the sound it produces and of the quantity of the voices, by referring or applying those sounds to those voices. And I say this when such a number is considered universally in every interval. But when it is considered particularly only in those intervals that are **consonant**, one could say it is the ratio of the proportions which are the forms of the **consonances** considered primarily in Music. These are the ones shown above, contained within the parts of the **Senary number** <note>The number six, which Zarlino believes contains the ratios for all basic musical harmonies.</note>, which are found through artifice in the parts of a sounding body and related in the aforementioned way. And because the differences found between voices and between low and high sounds are not known except by means of sounding bodies, Musicians, considering this, chose a string made of metal or another material that would yield sound. This string was to be equal in every way in all its parts, as it is the sounding body least subject to change or variation, allowing them to have certainty in everything they sought. They held the opinion that the quantity of the sound of the string was equal to the number of parts considered within it. Having known its length and quantity according to the number of its measured parts, they could immediately judge the distances found between low and high sounds, or vice versa, and know the proportion of each interval. them, according to the diversity of the parts to their whole. We can simultaneously know that the Whole is the 
cause of the low sound, and the parts—the smaller they are—are the cause of the high sounds. By this means 
and in this way, therefore, as a more certain path following the advice of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century scholar whose "Harmonics" sought to reconcile mathematical theory with what the ear actually hears.</note>, joining reason to the senses, 
Musicians first investigate the ratios of the **consonances** <note>Intervals that sound pleasing and stable to the ear.</note>, and then of every other Interval, and 
every difference found between low and high sounds. By having respect for the Voices and the Sounds, which 
are the matter of every musical interval, and for the numbers and proportions which (as I have said 
at other times) are their form—joining these two things together—they said that **Sonorous Number** is the true 
**Subject** of Music, and not the **Sounding Body**. For although all bodies are capable of producing sounds, 
they are not all capable of generating Harmony, except when they are proportioned among themselves and 
contained under a certain determined form—that is, under the ratio of **harmonic numbers**.

## For what reason Music is said to be subalternated to Arithmetic, and 
## halfway between mathematics and natural science. Chap. 20.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting a seated figure in classical attire holding a book or tablet among architectural ruins.</image-desc>
But because the science of Music takes (as we have been able to see) Numbers from 
Arithmetic, and measurable Quantities—that is, Sounding Bodies—from Geometry, 
it thus makes itself subject to these two named sciences and is called a **subalternated science** <note>In the classical tradition, a "subalternated" science is one that borrows its principles and "subject matter" from a higher, more abstract science.</note>. 
Hence it should be known that there are two sorts of sciences: for some are called 
Principal or **Subalternating**, and some are Non-principal or **Subalternated**. The first 
are those which depend on principles known by natural light and sensory knowledge, 
such as Arithmetic and Geometry. These have certain principles known through the understanding of terms 
acquired by way of the senses—as one might say, that a **Line** is length without width, which is a principle 
proper to Geometry; or that **Number** is a multitude composed of several units, which is a principle 
proper to Arithmetic. This is in addition to the common principles, which are those that say: *The whole is 
greater than its part*; *The part is smaller than its whole*; and many others from which the Arithmetician 
and the Geometer derive their conclusions. The second sort are those which, besides their own principles 
acquired through the senses, have others that proceed from principles known in one of the superior and 
principal sciences; these are called **Subalternated** to the first, just as **Perspective** <note>Optics or the study of sight.</note> is to Geometry. 
This is because, besides its own principles, it has others that are known and approved in the science 
superior to it, which is Geometry. And it is the nature of the non-principal and subalternated science 
that it takes the same subject from the principal one, but adds an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property or quality that can be added to a subject without changing its essential nature.</note> for its difference. 
For if it were otherwise, there would be no difference of subject between the two—as is seen in 
Perspective, which takes as its subject the Line itself (which Geometry also uses) and adds to it by 
accident the quality of **Visibility**; and thus the **Visual Line** becomes its subject. The same 
happens also in Music, which, having Number as a common subject with Arithmetic, adds to 
this **Sonority** as its difference; thus it becomes subalternated to Arithmetic, holding **Sonorous Number** 
as its subject. Nor does Music only have its own principles; it also takes others from 
Arithmetic for the means of its demonstrations, for through these we then have the true knowledge of the 
science. It is certainly true that such principles and means are not all the conclusions found in Arithmetic, 
but only a part of them which the Musician needs. These are matters of **Relation**—that is, of 
proportions—and this is to show the properties of Sonorous Numbers, which also serves our purpose. 
Hence we too will take only those conclusions that we need and apply them to Sound or to the 
Voice, which are considered by **Natural Science** <note>original: "dal Naturale"; referring to Physics or the study of the natural world.</note> (as **The Philosopher** <note>Aristotle.</note> demonstrates). And I will have the 
boldness to say that Music is subalternated not only to Mathematics, but to Natural Science as well—
not in the part concerning Numbers, but certainly in the part concerning **Sound**, which is natural, and 
from which all melody is born.

every consonance, every harmony, and every melody: which is also confirmed by Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath who wrote extensively on the mathematical principles of music.</note> saying; that Music has its principles from natural science, and from that of numbers. And just as in natural things, nothing is perfect while it is in potential: but only when it is reduced to action [actuality]; so Music cannot be perfect, except when by means of natural or artificial instruments it is made to be heard: which cannot be done with Number alone, nor with Voices alone: but by accompanying both of these together; especially since Number is inseparable from consonance. For this reason, therefore, it will be manifest that Music cannot be called simply mathematical, nor simply natural; but rather part natural and part mathematical, and consequently intermediate between the one and the other. But because from natural science the Musician has the reason for the matter of Consonance, which are the Sounds and the Voices, and from Mathematics he has the reason for its form—that is, its proportion—therefore, since all things should be named after the most noble thing, we more reasonably say Music is a mathematical science than a natural one: seeing that the form is more noble than the matter.

## What Proportion is, and of its Division. Chapter 21.

<image-desc>Decorative initial L featuring foliate patterns and a seated figure in the background.</image-desc>Sounds and Voices, then, proportioned among themselves, which without any doubt have their being from natural things, generate and in actuality make heard Consonance, the governess of every modulation, through which one arrives at the use of Melodies, in which all the perfection of Music consists. It is true that for its generation there concur (as we shall see other times) two dissimilar sounds, which according to the form and the reason of the harmonic numbers, are proportionately distant from one another by the low and by the high. But it must be known that all those things from which sound can be born—such as Strings <note>original: "Chorde"</note>, Sinews, breathed Air, and other similar things—the Musician calls **Distance**; and the Form, or Reason of the Numbers, which is drawn from the measurement of the sonorous strings, he calls **Proportion**. But Proportion is immediately divided into two parts, namely into **Common** and **Proper**. The first is the comparison of two things together, made in one and the same attribute or univocal predicate; like comparing Joseph and Francis in whiteness, or in some other quality in which they agree. The second (as Euclid <note>Greek mathematician (c. 300 BC) whose *Elements* established the geometric and numerical foundations for this theory.</note> maintains) is that certain habit or suitability which two finite quantities of the same proximate genus have, whether they be equal or unequal to each other. And it is said of a "same proximate genus": because one cannot say with reason that a Line is greater or smaller, or equal to a Surface, nor to a Body; nor that Time is greater, smaller, or equal to a Place: but indeed one Line is greater, smaller, or equal to another; and so one Body to another body; and other similar things. Because (as the Philosopher <note>A standard historical reference to Aristotle (384–322 BC).</note> teaches us) comparison should be made only in things that have a single meaning, and which are of one and the same proximate genus; and not in those that have multiple meanings and are of different genera, or absolutely of a single remote genus. Nor is Proportion found only in the aforementioned quantities: but in Weights, in Measures, and (as Plato <note>Greek philosopher (c. 428–348 BC) who integrated music and proportion into his cosmology.</note> wishes) in Powers and in Sounds, as we shall see; which proportion is never found in anything except in as much as one is equal, or greater, or smaller than the other: since the property of **Quantity** is to be called Equal or Unequal. And such proportion is found first in Quantity, and subsequently afterward in the other named things. I will now leave off speaking of the Common: since it does not serve our purpose, and I will again divide the Proper into the **Rational** and the **Irrational**. I will say the Rational is that which takes its name from numbers which contain or are contained; as from 2 which, being compared to Unity <note>The number 1, the fundamental building block of the number system.</note> in the ratio of containing, is named the **Double proportion**. Wherefore similar quantities are called **commensurable** and **communicating**: because both can always be measured by a common measure. The **Irrational**, then, is that which cannot be named by any rational number; like that of the Diameter and the Side of a Square: because no common measure can be given that is certain and that measures both entirely; and for this reason they are called **incommensurable** quantities. We must however note that every proportion found in numbers, which are **discrete quantity** <note>Quantity composed of distinct, separate units, such as people or numbers.</note>, is also found in **continuous quantity** <note>Quantity that is not separated into parts, such as a line, time, or a physical string.</note>: since all numbers are commensurable and communicating, because they are at least numbered by Unity; which does not happen in the continuous, in which infinite ratios are found that are not found in the discrete; and this because each proportion which is found in a genus of continuous quantity,
is found

is also found in another; wherefore just as two straight lines agree with each other; so too do two Surfaces, two Bodies, two Times, two Places, two Sounds, and other similar things: but the same does not occur in Numbers, or **discrete quantity**. <note>The author is contrasting geometry (continuous) with arithmetic (discrete). In geometry, a line can be divided infinitely, leading to "irrational" proportions like the diagonal of a square, whereas musical theory of this era relies on whole numbers.</note> Where it is manifest, that proportions in the continuous are of greater abstraction than those found in the discrete: since every **Arithmetic** proportion is rational; but **Geometric** ones are both rational and irrational. But because **Irrational** proportions do not serve our purpose, I will leave them aside, and I will take the **Rational** ones, which are likewise divided into the proportion of **equality**, and that of **inequality**. I say then that the **proportion of Equality** is that which is found between two quantities that are equal to each other; such as 1 to 1; 2 to 2; 3 to 3; and following the others; or two sounds, or two lines, or two surfaces, or two bodies equal to each other; which truly does not serve our purpose, being naturally indivisible: because in its extremes one finds no difference at all; and one cannot say that one quantity is greater than the other; and this happens because **Equality**, or similarity, in the view of the Musician, does not give birth to any consonance. <note>In Renaissance music theory, a "consonance" requires a relationship between different pitches. Two identical notes (a unison) are the source of harmony but are not considered a consonance in themselves because they lack variety.</note> The **proportion of Inequality** then, which is that of which I intend to reason, is when two quantities, one greater than the other, are placed in comparison, so that one contains, or is contained by the other; such as the **Binary** <note>original: "Binario" — the number two</note> compared to **Unity** <note>original: "Vnità" — the number one</note>, or vice versa. And this is likewise divided into two parts, that is, into that of **Greater inequality**, and that of **Lesser**: because when one compares the greater number to the lesser, if the greater contains that lesser simply, without having any other consideration, then the proportion of greater inequality is born: but comparing the lesser to the greater, if the lesser, without having any other regard, is contained by the greater, then the proportion of lesser inequality is born.

### In how many ways one Quantity is compared to another. Chapter 22.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'L' depicting two figures, one seated and one standing, in an architectural interior setting.</image-desc>
**L**ike-containing one another, and being contained, is not always taken simply, but indeed in another way. Wherefore, having considered such comparison more minutely, from each of these genera five others are born: because the greater number can be compared to the lesser in five ways and no more; and so by the contrary, the lesser to the greater: since in the proportion of greater inequality, the greater number contains in itself the lesser more than once entirely: or only once, and in addition a part of that lesser, called an **Aliquot part** <term>Aliquot part: A part that divides the whole number exactly, such as 2 being an aliquot part of 6.</term>; or it contains the lesser only once, and in addition a part of it called a **Non-aliquot part** <term>Non-aliquot part: A part that does not divide the whole number exactly, such as 2 being a part of 5.</term>. The greater number also contains the lesser more than once, and in addition an aliquot part of it, or contains it several times, and in addition a non-aliquot part. From the first way originates that genus of proportion called **Multiple**; from the second, that which is called **Superparticular**; and from the third, that which is named **Superpartient**. And these are called simple genera: because from the fourth way another is generated called **Multiple superparticular**; and from the fifth and last is born that which is called **Multiple superpartient**; which genera are composed from the first and the other two following; as is understood from the name of each by itself; and they are called **Compound**. In the proportion of **Lesser inequality** then, the lesser number similarly is contained by the greater in five ways, and no more; and thus one has five other genera, called those of lesser inequality; and they are named by the proper names of the aforementioned, adding only for their difference this particle **Sub**, which means "Under" <note>original: "Sotto"</note>, and they are named **Submultiple**, **Subsuperparticular**, **Subsuperpartient**, **Submultiple superparticular**, and **Submultiple superpartient**; of which the first three are likewise called simple: but the other two are called compound. And these last five genera not being suited to the generation of musical consonances, as we shall see in the second part, I will therefore not reason about them any further.

## What an Aliquot and Non-Aliquot Part is. Chapter 23.

WE MUST observe that mathematicians call an *Aliquot part* <note>In modern terms, an "aliquot part" is a proper divisor: a number that divides into a larger number without leaving a remainder.</note> that quantity which, when taken as many times as possible within a larger quantity, results exactly in the entirety of its whole. Thus, the *Binary* (the number 2) is called an *aliquot part* of the *Senary* (the number 6); because when taken three times, it results exactly in its whole, which is 6. *This is called the Multiplicative part by Campanus <note>Johannes Campanus of Novara was a 13th-century mathematician whose commentary on Euclid was a standard text in the Renaissance.</note>; because it entirely counts and measures its Whole.* Then, they call a *Non-aliquot part* that which, when taken as many times as possible, does not result exactly in its whole, but rather results in more or less. Just as the *Binary* is called a *non-aliquot part* of 5; for when taken twice it makes 4, and taken three times it makes 6. Therefore, such a part is named *Aggregative* by the same Campanus; for when added to another quantity, it yields its whole; just as adding 4 with the unit (1) yields 5. *And this is not properly, but rather improperly, called a "part."*

---

## On the production of the Multiple genus. Chapter 24.

ALTHOUGH the aforementioned five final genera of the proportions of greater inequality (as we have seen above) are finite in number, one should not think that their species are finite. For, like numbers (following their natural order to infinity), they can be increased infinitely. And although such species could be infinite, nonetheless **Music** contents itself with a small portion that is finite and closer to simplicity; it does not accept the infinite. This is because whatever is further from its origin is less pure and less simple; it is less grasped by the senses and less understood by the intellect. The opposite occurs when it is closer: then not only do the senses grasp it, but the intellect also learns it. Thus, one sees in numbers that the further they are from **Unity** (which is simple), the less simple and pure they are, and the less they are grasped by the senses and understood by the intellect. But on the contrary, the closer they are, the simpler they are found to be, and they are better known to the feelings and the intellect, because they participate in such simplicity.

The same occurs with the extreme sounds or voices of any <term>consonance</term> <note>A combination of notes that sounds pleasant or "stable" to the ear.</note>: the closer and more united they are to each other, the more intelligible they are. But if it happens that they extend too far into the high or low registers, the sense abhors it; nor can it have such ready knowledge of it. For such a distance is only understood with difficulty, whether by natural or artificial instruments. And although they could extend far toward the high and the low, nonetheless they could not proceed further than what is permitted by nature and art. 

But because all harmonic sounds, which are rational—that is, they have a determined and rational interval or proportion between them—are necessarily subject to the logic of number; because their extremes, compared to one another, necessarily fall under the logic of one of the species of the named genera; having reasoned about them up to this point, I will now come to reason on the manner in which their species are generated. 

Therefore, starting from the first, which is simpler than any other, called the **Multiple**; we can have knowledge of all its species by first arranging the natural order of Numbers, starting from Unity and proceeding to infinity if necessary. And then, make the comparison of the Binary (2), Ternary (3), Quaternary (4), and the other numbers in order to that Unity. In doing so, we will find in each relation various species of proportions: for comparing the Binary to unity, such a proportion will be called **Double** <note>original: "Dupla"</note>, after its <term>denominator</term> <note>In this context, the number that "names" the proportion.</note>, which is 2. Then, comparing the Ternary, a proportion will be born that will be named **Triple** <note>original: "Tripla"</note>, likewise from its denominator, which is 3; and so following in order. In such a way, by always making the comparison of each number to unity, we will have the species of the first genus called Multiple, as are those placed below:

## What the Denominator is, and in what way it is found; and how, between two proposed proportions, one may recognize the greater or the lesser.
### Cap. 25.

WE MUST observe that the *Denominator* (as *Euclid* <note>Euclid of Alexandria, the Greek mathematician whose "Elements" provided the geometric and numerical foundation for Renaissance theory.</note> maintains) is the name given to that number according to which a part is taken within its whole; and it is properly called by some an *Aliquot part* <note>A "proper divisor": a part that divides into the whole exactly with no remainder.</note>; and by others a *Quotient*: for it denotes how many times the greater term of the proportion contains the lesser. It is that which is produced by the division of the greater term by the lesser in any proposed proportion of any genus whatsoever. Just as, for example, by dividing the greater term of the *Dupla* <term>Double (2:1 proportion)</term>—which is found to be the first in the *Multiple* genus—which is 2, by the *Unity* (1), which is the lesser, the result will be 2. I say that this 2 is the *Denominator* of such a proportion: because the *Binary* (2) contains that *unity* twice, and the unity divides the binary exactly into two parts. Similarly, we shall say that 3 is the denominator of the *Tripla* <term>Triple (3:1 proportion)</term>; and 4 the denominator of the *Quadrupla* <term>Quadruple (4:1 proportion)</term>: since 3 contains the unity three times, and 4 contains it four times; and so it goes for all the others following. And such denominations are called *Simple*: because they are named after simple numbers, which are 2, 3, 4, and others like them.

But if, in the *Superparticular* genus <note>The genus of proportions where the larger number contains the smaller number once plus one single part (e.g., 3:2, 4:3).</note>, we divide the terms of the *Sesquialtera* <term>One-and-a-half (3:2 proportion)</term> in the manner described—that is, the greater by the lesser—the result will be 1 1/2. I say that this is the denominator of the *Sesquialtera*: since its greater term, 3, contains the lesser term, 2, one time, with one half-part remaining. According to the custom of mathematicians, this is written in such a way: 1/2. Such a denomination is called *Compound*: because it is composed of the unity and one of its parts. It is quite true that the parts that arise in such a way are sometimes called *Aliquot*, and sometimes *Non-aliquot* <note>A "non-aliquot" part is a quantity that does not divide the whole exactly (a remainder exists or it requires multiple parts).</note> of the lesser term contained in the proportion; but the number placed above the line is called the *Numerator* of such a part, and the one placed below is the *Denominator*.

From where this little word *Sesqui* originates, and what it signifies, is not an easy thing to know, were it not for what *Augustine* <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose treatise "De Musica" influenced medieval and Renaissance music theory.</note> maintains. He (reading it as *Sesque* and not *Sesqui*) thinks that it is said as if from *Ab sque*, that is from *Absque se* <note>original: "Absque se"; Latin: "without itself" or "apart from itself."</note>, which means *Without itself*: because

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 34 regarding the "Denominator" of a proportion—the numerical value resulting from dividing the larger term by the smaller—and focuses on the linguistic roots and classification of complex ratios used in musical tuning.</meta>

which (if I am not mistaken) takes the naming of the proportions from the part of the greater number by which it exceeds the lesser, in the terms or numbers of the proportions of the *Superparticular* genus <note>original: *Superparticolare*. A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number once, plus one "part" or unit (e.g., 3:2, 4:3).</note>; which he calls *Sesquialter* <note>original: *Sesquati*</note> numbers; and those of the *Multiple* genus, he calls *Complicated* numbers. And although there have been some who held the opinion that this is merely a syllabic addition and signifies nothing, having been invented only to be able to pronounce said species more conveniently, this seems to me to have been said with little consideration. Those who said that *Sesqui* <note>A Latin prefix meaning "one and a half," though here the author debates its broader meaning in ratios.</note> means "the whole" have spoken better; and that *Sesquialtera* is named from that word, which is Latin, and from *Altera*, likewise a Latin word used when speaking of only two, meaning "other"—as if to say a proportion whose greater term contains the whole of the lesser once, along with one of its two parts. And this is well said: for if it were otherwise (as some want, who claim *Sesqui* means "as much again" and "half"), one could not adapt such a word to the others, such as in the *Sesquiterza* (4:3), the *Sesquiquarta* (5:4), and other similar ones.

Nevertheless, it should be
noted that the Denominator of any proportion is found in two ways: that is, either in pure numbers, or by adding parts to these. And we can find this second way in four manners: for sometimes we will find the Unity and a single part; and sometimes the Unity and multiple parts; or we will find some whole number and a single part; or some whole number added to multiple parts. If we find simple numbers, we must name the proportion simply, according to what was shown in the species of the *Multiple* genus; if we find the unity added to a single part, we must name it according to how those of the *Superparticular* genus were named above.

When, however, the unity is found with multiple parts, then, leaving the unity aside, one places the particle *Super* before the Numerator of the parts, and this other particle *Partient* <term>from *partiente*, meaning "partitioning"</term> before the Denominator; and the naming of the proportion is composed of these two particles and the terms of the parts. For example, one can see in the first species of the *Superpartient* genus <note>original: *Superpartiente*. A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus more than one part (e.g., 5:3 contains 3 once plus 2 parts of 3).</note> that the proportion called *Superbipartient-third* <note>original: *Superbipartienteterza* (5:3)</note> is named from 1 and 2/3, its denominator: since if the greater term of such a proportion, which is 5, is divided by 3, which is the lesser, the result is 1 and 2/3. Thus, taking the numerator of the parts, which is 2, and adding the particle *Super*, we say *Superbi-* <note>Super-two</note>; then taking the 3 of the denominator with the second particle *Partient*, we say *Partient-third*; and so, joined together, it is called *Superbipartient-third*; which is done in the others as well, according to their denominator.

But when the denominator is composed of a
whole number and only one part, the proportion is first named from the number, as was said of the *Multiple*; then the part is added in the manner I declared for the *Superparticular*: since such a proportion is necessarily found in the first composite genus called *Multiple-superparticular*; as can be seen in the *Double-sesquialtera* <note>original: *Duplasesquialtera* (5:2)</note>, which is named from 2 and 1/2: because its greater term, which is 5, contains the 2, which is the lesser, two times, plus one-half part of the lesser; so that from the 2 it takes the name of *Double*, and from the part, which is 1/2, it takes that of *Sesquialtera*.

When, then,
the denominator is contained by a whole number and multiple parts, then the proportion is named primarily from the number, in the manner shown in the *Multiple*; then the parts are added, naming them as we did in the *Superpartient* genus: because such a proportion necessarily falls into the second composite genus, called *Multiple-superpartient*. We have the example of this in the *Double-superbipartient-third* <note>original: *Duplasuperbipartienteterza* (8:3)</note>, which is the first species of such a genus; as we shall see, named for the reasons stated from 2 and 2/3, its denominator.

It would be long if I wished to provide examples of every species; but because many of them can be seen in their proper place, I will not extend myself further on this now. I will only say this in conclusion: that every proportion is greater than another (as *Euclid* informs us) by as much as its denominator makes it; and this is true in every genus of proportion. This is manifest: since the *Double* (2:1) is without any doubt greater than the *Sesquialtera* (3:2), as its Denominator of 2 is greater than the 1 and 1/2 Denominator of the *Sesquialtera*; and the same can be said of the others.

### How the Superparticular genus is born. Chapter 26.

The second genus of proportions of greater inequality <note>Ratios where the first number is larger than the second.</note> arises in this way: leaving aside the Unit from one side of the aforementioned natural order of numbers, and starting from the Binary [2], following that order step by step; if we compare the larger number to the nearest smaller one, the **Superparticular** genus <note>original: *Superparticolare*. A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus one single part of it (e.g., 3:2, 4:3).</note> will be produced from such a comparison. Its first species is the **Sesquialtera** [3:2], by comparing the Ternary [3] to the Binary [2]. Then, when the Quaternary [4] is compared to the Ternary [3], the second species is born, called **Sesquiterza** [4:3], and so on for the others in order. Each of these (as I have said) is named after its own proper denominator, or aliquot part <note>A part that divides the whole exactly, such as a half or a third.</note>. Thus it can be seen that if, in any proportion, the part by which the larger number exceeds the smaller is half of that smaller number, it is called *Sesquialtera*; and if it is the third part, it is called *Sesquiterza*; and in short, all other species, even if they were infinite, are named after their parts, as can be seen in the example below.

### On the production of the Superpartient genus. Chapter 27.

The species of the third genus, called **Superpartient** <note>original: *Superpartiente*. A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus two or more parts of it (e.g., 5:3 contains 3 once, plus 2 thirds).</note>, are infinite: for some are called Superbipartients, some Supertripartients, and some Superquadripartients; proceeding thus to infinity, according to the natural order of numbers. Wherefore the Superbipartient is found between two numbers differing from each other by the Binary [2], provided they are larger than it and it cannot be their common measure. These numbers must be **Prime to one another** <note>original: *Contra se primi*. Numbers that share no common divisor other than 1.</note>, whose nature and property is such that they are radical terms <note>Numbers in their lowest mathematical form.</note> of whatever proportion they contain. Leaving then the Binary [2] aside, as it serves little purpose here, we will take the Ternary [3] and the Quinary [5], which are the first in the natural order of numbers to observe such a law: for if we compare the larger to the smaller, we will have the proportion called **Superbipartient-third** [5:3]: since 5 contains

## Of the Multiple superparticular genus. Chap. 28.

The Fourth genus, called **Multiple superparticular**, arises by adding the smaller term of any proportion of the <term>Superparticular</term> genus <note>Ratios like 3:2 or 4:3</note> to the larger, adding always the same smaller number to the number that results from such an addition. Wherefore, if we add the <term>Binary</term> [2]—the smaller term of the <term>Sesquialtera</term> [3:2]—to the larger, which is the <term>Ternary</term> [3], the <term>Quinary</term> [5] will result <note>creating the ratio 5:2</note>; to which, by likewise adding that same Binary, the <term>Settenary</term> [7] will be born <note>creating 7:2</note>, and so the others to infinity: so that by observing the same rule in the others, one may have infinite species; as can be understood in the figure placed below.

But if we observe the method that we followed in the production of the **Multiple Superparticular** <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number multiple times, plus one single part (e.g., 2 and 1/2).</note>; namely, adding the smaller term of the proportions of the **Superpartient** genus <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus multiple parts (e.g., 5:3, which is 1 plus 2/3).</note> to the larger term; and to the result always adding that same smaller term, continuing to infinity (if that were possible), this addition will create the fifth and final genus, called **Multiple Superpartient** <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller multiple times, plus multiple parts (e.g., 8:3, which is 2 plus 2/3).</note>; of which (not being a very difficult matter) I will not go on to speak further; it being sufficient only to provide the examples, so that they may be a guide and light to the understanding of this rule; and they shall be those placed below. ## On the nature and properties of the named Generi. Chapter 30.

FROM what has been shown above, therefore, one can understand that the genera and species of the proportions of **lesser inequality** <note>Ratios where the first number is smaller than the second, like 1:2.</note> are born among numbers in that same way that those of **greater inequality** <note>Ratios where the first number is larger than the second, like 2:1.</note> are born. No other difference is found from one to the other, except that in the former, the comparison is made of the smaller term to the larger, in terms of how one is contained by the other; and in the latter, the comparison is made of the larger term to the smaller, in terms of how one contains the other. And thus, both that of greater and that of lesser inequality come to be produced at the same time and exist within the same subject. 

But according to my judgment, the proportions of **lesser inequality** can be considered otherwise and also called **Rational** (so to speak) and **Privative**; and those of **greater inequality**, **Real** and **Positive**. And for a greater understanding of this, and also to know the nature of these genera, one must know that **Equality** <note>The ratio 1:1.</note> being like the element <note>The basic building block.</note> of proportions, it comes to be the principle of **Inequality** (as **Boethius** and **Jordanus** maintain) <note>Boethius was a 6th-century philosopher whose "De Institutione Musica" was the standard music theory text for a millennium; Jordanus de Nemore was a 13th-century mathematician.</note> and holds the middle place between the genus of greater inequality and that of lesser. 

And being so, it is by its nature simple; for (as can be seen) whether multiplied or divided, that proportion which is found in the whole is also found in each of its parts; and it is always permanent, and retains its being in any genus of inequality. This is clearly seen to be true; because by removing a **Double** from another **Double** in the genus of greater inequality—in the manner that we will see further on—and similarly in that of lesser inequality by removing a **Subdouble** <note>The 1:2 ratio.</note> from another, one arrives immediately at **Equality**. This is because (according to the opinion of **Boethius**) every **Inequality** is resolved into **Equality**, as if into the element of its own genus. This does not happen with proportions of inequality, which are changeable; when these are multiplied or divided, the proportions of the whole are different from those of their parts; and the larger proportions have no place among the terms of the smaller ones; as can be seen from the **Double**, which, being larger than the **Sesquialter**, has no place between

<summary>This page concludes the categorization of complex proportions and introduces Chapter 30, which explores the philosophical and mathematical relationship between "greater" and "lesser" ratios, establishing Equality (1:1) as the fundamental source from which all inequalities arise.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theoretical discussion on proportions, specifically focusing on how "lesser inequality" (ratios where the first number is smaller than the second) acts as a mathematical "privation" or subtraction from "greater inequality."</meta>

# First

...within its terms; as is manifest: for wishing to take the **Double** ratio <note>The ratio 2:1.</note> contained between these terms 2 and 1 from the **Sesquialter** <note>The ratio 3:2, often representing the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> contained between these 3 and 2—in the manner that I intend to show—there arises the **Subsesquiterce** <note>The ratio 3:4, the inverse of a 4:3 Sesquiterce or perfect fourth.</note> between these two, 3 and 4. This is contained in the second genus of <term>lesser inequality</term> <note>Ratios where the first number is smaller than the second, such as 1:2 or 2:3.</note>, called **Subsuperparticular**; which, by being of a different genus from the first two proposed, gives a manifest sign that the Sesquialter is deprived of as much quantity as that by which the Sesquialter is exceeded by the Double; that is, it is deprived of a Sesquiterce. And this is most true: for by adding the Sesquialter to the Sesquiterce, the Double is immediately born. Whence the Subsesquiterce comes to be only the reason of that proportion which is missing between the terms of the Sesquialter to ascend to the sum and quantity of the Double. This defect is manifested by the particle *Sub* <note>Latin for "under."</note> that is added to it, which in composition sometimes denotes diminution; wherefore, from its effect, we can call it **Privative**.

I say **Privative**, not because it has the power to deprive any proportion of its quantity, but because it declares the proportion to which it is added to be deprived within its terms and diminished by as much quantity as its name implies. And this is not said without purpose: for just as it is impossible that any greater number can be taken out of a smaller number in fact, so too is it impossible that from a smaller proportion, a larger one can be taken away in fact; it being necessary that the quantity from which another is taken be either greater than or equal to the one we intend to remove. However, operating in the manner I am about to show, from a **Double** we can always take a **Sesquialter**, and a **Sesquiterce** will remain; and from a **Sesquialter** we can take another, and **Equality** <note>The ratio 1:1.</note> will result. But we can never take a Double from a Sesquialter without some quantity being missing; which will always appear in the product of subtracting one from the other, as we shall see. It will demonstrate such a deficiency: the Double being greater than it by a Sesquiterce, and the Sesquialter being diminished by such an amount, as has been seen.

Therefore, no one should marvel if I liken the proportions of <term>greater inequality</term> <note>Ratios where the first number is larger than the second, representing the "presence" of a musical form.</note> to **Habit** <note>original: "Habito". In a philosophical sense, this refers to a state of being or the possession of a quality.</note>, having called them **Positive**, since they give the reason for the proportions—that is, the form that gives being to a determined real subject. And those of **lesser [inequality]** to **Privation**, naming them **Rational** and **Privative**: for they negate the proportion they represent in the named subject, and are deprived of one of their real terms because they do not exceed Equality, but are less than it. 

Wherefore, the genus of greater inequality being different and opposite to the genus of lesser, taken in this way, it is necessary that both be considered under different reasons: the first under the reason of Habit or Position, and the second under the reason of Privation, as I have said. And yet they must also be considered as two opposites corresponding to one another in the third mode of Opposition: for the genera and the species placed under one correspond (considered under the reason of Habit) to the genera and species placed under the other (considered under the reason of Privation); in almost the same way that Ignorance corresponds to Science, Darkness to Light, and the like. They must also be considered as two opposites corresponding to their middle, namely to **Equality**, which is like the subject of Habit and Privation: for such things occur around it. 

Nor do I wish to have said this without some foundation: for just as the subject of a non-natural habit and an imperfect privation is fit to receive now one, now the other, by succession, and retains that which presents itself to it until it is deprived of it—just as we see in the Air, which is fit to receive now light and now darkness, and is only as bright as the light stays near it and does not separate from it—so Equality is fit to receive now the proportion of greater, now that of lesser inequality. And just as the subject maintains in its quality the thing it receives, and for this reason does not vary in its substance, so Equality does not change that proportion of whatever genus accompanies it; nor does it vary when any proportion of whatever genus is added to or taken from it, its terms being (as I have shown) immutable and invariable. 

And because just as privation is always in the subject when the habit is removed, and the habit (or the aptitude) is there when the privation is removed; similarly, when any proportion of greater inequality is removed from Equality, there immediately follows an almost similar contrary of those of lesser [inequality]. And that of greater inequality is introduced when that of lesser is removed: just as by removing a **Double**, a **Subdouble** <note>The ratio 1:2.</note> results; and by removing the Subdouble, the Double is born. But because every extreme has its middle, and the middle is that which is equally distant from its extremes—the two genera of inequality being two extremes equidistant from Equality—therefore I have said that Equality holds the place of the middle between the one and the other of the named two genera of inequality, in the way that can be clearly seen in the figure placed below.

<summary>Zarlino explains that mathematical ratios of "lesser inequality" (where the first term is smaller) act as the "privation" or negative opposite of "greater inequality" (where the first term is larger). He establishes Equality (the 1:1 ratio) as the neutral midpoint between these two extremes, comparing it to how air can receive either light or darkness.</summary>

And although these examples are placed only within the terms of some species of the first two genera of <term>greater inequality</term> <note>Ratios where the first number is larger than the second, like 2:1.</note> and <term>lesser inequality</term> <note>Ratios where the first number is smaller than the second, like 1:2.</note>; nevertheless, one must also understand those of the other species, which I have left out for the sake of brevity. I believe that these alone are sufficient to show what we have proposed: therefore, anyone who is desirous of seeing the other species of such genera may investigate them for themselves, having regard for what was shown above. Now, from what has been said, we can understand for what reason we can call the proportions of greater inequality **Real** and **Positive**, and those of lesser inequality **Rational** and **Privative**; and we can also say that they are two extremes, between which **Equality** is found situated in the middle. Similarly, we can know the nature and property of each of these genera and what their true office is. When, therefore, we wish to name any proportion of the genus of lesser inequality, we can accompany it with this particle *Sub* <note>Latin: "under."</note>; those that are of the other genus we shall set down without such an addition. And so that the proportions of one of the two opposite genera may be known from those of the other, we will observe this order when necessary: we will place the greater terms of those proportions that are of the genus of greater inequality on the left side, and the lesser on the right, in this manner: **3 & 2**. The terms of those that are of the genus of lesser inequality we will place to the contrary in this manner: **2 & 3**. Meanwhile, those of Equality may be placed without any difference of position, being by their nature invariable.

## On the Multiplication of Proportions, Chapter 31.

HAVING sufficiently shown how proportions are born and their names, we shall begin to reason about their operations, which are five: **Multiplying**, **Adding**, **Subtracting**, **Dividing**, and **Finding their Roots**. Regarding the first, we must know that there have been some who held the opinion that Multiplying and Adding were the same thing; and some held the opposite, that they were two separate operations; and they held the same regarding Subtracting and Dividing. But leaving disputes aside, I will demonstrate with examples that such operations are not the same thing, but separate operations—a thing very useful and necessary for our present business. Coming then to the purpose, I say that **Multiplying** is an arrangement of several proportions in a continuous order, placed one after the other in such a way that the lesser term of one is the greater of the next, and so conversely. But **Adding**, I say, is a gathering...

<meta>This page transitions from the general classification of ratios (proportions) to the specific mathematical operations required to combine them. The author is explaining how to "multiply" proportions—what we would today call finding a common denominator or creating a continuous string of ratios—to understand how musical intervals stack together.</meta>

First Part

...a gathering of several proportions joined together under a single name. Multiplication can be done in two ways; the first is when one proportion is multiplied by another, or more; starting from the **left** side and moving toward the **right**; which method we shall name **Subjoining** <note>original: "Soggiungere"</note>. The second is when we proceed in the opposite direction; that is, from the **right** toward the **left**, which method we shall call **Prefixing** <note>original: "Preporre"</note>. And because these two methods are necessary and useful, we will show the operation of both.

Beginning then with the first, I say that if we had to multiply together two or more proportions of the same genus or of different ones (which does not matter), we will first arrange the proportions contained in their <term>radical terms</term> <note>The smallest whole numbers that express the ratio, such as 3:2 instead of 6:4.</note>, one after the other in order, according to how we intend to multiply them. Taking the larger term of the second proportion to be multiplied, placed on the **left** side, we will multiply it by the larger and the smaller term of the first; then we will multiply this by the smaller term of the second; and we will have three numbers containing two continuous proportions. Now we will multiply these by the larger term of the proportion that is to be multiplied, which is third in the aforementioned order, starting from the **left** and gradually coming toward the **right** side. This done, again taking the smaller term of such a proportion, we will multiply it by the smallest of the previous products; and four terms or numbers will result, in which the multiplied proportions will be contained. 

And whenever there is a need to subjoin to these proportions yet another proportion, we will always multiply the resulting numbers by the larger term of the proportion we wish to subjoin, and the smallest of the results by its smaller term; and from such multiplication we will always have what we seek. But because examples move the intellect toward the understanding of a thing much more than words do, especially in the operations of numbers, and desiring to be understood, I will come to an example. 

Let us suppose, then, that we have to multiply together four proportions contained in the <term>Superparticular genus</term> <note>Ratios where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3/2, 4/3).</note>; and let these be a **Sesquialter** <note>A 3:2 ratio, representing a musical fifth.</note>, a **Sesquiterce** <note>A 4:3 ratio, representing a musical fourth.</note>, a **Sesquiquarter** <note>A 5:4 ratio, representing a major third.</note>, and a **Sesquiquint** <note>A 6:5 ratio, representing a minor third.</note>. First, we will place them one after the other, according to the order in which they are to be multiplied, so that they are expressed in their radical terms in this way: $^3/_2, ^4/_3, ^5/_4, ^6/_5$. 

Then we will multiply the larger term of the Sesquiterce, which is 4, by the 3 and 2 (the terms of the Sesquialter); from this multiplication, we will have 12 and 8, which likewise contain the Sesquialter. This is because the terms of any proportion multiplied by any number do not change their value; as is manifest through the proof in Proposition 18 of the 7th book of <term>Euclid's Elements</term> <note>Euclid was a Greek mathematician; his "Elements" was the standard textbook for geometry and number theory.</note>, and by what <term>Boethius</term> <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De Institutione Musica" transmitted Greek music theory to the Middle Ages.</note> says in Chapter 29 of the 2nd book of his *Music*. These numbers we will place under a straight line on the page, which divides them from the proposed proportions. 

Having done this, we will multiply together the smaller terms of these two proportions, and 6 will result; which we will place on the **right** side next to the 8. Thus, we will have multiplied said proportions together; that is, subjoined the Sesquiterce to the Sesquialter between these terms: 12, 8, 6. Now, to subjoin the Sesquiquarter to these, we will multiply these terms by its larger term, which is 5, starting from the **left** side and moving toward the **right**, and we will have 60, 40, 30. This done, we will multiply the smallest of the first three, which is 6, by the smaller term of the Sesquiquarter, which is 4, and 24 will be born; which, placed with the others, will give this order: 60, 40, 30, 24, containing the Sesquialter, the Sesquiterce, and the Sesquiquarter proportions. 

We will do the same when we wish to multiply the Sesquiquint to these: for by first multiplying the aforementioned four terms by its larger term, which is 6, there will result 360, 240, 180, 144. Then, having multiplied the smallest of those shown, which is 24, by the smaller term of that proportion, which is 5, it will give 120; which, placed in its spot, will give us five numbers or terms from such multiplication: 360, 240, 180, 144, 120, containing those proportions. Just as 360 and 240 contain the Sesquialter; the Sesquiterce is between 240 and 180; between 180 and 144 is the Sesquiquarter; and between 144 and 120 is the Sesquiquint; even though they are not found in their radical terms, as seen in the example below.

## The Second Way of Multiplying Ratios. Chapter 32.

WHEN IT HAPPENS that in multiplications there is a need to prefix one ratio to another, we will proceed in this way: first, we will multiply each term of the first ratio by the smaller term of the second ratio (placed on the left side), starting from the smaller; then, we multiply the larger term of one by the larger term of the other together. From this multiplication, we will have three terms containing these ratios. Next, by multiplying these products by the larger term of the third ratio, and the largest of those products by the largest term again, we will achieve our purpose. 

If we take, for example, the smaller term of the <term>Sesquiquarta</term> <note>The ratio 5:4, which in music forms a Major Third.</note> used in the previous chapter, which is 4, and multiply it by the terms 5 and 6 of the <term>Sesquiquinta</term> <note>The ratio 6:5, which forms a Minor Third.</note>, the result will be 20 and 24. We will place these, as we did above, under a straight line. Then, having multiplied the larger term (5) of said <term>Sesquiquarta</term> by the larger term (6) of the <term>Sesquiquinta</term>, the result will be 30. Placing this next to the 24, it will give us three terms: 30, 24, 20, which contain the multiplied ratios. 

But to multiply the <term>Sesquiterza</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, which forms a Perfect Fourth.</note> with these, we will take its smaller term, which is 3, and multiply it by the three products, starting from the right and moving toward the left side; we will get 90, 72, and 60, arranging them one after the other under their factors (which are 30, 24, and 20). Again, multiplying the larger term (4) of the <term>Sesquiterza</term> by 30, the result will be 120. After we have added this to the three aforementioned numbers, it will yield this order: 120, 90, 72, 60, containing the <term>Sesquiquinta</term>, the <term>Sesquiquarta</term>, and the <term>Sesquiterza</term> ratios. 

If we wish to multiply the <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, which forms a Perfect Fifth.</note> with these, we will take its smaller term (2) and multiply it in the manner described by the four products; we will have 240, 180, 144, and 120. We will then multiply its larger term (3) by the largest term of the products (120), and 360 will be born. This, accompanied by the four products, will give the entire multiplication among these terms: 360, 240, 180, 144, 120, which contain the four named ratios, as seen in the example below, similar to what we showed in the previous chapter.

## On Adding Ratios. Chapter 33.

Adding ratios (as I have said) is nothing other than reducing as many as one wishes, of one or of different kinds, under a single name. This "name" is found in the extreme numbers or terms of these ratios when they are multiplied together, with this difference: these extremes are mediated <note>The numbers between the highest and lowest remain visible, showing the constituent steps.</note> by other ratios, but those that arise from adding are immediate <note>Only the start and end points are shown, hiding the internal steps.</note>, as we shall see.

Then, multiply the larger terms by one another, starting with the first two, then the product of those by the third, and the result of that by the fourth, and so on step by step; and

### On Subtracting Ratios. Chapter 34.

The third operation is called Subtraction, which is nothing other than taking a smaller ratio or quantity away from a larger one to know the differences, or by how much one quantity exceeds or is exceeded by the other. This operation is done in this manner: First, one must arrange the <term>radical terms</term> <note>The smallest whole numbers that express a ratio (e.g., 2:1 instead of 4:2).</note> of the ratios in the form of a square figure, so that the terms of the larger ratio are in the upper part and those of the smaller are in the lower, one beneath the other. Take care, however, that the larger terms of both ratios occupy the left side and the smaller terms the right. This done, we will multiply the terms crosswise: that is, the larger term of the upper ratio by the smaller of the lower; and likewise the larger of the lower ratio by the smaller of the upper. We will place the products perpendicularly beneath the multiplied terms placed above, dividing them from the ratios with a horizontal straight line. From these products, one will then see how much one ratio exceeds the other, and the difference found between them. 

Wishing, then, to take a <term>Sesquiterza</term> from a <term>Sesquialtera</term>, and to know by how much the <term>Sesquialtera</term> surpasses the <term>Sesquiterza</term> and the difference found between them, we will operate in this way. We will first arrange the terms of the ratios in the manner seen in the example below. Then, having drawn a horizontal straight line underneath, we will place below it the terms produced by the multiplication of one term with the other. Starting then from 3, the larger term of the <term>Sesquialtera</term>, we will multiply it by 3, the smaller term of the <term>Sesquiterza</term>, and the product, which is 9, we will place perpendicularly under the 3 (the larger term of the <term>Sesquialtera</term>) below the line on the left side. This will be the larger term of the resulting ratio that contains the difference we seek. This done, we will multiply 4, which is the larger term of the <term>Sesquiterza</term>, by 2, which is the smaller of the <term>Sesquialtera</term>; and the product, which is 8, will be the smaller term of the ratio containing the aforementioned difference. Once placed under the designated line perpendicularly beneath the 2 (the smaller term of the <term>Sesquialtera</term>), we will have the <term>Sesquiottaua</term> ratio <note>A 9:8 ratio, which in music is a Major Second or a Whole Tone.</note> contained between 9 and 8. This, I say, is the difference of how much one is greater than the other, as is seen here.

## On Partitioning or Dividing Proportions; and What Proportionality Is. Chapter 35.

It should be noted that by this fourth operation, I mean nothing other than the Division or Partitioning of any proportion, which is achieved by placing a certain calculated number between its extremes; this number is called the **Divisor**, because it divides that proportion into two parts. This division is what mathematicians call **Proportionality** or **Progression**. Therefore, it seemed appropriate to me to first declare what this name "Proportionality" signifies, and then proceed to the operations. Proportionality, then, according to the mind of **Euclid** <note>Greek mathematician (c. 300 BCE), author of the Elements.</note>, is a similarity of proportions found between at least three terms containing two proportions. And although among mathematicians (as **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 CE), whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory text for centuries.</note> demonstrates) there are ten types of proportionality—or eleven according to the mind of **Jordanus** <note>Jordanus de Nemore, a 13th-century mathematician.</note>—nevertheless, the first three are the most famous and approved by the ancient philosophers **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and **Aristotle**. These three are considered and embraced by the musician, as they serve his purpose better than the others. Of these, the first is called **Arithmetic**, the second **Geometric**, and the third **Harmonic**. Since I wish to discuss something about each of them, we shall first see what each one is separately.

Beginning then with the first, I say that **Arithmetic** division or proportionality is that which, between two terms of any proportion, will have a middle term arranged in such a way that while the *differences* of its terms are equal, its *proportions* will be unequal. Conversely, I say that **Geometric** division or proportionality is that in which the proportions (by virtue of the aforementioned middle term) are equal, while its

# On Proportionality, or Arithmetic Division. Chap. 36.

One may, therefore, divide any proportion according to arithmetic proportionality once we have found a Divisor which, when placed in the middle of the terms of the proportion to be divided, will divide it in such a way that—the differences of the terms being equal (as has been said)—its proportions will be unequal. In this way, the smaller proportions will be found among the larger numbers, and the larger proportions among the smaller numbers; a characteristic that belongs only to arithmetic proportionality. We can find this easily when, having added the terms of the proposed proportion together, we divide the sum into two equal parts: for that number which results from such a division will be the sought-after Divisor, which will divide the said proportion into two parts according to the conditions mentioned above. Nevertheless, one must note that if the proposed proportion is in its <term>radical terms</term> <note>original: "termini radicali"; the lowest whole-number ratio, such as 3:2 instead of 6:4</note>, the aforementioned method cannot be followed: for it will necessarily be contained by <term>relatively prime</term> numbers <note>original: "Contrafeprimi"; numbers that share no common factor other than 1</note>, which when added together will produce an odd number that cannot be divided into two equal parts—that is, into two whole numbers. Therefore, wanting to find such a divisor and avoid <term>fractions</term> <note>original: "numeri rotti" (broken numbers)</note>, which are not accepted by the arithmetician, we will always double the said terms, which will result in two even numbers that do not change the original proportion. Now, this being done, by adding the said even numbers together and dividing the sum into two equal parts, the result will be the sought-after Divisor.

And let it be as an example: suppose we wished to divide the <term>Sesquialtera</term> proportion <note>A 3:2 ratio, which corresponds to the musical interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note>, contained between these radical terms 3 and 2, according to arithmetic division. Since these numbers are relatively prime, they must be doubled: which being done, we will have 6 and 4 containing the <term>Sesquialtera</term>. These added together result in 10, which when divided into two equal parts gives 5. Thus I say that 5 will be the Divisor of the proposed proportion. For besides establishing equal differences in such a proportionality, it also divides the proportion (as is proper for such proportionality) into two unequal proportions, in such a way that the smaller proportion is found among the larger numbers, and conversely the larger proportion among the smaller; as between 6 and 5 is the <term>Sesquiquinta</term> <note>A 6:5 ratio or Minor Third.</note>, and between 5 and 4 is the <term>Sesquiquarta</term> <note>A 5:4 ratio or Major Third.</note>; as is seen here.

## On Geometric Division, or Proportionality. Chap. 37.

GEOMETRIC DIVISION is performed when the Divisor is placed between the extremes of any proportion in such a way that it maintains the conditions touched upon in the preceding chapter. Thus, it should be known that every other proportionality is of such a nature that it only divides the proposed proportion into two unequal parts; but the property of the Geometric is to always divide it into two equal parts. Because of this effect, it is properly called Proportionality, since between its greater terms and its lesser terms the proportions are equal; and the product of the Divisor multiplied by itself is equal to the product of the extreme terms of said Proportionality multiplied together. 

But to find such a Divisor, we shall observe this rule: once we have proposed whatever proportion we wish to divide, contained in its <term>radical terms</term> <note>The "radical terms" refers to the ratio reduced to its lowest possible whole numbers.</note>—to avoid the length of the operation, the effort, and the many errors that occur—we shall first multiply those terms by one another. Then, we shall take the <term>square root</term> <note>original: "Radice quadrata."</note> of the product, which will be a number that, when multiplied by itself, will yield exactly that product; and such a root shall be the sought-after Divisor. 

And so that I may be more easily understood, I shall come to an example. Let us take the <term>Quadruple</term> proportion <note>A 4:1 ratio, which in music represents two octaves.</note> contained in its radical terms 4 and 1. Wishing to divide it Geometrically, we must first multiply the said terms by one another, and thus we will have 4. Then, having taken its square root, which will be 2, we shall say that this number is the geometric Divisor of such a proportion. This is because the product resulting from multiplying [the divisor] by itself is equal to that which arises from the multiplication of the proposed terms multiplied together; for 4 multiplied by unity yields as much as 2 multiplied by itself, as is seen in the figure. The Quadruple is therefore divided into two equal parts by such a Divisor; that is, into two <term>Duplas</term> <note>original: "Duple"; 2:1 ratios, or octaves.</note>, one of which is found to be between 4 and 2, and the other between 2 and 1. 

But one must take note: although the property of Geometric proportionality is to divide any proportion into two equal parts, this is done universally in continuous quantity; because

...because in discrete quantity <note>The study of individual numbers, as opposed to continuous measurements like lines.</note> not all proportions are divisible in this way: since numbers do not allow for the division of the unit <note>In traditional Pythagorean arithmetic, the number 1 (the unit) was considered indivisible.</note>. Therefore, just as it is impossible to rationally divide any proportion into two equal parts when it is contained within the <term>Superparticular</term> <note>A ratio where the numerator is the denominator plus one, such as 3:2 or 4:3.</note> genus—as **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was a standard textbook.</note> affirms in his **Music**, and **Jordanus** <note>Jordanus de Nemore, a 13th-century mathematician.</note> in his **Arithmetic**—because no other number falls between its terms except the unit, which cannot be divided; so too will it be impossible to divide those of the other genera that come after this one. This is because those proportions which can be divided are contained in the <term>Multiple</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number is a whole-number multiple of the smaller, like 2:1 or 4:1.</note> genus, and have a square number at one of their extremes and the Unit at the other; and thus they are capable (as the same **Jordanus** affirms) of such division.

Thus, from Geometric proportionality, we can have two types of division: the <term>Rational</term> and the <term>Irrational</term>. I call the <term>Rational</term> that which is performed by way of rational numbers, so that its <term>Divisor</term> <note>The mean term or middle number.</note> is exactly the <term>Square root</term> of the product of the multiplication of the terms of a proportion; and the parts of such a division can be named, as is shown in the example containing the terms 4, 2, 1. But the irrational is that which is done by way of measurements, and also by numbers which are called <term>Surds</term> <note>original: "Sordi"; Latin: "surdus" (deaf/silent). In mathematics, a surd is an irrational number, typically a square root that cannot be simplified to a whole number or fraction.</note> and <term>Irrational</term>. This is because such a division cannot be performed or even described with rational numbers or similar measures in any way. This occurs when we cannot obtain an exact <term>Root</term> from the product; as would happen, for example, if we wished to divide a <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>The 3:2 ratio, which corresponds to the musical interval of a fifth.</note> in this manner. For when the terms (which are 3 and 2) are multiplied together, the product is 6; from 6, one cannot extract such a root—that is, one cannot find a number which, multiplied by itself, makes 6.

It is quite true that such a number can be named according to the custom of Mathematicians in this way, by saying "Root 6"—that is, the <term>Square root</term> that could be extracted from this number, if it were possible—and this would be its <term>Divisor</term>. But such a <term>Root</term> or number, which is seen in the example below, will always be called <term>Surd</term> and <term>Irrational</term> for the reason given. And because one cannot have the rational root of such a number, the parts of this division cannot be named or described, even though its extremes are comprised of Rational numbers. Therefore, for the reasons stated, such a division will always be called <term>Surd</term> and <term>Irrational</term>, and it is not considered by the Musician.

## How one may extract the square root from numbers. Chapter 38.

We shall now see in what manner one may extract the **square root** from numbers. First, having written down the number from which we wish to find the root, we will begin from the first digit placed on the right side of the said number, placing a dot beneath it. This done, skipping the next digit, we will place another dot under the third, and likewise under the fifth in order, always skipping one digit, even if there were many. Then, beginning from the last dot placed on the left side, we will find a **square number** <note>A number produced by multiplying an integer by itself, such as 4, 9, or 16.</note> that is equal to the whole number found from that dot backward toward the left side, or is closest to it, provided it does not exceed it. We shall place the **root** <note>The number which, when squared, produces the square number.</note> of this under the said dot; and we shall subtract the square from the number placed from the last dot backward, and whatever remains we shall always place above this number. Furthermore, we shall double the root that was placed under the dot, and the resulting value we shall place under the digit that immediately follows that dot on the right side, arranging the digits one by one toward the left. This done, we shall see how many times the double of the root is contained within that number which is placed above the root and its double; and the result, which will be the root of another square number, we shall place under the next dot, multiplying it by the result of the doubling, and subtracting the product from the number placed above. But one must take care that there remains a number which is equal to the square number of this root, so that when one is subtracted from the other, nothing remains. In this way, we will have exactly the true square root of the proposed number, which will be contained among the roots of the squares placed under the dots. And if a number remains which is greater than the square, then one cannot obtain anything but an **irrational and surd root** <note>A "surd" is an older mathematical term for an irrational root (one that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction or whole number).</note>, in the manner I have demonstrated elsewhere; and it will be necessary to turn to **continuous quantity** <term>Continuous quantity: Measurements like lengths or areas in geometry, as opposed to discrete numbers used in arithmetic.</term>, operating in the manner I intend to show in the second part. And because it is a very difficult thing to treat this matter in general terms, we shall therefore come to a particular example, so that what has been said may be understood. Let us suppose, then, that one wished to extract
