## On Division, or Harmonic Proportionality. Chapter 39.

**HARMONIC DIVISION**, or proportionality, occurs when a <term>Divisor</term> <note>A middle value used to split a larger ratio into two smaller ones.</note> is placed between the terms of a ratio in such a way that, in addition to the conditions mentioned in Chapter 35, the larger proportions are found between the larger terms, and the smaller proportions between the smaller terms. This is a property found only in this proportionality, which is properly called <term>Mediocrity</term> <note>From the Latin 'mediocritas', meaning 'the mean' or middle state.</note>; for among sounds, the middle string of three strings tuned according to its terms produces with its outer strings 그 sweet concord called **Harmony**. Thus <note>original: "Pietro d'Abano"</note> Pietro d'Abano <note>A famous 13th-century physician and philosopher.</note>, commentator on the *Problems* of Aristotle, said very well that "The middle is that which generates harmony."

We can easily find such a Divisor when, taking the <term>radical terms</term> <note>The simplest whole-number form of a ratio.</note> of the proportion we wish to divide, we first divide them by **Arithmetic Proportionality**; then, having multiplied its outer terms by the middle term, the products will be the outer terms of the Harmonic division. Likewise, by multiplying the largest by the smallest, the middle term of this proportionality—that is, the Divisor—will be produced; for such terms will be arranged according to the conditions described above.

Therefore, if we wish to harmonically divide a <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, which creates the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note>, contained between these radical terms 3 and 2, we will first divide it arithmetically according to the method shown in Chapter 36; and we will have such proportionality between these terms: 6, 5, 4. We will then reduce this to the harmonic by multiplying the 6 and the 4 by the 5; then the 6 by the 4, and we will have from the products the sought division, contained between these terms: 30, 24, 20; as seen in the following figure. For the proportion found between 6 and 4 (which are the differences of the harmonic terms) is the same as that found between 30 and 20 (which are the extremes of the <term>Sesquialtera</term> that was to be divided). This ratio remains divided into a <term>Sesquiquarta</term> <note>The ratio 5:4, a Major Third.</note> contained between 30 and 24, and a <term>Sesquiquinta</term> <note>The ratio 6:5, a Minor Third.</note> contained between 24 and 20. And thus, between the larger terms the larger proportions are found, and between the smaller the smaller; as is the nature of such proportionality.

## Consideration of what has been said regarding Ratios & 
## Proportionality. Chapter 40.

*THERE is no doubt, since Ratio is (as I have said at other times) the Relation of one quantity to another, made under the same immediate genus, that it can be considered in only two ways. First, insofar as one quantity counts, or is counted by the other; second, insofar as one is measured by the other. In such a way that from this first mode, ratios and arithmetic proportionalities have their origin; and from the second, the Geometric ones. There being, therefore, two modes and no more from which these two sorts of ratios and proportionalities are born, truly every other depends on and has its being from them. Hence, harmonic proportionality being very different from the two mentioned, it necessarily comes to be composed of these two. And although it is seen to be different from both the one and the other, it is nonetheless joined to them in such a way that the variety possessed by the two touched upon above is moderated within it with a pleasant variety. For one sees it sometimes to be far from the Arithmetic and approaching the Geometric; and sometimes the contrary. Similarly, at times it is seen with most admirable order to resemble both the one and the other, and at other times to be very different from both. So that even if other reasons were lacking, from this alone one can believe and know that it has acquired the name of Harmonic proportionality. Nor, to say that it is composed of the two mentioned, should it seem strange to anyone: because the Musician (as I have said elsewhere) takes not only Numbers from Arithmetic, but from Geometry he also takes other Quantities. And just as the pure Mathematician considers both quantities as distant from matter—if not in terms of their existence, at least in terms of their logic—so the Musician, not being a pure mathematician, considers not only the form, but the matter also of the Consonances; <note>In this context, Zarlino is using "form" to mean the mathematical ratio and "matter" to mean the physical sound produced.</note> that is, the Voices and the Sounds as the matter, and the Numbers and Ratios as the form. But because (as I have said elsewhere) the logic of the Voices and of the*

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 40 regarding how musical ratios are derived from mathematical principles. It shifts from the theoretical definitions of arithmetic and geometric proportions to the practical application of harmonic proportionality through the division of a sounding string.</meta>

First Part
Page 52
Header: First

Low and high sounds cannot be known, except by means of some **sounding body** <note>original: "Corpo ſonoro"</note>, which is subject to **continuous quantity** <note>In Renaissance science, "continuous quantity" refers to things that can be measured, like a line or a string, as opposed to "discrete quantity," which refers to things that are counted, like numbers.</note>: therefore, in finding such ratios through the medium of a sounding string, and making use of both types of quantity, the musician subjects his science to Arithmetic and Geometry. From this, he needed to find a **Proportionality** <note>A relationship between three or more terms where the ratios between them follow a specific rule.</note> which, while dealing with discrete quantity, was not far from the continuous; and that it should suit the nature of the two mentioned sciences, so that in sounding bodies every consonance could be discerned, arranged according to the form of the **harmonic numbers**. And because the parts of the sounding quantities, from which consonances are born, are ordered and divided by the Musician according to the ratio of numbers—which are their forms—and their progressions are without doubt arithmetic; from this it arises that one sees no division or harmonic proportionality belonging to musical harmonies that is not likewise found in Arithmetic. For those proportions which Harmonic science gives us, Arithmetic grants the same, though in a different way. And this is not without reason: because Arithmetic attends to nothing other than the multiplication of Unity, placing it in the natural order of numbers in the first place, the **Binary** <note>The number 2.</note> in the second (from which the **Double** <term>Dupla</term> ratio immediately arises), the **Ternary** <note>The number 3.</note> in the third, and so on for the others in order.

But Harmonic science, on the other hand, attends to its diminution—that is, the diminution or division of the sounding body—counting or multiplying its parts according to the ratio of the proportions contained in the natural order of numbers. For when it is diminished by one half part, between the whole and the half we have the form of the consonance **Diapason** <note>An Octave (2:1 ratio).</note>, which holds the first place in the progression or natural order of consonances and other intervals. Then, diminished by two-thirds, we have that of the **Diapente** <note>A Perfect Fifth (3:2 ratio).</note>, which holds the second place between the half and a third part; or rather, we have the form of the **Diapason-diapente** <note>A Twelfth (3:1 ratio), composed of an octave plus a fifth.</note> between the whole and the third part. Similarly, we have the form of the **Diatessaron** <note>A Perfect Fourth (4:3 ratio).</note> or the **Disdiapason** <note>A Double Octave (4:1 ratio).</note> when diminished by three-fourths; that is, one between the third and the fourth part, and the other between the whole and the fourth part. One would also have that of the **Ditone** <note>A Major Third (5:4 ratio).</note> when it was diminished by four-fifths; and that of the **Semiditone** <note>A Minor Third (6:5 ratio).</note> when it was diminished by five-sixths; and that of the other intervals in order, which would be long to discuss particularly for each one. 

Diminishing it in such a way, it retains the nature of continuous quantity; and in diminishing, it counts or multiplies the parts according to the ratios of the proportions contained in the natural order of numbers, and thus resembles discrete quantity. And although harmonic proportionality has the same ratios found in Arithmetic—because the forms of consonances (as we have seen) are contained between the parts of the **Senario** <term>Senario</term> <note>The number six; Zarlino famously argued that all perfect and imperfect musical consonances are derived from the first six integers.</note> number, which are in arithmetic progression—nevertheless, in Arithmetic, the proportions between the smaller terms are larger, and between the larger terms they are smaller; in Harmonic, the contrary is found: the larger proportions are in the larger terms, and the smaller in the smaller. 

And such diversity arises because one deals with pure numbers and the other with sounding quantities; they proceed in opposite ways. That is, one proceeds by the increase and the other by the diminution of its principle, as I have shown; yet each of them does not depart from the natural progression found in the order of proportions placed in numbers. Thus, in Arithmetic, numbers are units placed together, and in Harmonic, they are the parts of sounding quantities. 

And so that these things may be better understood, we will give an example. Let us place the line AB below, which for the Arithmetician shall be Unity, and for the Musician a sounding body—that is, a string—and let it be one foot long. I say that wishing to give an arithmetic progression, it will be necessary to leave it whole and indivisible, because proceeding arithmetically, it is not permitted that Unity be divided. Let such a progression then be contained by three terms in this manner: so that the **Triple** ratio is divided by the middle term into two parts. It will be necessary to proceed in this way: that is, to first double (if it were possible) the said line, in the same way we see Unity doubled in the Binary, which follows Unity without any intermediary. Thus, having doubled it, we will have the line AC, two feet long. If we compare the doubled line AC to the line AB, we will find between them the **Double** ratio, which is first in the natural order of proportions, just as it is found in numbers between the Binary and Unity. Now, to give the third term of such a progression, we will make the line AC three feet long, so that it reaches point D; since the Ternary immediately follows the Binary. We will then have between DA and BA the **Triple** ratio; for AD is measured exactly three times by AB, or AD contains AB three times, just as in numbers the Ternary contains Unity three times. And so such a ratio will remain mediated and divided into two parts by AC: that is, into one Double ratio (CA and BA) and one **Sesquialtera** <note>A 3:2 ratio, or a Perfect Fifth.</note> (DA and CA), in arithmetic proportionality, just as between the...

[Image: A horizontal line labeled with points A, C, D, and B from left to right. Above point A is the number 6, above point C is 3, and above point D is 2. Arcs above the line indicate proportions: "Dupla" between A and C; "Sesquialtera" between C and D; and "Tripla" spanning from A to D.]

**Arithmetic progression** are units multiplied; so those of the **Harmonic** are the number of parts counted in the **Sounding Body** <note>original: "Corpo sonoro"</note>, which arise from its division. This is because in the former, one considers the multiplication of Unity contained in this order: 3, 2, 1; and in the latter, one considers the multiplication of the parts in the divided subject, contained between these terms: 6, 3, 2. For if we consider the Whole divided into parts, we will find that the line CD is the smallest part of the line AB, and measures AB six whole times, CB three times, and DB twice. Now it can be seen that between the larger terms of the harmonic progression are contained the larger proportions and the **low sounds** <note>original: "suoni gravi"</note>; and between the smaller terms, the smaller proportions and the **high sounds** <note>original: "suoni acuti"</note>. This is because these latter are produced by strings of lesser extent, and the former by those of greater extent. Thus we can also see that just as in Arithmetic (granted it could be done in the manner shown) one would proceed from high to low by multiplying the string; so in the harmonic, by the contrary, one goes from low to high by diminishing it. In arithmetic progression or proportionality, the intervals of smaller proportion would have their place in the low range, contrary to the nature of harmony, whose proper character is to have low sounds of larger interval than the high ones, and these latter, by contrast, of smaller interval. But because all those proportions found in the arithmetic progression, following the natural order of proportions, are also found in the harmonic progression in that same order, we can see in what way one should take the meaning of the words I spoke in Chapter 15: namely, that within the parts of the **Senario** <term>The number six; Zarlino believed the first six integers contained the "forms" of all perfect musical consonances.</term> are contained all the **Forms** of the simple musical consonances possible to be produced. And one sees how those consonances called "Perfect" by practitioners are naturally placed within it in harmonic division. For when they are arranged on the sounding body, these terms—60, 30, 20, 15, 12, 10—which are the ratios of its parts, would be seen to be interspersed in that...

Part One

...the same manner that they are seen mediated in the parts of this **Senario** <note>The *Senario* refers to the first six natural numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), which Zarlino believed contained the ratios for all perfect musical consonances.</note>; even if they were ordered in a different way. Similarly, one can understand in what sense the words of the most learned **Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples** <note>original: "Giacopo Fabro Stapulense," a 15th-century French humanist who wrote *Musica Libris Demonstrata Quatuor*.</note>, placed in the 34th [proposition] of the 3rd book of his *Music*, should be understood, and how great the necessity of **harmonic proportionality** is; and in what way—being in agreement with **Arithmetic** regarding the quantity of proportions—it is then in disagreement regarding the method of proceeding and their placement. But this should not cause wonder, considering that every effect naturally follows the property and nature of its cause. And because both of these proportionalities use numbers, which are by nature communicating with each other—or at least have a common measure between them, which is (when no other number is present) **Unity** <note>In Renaissance mathematics, "Unity" (the number 1) was considered the source or "atom" of all numbers rather than a number itself.</note>—therefore every ratio between them is **rational**.

But **Geometry**, whose subject (absolutely speaking) is **Continuous Quantity** <note>Continuous quantity refers to things like lines or shapes that can be divided infinitely, whereas numbers are "discrete quantity."</note>, divisible potentially into infinite parts, considers not only rational ratios, but irrational ones as well, as I have said elsewhere. For it is an easy thing for the Geometer, by virtue of his principles, to divide any line into three parts that are geometrically proportionate to each other; or it will be easy for him to place one or more middle lines between two extremes that are proportionate with the first, as we shall show in the Second Part. But the **Arithmetician** or the **Musician** can never find a middle term for every proposed proportion that divides it into two equal parts; for between the terms of their proportionalities, no middle number falls that can divide it according to the purpose. And although the **Quadruple** <note>A 4:1 ratio, representing a double octave.</note> is sometimes seen divided by the Musician into two equal parts—that is, into two **Duplas** <note>2:1 ratios, or octaves.</note>—such a division is not simply made by the Musician as a Musician, but he usurps such a division as a **Geometer**.

### That Number is not the proximate and intrinsic cause of Musical Proportions, nor of Consonances. Chapter 41.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a scholar seated at a desk or lectern with an open book, surrounded by stylized floral ornamentation.</image-desc>
**ALTHOUGH** I have said above that **Sounds** are the matter of consonances, and **Numbers** and proportions are their form, one must not believe because of this that Number is the proximate <note>The most immediate or direct cause.</note> and intrinsic cause of musical proportions, nor even of consonances; rather, it is the remote and extrinsic cause, as we shall see. Whence it should be noted that, since the proper end of the Musician (as the Philosophers and especially **Eustratius** <note>Eustratius of Nicea, a commentator on Aristotle's Ethics.</note> hold) is to sing with modulation, or to play every instrument with **harmony** according to the precepts given in Music—likewise to be useful and to delight, just as is the end of the Poet—having regard for such a thing as that which naturally pushes him to work, he first takes the instrument in which the matter is prepared, namely the **strings**. Then, to achieve the desired end, by introducing into them the **form** of the consonances, he reduces them to a certain quality and a certain temperament, placing a proportioned distance between them, and stretching them so that, when struck by him, they then render perfect concord and excellent harmony.

And although four things concur here, just as they concur in every other operation—namely the **End** of the action, which is always regarded, and that is Playing with harmony, or being useful and delighting, which is called the **final cause**; the **Agent**, that is the Musician, who is named the **efficient cause**; the **Matter**, which is the strings, and is called the **material cause**; and the **Form**, that is the proportion, which is called the **formal cause**—nevertheless, these last two are **intrinsic causes** of the thing, and the Agent and the End are **extrinsic causes**. This is because the latter do not belong to its nature or its being, while the former are essential parts of it; for every corruptible thing is composed of matter and form. And **Matter** is said to be that from which the thing is made and remains in it, just as the sounds from which the Consonance is made; and **Form** is that species, or likeness, or let us say example, which the thing retains in itself, by which it is called such; just as proportion is in the Consonance. And this is called an intrinsic cause, to distinguish it from the extrinsic, which is (so to speak) the Model or Example, in whose likeness something is made; such as that of the Consonance, which is the proportion of number to number. Nevertheless, it must be noted that of these causes, some are called **Primary** and some **Secondary**; and such an order of first and second can be understood in two ways: first, according to a certain order of numbers, in which one thing is first and remote, and the other second and proximate; secondly, it can be understood according to the order comprised by reason in a single cause, which is placed between the **Universal** and the **Particular**. For naturally the Universal is first, and then the Particular. In the first way, we say that cause is...

<meta>This page continues Zarlino's philosophical investigation into the nature of musical intervals. Having previously discussed the mathematical properties of the "Senario" and the distinction between continuous and discrete quantity, he now applies Aristotelian logic to distinguish between the "Number" (the abstract mathematical model) and the "Proportion" (the formal cause of sound). He then transitions into a practical chapter on reducing musical ratios to their simplest forms.</meta>

Part [One]

*...to be first, which gives virtue and power to the second to act; just as it is said regarding the **efficient cause** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the agent or "efficient cause" is that which initiates change or generation.</note>, that the Sun is the first cause (though a remote one) of generation; the animal is then the second and proximate cause of such generation, because it gives to the animal the virtue and the power to generate. But in the second way, the **Genus** is the first, and the **Species** is the second. Wherefore I say that the first and universal cause of Health is the artisan, and the second and particular cause is the Physician, or rather a specific Physician. It is indeed true that the first and second causes of the first way are different from the first and second of the second way: for in the second way they are not actually distinguished from one another; neither the more universal from the less universal, nor the latter from the singular; rather, they are distinct only in the intellect. But in the first way they are distinct, since one is contained by the other, and not the reverse. And these two ways (especially regarding the second) are found in all types of causes: for in the **material cause**, metal is the first cause of the knife, and iron the second; just as in the **formal cause** (coming to an appropriate example for our purpose), the first cause of the **Diapason Consonance** <note>The *Diapason* is the musical interval of an Octave, characterized by the 2:1 ratio.</note> is number—that is, 2 and 1—and the second is the **Double Proportion** <note>original: "proportione Dupla," the ratio of 2:1.</note>, and so on for the others in order.*

*The Proportion, therefore, is the formal, intrinsic, and proximate cause of consonances, and Number is the universal, extrinsic, and remote cause; it is like the model of the Proportion, by which the **sounding bodies** <note>original: "corpi sonori," referring to physical objects that produce sound, such as strings or pipes.</note> must be regulated and proportioned so that they formally render the consonances. And **the Philosopher** <note>A standard Renaissance reference to Aristotle.</note> hinted at this while defining what Consonance was, saying: **It is a ratio of numbers in the high and the low** <note>original: "ragione di numeri nell'acuto, & nel graue."</note>; meaning the ratio according to which the said sounding bodies are regulated. Thus he did not say that it was "number" absolutely, but a "ratio of numbers"; which can be seen more expressly in musical proportions contained within the aforementioned bodies. For one does not find in them any species or form of number: since if we take their extremes, measuring them by number, after such a measurement is made, these bodies remain in their first integrity and continuity as they were before; nor is any number formally found in them that constitutes any proportion. For even if we take a part of a string in place of a unit, and by repeating it we come to know its quantity and its proportion according to determined numbers—and consequently the proportion of the sounds produced by the strings, that is, from the whole and the parts—we cannot say anything except that such numbers are that Model and that Form of the sounds, which are the **exemplary cause** and extrinsic measure of those sounding bodies that contain musical proportions; which, without their help, could only with difficulty be found in **continuous quantities** <note>Continuous quantities are physical dimensions like lengths of string that can be divided infinitely, as opposed to discrete numbers.</note>. Number, then, being the sole cause of making the proportions of consonances (and any other musical interval) known and artificially discovered, is necessary in Music; in so much as through it one may more expeditiously speculate upon the differences of sounds—according to the high and the low and their properties—and with more certainty than one would by measuring sounding bodies with Compasses or other measures. This is done after having first learned through manifest experience how they are measured according to their length with proportion; and when struck together, they move the hearing according to the high and the low, no differently than how they are considered in pure numbers according to reason. But to conclude, I say that just as number cannot in any way be the intrinsic and proximate cause of such proportions, so it cannot be the intrinsic and proximate cause of consonances, as I have declared.*

## On the finding of the Roots of proportions. Chap. 42.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'R' within a rectangular border, containing a landscape scene with trees and a building.</image-desc>

Returning now, according to the order begun, to the fifth and final operation called the *Finding of the Roots*, I say that such an operation is nothing other than reducing proportions to their first **radical terms** when they are found outside of them. For proportions that are contained between non-radical terms—that is, between **composite numbers** <note>original: "Tralorocomposti," referring to numbers that share a common factor and can therefore be reduced.</note>—besides being more difficult to recognize, also make their operations difficult. Therefore, so that one may have a easier knowledge of them and use them more easily, I will now provide the method of reducing them to radical terms—that is, to **coprime numbers** <note>original: "Contraseprimi," numbers that have no common divisor other than 1, representing the ratio in its simplest form.</note>, which are the smallest numbers by which they can be contained, as I have said elsewhere. And because not only proportions contained between two terms, but also every order of multiple multiplied proportions can be contained by composite numbers, I will first show in what way those contained between only two terms can be reduced to their radical terms, and afterward I will show how the others can be reduced. Starting then from the

--- Page 74 ---
<meta>This page continues Zarlino's discussion on the mathematical foundations of music. Having established the philosophical distinction between formal and material causes in the previous section, he now provides practical instructions for simplifying musical ratios—what he calls finding the "root" of a proportion. This is essential for determining the simplest integer representation of musical intervals.</meta>

First [Part]

...first we shall maintain this order: being proposed any proportion we wish, contained between numbers that are **composite among themselves** <term>Numbers that share a common divisor other than one</term>, we will seek to find a larger number which commonly measures the terms of the proposed proportion; by which, dividing these terms, the products will be the roots, or **radical terms** <note>The "radical terms" are the smallest whole numbers that express a specific ratio (e.g., 3:2 for a perfect fifth).</note> of such a proportion. Wishing then to find such a number, we will first divide the greater term of the proportion by the lesser, and then this [the lesser] by that number which remains after such division. And if a number should again remain, we will divide the first remaining number by the second; and this by the third; and so on, step by step, until a number is found that divides the other exactly, without anything remaining; and this will be the number sought: by which, then dividing each term of the proposed proportion, the products will be the minimum numbers and radical terms of the proportion. Let us suppose then that we wish to find the **Root** of the proportion contained between these terms, or numbers: 45 and 40, which are **composite among themselves**; we will first divide 45 by 40, and it will be 1, with 5 remaining. Then, leaving aside the unit [1], as it serves little to our purpose in this as well as in other divisions, we will take the 5, which will divide 40 exactly, without anything remaining; and this will be the greater number sought, which will measure both of the two proposed terms. Wherefore, dividing 45 by 5, there will come 9; and dividing 40, we will have 8. Which numbers, without doubt, are **relatively prime** <term>Numbers that have no common divisor other than one</term>, and the minimum terms, or the **Root** of the proposed proportion, which was the **Sesquioctave** <note>original: "Sesquiottaua." The 9:8 ratio, which corresponds to a whole tone in music.</note>.

## How one can find the Root of several proportions multiplied together. Chapter 43.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial M with floral patterns</image-desc>
**BUT** wishing to find the Root of an order of several continued terms, such as those that arise from the multiplication of several proportions placed together; or those that come from **harmonic proportionality**, which are without doubt terms or numbers **composite among themselves**; we shall proceed in this manner. We will first find, by the Third [Proposition] of the Seventh [Book] of **Euclid** <note>Euclid's *Elements*, Book VII, Proposition 3: "Given three numbers not prime to one another, to find their greatest common measure."</note>, a greater number that commonly divides or measures each of the numbers contained in such an order; by which we will then divide each of them; and the products that come from such division will be the Root of that order. Let there be, then, the four <note>Though the text says "four," the list contains five numbers: 360, 240, 180, 144, 120.</note> following terms or numbers **composite among themselves**, namely 360, 240, 180, 144, 120, produced by the multiplication performed in Chapter 31 or 32; which we wish to reduce into an order of **relatively prime** numbers, that is, to their root. I say that it is necessary first to find, in the manner shown in the preceding chapter, a greater number that commonly measures the two greatest terms of those proposed, which are 360 and 240; and such a number will be 120, because it divides or measures 360 three times, and 240 two times. We will then see if it can measure 180; but because it cannot measure it, it is necessary to find another similar number which commonly divides or measures 180 and 120, operating according to the rule given, which will be 60. And this, by the corollary of the Second [Proposition] of the Seventh [Book] of Euclid, will commonly measure the three greatest of the proposed terms, and also 120; for it measures 360 six times, 240 four times, 180 three times, and 120 two times. It is true, however, that it cannot measure 144; wherefore it will be necessary to find another greater number that measures it together with the others: wherefore, having found it according to the method shown, we will have 12, which will not only measure 144, but the others as well, as can clearly be seen. And because such a number measures even the smallest of those proposed, namely 120; therefore I say, that 12 is the greater number sought, which commonly measures each of the five proposed terms or numbers: for if we divide each of these numbers by 12, which was the last greater number found, there will come 30, 20, 15, 12, 10. And among these terms, I say, is the Root of the proposed order: because without doubt they are **relatively prime** numbers; as can be examined in its example. Wherefore, observing such a rule, one can have the radical terms not only of any order containing four, five, and six proportions, but even more, even if one proceeded (so to speak) to infinity.

## On the Proof of each of the shown operations. Chapter 44.

*BECAUSE man in his operations can easily err, especially in the handling of numbers, sometimes inadvertently placing one number in the place of another; therefore, so as not to leave behind anything that might be useful to students, I have wanted to add the method by which we may know if any error is found in the operations, so that once found, we may correct it. Thus, beginning with the first, which was **Multiplication**, I say: that when we have multiplied many proportions together, the terms produced by such multiplication will be (as has been said elsewhere) outside their **radical terms** <note>The "radical terms" are the smallest whole numbers that express a specific ratio, like 3:2 for a perfect fifth.</note>; so that wishing to know if the said proportions are contained in such terms without error, we will first take two terms, between which we imagine ourselves to have placed some proportion, and we will divide them by their radical terms—that is, the greater by the greater, and the lesser by the lesser; and if the results of such division are equal, such proportion will be contained in its terms without any error; and if it were otherwise, the opposite would be true. Wishing then to know if the **Sesquialtera** proportion <term>A ratio of 3:2, representing the musical interval of a perfect fifth</term>, placed between these numbers 360 and 240, is correctly contained; we will take its radical terms 3 and 2, by which we will divide 360 and 240 in this manner: 360 by 3 and 240 by 2. From each part will come 120; whereby such equality demonstrates that the said proportion is contained between the proposed numbers, even though they are not radical. But when one of the products comes out larger than the other, it would be a manifest sign that an error had been committed in such multiplication. We can also see the same thing by multiplying the greater of the proposed products by the lesser radical term of the proportion, and the lesser by the greater; that is, 360 by 2 and 240 by 3: for then both products would come out equal, namely 720; which would show us that such proportion is contained between the proposed products without error.*

*And although the **Addition** of proportions can be the proof of **Multiplication**, and Multiplication that of Addition, we still cannot see if there is any error in their middle terms except in the shown manner. But truly, the true proof of Addition is **Subtraction**: for if we subtract the added proportions one by one from the product of the Addition, without any fail we can know such a sum was made without error when at the last we arrive at **Equality** <note>A ratio of 1:1, where the two numbers are the same.</note>. If we therefore take the product of the sum placed in chapter 33, which is the **Triple proportion** <term>A ratio of 3:1</term>, and subtract the added proportions one by one, beginning from the largest, which was the **Sesquialtera** (3:2), the **Double** (2:1) will remain; from which subtracting the **Sesquiterza** (4:3), the Sesquialtera (3:2) will remain. Then, taking from this the **Sesquiquarta** (5:4), the **Sesquiquinta** (6:5) will remain, from which the last proportion being taken (which was likewise the Sesquiquinta), one will undoubtedly arrive at Equality. This will let us know that no error is found in such a sum; but it certainly would be if at the end there remained a larger proportion to be taken from a smaller one, or vice-versa. The proof of Subtraction (as I have said elsewhere) is Addition; and because I have reasoned sufficiently there of such things, it is not necessary that I repeat anything here. But in **Division**, when in the equal division of proportions, the terms contained in the **Geometric proportionality** are not found placed in the manner I have shown above, then it would be a manifest sign of error; just as there would also be error in the **Arithmetic** and in the **Harmonic** <note>These refer to the three types of mathematical means used to divide musical intervals.</note>, when their terms were placed otherwise than in the declared manner; and if the Proportions, or any continued order of proportions, were outside their radical terms when they were not found placed in **Coprime** numbers.*

*Now it seems to me that all I have said above is sufficient to show the principles of Music, which if we do not know, we can never have good knowledge of the following things, nor ever reach a perfect end. Wherefore everyone who desires to acquire this science must strive with all his power to possess them perfectly, so that he may acquire worthy praise and honorable fruit from his labors.*

### ->THE END OF THE FIRST PART.<-

# THE SECOND PART
## Of the Harmonic Institutions
### BY MASTER GIOSEFFO ZARLINO
### OF CHIOGGIA.

---

### How Music was in the beginning simple, crude, and poor in consonances. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'P' featuring two figures (possibly cherubs or mythological beings) in a landscape or architectural setting.</image-desc>
SINCE in the First Part we have sufficiently reasoned about Numbers and Proportions, it is reasonable that we now speak in detail—as the subject requires—about those things which Music considers in general. These include Sounds (or Pitched Voices), Intervals, the Genera <note>The "Genera" refer to the three types of tetrachord scales in ancient Greek music: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note>, the Orders of Sounds, the Modes, Mutations, and Modulations. But before we come to such a discussion, I will show in what way Music was simple in the beginning and how it was used by the ancients. Then, having seen how Sounds and Voices are born and having classified them, I will come to my main purpose. I say, therefore, that although Music in our times has reached such a degree and perfection of harmony regarding the use of all those consonances <term>Intervals that sound pleasing and stable when played together</term> that can be found—some of which were not even considered by the ancients, and to which it seems almost nothing new can be added—nevertheless, there is no doubt that in the beginning (as happened with the other sciences) it was not only simple and crude, but also very poor in consonances. That this is very true is shown by what Apuleius narrates of it, saying: that in the beginning only the Pipe <note>original: "Piffero"</note> was used, not with holes like those made in our time, but without them, in the likeness of a Trumpet. Nor were so many types of concerts made with varied instruments and varied modes; rather, the ancients refreshed their spirits and gave each other pleasure and solace with the aforementioned Pipe alone, without any variety of sound. And they used such a Pipe in their public spectacles and in their Choirs when they recited Tragedies or Comedies, as Horace declares, speaking in this manner:

> The pipe—not as now, bound with brass and a rival to the trumpet, but slender and simple with few holes—was useful to accompany and assist the choruses;
<note>original Latin: "Tibia non, vt nunc, oricalcho vincta, tubæque Æmula, sed tenuis, simplexque foramine pauco Adspirare, & adesse choris erat vtilis;" from Horace's *Ars Poetica*.</note>

To which later Hyagnis the Phrygian, a man learned in Music in those times (who was the father and teacher of Marsyas), added the holes and began to play it with varied sounds. He was the first who made two Pipes sound with a single breath, and who played such an instrument with the right and left hand; that is, he mixed the low sound with the high using right-hand holes and left-hand holes. The ancients also used in the beginning the Cithara or the Lyre with only three or four strings, of which Mercury was the inventor (as Boethius maintains). These were arranged in such a way that the first with the second, and the third with the fourth, contained a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>; and the first with the third, and the second with the fourth, contained a Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>; and again, the second with the third contained a Tone <note>A whole step.</note>, and the first with the fourth an Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. And this order was kept until the time of Orpheus, after which it was increased in various instruments. First, Chorebus of Lydia added the fifth string; then the aforementioned Hyagnis added the sixth; but the seventh was added by Terpander of Lesbos. And this number of strings truly (as Clement of Alexandria says) was contained in the ancient Lyre or Cithara. Later, the eighth was added by Lycaon of Samos; although Pliny attributes the invention of this string to Simonides, and the ninth to Timotheus. Boethius, however, claims that this string was added by Prophrastus of Periota, the tenth by Estiachus of Colophon, and the eleventh by the same Timotheus. But however it may be, Suidas attributes the addition of the Tenth and the Elev-

Part [Header]

...tenth string by Timotheus the Lyricist. And it is certain that many others added so many to them that they grew to the number of fifteen. They then added the sixteenth string to these, and went no further, being content with that number; and they placed them in the order that we will show further on, dividing them by Tones and Semitones into five Tetrachords <note>A group of four notes spanning a specific musical interval, used as the building block of ancient Greek scales</note>: observing the ratios of the Pythagorean proportions, found in the hammers by Pythagoras, in the manner that I showed in the First Part; which contained those same ratios that were found among the strings of the aforementioned Cithara, or Lyre found by Mercury; and which are seen in the following example:

| String Name | Weight / Ratio | Greek Note Name | Musical Interval |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **First string** | 12 | Parhipate hipaton | **Diapason** (Octave, 12:6) |
| **Second string** | 9 | Parhipate meson | **Diapente** (Fifth, 12:8 & 9:6) |
| **Third string** | 8 | Lichanos meson | **Diatessaron** (Fourth, 12:9 & 8:6) |
| **Fourth string** | 6 | Trite diezeugmenon | **Tone** (Whole Step, 9:8) |

Because the largest hammer (as they say) weighed twelve pounds, the next weighed nine pounds, and the third eight pounds: but the fourth and smallest weighed six pounds; from which numbers Pythagoras derived the ratios of the musical consonances <term>Intervals that sound pleasing and stable when played together</term>, which among the ancients were five, as Macrobius narrates; and they arise from five numbers, the first of which they called **Epitrito** <note>original: "Epitrito"; the 4:3 ratio</note>, the second **Hemiolio** <note>original: "Hemiolio"; the 3:2 ratio</note>, the third **Double**, the fourth **Triple**, and the fifth **Quadruple**, with one dissonant interval, which they estimated to be the principle of every consonance, and they called it **Epogdoo** <note>original: "Epogdoo"; the 9:8 ratio, or a Whole Tone</note>. In such a way that the **Diatessaron** <note>the interval of a Fourth</note> was contained by the *Epitrito*, the **Diapente** <note>the interval of a Fifth</note> by the *Hemiolio*, the **Diapason** <note>the interval of an Octave</note> by the *Double*, the **Diapason-Diapente** <note>An octave plus a fifth</note> by the *Triple*, the **Double Diapason** <note>Two octaves</note> by the *Quadruple*, and the **Sesquioctave Tone** <term>A whole tone defined by the 9:8 ratio</term> by the *Epogdoo*. 

To these consonances Ptolemy added the **Diapason-Diatessaron** <note>An octave plus a fourth</note>, contained by the *Double Superbipartient Third* proportion between 8 and 3; as can be seen in his *Harmonics*; which consonance is also mentioned by Vitruvius in chapter 4 of the Fifth book of *Architecture*. And truly the ancients did not know other consonances than those mentioned above; all of which are called **Perfect** by modern Musicians: and they did not consider as consonant those intervals that moderns call **Imperfect Consonances**; namely the **Ditone** <note>A major third</note>, the **Semiditone** <note>A minor third</note>, and the two **Hexachords** <note>Six-note spans</note>; namely the major and the minor; as Vitruvius clearly demonstrates in the named place, saying: that on the Third, Sixth, and Seventh strings the consonances cannot be made; and he says this with respect to the lowest string of every Octave: Which can also be seen in every other author, both Greek and Latin. 

And from this we can understand the imperfection that was found in ancient Harmonies, and how poor the ancients were in consonances and concerts. And even if someone, moved by the authority of the ancients (which is truly great) rather than by reason, wished to say that beyond the named perfect consonances, no other consonance can be found; I would not hesitate to affirm such an opinion to be false: because it contradicts the senses, from which all our knowledge originates: Since no one of sound mind will deny that beyond the aforementioned perfect consonances, the imperfect ones are also found, which are as delightful, charming, resonant, sweet, and harmonious as can be said to those who have not corrupted their sense of hearing; and they are so much in use, that not only the skilled singers and players of any kind of instruments use them in their harmonies; but even those who, without having science, sing and play by practice alone.

# For what reason the ancients in their Harmonies did not use imperfect consonances, and why Pythagoras forbade passing beyond the Quadruple. Chapter 2.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' at the start of the first paragraph, featuring foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

*NOR should we wonder that the ancients did not accept such consonances <note>Referring to "imperfect" consonances like thirds and sixths, which were not considered pleasing intervals in the strict Pythagorean system</note>; for they placed the greatest faith in the doctrine of Pythagoras. He, being a most diligent investigator of the profound secrets of Nature, did not wish to accept them among the consonances because he was a lover of simple and pure things. He delighted in all things as long as their matter did not depart from simplicity; in that simplicity, he investigated secret things—namely, their causes. He held the opinion that when things are found to be simple, there is in them both firmness and stability; but when they are mixed and diverse, there is inconstancy and variety. And because he estimated that no firm reason could be had for these [mixed things], he rejected them without proceeding further. Therefore, only those consonances pleased him which agreed with one another by reason of numbers that were simple and possessed their purest nature. These are those that arise from the Multiple and Superparticular genres <term>Mathematical classifications of ratios: Multiples (like 2:1, 3:1) and Superparticulars (where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, like 3:2, 4:3)</term>; and they are the five shown previously, contained within the number four (the Quaternary). He rejected those comprised of numbers found beyond the Quaternary <note>The number four, or the Tetractys, was sacred to Pythagoreans as the source of all harmony</note>, which enter into other genres of proportion. From these proportions arose their Ditone, the Trihemitone (or Semiditone), and other similar intervals, as we shall see <note>The Ditone is a Major Third and the Semiditone is a Minor Third; in the Pythagorean tuning of the time, their mathematical ratios were considered too complex to be "consonant"</note>. Nor did he place among the consonances the Ditone and the Semiditone contained in the Superparticular genre, which I showed in the first part. For he knew very well (as I believe) their nature, and saw that from the mixture of such imperfect consonances with perfect ones, the two Hexachords <term>Six-note scales</term> could be born—namely the major and the minor—which are contained in the Superpartient genre, as their forms manifest to us. He thus approved only those consonances as the most simple and noble which have their forms among the parts of the number four: because from them no sound can be born that is not consonant. And perhaps the Pythagoreans held this number in the highest veneration for no other reason than that they saw such simplicity of harmony arose from it; hence they held the opinion that it belonged to the perfection of the Soul. They held this as so true that, wishing to have undisputed faith granted to what they affirmed, they would say (as Macrobius says): "I swear to you by him who gives to our soul the number four." The Divine Philosopher <note>Pythagoras</note> therefore forbade passing beyond the Quadruple <term>A ratio of 4:1, representing a double octave</term>; because beyond it (as the Platonic Philosopher Marsilio Ficino says in the Compendium of Plato's Timaeus) he heard no harmony. This is because, proceeding further, the Quintuple arises between 5 and 4, and the Superbipartient between 5 and 3, which generates dissonance. To be sure, if Ficino's words were taken literally, they would be misunderstood; for the Quintuple is not found between 5 and 4, but rather between 5 and 1. Therefore, I judge that either this text is incorrect and that Unity <note>the number 1</note> should be put in place of 4, or that such words are to be understood in this way: that proceeding beyond the Quadruple, by adding the number five (the Quinary) to the number four—that is, adding the Sesquiquarta <note>The ratio 5:4, a Major Third</note> to the Quadruple proportion in this form: 5. 4. 3. 2. 1.—the Quintuple proportion is born between 5 and 1, and similarly the Superbipartient-third between 5 and 3. This departs from the simplicity of numbers and is contained in the third genre of proportion called Superpartient <term>A complex ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number once, plus more than one part of it remaining (e.g., 5:3)</term>. This genre, Pythagoras said, was not fit for the generation of musical consonances, as is seen in the example below. For this reason, then, and no other, I believe Pythagoras forbade overstepping the Quadruple. To be sure, some others say the Philosopher wished that one should not overstep the Quadruple in songs—meaning the number of fifteen strings contained within the Disdiapason <term>A double octave range</term>. For he judged that every excellent voice (Nature having set a limit to all things) could naturally ascend from the low to the high or descend through fifteen notes without discomfort; and that whenever one passed further, whether into the low or the high, such voices were no longer natural but forced, bringing annoyance to the listeners. But of these two reasons, the first (in my judgment) is better and more to the point. It is no wonder, then, that the ancients did not receive such consonances, since they were forbidden by Pythagorean laws from overstepping the Quadruple.*

## Question concerning the discovery of Pythagoras. Chapter 3.

NOW, regarding the aforementioned discovery of Pythagoras, a doubt arises: in what way could harmony emerge from those two hammers that contained the **Sesquioctave** <term>The ratio of 9:8, which defines the distance of a whole tone</term> proportion, which is the form of the **Tone**, which is without any doubt a dissonant interval? To this one can respond and say it is reasonable that the blacksmiths of those times did not strike with their hammers all at once while beating the iron, but rather one after the other, as we see and hear done today. Thus, it is credible that when the Philosopher <note>Referring to Pythagoras</note> passed by the blacksmiths' shop by chance, the first thing that presented itself to his senses was a certain harmonic order of sound, and that it was very pleasing to him; by this, he was moved to want to investigate the reason for harmonic sounds. 

But because the hammers were struck one after the other, the Tone could not offend the hearing as it would have offended if they had all struck at once; for **Consonance** and **Dissonance** are heard between two sounds that strike the hearing at the same time. Therefore, it cannot be said that Pythagoras in that act heard anything dissonant in a way that could offend him—especially having first removed the fifth hammer, as Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), the Roman statesman and philosopher whose writings on music were the standard textbooks for over a thousand years</note> says, because it did not accord with the others.

And that this is true, Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer; original: "Macrobio"</note> clearly demonstrates when he says that as Pythagoras was passing by a public road by chance, certain sounds reached his ears that responded to each other with a certain order; these arose from the hammers of some blacksmiths who were beating a red-hot iron. He says they were sounds that "responded with a certain order," and he does not say they were "consonant sounds." By this, we can see that such an interval could not cause him any annoyance, just as we ourselves can hear in any of our melodies <note>original: "modulatione"</note>; the sense is not offended by the progression of such an interval, nor by any other, provided it arises from resonant and harmonic numbers. 

Having then found that this proceeded from the quantity of the weight of each hammer, the Philosopher began from the weights found to investigate musical proportions and harmonic numbers, testing one sound against the other with their weights. He found their logic in the aforementioned numbers and recognized those proportions that gave consonances and those that made dissonances. Hence Boethius, in Chapter 10 of Book 1 of his *Music*, wanting to show in practice those proportions that were the true forms of consonances, speaking of each of them, adds one of these words: *Consonancy* <note>original: "Consonantia"</note> or *Concordance* <note>original: "Concinnentia"</note>. But when he comes to the **Sesquioctave**, without adding anything to it, he says only that the **Tone** resonated—intending to imply that such a proportion was not placed by the Philosopher among those that create Consonance.

### Second Part: Of Ancient Music. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'M' featuring a leafy, scroll-work pattern inside a square frame.</image-desc>

BUT IF ancient Music (as I have shown above) possessed such imperfection, it does not seem credible that Musicians could produce so many various effects in human souls, as are recounted in histories. For one reads that at times they moved the soul to anger, and at other times they drew it back from anger to gentleness; now they induced weeping, now laughter, or other similar passions. And it seems all the less credible because, music being today reduced to such perfection that one can hardly hope for better, we do not see it produce any of the aforementioned effects; thus one might rather say that modern music, and not the ancient, is imperfect. Because such a thing could generate no small doubt in the minds of readers, before going any further, it seemed appropriate to me to reason through certain things regarding this matter. First, I will demonstrate in what manner Music was put to use by the ancients; then, what subjects they recited in their songs, and who the ancient Musicians were. Beyond this, I will discuss what was powerful enough to induce man into diverse passions, and in what way Melodies could move the soul and instill in it various characters; and lastly, by what Genre of song such effects were operated.

Beginning then with the first point, I say that although Music in ancient times performed many marvelous things, as one reads, and although it is said that today it no longer performs any of the things named, anyone who wishes to examine everything minutely will find that Music even at present is not deprived of making such effects; and one might perhaps see some effects of no small importance with great wonder. It is quite true that modern practice is so varied and far from ancient practice that it would be almost impossible to believe it if many worthy and honored writers, who lived long before our age, had not made mention of such things. For the Musicians of those times did not use Music with so many varied types of instruments (leaving aside those they used in Comedies and in their armies), nor were their songs composed of so many parts; nor did they make their concerts with as many voices as we do now. Instead, they practiced it in such a way that, to the sound of a single instrument—that is, a Pipe <note>original: "Piffero"</note>, or a Cithara, or a Lyre—the Musician simply accompanied his voice, and in this way provided pleasing pleasure to himself and his listeners. In this manner Homer introduces Achilles, Phemius, and Demodocus singing; similarly Virgil introduces Iopas, Horace introduces Tigellius, Silius Italicus introduces Teuthras, and Suetonius writes that Nero did the same.

The same was done by those whom the Greeks call Rhapsodes, who were reciters, interpreters, and singers of the verses of Poets; among whom was Ion, as Plato demonstrates in his work on *Poetic Fury* <note>Referring to the dialogue *Ion*</note>. He interpreted the verses of Homer to the sound of the Lyre, and was so devoted to him and had made him so familiar that he did not wish to explain any poet other than him. When there were two who sang, they did not sing together and at the same time, as is done today; but one after the other. They named such a way of singing **Alternating Song** <term>original: "Cantare a vicenda"; a style of singing where performers trade verses back and forth</term>, in the way that the shepherds Daphnis and Menalcas sang in Theocritus, and Damoetas and Menalcas in Virgil.

The lyric Poets also used to sing their poems and compositions with various types of Verse to the sound of the Lyre or the Cithara in their musical contests. They did this gathered together in a circle to the number of fifty during some of their festivals; and such a gathering was named a **Chorus** <term>original: "Choro"; here referring specifically to the dithyrambic chorus of ancient Greece</term>. They sang the praises of the Gods and of those who had been victorious in the Olympic games; and they received an Ox as a prize for their singing. The country folk also used to offer their vows to the Gods for the fruits of the earth in this way: gathered in a chorus near an altar upon which was the sacrificial victim, sometimes processing and sometimes turning in a circle, they sang certain types of verses to Bacchus to the sound of the Pipe. And such a Pipe did not resemble those used now; for in those times they were made from the leg bones of Cranes. Thus, these instruments were called **Tibiae** by the Latins, as that part of any animal is named *tibia* in the Latin tongue. Nor was there any need then for a greater instrument, for the people who gathered in such places were few, and were more dedicated to hardship and labor than to festivals and games. They likewise had the custom of representing their Tragedies and Comedies by singing, and Horace alludes to this, saying:

> If you desire an applauder who waits for the curtain and will stay seated until the singer says: "give your applause."
<note>original Latin: "Si plausoris eges aulaea manentis, & vsque Sessuri, donec cantor, vos plaudite dicat." from Horace's *Ars Poetica*.</note>

And it was the custom (as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> affirms) that the Poets themselves recited the Tragedies and Comedies they had [written]...

I also believe that the Orators spoke to the people to the sound of some instrument, although in my opinion such a custom lasted only a short time. Cicero, in the speech he made in favor of Publius Sestius—which remains imperfect—mentions it; and also at the end of the third book of *The Orator*, speaking of Gaius Gracchus, he demonstrates this, even though it seems somewhat strange to Aulus Gellius. And we should not marvel at this, since the art of Oratory had its beginning (as Strabo holds) from poetry, and the Poets spoke to the people by singing verses to the sound of the <term>Cithara</term> <note>An ancient Greek musical instrument similar to a lyre but with a larger sound box.</note> or Lyre, drawing them to do their will; as Ariosto clearly demonstrates, saying:

The ancients also sang to the sound of the Pipe, reciting various songs composed in verse; and they did this at times when two were together, one of whom knew how to sing and the other how to play, as the Poet hinted when he introduced Menalcas saying these words to the shepherd Mopsus:

> You blow the light reeds, I recite the verses:
> <note>Original Latin: *Tu calamos inflare leueis, ego dicere versus*</note>

Because one was a skilled player of the Pipe, and the other sang excellently. It was also a custom among the ancients to jump and dance while the Musician recited something to the sound of the Lyre, Cithara, or some other instrument; as is seen in Homer’s *Odyssey*, where Demodocus sang to the sound of the Cithara while the Greeks jumped and danced. Similarly Virgil, imitating him in the first book of the *Aeneid*, says that Iopas sang to the sound of the Cithara, and

> The Tyrians redouble their applause, and the Trojans follow;
> <note>Original Latin: *Ingeminant plausu Tyrij, Troesq; sequuntur*</note>

> Some beat the dances with their feet and recite songs.
> <note>Original Latin: *Pars pedibus plaudunt choreas, & carmina dicunt.*</note>

Similarly Horace (although he makes no mention of singing) says:

> Thus the flute-player added movement and luxury to the ancient art.
> <note>Original Latin: *Sic priscæ motumq; & luxuriam addidit arti / Tibicen.*</note>

One could have infinite examples of this, which I now leave aside for the sake of brevity; since the Odes of Pindar give undoubted evidence of it. For they are divided into three parts, of which the first is called <term>strophe</term> <note>Greek: στροφή, meaning "turning."</note>, the second <term>antistrophe</term> <note>Greek: ἀντιστροφή, meaning "counter-turning."</note>, and the third <term>epode</term> <note>Greek: ἐπωδός, meaning "after-song."</note>, and they are included under lyric verses. The ancients sang them to the sound of the Lyre or Cithara and danced or jumped in such a manner that when the dancers turned from the right side toward the left, they sang the first part; and when they went from the left to the right, they sang the second; and they came to rest when they sang the third. This manner of dancing or jumping has lasted until the present day among the Cretans and those who inhabit the island of Cyprus. The ancients, therefore, used Music in the manner we have described, accompanying the voice with a single instrument; and if at times they used several types of instruments, they accompanied the voice with them, just as is still the custom today among barbarian peoples in some parts, and especially in the Levant, as I have many times heard from men worthy of trust. # Second Part

[...the] Trumpet, of which they <note>Likely the Tyrrhenians or Etruscans, based on common Renaissance histories of music.</note> were the inventors, as some claim; the Arcadians invented the Panpipes; the Sicilians certain instruments which they called <term>pyktides: a type of ancient stringed or wind instrument, often associated with mourning or simple folk music</term> <note>original Greek: πύκτιδας</note>; the Cretans the Lyre; the Spartans the Pipe; those of Thrace the Horn; the Egyptians the Timpanum; and the Arabs the Cymbal. The Romans made use of certain types of Pipes <note>The Italian *pifferi* here refers to the Roman *tibia*, a double-piped reed instrument.</note> in their comedies, which they called "Right" and "Left"; from these, the spectators could understand the genre of the comedies that were about to be performed. For when the comedy contained serious and grave matter or subject, one heard the low, grave harmony of the Left pipes; when it was instead playful and festive, the harmony arising from the Right pipes was high-pitched; and if it was mixed, the musical melodies were a tempered blend of both types of harmony. And such melodies were not made by the Poet who had composed the comedy, but by one skilled in the art of Music, as can be seen at the beginning of each of Terence's comedies. These melodies varied in Mode or Tone, whichever we wish to call it; and they played them before they began to perform the comedy, so that the subject matter contained within it (as I have said) could be known beforehand by the spectators.

Nevertheless, in our own times, such types of pipes are still unknown; although Servius, in the ninth book of Virgil's *Aeneid*, commenting on the verse *O truly Phrygian women* <note>original Latin: *O uere Phrygiæ*</note>, shows that there were two kinds, one of which he names Seranian pipes, and the other Phrygian. The first were "Equal"—and so he calls them—because they had their openings equal and identical; the second were "Unequal," because their openings were not the same. Servius then cites the authority of Marcus Varro, wishing to declare which are the Right and Left pipes, saying: that the Right Phrygian pipe has a single hole, while the Left has two, of which one has a high sound and the other a low one. But these words are different from those placed in the first book, chapter two, of *On Agriculture* <note>original Latin: *De Re Rustica*</note>, where he says that one type of pipe played the modes of a single verse in a high voice, and the other in a low voice. Thus, following further down, one can understand from his words that the Left pipe sent out the low sound, and the Right the high sound.

And this can be confirmed by the authority of Pliny, who, speaking of water-reeds, says that they used to be cut at a suitable time around the star Arcturus, up until the time of Antigenidas the piper, when simple music was still used in those days; and once prepared, they began to be good after several years. Even then, it was necessary to use them very often and almost "teach" them to play, because the reeds <note>The vibrating tongues or "lamellae" of the instrument.</note> came to touch one another, which was very useful for portraying character in the theaters. But after variety and the "wantonness" of songs arrived, they began to cut them before the Solstice, and they were good by the third year; this was because they had their reeds more open and more suited to varying the sounds, which they still are today. But at that time, it was the opinion that those which came from the same stalk would harmonize together; and that the part near the root was suited to the Left pipe, and the part near the top to the Right.

Pliny says this, and it seems to me well said: because the parts near the root are necessarily thicker than those toward the top. Thus, every day we see through experience that since their body is larger and wider, it also renders a lower sound; just as the opposite is seen in those that are smaller and more narrow. This is also seen and heard in the instruments called Organs, whose pipes render lower sounds the wider they are, and higher sounds the narrower they are.

But to what has been said, there seems to be a contrary opinion by an uncertain author of a Greek Epigram that begins *the wise man at the kithara* <note>original Greek: τὸν σοφὸν ἐν κιθάρῃ</note>; for he calls the low string the "Right Hypate" <note>original Greek: δεξιτερὴν ὑπάτην</note> and the high string the "Left Nete" <note>original Greek: λαιὴν νήτην</note>. But this matters little: because if the matter is well considered, it fits both ways. The parts of every instrument can be considered and named in two ways: first, in relation to us; second, in relation to the instrument itself. In relation to us, the part of the instrument placed on the right hand is called "Right" and renders high sounds, as is seen in Organs, Monochords, and other similar instruments; and that placed on the left is called "Left" and renders low sounds. But in relation to the instrument, that which is right to us is left to it; and conversely, that which is right to it is left to us—just as one can see in two people wrestling together, that the right side of one is the left of the other, and the left is the right. It is therefore not inconsistent if one names "Right" that part which another calls "Left," as such parts are considered differently according to their various perspectives. In this manner, then, Music was put into use by the ancients; and how different this manner is from modern usage, everyone can always see for themselves; just as they may also see elsewhere how different their harmony was from the modern. But what subjects they recited in their songs, the following chapter will make manifest.

## The subjects that the ancients recited in their songs, and regarding certain musical laws. Chapter 5.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap "L" depicting a seated classical figure, possibly Apollo or a personification of Music, playing a lyre within a circular frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc>
**Ancient musicians** in their songs recited subjects and topics very different from those contained in modern songs. For they recited grave and learned things, elegantly composed in various verses—namely, the praises of the Gods, such as those contained in the *Hymns of Orpheus*; the illustrious deeds of men victorious in the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games, such as those contained in the *Odes of Pindar*. Or they sang wedding songs, similar to those of Catullus. One could also hear funeral arguments, lamentations, love stories, and things belonging to banquets; and to certain songs they added specific prayers, which they called <term>Epilimie: ancient prayers or apotropaic songs intended to ward off pestilence</term>, to drive away the plague. They sang comic and tragic subjects, and other similar things full of severity and gravity, as Galen clearly demonstrates to us, saying: that in ancient times at banquets, it was customary to pass around the <term>Lyre</term> or <term>Cithara</term>, to the sound of which were sung the praises of the Gods, of illustrious men, and other similar things. He laments that in his own time (as is also done by many today), it was instead customary to pass around glasses full of white and red wines. Just as the ancients rejoiced in having passed their time virtuously with Music, so then and at present, many gloried and glory in having eaten and drunk a great deal, recounting the number of glasses they have emptied. Similarly, Cicero says that guests were accustomed to singing at banquets to the sound of the <term>Piffero</term> <note>The Italian *piffero* here refers to the ancient *tibia*, a reed pipe.</note> the praises and virtues of illustrious men, citing the example of **Themistocles**, already commemorated in the First Part. And in the book on famous orators titled *Brutus*, he says these words: "Would to God that those verses could be found, which Cato, many centuries before his age, left written in the book of *Origins*, stating that they had been sung at every banquet, concerning the praises of famous and illustrious men." Such subjects were also sung to the sound of the pipe at their deaths, as Cicero himself affirms in another place. And the mournful songs, following the Greeks, the Latins called <term>Neniae: funeral dirges or ritual laments</term>. Truly, Music was given to us for no other end than this, which Horace manifests in these verses:

> The Muse granted to the strings [the power to tell of] gods and the children of gods,
> And the victorious boxer, and the horse first in the race,
> And the cares of youths, and the freedom of wine.
> <note>original Latin: Musa dedit fidibus diuos, puerosque deorum, / Et pugilem victorem, & equum certamine primum, / Et iuuenum curas, & libera vina referre.</note>

And, as Plato demonstrates in the *Protagoras*, the ancients taught all these subjects to their youth, so that they would have to sing them to the sound of the Lyre or the Cithara. Whence Homer writes of **Achilles**:

-> He sang of the glories of men <note>original Greek: ἄειδε δ’ ἄρα κλέα ἀνδρῶν</note> <-

That is, he sang the praises of men to the sound of the Cithara. And of **Demodocus** he says: that he sang the glorious deeds of men, the contention of Ulysses with Achilles, the fable of Venus and Mars, and the Trojan Horse. **Phemius**, also in the *Odyssey*, excuses himself to Ulysses, saying: that he sang to the Gods and to men. From this, one must think that he sang only grave and severe things, having already sung the mournful and funeral return of the Greeks to their homeland. And although he sang of the adultery of Mars and Venus, he did not do so to praise such wickedness, but to steer the Phaeacians away (as Athenaeus says) from their dishonest lusts and pleasures. In such a manner, Virgil also describes the long-haired **Iopas** with his Cithara:

> He makes the golden lyre resound with what the great Atlas taught. 
> He sings of the wandering moon, and the labors of the sun: 
> Whence the race of men and beasts, whence the rain and fires: 
> Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, and the twin Bears: 
> Why the winter suns hasten so to dip themselves in the Ocean, 
> or what delay hinders the slow nights.
> <note>original Latin: Cithara crinitus Iopas / Personat aurata, docuit quae maximus Atlas. / Hic canit errantem Lunam, Solisque labores... [to the end of the quote]</note>

And likewise **Creteus**, a friend to the Muses,

> Always sang of horses, and the arms of men, and battles.
> <note>original Latin: Semper equos, atq; arma virum, pugnasq; canebat.</note>

**Nero** also, according to Suetonius in the life of this wicked Emperor, sang the fable of Niobe to the sound of the Cithara; and he sang many other tragedies in a mask, such as *Canace in Labor*, *Orestes the Murderer of his Mother*, *Oedipus Made Blind*, and *Hercules Furens*. And Lucian says that the arguments and subjects of songs among the ancients were those things that had happened from the beginning of the world until the times of Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt. These, it seems to me...
