->Second<-

(according to what he tells) that they are almost all those things that Ovid writes in his *Transformations* <note>original: "Trasformazioni," referring to the *Metamorphoses*</note>; and to such songs they danced. They recited all these things under a specific Harmony, with specific Rhythms, Verses, and Percussions <note>In this context, "percussions" refers to the rhythmic beat or measure of the music</note>; even though they were varied in every manner of melody. And so, with such numbers, beats, modes, and concords, and with the human voice, they expressed suitable subjects and good morals. They then named such specific structures **Laws**: for a **Law** in Music is nothing other than a way of singing which contains within itself a determined concord, rhythm, and meter. And they were called thus because it was not permitted for anyone to change or innovate anything within them, neither in the harmonies nor in the rhythms and meters. However, there are some who say they were called Laws because, before civil laws were written down, these laws were sung in verse to the sound of the Lyre or Cithara, so that the people would more easily retain in their memory what they ought to observe.

But be that as it may, these Laws were of three sorts: some were called **Citharistice**, which were sung to the Cithara or Lyre; and some **Tibiarie**, which were sung to the sound of the Pipes <note>The *Tibia* or *Aulos*, a double-reed ancient woodwind instrument</note>. The third sort were called **Common**, and they were sung to the sound of both types of the aforementioned instruments. And although such Laws were many, nevertheless each had acquired its own name, either from the people who used them, from the rhythms and meters, from the musical modes, from their inventors, from those who loved them, or from their subject matter. From the peoples, they were named the **Aeolian** and the **Boeotian**; from the rhythms and meters, the **Orthia** and the **Trochaic**; from the modes, the **Acute** and the **Tetraedian**; from the admirers and inventors, the **Terpandrian** and the **Hieracian**; and from the subjects, the **Pythic Contest** and the **Currule**. These laws (as Plutarch maintains) were published by **Terpander**, who, having first divided the Citharistice, gave names to their parts. The Tibiarie laws had many names, which I will omit to avoid being long-winded; these (according to what is said) were discovered by **Cleon** in imitation of Terpander.

The **Orthian law** belonged to Pallas Athena and contained subjects of war. It was a species of modulation in Music which Aulus Gellius calls the *Orthian verse*; perhaps it was named in such a way from the "outer numbers" <note>irregular or extraordinary meters</note> which are fast and resonant. This is because the Greeks use the term <term>ὄρθios: orthios, meaning shrill or high-pitched</term> for that which we call Resonant; although many interpret it as the Song belonging to a battlefield or an army of men-at-arms. The **Trochaic** was a signal that the ancients gave to soldiers with song or the sound of the Trumpet; and the **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans</note> used in their armies the song of the **Castorian law** to kindle the spirit of the soldiers to take up arms against enemies; and such a law was composed under a rhythm called **Embaterio** <note>A dactylic marching rhythm</note>. The **Currule** acquired its name from the subject it contained—that is, from the story in which it was narrated how Hector, son of King Priam, was dragged by chariots around the walls of Troy. I wanted to provide this brief explanation of these Laws so that it can be seen they were composed of rhythmic verse, perfectly suited to move and generate various passions in the soul.

It will also not be out of place for us to see in what manner the musicians of old recited any of the aforementioned Laws while singing to the sound of the Pipe, so that we can understand how they could recite the others. This example shall be the **Pythic Contest**, of which Horace makes mention, demonstrating the qualities of the musician who had to recite it, saying:

> The flute-player who sings the Pythian songs has abstained from love and wine; he has practiced first and stood in fear of his teacher; <note>original Latin: "Abstinuit Venere, & Vino, qui Pythia cantat Tibicen, didicit prius extimuitque magistrum"</note>

These requirements were known all too well by **Nero** (as one reads in Suetonius), who abstained from eating apples and used vomiting and enemas to purge his chest thoroughly so that he would have a clear and clean voice while performing on stage. The subject of this law was the **Battle of Apollo with the serpent Python**, which gives the name to the fable; and the name of the entire melody was **Delona**, perhaps named because Apollo was born on the island of Delos. This law (as Julius Pollux shows) was divided into five parts: the first they named **Rudiment** or **Exploration**; the second, **Provocation**; the third, **Iambic**; the fourth, **Spondee**; and the fifth and last, **Ovation** or **Dance**. The performance (as I have said) was a representation of the fight between Apollo and the Dragon. In the first part, it was recited how Apollo investigated and contemplated the place to see if it was fit for battle. In the second, it declared the method he used to provoke the Serpent to battle. In the third was the combat itself; and this part contained a way of singing to the sound of the Pipe called <term>ὀδοντισμός: odontismos, or "gnashing of teeth"</term>, because the serpent ground its teeth when struck by arrows. In the fourth, the victory of Apollo was recounted; and in the last, it was declared how Apollo celebrated with dances and leaps for the victory he had received. It would be no great wonder if the ancients had leaped and danced when such a law was recited, for they also used to leap and dance in their Tragedies and Comedies; and to each of these, they had adapted its own proper manner:

Part 67

Since (as Athenaeus <note>Athenaeus of Naucratis, a Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae*</note> shows) they had discovered a species of dance called **Emmelia**, and for Comedy one called **Cordax**. There was also among them a species of satirical dance, which they called **Sicinnis** <note>original: σίκιννις</note>, and it was established by Bacchus after he had subdued India. This was one of the **Tibiarian Laws** <note>Musical compositions for the *tibia* or pipes</note>, in which the Rhythms, the Measures, the Styles, and the Harmonies were changed according to what the subject matter required. They also had the dance called **Carpea**, which I shall omit recounting: because it is set down by Athenaeus so clearly that everyone reading it will be able to know what it was, and in what manner they used it; and from these two—that is, from the **Pythian Contest** and from the **Carpean dance**—one will be able to discern in what way the ancients recited the other Laws. We can now see from what has been said that Music had several parts: namely Harmony, Rhythm, Meter, and the Instrument, from which this part was called **Instrumental** <note>original: "Organica"</note>. There was also Poetry and Dance; and these parts sometimes all concurred in one composition, and sometimes the majority of them. Nor was it permitted (as I have said at other times) to change or innovate anything, lest the inventor of such a change should have to suffer punishment. And such custom lasted a long time; whereby, Music being preserved in such a state, its reputation was also preserved. 

Afterward, it was reduced little by little to the state in which we see it today; the people having given themselves over to gluttony and luxury, caring little for such things, the Musicians took greater license, and together with many other things, they and Music lost their ancient gravity and reputation. This is seen described by Horace when he says:

> After the victor began to extend his fields and embrace the city with wider walls, and the genius was appeased on festive days with daytime wine without penalty, a greater license was added to both rhythms and modes:
> <note>original: "Postquàm cœpit agros extendere victor, & urbem Latior amplecti muros, vinoque diurno Placari genius festis impune diebus, Accessit numerisque, modisque licentia maior"</note>

And further on he continues, saying that which I have commemorated above; namely:

> Thus the flute-player added movement and luxury to the ancient art.
> <note>original: "Sic priscæ motumque & luxuriam addidit arti Tibicen."</note>

And then he also follows by saying,

> Thus also did voices grow for the austere strings.
> <note>original: "Sic etiam fidibus voces creuere seueris."</note>

Wherefore it is to be noted that Horace names the ancient strings "austere": because (as I have said) the ancients recited nothing but austere and grave things to their sound. In such a way, then, the ancient Musicians—in the age when Music flourished most and was in greatest prize and reputation—recited the narrated subjects in their songs. But which things, and in what manner they are recited by the moderns, and which have been cast aside, everyone who has knowledge of Music will be able to judge and see for himself.

## What the Ancient Musicians Were Like. Chapter 6.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' with an illustration of a figure seated among foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>

IT IS NOT a difficult thing to know who the ancient Musicians were: since in ancient times these, the Poets or Diviners, and the Sages were judged to be one and the same thing. This was because Music was contained within Poetry in such a way that the ancients, by this word "Music," did not only understand this science which principally treats of Sounds, Voices, and Numbers (as I have said elsewhere), but they also understood the study of humane letters joined with it. Thus the Musician was not separated from the Poet, nor the Poet from the Musician: because the Poets of those times being skilled in Music, and the Musicians in Poetry (as Strabo maintains), both were called by one of these two names, Musician or Poet. And this is manifest from what Plutarch says: That Heraclides, in his collection of ancient Musicians and the Inventors of such art, maintains that Amphion—son of Jupiter and Antiope <note>original: "Antipa"</note>, builder of the walls of Thebes—was the first to discover the song of the **Cithara** <note>original: "Cetera," an ancient stringed instrument</note> and its poetry; and that he was not only a Musician, but also a Poet, and the inventor of the named instrument, as Pliny also writes; and that he accompanied the voice to its sound. And following further, he says that Linus of Negroponte <note>Referring to Linus of Euboea; Negroponte was the medieval Italian name for the island</note> composed Lamentations and Hymns in verse. From which it can be believed that he was not only a Poet, but also a Musician: since the same Pliny says that he sang to the sound of the Cithara. Plutarch continues, saying that Philammon of Delphi composed [songs on] the birth of Latona and Diana, and that Demodocus of Corfu, an ancient musician, composed [on] the ruin of Troy, and that in a poem he celebrated the marriage of Venus and Vulcan. It is not a doubtful thing that he was a Musician: because this is manifest from what has been said before. Terpander also was a Musician and Poet, as [he] clear-

# Second [Part]

...as *Plutarch* clearly demonstrates, saying that he composed the prefaces to his verses to the sound of the **Cithara** <note>The "cetera" or cithara was a stringed instrument of the lyre family, central to ancient Greek music and education.</note>. *Apollo* likewise was not ignorant of these two things, as *Horace* shows, saying:

> Lest by chance the Muse skilled in the lyre, 
> and the singer Apollo, be a cause of shame to you. <note>original Latin: "Ne forte pudori / Sit tibi musa lyræ solers, & cantor Apollo"</note>

For he mentions first the player of the Lyre, as one who (as some believe) was its inventor; then he calls him a Poet by the name of Singer. I will refrain from recounting who *Orpheus* and *Arion* were, for it is well known that they were not only Musicians, but also most celebrated Poets. *Hesiod* was also placed among the Musicians, even though he never used to accompany his singing with the sound of the Lyre; for he used a laurel wand, with which, by striking the air (as *Pausania* relates), he made a certain sound to which he was accustomed to sing his poems. For this reason, the ancients made a statue of him with the **Cithara** upon his knees, and placed it among those of *Thamyris*, *Arion*, *Sacadas*, and other most noble and excellent Musicians, so as not to deprive him of such honor.

*Pindaro* was similarly a Musician and Poet, as can be understood from his works, and also from what *Alexander the Great* did; for when he had *Thebes* leveled and ruined, he had these words written above Pindar's house (as *Dio Chrysostom* says): <note>original Greek: πινδάρε τᾶ μουσοποιᾶ τὼ σέγλω μὴ καίετε</note> *Do not burn the house of Pindar the music-maker.* And to go no further, the most holy *David*, King of *Jerusalem* and great Prophet, is called by *Basil the Great* not only a Musician, but also a Poet of sacred songs. He is also called by the most learned *Jerome* the "Simonides," "Pindar," "Alcaeus," "Horace," "Catullus," and "Serenus" [of the Hebrews], because he wrote the sacred *Psalms* in an elegant style in lyric verse, in the manner of *Horace* and those others named. And it can be believed that he often sang them to the sound of the **Cithara**, in the way he sang when he drove out the evil spirit from *Saul*. 

Thus there is no doubt that, having been a Poet, he must also be named a Musician; for *Holy Scripture* calls him in many places **Psaltes** <term>Psaltes: A Greek term for a singer who accompanies themselves on a stringed instrument</term>, which means Singer or Player, and names his divine Poem the **Psaltery**. And of this *Origen* is a witness in Homily 18, chapter 24 of the book of Numbers, saying: *What shall we say of Music? Of which the most wise David had every science, and had gathered the discipline of all Melody and Rhythms, so that from all these things he could find sounds with which he could mitigate, by playing, the King who was troubled and molested by the evil spirit.* *Augustine* says the same in Book 17, chapter 4 of *The City of God*, as can be seen there. 

Every reason, therefore, persuades us to believe that the ancient Poets sang their poems themselves, and that they had joined Music with Poetry. For if it had been otherwise, they would not have used this word "Sing" so often in their compositions, as *Homer* did, who began the *Iliad* in this way:

*Sing, Goddess, the wrath* <note>original Greek: Μῆνιν ἄειδε θεὰ</note>; and *Hesiod*, who began the *Theogony* in this manner: *From the Muses of Helicon let us begin to sing* <note>original Greek: Μυσάων ἑλικωνιάδων ἀρχώμεθ’ ἀείδειν</note>. To these we shall add the prince of Latin poets, *Virgil*, who began his *Georgics* in this way:

> What makes the crops joyous, under what star to turn the earth,
> Maecenas, and to join the vines to the elms,
> is fitting; what care for oxen, what cultivation for keeping 
> the flock, and how much experience for the frugal bees,
> from here I shall begin to sing. <note>original Latin: "Quid faciat lætas segetes..."</note>

And to his *Aeneid* he gave such a beginning: *Arms and the man I sing.* So also *Ovid* begins the *Fasti* with these verses:

> The seasons with their causes distributed through the Latin year,
> and the signs that sink beneath the earth and those that rise, I shall sing. <note>original Latin: "Tempora cum causis Latium digesta per annum..."</note>

Following all of these, *Petrarch* began one of his songs in this manner:

> In the sweet time of my early age,
> Which saw the birth, and still almost in the blade,
> Of the wild desire that grew to my harm,
> Because by singing, grief becomes less bitter,
> I shall sing how I lived in liberty;

And the modern *Ariosto*, to follow such custom, he too began his elegant poem in this way:

> Of ladies, knights, of arms and loves,
> Of courtesies and daring deeds I sing.

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the historical unity of music and poetry, transitioning into a discussion on the "divine fury" that inspires both musicians and poets, and how ancient poets were often seen as prophets of Christian truths.</meta>

Part.

But why do I wander further, if **Terence** <note>Publius Terentius Afer (c. 185–159 BC), a Roman playwright.</note>, the comic poet, demonstrates to us that Poetry and Music are joined, and almost the same thing, by calling it **Musical Study**? It is no wonder, then, if Musicians and Poets were anciently reputed to be the same thing. And if the Poet is sometimes called by the Latin word ***Vates*** <note>original: "Vates"</note>, which also applies to a **Soothsayer** <note>An "indovino" or diviner who predicts the future.</note>, it is not out of place: for both (according to the opinion of **Plato**) are moved and agitated by the same divinity, or divine alienation of the mind, and by the same fury. For this reason, **Homer** names the Musician ***self-taught*** <note>original Greek: "αὐτοδίδακτος" (autodidaktos), meaning one taught by oneself or by God.</note>: because he sings not by human instruction, but inspired by the Gods, which is seen from the words he adds, which say:

->God implanted all kinds of songs in my mind.<-
-><note>original Greek: "θεὸς δ᾽ ἐμοὶ ἐν φρεσὶν οἴμας παντοίας ἐνέφυσεν"</note> that is: Because God produced in my mind every one of my songs.<-

# Second Part

> *He remembers also that it is in the fates that a time will come when the sea, when the earth, and the seized palace of heaven shall burn, and the laborious mass of the world shall struggle.*
> <note>original Latin: "Esse quoque in fatis reminiscitur, affore tempus / Quo mare, quo tellus, correptaq; regia cœli / Ardeat, & mundi moles operosa laboret." From Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book I, describing the eventual destruction of the world by fire.</note>

There are many examples of such things; but setting them aside for a moment, we shall turn to those in the Sacred Books. There we will find the authority of the most holy Apostle Paul, who, writing to Titus and citing a sentence by the poet Epimenides <note>A semi-mythical Greek seer and philosopher-poet from Crete (7th or 6th century BC).</note>, calls him a prophet, saying: **a prophet of their own** <note>original Greek: "ἴδιος αὐτῶν προφήτης" (idios autōn prophētēs). From Titus 1:12.</note>; which means, a prophet belonging to them, that is, to the Cretans. Since at that time a Musician, a Poet, or a Soothsayer <note>An "indovino" or diviner.</note> were called by a common name, it was also fitting that the name of **Sage** <note>Sapiente</note> should be applied to them. For (as Plato informs us) it belongs to the true Musician to know and have cognition of all the sciences, and the same applies to the Poet, according to the opinion of Strabo <note>Greek geographer and philosopher (c. 64 BC–24 AD).</note>. For this reason, the Poet alone deserved to be called Sage by the ancients. It followed that in those times, the cities of Greece had their children learn Poetry, not only for the sake of pleasure, but for the sake of chaste moderation. Thus the Musicians—who taught Poetry, Singing, and the Modes <note>The musical scales or "modi" of the ancient world.</note> played on the Lyre, the Kithara, or the Pipe—made it their profession and claimed the power not only to be correctors and emenders of morals, but even had themselves called "masters." Homer confirms this with these words:

> *For there was with him a singing man, to whom*
> *Atrides, going to Troy, gave many commands*
> *That he should keep his wife chaste.*
> <note>original Greek: "Πὰρ γὰρ ἔην καὶ ἀειδὸς ἀνήρ, ᾧ πόλλ' ἐπέτελλεν / Ἀτρείδης Τροίην δὲ κιὼν εἴρυσθαι ἄκοιτιν" (Odyssey III, 267–268). "Atrides" refers to Agamemnon.</note>

Rightly, then, did the ancients repute Musicians, Poets (or Soothsayers), and Sages to be one and the same thing.

### What things in Music have the power to induce various passions in man. Chap. 7.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a landscape with buildings and foliage.</image-desc>
If I did not fear being considered a slanderer, I would now like to demonstrate in part the ignorance and the audacity of certain modern musicians. Because they know how to put together four or six musical figures, they preach about themselves as if they were the greatest things in the world, thinking nothing of the ancients and holding any of the modern composers in low esteem. If one were to hear them, one would undoubtedly say that these men were worth more in the art of Music than Plato and Aristotle were in Philosophy. Sometimes, after having racked their brains for many days, they put forth some of their compositions with such reputation and pride that they seem to have composed another *Iliad*, or another *Odyssey* far more learned than that of Homer. Poor souls, they really ought to realize their error. For one does not hear of the chastity or honesty of any woman being preserved through their compositions, as one of the ancients once did for the chastity of Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon, as Homer and Strabo left in writing. Nor does one hear that Music in our times has compelled anyone to take up arms, as one reads in many sources—and especially in Basil the Great <note>A 4th-century Church Father.</note>—regarding Alexander the Great, who was spurred to such an effect by the musician Timotheus <note>Timotheus of Miletus, a famous and innovative Greek musician.</note>. One does not hear, either, that by their singing they have made any furious person become mild, as Ammonius <note>Likely referring to Ammonius Hermiae, a philosopher.</note> shows regarding a young man of Tauromenium, who through the wisdom of Pythagoras and the virtue of the Musician, was changed from a madman into someone human and pleasant. On the contrary, one hears instead how the shameful and filthy words contained in their songs <note>original: "cantilene." While this can mean "chants," here it refers to contemporary polyphonic songs.</note> frequently corrupt the chaste minds of the listeners. And although these men are worthy of every blame and punishment, those who—instead of admonishing them for their foolishness—take great pleasure and rejoice and greatly praise such songs are even more to be rebuked and punished. By doing so, they show outwardly how well they are composed in their inner character. But we should not wonder at this, since the lewd soul (as Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher and musical theorist.</note> says) either delights and enjoys lewd Modes, or by seeing them often, becomes soft and effeminate: for every like seeks its like. But let us leave these men for now, since these and other similar errors could be long lamented but not easily amended; let us return to our first purpose, and say that we ought greatly to

# Part

...to praise and revere the ancient musicians: since by their virtue, and through the medium of Music practiced in the manner shown, such and so many marvelous effects occurred that to recount them all would seem incredible. *But so that these things do not appear to be fables or strange to hear, we shall look into what the cause of such movements might be. Thus, if we examine the whole matter, we shall find that there were four things that always concurred together in such effects, and if any one of them were missing, nothing or very little could have been seen. The first, then, was Harmony, which arises from sounds or voices; the second was the determinate <term>Number</term> <note>In this context, "Number" refers to rhythm and the poetic meter of the verse.</note> contained in the verse, which they called Meter; the third was the Narrative of some matter containing a certain character, and this was the <term>Oration</term> <note>The "Oration" refers to the text, lyrics, or speech being delivered.</note> or Speaking; the fourth and last was a well-disposed <term>Subject</term> <note>The "Subject" refers to the listener and their specific psychological or emotional state.</note> ready to receive a certain passion. I have said this because if we take simple Harmony, without adding anything else to it, it will have no power to produce any external effect of those narrated above; although it might have the power, in a certain way, to dispose the mind intrinsically to express certain passions or effects more easily, such as laughter or pleasure. That this is true we can understand from this: if someone hears a melody that expresses nothing but the harmony, he takes pleasure only in it because of the proportion found in the distances between the sounds or voices; and he is prepared and disposed intrinsically in a certain way toward joy or sadness; but he is not induced by it to express any extrinsic effect, like laughing or crying, or doing anything manifest. If to such harmony the determinate and proportioned Number is then added, it immediately gains great strength and moves the soul; as is seen in Dances, which often induce us to accompany them with certain external movements of the body, and to show the pleasure we take in such a proportioned addition. Then, by adding to these two things the Oration—that is, Speech—which expresses character by means of the narration of some history or fable, it is impossible to say how great the power of these three things added together might be. It is certainly true that if the disposed Subject—that is, the Listener who hears these things willingly and delights in them—were not present, no effect could be seen, and the Musician would achieve little or nothing. For just as it happens to a Soldier, who, being naturally inclined toward matters of war, is little moved by those that treat of peace and quiet, and yet is sometimes altered by discussions of arms and field matters which delight him greatly; so also the talk of arms brings little or no delight to a man who is by nature peaceful, quiet, and religious; and talk of things of peace and celestial glory will often move his soul and compel him to weep. And just as chaste discussions move the Lustful man but little, so others that are lewd and filthy annoy the temperate and chaste man. For everyone willingly hears talk of those things in which he most delights, and is highly moved by such discussions; and on the contrary, he hates those that are not conformed to his nature, and thus cannot be moved by such talk. For this reason, if Alexander, son of Philip King of Macedonia, was induced by the musician Timotheus and by Xenophantus <note>Timotheus of Milete and Xenophantus were famous ancient Greek musicians; Alexander the Great was said to have been moved to take up arms just by hearing their music.</note> (as some claim) to take up arms with great fury, we should not be surprised: because he was so disposed that he willingly and with great pleasure heard discussions dealing with matters of war, and by such discussions he was induced to do marvelous things. Wherefore a certain man demonstrated this well to some who marveled that Music had such power, saying: "If this Xenophantus is a man as valiant as they say, why does he not find some melodies to recall him from battle?" Meaning to imply that it was not a great thing, nor of much art, to push a man in the direction toward which he is naturally inclined; but rather it is a marvelous thing to withdraw him from it. And so it is indeed. Therefore, if Alexander attended to nothing else but those things which could lead him to immortal glory—which were arms—it was not difficult to induce him to perform the narrated effects. How thirsty he was for such glory can be understood from this: that he sought to surpass everyone, and was envious of no one except for the fact of their fame in arms; for he never considered himself inferior to anyone in such things, though he did feel it toward Achilles, for having had Homer, who sang of him in such a sublime style. This he demonstrated, for one reads that:*

> *When Alexander reached the famous tomb*
> *Of fierce Achilles, sighing he said:*
> *O fortunate one, who had so clear a trumpet*
> *That wrote of you with such a lofty style.*
> <note>Original: "Giunto Alessandro alla famosa tomba / Del fero Achille, sospirando disse, / O fortunato, che si chiara tromba / Hauesti, che di te si alto scrisse." These verses are from Petrarch’s Canzoniere (Sonnet 187). The "trumpet" is a metaphor for the poet Homer.</note>

Such a Subject is therefore required: since without it (as I have also said) nothing or very little would be seen. And although the aforementioned things concur in such movements made by Music, nevertheless...

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical investigation into why ancient music was credited with miraculous effects on the human spirit. Building on the previous distinction between Harmony, Rhythm (Number), and Text, the author now argues that the "Melody" (the combination of all three) derives its primary emotional power from the text or "Speech."</meta>

# Second [Part]

The prize and honor are given to the composite of the first three elements, which is called **Melody**. For although **Harmony** alone has a certain power to dispose the soul and make it joyful or sad, and although its strength is doubled by **Number** <note>In this context, rhythm or poetic meter.</note> when put into action, these two things joined together are not powerful enough to generate any external passion in a subject in the manner described. This is because they acquire such power from **Speech**, which expresses specific human characters and morals.

And we can see that this is true: for Alexander [the Great] was not moved by harmony alone, nor even by harmony accompanied by rhythm, but rather (as **Suidas**, **Euthymius**, and others claim) by the <term>Orthian law</term> <note>A traditional ancient Greek musical "nomos" or rule, often vigorous and martial in character.</note> mentioned above, and by the **Phrygian Mode**. By this mode, and perhaps also by that "Law," the aforementioned young man of **Tauromenium** <note>An ancient city in Sicily, modern-day Taormina.</note>, while drunk, was driven (as **Boethius** relates) to want to burn down the house of his rival where a courtesan was hidden. **Pythagoras**, recognizing this, commanded the musician to change the Mode and play the **Spondee** <note>A slow, solemn rhythm consisting of two long beats, used here to calm the youth's agitation.</note>, with which he pacified the youth’s anger and restored him to his original state.

Likewise **Arion**, the musician and inventor of the <term>Dithyramb</term> <note>A wild, passionate choral hymn dedicated to Dionysus.</note> (according to the opinion of **Herodotus** and **Dio Chrysostom**), took the courage to cast himself into the sea, having (in my opinion) first sought to compose for himself an intrepid and manly spirit by means of that "Law" (as **Gellius** posits), so that he could do such a thing without any fear.

Now we can see that such movements were made not by the virtue of the first parts of Melody, but by the whole—that is, by Melody itself—which has great force within us by virtue of the third part, namely the **words** that concur in its composition. For **Speech** by itself, without harmony and rhythm, has great power to move the soul. Indeed, if we consider this, we shall see that sometimes when we hear a fable or history read or recounted, we are compelled to laugh or cry; sometimes it induces us to anger and rage, and sometimes it makes the sad become joyful, and vice-versa. Speech, therefore, induces us to fury and pacifies us; it makes us cruel and softens us. How many times has it happened that, by simply reading some pitiful history or novella, the listeners have been seized by such compassion that, despite themselves and after some sighs, they were forced to shed tears? On the other hand, how many times has it occurred that, while reading or narrating some joke or prank, some have nearly burst from laughter?

And it is no wonder: for most of the time, if something worthy of commiseration is represented to us, the soul is moved and induced to weep. And if we hear something that has a quality of ferocity and cruelty, the soul declines and bends in that direction. **Plato** is a witness to this (besides it being obvious) when he says: *whenever any of us hears **Homer** or any other tragic poet imitating one of the heroes afflicted by grief, crying out loudly and weeping over his fortune with mournful ways, beating his breast with his fists, in a certain way we take delight; and having a certain inclination toward these things, we follow them and are simultaneously seized by such passions, and we praise him as a good poet who greatly moves our soul.*

**Aristotle** confirms this even more expressly, saying: *it is further seen that men, hearing imitations, have compassion for those cases, even though they are without rhythm and without melody.* But if speech (as we have seen) has the power to move souls and bend them in different directions without Harmony and without Rhythm, it will have even greater force when joined with **Numbers** and with **musical sounds** and **voices**.

And such power is made clearly manifest by its opposite: for we see that those words move the soul less when they are uttered without melody and proportion than those uttered in the proper musical ways. Therefore, Speech has great force by itself, but it has much more force when joined to harmony, because of the similarity that harmony has with us and the power of Hearing. For nothing is so joined with our minds (as **Cicero** says) as **Numbers** and **Voices**, through which we are moved, inflamed, pacified, and made languid. Is it not a great marvel (he says) that rocks, wildernesses, caves, and dens respond to voices? And that cruel and ferocious beasts are often made gentle by song and are stopped by it?

Nor should we wonder at this: for if seeing a history or fable merely painted sometimes moves us to compassion, sometimes induces us to laugh, and sometimes drives us to anger, how much more can speech do this, which expresses things better than any painter, however excellent, can do with his brush? Thus we read of one who looked at a painted image and was driven to weep; and of **Aeneas**, who, having entered the temple built by **Dido** in the new Carthage:

-> He sees the Trojan battles in order, <-
-> and the wars now publicized by fame throughout the whole world, <-
<note>original Latin: "Videt Iliacas ex ordine pugnas, / Bellaq; iam fama totum vulgata per orbem," from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 1.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how music affects the human soul, moving from the role of speech to the physiological and philosophical mechanisms—specifically how "Harmonies" and "Numbers" (rhythms) interact with the human "spirits" and "complexions" to shape moral habits.</meta>

# Second [Part]

...[deter]mine in bodies, by virtue of the aforementioned qualities, certain states similar (if I may say so) to the <term>complexions</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, a "complexion" is the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual.</note> found in Harmonies. Thus, we can easily understand how Harmonies are able to move the soul and dispose it toward various passions. For if someone is subject to a certain passion, whether with delight or sadness, and hears a harmony that is similar in proportion, that passion increases. This is because, as **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was a standard textbook for over a millennium.</note> maintains, "Likeness is a friend to everyone, while Diversity is contrary and hateful." 

But if it happens that one hears a harmony of a different proportion, that passion diminishes and a contrary one is generated. It is then said that such harmony "purifies" the listener of that passion through the destruction of one state and the generation of another, contrary thing. We see this when someone is troubled by a passion involving sadness or the "inflaming of the blood," such as Anger; if they hear a harmony of a contrary proportion containing some delight, then the Anger ceases and is destroyed, and immediately <term>gentleness</term> is generated. This also happens with other passions. Everyone naturally takes more delight in that harmony which is most similar, convenient, and proportionate to their own nature and complexion, and according to their current disposition, rather than in that which is contrary to it. 

These diverse dispositions in men arise from nothing other than the various movements of the **Spirit** <note>The "Spirit" (spiritus) was believed to be a subtle, vaporous substance that acted as the intermediary between the soul and the physical body, carrying sensory information and triggering motion.</note>, which is the primary organ of every faculty of the soul, both the sensory and the motive, whether through alteration or local motion. From these movements, there sometimes occurs a gathering, sometimes a "boiling," and at other times a dilation of the Spirits. These movements arise not only from the diversity of musical Harmonies but from **Numbers** <note>In this context, "Numbers" refers to rhythm and poetic meter.</note> alone, as is evident. For while we attentively listen to the reading or recitation of Verses, some keep a man in a certain modesty; some move him to liberal and delightful things; some incite him to light and vain things; and others lead him into a violent motion. On this point, it will suffice to give only the example of **Archilochus**, of whom **Horace** says:

> Rage armed [Archilochus] with his own iambic [verse]. <note>Original Latin: "Proprio rabies armauit Iambo." Archilochus was a Greek poet famous for his biting, aggressive iambic poetry.</note>

From these things, one can understand how Melody and its parts can, with a certain disposition, diversely change the passions and the character of the soul. But because I said above that everyone naturally delights most in the harmony most similar and proportionate to their nature or complexion, and according to how they are disposed, I must note why I said "according to how they are disposed." I say now that Melody can change the character of the soul because, undoubtedly (following the doctrine of the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle.</note>), moral virtues and vices are not born within us; rather, they are generated through many repeated habits, whether good or bad. In the same way, by playing or writing poorly many times, one becomes a poor player or writer; or conversely, by practicing well many times, one becomes good and excellent.

Similarly, in moral virtues, he who often practices injustice becomes unjust; and he who practices justice becomes just, just as he who accustoms himself to fearing dangers becomes timid, and he who disregards them becomes bold. Thus, as the actions are, so are the habits; from good actions, good habits are born, and from bad actions, bad ones. Since Harmonies and Numbers are similar to the passions of the soul, as **Aristotle** affirms, we can say that becoming accustomed to Harmonies and Numbers is nothing other than becoming accustomed and disposed to various passions and different moral habits and characters of the soul. For those who hear Harmonies and Numbers feel themselves transformed according to the soul's disposition—sometimes into love, sometimes into anger, and sometimes into boldness. This happens for no other reason (as I have said) than the similarity found between the aforementioned passions and the harmonies. This is evident because one who has heard a certain kind of Harmony or Numbers many times will take greater delight in it, having already become accustomed to it.

However, for a better understanding of what has been said, we must note that although **Number** is taken (as we saw in the First Part) as a multitude composed of many units, and for the "Air" (as I shall call it) of a song—as the **Poet** <note>Virgil, in his Eclogues.</note> meant when he said:

> I remember the rhythm, if I could only keep the words; <note>Original Latin: "Numeros memini, si verba tenerem."</note>

and in many other ways; nonetheless, in this place, it is nothing other than a certain measure of short or long time. In this measure, one perceives the proportion or measurement of two or more movements compared together, according to a reciprocal ratio of the time of those movements. This is seen in the "feet" of the **Meter** and the **Verse**, which are composed of several Numbers in a certain order or determined space. **Meter** or **Verse** is a certain composition and order of feet, invented to delight the ear; or truly, it is an order and composition of several voices, finished with Number and mode. I could now explain the difference found between Meter and Verse, but for brevity, I wish to pass over it; for those who desire to know it may read Chapter 2 of the third book of **Augustine's** *On Music*, and they will find their every desire satisfied.

Part.

*One must only take care to notice that Rhythm is different from Meter and from Verse in this: that Meter and Verse contain within themselves a certain determined space, while Rhythm is more universal and has its spaces free and not determined. Thus, Rhythm is like the Genus, while Meter and Verse are less universal and are like the Species; for from the former one receives the quantity or the matter, and from the latter the quality or the form. Some others say that Meter and Verse are reason with modulation, and Rhythm is modulation without reason. But let this be said sufficiently regarding such matters.*

### In which genus of Melody the narrated effects were produced. Chapter 9.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial R featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>FINDING *that in Music, as we shall see elsewhere, there are three sorts of Melody—one of which was called* <term>Diatonic</term> <note>The most common musical scale, similar to the white keys on a modern piano.</note>, *the other* <term>Chromatic</term> <note>A system using smaller intervals (half-steps), often associated with more intense or "colored" emotions.</note>, *and the third* <term>Enharmonic</term> <note>The most complex ancient system, utilizing microtones smaller than a half-step.</note>—*there have been some who, led by a false reasoning, held the opinion that the effects of Music narrated above were not, nor could have been, produced in the first of the named genera, but rather in the latter two, namely in the* **Chromatic** *or in the* **Enharmonic**. *Their reason is that if they had been produced in the* **Diatonic** *genus, one would see such operations even in our own times, since only that genus, and not the others, is practiced by Musicians. They argue that every cause put into action never fails its effect unless it is hindered by some supervening accident. Therefore, not seeing such things now (as they say), they do not want to believe that in the past they were produced in the aforementioned genus, but rather in one of the other two named. Truly, these people are greatly deceived; for they suppose a false thing to be true and treat two different causes as if they were similar. The first is proven false by this reason: that Music never ceases, in diverse ways and at diverse times, to operate and produce various effects according to the nature of the cause and according to the nature and disposition of the subject* <note>In this context, the "subject" is the person listening to the music.</note> *upon which it works such effects. Thus we see even in our times that Music induces various passions in us, in the same way it did anciently. For at times one sees that when some beautiful, learned, and elegant Poetry is recited to the sound of an instrument, the listeners are greatly moved and incited to do various things, such as laughing, weeping, or other similar things. And of this, experience has been seen in the beautiful, learned, and graceful compositions of* **Ariosto** <note>Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533), a famous Italian poet whose "Orlando Furioso" was often set to music.</note>. *When reciting (among other things) the piteous death of* **Zerbino** *and the tearful lament of his* **Isabella**, *the listeners wept, moved by compassion, no less than* **Ulysses** *did when seeing the most excellent musician and poet* **Demodocus** *sing. So, even if one does not hear that Music today works upon diverse subjects in the manner it once worked upon* **Alexander** <note>Referring to Alexander the Great, who was famously said to have been moved to take up arms or calm down by the playing of the musician Timotheus.</note>, *this may be because the causes are different and not similar, as these people presuppose. For if such effects were produced by Music anciently, it was also recited in the manner I showed above, and not in the manner used at present—with a multitude of parts and so many singers and instruments that at times one hears nothing but a din of voices mixed with diverse sounds, and a singing without any judgment or discretion, with a disjointed uttering of words. One hears nothing but din and noise; therefore, Music practiced in such a way cannot produce in us any effect worthy of memory. But when Music is recited with judgment and more closely approaches the use of the ancients—namely, in a simple way, singing to the sound of the Lyre, the Lute, or other similar instruments certain matters that are Comic or Tragic and other similar things with long narrations—then its effects are seen. For truly, those songs can move the soul very little in which a brief matter is recounted with brief words, as is the custom today in certain little songs called* **Madrigals** <note>Short, often complex vocal compositions for several voices, which the author argues are too brief and fragmented to have a deep moral impact.</note>, *which, although they delight much, do not have the aforementioned power. And that it is true that Music delights more universally when it is simple than when it is made with much artifice and sung with many parts can be understood from this: that one hears with greater delight a single person singing to the sound of an Organ, Lyre, Lute, or other similar instruments, than one hears many. And if indeed many singing together do move the soul, there is no doubt that universally those songs whose words are pronounced by the singers together are listened to with greater pleasure than learned compositions in which one hears the words interrupted by many parts. By this thing, it is seen that the causes of the effects are very diverse and different from one another, and not similar as these people claim. Thus it would be no wonder if even one of the narrated effects were not seen at present. But I hold and believe for certain that if modern Musicians were such as the ancients were, and Music were practiced as it once*

Second Part

[The argument] was made that the effects would be heard much more in our own times than those we read about regarding the ancients: because at present, the multitude of Musicians is greater than it once was. But let us now leave these matters, for they are nearly obvious to anyone who has judgment, and let us seek to refute their opinion with lively and effective reasons, showing them their error. This will be easily done by one inconvenience that would follow, among many others: that if what they say were true, it would follow that the **Artificial** could do more than the **Natural**, since it would surpass it in bringing such effects into being. This is because the <term>Diatonic genus</term> <note>The standard musical scale consisting of whole steps and half steps, considered "natural" because it aligns with the simplest mathematical ratios.</note> is natural, and the other two are artificial, as can be understood from the words of **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect and engineer whose writings on music theory were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>, which say: "The genera of songs are three; the first is that which the Greeks call *Harmonia* <note>original: "Harmonia." Here Vitruvius uses this term to refer to the Enharmonic genus.</note>, and it is a modulation conceived by art, and its song has great gravity and no small authority. The **Chroma** then, with subtle diligence and a density of intervals, has a sweeter delight; and the **Diatonic**, for being natural, is easier due to the distance of its intervals." **Boethius** <note>An early 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music textbook of the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> also names it, more than any other, "hard and natural." And he says "more natural" because each of these genera is natural in terms of sounds and voices, but not in terms of intervals; for the shortening and lengthening of intervals belongs to art and not to nature, as we shall see elsewhere. **Franchino Gaffurio** <note>A leading Italian music theorist of the late 15th century.</note> even says that the **Chromatic** is artificially made for the ornament of the **Diatonic**, and the **Enharmonic** is called the perfect ornament of the natural and artificial Diatonic and Chromatic musical system; he also says that the Diatonic <term>tetrachord</term> <note>A series of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> is natural.

Similarly, another great inconvenience appears: for in striving to defend their opinion, they place the **Effect** before the **Cause** by a vast span of time, which is against all reason; since every cause is either before the effect or occurs together with it. But truly, long after such effects occurred, there followed not only the Inventors, but even the Invention of such genera. Of this **Plutarch** is a witness, who says: that the Diatonic is the most ancient of all genera; for everything in Music having previously been Diatonic, a long time later the Chromatic genus was found (as we shall see) by **Timotheus of Miletus**, the Lyric poet, son of Terpander, or of Neomysus, or perhaps of Philopides, as **Suidas** and **Boethius** maintain. **Aristotle** mentions him as a discoverer of new things (as I believe) in his *Metaphysics*, saying: "If Timotheus had not existed, we would not have many Melodies; nor would he have acquired such things if **Phrynis** <note>A celebrated Greek musician of the 5th century BC, known for his innovations.</note> had not existed before him." And if he was the one who, by means of Music, worked that most marvelous effect upon **Alexander** as we have said above, he lived in the **111th Olympiad**, which is around the year 338 before the year of our Salvation; for Alexander reigned in those times. And yet one reads of many other marvelous effects produced by Music before this man was even named, as we shall see. After him came **Olympus**—as Plutarch reports the opinion of **Aristoxenus**—who was the first to discover the Enharmonic genus, everything in Music having previously been Diatonic and Chromatic.

Reasonably, such effects should have happened after the Inventors and after the Invention, so that (according to the truth) the causes would be before the effects; but let us look closer if we wish to perceive the folly of these people. I find in history that **Pythagoras**, by whose skill Music worked the aforementioned effect upon the young **Taorminian** <note>A famous anecdote where Pythagoras used a specific musical mode to calm a drunken youth who was trying to burn down a house.</note>, lived during the time that **Servius Tullius** reigned in Rome, and in the times of **Cyrus**, King of Persia, around the year 600 before the coming of the Son of God, in the time of **Zedekiah**, King of the Jews, about 260 years before the time of Alexander. How then could the two named genera [Chromatic and Enharmonic] perform anything, if they were discovered by their Inventors a long time afterward? Furthermore, **Homer**, the most famous poet, wrote in heroic verse the misfortunes and diverse cases of **Ulysses**, and how he was provoked to weep by **Demodocus**, and said that he was recognized by **Alcinous** by his weeping; nonetheless, Homer lived about 490 years, more or less, before Pythagoras, and 160 years before Rome was built, in the times when **Jehoshaphat** reigned in Judea. Further still, **David the Prophet**, who many times drove away the evil spirit of **Saul**, was about 20 years before Homer, according to what I have been able to gather from histories, and more than 700 years before that same Timotheus. Oh, the great folly of these people! How can it be that if the cause they propose did not exist until so many and so many years later, any effect could issue from it? Truly, if they had placed the cause and the effect together, such things would at least have been said with some reason; but because (being men) they were able to err like many others, it is necessary to hold them excused. If, therefore, those marvelous effects which we recounted above were not performed by means of the Chromatic, they were even less likely to have been done by means of the Enharmonic, for this was discovered much later. Since such effects were not performed by means of these two genera, it follows that they were performed by means of the...

But let us suppose that Timotheus, the inventor of the <term>Chromatic genus</term> <note>A musical scale using "colored" or altered notes, often contrasted with the simpler, "natural" Diatonic scale.</note>, was not the one who moved Alexander to take up arms, as some might say, following the opinion of **Suidas** <note>original: "Suida." But in what manner the Ancients proceeded in their harmonies, we shall see elsewhere; wherefore, returning now to our principal intention, I shall begin to discuss the origin of Sounds and Voices: since they are considered by the Musician as the first elements of his science.

### Of Sounds and Voices, and how they are born. Chap. 10.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'F' containing stylized foliage and a small human figure.</image-desc>
IT IS NECESSARY then to know that if all things were immobile, and one could not move toward another, or one could not move or push another, Movement would necessarily be lacking; and Sounds and Voices would be lacking, and consequently every musical Consonance, every Harmony, and every Melody: since Sounds and Voices are born from nothing else but the violent percussion of the Air, which without any doubt cannot be had without Movement. For their generation, therefore (as **Aristotle** <note>Zarlino refers to Aristotle's theories on acoustics found in 'De Anima' (On the Soul).</note> maintains), three things necessarily concur: first, that which strikes; second, that which is struck; and the medium in which the Sound is received. I say that which strikes and that which is struck: because from percussion Sound is generated, Sound being especially (as **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose works on music were foundational for the Renaissance.</note> declares it) a percussion of air, unbroken until it reaches the hearing; in which is required that which strikes, as the agent; and that which is struck, as the patient; just as in movement one always seeks that which moves and that which is moved. After these, the Medium concurs, in which the Sound is received as in its own subject; and this is the Air: since for Sound to be generated, it is necessary that what strikes touches the struck in such a way that in touching it makes a blow: but not without local movement, in which the middle Air moves between that which strikes and that which is struck, and reaches our ears, moving the Sense of Hearing. Wherefore what the Philosophers say is true: that local Movement is always made in some Medium, and never in a Vacuum. It is indeed true that Sound can be born in many ways: first, when two hard bodies are struck together, such as the Anvil and the Hammer; and Aristotle confirms this, saying that Sound is born from the collision or rubbing together of two solid and hard bodies which strongly break the air. Secondly, it is born when a liquid body strikes a hard and firm one, such as the air striking a tree with violence; or on the contrary, when a liquid body is struck by a hard and firm one, such as when the air is struck by a rod. Similarly, when two liquid bodies run together or meet, such as two running waters; or when some wind or other vapor quickly pushes one part of the air over another, as happens when **Artillery** or some similar thing is discharged. And Sound is not only born in these ways, but also when any part of a body is separated from another, as is done by the splitting of wood, or by tearing Velvet, Cloth, Linen, or other similar things; in which effects the violent percussion of the air always concurs. And just as when a stone is thrown into the water, a small circle is immediately made in it, and it becomes larger as far as the movement permits—for being exhausted, it stops and proceeds no further—so it happens with sounds in the air, and with Voices: that the circles made in it spread out and become larger, as—

Second [Part]

...is permitted by the movement; and in such a way it strikes the ears of those standing by. It happens, however, that just as the waves that form circles [in water] are weaker and of less power the further they are from their origin, and are less perceived by the eye; so too sounds, or voices, strike the hearing more weakly the further they are from their source, and render themselves more obscure to the hearing, and are less understood by it; then, once the movement is exhausted, they are heard no longer. But if by chance it should happen that something should create an obstacle to the aforementioned waves, or circles made in the water, or prevent them from becoming larger as much as was granted to them by the nature of the movement; those circles return, decreasing, back to where they had their beginning, and the movement ceases. The air does this same thing: if something opposes it, it immediately returns to its beginning—that is, to the origin of its movement—and from this reflection a new sound is made in our ears, which they call an **Echo**. 

From movement, therefore, as the principal cause, **Sound** is made; in whose likeness **Voices** are also born, although differently from how sounds are produced. For their generation, not only are the named things concurring in the birth of sounds required, but moreover, it is necessary that there be two highly necessary natural instruments, which are the **Lungs** and the **Throat**. The Lungs, I say, which like a **Bellows** draw in the air and send it out; and the Throat, in which the expelled air strikes. Since the voice is a sound, and sound is generated (as I have said) by percussion, it is necessary that when the voice is generated, the air sent from the Lungs strikes the Throat—that is, the pipe which is called the <term>vocal artery</term> <note>original: "Arteria vocale." In Renaissance anatomy, the trachea or windpipe was often called an "artery" because it was believed to carry the "vital spirit" or air.</note>—and by such percussion it is generated. And although many sounds are born from the Lungs and the Throat, they are not all to be named "Voices," such as a **Cough** or other similar noises; but only those that are articulated and are those that signify something. From these are born **Speeches**, which are proper to man; for the generation of which all those natural instruments are needed that I commemorated in the First Part. These are considered by the Musician because they serve his purpose; but not the first ones [like coughs], which are not fit to make any <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "concento." Referring to a harmonious blending of sounds or a musical concert.</note>. 

Now we can see the difference found between **Sound** and **Voice**: for Sound is that which is only heard, and is the percussion of unreleased air (as I have said) that reaches the hearing and represents nothing to the intellect; and Voice is the percussion of breathed air at the vocal artery, which is sent out with some significance—leaving aside the **Barking of dogs** and other similar things, which do not serve our purpose here. Thus we can say that Sound is like the **Genus**, and Voice is like the **Species**: for every voice is a sound, but not the reverse.

### From what low sounds are born, and from what the high. Chapter 11.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'D' at the beginning of the chapter, set within a square frame with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>
From Movement, then (as we have seen above), are born Sounds and Voices. But because some movements are equal and some unequal, and of these some are slow and rare, and some fast and frequent; it is therefore necessary to know that from the first [slow] come <term>grave sounds</term> <note>Low-pitched sounds.</note> and from the second [fast] come <term>acute sounds</term> <note>High-pitched sounds.</note>. This is manifest to the senses: for if we take a musical instrument in which many strings are stretched, and we strike some of them equally together, so that the strike made to one is no stronger than that made to the other, we will find in the strings that give the lowest sounds, the movements are slower and rarer, and their sound lasts longer; and in the highest ones, the movements are faster and more frequent, and the sounds fail more quickly. 

This is because the looser strings strike the air weakly, and the sound born from them lasts longer, and this is due to the slowness of the movements. But those that are more stretched strike the air vigorously and with speed, and the sound proceeding from them is less durable: because by the velocity of the movements, it ceases so much sooner and reaches its end. Every day we see by experience that the tighter string renders a higher sound; and if we pull it more than it is pulled, we find in it faster movements, and the sound made higher than it was before. And if we slacken it, its movements are slower, and the sound produced by it lower; since the slower the movement is, the closer it is to its end—that is, to stopping; and the lower the sound is, the closer it is to <term>silence</term> <note>original: "taciturnità." Literally "taciturnity," but here referring to the state of being quiet or still.</note>. One must, however, understand that slowness which is found at the end of violent movements: for such movements are by their nature vigorous and fast in the beginning, and in the end they are weak and slow, as they gradually lose their velocity. And this slowness is found in the string when it is close to stopping: for then it is weaker and looser. Wherefore the movement of any struck string is fast in the beginning,

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physics of sound, moving from the human voice and echoes to the mechanical behavior of vibrating strings and the mathematical nature of musical intervals.</meta>

Part [Two].

*...renders a great sound: but little by little, as the movement weakens, it goes on losing it. Low <note>original: "graui"</note> sounds are also born from thick strings, and high <note>original: "acuti"</note> sounds from thin ones; because the high sound is born not so much from the speed of the movement as from the thinness of the string, which is more penetrative in the air. Nor should we imagine that whenever a string is struck, it generates only one sound; rather, we must be certain that the sounds and percussions are many, and that as many times as the air is struck by that string, it renders as many different sounds, according to the speed or slowness of the movements made in that string; and it strikes the air until such a string stops trembling. It is quite true that the differences of the low and high sounds born from the string are not audible; which can happen not only from the percussions, which are fast and joined in such a way that they seem to us as one alone, but also because of the tiny intervals found from one sound to the other, of which the hearing is not capable, both because of their smallness and because they are very closely joined. Wherefore the hearing remains deceived in the audible thing, almost in the same way that sight does in the visible thing; for if someone takes a burning ember in their hand and turns it quickly around, it will seem that there is a circle of fire in the air; nevertheless, according to the truth, it will not be so, because from the speed of the united movement and from the shape of such a figure, which has no angles, the eye will remain deceived. Since, therefore, low sounds are made from slow and rare movements, and high ones from fast and frequent ones, we can say that from the addition of movements, high sounds are made from low ones; and conversely, from the diminution of movements, low sounds are made from high ones. So that high sounds being made by the greater part of the movements and low ones by the lesser, from such a difference, which consists in a certain plurality, it is necessary that they fall under number; and that when their greater number is compared to the lesser, that comparison and proportion is found between them which is found between simple numbers in discrete quantity <note>Discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted, like individual objects or integers, as opposed to continuous measurements like length.</note>. And just as such movements compared according to number are partly equal and partly unequal to each other, so too sounds are partly equal and partly distant from each other by inequality. Wherefore, in those that are not discordant by any inequality, no **Consonance** can be found, nor even its opposite, which is **Dissonance**: for **Consonance** is the agreement of several sounds different and unequal among themselves, reduced into one; and **Dissonance** (as we shall see elsewhere) is a mixture of low and high sound that offends the ear. Therefore, just as from quantities that are unequal to each other, one compared to the other (in the way we saw in the first part) five types of proportion are born, called proportions of greater inequality, of which the species are infinite; so also from the comparison of sounds unequal to each other, five types and infinite species are born. And although sounds are found in action in the air, as in their own proper subject, and we can have no certain knowledge or determined reason of them through the subject—because the boundaries <note>original: "termini"</note> of sounds are unknown to us—nevertheless, insofar as they are born from **Sonorous Bodies** <term>Sonorous bodies: Physical objects capable of producing sound, like strings, pipes, or bells, which can be measured mathematically to understand musical intervals.</term>, which are commensurable quantities, and are found in them in potentiality, we have perfect knowledge of them from their measurement; because their boundaries are known, since from the division of strings (as I said in the First Part) we derive the ratios <note>original: "ragioni"</note> of low and high sounds and their differences, and this according to the number of the parts that measure them; from which number we come to be certain of the quantity of sounds; and not only of them, but also of **Voices**, which are undoubtedly sounds; applying, however, those sounds that are born from sonorous bodies to the voices, which are produced by human bodies.*

->What Consonance, Dissonance, Harmony, and Melody are. Cap. 12.<-

**FROM** slow and fast movements, then, proportioned together, is born **Consonance**, considered principally by the musician, which, declaring once again, I say is a mixture of low and high sound that reaches our ears sweetly and uniformly, and has the power to change the sense [of the listener]. Or it is (according to how **Aristotle** defines it) the ratio of numbers in the high and low. From which definitions we can understand that Consonance is born when two sounds, which are different from each other without any middle sound, join harmoniously in one body; and it is contained by a single proportion. But because of two opposites, when one is found to exist, it is necessary that the other also be found, and that one should have the same science of both;

Second [Part]

However, since Dissonance is the opposite of Consonance, it will not be difficult to know what it is: for it is a mixture of a low <note>original: "graue"</note> and a high <note>original: "acuto"</note> sound which reaches our ears harshly. And it is born in such a way that while such sounds do not wish to unite with one another, because of the disproportion found between them, and they strive to remain in their own integrity, by offending each other they provide a bitter sound to the hearing. Nor are there only two sounds found distant from each other by low and high pitch that harmonize <note>original: "consuonino"</note>; but such sounds are also often heard with other sounds placed between them, which render a sweet concord, as is evident; and they are contained by many proportions; therefore musicians call such a composition *Harmony* <note>original: "Harmonia"</note>. Wherefore it should be noted that *Harmony* is found in two sorts, one of which we shall call *Proper*, and the other *Improper*. 

The *Proper* is that which Lactantius Firmianus <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author</note> describes in his work *On the Workmanship of God* <note>original: "Opera di Dio" / Latin: "De Opificio Dei"</note> saying: Musicians properly name *Harmony* the concord of strings or of voices sounding together in their modes, without any offense to the ears; understanding by this the concord that arises from the modulations made by the parts of each song <note>original: "cantilena"</note>, until they have reached the end. *Proper Harmony*, therefore, is a mixture of low and high sounds, whether mediated or not mediated <note>referring to whether there are middle pitches between the highest and lowest notes</note>, which strikes the sense sweetly; and it arises from the parts of each song through the progression they make by according together until they have reached the end; and it has the power to dispose the soul to diverse passions. And this *Harmony* arises not only from consonances but from dissonances as well: because good musicians apply every study to ensure that in their Harmonies the dissonances accord, and that they harmonize with a marvelous effect. In this way, we can consider it in two modes, that is, *Perfect* and *Imperfect*: the *Perfect*, when many parts are found in a song, which go on singing together in such a way that the extreme parts are mediated by the others; and the *Imperfect*, when only two parts go on singing together, without being mediated by any other part. 

The *Improper* harmony is that which I declared above, which can sooner be called a *Harmonious* consonance than *Harmony*: since it does not contain any modulation in itself, even though it has the extremes mediated by other sounds; and it has no power to dispose the soul to diverse passions like the harmony called *Proper*, which is composed of many *Improper Harmonies*. And although it seems that Proper Harmony does not have such force by itself, it nevertheless acquires it by means of Number <note>referring to rhythm and meter</note> and Oration <note>original: "Oratione," meaning the text or speech</note>, that is, the Speech or the Words that accompany it; which move the listener more or less according to how much they are accommodated to the Rhythm, or rather to the Meter with proportion. Wherefore from all these three things added together—that is, from *Proper Harmony*, from *Rhythm*, and from *Oration*—there is born (as Plato wishes) *Melody*.

## Division of Voices. Cap. 13.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring two figures in an outdoor setting with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

And although Consonance, Dissonance, and Harmony can be born not only from voices but also from sounds [of instruments]; nonetheless Melody, into which Oration enters, cannot be born except from voices. However, not every voice, even if it is articulated, is fit for its generation: since voices are not all of one species. Wherefore it is necessary to know that human voices (as Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477 – 524 AD), whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory text of the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> posits) are divided into three parts, of which some are called *Continuous*, some *Discrete*—or we might say *Suspended* with an interval—and some are those that participate in the nature of each of those named. 

The *Continuous* are called by the Greeks *synecheis phōnai* <note>original: "συνεχὰι φωναὶ"</note>, and they are those which we use in domestic and familiar reasoning, with which, without changing pitch, we read Prose or Verse. The *Discrete*, which the Greeks call *diastēmatikoi phōnai* <note>original: "διασηματικὰι φωναὶ"</note>, are those with which we sing every sort of song, ordered by proportioned musical intervals found in modulations; and these alone are those that serve our purpose: because from them every modulation has its being, from which all sorts of *Harmony* are born. Different from these two sorts are those added by Albinus <note>A scholar mentioned by Boethius, likely Albinus the Platonist</note>; as Boethius shows in chapter 12 of the first book of *Music*; which participate in the nature of the two named: since they are those with which we read every sort of Poetry, not like Prose without change of pitch, nor yet distinctly with determined intervals as is used in songs; but in a certain way that pleases us more, observing those accents given to the words according to what the subject matter contained therein requires. And although Continuous Voices can be infinite, since speaking and reading can continue for a long time without any limit, and the Discrete have no prescribed limit for ascending to the high or descending to the low; nevertheless nature gives an end to the one...

It also begins a classification of the human voice into continuous, discrete, and intermediate types based on classical music theory.</summary>

to one, and to the other: Because the human spirit, together with time, brings an end to the continuous [sounds]; allowing each person to speak, and similarly to read, as much as is permitted by his nature and by time; and the Nature of men gives an end to the discrete [sounds]; because man naturally ascends or descends with his voice only as much as his nature can endure. To those sounds, then, that participate in the nature of the first two, both of the named factors bring an end. Therefore, the Discrete sounds are those which are suitable for modulations, for harmonies, and for melodies, of which (leaving the others as of little use to us) our discourse will be made.

### What Song and Modulation are; and in how many ways one can sing: Chapter 14.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' depicting a rural landscape with buildings, trees, and a seated figure in the foreground.</image-desc>
DISCRETE voices, or those suspended by an interval, are therefore those which are principally
considered by the Musician; then the Sounds applied to them: because from these and those,
without any difference, every one of our songs <note>original: "Cantilena"</note> is formed. This everyone calls
Song <note>original: "Canto"</note>, from Singing; which is modulation that arises principally from the human voice. I say
principally: because "Song" is also used for the harmony that arises from the Sound of
artificial instruments; and even for the Song of any animal; as can be seen in the song of the 
Swans, of which Virgil, speaking, said;

> *Just as they, returning, play with whirring wings,* <note>original: "Vt reduces illi ludunt stridentibus alis,"</note>
> *And have circled the sky in a flock, and given forth songs:* <note>original: "Et cœtu cinxere polū, Cantusq́; dedêre:" — Virgil, Aeneid, Book I.</note>

And this last mode is not to our purpose, but the 
first two: because in them every Harmony and every Melody is understood. But Modulation is a movement 
made from one sound to another through various intervals, which is found in every sort of Harmony and Melody; 
<margin>a</margin> we use it in two ways: first when we move from one sound to another without variation of time, with 
various intervals, making no Proper harmony, proceeding equally from one interval to another through 
the same time; as is done in Plainchants <note>original: "Canti fermi" — the traditional, unmeasured chant of the Church</note>; And this is called Modulation improperly: because it contains 
only a simple progression, without any consonance; from which effect it is seen that such modulation has the 
quality of imperfection: since it lacks its own proper end. But the other way is called so properly, when 
through its means we arrive at the use of Harmony and Melody, as its own proper end; as we do 
in Figured Song <note>original: "Canto figurato" — measured music or polyphony</note>; in which we sing not only with simple flexions, and simple elevations, and lowerings 
of voices, but we also move from one interval to another with fast and slow movements, according to the time 
shown in its singable figures <note>musical notes or notation</note>. Wherefore, touching then various consonances, from our singing 
is formed every sort of harmony and melody, which cannot be born except with the help of consonances; 
although we can have modulation without proper harmony, and without any consonance, and without melody. 
We can nonetheless have modulation in three ways; first when we sing by name each 
string, or sound, with the name of one of these six syllables, *Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La*, according to the method 
found by Guido of Arezzo <note>original: "Guidone Aretino" — the 11th-century monk who invented the precursor to modern solfège</note>, as we shall see in its place; which method the Practitioners call 
Solfizizing <note>original: "Solfizare"</note>, and it cannot be done except with the voice. Then, when we utter only the 
sound, or the voice, and the intervals described, as artificial instruments do. But the last way is when 
we apply words to the singable figures, which is proper to the Singer: because from this manner of 
singing, Melody is born, as we have seen.
