### What an Interval is, and its species. Chapter 15.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' illustrating a classical architectural structure with arches and columns.</image-desc>
SOME things are in Music that are called Elements, of which some are attributed 
to Nature, and some to art. Those that are attributed to nature are the High Pitch <note>original: "Acuto"</note>, 
the Low Pitch <note>original: "Graue"</note>, and the Interval: because it is necessary (using the words of Cicero) that 
its extremes sound lowly on the one side, and highly on the other: Whence it is manifest, 
that the High and the Low are the extremes of the Interval. The things that are attributed to 
Art are the Extension of any string; the making of it low, or high; Consonance; Concord <note>original: "Concento"</note>; and 
every proportionate Composition; whether in voices or in sounds, which does not matter; all of which things fall into 
the consideration of the Theorist <note>original: "Speculatiuo"</note>. It is indeed true, that there are some other things, which only belong to the Practitioner <note>original: "Prattico"</note>;

<header>Second [Part]</header>

And these are *Playing*, *Singing*, & *Composing*: because they are born from exercise & long use. But the other accidents—which are many, and which occur in compositions and in songs <note>original: "cantilene"</note>—are not only within the consideration of the *Practitioner*, but also the *Theorist* <note>original: "Speculatiuo"</note>. The *Interval* <term>Interval: the distance in pitch between two sounds</term>, then, which is attributed to nature, is named in two ways, according to *Aristides Quintilianus* <note>A 2nd or 3rd-century Greek music theorist</note>, namely *Common* and *Proper*. It is called *Common* because every magnitude bounded by certain limits is called an *Interval*, considering the space found between one extreme and the other; and of this I do not intend to speak, as it is very far from our consideration. It is called *Proper* because the distance from a low sound to a high one is called an *Interval*; and this is considered by the Musician. It is found in twelve types, namely *Major*, *Minor*, and *Equal* (always comparing two together); *Consonant*, *Dissonant*, *Simple*, *Composite*, *Diatonic*, *Chromatic*, *Enharmonic*, *Rational*, and *Irrational*. *Major*, like that of the *Diapason* <note>Octave</note> compared to that of the *Diapente* <note>Perfect Fifth</note>. *Minor*, like that of the *Diatessaron* <note>Perfect Fourth</note> compared to that of the *Diapente* or the *Diapason*. *Equal*, such as one *Diatessaron* compared to another; and I say this with respect to the proportion of number to number, and not otherwise. *Consonant* is said of the *Diapason*, the *Diapente*, the *Diatessaron*, and all others that have their ratios <note>original: "forme"</note> among the parts of the *Senary number* <term>Senary number: the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, which Zarlino identified as the source of all musical consonance</term>. *Dissonant*, like that of the *Tone* <note>Whole step</note>, and all those smaller than it. *Simple* is the name for that which is not divided by another sound, which the Greeks call *diastema* <note>original: διάστημα, meaning "interval" or "distance"</note>: since its extremes follow one another without any middle [sound]. *Composite* is said of that which is divided by other sounds, called by the Greeks *systema* <note>original: σύστημα, meaning "a whole composed of parts"</note>. *Diatonic* is that of the *Major Tone*. *Chromatic* is that of the *Minor Semitone*, and *Enharmonic* that of the *Diesis* <note>A very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone</note>, as we shall see. The *Rational* is then called that which can be described with numbers, just as the Interval of the *Diapente* is circumscribed by these two terms, 3 & 2; and the *Irrational* is that which in no way can be described [by ratios], as I showed in the First Part when we reasoned about Proportions. All these things are considered by the Musician, as we will see further in our reasoning, because they are very necessary for the knowledge of the Art and the Science [of music].

### What Genus is, and of the three Genera of Melody, or Song among the ancients, and of their species. Chapter 16.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'E' containing an engraved scene of a building in a landscape.</image-desc>

And although it can be said that *Genus* is that which has many species beneath it; nevertheless, the Musician also intends it to be the division of the *Tetrachord* <term>Tetrachord: a scale of four notes spanning the interval of a Perfect Fourth</term>, which demonstrates many different forms and gives a certain mode of *Harmony*, or *Universal Melody*. Whence *Ptolemy* in chapter 12 of the First Book of *Music* says that *Genus* in harmony is nothing other than a certain habit or suitability of sounds which together compose the *Diatessaron*. But the *Tetrachord* is an order of sounds contained between four strings, whose extremes are found distant from each other in *Sesquiterza* proportion <note>The 4:3 ratio</note>. And it is called *Tetrachord* from *tetras* <note>original: τετράς</note>, a Greek word meaning Four, and from *chorde* <note>original: χορδή</note>, which signifies String: that is, [a system] of four strings. However, it should be noted that among the Ancient musicians there were three genera of *Melody*, or *Song*; the first of which they called *Diatonic*, the second *Chromatic*, and the third *Enharmonic*. They were named Genera because from the various divisions that many made of the *Tetrachord*, different species of modulations were born, each of which was later reduced under one of the three named heads, according to which they most closely approached or retained the form of the most ancient species. I will now omit the various divisions made by *Aristoxenus*, among which are found two species of the *Diatonic*, one of which he named *Soft* and the other *Tense*; and similarly three species of the *Chromatic*, namely *Soft*, *Sesquialter*, and *Tonic*; and one species of the *Enharmonic*. Similarly, I will set aside the divisions of *Archytas*, those of *Didymus*, and those of *Eratosthenes*; which, having been rejected with many arguments by *Ptolemy* (as appears in chapters 12 and 13 of the First Book and in 13 and 14 of the Second of his *Music*; and similarly in chapters 15, 16, & 17 of Book 5 of *Boethius*), do not serve our purpose. I will set down only those divisions made by *Ptolemy*, as they have been accepted by the majority of Musicians as the best, because they are more rational and more consonant to the *Hearing*. Having first shown the forms contained in the various *Tetrachords*, adding to them the first species of the named genera put into use by the most ancient [musicians], I will thereafter show the order of each, contained in the *Greater System* <note>The "Sistema massimo" or Greater Perfect System of ancient Greek theory</note>, divided into five *Tetrachords*; and together I will show the divisions of the *Monochord* <term>Monochord: a single-stringed instrument used to measure musical ratios</term> for each species. By these, one may see the utility the Ancients could have gained from each, had they wished to practice

the portions are ordered in arithmetic progression. This genus [the Diatonic] was used in antiquity more than any other, especially in its first species, as can be seen in the writings of many ancients; and now more than ever it is used in the third species, although it is used in ways different from those the ancients used, and with the use of imperfect consonances <note>Thirds and sixths, which were not considered "perfect" like the octave or fifth</note>, as we shall see elsewhere. Ptolemy compared this genus to two other diverse types—namely, the Theological and the Political—because of the similarity and suitability of its order, majesty, and excellence, which are very much in conformity with those two. For just as it is more honorable to prefer public things over private ones, and Metaphysical or Theological things over natural and mathematical ones (since the second are ruled and preserved by the first, and without them would have no being), so it is just and honorable that this genus be preferred over the other two as more noble and excellent, since the others derive their being from it. This is because the Diatonic virtually contains the Chromatic and the Enharmonic, and ultimately produces them in practice, but not vice versa. It was truly just for Ptolemy to give every preeminence to this genus, since as the generator it is undoubtedly much more noble than that which is generated. 

Wherefore I am moved to laugh at those who, without assigning any reason or authority, say that this genus was used in ancient times in public festivals for the use of common ears, and that the other two were used among private lords. But I think these people have never seen Ptolemy, or if they have seen him, they have not understood him. I will not expand now on demonstrating how it was used, for I believe that what I said in Chapter 4 will suffice to show that it was used magnificently and with great excellence by the skilled ancient musicians. 

But I shall come to the second genus, called Chromatic <note>From the Greek 'chroma', meaning color, suggesting a modification or "coloring" of the Diatonic</note>, of which there were three species: the ancient one and the two of Ptolemy, one of which he called "Soft" and the other "Intense." The ancient Chromatic was that which, in its modulation in every tetrachord, proceeded from the low to the high by an interval of a minor semitone (contained by the shown proportion of the first Diatonic species), and by another semitone somewhat larger than this, of the proportion of 5 over 76 <note>original: "Super 5. partiente 76"</note>, and an interval containing three semitones, called by Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher</note> an "uncomposite trihemitone," because in that genus it could not be divided by any other string; and it was contained by the proportion of 3 over 16 <note>original: "Super 3. partiente 16"</note>, as can be seen below. 

The Soft [Chromatic] was that whose strings were ordered in such a way that the first (the lowest) and the second contained the sesquivigesimaseptimal proportion <note>28:27</note>; this with the third contained the sesquiquattuordecimal <note>15:14</note>; and the third with the last (the highest) the sesquiquintal <note>6:5, a minor third</note>. This was a consonant interval, as shown by the terms of its proportion, which are fundamentally found located between 6 and 5 in the parts of the Senary Number <note>The number six, which Zarlino considered the source of all musical intervals</note>, as can be seen in Chapter 15 of the First Part; and it will return to our purpose in the composition of the Chromatic order in the promised instrument, and will create the consonant trihemitone. Such a tetrachord proceeded from high to low in the opposite direction through the same intervals, as seen in the figure below. 

The Intense [Chromatic] was that whose strings were ordered in such a manner that in its tetrachords, the first and lowest string was distant from the second by a sesquivigesimaprimary proportion <note>22:21</note>; this was distant from the third by a sesquiundecimal <note>12:11</note>; and the third from the fourth by a sesquisextal <note>7:6</note>;

...understood by the Moderns until now; indeed, the true use of it, and that of the Chromatic, is very far from the truth. Ptolemy compared this genus to two other diverse types—namely, the Natural and the Moral—for no other reason than the common reduction of its size, which it possesses over the others. For just as the natural deals with those inferior things, which are the least noble in the world; and the moral deals with a single individual, who is outside of Number; so this genus goes about dealing with those intervals which are the least noble and the smallest in harmonic modulations. This is called **Enharmonic**, as if to say "Optimally and Aptly joined," or (as some would have it) as if "Inseparable." But in what manner its strings are put into use, we shall see elsewhere.

### For what reason each of the Intervals contained in the shown Tetrachords is called Incomposite. Chapter 17.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q depicting a man in a landscape.</image-desc>
**ALTHOUGH** I have said that the <term>Trihemitone</term> <note>A minor third, literally "three half-tones"</note> in the Chromatic genus, and the <term>Ditone</term> <note>A major third, literally "two tones"</note> in the Enharmonic, are called **Incomposite** <note>original: "Incomposti"; meaning they are simple or uncompounded intervals that are not divided into smaller steps within that specific system</note>; nevertheless, all the other intervals of each of the named genera, in every one of their species, are also called Incomposite. This is because (as Boethius says) each one is placed whole in its species, and without any middle division. And even if the word "Incomposite" is often taken for what we usually call "Without ornament" or "Without any elegance," nonetheless Boethius takes it to mean "Without any composition." He wishs to show us that these intervals are the **Elements** of which each of the shown species is composed. For something is called an Element when it is the primary thing from which everything else is composed, and it is found within that thing indivisibly according to its form. 

Hence, just as we say that Letters are the first elements of words; and that the elements of mixed things are Earth, Water, Air, and Fire; and that the first elements of any science are the first principles, which are indemonstrable in that science; so too it is said that the first elements of the genera of melody or song are the shown intervals. For every harmonic modulation is composed of them primarily; and ultimately, every composition of multiple intervals for each genus and each species is terminated and resolved into them. Each is indivisible within its genus or species in every <term>Tetrachord</term> <note>A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth</note>. For if they were divisible while the outer strings of each Tetrachord remained in their quality, it would no longer be called a Tetrachord, but a Pentachord (five strings), or a Hexachord (six strings); or it would be called by another name according to the number of strings it contained. 

And this is not contrary to what I said in the First Part—namely, that every interval is at least divisible into two parts—since at that time they were not being considered as primary elements, as they are considered at present. Boethius, therefore, has named each of them **Incomposite** for no other reason than to denote to us that they are the primary elements of such genera, and that, in forming each of the shown Tetrachords, they receive no division: because every sort of Melody and Song is principally composed of them as Elements.

### In what way any resonance or Interval can be accommodated to its proportion. Chapter 18.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P depicting a man in a landscape with a large tree.</image-desc>
**SINCE** Sounds are found primarily in potentiality within the continuous quantity called the "Sonorous Body," and formally thereafter in the Air as their true subject (in the manner I have said elsewhere); and since no ratio can be had of them except by means of the named bodies; nor even of Voices, except in insofar as Sounds are applied to them; therefore, having reasoned in the First Part about Numbers and Proportions—which are (as has been said) the **Forms** of consonances—I will now come to show the method held in accommodating Sounds, or Consonances, and any interval in sonorous Quantities to its proportion. This is so that afterward we may come to the composition or division of the <term>Monochord</term> <note>A single-stringed instrument used by ancient and Renaissance theorists to measure musical intervals mathematically</note>. 

But first, it is necessary to find a plank—or board, as we might call it—that is very flat and two <term>braccia</term> <note>A traditional unit of length roughly equal to an arm's length (about 23-27 inches)</note> long (more or less, it does not matter); which should be at least four fingers wide and two or more thick, so that it cannot bend in any part; and so that it is equal in its surface or flatness on all sides. Once this is found, we shall draw a straight Line down the middle of it lengthwise, falling perpendicularly from one end of the said board to the other, so that it might be more convenient to measure,

measure, or divide; and such a Line will serve in place of a string. From the ends of this, it is then necessary to place two immobile **bridges** <note>original: "Scannelli"; the fixed supports at either end of a monochord</note>, over which, after the measurement is made, one or more strings can be stretched according to need. But it should be noted that none of them should be higher than the edge of a knife, and that they should be equal, and that they form four right angles on the said surface. This done, one must take the <term>radical terms</term> <note>The lowest whole numbers that express a mathematical ratio, such as 2:1 or 3:2</note> of the proportion of the consonance or interval that one wishes to accommodate; which will be in <term>discrete quantity</term> <note>Quantity that can be counted, i.e., whole numbers</note>—that is, in Numbers; and divide the whole Line, starting from one of the immobile bridges at the points over which the strings will be placed, to the other, into as many equal parts as units contained in the greater radical term of that consonance or interval. 

Then one must take for the smaller term as many parts of that line as units this term contains, always starting from the right side and coming toward the left; and between the whole of the line—which represents the low sound, or the greater term of the proposed consonance or interval—and the part or parts that remain, which are taken for the high sound or for the smaller term, we will have accommodated such a consonance or interval to its proportion. Because (as I have said at other times) Musicians hold this to be true: that the proportion of one sound to another in any musical interval is the same as the proportion of its strings according to their length, provided they are stretched under the same quality <note>Meaning the strings must be of the same thickness, material, and tension for the mathematical division of length to correspond accurately to the musical pitch</note>. 

But let us come to an example, so that what I have said may be more easily understood. Let the line **a-b** be placed in the position of a string, upon which one wishes to accommodate the consonance <term>Diapason</term> <note>original Greek: "diapasōn," meaning the interval of an octave</note> to its proportion. First, one must find the radical terms of its proportion, which are 2 and 1; then, having found them, divide the line into two equal parts according to the number of units included in the greater term at point **c**. This done, I say that between line **a-b**, which is the whole, and **c-b**, which is one part, we will have accommodated the consonance of the Diapason to its proportion. For just as **a-b** is the whole of the line and **c-b** is its half, and they are in <term>continuous quantity</term> <note>Quantity that is measured by length or size rather than counted</note> in a <term>Double proportion</term> <note>A 2:1 ratio</note> according to length;

# Another way to accommodate consonances to their proportion. Chapter 19.

One could also achieve this goal by following the method taught by **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century Roman philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory textbook for a millennium</note>; that is, by first adding together the <term>radical terms</term> <note>The lowest whole-number representation of a ratio, e.g., 3:2</note> of the proportion that contains the consonance, then dividing the entire line or string into as many equal parts as there are units in the sum. By taking as many parts from the left side toward the right as there are units in the greater term, that portion of the string taken—along with the remainder on the right side (which will necessarily have as many parts as units in the smaller term)—will contain the proposed consonance. 

For example: if we wanted to accommodate the Perfect Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> to its proportion on the underlying line **a b**, it would first be necessary to find the radical terms of its proportion, which are 3 and 2. Then, adding them together, we would have 5. For this number, it would be necessary to divide the underlying line **a b** into five equal parts and take the three parts placed on the left side (according to the number of units in the greater term of the proportion, which is 3) at point **c**. We would then have string **a c**, which, when struck together with **c b**, would give us the Perfect Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> consonance, as intended. This is because **a c**, representing the low sound, would contain three parts of the said line or string **a b**, and **c b**, representing the high sound, would contain two parts—which are compared to one another in the <term>Sesquialtera</term> proportion <note>The ratio of 3:2, where the larger number contains the smaller number once plus a half</note>.

# How one can hear any consonance adjusted to its proportion. Chapter 20.

AND BECAUSE in Music, we employ not only reason but also sensory perception to judge sounds and voices—since when one is not discordant with the other, we have true and perfect knowledge of the consonances—it is now necessary that I demonstrate the way to submit everything that has been achieved through reason to the judgment of the senses. This is so we can be certain that sense and reason are in agreement and that the arguments repeatedly put forward are not in vain. Therefore, after having stretched two or more strings over the aforementioned surface, resting them upon the two fixed bridges <note>original: "scannelli immobili"; these are the nuts at either end of the instrument</note>, it is necessary that they be tuned together in perfect unison. Once this is done, they should be treated as if they were a single string. 

After this, find as many movable bridges <note>original: "scannelli mobili"</note> as there are strings stretched over the surface—I say "movable" so that they can be moved from one place to another as needed. These should be made of such a length that they touch only one of those strings, and tall enough so that they do not exceed the height of the fixed ones, being all of the same height and manufactured in this manner, or another, provided they meet the qualities I have described. 

Once you have arranged things in this way, if we take one of these bridges and place it under any of the stretched strings so that the string rests upon the bridge at point **c** (as placed in the example in Chapter 18), and if one strikes the string **cb** on the right side along with another string without a bridge (for I will always place the high-pitched sounds <note>original: "suoni acuti"</note> on this side, both because of the terms of their proportions and because they are found on this side in musical instruments), between the sound of this string, which will be **ab**, and the sound of **cb**, one will hear the consonance of the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. 

But if we mark a third string at point **d** with one of the movable bridges, as seen in the second example in the place mentioned, by striking this together with one of the unmarked strings (that is, **db** with **ab**), the sounds born from these two strings will create the consonance of the Perfect Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>. Similarly, if we strike strings **ab** and **cb** together with **db**, we will hear the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> mediated by **db**, divided by harmonic proportionality into a Perfect Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> (**ab** and **db**) and a Perfect Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> (**db** and **cb**); which (as I have said at other times) joined together create the consonance of the Octave. 

Furthermore, if we wish to hear the Perfect Fifth already accommodated in the preceding chapter, it will suffice simply to place one of the movable bridges at point **c**; for by striking the strings **ac** and **cb** on the right and left sides, one can undoubtedly hear that consonance. In this division, a single string is sufficient; however, it is true that this method is more difficult than the first. In the first method shown, more than one string is needed, as we have seen, and it is a more...

### On the multiplication of consonances. Chapter 21.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a landscape with a building and clouds.</image-desc>
I STATED in the First Part that every proportion <note>original: "Proportione"</note> found in discrete quantity <note>discrete quantity refers to whole numbers used in arithmetic</note> also has a place in continuous quantity <note>continuous quantity refers to physical measurements like lines or strings in geometry</note>. This is because every proportion is found within the latter. I say again that proportions not only have a place in such quantity, but they can also be multiplied, divided, and subjected to any other operation, as we shall see below. Having shown how one can fit consonances to their proportions in continuous quantity—that is, in sounding bodies—I will now show the method one must follow when wishing to fit many of them one after another. This is done in such a way that the high end <note>original: "estremo acuto"</note> of one interval placed in the low range becomes the low end <note>original: "estremo graue"</note> of the next interval placed in the high range. We can call this method "Multiplying," for to arrange consonances in this way is nothing other than multiplying their proportions by placing them before or adding them to one another.

But because I showed in the First Part that multiplication in numbers can be done in two ways, I also want to show two ways of multiplying consonances (so that this operation corresponds to that of the numbers), which will be very necessary. The first will correspond to the multiplication described in Chapter 31 of the First Part, called "Appending" <note>original: "Soggiungere"</note>, which is done when one begins from the left and moves toward the right. The second will correspond to the multiplication in Chapter 32, which proceeds in reverse—from the right side to the left—and is called "Pre-posing" <note>original: "Preporre"</note>. 

Beginning then with the first method, we will first arrange the radical terms <note>the lowest whole numbers of a ratio, e.g., 3:2 for a Fifth</note> of the proportions of the intervals we wish to multiply one after another in order, according to the method shown in Chapter 31 of the First Part. Then, we will fit the first consonance placed on the left side to its proportion in the low part of the string (as we did above). To append the next one to this, we will always take that part of the string (or line) that represents the high sound of the fitted consonance, leaving aside the part taken for the low sound. Upon that line, we will fit the second consonance or interval, dividing it into as many parts as there are units contained in the larger term of its proportion. Between this divided line (representing the larger term) and the parts representing the smaller term, we will have multiplied the second consonance to the first. By always taking the smaller line representing the high sound of the multiplied consonance and dividing it according to the terms of the proportion of the consonance we wish to append (setting aside the low part), we will achieve our purpose.

Suppose we wish to Multiply or Append a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> to a Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>; and to the Fourth, a Major Third <note>original: "Ditono"</note>; and to this, a Minor Third <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>. It is first necessary to know the radical terms or lowest numbers of the proportions of these consonances and place them one after another in the order we wish to multiply them, in this manner: <gloss>3 4 5 6 / 2 3 4 5</gloss> <note>These represent the ratios 3:2, 4:3, 5:4, and 6:5</note>. 

Then, starting from the Fifth, whose terms are 3 and 2, we will fit it to its proportion on the line **a b** below, in the manner I showed in Chapter 18; we will have the proportion of that consonance between **a b** and **c b**. Now, to append or multiply the Fourth to it, we will take **c b** (which represents the high sound of the Fifth), leaving **a c** aside. By fitting the Fourth to its proportion upon this line, we will have our result between **c b** and **d b**. To then append the Major Third to these, leaving aside **a d** and taking **d b**, we will divide it into five equal parts; by taking four of them, we will have joined the Major Third to the two previously fitted consonances between **d b** and **e b**. Then, taking **e b** and fitting the Minor Third upon it in the shown manner, we will have appended or multiplied (according to our goal) the Minor Third to the first three consonances between **e b** and **f b**, as seen in the figure. And this is the first method of multiplying, called Appending.

## On the second method of multiplying consonances. Chapter 22.

IN the second method, it is necessary (having first placed in order the <term>proportions: the numerical ratios that define musical intervals</term> of the <term>consonances: pleasing combinations of notes</term> that you wish to multiply) to first find the extreme strings that can arise from such a multiplication. These can easily be found when we sum their proportions together, contained in their <term>radical terms: the simplest whole-number form of a ratio, such as 3:2 instead of 6:4</term>. We then divide the <term>string: the sounding length of a monochord</term> into as many equal parts as there are units contained in the larger term of the proportion resulting from that sum. Then, by taking as many parts from the right side as there are units contained in the smaller term of that product, we will achieve our goal. This is because the whole string and these parts will be the ones we seek, which serve our purpose. 

To multiply these consonances, we will divide the high extreme string into as many equal parts as there are units in the smaller term of the first proportion, placed in the high range on the right side. Using the same logic, by adding enough parts to reach the number of units contained in the larger term, we will have accommodated that consonance in the high part according to its proportion between the divided string and the one increased by the addition of the part. If we then wish to prefix or multiply another interval to this one, we take the string that gives the low sound of the already placed consonance (which will serve as the high sound for the one we want to multiply) and divide it into as many parts as there are units in the smaller term of the proportion containing the consonance we wish to multiply. Furthermore, by adding as many parts as are equal to its larger term, we will have the second consonance placed before and multiplied by the first, situated between this string (which will give the low sound) and the divided one (which will produce the high sound). I say the same for the others; but let us come to an example. 

Suppose we want to multiply together a <term>Major Third: an interval of four semitones, originally called a Ditone</term>, a <term>Minor Third: an interval of three semitones, originally called a Semiditone</term>, and a <term>Perfect Fourth: originally called a Diatessaron</term>, in such a way that the Perfect Fourth is placed in the high range, the Major Third in the low range, and the Minor Third occupies the middle. I say that we must first set the terms of the proportions of these consonances in order, in the way they are to be multiplied. To find the extreme strings of this multiplication, we will sum the proportions together in the manner I showed in Chapter 33 of the First Part <note>In 16th-century music theory, "summing" proportions refers to multiplying the fractions together: (5/4) * (6/5) * (4/3) = 120/60</note>. These will be 5/4, 6/5, and 4/3, and we will have an <term>Octave: a 2:1 ratio, originally called a Duple</term>, contained between these terms of 120 and 60;

# Second [Part]

...which, reduced to its **radical terms** <note>the simplest whole-number form of a ratio</note>, will be found between 2 and 1. Having done this, we will divide the line *a–b* into two equal parts at point *c*, and we will have *a–b* and *c–b*, which will be in a **double proportion** <note>original: *proportione dupla*, or a 2:1 ratio</note>, and these will become the extreme strings of such a multiplication.

Now, we will first arrange the **Perfect Fourth** <term>Diatessaron: an interval spanning four notes of a scale</term> in its proportion in the high part <note>original: *parte acuta*</note>, by dividing the line *c–b* into three equal parts, according to the number of units contained in the smaller term of its proportion <note>the ratio of a Fourth is 4:3</note>. Then, by adding a fourth part at point *d*, we will have the line *d–b*, which will contain four parts, according to the number of units included in the larger term of the proportion, and this will give us the **low sound** <note>original: *suono graue*</note> of the Perfect Fourth. 

Thus, between *c–b*, which contains three parts, and *d–b*, which contains four parts, the **Sesquiterza** <term>Sesquiterza: a ratio of 4:3, where the larger number contains the smaller plus one-third of it</term> proportion will be contained; and between them the Perfect Fourth is arranged in the high register in its true proportion—as could be seen by providing the reasons in the manner shown above in chapters 18 and 19, which for brevity are omitted. 

But to multiply and place the **Minor Third** <term>Semiditono: literally a "half-ditone," known today as a minor third</term> before this, we will divide *d–b* into five parts, for the smaller term of its proportion <note>the ratio of a Minor Third is 6:5</note>; and by adding another part at point *e* for its larger term, between *e–b* and *d–b* we will have placed the Minor Third in its proportion, positioned before the Perfect Fourth. And between *a–b* and *e–b* we will have the **Major Third** <term>Ditono: literally "two tones," known today as a major third</term> placed before the Minor Third. This is because between these two strings is found the **Sesquiquarta** <term>Sesquiquarta: a ratio of 5:4</term> proportion; since *a–b* contains *e–b* once plus one-fourth of it. This proportion is without any doubt its proper form, as has been seen elsewhere. 

We can therefore say that between the extremes of the **Octave** <term>Diapason: the interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency</term>, starting from the high extreme, we have placed the three named **consonances** <note>pleasing musical intervals</note> in their proportions, having multiplied and placed them one before the other: that is, between *d–b* and *c–b* the **Perfect Fourth**; between *e–b* and *d–b* the **Minor Third**; and between *a–b* and *e–b* the **Major Third**, as seen in the figure. If we wish to hear these, by operating in the manner shown and with the help of **movable bridges** <term>Scannelli mobili: small wooden blocks used to change the vibrating length of a string on a monochord</term> placed under the strings, we can be made clear not only regarding this but every other doubt that might occur on the subject.

# How any chosen consonance, or interval, is rationally divided. Chapter 23.

AFTER multiplication—if we wish to follow the order established in the first part regarding the operations of **Proportions** <note>the mathematical ratios used to define musical intervals</note>—Summation and Subtraction would immediately follow. However, because they are not strictly necessary, we will only look at the manner in which musical intervals are divided. This is nothing more than placing a middle string between two extremes, which divides the interval into two parts. This division is of two kinds: **Rational** and **Irrational**. The Irrational does not serve the Musician’s purpose except by accident, but the Rational is of three types: namely, **Arithmetic**, **Geometric**, or **Harmonic**. These correspond to the Proportionalities found in **discrete quantity** <term>Discrete quantity: mathematics involving distinct numbers, like 1, 2, 3</term>, in the manner shown in the First Part. Even though any consonance or any other interval could be divided into two parts by a middle string at random and without further thought, such a division is not considered by the Musician, for it oversteps the boundaries of his Science. 

Therefore, a consonance is divided in **Arithmetic proportionality** when its extremes are mediated or divided by a middle string such that the smaller part of the division is heard between the middle and the **low sound** <note>original: *graue*</note> of the consonance, and the larger part is heard between the middle and the **high sound** <note>original: *acuta*</note>. Conversely, it is divided **Harmonically** by such a string when the two members of the division are situated and placed opposite to those mentioned above: in such a way that the larger part occupies the low position and the smaller the high. This occurs in the division of the **Octave** <term>Diapason: the interval of an eighth</term>; when it is divided by a middle string into a **Fifth** <term>Diapente</term> and a **Fourth** <term>Diatessaron</term>, in the Arithmetic division the Fourth holds the low position and the Fifth the high; in the Harmonic division, the opposite occurs—the Fifth is found in the low and the Fourth in the high, as demonstrated by the division of each in discrete quantity. 

A consonance or other interval is divided in **Geometric proportionality** when its extreme sounds are mediated by a middle string in such a way that the two parts arising from the division are not larger than one another in proportion; rather, the part placed in the high register is of the same quantity and proportion as the one in the low. This occurs when the **Double Octave** <term>Disdiapason: an interval of a fifteenth, with a 4:1 ratio</term> is divided into two Octaves by a middle string; both parts are, without any doubt, contained by the **Double proportion** <note>original: *proportione Dupla*, or 2:1</note>. 

For greater convenience, these divisions will first be made with numbers, and then their proportions will be applied to **continuous quantity** <term>Continuous quantity: physical measurements, such as the length of a string</term> upon the sounding strings. But because—as I have said many times—every arithmetic and harmonic division is only rational, while the geometric can be both rational and irrational; and since the rational is easy to perform, while the Irrational is sometimes more relevant to the Musician than the Rational, before I go any further, I will demonstrate how every Consonance and every musical interval (no matter how small) can be divided not only into two parts, but even into many equal irrational parts when necessary. I will first show a brief and efficient way to divide it into only two parts, and then I will provide the method to divide it into more parts when needed.

# How any chosen Musical interval can be divided into two equal parts. Chapter 24.

TO show how any musical interval can be divided into two equal parts, it will serve our purpose well to use the Ninth [Proposition] of the Sixth [Book] of **Euclid** <note>A Greek mathematician known as the "Father of Geometry"</note> according to **Campanus** <note>Campanus of Novara, a 13th-century mathematician who edited Euclid</note>; or the 13th [Proposition] and fifth Problem according to **Theone** <note>Theon of Alexandria, a 4th-century scholar</note>, which says: *Given two straight lines, we can find a mean proportional.* This is effectively the same as saying: *Given two sounds, we can find a proportional middle sound for them.* 

This is the method: Let us suppose that in the example below, the Octave consonance is arranged according to its proportion between string *a–b* and string *c–b*; and it is necessary to find a middle string that, placed between these two, divides it geometrically into two equal parts. We will first extend the line *a–b*, starting from point *b* toward the right side, until point *d*, in such a way that *b–d* is equal to *c–b*, and we will have the line *a–d*. Having done this, we will describe a semicircle, whose diameter...

# Part.

Geometry, in teaching how to find two mean proportional lines between two proposed ones, makes it clear that without the aid of an instrument, named by some the **Mesolabe** <term>Mesolabe: an ancient mechanical instrument, often attributed to Eratosthenes, used to find mean proportionals—essentially the geometric means—between two line segments</term>, every effort would be vain and useless; therefore, before I go any further, I will show the method of constructing the Instrument; and afterwards, I will teach how to find the lines. One must, therefore, first prepare a board or very flat table, even in its surface, which is at least one foot wide and as long as one wishes—though the longer it is, the more convenient it will be. Having reduced it to a long rectangular shape <note>original: *figura quadrata lunga*</note> containing four right angles at its corners (to be able to operate better and without any error), we shall diligently make a channel upon it. We do this by placing two thin, carefully made rulers or strips along the sides of the said table or board, so that, being equidistant, the edges of the channel come to be as high as the back of a knife, and no more. Once this is done, we shall make three very thin rectangular figures of metal or wood, which Geometers call **Parallelograms**, having four right angles; these should be as long as the channel is wide, and as wide as one wishes, provided they are constructed in such a way that one is equal to the other—that is, the sides of one are equal to the sides of the other. Then, on two of them, we shall draw a diagonal line from the upper left corner to the lower right corner of each, in such a way that the surfaces are divided into two equal **Right-angled triangles** <note>original: *triangoli Orthogonij*</note>, as is seen here.

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram depicting the Mesolabio, an instrument for finding mean proportionals. The diagram shows a large rectangular frame (labeled d, e, f, g) containing three overlapping rectangles. The first rectangle (h i k l) is fixed on the left. The second (n o p q) and third (r f t u) rectangles have diagonal lines (n q and r u) and are shown as if they can slide horizontally. We shall then place the Squares in the said channel one after another in this manner: the first, without a diagonal, shall be on the left side and remain immobile; then the others, which have the diagonals—namely the second and the third—in order on the right side, so that the right side of one is placed over the left of the other; and thus we will have made the said Instrument. It shall be $defg$; and let $hikl$ be the first immobile square without a diagonal; the second $nopq$, whose diagonal is $nq$; and the third $rftu$, whose diagonal is $ru$. Let us now suppose that we must find a mean proportional string which divides the **Diapason** <term>Diapason: the Greek term for the Octave interval</term> consonance—contained by the **Double ratio** <term>Double ratio: the 2:1 ratio representing the octave</term>—into two equal parts between the two given strings or lines $ab$ and $cb$; and let these be equal to the $ab$ and the $cb$ placed in the preceding chapter. We shall first make the right side of the first square, namely $lk$, equal to $ab$ at point $m$, making it $lm$. Then we shall take the second square and slide it under the first until its diagonal $nq$ cuts the side $kl$ of the first square at point $m$; thus the first and second squares will remain fixed. We shall then make the right side of the third square, namely $ut$, equal to $cb$ at point $x$; and having placed a very fine thread at point $m$, which will be the $mx$ of the example below, we shall stretch it until it passes through point $x$. Now we shall slide the third square under the second until the side $pq$ is cut by the diagonal $ru$ and by the said thread at a single point, which will be $y$; and that part of the right side of the second square which remains under the thread, which is $qy$, will be the sought-after proportional line or string, as is seen in the figure.

And this is manifest by the preceding demonstration: for the mean proportional line $qy$ found in the Mesolabe between $ab$ and $cb$ is equal to the $be$ found in the preceding chapter. This could be proven if one were to describe on a flat surface all the lines made in the Mesolabe, first extending the line $mx$ to point $z$ according to the **Second Postulate** <note>original: *Seconda dimanda*</note> of the first book of Euclid. For then we would have three triangles containing a right angle, namely $lmz$, $qyz$, and $uxz$; from which it would be demonstrated by the Principles and Demonstrations of Euclid that the whole is true—as by the **Second Common Notion** <note>original: *Secondo parer commune*</note> and by the ninth; by the 28th and by the second part of the 32nd of the first book; by the second, fourth, and sixth of the Sixth book; and by the eleventh of the Fifth; all of which I omit, because I have treated such matters extensively in my *Harmonic Demonstrations* <note>Zarlino refers here to his own work, *Dimostrationi harmoniche* (1571)</note>. It will suffice for me, then, to say only that when one wishes to find more mean lines or proportional strings—that is, wanting to divide any Musical Interval into more parts—it is necessary to use the method shown. One must, however, note that for every line or string one wishes to add beyond the one found, it will be necessary to also add another Parallelogram or Square with its diagonal, made in the same manner and size as the first ones; then ensuring that the right sides of every Square come to be marked at the same point by the diagonals and by the thread in the manner shown.

## MESOLABIO
<term>Mesolabe: A mathematical instrument used to find geometric means. In music theory of this period, it was used to divide musical intervals (like the octave) into equal parts, which was a significant challenge for Renaissance theorists.</term>

*Note that one must always place the first square, which is immobile, without a diagonal line <note>original: "diametro"</note>; its right side must be intersected by the diagonal of the following square at the point representing the length of the longer proposed line. The right side of the last square should be intersected by the wire <note>original: "filo," referring to the sliding string or diameter used in the diagram</note> at the point marking the length of the shorter proposed line, according to the given method. If the longer proposed line were longer than the square placed in the Mesolabe, nothing could be done. However, it is quite true that by taking half of each of the two proposed lines, the goal can be achieved: for after the work is finished, the mean proportionals found can be lengthened according to the ratio of the part taken from the proposed lines; and thus, everything will turn out well.*

### How Consonance is made divisible. Chapter 26.

But because everything that has the power to change the *Senses* is called a *Passible Quality* <term>Passible Quality: In Aristotelian philosophy, a quality that can be perceived by the senses or that results from an "affection" or change in matter</term> by the *Philosophers* <note>The "Philosopher" almost always refers to Aristotle</note>; one should know that since *Consonance* is undoubtedly *Sound*, and possesses such power (as stated in its explanation above), it can also be called a *Passible Quality*. This is because (as the *Philosopher* maintains) it is drawn out of the power of the striker and the struck, as I have shown above. On this point, one might reasonably doubt how *Consonance* can be divided or multiplied, since it is neither Number nor Proportion: for division or multiplication belongs only to *Quantity*, and is its specific property.

Responding to this doubt, I say that although *Quantity* is divisible and multipliable essentially and by itself, it cannot be denied that *Quality* can also be divided and multiplied by accident <note>In logic/philosophy, "by accident" means a property is shared through a relationship with something else rather than through its own essence</note>. This is because it is subject to *Quantity*; when the latter is divided or multiplied essentially and by itself, the *Quality* is simultaneously divided or multiplied—not properly, but certainly by accident, as I have said. This can be seen by giving a suitable example in the division of the *heavy* and the *light* <note>original: *graue, & leggiero*</note>, which things are not *quantities*, but rather *qualities*; they do not undergo division except insofar as they are subject to a *divisible* body, to which division properly belongs;

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 96 regarding how "Consonance"—though categorized as a "passible quality"—can be considered divisible. division; in its division, even though accidents <term>Accident: In Aristotelian philosophy, a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing, such as color or sound, which cannot exist without a physical subject.</term> are indivisible in themselves, they are nonetheless accidentally divisible. This is because they have their being essentially in things that are divisible; as can also be seen in the **Color** placed in **Wood**, for when such wood is essentially divided into many parts, the color is likewise divided by accident into many parts. Thus, I say on this subject that although Consonance is in itself indivisible, being a quality, nonetheless when the sonorous bodies are essentially divided into many parts (as I have shown), it also becomes divisible by accident, according to the division of its Subject, which are those sonorous bodies. We can therefore say that although Consonance by itself is not divisible, it is nonetheless divisible by accident through the division of its subject; and so, from what has been said above and from what was said in Chapter 41 of the First Part, one can see how Aristotle’s definition of Consonance can be understood, where he says: *That it is a ratio of numbers in the high and the low* <note>original: "ragion de numeri nell' acuto, & nel graue"</note>; and how one might respond to all those who, with sophisticated arguments, wish to oppose such a definition.

# What the Monochord is, and why it is so called.
## Cap. 27.

HAVING SEEN all these things, I will now come (according to my primary intention) to the ordering, or composition, or let us say division, of the Monochord of each species of the three named genera <note>The three genera of ancient Greek music: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note>: but first we shall see what the Monochord is. I say, then, that the Monochord is that instrument, or any other similar to it, which I showed above in Chapter 18, which has been called differently by many. For Ptolemy and Boethius call it the **Harmonic Rule** <term>Regola harmonica: A scientific instrument used to measure the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</term>, and some of the Greeks call it the **magas** <term>μαγὰς: Originally a bridge on a stringed instrument, but here referring to the instrument itself.</term>; it is an instrument of a single string, with which—adding the judgment of reason through the power of harmonic proportionality—we investigate the ratios of musical consonances and every part of them. In it are found and accepted many sounds, which we place according to the degrees of the low and the high in their proper places, and we describe them with their own names, so that through this artifice we may learn to practice modulations and harmonies. And Pythagoras (according to Boethius) was the inventor of this instrument. This name Monochord derives from two Greek names joined together: from **monos** <note>original: μόνος</note>, which means **Solo** or **Single**, and from **chorde** <note>original: χορὴ</note>, which means **String**; that is, an instrument of a single string. This is so even though that instrument played with doubled strings, known by everyone today as it is in common use, is also called by this name: but that is not relevant to our purpose.

# On the Division, or Ordering, of the Monochord of the first species of the diatonic genus, called Ditonic Diatonic; on the name of each string; and who was the Inventor of this Genus and its order.
## Cap. 28.

TO ARRIVE at the Ordering, or Division, as we wish to call it, of the Monochord of the first species of the first genus, called by Ptolemy **Ditonic Diatonic** <term>Diatonico diatono: The "natural" scale of the Greeks, built on two whole tones and a semi-tone, often associated with Pythagorean tuning.</term>, we must first take care to order it, or divide it, into five Tetrachords <term>Tetrachord: A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</term>, so that we follow the custom of the Ancient musicians. The first of these we shall call **Hypaton** <term>Hypaton: Literally "the principal" or "highest" in rank, though it refers to the lowest-pitched notes in the Greek system.</term>, because it holds the lowest part; the second **Meson**, meaning **Middle**, since it holds almost the middle place and is higher than the first; the third **Diezeugmenon**, or **Separated**; and the last of the four, which comprise the Fifteen strings (as we shall see), we shall name **Hyperboleon**, or **Excellent**. To these we shall then add the Fifth, and we shall call it **Synemennon**, meaning **Conjoined**; and we shall have an order of Sixteen strings, contained in the **Disdiapason** <term>Disdiapason: A double octave, the standard range of the Greek "Greater Perfect System."</term>, which the Greeks call the **Greatest System** <note>original: "Sistema massimo"</note>. But it should be noted that the Ancients divided or ordered their Monochord by Tetrachords, and not by Pentachords or Hexachords, for two reasons. First, because they held that the **Diatessaron** <term>Diatessaron: The interval of a perfect fourth.</term>, which was contained within the extremes of the Tetrachord, was the first consonance, because it was the smallest of all the others; second, because one can always add to the Tetrachord from the high side that interval which is placed in the low part of that same Tetrachord, or conversely, place in the low what is found in the high, which will always yield the consonance of the **Diatessaron** in every species of harmony for every genus. Second Part

...fit comfortably into the Fifth <term>Diapente: The musical interval of a perfect fifth.</term>, nor even into the Hexachord <term>Essachordo: A scale of six notes.</term>: since by taking a low interval of the Fourth <term>Diatessaron: The musical interval of a perfect fourth.</term> and adding it to the high, or conversely, taking that which is placed in the high and putting it in the low, one could not always maintain the consonance of the Fifth; even though one could have the number of strings from which the Fifth is named. Therefore, the Greeks, having this awareness, created the Ordering, or Division, of the Great System <term>Sistema massimo: Also known as the Greater Perfect System, the standard framework of Greek music theory.</term> by Tetrachords <term>Tetrachord: A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</term>, and not by Pentachords or Hexachords. Wishing then to give a beginning to such an order or division, following the custom of the Ancients not only in this but in every other division; for its foundation we shall first accommodate in the lowest part the Sesquioctave Tone <note>The "Tuono sesquiottauo" is the ratio 9:8, the standard whole tone in Pythagorean tuning.</note> according to its proportion; so that the lowest string, called by the Greeks *Proslambanomenos* <note>original: "Proslambanomenos", meaning "the added note."</note>, with the high string of the second Tetrachord called *Mese* <note>original: "Mese", meaning "the middle."</note>, contains and makes heard the consonance of the Octave <term>Diapason: The musical interval of an octave.</term>. To this Tone we shall add the first Tetrachord, and to this the second. Afterward, we shall add to this the interval of the Tone contained by the Sesquioctave proportion. Adding then to this the third Tetrachord, and to the third the fourth, in its highest part; we shall have fifteen strings contained by such an order. This being done, we shall add above the string *Mese* the fifth Tetrachord, and thus we shall have the ordering or division of the first diatonic species, contained within sixteen strings and among five Tetrachords, in the manner we shall see. Of this order, I believe the inventor was Terpander of Lesbos, when he reduced the first seven ancient strings into one, joining them by two Tetrachords, as can be seen in the second example of chapter 20 of the first book of the *Music* of Boethius; which were afterward reduced by Lycaon of Samos to the number of eight, and divided into two separate Tetrachords; as is manifest from the third example placed by Boethius in the aforementioned place. It was afterward increased by others in such a manner that it reached the number of sixteen strings, in the way I intend to show; although some wish for Pythagoras to be the Inventor of this first genus and this first species, and of the first species of the two following Generi. But be that as it may, Pythagoras was the one who discovered the ratio of Sounds, in the manner I have shown in the First Part. Wishing then to show the order of this first species, and the division of its Monochord contained by five Tetrachords, in order to be able to place it under the judgment of the senses; so that I may afterward reason more freely upon what I have to say (not deviating from the custom of the Ancients), once one has prepared an instrument similar to that which I showed above in chapter 18; after having accommodated in it a line that passes from one end to the other through the middle, in the manner seen in the example below, which will be AB; we shall first accommodate to its proportion the Sesquioctave Tone, which will be between AB and CB, in the manner I have taught elsewhere. To which we shall immediately join the first Tetrachord called *Hypaton* <note>original: "Hypaton", meaning "the lowest" or principal ones.</note> in this way: once its extremes have been accommodated to their proportion, which will be CB and DB, without being mediated by any middle string; we shall multiply in their midst its middle strings, contained by their proportions. But it must be noted that not only in this, but in any other division, one must accommodate and multiply the intervals in such a way that the larger ones, contained by larger proportions, are always multiplied before the others; so that one may avoid, along with much labor, infinite errors that could arise: For having first multiplied those that are larger, necessarily and with little effort (as we shall see), the smaller ones also come to be accommodated. This will be manifest by multiplying the intervals of the Tetrachords, accommodating the middle strings proportionately in their place: Since after one has accommodated the two Sesquioctave tones to their proportion, multiplying them in the manner I showed in chapter 22; we shall have placed in the high the first Tone between EB and DB, and the second in the low between FB and EB. And because every Tetrachord of this species is composed of two Sesquioctave intervals and the proportion *Super 13. partiente 243* <note>This ratio, 256:243, is the Pythagorean minor semitone or "limma."</note>, which is the form of the minor Semitone; FB and EB being a Tone, and similarly EB and DB; it follows that CB and FB is the interval of the Semitone, which is the supplement of the two Tones to the perfection of the Tetrachord. And this is manifest: for if we take from the Sesquitertia <term>Sesquitertia: The ratio 4:3, which defines the musical Fourth.</term>, which is the form of the Tetrachord, two Sesquioctave proportions, there will remain the proportion *Super 13. partiente 243* containing the minor Semitone. This done, to add to the said Tetrachord the second called *Meson* <note>original: "Meson", meaning "the middle" ones.</note>, we shall accommodate it in the way the first was done, above the line DB; and there will come GB and DB, which will be the extremes, and HB and GB will be the high Tone, and the low will be IB and HB. But DB and IB, for the reasons stated, will be the minor Semitone. To this Tetrachord we shall join the Sesquioctave Tone, by which we shall separate the Third from this, and such separation we shall call, with Boethius, *disjunction* <note>original Greek: διάζευξις (diazeuxis), meaning a gap or disjunction between tetrachords.</note>, which means Division, from which name the third Tetrachord is called Die-

### Part

...*zeugmenon* <note>original: "zeugmenon," Greek for "disjunct" or "separated."</note>, that is, **Separated**. And this separation is found only where two <term>Tetrachords: A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</term>, through the interposition of a **Tone** <note>The "disjunctive tone" that separates two tetrachords in the Greek system.</note>, are detached from one another. But when the highest string of one is the lowest string of the other, then they are joined to each other, and such a union is called **Συναφή** <note>original: "Synaphē," meaning "conjunction" or "connection."</note>, that is, **Joining**; as the same **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose work "The Principles of Music" transmitted Greek theory to the Middle Ages.</note> demonstrates in chapter 24 of the first book of *Music*. Having added, then, the Tone to the *Meson* <note>The "middle" tetrachord.</note> tetrachord, which will be contained between the points K B and G B, we shall then without any middle step multiply the third tetrachord to K B, dividing the said line in the manner shown; once this is done, we will have its outer strings K B and L B, with M B and N B in between, which give us the division of the Tetrachord into two Tones and one Semitone. Now, above the string L B, we shall place the fourth tetrachord, called ***Hyperboleon*** <note>The "highest" or "extreme" tetrachord in pitch.</note>, operating as was done with the others, and we will have L B and O B, which are its outer strings, and P B and Q B, which are the middle ones, which make the division into two tones and one semitone according to the established order; so that we shall have an order, or division, of **Fifteen strings**; to which we will add the last tetrachord called ***Synemmenon*** <note>The "conjunct" tetrachord, used for modulation.</note>, joining it to the second in this way: that is, making the usual division above the string G B, and between it and M B, we will have the outer strings, whose middle ones will be N B and R B. It is quite true that only the string R B will be added anew, because the others are common to the other tetrachords. Hence, I believe that such a string was added for two reasons: one to give the understanding that every Tone can be divided into two Semitones; the other to acquire a <term>Diatessaron: A perfect fourth.</term> toward the high end, starting from the string *parhypate meson*. And if it were added for some other reason, this is of little importance; and whatever the case may be, we shall have by such an addition even the **greater semitone** between R B and K B, contained by the ratio of 2187 to 2048 <note>A mathematical ratio representing the Pythagorean "apotome."</note>, called by the Greeks **λεῖμμα** <note>original: "leimma," meaning "remainder."</note>, which when added to the minor one called **ἀποτομή** <note>original: "apotome," meaning "a cutting off."</note>, gives us the Sesquioctave Tone <note>The 9:8 whole tone.</note>: because the string R B of this tetrachord divides the Tone G B and K B into two parts, which are those named. This, then, will be the entire division, or composition, of the Monochord of the ***first species of the Diatonic***, called the **Diatonic Diatonos**, divided or rather ordered according to the mind of the ancient ***Pythagoreans*** into five tetrachords, in which are contained fifteen intervals between sixteen strings; these strings I have described with their ancient names, and noted with their proportions, multiplied according to the methods shown above in chapters 32 and 33 of the First Part, for a greater understanding of what has been said. And although the Ancients named the strings of this arrangement with the names I have shown, which are very different from those we have at present, this is not of great importance: since it is granted to the first inventors of things to name them from their cause, or from their effect, or simply at their pleasure. The Ancients, then, named the strings of their citharas <note>An ancient Greek string instrument similar to a lyre.</note> with such names because Music—as Boethius recounts according to the opinion of **Nicomachus**—was in the beginning so simple that only the **Quadrichord** <note>A four-stringed instrument.</note> was used, which **Mercury** invented (as has been said elsewhere) in imitation of the "world music" of the four elements; it was later reduced by **Terpander** to the number of seven strings, in imitation of the seven planets. And of these strings they called the lowest ***Hypate***, that is, Principal, or greater, and more honored; hence they also named Jove ***Hypaton***, and the **Consuls** <note>Roman magistrates.</note> took the aforementioned name because of the excellence of their dignity. The second was called ***Parhypate***, because it was placed next to the *Hypate*. The third they called ***Lychanos***: since the Greeks call by that name the finger we call the **Index**, from the light touching done with it, and also because in playing the said string, that finger was put to use. ***Mese*** is the name of the fourth: since among the seven it was placed in the middle. The fifth is ***Paramese***, that is, placed next to the *Mese*. The sixth is ***Paranete***: because it was near the *Nete*. But the seventh they called ***Nete***, almost as if ***Neate***, that is, Lowest <note>In ancient lyres, the highest-pitched string was physically lowest in position, near the ground.</note>. When this order was later increased in the manner shown, they named them from the names above, adding the name of the Tetrachords in which they were placed; and the lowest string of this order they called ***Proslambanomenos***, that is, **Acquired** <note>Or "Added note."</note>, since they added it so that with the eighth string called *Mese* it would make the consonance of the ***Diapason*** <note>The interval of an octave.</note> heard. And not only were the strings of this species named with such names in this first genre, but the others as well for every other species in every genre, because every species is divided or ordered into five tetrachords, as we shall see.

Part 2.

## That the Ancients attributed certain strings of their instruments to the celestial spheres. Chapter 29.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'L' featuring a seated figure in a pastoral landscape with a tree.</image-desc>THE OPINION that the Ancients held, especially the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that the universe was ordered by numerical and musical ratios.</note>, concerning the **harmony** or **concert of the Heavens**, gave them cause to contemplate various things regarding this matter. From the diversity of their opinions, different principles and various reasons arose. For some held the opinion that the **Firmament**, or what we might call the Sphere of the fixed stars—which of all others is the fastest in its daily motion (as **Plato** affirms)—sent out a sound higher <note>original: "acuto," meaning high-pitched.</note> than any other Sphere. They were perhaps led by this reasoning: that the body which moves most quickly causes the highest sound; therefore, since the superior bodies of Heaven move more quickly than the inferior ones, they concluded that such bodies produced the highest sound. On the other hand, there were some who held the contrary: that the Sphere of the **Moon** produced the highest sound, forming this reason: larger bodies return a greater and lower <note>original: "grave," meaning low-pitched.</note> sound than smaller ones do, as is perceptibly understood. Since the superior celestial bodies are larger than the inferior ones, it follows that the larger superior bodies send out greater and lower sounds than the inferior ones. Those who favored the first opinion were many, among whom is **Cicero** in the sixth book of the *Republic*, as can be seen by the words placed in chapter 4 of the First Part; this opinion **Ambrose**, the Holy Doctor, recounts in his *Hexameron* <note>A commentary on the six days of Creation.</note>. But among modern writers is found **Battista Mantovano**, a most elegant poet, who reveals this opinion to us with these words:

> The heavens rang, and a harmony was heard from far on high,
> a mixed melody; one part, driven faster,
> echoed more brightly and with a high song,
> while the slow part moved with a lower sound.
> <note>original Latin: "Insonuere poli, longéq; auditus ab alto / Concentus, mixtumq; melos, pars ocyus actâ / Clarius, & cantu longé reſonabat acuto, / Tarda ibat grauiore ſono."</note>

It is true that what he says can be adapted to either of the two narrated opinions. For if we wish to attribute the slowness of annual movement to the Sphere of **Saturn**, its movement is truly slower than any other Sphere, as Plato shows in his *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue concerning astronomy and wisdom.</note>, given that it completes its revolution in thirty years; and this would favor those who hold that larger bodies make the lower sound. But if the slowness is attributed to the daily <note>diurnal</note> motion, it will favor those who support the first opinion, and it will be necessary to understand the opposite; for there is no doubt, as seen by the senses, that the movement of the Sphere of the Moon is not slower than any other when it moves from East to West. But whether it be slower or faster, as one wishes, matters little to us; therefore, we will leave the care of their slowness or speed to the **Astronomers**. Of the other faction, many are found. For **Dio** <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian.</note> the historian, recounting the reason why the Days were named after the celestial Spheres and are not numbered according to their order, begins to give such a reason according to the opinion of the **Egyptians**, starting from the Sphere of Saturn and coming to that of the Sun, placing one and the other as the extremes of the consonance **Diatessaron** <note>The musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, leaving out the two middle ones, namely that of **Jupiter** and that of **Mars**. Then from that of the Sun, he goes to that of the Moon and forms another **Diatessaron**; similarly from this to that of Mars; and from Mars to **Mercury** he makes two others; so that always leaving the two middle Spheres, he gives the reason for such a problem, always returning circularly to the first Sphere. Thus it is seen that, starting from the Sphere of Saturn and coming to that of the Sun, and from this to that of the Moon, he places the first as that which makes the low sound; and coming toward the other Spheres, he places them as those that make the high sounds. For it is the custom of the majority of those who treat Music to place the low sound first in their arguments, as something more reasonable, and then the high. Nor should it seem strange if Dio returns from the Sphere of the Moon to that of Mars, making a reversed order, proceeding from high to low, contrary to what he had shown before; for it is enough for him simply to show the reason for such a thing by that means, even though this reason is not very sufficient to favor such an opinion. There is also the opinion of the Ancients that **Pliny** places in his *Natural History*, first of the celestial Harmony, then of the order; where he says that the Sphere of Saturn makes the **Dorian** sound, that of Jupiter the **Phrygian**, and the others in order other **Tones** <note>In this context, musical modes or scales.</note>. Thus there is no doubt that, the Dorian being held by the majority of Musicians as lower than the Phrygian, the sphere of Saturn is the one that produces the low sound.

It cites authorities like Plato, Cicero, and Pliny to link the planets to specific musical intervals (like the Diatessaron) and modes (like the Dorian).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 29 regarding how ancient philosophers mapped the musical scale onto the cosmos. Second [Part]

not deep <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "...less deep."</note>. Beyond this (leaving many others aside), there is **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the primary source for medieval and Renaissance music theory.</note>, who, as if reciting the opinion of others, attributes the string **Hypate** to **Saturn**, which is the deepest of all <note>original: "gravissima." In ancient Greek music theory, *Hypate* refers to the lowest notes of the scale, though the word literally means "highest," referring to its physical position on the lyre.</note>; then later, he attributes to the same sphere (following the first opinion likewise recited by him) the high sound, and the low ones in order, attributing the lowest to the **lunar globe**. From these differences it arose that the **Philosophers**, wishing to show in action that harmony which they knew by reason to be in the celestial spheres, attribute to each—as they were of different opinions on the location of the low and high sounds—different strings of their instruments, arranged in various ways.

For those who favored the first opinion attributed to the sphere of the **Moon**, the Planet closest to us, the string **Proslambanomenos** <note>The "acquired note," the lowest pitch in the Greek Greater Perfect System.</note>, because it makes a lower sound than any other; to that of **Mercury** the **Hypate hypaton**; and to the other spheres the other strings in order, according to how they are placed in the figure shown above. But those who had the contrary opinion attributed the string **Hypate meson** to the sphere of Saturn, because they thought it made the deepest sound of any other sphere; the **Parhypate** to **Jupiter**; **Lychanos** to **Mars**; and **Mese** <note>The "middle" note, serving as a structural anchor in the Greek scale.</note> to the **Sun**; and so to the others they attributed other strings, according to the shown order. And just as they were of various opinions regarding what I have said, so also they were different in placing the strings on their instruments. For those who held the opinion that Saturn made the high sound and the Moon the low...
