...placed the high-pitched strings in the soprano position of the instrument, or on the right side, and the low ones in the lowest place, or on the left side; and those who held the contrary opinion did the opposite: for they placed the low notes in the upper part, or on the right side, and the high notes in the lower part, or on the left side. But **Plato** assigned a **Siren** to each sphere (as I have said before in the First Part), which is to say one of the nine **Muses**, who sends forth (as he says) her own voice or sound, from which the harmony of the Heaven is born. And although he does not set down their order, nevertheless the most learned **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar who revived Neoplatonism; here referring to his commentary on Plato's *Phaedrus* regarding "poetic frenzy."</note> provides it in his work on Plato's *Poetic Frenzy*. He applies the Muse named **Thalia** to the first lunar sphere, **Euterpe** to Mercury, **Erato** to Venus, **Melpomene** to the Sun, and so on with the others in order, as is seen in the figure. It is indeed true that he attributes **Calliope** to every sphere, to indicate to us the concord that arises from the voices of them all. But because (as **Pliny** says) these things are investigated more for subtle delight than for necessity, I will make an end of it, having reasoned enough on such matters, and I shall come to show in what way the aforementioned sixteen strings were named by the Latins.

## How the aforementioned Sixteen strings were named by the Latins. Chap. 30.

And although the ancient Greeks, in the construction or division of the <term>Monochord<gloss>a single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals</gloss></term>, considered only sixteen strings, divided into five <term>Tetrachords<gloss>a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth</gloss></term>, and did not attempt to go beyond this for the reason stated above; nevertheless, the Moderns, not content with such a number, increased it, going further now into the low range and now into the high. For **Guido d'Arezzo** <note>An 11th-century music theorist regarded as the inventor of modern staff notation.</note> in his *Introductory*, besides the named strings, added others to a total of twenty-two, and arranged them into seven <term>Hexachords<gloss>a six-note scale; from the Greek "hexa" (six) and "chord" (string)</gloss></term>. This arrangement was, and is more than ever, accepted and embraced by the majority of practical musicians, since in it the strings are placed and ordered in the manner of the **Pythagorean** ones shown. And because each Hexachord is composed of six strings, it is named for that number, which means "of six strings." It is indeed true that to each of these, for the convenience of singers, he added some of these six syllables—namely **Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La**—taken from the **Hymn of Saint John the Baptist**, which begins in this way:

> **Ut** queant laxis **Re**sonare fibris **Mi**ra gestorum **Fa**muli tuorum,
> **Sol**ue polluti **La**bij reatum **Sancte Iohannes**;
> <note>original Latin: "So that your servants may sing the wonders of your deeds with relaxed vocal cords, wash away the guilt from our polluted lips, O Saint John."</note>

And he linked them with such skill and in such a manner that each contains all the species of the <term>Diatessaron<gloss>the interval of a perfect fourth</gloss></term>, of which there are three, as we shall see in the Third Part; placing the semitone, bounded by these two middle syllables **Mi** and **Fa**, in the middle of each. But he first added to the string **Proslambanomenos** <note>the lowest note in the Greek system</note> in the low part a string a whole tone away, and marked it with a Greek capital letter in this way: **Γ** <note>the letter Gamma</note>; and the others then with Latin letters, to show us that Music (as some maintain) was first discovered by the Greeks and put into use, and that at present it is honorably possessed, embraced, and increased by the Latins. And to the aforementioned letter he added the first of the six syllables, namely **Ut**, in this way: **Γ, ut**, which means **Gamma-ut**; and thus he named the added string with that name, and it is the first string of his arrangement. He then called the **Proslambanomenos** of the Greeks **A-re**, putting together the first Latin letter and the second syllable of those shown; and it was the second string of his *Introductory*. The third then—that is, the second Greek string, called **Hypate hypaton**—he named **♮, mi**, putting together the second Latin letter and the third following syllable. He placed this square letter <note>The "square b" (b quadro), ancestor of the natural ♮ and sharp # signs.</note>, different from the round **b** <note>The "round b" (b molle), ancestor of the flat sign ♭.</note>, to show us the difference of the semitones that these two strings make: for they are not in the same place, although they are joined as if in the same letter, as we shall see elsewhere. He then named the fourth **C, fa-ut**, and the rest in order up to **Nete hyperboleon** <note>the highest note in the Greek system</note>, applying to them one of the first Latin letters—namely A, ♮ (or b), C, D, E, F, G—writing them in the first order in capitals, in the second in small letters, and in the third doubled, as they are seen in the *Introductory*. But above **Nete hyperboleon** he added another five strings in the third order, namely **bb-fa**, **♮♮-mi**, **cc-sol-fa**, **dd-la-sol**, and **ee-la**; and he did this to finish the last two Hexachords, of which one begins on F and the other on G; and in this way the Greek strings acquired another naming. This order was held by Guido (as I believe) perhaps not without consideration, applying these syllables to the sounding strings, multiplied by the number **seven** (the **Septenary**): because he understood that the **Senary** (six) contained the diversity of the Tetrachords, and that in the Septenary there were seven sounds or voices, one from the other by natural division entirely varied and different; as can be seen,

These opinions would not be dismissed if they were according to the intent of such authors and were not far from the truth. However, since the Poets undoubtedly followed the opinion of Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle, and other most excellent ancient Musicians and Philosophers, it cannot be said that they ever had any intention of placing the Semiditone, the Ditone, and the two Hexachords in the number of consonances, for the reasons mentioned above in Chapter 10. But if anyone should say that in the Diapason there are found not only Seven sounds, or different voices, but even more, as can be seen in artificial instruments—which argues against what I have said above—it would be answered that it is true that many different sounds are found within the Diapason beyond the Seven named; but such sounds are not ordered according to the nature of the <term>Diatonic genus</term> <note>The standard arrangement of whole tones and semitones in Western music.</note>, nor are they derived through any division from <term>Harmonic Proportionality</term>.

### Consideration of the shown Division, or Ordering, and of the other species of the Diatonic genus set down by Ptolemy. Cap. 31.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter S, depicting a figure within a classical architectural frame surrounded by floral elements.</image-desc>

IF WE wish to examine the shown division or ordering, there is no doubt that we will find in it a great imperfection: for it is deprived of those intervals that are presently accepted as consonant by all Musicians of common opinion, which are the Semiditone, the Ditone, and their composites, which are continually heard in their compositions. And although these intervals, as far as the name is concerned, are found in the said division, they were not considered consonant by their inventors: because truly they are not. That this is true will not be difficult to show, provided we believe these Principles: first, that from no other genus or species of proportion except the Multiple and <term>Superparticular</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number is equal to the smaller number plus one (e.g., 3:2 or 4:3).</note> (as Ptolemy, Boethius, and the better part of all Musicians maintain) can the form of any interval be born that is fit for the generation of any consonance. Second, that any two simple intervals contained by the same proportion, of whatever genus or species they may be (except those having their form from the <term>Dupla</term> <note>A 2:1 ratio, the octave.</note>), when joined together do not make any consonance between their outer extremes, as can be seen by putting it to the test. Besides this, that no Interval whose form is found in its radical terms outside of the <term>Senary number</term> <note>The number six; Zarlino's theory was that all musical consonances are derived from the first six integers.</note> is consonant. And such Principles will be the foundation of this reasoning, by which I will prove what I have said is true in this manner. A thing is said to be perfect (according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note>) beyond which nothing can be desired that contributes to its perfection. Since, therefore, in such a division perfect harmony can be desired—being deprived of many consonances, which are those already named that make perfect harmony—there is no doubt that it is imperfect. For if we take the extremes of the proportion of the Ditone and the Semiditone already shown, which are the <term>Super 17-partiente 64</term> <note>A complex ratio (81:64) representing the Pythagorean major third.</note> and the <term>Super 15-partiente 81</term> <note>A complex ratio (96:81) representing the Pythagorean minor third.</note>, which without doubt are in the <term>Superpartient</term> <note>A complex mathematical ratio that is neither multiple nor superparticular.</note> genus; by the first of the said Principles we can be clear about what I have said: because these two proportions, being contained in the said genus, are not in any way consonant; hence, not being consonant, they are necessarily dissonant. It can also be proved by the second principle that the Ditone is inharmonic <note>Literally "un-consonant."</note>: because in it, two <term>Sesquioctave</term> <note>The 9:8 ratio, a whole tone.</note> proportions are joined together. The third principle also demonstrates that neither the Ditone nor the Semiditone already shown are consonant: because the proportions that are the form of such intervals have no place among the parts of the Senary number. And now the same could be said of the major and minor **Hexachord** <note>A scale of six notes.</note>; because they are composed of the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, which is a consonance, and of the **Major Third** <note>original: "Ditono"</note> or the **Minor Third** <note>original: "Semiditono"</note> shown, which are dissonant; but for the sake of brevity I will set such reasoning aside. If, therefore, such intervals are not consonant, it is impossible for such an order to be perfect, as it lacks those things that contribute to its perfection. From this, one can easily understand the great error of those who labor obstinately to show that the aforementioned intervals are consonant, and that they are the ones used today by musicians in their harmonies. At the same time, one can see how little they have understood **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose works were the primary source for medieval music theory.</note> when they try to use his authority to prove their false opinion as truth.

But if they purely desire the authority of the Ancients alone, and not the reasons provided by the Moderns, what **Vitruvius** <note>An ancient Roman architect and engineer who wrote on the mathematics of music.</note> says on this subject will suffice to show them their great error. He clearly states that the Third, the Sixth, and the Seventh strings cannot produce consonances; and this is understood when they are added to the first. And although many species are found in this genre, as I have shown, only one of them is the one that gives us all the consonances and the perfection of harmony. Therefore, if only one species provides what is truly necessary, what was the need for the other species? Truly, they were not needed considering music in its modern use; but considering it according to the use of the Ancients, they were not out of place, because they had little or no consideration for such consonances, and all their harmony consisted in the melody <note>original: "modulatione"</note> of a single part.

Thus, it can be said that for them, even a single species of melody for each genre was enough (excluding the Modes, of which we will speak in the Fourth part). The various divisions of the **Tetrachords** <note>A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note> were matters that belonged more to the Speculative <note>The theoretical or mathematical study of music.</note> part than to the Practical. For even if they had wanted to put every species of every genre into perfect use, it would have been impossible, as we shall see. And so that this does not seem strange, having seen above the division of the first species of the **Diatonic**, I will come to the divisions of the other species added by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the Greek astronomer and music theorist.</note>, which (as he said) were very agreeable and pleasing to the ear. Their proportions (as can be seen for each Tetrachord) are subject to the **Superparticular** <note>A mathematical ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 4:3, which were considered the most "pure" ratios in ancient theory.</note> genus; for he was of the opinion that in this genus of proportion, a great power was found in harmonic melodies.

I will skip discussing the second species set down by Ptolemy, which he calls the **Syntonic Diatonic**; for I intend to discuss it at length and show that in it is found the perfection of harmony. I will instead come to discuss the First species, which he names the **Soft Diatonic** <note>original: "Diatonico molle"</note>; and I will show how much imperfection is found in it. I say, then, that after we have joined together the first two Tetrachords of this species—namely the *Hypaton* and the *Meson*—adding the *Proslambanomenos* string in the bass, so that they contain the consonan-

this example. We should not believe, however, that the **Equal Diatonic** is far from imperfection: for if one were to believe this, everyone will be made certain by the strings placed here below. Whence it can be held as true that the Ancients, in their melodies, had greater respect for the **modulation** <note>The melodic movement or "flow" of the song.</note> (as has been said) than for the perfection of the harmony; and this is now manifest: since even if they had tuned the strings of their instruments according to the shown proportions and divisions, it would have been impossible for them ever to have drawn perfect harmony from them. This is because for its perfection, not only do the perfect consonances concur—such as the **Octave**, the **Fifth**, and the **Fourth**—but also the imperfect ones, such as the **Major Third**, the **Minor Third**, and both **Hexachords**. Nor is such a defect found only in the shown species of this first genre; but also in all the other species of the other two following genres; as I am about to demonstrate, coming step by step to the division or composition of the first species of the second genre, called **Chromatic**.

## On the Chromatic genus, who its inventor was, and in what manner he might have discovered it. Chapter 32.

Wishing then to discuss the second genus of Melody, called **Chromatic**, I say that **Timotheus of Miletus** <note>A famous and controversial Greek musician of the 5th century BCE known for his innovations.</note> (according to **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> and **Boethius**) was its inventor. For having added a string above those found on the ancient instrument, and having first received a modest harmony, by multiplying it in such a way, he turned it into the said genus, which is undoubtedly softer than the **Diatonic**. For this reason, the **Lacedemonians** <note>The Spartans, known for their strict social discipline.</note>, who always took care that nothing should be changed in their Republic, banished him from Sparta. They believed that music increased in such a manner greatly offended the souls of the youth to whom it was taught, and hindered them or withdrew them from the modesty of virtue. And to show that if anyone in the future had the audacity to add or renovate anything further in Music, they would not pass without due punishment, they hung (as **Pausanias** <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century CE.</note> says) his **Lyre** <note>original: "Cetera"</note> in a prominent place so that everyone could see it. 

But because Pausanias says that the strings Timotheus added to the Ancient Seven were four, and Boethius says (as we have seen) that it was one; therefore (not to leave such a matter without some consideration) taking up our argument from a bit earlier, I say: That the **Diatonic genus**, before any other genus was discovered, and before **Pythagoras** found the ratios of numbers, was produced by nature in the form that we see in its perfect consonances. Of this, the **Lyre of Mercury** <note>The mythical origin of the lyre, attributed to the god Hermes (Mercury).</note> bears witness, which was found around the year 1655 before the year of our Salvation. Its strings (as Boethius shows, and as was shown above in chapter 9) were ordered in such a way that in them one perceived not only **Geometric** and **Arithmetic** proportionality, but **Harmonic** as well, as can be seen between the terms of their proportions; so much so that some held the opinion that it contained within itself a maximal and perfect harmony. 

But the other two genera were discovered much later, after a great space of time, and were placed within the **Diatonic**. Hence, having been put together in such a way, many Ancient Musicians—among whom are **Ptolemy**, **Bryennius**, and **Boethius**—were of the opinion that the last two were nothing other than the **thickening** <note>original: "inspessatione," referring to the process of dividing a large interval into smaller, denser ones.</note> of the first genus. This is because they called every **Tetrachord** <note>A scale segment of four notes.</note> "thickened" when it made the highest interval greater in quantity than the first two lower ones; and this truly is a characteristic of these last two genera, as can be seen in their first Tetrachords, placed above in chapter 16. with diligence, we will find that the outer strings of the **Diatonic** <term>Diatonic: the standard musical scale consisting of whole tones and semitones</term> are immovable and common to the other two genera, not only in their proportions but even in their position. And we will find that the two middle strings (even though they remain without variation in their proportions) are varied in their position. We will also find that this **Thickening** <term>thickening: known as *pyknon* in Greek theory, this refers to the narrowing or crowding of intervals within a tetrachord</term> is created primarily by the addition of a string placed between the second and the third strings of the **Diatonic** scale. This string, together with the highest note, contains a **Trihemitone** <term>trihemitone: an interval of three semitones, equivalent to a minor third</term>; and together with the first low note, along with the second and the last, it constitutes by itself a new **Tetrachord** <term>tetrachord: a series of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth</term>, which (for the reasons stated in chapter 16) is called **Chromatic**.

Then, through the addition of another string placed between the first and the second low **Diatonic** strings, the third genus arises, called **Enharmonic**. This is because it divides the **Semitone** into two parts, that is, into two **Diesis** <term>diesis: here referring to a quarter-tone, the smallest interval in ancient Greek music</term>; and in this way, this string—along with the lowest note, the second Diatonic note, and the last—makes by itself another tetrachord called **Enharmonic**.

And although the second **Diatonic** note changes into the third **Enharmonic** note in terms of its position, and because of this loses its name, it nonetheless does not change its location or its proportion, but remains of the same quantity it was before. It can be seen, then, that such **Thickening** is achieved by the addition of two middle strings into the **Diatonic tetrachord**, which create the other two named genera within said tetrachord. Thus, where there was previously only one genus, there are now three joined together; from one Genus, three Generi are made; and from a **Tetrachord** that existed before, a **Hexachord** <note>A six-note grouping.</note> is made, containing the three named Genera and their tetrachords, as can be seen in the example placed below. The outer strings of this example—that is, the low and the high—are common and stable, being the first and last in every tetrachord of each genus. But the Second string is the specific second string of the **Enharmonic tetrachord** and is not common to any other genus. The same is true for the Third, which is common to each genus, even though it is the third note of the **Enharmonic** and has changed its name, while keeping its own name in the other two and similarly holding the second place in their tetrachords. The Fourth note is then specific, being the third of the **Chromatic tetrachord**. Likewise, the Fifth, being specific to the **Diatonic**, becomes the third string of its own tetrachord.

The **Diatonic tetrachord** was "thickened" in this manner by the other two genera by their inventors (according to the opinion of some) for no other reason than so that, in one single instrument, with those strings naturally ordered and divided in the **Diatonic** genus, and with the **Chromatic** and **Enharmonic** additions discovered later through artifice, one could have greater sweetness in the harmonies. The number of strings in the usual instrument having been subsequently increased by many up to fifteen, and divided into four Tetrachords—as can be seen in the eighth example of the aforementioned passage by *Boethius*—*Timothy* returned the Tetrachord to its place, which had previously been removed from that instrument by *Lycaon*. It was the fifth in that order, and he called it *Synemennon*, as it was called before, that is, "Conjoined." And this addition gave rise to a Tetrachord different from the others: since the *Trite synemennon* placed between the *Mese* and the *Paramese* divides the Tone into two Semitones, as can be seen above in chapter 28. 

And these, I believe, are the four strings that *Pausanias* says *Timothy* added to the *seven* ancient ones. These strings are truly the *seven* principal and essential strings of the **Diatonic** genus <term>Diatonic: the standard scale consisting of tones and semitones</term>, as I have shown above in chapter 30: and they are the first *seven* contained in the first two Tetrachords of the division placed in chapter 28. *...otherwise, I do not see how what **Pliny** says in his **Natural History** <note>original: "Historia naturale"</note> could be true: that **Timotheus** was the one who added the ninth string to the usual instrument. And although **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on music transmitted Greek theory to the Middle Ages.</note> in Book 1 makes no mention of this **Tetrachord** <term>tetrachord: a series of four notes spanning a perfect fourth, the building block of Greek scales</term>, he nonetheless places it in the divisions of the **Monochord** <term>monochord: an ancient scientific instrument with a single string used to measure musical intervals</term> that he provides in the other books. And because perhaps someone might say that, since the added tetrachord was **Diatonic** <term>diatonic: the standard musical scale of whole tones and semitones</term> and not **Chromatic** <term>chromatic: a musical style using smaller intervals (semitones) and jumps of a minor third</term>, it could not produce any melody other than a diatonic one, nor could it serve the chromatic genus—given that it does not contain within itself those proportions found in the chromatic tetrachords shown by Boethius—I respond that it was truly diatonic. However, this does not mean it could not form the Chromatic, by proceeding from the string **Mese** <note>The "middle" or central note of the Greek system.</note> to the **Trite synemmenon**, and from this to the **Paramese**, and from the Paramese to the **Nete synemmenon**, all of which together form a chromatic tetrachord.*

*And even though its proportions are very different from those given by Boethius, this matters little: for the diversity of the genus arises only from the change and variation of the intervals. This can be perfectly achieved by playing from low to high with a **Semitone** in the first interval, and another in the second, and finally placing a **Trihemitone** <term>trihemitone: an interval of three semitones, roughly equivalent to a minor third</term> in the third; and thus proceeding from high to low in the opposite way. And if indeed (as I have said) the proportions are different, this may arise because Timotheus, having discovered this genus and wanting—or perhaps some other musician wanting—to bring it under the rule of mathematical ratios, found the melody of the Chromatic tetrachord to be very different from the Diatonic. They also wanted the proportions of its intervals to be different, because such differences, being very small, are difficult to perceive. Hence, it is to be believed that afterwards, the various opinions, reasons, and principles held by the musicians of those times induced them to discover different intervals; since they were not content with a single species of melody and harmony for each genus, they created many species within each genus (dividing the tetrachord in many ways), as I have shown above.*

*And while it is difficult to narrate exactly how Timotheus could find or investigate this genus—since no writer has yet been found who describes it—nonetheless, it can be shown with some reason. Since the named strings were arranged in such a way, and the potential for the melody was within them, Timotheus, while practicing in the Diatonic genus, may have tried many times to pass through the added tetrachord with his melody, touching the **Trite synemmenon** after the **Mese**, then passing from there to the **Paramese**, and even reaching the **Paranete synemmenon** or **Trite diezeugmenon** (which are the same string, even though the tetrachords they serve cause their names to change). Then, considering that the passage made through these strings rendered a certain variety, and after longer consideration of this, he sought to play through every tetrachord in such a manner. For it would have been, if not impossible, at least too difficult to have had any consideration of such a thing if he had not first heard the melody. But let enough be said of this, so that we may come to the ordering of this genus by showing its division.*

### Division of the Chromatic Monochord. Chapter 33.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' depicting a landscape with figures and buildings.</image-desc>

*Since, therefore (as we have seen), the first, second, and fourth strings of every Diatonic tetrachord are—without any variation or change of position or proportion—common to and essential for the Chromatic genus, it remains only for us to see in what way the third string can be added to these same three strings for each tetrachord. This third string must contain the **Trihemitone** with the fourth string and be specific and essential to this genus, so that we may have, in the briefest way possible, the perfect tetrachord and the division of its monochord. Therefore, setting aside only the third string of every tetrachord from the previously shown Diatonic monochord (as they are specifically diatonic), and excepting the strings **NB** and **MB** which are common to both genera, we shall add the third string to the second. This is done by always dividing that line which is placed in the position of the fourth string into sixteen parts (for the smaller term of the proportion that contains the Trihemitone, in the manner I showed above in Chapter 22). By adding three parts to it, which will be equal to the larger term of the proportion <note>creating a 19:16 ratio</note>, the resulting length will be the length of the **sought-after string** <note>original: "ricercata chorda"</note>. search for the Third string. In such a way that between string *a-B*, which contains 19 parts, and *D-B*, which contains 16, we will have placed in its proper proportion the Trihemitone <note>original: "Trihemituono"—a musical interval spanning three semitones, roughly equivalent to a minor third.</note> in the first tetrachord called Hypaton; and between strings *F-B* and *a-B*, the higher-pitched Semitone. And I prove that this is true because if, from the said Tetrachord—that is, from the Sesquiterza proportion <note>original: "Sesquiterza"—the 4:3 ratio representing a musical Fourth.</note>—we subtract the minor Semitone placed between *C-B* and *F-B* on the lower side, and the Trihemitone placed between the shown strings (contained under the ratio of 19:16) <note>original: "Super 3 partiente 16"—literally '3 over 16', meaning the ratio 19:16.</note>, there will necessarily remain the sharper Semitone, contained by the ratio of 81:76 <note>original: "Super 5 partiente 76".</note>. Thus, between strings *C-B*, *F-B*, *a-B*, and *D-B*, we will have the first chromatic tetrachord, called Hypaton <note>The "lowest" of the tetrachords in the Greek system.</note>. And to place such a string in the other tetrachords, we will divide strings *G-B*, *M-B*, *L-B*, and *O-B* in the same manner, and we will have strings *b-B*, *e-B*, *c-B*, and *d-B*, which will be those noted below with the terms containing their proportions, as seen in the figure. Here it should be noted that the names of the strings in the Chromatic and Enharmonic genera are not changed from those of the Diatonic, even though in these last two genera two additional strings are found that are not in the Diatonic. This arises from the variety of intervals created by the Third string of this genus; but there is no other difference in name, except that in the Diatonic the Lychanos <term>Lychanos: Ancient Greek for the "index finger" string; its tuning was the primary marker of the musical genus.</term> is called the Diatonic Lychanos, in the Chromatic it is the Chromatic Lychanos, and in the Enharmonic it is named the Enharmonic Lychanos; as we will see further below in the order or composition of the Diatonic Monochord, thickened with the strings of these two genera.

### Considerations on the demonstrated division, and on some other species of this genus found by Ptolemy. Chapter 34.

IT is not believable—if the Diatonic genus, among those species we have shown, is found to be imperfect—that the Chromatic should be more perfect than it. This is because in its species, it is not only deprived of those consonances that practical musicians call "Imperfect" <note>Referring to major and minor thirds and sixths, which were often considered "imperfect" compared to the "perfect" fifth and octave.</note>, but it is even deprived in many places of the "Perfect" ones. For if in the first species of the Diatonic, which Ptolemy calls the *Diatonic Ditone* <note>original: "Diatonico diatono"—the Pythagorean tuning where the third is a sharp, dissonant interval (81:64).</note>, the Fourth <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note> is found five times among its strings, and the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> four times; in the demonstrated division, the Fourth is found only four times, and the Fifth only a single time, from the *Proslambanomenos* to the *Hypate meson* <note>The interval between the absolute lowest note and the fourth note of the scale.</note>. And if anyone wished to say that his Trihemitone was consonant, and that it was the minor Third or the Semiditone <note>original: "Semiditono"—another term for a minor third.</note> which is placed in our times by practical musicians among the number of Consonances, it can be answered with truth that this is not so. This is because its proportion is contained in the *Superpartient* genus <note>A category of mathematical ratios where the larger number contains the smaller number plus a remainder greater than one.</note> as 19:16 <note>original: "Supertripartiente 16".</note> which (as I have said other times) is not suited to the generation of consonances. Anyone can certify this for themselves when they bring into actual sound the notes arising from strings stretched according to the aforementioned proportions; for they will truly hear that they make no consonance at all, as they do not have their form among the parts of the *Senario* <term>Senario: The "number six." Theoretical musicians of this era believed that all harmonious musical intervals must be derived from the ratios of the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.</term>. And although, besides the shown species of Chromatic, Ptolemy found others...

two others (as I have mentioned elsewhere), one of which he calls the **Soft Chromatic**, and the other the **Intense Chromatic**, both of which he approves as good. Although their intervals are contained within the superparticular genus <note>original: "Superparticolare"—a mathematical ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 4:3. Zarlino considered these the most "natural" ratios.</note>, not all of them are suited to the generation of consonance and perfect harmony. The exception is that which is found in the **Soft Chromatic**, between the two highest strings of each of its Tetrachords; this is called a **Semiditone** in the Diatonic genus, and in the Chromatic they call it a **Trihemitone** <note>original: "Trihemituono"—a minor third, spanning three semitones.</note>. And it is truly consonant: since the **Sesquiquinta** <note>The 6:5 ratio.</note>, which is contained within the superparticular genus, is its form; and its terms are contained among the numbers that are parts of the **Senary** <note>original: "Senario"—the number six, which Zarlino argued was the foundation of all musical beauty and harmony.</note>, as can be seen in Chapter 15 of the First Part. And although this species is adorned with this interval, it nevertheless has the same imperfection found in the other species contained in the Diatonic genus: because in many places it is lacking the **Diatessaron** <note>A perfect fourth.</note>, and the **Diapente** <note>A perfect fifth.</note> as well, as can be seen among the eight lowest strings of its Monochord in the example provided above. Among these, one also finds the **Minor Hexachord** <note>A minor sixth.</note>, which modern practitioners include among the consonant intervals. The second species, called **Intense Chromatic**, has this same imperfection—indeed, I would say a greater one: since among the strings of its Tetrachords, no consonance is found (as can be seen), except for the **Diapente** between the first low string and the eighth, which is also found in the others.

## Who the Inventor of the Enharmonic genus was, and in what manner he discovered it. Cap. 35.

IT is not a difficult thing to know who the Inventor of the **Enharmonic genus** was, although it is difficult to show the method he used to find it. For **Plutarch**, and many others as well, citing the authority of **Aristoxenus** <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who wrote extensively on music theory.</note> with words that are not very clear, say that **Olympus** (according to the opinion of the musicians of those times) was the first who discovered this genus; prior to this, everything was **Diatonic** and **Chromatic**. Hence, they thought that such an invention proceeded in this way: that while Olympus was practicing in the Diatonic, and frequently shifting the Mode to the *parhypate diatona* <note>The second-lowest note in a Greek tetrachord.</note>, departing sometimes from the *Mese* <note>The central "middle" note of the scale.</note> and sometimes from the *Paramese* <note>The note just above the middle.</note>, and passing over the *Lychanos diatona* <note>The "index-finger" note, the third string of the tetrachord.</note>; considering the beauty and suitability of the character that arose from the singing of the voices; having greatly marveled at the conjunction, which stood by reason, which the Greeks call a **system** <note>original: "σύστημα"—a composite musical scale or structure.</note>, and em-

## Of the Division, or Composition, of the Enharmonic
## Monochord. Chapter 36.

BEING (as we have seen above in Chapter 32) that the First, Second, and Fourth strings of every **Tetrachord** <note>A scale of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> of the first species of the **Diatonic** genus are essential strings of the **Enharmonic**; although they are common to both of these two genera; and as we have seen, the second Diatonic string becomes the third Enharmonic string; it is only necessary that we seek to place the Second string in the Tetrachord between the two lowest Diatonic ones. This string will divide the **Semitone** contained between them into two parts, that is, into two **Diesis** <note>In the Enharmonic genus, a Diesis is a very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone, created by splitting a semitone.</note>, according to the proportions shown above in Chapter 16. Therefore, to follow the brevity that is a friend to students, we will simply divide into two equal parts the differences between the larger and smaller terms of the Semitones. These are the parts of the string by which the longer strings (which produce low sounds) exceed the shorter strings (which produce the high sounds) of such Semitones. We will place a middle string of a length equal to the shorter one plus half of the difference, and we shall achieve our purpose without any error. This is because between two equal parts of any string that are measured by another common quantity or measure, one finds a continuous **Arithmetic Progression** when comparing them to the Whole. The differences found between the proportions of these three strings become equal, which causes the proportions to be arranged in **Arithmetic Proportionality**; and this is very convenient. Indeed, between those proportions which are the forms of the two Diesis—512, 499, and 486—one finds the same proportionality, because their differences on each side are 13, as can be seen in the figure below. We shall then take the Compass,

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the arithmetic division of a musical interval. A large arc labeled "Differences" spans the values 512 and 486. Below it, two smaller arcs meet at the value 499, with the number 13 written under the peak of each small arc to indicate the equal difference between 512–499 and 499–486. At the bottom, two boxes are labeled "Minor Diesis" and "Major Diesis" respectively.</image-desc>

and we will divide each of the said differences into two equal parts for every Tetrachord of the first species of the Diatonic, which are CF, DI, KN, LQ, and GR; at the points f, g, h, i, k. Together we will have the strings fB, gB, hB, iB, and kB, according to our purpose. Having placed the **Diesis** of smaller proportion in the low range, and that of larger proportion in the high range—as can be seen in the Division—it also contains an order of proportions, contained in their radical terms, and the names of the strings of such an order.

<header>Part 2</header>

# Consideration on the previously shown division, or composition, and on that species of this genus which Ptolemy discovered. Chapter 37.

IF WE, THEN, diligently examine every interval—that is, the terms of every ratio of this division or composition—we will find that same imperfection that we have found in the other two genera <note>The Diatonic and Chromatic genera discussed in earlier chapters.</note> in their various species. This is primarily because every one of its tetrachords <note>A grouping of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note> is deprived of that consonant interval which is called the Major Third <note>original: Ditono</note>; for in its place, one finds a Major Third with the ratio of 81:64 <note>original: Super 17. partiente 64</note>, which is truly dissonant. And because someone might perhaps believe that the species of Enharmonic which Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Alexandrian polymath whose musical theories Zarlino deeply respected.</note> discovered produced perfect harmony—since in every one of its tetrachords it possesses the consonant Major Third, contained by the 5:4 ratio <note>original: Sesquiquarta</note>, and the Major Sixth <note>original: Essachordo maggiore</note>, contained by the 5:3 ratio <note>original: Superbipartienteterza</note>, which (as I have shown in the First Part) have their lowest terms among the numbers of the Senario <note>The numbers 1 through 6, which Zarlino considered the foundation of all musical beauty.</note>—I therefore say that even this species cannot be far from imperfection. This is because many strings within it are found to have no relationship toward the bass nor toward the high notes with any other string that can give any consonance, such as the Perfect Fifth <note>original: Diapente</note>, the Perfect Fourth <note>original: Diatessaron</note>, the Major Third, or the Minor Third <note>original: Semiditono</note>. Instead, they are entirely outside of any such ratio, as can be understood in the eight strings placed below, ordered according to the nature of their tetrachord. We can now see how much utility is brought to us by any...

Whence I will say, as a final conclusion, that each of the shown divisions, whatever it may be, is not suited to the generation of perfect harmony. For the construction or manufacture of an instrument which possesses each of the said three genera in the most perfect way possible, one could choose for the Chromatic Minor Third <note>original: Trihemituono Chromatico</note> the one by Ptolemy placed in the "Soft Chromatic," which is contained by the 6:5 ratio <note>original: Sesquiquinta</note>; and for the Enharmonic Major Third, the one shown above, which is contained by the 5:4 ratio. These intervals—or consonances, as we may wish to call them—are also contained in the Syntonic Diatonic of Ptolemy, where one is called the Minor Third and the other the Major Third, as we shall see elsewhere. It is quite true that such intervals are considered in every Diatonic tetrachord as composed, or divided into two other intervals; but in the other two genera <note>The Chromatic and Enharmonic.</note>, they are considered simple and without any further division.

<header>Part Two</header>

# On the Composition of the Diatonic Monochord, Interspersed with Chromatic and Enharmonic Strings. Chapter 38.

HAVING completed the Division, or Composition, of the Monochord for each species of every genus separately, it will not be out of place to show how the strings of the *First species of the Diatonic* may be interspersed, on a single instrument, with the strings of the *first species* of the other two genera—that is, the *first species of the Chromatic*, already shown, and the *first species of the Enharmonic*. I do this so that no one might believe that by joining these three species together on one instrument through such interspersion, one could achieve perfect harmony. For although the number of strings is increased, it does not make the *Diatonic* any more perfect than it was before. Since it is interspersed in such a way, it still lacks the consonant *Major Third* <note>original: Ditono</note> and *Minor Third* <note>original: Semiditono</note> just as much as it did before this *Interspersion* was made; as can be clearly seen by testing it. And such imperfection is found not only in this particular interspersion, but it would also be found even if the same *Diatonic* were interspersed with the strings of the *Soft Diatonic*, those of the *Tonic Diatonic*, or those of the *Equal Diatonic* mentioned above in *Chapter 31*, or even if one added the strings of the *Intense Chromatic*—all of which are species discovered by *Ptolemy* <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and music theorist.</note>.

Therefore, as we have seen, when the *Diatonic* is interspersed in this way by the *Chromatic* in the high part by one string (which, with the highest string of each *Tetrachord* <note>A group of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note>, forms a *Minor Third* <note>original: Trihemituono</note>), and by the *Enharmonic* in the low part by another string (in such a way that with the first low string and the second of every *Diatonic Tetrachord*, it creates two *Diesis* <note>Small intervals, roughly a quarter-tone in the Enharmonic system.</note>), there are six strings found in every *Tetrachord* increased in this manner. Because of this number, it can truly be called a *Hexachord* <note>original: Essachordo; literally 'six strings'.</note>. From this, it follows that this arrangement contains *Twenty-six* strings in total, as can be seen in the example placed below.

Of these strings (as *Boethius* <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, the 6th-century philosopher whose "Fundamentals of Music" transmitted Greek theory to the Middle Ages.</note> informs us), some are entirely *Stable*, some are entirely *Mobile*, and some are neither entirely stable nor entirely mobile. Those that are entirely *Stable* are the *Proslambanomenos*, the two *Hypaton*, the *Mese*, the *Nete Synemmenon*, the *Paramese*, and the other two *Netes* <note>Zarlino is listing the standard names of strings in the Ancient Greek "Greater Perfect System."</note>. This is because in each genus they do not change place or position, nor do they change their name; thus they retain their name simply without any addition. But the *Mobile* ones are the *Paranete* and the *Lichanos*, to which, besides their proper names, the name of their genus is added—calling them now *Diatonic*, now *Chromatic*, and now *Enharmonic*. This is because the *Diatonic Paranete* is in a different place than the *Chromatic Paranete* and the *Enharmonic Paranete*; and likewise, the *Chromatic Paranete* is different from the *Enharmonic Paranete*. The same can be said of the others, as they change in every genus.

Those that are neither entirely stable nor entirely mobile are the *Trite of the Diatonic* and those of the *Chromatic*, and the *Lichanos* and the *Paranete of the Enharmonic*. These remain stable in the first two genera, but in the *Enharmonic* they vary in name and position; since they are transposed, and from being second strings they become the *Third* strings of the *Tetrachords* of this genus. From what has been said and shown, therefore, one can easily recognize how arrogant anyone would be who wished to affirm that such genera and their species could be used simply, with all perfection, at our pleasure, or even mixed. For never, in any way or at any time, were they used perfectly by the *Ancients*, whether mixed or simple.

The matter therefore stands thus: not only are the *first species* of the said genera found to be imperfect, whether separate or joined together, but even those discovered by *Ptolemy* are imperfect—except for the *Syntonic Diatonic* <note>original: Diatonico sintono; the system of "Just Intonation" that Zarlino championed as the basis for modern music.</note>, as can be seen through experience. For this reason, I cannot imagine for what purpose the *Ancients* discovered so many divisions in every genus, which did nothing or very little for the perfection of harmonies, unless it was that they were useful then to the *Speculative* <note>Theoretical or mathematical study.</note> part of music, to demonstrate the truth of those things belonging to *Practice*. Or perhaps (as some believe) because through such divisions they could come to a true understanding of the composition of every Machine, and form with due proportion the *Vessels* that resonated in their *Theaters*, placing them afterward in the appropriate locations. But be that as it may, it is enough that from this we can recognize how much imperfection Music would have if one wished to use only the intervals shown here; and we can recognize the folly of those who would stubbornly affirm that such intervals were those from which the true...

*...true and legitimate consonances that we use today, which are born from the true and legitimate harmonic numbers that provide us with perfect harmony. But because none of the divisions shown so far suit our purpose—since they all contradict both reason and the senses—I desire to show the division that arises from the true and natural sounding numbers, which we use at present. I also wish to demonstrate in what manner one can use the Chromatic and the Enharmonic genera added to the Diatonic. Ceasing to speak further of the species already shown, I shall come to demonstrate (according to my purpose) the Division, or Construction, of the Intense Diatonic Monochord <note>original: "Diatonico sintono"</note>, thickening it with Chromatic and Enharmonic strings, as the sounding and true harmonic numbers shall allow.*

## That Ptolemy's Intense Diatonic is that which has its being
## naturally from the harmonic numbers. Chapter 39.

<image-desc>Large woodcut ornamental initial 'A' decorated with foliage and bird-like motifs.</image-desc>BEFORE I come to the aforementioned Division or Construction, I wish first to show for what reason I have said that the Intense Diatonic <note>A tuning system proposed by the ancient geographer and astronomer Ptolemy, which Zarlino championed because it accommodates the major and minor thirds used in Renaissance music.</note> arises from the true harmonic numbers. For after its division or composition is made, I will come to its "thickening" <note>The process of adding extra notes from the Chromatic and Enharmonic scales into the standard Diatonic scale.</note>; so that (according to modern use) we may use harmonies in the most perfect way granted to us. Therefore, to show this, I will propose this conclusion: that the Tetrachord <note>A scale of four notes.</note> of this species, placed in Chapter 16, is divided or ordered according to the nature and properties of the harmonic numbers. This is because it has its being within the strings of the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, divided in its parts into seven intervals, according to the property of the said numbers. <margin>Note that / I speak / of the / numbers / <unclear>...</unclear></margin> And so that I may demonstrate this, I will take as a foundation the division of the said Octave into its parts, according to the nature of Harmonic Proportionality. Its form is contained by the Double proportion <note>The ratio 2:1.</note>, which is the first proportion in the multiple genus, between these radical terms: 2 and 1. If we then divide this proportion into two parts harmonically (according to the method shown in Chapter 39 of the First Part), from such a division will come a Sesquiterza <note>The ratio 4:3, representing a perfect fourth.</note> and a Sesquialtera <note>The ratio 3:2, representing a perfect fifth.</note>, from which the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> has its true form. This is placed on the right side of the figure below—that is, in the low part of the harmony, for that is its true place. The Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> will then be accommodated on the right side—that is, in the high part—and will have its true form from the Sesquiterza proportion. These parts will be (as I have also said elsewhere) the first and principal parts of the Octave. Taking then the larger of these two, which is the Fifth—since the Fourth is not capable of harmonic division <note>Meaning it cannot be divided into two smaller ratios using only the simple whole numbers Zarlino prefers.</note>—we will make two parts of it, dividing its proportion (contained in its radical terms 3 and 2, placed in the first rank of the Superparticular genus) in the manner shown. Once this is done, we will have two parts: one larger, contained by the Sesquiquarta proportion <note>The ratio 5:4.</note>, which we shall call the Major Third <note>original: "Ditono"</note>; the other smaller, contained by the Sesquiquinta proportion <note>The ratio 6:5.</note>, which we shall name the Minor Third <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>. Of these, the larger will hold the low part, which is its natural place, and the smaller will hold the high part. These will be the second parts of the Octave, and the first parts of the Fifth, between which they are placed. In this way, we will have made three parts of the Octave, acquired by means of harmonic proportionality. Each of these (besides having its origin from proportions contained in the Superparticular genus) also has its radical terms placed among the parts of the Senario <note>The "number of six"—the integers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, which Zarlino believed were the source of all musical perfection.</note>, as can be seen in the figure. All these parts are called Consonances by the Moderns, and they truly are, as experience demonstrates to us. From these, we can begin to see how much similarity they have with those intervals placed between the strings of the named Tetrachord. For within it are found those parts that arise from the division of the Fifth: first the larger, placed in the low range, contained by the Sesquiquarta proportion, between the last high string and the second low string; and the smaller placed toward the high range, contained by the Sesquiquinta proportion, between the first low string and the third high string of the said Tetrachord. And although all these intervals are consonant, nonetheless those that are the first parts of the Octave are called Perfect Consonances by the moderns; whereas the others, which are its second parts and the first parts of the Fifth, they name Imperfect Consonances. We will then accommodate the extremes of the Fourth among those of the Fifth in such a way that the low string of the Fourth is the low string of the Fifth; or we will accommodate the extremes of the Fifth in such a way that the high string of the Octave is the high string of the Fifth. Once this is done, there is no doubt that the high string of the Fourth, or rather the low string of the Fifth, will fall between the...

In such a manner, then, we shall have the perfect division of the *Octave*, divided into seven intervals, according to the nature of the true harmonic numbers, which are found arranged among eight strings, which by the Moderns are noted with these seven letters: C, D, E, F, G, a, b, and c. And this division is made in every proper way: for if in this manner we divide the *three-to-two* proportion <note>original: *Sesquialtera* (the ratio of a musical Fifth)</note> according to harmonic proportionality, there will come two proportions: namely, the *five-to-four* <note>original: *Sesquiquarta*</note> and the *six-to-five* <note>original: *Sesquiquinta*</note>. ...necessarily placed in the named *Tetrachord* <term>Tetrachord: A scale of four notes spanning a Perfect Fourth</term>: for the *Major Third* <note>original: Ditono</note> is exceeded by the *Fourth* <note>original: Diateſſaron</note> by that exact amount. And if he placed it in the lower part of the *Tetrachord*, he did this to follow the custom of the Ancients—the first inventors of the musical Genres shown—who primarily placed the smaller interval in the lower part of their *Tetrachords*, and then the larger ones in order. They did this (as I believe) thinking that the first interval in music should be the smallest rational interval that could be found, as can be seen (from what I can gather) in Book 1 of the *Posterior Analytics* <note>Aristotle's work on logic and demonstration</note>, and in Book 10 of the *Metaphysics* in Chapter 2, where Aristotle places the *diesis* <term>diesis: here referring to the smallest melodic interval or semitone</term> as the beginning of this kind of melody. 

But there is no doubt that such a *Semitone* is always placed (as can be seen) when proceeding from low to high, after the *Minor Tone* and before the *Major Tone*, within the composition and conjunction of the *Tetrachords*, just as the nature of harmonic numbers requires, which primarily give us the larger intervals and then the smaller ones in order. And the necessity of the *Semitone* interval is so great that without its mediation, one cannot proceed from the *Major Third* to the *Fourth*: because wanting to pass from the *five-to-four* proportion <note>original: Sesquiquarta</note> to the *four-to-three* proportion <note>original: Sesquiterza</note>, it is necessary to arrive there by means of the *sixteen-to-fifteenth* proportion <note>original: Sesquiquintadecima</note>, which is its true form. 

This interval is called the *Major Semitone* to distinguish it from that quantity by which the *Minor Third* <note>original: Semiditono</note> is exceeded by the *Major Third*, which is contained by the *twenty-five-to-twenty-four* proportion <note>original: Sesquiuenteſimaquarta</note>, called the *Minor Semitone*. And although it does not originate from harmonic proportionality as I have said, it is nonetheless very well placed in the said *Tetrachord* for many reasons. First: because when joined to the *Major Tone*, we have the *Minor Third*—or a composite *trihemitone* <note>an interval of three semitones</note>; second, because when joined to two *Tones* (that is, the major and the minor), we have the *Fourth*. Beyond this, by placing it near the *Fifth* <note>original: Diapente</note>, we can obtain the *Minor Sixth* <note>original: Eſſachordo minore</note>, as can always be seen by examining the intervals placed in the figure above. 

We shall conclude, then, that since all the intervals of Ptolemy's *Intense Diatonic Tetrachord* originate from the harmonic division of the *Octave* into its parts, this *Tetrachord* is also divided and ordered according to the nature and properties of harmonic numbers, as I have stated. But let us come now to the division, or composition, of the *Monochord* <term>Monochord: An ancient scientific instrument with a single string used to demonstrate musical ratios</term>.

# On the division of the Syntonic Diatonic Monochord made according to the nature of sonorous numbers. Chapter 40.

Once we have **PREPARED**, according to the method shown, a board or table in which the line **A B** represents the string upon which we are to make this division; in order to arrange and place each of its <term>tetrachords<note>A group of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note></term> in order, following the method used in other divisions, we will first place the **Major Tone** at its proper ratio. We will then have **A B** and **C B**, of which the first will contain nine parts (the larger term of its ratio) and the second eight (the smaller term); in this way, we will have accommodated the said Tone between them. To this, we will then add the first tetrachord, called the <term>Hypaton<note>original: Hypaton; the "lowest" tetrachord in the Greek system.</note></term>, by dividing **C B** into four equal parts for the larger term of its ratio; then, taking three parts for the smaller term, we will have placed the outer boundaries between **C B** and **D B**. 

Wishing then to divide it into two Tones and one Semitone, according to the logic of the intervals and ratios of said tetrachord, we will first accommodate the **Minor Tone** at its ratio by dividing **D B** into nine equal parts for the smaller term of its ratio; then, adding another part toward the lower pitch, we will have placed the Minor Tone between **D B** (which contains nine parts) and **E B** (which contains ten). To this, we will immediately prepend the **Major Tone**, dividing **E B** into eight parts and adding a ninth part; thus, between **F B** and **E B**, we will have our goal. 

Consequently, the **Major Semitone** will necessarily be placed between **C B** and **F B**, as can be proven: for if we add to a five-to-four ratio <note>original: "Sesquiquarta", producing a Major Third</note> the sixteen-to-fifteen ratio <note>original: "Sesquiquintadecima"</note> that contains such a Semitone, the result will necessarily be the four-to-three ratio <note>original: "Sesquiterza"</note> that encompasses the outer limits of the tetrachord. We can see the same thing clearly from this: if we take a nine-to-eight ratio <note>original: "Sesquiottaua"</note> and a ten-to-nine ratio <note>original: "Sesquinona"</note> away from the four-to-three ratio, the sixteen-to-fifteen ratio remains. The first tetrachord will thus be placed in its proper location, divided into two Tones and one Semitone, according to the nature of such a tetrachord. 

We will then add to this the second tetrachord, called the <term>Meson<note>The "middle" tetrachord.</note></term>, and the others in order, following the method held in the other divisions. We will have the *Meson* between **D B**, **I B**, **H B**, and **G B**; the <term>Diezeugmenon<note>The "disjunct" tetrachord.</note></term> between **K B**, **N B**, **M B**, and **L B**; the <term>Hyperboleon<note>The "highest" tetrachord.</note></term> between **L B**, **Q B**, **P B**, and **O B**; and the <term>Synemmenon<note>The "conjunct" tetrachord, often used for B-flat.</note></term> between **G B**, **S B**, **N B**, and **R B**. 

In this division, we will also have 17 strings, among which will be found not only the **Minor Semitone** between **S B** and **K B**, but even the smallest interval of this division: the difference found between the Major and Minor Tone, which is called the **Comma**. This is contained in the eighty-one-to-eighty ratio <note>original: "Sesquiottanteſima"</note>. This interval arises from the joining of the *Synemmenon* tetrachord to the *Meson* tetrachord at the *Mese* string. This is because the high string of the said *Synemmenon* divides the middle interval of the *Diezeugmenon* into two parts: a Minor Tone in the lower part, and the **Comma**, which occupies the high part of that division; one of these is placed between **N B** and **R B**, as can be seen, and the other between **R B** and **M B**. 

And although the interval of the **Comma** is not usable in any <term>genus<note>A classification of melodic scales (Diatonic, Chromatic, or Enharmonic).</note></term>, it was not born without use: for by its means, many consonances are acquired. First, a **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> placed between **R B** and **O B**, and then a **Minor Third** <note>original: "Semiditono"</note> placed between **R B** and **Q B**, which could not be had without its help. Because this interval is so minute, it would greatly annoy the hearing if one tried to use it, especially in man-made instruments; however, Nature first, and then Art, have found a remedy (so to speak) for such a disorder. This interval in the **Voices**—which by their nature can bend in every direction—is accommodated in such a way that it is not heard; and in man-made instruments, it is divided through a "distribution" <note>An early reference to temperament.</note> made across many intervals among eight strings, as we shall see elsewhere. 

Thus it should be noted that although the strings of this division are named with **Greek names** according to the order held in others, nevertheless, to follow the custom of the **Moderns**, I have also marked them with the **Seven letters** found by **Guido** <note>Guido d'Arezzo, the 11th-century monk who developed the precursor to modern staff notation.</note>. I have marked not only the string **R B** but also **M B** with the letter **d**, so as not to confuse the order observed by Guido himself. So, while in the instrument shown the said **Comma** is contained between these two strings and is usable, in modern instruments such as **Organs**, **Harpsichords**, **Monochords**, **Arpichordi**, and other similar ones, such an interval is not found; for their strings are reduced to the number of **Pythagorean** strings. But if we wish to find any consonance whatsoever on the shown Monochord that is possible to find therein—whether harmonically or otherwise mediated—once we have drawn three, four, or more strings over it as needed, we will be able to achieve our purpose, and*

# On the division of the Syntonic Diatonic Monochord made according to the nature of sonorous numbers. Chapter 40.

Once we have **PREPARED**, according to the method shown, a board or table in which the line **A B** represents the string upon which we are to make this division; in order to arrange and place each of its <term>tetrachords<note>A group of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note></term> in order, following the method used in other divisions, we will first place the **Major Tone** <note>The ratio 9:8.</note> at its proper ratio. We will then have **A B** and **C B**, of which the first will contain nine parts (the larger term of its ratio) and the second eight (the smaller term); in this way, we will have accommodated the said Tone between them. To this, we will then add the first tetrachord, called the <term>Hypaton<note>The "lowest" tetrachord in the Greek system.</note></term>, by dividing **C B** into four equal parts for the larger term of its ratio; then, taking three parts for the smaller term, we will have placed the outer boundaries between **C B** and **D B**. 

Wishing then to divide it into two Tones and one Semitone, according to the logic of the intervals and ratios of said tetrachord, we will first accommodate the **Minor Tone** <note>The ratio 10:9.</note> at its ratio by dividing **D B** into nine equal parts for the smaller term of its ratio; then, adding another part toward the lower pitch, we will have placed the Minor Tone between **D B** (which contains nine parts) and **E B** (which contains ten). To this, we will immediately prepend the **Major Tone**, dividing **E B** into eight parts and ad...

## That in modern artificial instruments none of the shown Diatonic species are used. Chapter 41.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' containing a landscape scene with buildings and a figure walking.</image-desc>

**And** although the true and natural forms of all those consonances that can possibly be found are present in the illustrated Monochord, we must not believe for this reason that in modern instruments—such as **Organs**, **Harpsichords**, **Harps**, **Monochords**, and others—such consonances are found in their true and natural form. To believe so would be a great error. This is because the strings of such instruments are determined by the **Pythagorean** numbers <note>original: "chorde Pithagorice"; the tuning system used in the Middle Ages based on pure mathematical ratios (3:2 fifths), which resulted in harsh, "out-of-tune" thirds.</note> contained in the **Diatonic ditone** <term>Diatonic ditone<note>Also known as the Pythagorean Diatonic; a scale where the major third is made of two identical whole tones (9:8), making it wider than a natural, "pure" third.</note></term> shown above in chapter 28. In those instruments (following the order of the intervals of the Tone and Semitone already shown), when one hears the intervals of the **Ditone** <term>Ditone<note>The Major Third.</note></term> and the **Semiditone** <term>Semiditone<note>The Minor Third.</note></term>—which are consonant—it is impossible to find a single interval among them in its true and natural form or proportion, except for the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> and the **minor Semitone** located between the notes *a* and *♮, ♭*.

This is because the number of their strings cannot produce the intervals found in the **Syntonic Diatonic**; nor do they even encompass those of the **Diatone Diatonic** <note>The Pythagorean system.</note> we showed. In that system, the **Ditone** and **Semiditone** are dissonant intervals (as we have seen), yet on these modern instruments, they are consonant—as anyone can hear—even though they are outside their true and natural form. And this is indeed the case: for all those intervals found in said instruments (excepting the two mentioned) are **tempered** by musicians when tuning them. Because they are outside their true forms or proportions, they are reduced into such a **temperament**—by increasing or decreasing them by a certain amount for that purpose, in a manner we shall see later—so that the Hearing is satisfied with them.

Moderns call this temperament **Participation** <term>Participation<note>original: "Participatione"; Zarlino’s term for temperament, where the "perfection" of certain intervals is shared or distributed among others to make the whole instrument playable in all keys.</note></term>, about which I do not know if anyone else has yet reasoned or shown anything. Some claim it was done or discovered to reduce the number of strings of the **Syntonic Diatonic** monochord to the number of Pythagorean strings contained in the **Diatone**. This was done so that all consonances, both perfect and imperfect, which are necessary for the generation of **perfect Harmony**, could be placed among them; and so that the player might be more free while playing, and the harmony coming from such instruments could be heard with greater satisfaction by the ear than would have been possible if one had wanted to stick to the number of strings in the Syntonic Diatonic. 

Had they done so, it would have been necessary to frequently use the interval of the **Comma** <term>Comma<note>A tiny mathematical discrepancy between intervals (like the difference between a major and minor whole tone).</note></term>, adding it to or taking it away from certain intervals to acquire many consonances—especially when wanting to move from the low register to the high, or conversely from one consonance to another. This would have brought not only difficulty to the player but also little delight to the listeners, for in such a case one would have heard "I know not what" of a sadness or harshness that would have caused no small annoyance.

Furthermore, although some say that this **Temperament** or **Participation** was discovered studiously so that through it these instruments might come to **imitate Nature** (which ought to be imitated in all things as much as possible), I believe otherwise. They argue that just as one can proceed naturally with the voice through its intervals from low to high and vice versa without any inconvenience, so too should one be able to pass from high to low on these instruments without any impediment or offense to the Senses. However, I truly believe that such Temperament or Participation was introduced **by chance** and not by study. 

What moves me to believe this is that there is no doubt that neither the **Ditone**, nor the **Semiditone**, nor the two **Sixths** <note>original: "Essachordi"</note>, nor many other intervals which are now consonant to us, were ever received into the number of consonances by any of the Ancients (as can be understood from their writings). Nor did they truly use them as consonances in the way we use them, especially since they always used the Pythagorean number of strings, as can be seen from the strings placed in many ancient instruments. Therefore, it is believable that some person skilled in Music, after a certain space of time—first by chance, and then having conducted many experiments—reduced them on the same instrument...

## What must be observed in tempering, or rather tuning, the intervals of every modern artificial instrument, reducing the number of strings from the Syntonic Diatonic to the Diatonic; and that such intervals are not natural, but rather accidental. Chapter 42.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' featuring a male figure in a landscape setting.</image-desc>

**SO THAT** the Studious Reader may know with what reasoning and by how much each interval in the said instruments comes to be tempered, and the method they must follow if they wish to perform the **Participation** <note>original: "Participatione"; a term used by Renaissance theorists to describe "tempering" or "sharing" the tuning discrepancies across the scale to make all keys playable.</note> in such a way that it does not offend the sense of hearing, I will now take up this task. I will show at the same time in what manner the 17 strings, placed in the **Syntonic Diatonic** <term>Syntonic Diatonic<note>Also known as Ptolemy’s Intense Diatonic, this scale uses pure ratios (like 5:4 for a major third) which sound beautiful but create mathematical overlaps that make tuning a fixed-pitch instrument like a piano or organ very difficult.</note></term>, are reduced to the number of sixteen contained in the Diatonic scale. To do this, one must note that if we wish to create such a Temperament or Participation with logic and foundation, it is necessary to divide the **Comma** <term>Comma<note>A tiny interval—specifically the "Syntonic Comma"—which is the small difference in pitch between a major third reached by four perfect fifths and a pure major third.</note></term> (contained between the strings RB and MB) into seven equal parts. These must be distributed among the seven intervals contained within the eight strings of the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, so that we can reduce the two shown strings that contain the Comma into one single string. But this must be done so that the intervals remain in their natural form as much as possible, so that the hearing is not offended. Each consonance, both in the low and the high range, and every other interval, however small it may be, must be equally increased or diminished by a certain and fixed quantity across all intervals of similar proportion.

This will work very well if one ensures that every **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> remains diminished and imperfect by two-sevenths of a Comma; and that the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> takes an increase of that same amount. This is only right: since the Octave always remains immutable and in its true and natural proportion, and is comprised of these two parts <note>A fifth plus a fourth equals an octave.</note>, whatever is taken from one must necessarily be given to the other, so that when they are joined together, a perfect Octave is heard at the outer ends.

Next, the **Major Third** <note>original: "Ditono"</note> will be made imperfect by one-seventh of a part, and the **Minor Third** <note>original: "Semiditono"</note> will be diminished by that same amount. Since these two consonances combine to complete the Fifth, and the Fifth is diminished by two-sevenths, it is necessary that such a diminution be divided between these two intervals. By making the Major Third imperfect by one-seventh and the Minor Third by another seventh (which totals two-sevenths), these two consonances, which are parts of the Fifth, come to be diminished by the same total quantity as the whole.

As for the parts of the Major Third—which are the **Major Tone** and the **Minor Tone**—they will be made imperfect in this way: four-sevenths of the Comma will be taken from the first, and the second will be made larger by three-sevenths. Thus, between them, they will have that same imperfection that their Whole has; that is, they will be imperfect by one-seventh. <note>In this math, -4/7 + 3/7 = -1/7.</note>

The **Major Semitone** will then be given an increase of three-sevenths of a part. Since it is the smaller part of the Minor Third, and the Major Tone is the larger part, one will find between these two parts the same deficiency found in the Minor Third; that is, they will be diminished by two-sevenths. Both the **Major Sixth** and the **Minor Sixth** <note>original: "Essachordo maggiore & minore"</note> will both take an increase of one-seventh of a part. This is because the first is composed of a Fourth and a Major Third, and the other likewise of a Fourth and a Minor Third. Since the Fourth takes an increase of two parts, and the Major Third and Minor Third are each diminished by one-seventh, these Sixths truly end up increasing by that amount <note>2/7 increase minus 1/7 decrease equals 1/7 net increase.</note>.

In this way, having finally proportioned the instrument, every consonance and every interval from the largest to the smallest—excluding the Octave and the Minor Semitone shown—will be outside of its true proportion. However, they will not be far from their true form, so the hearing will still be satisfied. This, then, is what must be observed when desiring the Participation or Distribution of the Comma in every one of our instruments, so that every species of consonance becomes equally increased or diminished. Wherefore, every expert of sound should take note,

He details exactly how much to diminish or increase fifths, fourths, thirds, and tones to create a balanced, playable scale that remains pleasing to the ear.</summary>
