<meta>Continuity: This page continues from the previous discussion on tempering the Syntonic Diatonic scale for modern instruments. The previous page ended with the beginning of the word "notice" (avver-).</meta>

...notice, that wishing to temper, or rather tune the aforementioned instruments, it will be necessary to stretch or proportion each **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> in such a manner that its high extremes lean toward the low, according to the stated quantity that I am about to show; or rather that the low notes lean more toward the high, according as it shall be more convenient in the tuning or tempering of said instruments. Similarly, each **Fourth** <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note>, to which is given the quantities taken away from the Fifth, must be increased in such a way that its every high extreme is further from the low by that much quantity, and the low similarly from the high. And although these intervals are in such a manner now increased and now diminished, the **Hearing** (as I have said) does not for this reason abhor such a distribution. Since the quantity that is removed or added to such intervals is minimal and almost imperceptible, and being not very far from their true forms, the sense is satisfied. Nor should we wonder at this: because what happens to the Hearing is what usually happens to the other senses, and especially to **Sight**, which sometimes does not notice a minimal quantity for being almost imperceptible. This is as it happens when, if one removes or adds two, three, or more handfuls of grain to a great mountain, one cannot notice such a thing; but one would certainly notice if a great part were removed or added. 

But if anyone should say that by putting into use **Consonances** that are outside of their true proportions—which, without doubt, are not without sweetness—that the true and legitimate consonant intervals were these and not those which I have already shown, he would truly be in error. For although the intervals already shown are not found to be in the named instruments, it does not follow that they are not the true and natural ones, and that they are not those which perfectly produce every consonance that is possible to be produced. Nor does it follow that they cannot be put into practice and heard: because they can be heard whenever one wishes; just as it also does not follow that a man is not capable of laughter <note>original: "risibile"</note> because he does not laugh always: for even if he does not laugh now, he is at least capable of laughing when he wants. And although in the said instruments tempered in such a manner, one cannot use the consonances in their perfection (that is, in their true and natural form), it is nonetheless possible to be able to use them when one wishes to tune their strings under the ratio of their true and natural proportions. 

And this I say because many times I have made the experiment upon an instrument which I had manufactured for this purpose; although such a test can also be made upon any other instrument, and especially upon **Harpsichords** or **Clavicembalos**, which are very suitable for this purpose. And if anyone should say that when such instruments were tuned perfectly, one would come to lose several consonances that are found in other instruments, this matters little: for it is enough for me only that no one can contradict with truth what I have said above, and say that such consonances cannot be put into practice in their true forms or proportions. For even if one could not practice harmonies in them with that convenience and freedom found in common instruments, it would not mean that one could not hear in them every consonance and every harmony in its true form. 

But if such inconveniences (so to speak) are found in artificial Instruments, nonetheless among **Voices**, as we shall say another time, such considerations are not found: for they reduce everything to its perfection, as is right. This is because Nature, in making things, is far superior to Art; and Art, in imitating, makes everything imperfect, while Nature (impediments removed) reduces everything to perfection. In such a way, then, one will come to temper each of the named instruments; in which the distribution of the **Comma** <term>Comma<note>A very small interval resulting from the difference between pure musical ratios, such as the difference between twelve Fifths and seven Octaves.</note></term> will be made into seven intervals, as I have said; nor would it otherwise turn out well, wishing to acquire the perfect and imperfect consonances together in the best way that can be done; so that every similar interval, both in the low and in the high, comes to be equally increased or diminished by its quantity; and one no longer has to place the doubled string *d*. 

And if it should seem strange to anyone that such things occur in Music, he should remember that not only in this science, but in every other as well, in every art, and in every other created thing, great imperfection is found. And this, I believe, was the will of **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Iddio Ottimo Maſſimo"</note>; so that, seeing the imperfection of these inferior things, we may turn our intellect to the contemplation of His Infinite Wisdom, in which every thing is found to be not only **Perfect**, but even **Excellent**.

He argues that natural singing voices remain superior to artificial instruments because they can achieve the "perfect" natural proportions that instruments cannot.</summary>

### Demonstration from which it can be understood that the shown Tempering, or Distribution, is reasonably done, and that it cannot be done in any other way. Ch. 43.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' showing a landscape with buildings or ruins under a sky with clouds.</image-desc>
I SHALL now proceed to demonstrate the reason for such **Tempering** <note>original: "Participatione"; referring to the "sharing" or distribution of a small interval to tune an instrument</note>. It must be known that there have been some who held the opinion that the interval of the **Comma** <note>original: "Coma"; a tiny acoustic discrepancy between notes reached by different mathematical paths</note> shown above should be distributed between those two intervals closest to it—one in the high register and one in the low—by dividing it into two equal parts. They would increase each of these two intervals by half a Comma while leaving all other intervals in their natural forms. Truly, it seems to me they are much mistaken for many reasons. First, because only those two intervals near the Comma would participate in its division, while none of the others would, making the instrument's proportions unequal. One would hear a **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> and a **Fourth** <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note> where one interval is larger than the other. Furthermore, those intervals where this distribution was made would become dissonant because of the great distance they would have from their true forms. The **Whole Tones** <note>original: "Tuoni"</note> near such a Comma, participating in one of its parts, would be contained by a proportion that could not be added to a Fifth, a Fourth, or a **Minor Third** <note>original: "Semiditono"</note> to form any consonance. And although they say experience shows that these intervals, increased or diminished in such a way, do not depart from their proper form so much that the hearing suffers—no differently than if the Comma were not distributed that way—this is not true. Therefore, I believe these people have never made any trial of this. The sense of hearing itself makes it manifest that they are dissonant. Anyone can prove this for themselves by dividing the said Comma into two equal parts, as I showed above in Chapter 24. For once the resulting parts are added to the two **Minor Whole Tones** <note>original: "tuoni Sesquinoni"; intervals with a 10:9 ratio</note> that are near them, everyone will be able to recognize that what I have said is the truth, and that one must seek to distribute such a Comma in another way so the hearing is not offended.

But because I said above that during this distribution, some **Consonances** <note>original: "Conſonanze"</note> or other intervals are diminished by two, four, or even one-seventh part of the said Comma; and similarly, some are increased by one, two, or three-seventh parts; finally, not only every Fifth, every Fourth, every **Major Third** <note>original: "Ditono"</note>, and every Minor Third (which are consonant intervals) are increased or diminished equally and remain equal in the low, middle, and high registers of the instrument, but so too are the dissonant ones: the Major Whole Tone, the Minor Whole Tone, and the Major and Minor Semitones. I hold this to be even more true because a manifest sign shows us that such a distribution is good and done with every justification. For the **Minor Semitone** <note>original: "Semituono minore"</note>, which is contained by the proportion 135:128 <note>original: "Super 7. partiente 128"</note> and is not used in the **Diatonic genus** <note>a standard arrangement of whole and half steps</note>, and is found between the strings SB and KB, becomes smaller by the whole Comma <note>original: "Sesquioitanteſima"; the ratio 81:80</note>. Thus, it remains in the proportion 25:24 <note>original: "Sesquieuteſimaquarta"</note>. Consequently, its proportion remains **rational** <note>expressible as a simple whole-number ratio</note>; the others, however, once all the **Octaves** <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note> (contained in the **Double** <note>original: "Dupla"; 2:1</note> proportion) are removed, are **irrational** and unknown. This is because the parts removed from or added to rational quantities (their first natural forms) are irrational when the division of the whole into parts is irrational; that which results is likewise irrational. Just as that which is born from the addition or subtraction of a rational quantity from an irrational one is irrational, so too is that which comes from the subtraction or addition of an irrational proportion from a rational one. But this does not happen with rational proportions, for everything that is born from adding or subtracting one quantity from another is rational. Therefore, this distribution, which is made by adding or removing such parts, cannot for any reason be rational, nor can it be named or described with specific numbers in any way, since the division of the Comma into seven equal parts is not rational. To show, then, that such a distribution must necessarily be made in the said manner and no other, we shall proceed in this order: we will first take only twelve strings of the **Monochord** <note>original: "Monochordo"; a single-stringed scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals</note> placed above—namely FB, EB, DB, IB, HB, GB, SB, KB, NB, RB, MB, and LB—which will be sufficient.

<summary>Zarlino argues that a musical temperament must distribute the tuning error (the comma) equally across all intervals of an instrument rather than isolating it, ensuring the instrument sounds harmonious in all registers. He notes that while this process results in mathematically "irrational" ratios, it is acoustically necessary for a well-tuned instrument.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the mathematical demonstration of musical temperament (the "Distribution") from the previous chapter, specifically focusing on the division of the Comma into seven parts to adjust fifths and fourths within the octave.</meta>

Part. 129

...serves to demonstrate the purpose; and then we will perfectly tune the strings FB and NB in such a way that they contain the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Octave (2:1 ratio)</note> consonance. We shall leave these unchangeable, and upon them we will begin to make this Distribution. Even though one could begin upon whichever strings one wished, we will do this to follow the majority of those who tune modern instruments, as they begin upon such strings. It must be noted, however, that I said "unchangeable"; it is necessary that the first string upon which the Distribution is founded be stable, and that every <term>Diapason</term> be reduced to its perfection—that is, in its true form, which is the <term>double proportion</term> <note>2:1 ratio</note>—because it does not suffer any mutability or variation. 

Assuming, then, that we have these stable strings, we will make the Distribution among those strings located between them, using the other strings placed outside of them. To begin, we will take the first <term>Diapente</term> <note>The Perfect Fifth (3:2 ratio)</note> placed in the low register, which will be FB and HB, contained by the <term>Sesquialtera proportion</term> <note>3:2 ratio</note>. Without moving FB in any other way, we will make HB lower in pitch by the quantity of two-seventh parts of a <term>Comma</term>, as I have said. We do this by first placing and multiplying the <term>Comma</term> onto the string HB, first adding to string IB the <term>Minor Tone</term> contained in the <term>Sesquinona proportion</term> <note>10:9 ratio</note> and dividing it into ten parts. Once nine parts of it are taken, between the string containing that quantity and HB (which is the high string of the <term>Major Tone</term> <note>9:8 ratio</note> IB and HB), we will have the <term>Comma</term>. This is because if we take the minor tone from the said [major] <term>Tone</term> (which will be IB) and the quantity of nine parts, the <term>Comma</term> will undoubtedly remain, contained by the <term>Sesqui-eightieth proportion</term> <note>81:80 ratio, known as the Syntonic Comma</note>. We will divide this into seven equal parts, according to the method shown above in chapter 25. 

Then, leaving aside the two highest parts of it and taking only the five placed in the low register, we will have—all at once with string aB—two consonances adjusted to their irrational proportions: the <term>Diapente</term> FB and aB, and the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The Perfect Fourth (4:3 ratio)</note> aB and NB. We will now take aB, which with MB contains the <term>Diapente</term> higher by two equal seventh parts of the said <term>Comma</term>. Having divided the <term>Comma</term> RB and MB into seven equal parts (as we did the first), and leaving the four highest parts—which are the two parts left so that we have the <term>Diapente</term> in its true proportion, and two other parts then for its diminution—the string bB will give us our intent. 

To this string, we will find the corresponding string in the low register in <term>double proportion</term> so that we can perfectly hear the <term>Diapason</term>. This will be done when, after having multiplied and placed the <term>Comma</term> before EB and divided it into seven equal parts, we take the four parts placed in the high register. Thus, between CB and this bB, we will have the sought-after consonance by means of string cB, according to our purpose. Since EB and MB correspond in equal sound in the <term>Diapason</term> consonance, and adding to both towards the low register four parts of the <term>Comma</term> (which are equal to each other), it follows that the ends of these additions are likewise equal and render the <term>Diapason</term> consonance. For, according to the Second and Third Common Notion of the first book of <term>Euclid's Elements</term>, if equals are added to equals, or taken away from equals, the results are similarly equal. We will also have between cB and aB a <term>Diatessaron</term> increased by two parts of the <term>Comma</term>, which will be equal in proportion to aB and NB. 

We will now make string GB correspond in <term>Sesquialtera proportion</term> to cB, adding the <term>Comma</term> to GB and dividing it according to the given method. Then, leaving the four parts placed in the high register and the two that follow toward the low, between cB and dB we will have another <term>Diapente</term> diminished by two parts of a <term>Comma</term>, and between dB and bB another <term>Diatessaron</term> increased by the same amount. Following this are dB and LB, which contain the <term>Diapente</term> diminished by one-seventh part; since we wish to diminish it by another part so that it matches the others in equal proportion, we will place the <term>Comma</term> before LB, divided like the others into seven intervals. Leaving the highest, we will take only the six placed in the low register, and from eB we will have our purpose. To this, we will find the corresponding string in <term>double proportion</term> in this way: we will divide the <term>Comma</term> placed before DB into seven parts, then taking the highest part, we will have fB, which with the said eB will give us the <term>Diapason</term> consonance in its natural form, and another <term>Diatessaron</term> equal in proportion to the others, which will be fB and dB, in its accidental form. 

Between fB and KB, there will then be a <term>Diapente</term> likewise in its accidental form, higher by one of those parts. Therefore, wanting to reduce it to its proportion, we will place the <term>Comma</term> before KB, divided in the given way; leaving the highest part for the surplus and the two following parts for the diminution, by means of string gB, we will not only have the true accidental proportion of the <term>Diapente</term>, but also that of the <term>Diatessaron</term> contained between gB and eB. It now remains to reduce the <term>Diapente</term> IB and NB, and the <term>Diatessaron</term> FB and IB, to their proportion. Thus we will add to IB the <term>Comma</term>, which after being divided into seven parts—and once we have taken the two lowest seventh parts—will, by means of string hB, give us the proportion of these consonances. That is, we will have increased the <term>Diatessaron</term> placed in the low register by that many parts, and made the <term>Diapente</term> smaller...

Now, to give its proper proportion to the string $S B$, which is found to be a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> away from $h B$, decreased by two parts; we will add the Comma to $S B$, and after it has been divided, we will take the four lower parts at point $i$; and between $i B$ and $h B$ we will have made the said Fourth equal to the others in proportion. In this manner, then, we will have increased or decreased equally not only every Consonance in its specific kind, but every other Interval that was contained between the said strings. From the twelve strings that were there before, we will have reduced them to the number of eleven, corresponding to the number of Pythagorean strings <note>the standard notes of the ancient Greek musical scale</note> placed above in chapter 28; these we can conveniently describe with Guido's letters <note>the alphabetical notation A-G used by Guido d'Arezzo</note>, without doubling the 'd' in any other way. And what I said above regarding the minor Semitone is seen to be verified: since it is found in its proportion between strings $S B$ and $K B$, and remains diminished at the low end (as seen in the demonstration) by the four parts of the Comma contained between $S B$ and $i B$; and at the high end by three parts, contained between $g B$ and $K B$; if we add these three parts to the first four, there is no doubt they will reach the number of Seven, making the whole Comma. But because (as I have said elsewhere) the Comma is contained by the ratio 81:80 <note>original: "Sesquiottantesima"</note>; therefore, if from the ratio 135:128 <note>original: "Super 7 partiente 128"</note>, which was the first form of the minor Semitone, which is rational, we take away the 81:80, which is also rational; the remainder will make the ratio 25:24 <note>original: "Sesquiae-tesimaquarta" [likely a misprint for sesquiventiquattresima]</note>, which is the rational form of such a Semitone. We can now see in what manner the parts of the Comma come to be distributed, with a certain equality, into every Consonance and every Interval. For this reason, we can hold for certain that this method is so much the better and truer as we see that every consonance and every interval—whether at the low end, in the middle, or at the end—is increased or decreased by the same amount, according as its proportion requires. Nor is it seen in any way that one is larger or smaller than the other; nor is it perceived that there is any remainder, however small, of any part of the said Comma. Indeed, if any of these things were found, it would be a manifest sign that such a Distribution was not made in the proper manner. Thus, I conclude that if one wished to attempt to make such a Distribution otherwise, such labor would be in vain and without fruit, as experience will always make manifest. Therefore, since such a thing cannot be done in any other way that works well in the aforementioned instruments, it follows that such a Temperament <note>original: "Participatione"</note> or Distribution is made perfectly, with the proper means, and without any error.

## On the Construction of the equally tempered diatonic Monochord, reduced to the number of Pythagorean strings. Chap. 44.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'P' set within a square border, decorated with classical foliage and vine motifs.</image-desc>

We can now show in what manner, with little effort and without any error, one can construct the Monochord, tempered in its intervals in such a way that it is found to be midway between the "Diatono" Diatonic <note>the Pythagorean tuning based on pure fifths</note> and that which is called the Syntonic Diatonic, discovered by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient astronomer and music theorist</note>. I hope this composition will be no less useful to all those who desire to know the temperament and the true proportion of its intervals, than it will be to those who build musical instruments and desire to know the logic and measure of any interval, in order to be able to proportion those of their instruments with reason. We must, therefore, first know that just as each term of any interval placed at its proportion upon any string can be made larger or smaller by a certain amount from whichever side one wishes—that is, from the low side or from the high side—by the proportion of the part of the string to its Whole that is taken or left from one of these two sides; so also it can be made lower or higher by that amount which is the proportion that the part of the string left or added at the low or high end has with its Whole, as has been seen in many places. Thus I say that after one has found a board or table that is very flat and well-prepared, as the others were arranged, we will place in the middle of it the line $a b$ in place of a string, upon which we will make the construction of the said Monochord. Upon this line, therefore, we will first arrange the Comma on the left side at its proportion, in the shortest and most expeditious way possible, in this manner. We will first arrange the Major Tone <term>Major Tone: an interval with the ratio 9:8</term> upon the said string at its proportion; then the Minor Tone <term>Minor Tone: an interval with the ratio 10:9</term>, so that the lower term of the Major Tone is also the lower term of the Minor Tone. Once this is done, the Comma <note>the mathematical difference between these two types of tones</note> will be located between the higher terms of each of these two Tones; for it becomes the difference found between the quantities of the one and the other, as the proof demonstrates to us. To this we will then add another, placing it at its proportion, as we did the first,

For since between the whole division and the parts $e b$ the Tone is placed in its true proportion, which is the Sesquioctave <note>original: "Sesquiottaua," the ratio 9:8</note>; if from the low part (that is, from the divided line) we remove all the proportion added to the string $c b$, which are the four highest parts of the Comma $a b$ and $c b$; there is no doubt that the divided whole remains diminished by that amount, and $c b$ takes its place. Thus, if the proportion placed between the divided whole and $e b$ remains diminished by so many parts, consequently the sounds arising from the strings drawn under such proportions will also remain diminished by that amount. Since (as I said in the First Part) musicians judge the proportion of sound to sound to be the same as the proportion of each part of the string to its whole. We will thus have made by this path the Major Tone—which is found between these two strings **A** and **♮** <note>the symbol for B-natural</note>—smaller by four parts of a Comma. We will immediately follow this with the Major Semitone, contained by the ratio 16:15 <note>original: "Sesquiquintadecima"</note>; which, when added to the Major Tone, makes the Minor Third <note>original: "Semiditono," literally a "half-ditone"</note>, contained by the ratio 6:5 <note>original: "Sesquiquinta"</note>, as I have said many times. And because the Semitone increases by three-sevenths of the Comma, and the Tone decreases by four; therefore, by taking three from four, one remains, which will be that part by which the Minor Third is diminished, as was said above. We will then take only one part of the Comma $a b$ and $c b$, which will be the one closest to $c$, and we will put it together with $c b$: then dividing this whole into six equal parts and taking five (which will be at point $f$), between the division and $f b$ we will have placed the Minor Third in its natural proportion; and between $c b$ and $f b$ we will have it diminished by one-seventh of the Comma, for the reasons already stated, and in its accidental form. In this way, we will have a third string, which we will mark with the letter **C**, and it will be the second of the first Tetrachord, which with **♮** will contain the Major Semitone, increased by three-sevenths. We will then immediately add the Tone to this, so that the first string with the fourth has the consonance of the Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. This is because those two parts, which were set aside before the line was halved, are added to it. in the Fourth <note>original: "Sesquiterza," the mathematical ratio of 4:3</note>; and while the higher note remains in its original state, that proportion is made larger by exactly the same amount that was added. But because between string *cb* and *eb* we have a diminished Major Tone, and between *eb* and *fb* an increased Major Semitone, between *fb* and *gb* we will therefore have a Minor Tone. This results from completing a Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> that has been increased by two parts of the Coma <note>a "comma" is a tiny mathematical difference in pitch between two notes, here being divided into seven parts for tuning</note>, as the calculation will always demonstrate. We will then have string **D**, which contains with **C** a Minor Tone increased by three parts of the Coma. This Tone occurs only in this location (and in its corresponding strings in the Octave <note>original: "proportione Dupla," or 2:1 ratio</note>), immediately following the Major Semitone when proceeding from low to high. Thus, I believe the difficulty found in tuning or tempering modern instruments—specifically the string **G** with **d**, and **d** with **aa**—arises from nothing else than the fact that strings **D** and **d** on said instruments take the place of the Coma. Consequently, two Minor Tones follow one another immediately, between strings **C** and **D**, and between **D** and **E**, as well as between those that correspond to these in the Octave ratio. To follow what we have begun, we shall add to string **D** another string that contains a Minor Tone with it on the higher side, which will be the second interval of the first Tetrachord <note>a four-note scale segment used as a building block in ancient music theory</note>. We will ensure that this added string, when compared to **A**, creates a Fifth <note>original: "Diapente," the 3:2 ratio</note>. But first, we must know its proportion, which is a diminution of two-sevenths of a Coma. We will therefore take the two parts closest to *c* located between *a* and *c*, and combine them with the whole of *cb*. We will then divide this entire length into three equal parts, according to the greater term containing the proportion of the Fifth. Then, taking two parts for the lesser term (which will be *hb*), we will have placed the Fifth in its true proportion between this and the divided line. The diminished Fifth, following the reasons previously given, will be between *cb* and *hb*. In this way, we will have string **E**, which will contain with **D** the aforementioned Tone, increased by the necessary parts; it will be the last high string of the first Tetrachord and the first low string of the second. To find the second string of this new group, which should be a Major Semitone away from **E** and a Minor Sixth <note>original: "Essachordo minore"</note> away from **A**, we must first know the logic of its proportion. As we have seen, this Sixth is increased by one-seventh of the Coma, just as the Major Sixth is also increased. Therefore, we will take the line *cb* diminished by one-seventh of the Coma *cb* and *db*, and divide the remainder into eight equal parts (since 8 is the greater term of the Sixth's ratio). Then, taking only five parts for the lesser term at point *i*, we will have the said Sixth in its true proportion between the whole of the divided line and *ib*, which will be string **F**; and between *cb* and *ib*, we will have it increased by that specific part. We will now add the seventh string to this sixth one, which will be a Major Tone away from it. But we must first know what proportion it has with the first string, and by how much this interval (called the Minor Seventh <note>original: "Eptachordo minore"</note>) increases or decreases. We find that its true proportion is the *Superquadripartientequinta* <note>a complex ratio of 9:5</note>, and that it increases by four of the aforementioned parts. This is because the interval added beyond the seventh string to reach the eighth string decreases by the same amount that the Seventh preceding it increases. Conversely, however much that interval is made larger, the Seventh is diminished by that much. And because the interval remaining to reach the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> is a Major Tone (which is diminished by four-sevenths of a Coma), the said Seventh is therefore increased by that many parts. The same is observed in accommodating the other strings, always paying regard to the interval that immediately follows the one you wish to tune. We will therefore take line *cb* diminished by the four parts closest to *c* (those placed between *c* and *d*) and divide it into nine equal parts. By taking five parts at point *k*, we will have placed the said Seventh in its true proportion between the divided line and *kb*; and between *cb* and *kb*, we will have it increased by four parts of the Coma. String **G** will thus be the seventh of this order and the third of the second Tetrachord. To these, we will add the eighth string, which will contain the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> with the first, simply by dividing *db* into two equal parts. This is because such a consonance remains in its perfection—that is, in the Double proportion <note>2:1</note>. At point *l*, we will have string **a** as intended. Between strings **A, ♮, C, D, E, F, G,** and **a**, we will have the Octave mediated by six strings and divided into seven intervals, each of which is increased or diminished according to the proportion that belongs to it, in the manner shown. *Monochord* <note>a scientific instrument with a single string used to demonstrate musical ratios</note> *in its intervals, according to their*

*that is, to accommodate the Major and Minor*

*25:24 proportion* <note>original: "Sesquiventesimaquarta"</note>*, which is rational;*

*twenty-four equal parts, and taking twenty-five*

## Whether in Songs we continue by singing the intervals produced by the true and sonorous numbers, or those shown; and concerning the solution of certain doubts. Chapter 45.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap 'H' within a square frame, depicting a figure (possibly a scholar or saint) seated in a landscape setting.</image-desc>

NOW a doubt may arise, considering what I have said above: whether among the parts of Songs or compositions—whose harmonies arise from natural instruments <note>By "natural instruments," the author refers to the human voice.</note>—one hears the true and legitimate intervals contained in their true forms, or rather those increased or diminished according to the method shown <note>Referring to "tempering," where intervals are slightly adjusted to fit the limitations of fixed-pitch instruments like the harpsichord.</note>. To this doubt, one can answer and say that truly those intervals contained in their true forms are heard, and not the others. This is because Nature (as the Philosopher <note>original: "Filosofo"; likely referring to Aristotle.</note> holds) is in all things always inclined to follow the good, and to desire not only the good and the delightful, but the best, and even that which is ordered toward the good. Therefore, since such intervals and consonances are ordered for the perfection of Harmony and Melody; and since these intervals are better and more delightful; and not only more delightful, but more greatly desirable; we naturally strive in vocal compositions to follow those that are produced in their true form, rather than the others, which by their nature are neither better nor more fit for the perfection of harmonies.

And such an inclination is seen to be within us by many evident signs. First: because everyone naturally flees the opposite of the good—that is, the evil and the bad—and not only that, but even the less good, and that which is an impediment to the good, and always chooses the best, or flees the most wretched. As we see, even every Science (as Plato says) with all its strength drives away depraved things and chooses the useful and most fit. And it is only right, since every art, and every doctrine, and similarly every act and every choice, seems to desire a certain good and every perfection; which, once acquired, it then strives with all its power to remain within and to preserve.

We see next that those intervals which are in their true forms are more greatly desirable than the others because they are better; and this we see every day with experience in hand. For both those who have a confused knowledge of the extremes of any consonance—without knowing how to discern the perfect from the merely increased or diminished, and lacking the reason of <term>Temperament</term> <note>original: "Participatione"; the mathematical adjustment of intervals.</note>—as well as those who possess such judgment and reason, whenever they wish to tune their instruments, they reduce the consonances to their perfection. The former do so because they do not know how to temper and proportion them; following that which delights them most, they believe that to be the form required to tune said instruments; and thus, deceived by the sense, they do not obtain what they desire. The latter, however, having the reason of Temperament, more easily increase or diminish them, and more quickly reduce them to that form required by the number of strings of such instruments, bringing their work to perfection.

And if it were true that both among voices and in instruments one heard only the consonances and intervals shown above, outside of their natural proportions, it would follow that those arising from the true <term>harmonic numbers</term> <note>The mathematical ratios (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) that define pure musical intervals.</note> would never be found in practice, but only in potentiality. Such potentiality would be vain and frustrated, since every natural power, when it is not brought into action for some time, is without any utility in nature. And yet we see that God and Nature never do anything in vain; therefore, it must be said that such power is sometimes brought into action. Since it cannot be brought forth by means of the instruments named above, it is necessary that it be brought forth by means of the voices; otherwise the <term>Sonorous</term> or <term>Harmonic Number</term> shown elsewhere—which is the cause of consonances and is found in sonorous quantities—would be entirely vain and superfluous in nature.

From what has been said, then, one can conclude that those intervals heard in vocal compositions are contained in their true forms, which are found (as I have said many times) among the parts within the <term>Senary Number</term> <note>original: "Numero senario"; the number six, which Zarlino identifies as the foundation of all perfect musical intervals.</note>. But perhaps someone might say: If nature is inclined to follow the good and the best, and if the intervals arising from harmonic numbers are better than others and consequently more consonant, why is it that we often hear in vocal compositions a certain something that is more like dissonance than consonance? To this, it can be said that it may proceed from many causes. First: because one of the singers might have imperfect or hindered hearing, which above all other things ought to be without any defect in those who practice Music. Next, because it could be that the voices of the singers are disproportionate to one another; where one is clear and sweet, and...

<meta>catchword: the other</meta>

<summary>Zarlino argues that human voices naturally sing pure mathematical intervals (based on the number six) because nature always seeks perfection, whereas instruments must use "tempered" or adjusted intervals.</summary>

the other, by contrast, being dark and graceless, cannot produce a <term>harmony</term><note>original: "concento"; refers to the pleasant blending of multiple voices or sounds.</note> that is good. It could also be that one of the singers has greater lung capacity and makes himself heard more than the other; or that one has
<margin>+</margin>such a nature that in singing he raises his voice more than he should in the high register, while the other willingly stretches toward the low; these things would be the reason that one would never hear any harmony that was good. But when the voices are proportionate to one another and well-united, without having any impediment, and are uttered by the singers with some discretion and good judgment—in such a way that one voice does not overpower the other—I hold for certain that such intervals would be heard as perfect. The listeners would take no small pleasure and contentment from the songs they heard, because besides the other effects that occur in singing the parts, one would sometimes hear certain accents and (as they say) certain <term>vocal runs</term><note>original: "tirate di gorgia"; a style of virtuoso vocal ornamentation involving rapid scales.</note> with some <term>diminutions</term><note>original: "diminutioni"; the practice of breaking a long note into many shorter, decorative notes.</note> that cannot be heard on artificial instruments. 

Perhaps someone will say here: "Let us grant that what has been said is true; does it not follow from this a great inconvenience: that whenever artificial instruments are accompanied by human voices, the latter can never be united with the former in any way?" I respond that whoever wishes to examine the matter minutely will find that this "inconvenience" happens infinite times; for it never, or only rarely, happens that voices and sounds accord so perfectly that no discrepancy is heard between them, even if it be minimal. And although it seems to many that they are united, this happens because of the small distance between them, which the hearing of those who do not have much practice or good judgment in musical matters cannot grasp. It is not, however, impossible for voices to unite perfectly with sounds without any inconvenience occurring—all the more so because (as I have said elsewhere) Nature always desires to approach the Good and the Better, provided it is known, which is desirable in itself; and it is her own nature to flee the Sad, which is abominable, and that which is an impediment to the good. 

Wherefore the Senses cannot suffer the dissonance that would be heard if the singer wished to follow naturally the intervals that arise according to the nature of <term>sonorous numbers</term><note>original: "Numeri sonori"; the simple mathematical ratios (like 2:1 for an octave) that produce pure musical intervals.</note>; and therefore the singer tries to unite the voices with the sounds as much as possible. And this is not difficult for him, because it is naturally granted to voices that they can bend in every direction—becoming high from low, and conversely, low from high—in whatever way is most convenient. Nor has Nature placed any limit or end upon them, except in the manner we saw in the First Part. But artificial instruments cannot do this, since they are stable and cannot be varied or changed in sound in any way, Art having placed a certain limit or end upon them. 

But let these two things accord and unite as perfectly as they wish; when they are later separated from one another, the voices will return to their perfection, and the instruments will remain in their first quality and quantity. Nor should this seem strange to us, since greater effects are seen in natural things when they approach or mix with one another. And this is seen not only in things that have some agreement between them, but even among those that are entirely contrary to each other. For they mutually take on the quality of one another (it being true that every Agent that performs an action undergoes some reaction in the doing) or one of
<margin>*</margin>them alone takes on the quality of its contrary; once separated, it returns to its first quality or nature and its first being. We can see this conveniently in Water, which is by nature cold and humid; when brought near its contrary—namely Fire, which is hot and dry—it takes on the quality of the Fire, becoming hot. But once separated, it returns to its first state—that is, it becomes cold. 

The same happens in other natural things, which by habit are never varied in their nature; as is seen in heavy things, whose nature is to move toward the center [of the Earth]. Even if they are violently thrown upward infinite times, they never take on the nature of ascending, but always decline downward, as is manifest in the Stone, which by its nature is always inclined to descend to the center. This same thing we can see in the human voice: although it is often forced by the sound of artificial instruments, it does not stop being itself, so that after it is unaccompanied, it returns to its first nature. 

Someone might even add, perhaps, that with greater pleasure and delight we most often hear the sounds and harmonies of artificial instruments—such as Organs, Harpsichords, Virginals, Lutes, and other similar ones—than we hear the harmony that arises from voices. And this is true because this can arise from the lack of proportion found among voices, and from the proportion and <term>temperament</term><note>original: "temperatura/temperamento"; the system of tuning where intervals are adjusted (tempered) so that the instrument sounds acceptable in multiple keys.</note> placed among the sounds of the instrument. For the good craftsman has sought to imitate nature in it as much as he could, and to reduce it to that perfection granted to it by Art, proportioning its intervals with such a temperament so that one does not exceed the other in any quality;

Thus, when the instrument remains in such an accord and <term>temperament</term><note>original: "temperatura"; the system of adjusting musical intervals to allow for different keys and pure-sounding harmonies.</note>, and in an invariable order of sounds, the Hearing is greatly delighted by the harmony that is born from it; especially since, by nature, it delights in a proportioned order. But if by chance such an order and temperament changes its quality, it seems that immediately those sounds that are born from it offend the ear exceedingly. We see this same thing happen often in voices, which, being disproportionate and poorly united, cannot be heard; but if they are proportionate and well-united, they greatly delight the senses. Therefore, without any doubt, a harmony and a <term>concord</term><note>original: "concento"; a harmonious blending of voices.</note> of voices is heard with greater delight than the concord that arises from any instrument whatsoever. This, then, is the reason why we sometimes hear with greater pleasure the sound of an instrument than the harmony born of voices; even if such an instrument is of little quality and its sounds are optimally proportioned, while the voices are good and resonant, yet among themselves disproportionate and poorly united. And this should not seem strange to us, since sometimes we see with greater delight, greater contentment, and more satisfaction a horse that is well-formed and proportioned than a man who is deformed and ugly; and yet Man is the most graceful and noble animal found among mortals, and one of the marvelous things that blessed God has created. But what can be said to this? Except that Nature exceedingly hates those things that are imperfect, disproportionate, and monstrous within their species, and takes greater pleasure in those that are closer to their perfection.

## On the Filling-in of the displayed Diatonic Monochord with the strings of the Chromatic genus. Chapter 46.

It remains now for us to see in what way we can usefully fill in <note>original: "inspessare"; literally "to thicken," referring to adding more notes/strings to the scale to make it more dense.</note> the Diatonic <term>Monochord</term><note>original: "Monochordo"; a single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals mathematically.</note> shown above with the strings of the Chromatic and Enharmonic genera. Thus, it should be noted that having added, in the composition shown, the <term>conjunct tetrachord</term><note>original: "Tetrachordo synemennon"; a group of four notes starting from the middle of the Greek scale.</note> with the <term>middle tetrachord</term><note>original: "Tetrachordo meson"; the second-lowest four-note grouping in the ancient Greek system.</note>; by such a conjunction, the whole tone placed between the string **a** and the **♮** comes to be divided by the string **b** into two parts: that is, into a **major semitone** and a **minor semitone**. Because of this, a new tetrachord is born by chance between the strings **a**, **b**, **♮**, and **d**; for between **a** and **b** one finds the major semitone; between **b** and **♮** the minor semitone; and between **♮** and **d** the <term>trihemitone</term><note>original: "Trihemituono"; an interval consisting of three semitones, roughly equivalent to a minor third.</note>, as can be seen in the four strings placed below.

| Fourth | Major Third | Tone |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Trihemitone** | | **d.** (Highest of the conjuncts) |
| **Minor Semitone** | | **♮.** (Next to the middle) |
| **Major Semitone** | | **b.** (Third of the conjuncts) |
| | | **a.** (Middle string) |

And because such a tetrachord does not resemble in any way any of the Diatonic tetrachords set down in Chapter 16, it cannot truly be said to be Diatonic; but it can certainly be said to be Chromatic. This is because it closely approaches the "soft chromatic" of <term>Ptolemy</term><note>original: "Tolomeo"; Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist.</note>, as it proceeds from the low to the high by a semitone in the first interval, similarly by another semitone in the second, and by a trihemitone in the third, according to the form of the Chromatic tetrachords already shown. So we can truly say that this is the true Chromatic tetrachord we seek, which is very useful and necessary for the filling-in of the displayed Diatonic Monochord. And if anyone wished to say that the Ancients placed the smallest interval in the lowest part of their tetrachords, and the others then in order of the larger interval, and that in this one we find first the major semitone and then the minor; to him I would answer that this matters little, since such a thing is not done without purpose. These intervals are naturally placed according to what the nature of <term>Harmonic Numbers</term><note>original: "Numeri harmonici"; the set of integers (1 to 6) that Zarlino believed governed all perfect musical intervals.</note> allows, which give us first in the lower part the parts, or rather

For this reason, we must take care to arrange the intervals in such a way that we can obtain all those consonances that are suitable for the generation of perfect harmony; we should not worry if the greater interval is placed in the <term>Tetrachords</term><note>A scale of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> before the lesser one, which might otherwise result in the loss of many consonances. The Ancients indeed had such a concern; but they did not compose their <term>harmony</term><note>original: "concento"; refers to the sounding together of multiple voices.</note> in the way that we do; and they held the opinion that greater intervals (as I have also said elsewhere) were composed of smaller ones. If, therefore, having placed the major semitone before the minor does not change anything, it will also not prevent such a Tetrachord from being <term>Chromatic</term><note>One of the three genera of ancient Greek music, characterized by the use of semitones.</note>; since it is neither Diatonic nor <term>Enharmonic</term><note>The third genus of Greek music, utilizing even smaller intervals called quarter-tones.</note>. And even though this is very different in its first two intervals from the "soft Chromatic," this also matters little, considering the little use that is derived from those intervals: given that they cannot provide any consonance, as would be manifest if one wished to use them. This Tetrachord, then, will become the form for the other four Tetrachords when we wish to densify the <term>Monochord</term><note>A single-string instrument used for measuring musical ratios.</note> described above in Chapter 40. It is quite true that if they were placed in such a Monochord containing those proportions, they would generate confusion rather than convenience, due to the multitude of keys and strings that would be added to find the consonances according to our purpose, beyond those already shown. However, we will only reduce the aforementioned Trihemitone among the diatonic strings in the manner shown, making it smaller in every Tetrachord by two parts of a <term>Comma</term><note>A very small mathematical difference between intervals.</note>, as we did above; and in this way, besides removing the inconvenience for the players, we will have avoided many things that would have been very strange to hear due to the passages made from one interval to another; which are not heard after the <term>Participation</term><note>original: "Participatione"; another word for temperament, the system of tuning where intervals are slightly adjusted to sound better across different keys.</note>. We will therefore arrange the Trihemitone in its own proper place in this manner: adding to the high string of every Tetrachord of the Monochord placed above, a string in the low range that is distant from it by a Sesquiquinta (6:5). This, once added to the high string mentioned above, will contain the sought-after Trihemitone; and similarly, it will divide the major tone of every Tetrachord into two parts, according to the ratio of the interval placed in said Tetrachord; so that between the first and second diatonic [strings], and between the added and the said high string, we will have the chromatic Tetrachord, according to our purpose. This string, then reduced to its proportion by means of the Participation, will give us the diatonic Monochord densified by chromatic strings in every Tetrachord; of which Monochord I will not extend myself further to demonstrate anything; because its order in modern instruments is already so widely used that by now it can be known by everyone. In this order, so that the chromatic strings might be more easily distinguished from the others, the one who arranged their <term>keyboard</term><note>original: "Tastame"; the layout or set of keys on a keyboard instrument.</note> in the way that is seen, made the keys colored; and perhaps he did this because he knew that "Chromatic" was said to be "Colored" from color, as was said above in Chapter 16. Nor was he content only to densify the aforementioned Tetrachords with such strings, dividing the Tone...

greater into two parts: but they also divided the lesser ones into two <term>semitones</term><note>The smallest interval in common use in Western music, half of a whole tone.</note>, one larger than the other; as can be seen in such instruments. And this, I believe, was done for the greater convenience of the players, so that they could express their modulations with greater freedom in both the low and the high registers, using varied <term>Modes</term><note>The specific patterns of notes or scales used in a composition.</note> and varied harmonies. The <term>colored strings</term><note>original: "chorde colorate"; refers to the strings on a keyboard or harp used for chromatic notes (sharps/flats), which were often stained or made of different materials.</note> were then marked by practical musicians in their melodies and noted with two signs; such as the <term>Trite synemmenon</term><note>The third string of the "synemmenon" (disjunct) tetrachord in Ancient Greek theory.</note> with this round letter 'b' of Guido, which they call <term>soft b</term><note>original: "b molle"; the ancestor of the modern flat sign (♭).</note>; and likewise all those that are consonant with it, both in the low and the high, by a <term>Diapason</term><note>An octave.</note>, or a <term>Diapente</term><note>A perfect fifth.</note>, or a <term>Diatessaron</term><note>A perfect fourth.</note>. The others they noted with this sign 𝄰, which they name <term>Diesis</term><note>Now used for a sharp sign, though historically it referred to a smaller interval.</note>; perhaps holding the opinion of <term>Philolaus</term><note>A Pythagorean philosopher (c. 470 – c. 385 BC).</note>, who (as <term>Boethius</term><note>An influential 6th-century Roman philosopher and music theorist.</note> recounts) said that the space by which the <term>Sesquiterza</term><note>A 4:3 ratio, representing a perfect fourth.</note> is greater than two tones was called a Diesis; which space some moderns call the minor semitone, because most of the time it is placed to create the interval of the semitone, as we shall see elsewhere. And when they wanted such a semitone to be sung in any part of their melodies, and they ascended from the low to the high, they placed the 'b': but when they descended from the high to the low, they placed the 𝄰, which even the most modern players do when, in ascending and descending by means of such signs or strings, they wish to place the tone. I believe this sign 𝄰 was introduced by some who dreamed that the tone was, or was composed of, nine <term>commas</term><note>A very small musical interval; Zarlino is critiquing the Pythagorean idea that a whole tone can be divided into nine equal parts.</note>; or that it could be divided at least into that many parts: for they wanted the major semitone to be five commas and the minor to be four; and for this reason, when they proceeded from the diatonic strings to the chromatic ones in the manner I have described, they placed this sign for the space of a semitone to denote this interval: because they held the opinion (as many moderns still do) that such an interval was the minor semitone and consisted of four commas; hence they marked the space with four little crossed lines, which are the four placed in that sign: seeing as they followed the order of the strings, the number, and the <term>Pythagorean proportions</term><note>Mathematical ratios used to define musical intervals according to the school of Pythagoras.</note> shown above. But how much these people deceive themselves can easily be understood from what we have said and seen above, and from what Boethius says in Chapter 15 of the third book of *On Music*, showing that the tone of <term>Sesquioctave</term><note>A 9:8 ratio, representing a whole tone.</note> proportion is greater than eight and less than nine commas. And in Chapter 14, he says that the minor semitone is greater than three commas and less than four. Therefore, if the tone is greater than eight and less than nine commas, and one cannot have any certainty of its quantity, it seems to me certainly a great arrogance to wish to state determinately a thing that Science places in doubt and leaves indeterminate. Thus, if this interval cannot be named with a determinate quantity, even less can those that are smaller be named, such as the major semitone, the minor semitone, and other similar ones.

## In what manner we can fill in the said Monochord with Enharmonic strings. Chap. 47.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a figure standing in a landscape with hills and a tree.</image-desc>
WISHING then to fill in the said instrument with Enharmonic strings, so that we have in every <term>Tetrachord</term><note>A four-note scale spanning a perfect fourth.</note> the major semitone divided into two <term>Diesis</term><note>In the Enharmonic genus, this refers to a quarter-tone interval.</note>, we shall place only one string in the middle of it in such a way that with one of the named diatonic or chromatic strings, it may be consonant, and we shall have our purpose. But before we proceed further, it seems to me that I ought to show the Proportions of the Tetrachord, so that when one wishes to fill in the <term>syntonic diatonic</term><note>Ptolemy's tuning system which favored pure major thirds (5:4).</note> monochord, the reason for its intervals may be known. For which reason one must observe that every Enharmonic Tetrachord proceeds from the low to the high by two Diesis and one uncomposed <term>Ditone</term><note>A major third.</note>; as has been said many times: we must choose that which has its intervals contained by proportions that can lead us to the use of perfect harmony; nor should we have regard for those that were placed in many Tetrachords by the Ancients: since they are not suited to the generation of perfect <term>harmonies</term><note>original: "concenti"; refers to the pleasant sounding together of notes.</note>, and do little for our purpose. Therefore we must choose those intervals that are useful; so that we do not end up multiplying things without any necessity. And it should be noted that I call those intervals useful which, when added to any other, give some consonance. Therefore, we shall first choose from the Tetrachords shown above that which is useful and suited to the purpose; then we shall add intervals contained by such proportions that, after the aforementioned Monochord has been filled in according to the reasons of the proportions that I am about to show, every string will have its corresponding diatonic or chromatic string that is consonant. The Ditone, then, that <term>Ptolemy</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer who wrote extensively on music theory.</note> places in his Enharmonic Tetrachord, found in Chapter 37, will be to our purpose: because it is a consonant interval, and its true form is found...

[concluded]...and the useful and necessary intervals that contribute to the constitution of every kind of harmony are already placed in their proper locations.

### That it is more reasonable to say that smaller intervals arise from larger ones, than to say that larger ones are composed of smaller ones; and that the modern Hexachord is better ordered than the ancient Tetrachord. Chapter 48.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'H' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or philosopher, within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>NOW I wish to satisfy the promise I made above, when I said I wanted to show why it is more reasonable that the larger intervals generate the smaller ones, rather than saying that the consonances or smaller intervals are composed of smaller units. Therefore, it should be known that (as I have said elsewhere) the ancient Greeks held the opinion that consonances and other larger intervals were composed of several smaller intervals. For this reason, they had a "Minimum" interval, which they considered indivisible, just as one considers "Unity" in Arithmetic; they called this the "First" of its kind. Aristotle mentions this in the 10th book of the *Metaphysics*, and (in my opinion) following the views of Aristoxenus, he places the <term>Diesis</term><note>In this context, the smallest melodic interval or "quarter-tone" used in ancient Greek music theory.</note> in music, just as he also places it in the first book of the *Posterior [Analytics]*, saying: <note>original: "ἐν δὲ μέλει δίεσις"</note> "and in melody, the diesis"; he intends for it to be the common measure of every consonance, just as Unity is the common measure of all numbers.

But it seems to me that they spoke beside the point. All consonances and other musical intervals, however small, have their origin in the division of the <term>Diapason</term><note>The interval of an Octave.</note>. Truly, the Octave is the first of its kind, the cause of all other intervals, and their common measure. Marsilio Ficino confirms this in his commentary on Plato's *Epinomis* when speaking of the form of this consonance: he says that the "Double" (the 2:1 ratio) is deemed a perfect proportion, primarily because it is the first among proportions, generated between Unity and the Binary (1 and 2). Furthermore, while it seems to depart from Unity, it restores that Unity by doubling itself. Beyond this, he says it contains every other proportion within itself, since the <term>Sesquialtera</term><note>The 3:2 ratio, which produces the Perfect Fifth.</note>, the <term>Sesquiterza</term><note>The 4:3 ratio, which produces the Perfect Fourth.</note>, and other similar ratios are within it as its parts.

All of this is verified by the Octave in music, whose form is this Double ratio. It is more perfect than any other consonance and suffers no change at its extremes; while it seems to move away from a certain unity of sounds, it restores that unity by doubling its parts. Similarly, it contains within itself (as I have said) every simple consonance and every tiny interval. Thus, it is no wonder that all the Greeks, by common consent, called it <note>original: "Διὰ πασῶν" (Dia pason)</note> "Through all"; for it is present in every other consonance or interval. If an interval is simple and smaller, it is one of the Octave's parts; if it is composite and larger, it is composed of the Octave and one of its parts, as I showed in Chapter 16 of the First Part.

This can be understood by the fact that Sounds partake more of <term>Continuous Quantity</term><note>Like a line that can be divided anywhere, rather than distinct, separate objects.</note> than <term>Discrete Quantity</term><note>Like a collection of individual coins or numbers that are counted.</note>. We can see this clearly: when we put together the <term>Diapente</term><note>The Perfect Fifth.</note> and the <term>Diatessaron</term><note>The Perfect Fourth.</note>, the first is contained by five strings and the second by four. Together they form the Octave, which is contained within eight strings, not nine, even though five and four added together make nine. This happens because they join at a common boundary, which is the nature of Continuous Quantity. This boundary is the highest string of the Fifth (when placed low) and the lowest string of the Fourth (when placed high), joined together in "harmonic proportionality." Or conversely, in an arithmetic joining, the highest string of the Fourth and the lowest of the Fifth would be this common boundary.

Just as it is an error to say that a divisible Whole is composed of its parts—since the Whole exists before the parts—it is an error to say that the Octave is composed of the Fifth, the Fourth, and other consonances. The Octave is prior to each of them. Therefore, I say that the Moderns divided their <term>Hexachord</term><note>A six-note scale (Ut-Re-Mi-Fa-Sol-La) used in medieval and Renaissance music.</note> into tones and semitones with better reason than the ancient Greeks did their <term>Tetrachord</term><note>A four-note scale used in ancient Greek music.</note>. The Greeks placed the smaller intervals at the bottom of their scales and the larger ones above; the Moderns did the opposite, placing the larger intervals at the base of their Hexachords and the smaller ones at the top, as is proper and as the harmonic numbers dictate, as could be seen in Chapter 39 above.

<summary>Zarlino argues that the Octave is the fundamental unit of music from which all other intervals are derived by division, rather than being built up from small "atoms" of sound. He uses this to justify the structure of the modern hexachord over the ancient Greek tetrachord.</summary>
<keywords>Octave, Diapason, Fifth, Fourth, Hexachord, Tetrachord, Aristotle, Marsilio Ficino, harmonic proportion, continuous quantity, musical intervals, music theory history</keywords>

### That each of the named Genera can be called both Genus and Species, and that every other division or ordering of sounds is vain and useless. Chapter 49.

NOR SHOULD we omit saying that we can call the aforementioned *Genera*, according to different respects, both *Genera* and *Species*: since they can be considered in two ways: first, regarding the use of the Ancients; second, regarding the use of the Moderns. Thus, considered according to the use of the Ancients—who sought more to vary their melodies than to achieve the perfect use of harmonies through the acquisition of all the consonances—we will find various divisions and different forms of tetrachords, as I have shown; these are reduced under one of these three headings: *Diatonic*, *Chromatic*, and *Enharmonic*. And because those things that are placed under a *Universal* are called *Species*, and that *Universal* which contains such *Species* under it is called a *Genus*, they may first be called *Species*: for each is contained under this most universal genus, *Melody* or *Harmony*. Afterward, they may be named *Genera*, because each of them has many *species* under it.

Considered then according to the use of the *Moderns*, with the acquisition of all the consonances and with the perfection of harmony, there is no doubt that we will have no more than one *Species* of each of them. For it is impossible that from other numbers, other proportions, and another order than that shown above, we could obtain the desired goal. Therefore, we must call them not *Genera*, but only *Species*: because they have nothing under them except individuals, which are this or that song. And they will likewise be subject to this universal genus, *Melody* or *Harmony*, of which the *Diatonic*, the *Chromatic*, and the *Enharmonic* will be the *species*. For this reason, considered in the first way, they can be called *Genera* and *Species*; but considered in the second way, they will be named only *species*.

And although the forms of the intervals of each *species* of these three genera, shown by *Ptolemy* in Chapter 16 of the *First Book of Harmonics*, are found located among the proportions of the *Superparticular* genus <note>A ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2, 4:3). Ancient theorists often argued only these could produce pure musical intervals.</note>; and *Boethius* is of the same opinion as *Ptolemy*—when he reproves the divisions of *Archytas* and writes against *Aristoxenus* and *Didymus*—that from no other genus of proportion than the *Multiple* <note>A ratio where the larger number is a multiple of the smaller (e.g., 2:1, 3:1).</note> and the *Superparticular* (which are the genera of the *Proportion of greater inequality*) can any interval arise that is fit for consonance, except for the *Double supertripartient-third* <note>The ratio 8:3, which produces the interval of an octave plus a fourth.</note>, from which the consonance of the *Octave plus a fourth* <note>original: "Diapason diatessaron"</note> is born; nevertheless, Nature, opposing such a law, grants us many other intervals which are approved by the senses and confirmed as consonant by everyone’s opinion. These are fit and very necessary for melodies and for the generation of harmonies in each of our *Species*, and they have their forms contained among other genera of proportion.

And although the reasons that *Ptolemy* brings against *Aristoxenus*, *Archytas*, *Didymus*, and many others have the power to make someone believe (without putting it to the test) that the perfection of the three *Genera* consists in the *Proportions* and *Intervals* of each *species* found by him; nonetheless (as I have shown), no perfection is found in them. Because I desired to show a way and an order by which one could come to the perfect knowledge of the *Science* and the knowledge of the true *Intervals*—which serve the purpose of harmonies practiced perfectly with *Voices* and with artificial *Instruments*—so that the senses would not be discordant with reason, it was necessary for me to depart from such a law. For otherwise, what usually happens to some who use an instrument to do something would have happened to me: they cannot bring their work to perfection with such means, and all their designs remain in vain.

Wherefore, if it is true what the *Philosopher* <note>Referring to Aristotle.</note> says, that *In vain and without any use are those things put into practice by which one wishes to reach a goal and then does not reach it*, I should by no means follow such a law, nor the *Divisions*, *Proportions*, and *Orders* found by *Ptolemy* or any other *Ancient or modern musician*, except for those of the *Syntonic Diatonic* <note>The specific tuning system favored by Zarlino, also known as Just Intonation, which allows for pure major and minor thirds.</note>. For if I had not wanted to depart from such a law and had chosen such orders to demonstrate the true proportion of each interval, and how one could build an *Instrument* in which harmonies could be practiced perfectly (as has always been my goal), and I could not have obtained from them what I desired, my effort would have been madness and my labor vain; and such a law and orders would have been entirely without any utility. For which...

->For what reason Consonances have their origin more from the Proportions of greater inequality, than from those of lesser. Chap. 50.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' containing a small woodcut illustration of a village or town with buildings and a bridge over water.</image-desc>

IT SEEMS to me now that I see some who doubt, and at the same time wish to know, why it is that the Proportions of lesser inequality <note>Ratios where the first number is smaller than the second, such as 1:2 or 2:3</note> are not suited to the generation of musical Consonances: seeing that one hears the consonance of the Diapason <note>original: *Diapason*; the interval of an octave</note> between two sounds, of which one is contained under the ratio of Unity <note>the number 1</note> compared to another that is contained under the ratio of the Binary <note>the number 2</note>, just as much as one hears it between two where one has the ratio of the Binary and is compared to that which is considered under the ratio of Unity. Since there is no other difference than the comparison, and the Sounds remain invariable, no reason can be given to convince us to say that such a Consonance is made more by the Double proportion <note>2:1</note>, contained in one of the genera of greater inequality, than by the Subdouble <note>1:2</note>, which is contained among those of lesser. 

To this doubt, some answer by saying that although every musical Consonance can be born from one or the other genus in terms of simple production, there is nonetheless a difference in the way they are produced: For in the production of Consonances, the *sonorous Number* <note>a number used to measure musical pitch</note> compared to another sonorous number is compared in a more perfect way according to the proportion of greater inequality, and more nobly still, than is done when comparing it according to the proportion of lesser inequality. Hence, since everything produced has a greater dependence on the more noble way of its production, it reasonably follows that the aforementioned Consonances have their origin more from the Proportions of greater inequality, as from a more noble thing, than from those of lesser. 

They also add another reason, saying: In the Genera of greater inequality, the larger term contains the smaller; and in those of lesser, the contrary is found. Therefore, taking the act of *containing* for the Form, and *being contained* for the Matter; and since the Form is more noble than the Matter; it is manifest that the sonorous Number compared according to the proportions of greater inequality is compared in a more perfect & more noble way than according to those of lesser. 

And although these reasons of theirs might satisfy the mind of someone, it nonetheless seems to me—taking the Proportions of lesser inequality in the way that was determined in Chapter 30 of the First Part, and as they truly ought to be taken—that they serve little to the purpose: because they suppose that every musical Consonance can be born from one or the other of the named genera in terms of simple production, which is made from number to number. But in fact, it is not so: because (as we have seen) the Proportions of greater inequality are contained under one genus, that is, under *Habit* <note>a state of being or possession</note>; and those of lesser under another, that is, under *Privation* <note>the absence or lack of a quality</note>. And the Proportions of greater inequality are Real & Positive; and those of lesser inequality are only Rational & Privative; and the first are greater than Equality, but the second are less. 

Since the terms of the first are real (because they are found among real things) and the terms of the second are not (since they have at most one real term), it is impossible that Consonances could have their origin from these; for Voices & Sounds are drawn from the power of a thing that strikes, and from that which is struck, which are real things and have their being in nature; just as are animate Bodies and sonorous ones. And because Consonance is Sound, or rather a Mixture of low & high sound; and since Sound is a natural thing that is born from artificial or natural Instruments that are found to exist among natural things; it cannot be said that consonances are born from the Proportions of lesser inequality, taken in the manner said: since they have nothing but one real term, whence they are called Rational & Privative only. Therefore, as these proportions are not suited to the generation of consonances, I say that they have their origin more from those of greater Inequality than from those of lesser. But so that what I have said does not appear strange to anyone—that is, that the Proportions of Lesser inequality have only one real term—it must be

<meta>observed</meta>

<summary>Zarlino explains why musical consonances are mathematically defined by proportions of "greater inequality" (where the larger number comes first, like 2:1). He argues that these ratios are "real and positive," whereas ratios of lesser inequality (like 1:2) are merely "rational and privative" and cannot physically generate sound.</summary>
