...observe that, since every *Proportion* is a *Relation*, in a *real Relation* there necessarily concur two real extremes, contained under the same immediate genus, as appears in its definition placed in *Chapter 21* of the *First Part*. But in a *Rational Relation*, it is not inconsistent for one extreme to be comprised under one genus and the other under another. This is because *Relation* (as *Aristotle* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Categories* or *Metaphysics*, where he defines relational categories.</note> maintains) is of two sorts—leaving aside those that do not serve our purpose. The first of these is when a relation is made between two natural things with one another, according to a certain thing that really belongs to both. And such a relation is twofold: for either it is founded upon *Continuous Quantity* <note>term: *Continuous Quantity* — Physical magnitude, such as a line or a solid body.</note> or *Discrete Quantity* <note>term: *Discrete Quantity* — Numerical units that are separate and distinct.</note>; or it is founded upon *Active Power* and *Passive Power*, insofar as they are principles of acting and of suffering <note>In this context, "suffering" or "patire" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note>. Of this second kind, one could say it can be considered in two ways: that is, insofar as such things are not joined in the act, wherefore they are called *active* and *passive*; and insofar as they are joined, and are called *Agents* and *Patients*. One could also say that all these *Relations* are real, provided they are founded upon natural and *created Active* or *Passive power*, and not upon the *Uncreated*. 

But for brevity I will leave everything else aside and speak only of that which is found in *Continuous Quantity*, comparing two lines or two finite quantities of the same genus to one another; or of that which is found in *Discrete Quantity*, when one number is compared to another in the manner I showed in the *First Part*. Therefore, these *Relations* are truly real and reciprocal: because from the very nature of the thing, every two numerical *Quantities* have a reciprocal order to one another in the ratio of the measure founded upon *Quantity*. And this is known because just as the *Half* <note>original: *Mezo*</note> regards the *Double*, not only by the apprehension of the Intellect, but also by its own nature; so the *Double* has regard for the *Half*. 

The second *Relation* is that which is founded upon two extremes that are not of the same genus or order; and this is likewise of two manners. One is when one of the extremes is natural and the other is of reason, and is founded upon the dependence of one upon the other; such as the *Sensible* and the *Sense*, and the *Intelligible* and the *Intellect*. For as to the act, the *Sense* depends on the *Sensible*, we having *Sense* so that we may feel. Similarly, *speculative Science* <note>Theoretical knowledge or study.</note> depends on the thing that can be known, and the *Intellect* from that which can be understood; which things, insofar as they have their being among natural things, are outside the order of *Sensible* and *Intelligible* being. Wherefore between *Science* and *Sense* there is a certain real relation, according to how they are ordered toward *Knowing* or *Feeling* things; but considered in themselves, they are outside this order, and in it there is no real relation to *Science* and *Sense*, but only a rational one, insofar as the Intellect apprehends them as terms of the relation of *science* and *sense*. Because (as *Aristotle* says) they are not truly called *relatives* because they refer to things, but because things refer to them; just as one sees that a *Column*, having neither right nor left side except insofar as it is placed to the right or left of a *Man*, does not create a real relation on its own part, but the *Man* does. 

The other relation is founded upon the imitation of a thing by another thing, such as the *Image* to the *Man*; whence it is called an *Image* because it imitates or represents the *Man*. But these relations are very different from the first two: because those are *real* and *reciprocal*, since one of their extremes refers to the other *reciprocally*; while these are not reciprocal: because the real relation stays only in one term, which is that which depends upon or imitates the thing; the other is then called relative only by relation: since the other extreme refers to it, and it is the term of such a relation. In such a way that just as the thing of which one can have knowledge has a relation to *Science*—this referring to that which terminates the dependence of *Science*—so the *Man* has a relation to the *Image*, because the *Image* refers to the *Man* and terminates its imitation. 

I say *therefore* in this regard, that in the first manner of the *First relation* are found the *Species* or *Proportions* contained in the genus of *greater inequality*, which are applied to the extremes of *any* musical interval; and this because the terms of both their extremes are real and have a reciprocal relation to one another. But in the relations of the Second kind are those *Proportions* contained in the genus of *lesser inequality*: since there is only one real term, placed in *Equality* <note>The ratio 1:1, which Zarlino views as the natural, stable foundation.</note>, which is situated among natural things and is always stable and remaining in every proportion, as I said in *Chapter 30* of the *First Part*; and the other is rational only and imagined. In such a way that the Relation is real only in one extreme, which is that which depends on or imitates the natural thing, and the other is called relative by relation: since the other extreme refers to it, and it is the term of such a *Relation*. It is therefore not inconsistent that *Proportions* of *lesser inequality* have only one real term, since sometimes the Relation is made of two things that are not comprised under the same genus or order, but rather under two different genera or orders, as we have seen; even though such proportions could be called *Real* when they are consi...

### Doubt concerning what has been said. Chapter 51.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, within an architectural frame.</image-desc>

Someone might perhaps say: Since proportions of lesser inequality are only Rational and not Real <note>In Renaissance logic, a "Real" relation exists in nature between two things, while a "Rational" relation exists only in the mind's way of categorizing them.</note>; how can that which the philosophers say be verified, when speaking of things that have a real relationship and mutual Action with one another, that no action proceeds from the class of lesser inequality? For the terms of these proportions are truly located among natural things. 

Wherefore, to satisfy such a question, I say that—since Action arises (according to the opinion of the Commentator <note>The "Commentator" usually refers to Averroës, the 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western science.</note>) from the victory of the thing that moves over the thing being moved—many philosophers, considering this victory from the side of the Agent, attributed to it the name of "Greater Inequality." For they saw very well that such a thing could not exist without some proportion between the one and the other; and because they also considered it from the side of the Patient <note>term: Patient — The thing that receives an action or is acted upon (from the Latin *pati*, to suffer or endure).</note>, they attributed to it the name of "Lesser." 

But because between the Agent and the Patient one can consider two things: first the Excess, and then the Defect; I say the Excess is on the part of the Agent in respect to the Patient, and the Defect is on the part of the Patient in respect to the Agent. Therefore, I am of the opinion that they would have done better if they had said that Action comes from the Proportion of Excess, and Passion from that of Defect. Since Proportion is a Relation, and such a Relation (as the philosophers maintain) is found in three manners: namely, Equality, Superposition, and Subposition <note>original: "Agguaglianza, Soprapositione, & Soppositione"</note>. 

Wherefore they could conveniently say that no Action comes from this proportion [of equality]; for between two things found to be of equal power and equal virtue, such that one cannot overcome the other, there comes no Action nor any Passion. But it does indeed occur in the others, because the Agent overcomes the Patient in virtue and power by a certain ratio of abundance, from which Action alone arises; or rather the Patient is overcome by the Agent, from which Passion arises—of which modes every philosopher speaks abundantly. 

And although the proportions of Superposition and those of Subposition are the same thing regarding the Subject and the Matter—because they are opposite only by relation—the proportion of the virtue and power of the Agent might be, let us say, 4, and that of the Patient 2; just as the proportion of the virtue of the Patient would similarly be 2 and that of the Agent 4. They would be found equal in distance, and the Agent would overcome the Patient with that proportion by which the Patient was overcome by the Agent; nonetheless, they are different as to reason and form. This is because Action is considered in one way, and Passion in another: first insofar as one overcomes the other, then insofar as one is overcome by the other. Thus the Agent overcomes the Patient according to Excess, and conversely, the Patient is overcome by the Agent according to Defect. 

For this reason, it is manifest that Excess and Defect are not the same thing according to Form and Reason, even though they are the same thing according to Subject and Matter. Having considered these proportions in this way, I say that such a proposition is verified when, by the proportion of the class of lesser inequality, we understand the proportion or relation of Subposition. But when one wishes to understand the class of lesser inequality in another way, such a proposition would have no truth in it, as anyone can see by reading and examining what was said in Chapter 30 of the First Part. 

Now, to put an end to this discussion of ours, I say that what I have said until now will be sufficient for what has been reasoned concerning the First Part of Music, called *Theoretical* or *Speculative* <note>term: Speculative Music — The study of music as a mathematical and philosophical science, focusing on ratios and the laws of the universe rather than performance.</note>. For it is necessary that we now see those things which are necessary for the understanding of the Second [Part], which is named *Practical*, which will be of great utility to every studious person and will be contained in the two following parts.

->THE END OF THE SECOND PART.<-

# THE THIRD PART
## Of the Harmonic Institutions
### BY MASTER GIOSEFFO ZARLINO OF CHIOGGIA,
### IN WHICH WE DISCUSS THE SECOND PART OF MUSIC CALLED PRACTICAL, THAT IS, THE ART OF COUNTERPOINT.

---

->*What Counterpoint is, and why it is so named.*<-
->Chapter One.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring floral patterns and a scenic background with classical architecture and figures.</image-desc>

HAVING until now in the two preceding parts reasoned sufficiently regarding the *First part of Music, called Theoretical or Speculative; and* having seen those things which are relevant *and* necessary to the *Musician;* it remains that in these two following parts, I reason about those things that coincide in the *Second part, which is called Practical, which consists in the composition of songs, or melodies, which are composed for two, or more voices;* which practitioners name the *Art of Counterpoint.* But because *Counterpoint* is the principal *Subject* of this part; therefore before anything else we will see what it is; *and* why it is so called. I say then that *Counterpoint* is that *Concordance,* or harmony, which arises from a body which has in itself various parts, *and* various modulations adapted to the song, ordered with voices distant from one another by commensurable *and* harmonic intervals; *and* it is that which in chapter 12 of the *Second part* I named *Proper Harmony* <note>original: "Harmonia propria"</note>. One can also say that *Counterpoint* is a mode of harmony, which contains within itself various variations of sounds, or of singable voices, with a certain ratio of proportions *and* measure of time: Or rather that it is a certain artful union of diverse sounds, reduced to concordance. From which definitions we can gather that the *Art of Counterpoint* is nothing other than a faculty which teaches how to find various parts of the song, *and* to arrange the singable sounds with proportionate ratio *and* measure of Time in the modulations. And because musicians formerly composed their counterpoints only with certain dots <note>The author refers to the "points" (punti) or dots that were used in early notation before modern note shapes were standardized.</note>, they therefore called it Counterpoint: because they placed one against the other, as we do at present, who place one Note against another: *and* they took such a Point to stand for the voice: for just as the Point is the beginning of the Line, *and* is also its end; so the Sound, or the Voice, is the beginning *and* end of the *Modulation:* *and* between them is contained the *Consonance,* from which *Counterpoint* is then made. It would perhaps have been more reasonable to call it *Countersound* <note>original: "Contrasuono"</note> than *Counterpoint:* because one sound is placed against another: but so as not to depart from common usage, I too have wished to call it *Counterpoint;* as if to say *Point against point;* or *Note against note.* It should be noted, however, that *Counterpoint* is found in two sorts, namely *Simple and Diminished.* *Simple* is that which has modulations composed only of consonances, *and* of equal figures <note>term: figures — the shapes of notes that indicate their rhythmic value</note>, whichever they may be, one against the other: But *Diminished* not only has parts composed of *Consonances,* but also of *Dissonances; and* in it is placed every sort of singable figure, according to the will of the Composer; and its modulations are ordered by intervals, or singable spaces; *and* the figures numbered according to the measure of its Time. The proper nature of Counterpoint is to ascend *and* to descend with diverse sounds, or voices, through contrary movements at one and the same time, through proportionate intervals that are suitable for consonance: for *Harmony* arises from nothing other than the diversity of things that are put together *and* are opposite to one another. And Counterpoint is judged all the more delightful *and* good, the more it is used with good grace, better methods, *and* with an ornate *and* beautiful progression; and this according to the rules required by the Art of good and correct— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword "tamente" indicates the next word is "correttamente" (correctly).</note>

### Of the invention of Clefs, and of singable Figures. Cap. 2.

<image-desc>Decorative initial E featuring a landscape with a house and trees.</image-desc>
AND BECAUSE every mathematical science consists more in **Demonstration**, to grasp its truth, than in disputes and opinions: given that once certain principles, called **Premises**, are granted by the adversary, the **Demonstration** is made, which makes everything clear, without difficulty, and resolved; therefore, wishing to come to the demonstrative act, it was necessary to find the means to bring demonstrations to our senses, so that we might be fully capable of understanding them. Hence, just as Mathematicians, seeing the necessity of the thing, devised certain **Ciphers** <note>original: "Cifere," meaning symbols or numerical characters</note>; not however separated from the matter, although they consider them apart from it, if not in their essence, at least according to reason; but rather joined to it; and these were Points, Lines, Surfaces, Bodies, Numbers, and infinite other characters, which are only painted on paper with certain colors, and used in place of the thing signified: So also did the Musicians, in order to be able to put their speculations and demonstrations into practice and place them under the judgment of the senses; since Voices and Sounds cannot in any way be written, nor painted on paper, nor in any other material; they devised certain signs or characters, which they called **Figures**, or **Notes**: and they governed them in the manner that we shall see further below. But they named the strings of their instruments and the voices of the melodies with one of these six syllables, placed in this order: *Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La*; just as I have shown in chapter 30 of the Second Part. Such an order they then called **Deduction**, or **Reduction** <note>A "Deduction" refers to the hexachordal sequence, the foundational six-note scale of the period.</note>, which is nothing other than a transposition of voices from one place to another: or (as they say) a natural progression of the six syllables shown above. But because such a **Deduction** can have its beginning in three places, namely on the string C, on F, and on G; therefore <term>Guido</term><note>Guido d'Arezzo, the 11th-century monk credited with inventing the musical staff and solmization.</note> divided his **Introductory** into three parts, applying the said syllables to three **Properties** in such a way; that when the first of the said syllables (followed by the others in order) began from the letter C, he intended that such an order or deduction be sung by the property which he called **Nature**; and when it began from the letter F, by that of the **round b**, or **soft** [b-flat], as we wish to call it: But when it had its beginning from the letter G, he intended it to be sung by that of the **square ♮**, or **hard** [b-natural]; and he said that the **Property** was a derivation of several voices or sounds from one same principle; or that it was a singular or particular **Deduction** of each ordered **Hexachord**. Wherefore one must know that Guido joined every **Deduction** with one of the **Greek Tetrachords**, adding to each **Tetrachord** two more strings at the lower end, such as that of *Ut* and that of *Re*: for every **Tetrachord** begins on the string of *Mi*; as was commemorated in the Second Part: so that every **Hexachord** contains each species of the **Diatessaron** <note>original: "Diatessaron," the interval of a Perfect Fourth.</note>, which are three; as we shall see in its place. The seat, then, or the place of the voices or sounds, which Musicians call **Strings**, he named **Clefs** <note>original: "Chiaui," literally "Keys."</note>; which are distinguished from one another by equidistant and parallel lines; including therein the spaces in between; even though the Voices or Sounds are not equally distant from one another. Thus he placed the first clef, which he named **Gamma Ut** <note>The Greek letter Γ (Gamma) was used to represent the lowest note of the medieval system.</note>, on the line; and **A re**, which is the second, in the space. Similarly he placed **B mi** on a line; and **C fa ut** in a space, and step by step he placed the others in such a manner; as they are seen in order in the **Introductory** named above, marking each with its own proper letter. But because at times such a thing could generate confusion, the more modern [musicians], perhaps remembering that it is in vain to do something by means of many things which can be done with few and done well, devised certain **Ciphers**; by which Singers might be guided, so that having left behind certain others, by those alone they might have knowledge of every modulation and every melody; and from them they might have notice of the **Spaces**, or **Intervals** of the **Tone**, of the **Semitone**, and of the others as well. These **Ciphers** were always called **Clefs**; standing in this analogy, that just as the door is opened by the **Key** and one enters the house and sees what is found within; so by such **Ciphers** the modulation is opened, and each of the named intervals is known. The opposite would certainly happen if they were removed: for then everything would be filled with confusion; as anyone can imagine. They then named those **Clefs** with the names noted in the example placed below, which, although at times some of them are placed upon the same of the five shown lines, are nonetheless distant from each other by five letters, that is, by a **Diapente** <note>original: "Diapente," the interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note>. They devised

<image-desc>A single musical staff displaying a series of notes in descending order of duration: Maxima, Longa, Breve, Semibreve, Minima, Semiminima, Croma, and Semicroma.</image-desc>

And their value is such that one is worth double the other: for they intended that the *Maxima* should be worth two *longs*, the *Long* two *breves*, the *Breve* two *semibreves*, and so on, in <term>Imperfect Time</term> <note>original: "Tempo imperfetto"; a rhythmic system where notes are divided into two equal parts</note>: because in <term>Perfect Time</term>, in <term>Mode</term>, and in <term>Prolation</term> <note>These terms refer to the complex mensural system where notes could be divided into three parts instead of two</note> they considered them in another way, as we shall see elsewhere. And according to what some believe, the *Breve* was the mother and the beginning of all the others: since the *Maxima* and the *Long* were later devised for its augmentation, and the *Semibreve* with the others following for its diminution. And although the Ancients in their compositions placed other signs and ciphers—such as the Signs of Time, Mode, and Prolation, Points, square <term>b</term> <note>B-natural</note>, round <term>b</term> <note>B-flat</note>, sharps <note>original: "Diesis"</note>, Rests, Ligatures, Signs of Entry <note>original: "Prese"</note>, Fermatons <note>original: "Coronate"</note>, Refrains, and a thousand others that may occur, a good part of which are still used by the moderns—nevertheless, I do not intend to speak except of those that are relevant to the purpose and as they become convenient. For I primarily intend to treat those things that are necessary and fall under the perception of hearing, whose object is truly Sound; leaving aside (as much as I can) those things that are strange and foreign to that sense.

### On the Elements that compose Counterpoint. Cap. 3.

HAVING therefore to reason about the composition of Counterpoint, it is necessary before anything else to know the Elements of which it is composed: for no one will ever know how to order or compose anything in any way, nor will they ever know the nature of the compound, if they do not first know the things that must be ordered or put together, and their nature or their reason. Whence I say that the Elements of Counterpoint are of two kinds: that is, Simple and Replicated. The Simple are all those intervals that are smaller than the *Diapason* <note>original: "Diapason," the Greek term for an Octave</note>: that is, the *Unison* (following in this the usage of Practical musicians), the *Second*, the *Third*, the *Fourth*, the *Fifth*, the *Sixth*, the *Seventh*, and the *Octave*, which is the *Diapason* itself. And the Replicated are all those that are larger than it: that is, the *Ninth*, the *Tenth*, the *Eleventh*, the *Twelfth*, and the others in order. Nor should anyone marvel that I have placed the *Diapason* among the simple intervals: since it is not truly a replicated interval, nor a compound one, as perhaps some think: for it is the first among the other intervals; and (as Boethius affirms) it is the first consonance. And being the first interval, it cannot be compound: since every compound is always after the parts of which it is composed, and the *Diapason* is first, and every other interval is after it. And this is seen because it has its form from the *Dupla* proportion <note>2:1 ratio</note>, which is the first of inequality; and the other consonances or intervals have their forms from the proportions that follow the *Dupla*; which are (as I have said elsewhere) the parts of the form of the Diapason, which arise from its division. Being therefore the *Diapason* first, it cannot be said that it is compound: for it would be necessary for it to be composed of intervals more simple and prior than its own. Nor can we say that it is composed of several *Unisons*, as some foolish people have been of the opinion; even though they are simpler than the *Diapason* and prior to it: for Unisons (as we shall see) are not intervals; but are like the *Point* <note>original: "Punto"</note>, which is a minimum indivisible thing that cannot be continued with another point, as Aristotle proves in the 6th book of the *Physics*. And to whoever should ask in what manner the *Diapason* is born, one could answer without any error that it is born in almost the same way that the Line is born, which is the first divisible quantity. Being therefore first...

### Third [Part]

first among the other musical intervals, and since it cannot be composed of <term>Unisons</term> <note>Two notes of the same pitch</note>, nor of other intervals however small, it can be concluded that it is simple and without composition. Being first, it is the mother, generator, source, and principle from which every other <term>Consonance</term> <note>A combination of notes that sounds pleasant or stable</note> and every other Interval derives: for that which is first is always the cause of that which follows, and not the other way around. And just as we say that Inequality begins from Equality, so must we say that the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note> begins from the Unison: because the Unison takes its form from the former, and in the latter, the form of the Octave is found. And so great is the friendship between these two that, because of their similarity and simplicity, the sense of hearing is moved by the sounds of the Octave in almost the same way it is moved by those of the Unison. And this happens primarily from the similarity they have together, as I have said: because every generator always generates that which is generated in its own likeness; and secondly, because both are Principles: that is, the Unison for Equality (from which Inequality begins) and the Octave for the <term>Double Ratio</term> <note>original: "Dupla"; the 2:1 ratio</note>, which is first among all other consonances and from which the other proportions of inequality begin.

And the Octave is simple in such a way that, although it is contained by two sounds different in their position (so to speak), they nonetheless seem to the sense to be a single sound: because they are very similar. This happens because of the proximity of the <term>Binary</term> <note>The number 2</note> to <term>Unity</term> <note>The number 1</note>, which are contained in the extremes of its form, which is the Double Ratio. Hence, such a form contains two principles: namely Unity, which is the principle of Numbers and is that among them which cannot be divided; and the Binary, which is the principle of the joining of units and is the smallest number that can be divided, and is measured by unity only twice—but it cannot be divided into two numbers, because it contains in itself no other number than the unit repeated. Therefore, just as the Binary has almost the same nature as Unity by being close to it, so the Octave has almost the same nature as the Unison, both by being close to it (as seen in the terms of their forms) and also because the extremes of their proportions are not composed of any numbers other than Unity. Thus, as the effect imitates the nature of its cause, and as harmonic numbers are the causes of harmonic sounds, it is reasonable that the sound also imitates their nature, and that the said two sounds of the Octave seem like a single sound. 

Such simplicity is also clearly recognized when any interval, whether consonant or dissonant, is added to either the low or high side of this Octave: for then it seems to be joined to almost a single sound. Whence we see that the <term>Octave plus a Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapason diapente"; a compound interval</note> moves the hearing in almost the same way as the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note> does; likewise the Octave with the <term>Major Third</term> <note>original: "Ditono"</note> acts as the Major Third does alone. And we hear the Octave with a <term>Whole Tone</term> <note>original: "Tuono"</note> to be just as dissonant as the Tone is, and both move the feeling in almost the same way; the same could be said of the others as well. And this cannot happen in any of the other consonances, as is manifest: because they are not as simple as the Octave is. This is clear to see: for if we add a Major Third to a <term>Minor Third</term> <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>, the extremes of such an addition will produce a Fifth. Similarly, if we join two Fifths, two Fourths <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, two Major Thirds, two Minor Thirds, or two others similar in proportion; besides the different sounds that will be heard in their extreme strings, the interval will also be dissonant: because neither extreme of any such interval has any reason or similarity to being the same sound, as those of the Octave do.

From this it arises that the simple consonances placed beyond the Octave have that same similarity they had when they were simple and placed within the extremes of that Octave. And I have said "simple" because one sees that every other interval placed beyond the Octave is born in a certain way that makes it seem to have its origin from one of those simple ones. Thus we see verified what I said in the First Part: that consonances and dissonances follow almost the same logic in multiplying as simple numbers do beyond the <term>Ten</term> <note>original: "Denario"</note>. For just as beyond ten one does not see any new number added, but only a replication of one of those smaller than it—since by adding Unity (which is first) to the Ten, the Eleven <note>original: "Undenario"</note> is born; then by adding the Binary, the Twelve <note>original: "Duodenario"</note> is born; similarly, by adding the Ternary and the others in order, numbers are generated that are similar in their termination to those simple ones that are added—so also beyond the said Octave, no new sound is added: but rather those same ones contained within it, which being finite, one always returns circularly to the first ones. 

Therefore, it can be concluded by the reasons given that the Octave should truly be called a simple interval, and not a replicated or composite one, given that it is like the Element of every other consonance and interval. Following then the custom of the Practitioners, we shall say that the simple Elements, or (as they say) the simple **Species of Counterpoint**, are seven and no more, leaving out the Unison: because it is not a consonance nor an Interval, as we shall see in its place; these are the Second, the Third, the Fourth, the Fifth, the Sixth,

## Division of the shown Species. Chapter 4.

BOETHIUS <note>A 6th-century Roman scholar whose musical treatises were the foundation of medieval and Renaissance music theory</note> In the 10th & 11th chapters of the Fifth book of *On Music*, following the opinion of <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>An ancient Greek astronomer and music theorist</note>, calls some of the Voices or Sounds <term>Unisons</term>, and some <term>Non-unisons</term>. Those he names Unisons which, either individually or added together, make one and the same sound. Then he divides those that are not Unisons and makes many parts; placing some as <term>Equisonant</term> <note>Sounds that blend so perfectly they seem like one</note>, some <term>Consonant</term> <note>Pleasant-sounding combinations</note>, others <term>Emmelic</term> <note>From the Greek word for "harmonious"; sounds suitable for melody but not necessarily consonances</note>, and some <term>Dissonant</term> <note>Harsh-sounding combinations</note>: and he even places finally the <term>Eccmelic</term> <note>From the Greek for "unmelodic"; sounds that do not fit into the musical scale</note>, which are very different from these. He calls those Equisonant which, when struck together, from their temperament and mixture of two different sounds, make in a certain way a simple sound: such as that of the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note> and also that of the <term>Double Octave</term> <note>original: "Disdiapason"</note>. But he names Consonant those that, although they make a compound or mixed sound (whatever we wish to call it), are nonetheless sweet: such as that of the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, and also that of the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, and those composed of these two and the Equisonants: such as the <term>Octave plus a Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapason diapente"</note> and the <term>Octave plus a Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diapason diatessaron"</note>. Then he calls Emmelic those that are not consonant but can nonetheless be perfectly accommodated to Melody; and these are those that join consonances together and can be placed between them: such as the <term>Tone</term> <note>A whole step</note>, which is the difference found between the Fifth and the Fourth, by which they are joined together from being consonances into an Equisonant Octave. Thus also the simple parts of these consonances can be called Emmelic, which although they are not consonant, can nonetheless be well accommodated to Melody. He then calls Dissonant those that do not blend together into any sound that is pleasing, but strike our senses bitterly and without any sweetness. Lastly, he names Eccmelic those that do not enter into the conjunction of consonances: as one might say (to give an example) the <term>Enharmonic Diesis</term> <note>An extremely small interval used in ancient Greek music</note>, which some people with little understanding of what Boethius meant have placed in the number of the Emmelic; and other similar intervals that cannot be added to others to join consonances together. This is the division that Ptolemy makes of such Species, as recited by Boethius: but I, to follow common usage and to avoid the difficulty that might arise, will divide them only into two parts: that is, into <term>Consonants</term> and <term>Dissonants</term>. The Consonants will be the Third, the Fourth, the Fifth, the Sixth, the Octave, and the replicated or compound ones; and the Dissonants will be the Second, the Seventh, and all those composed of one of these and the Octave. And because in the Second Part we have seen what Consonance and Dissonance are, leaving aside repetition for now, I will only provide an example of such division so that what has been said may be more easily discerned.

## Whether the Fourth is a consonance; and whence it happens that Musicians have not used it, except in compositions of many voices. Chapter 5.

It may perhaps seem a new thing to some that I have placed the Fourth in the number of the consonances, since until now practical Musicians have placed it among the dissonances. Therefore, so that one may have some knowledge of this matter, it must be noted that the Fourth truly is not a dissonance, but rather a consonance: as can be proven in three ways; first by the authority of the ancient Musicians, which is not to be despised; then by reason; and lastly by example. By the authority of the Ancients first, because by every learned Greek and Latin writer, it is placed among the consonances. **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist</note> (leaving aside infinite others more ancient than him) in many places of his *Harmonics* <note>original: "Harmonica"</note>, and especially in chapter 5 of the First book, names it a consonance. **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose "De Institutione Musica" was the standard medieval music textbook</note> does the same in his *Music* many times, and most especially in chapter 7 of the First book, and in the Eleventh of the Fifth. And **Dion** the historian in book 37, with the authority of those more ancient than him, calls it Harmony <note>original: "Harmonia"</note>. **Euclid** in the First chapter, and **Gaudentius** the philosopher in chapter 7 of their *Introductions*. **Macrobius** in the first chapter of the Second book of the *Dream of Scipio* <note>original: "Sogno di Scipione"</note> numbers it among the consonances. **Vitruvius** also, in chapter 4 of the Fifth book of *Architecture*, is of the opinion that it is a consonance; And **Censorinus** in that which he writes to Q. Cerellius, has the same opinion. 

It is proven then by reason in such a way: That interval which in a harmonic composition is heard to consort perfectly, when placed by itself, cannot by any means be dissonant. Since, therefore, the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The Greek term for the interval of a Fourth</note>, or Fourth, is of such a nature that when accompanied with the Fifth in a harmonic composition, it renders a sweet and harmonious concord; it follows that it is also a consonance outside of the composition: that is, when it is placed alone. The premise of such reasoning is manifest by its contrary; that is, by the dissonances, which are the Second and the Seventh, with their replicates; which, not being in any way consonant within a composition, are also of the same nature outside of the composition: as is manifest. 

Beyond this, it is proven by another reason: that whatever has a ratio of numbers in the high and in the low pitch is consonant: as is manifest by the definition of **The Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> placed in chapter 12 of the Second part; since the Fourth has such a ratio, it is manifest that it is a consonance. And this minor proposition is proven: since **Philoponus** <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note>, upon the Definition given by the Philosopher in the 2nd book of the *Posterior Analytics*, calls the <term>Sesquiterza</term> <note>The mathematical ratio of 4:3</note>, which is its true form, a Ratio of numbers. 

But because examples carry more weight with some than authorities and reasons; it is therefore necessary to come to the third proof. Hence I say that always, when such a consonance is reduced into action, in its true proportion or interval, everyone of sound judgment will say that it truly is a consonance; as everyone for themselves can always make the proof, tuning a **Lute** <note>original: "Liuto"</note>, or a **Violone** <note>A large, bowed string instrument</note> perfectly: for between the string they call the Bass, and 그that which they name the Bourdon; or truly between this one and that which they call the Tenor; and between those other three strings that are higher, they will hear that the <term>Diatessaron</term>, or Fourth, will make a marvelous concord. And if anyone should still wish to say that it is dissonant, this will happen because they follow the usage of the Practitioners; who, not knowing how to provide any reason, very wrongly call it so, and separate it from the number of the Consonances. But in fact it is not so: for when they are brought to hear it upon any instrument that is tuned perfectly, they are then satisfied. And if it were truly dissonant, as they say, we would not use it in our compositions: and similarly the modern Greeks would not place it in their songs for many voices; which are heard here in **Venice** <note>original: "Vinegia"</note> every solemn day in their ecclesiastical Chants, in which they place the <term>Diatessaron</term> in the low part, without placing as its base (so to speak) any other consonance. Here someone will perhaps say: from what did it arise then, that our Practitioners placed it in the number

of the dissonances? I believe this arose from the discord between the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed musical intervals should be governed by simple mathematical ratios</note> and **Ptolemy**. The Pythagoreans held that any interval contained in a ratio other than Multiple or Superparticular <note>Technical terms for ratios like 2:1, 3:1 (Multiple) or 3:2, 4:3 (Superparticular). The 11th (8:3) fits neither category</note>—as I have said many times—was not fit to create any consonance. Thus, they did not agree that the **Eleventh** <note>original: "Diapason diatessaron"</note>, contained in the **Double superbipartient tertian** proportion <note>The ratio 8:3</note>, was consonant. This was despite Ptolemy’s efforts to show the contrary by using this reasoning: just as the simple **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> is consonant, so too when added to the Octave, the outer strings of such an addition cannot be dissonant. For those sounds added to the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> seem almost to be added to a single sound, such is the nature of that consonance (according to what **Boethius** <note>A 6th-century Roman senator and philosopher whose works were fundamental to medieval music theory</note> shows). Seeing the dispute between these parties and that the reasons brought by both sides were good, the Latin musicians did not wish to be judges of this matter. Instead, so as not to grant a certain liberty to place this consonance and its simple form into songs without some consideration, they separated them from the number and order of the others. They did this not because they are truly dissonant—for they would not have allowed them to be placed in compositions—but so that they would be used with good order and judgment. That this is the truth can be seen: those who have had some judgment in Music have used it, not only accompanied by other consonances, but even without any other parts in songs for two voices. Among these was **Josquin** <note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), one of the most famous composers of the Renaissance</note>, who at the beginning of that part, **"And he rose again on the third day"** <note>original: "Et resurrexit tertia die"</note>, from the four-voice mass called **"The Armed Man"** <note>original: "l'Homme arme"</note>, placed such a consonance simply, without accompanying it with any other interval in the lower part. This can also be seen in many other ancient songs, which I do not include so as not to weary the Reader. And although such consonances are found in use only rarely, one nevertheless sees that they used them; and if they had been of the opinion that they were dissonant, I believe they would not have used them. Now, from what has been said, it can be seen that the Fourth and its replicates are consonant, and for what reason Musicians placed them among those intervals that are dissonant. In what manner it is then called **Perfect**, and in what way it is to be placed in compositions, we shall see in its proper place.

## Division of the consonances into Perfect and Imperfect. Chapter 6.

<image-desc>A large historiated drop-cap 'S' containing an etching of a landscape with a building or ruin, a prominent gnarled tree, and mountains in the distance.</image-desc>CONSONANCES are divided by Practitioners in such a way that some are called **Perfect** and some **Imperfect**. The Perfect ones are the **Unison**, the **Fourth**, the **Fifth**, the **Octave**, and their replicates; although **Aristotle** attributes such perfection to the Octave only, and certainly this is true, since the Fourth and the Fifth are midway between perfection and imperfection, as we shall demonstrate. The Imperfect ones are the **Third**, the **Sixth**, and those that arise from these when added to the Octave, as seen in the example placed below.

And they say the first ones are perfect, perhaps because they take their form from the proportions contained within the **Quaternary** number <note>The number four, or the Tetraktys (1, 2, 3, 4), which was sacred to Pythagoreans</note>, in the Multiple and Superparticular species, between 4, 3, 2, 1. This number (as I have said elsewhere) was held as Perfect among the Pythagoreans because from its parts, both those that divide it evenly and those that do not—which are the four shown numbers—there resulted another number which they likewise called Perfect: the **Ten** <note>original: "Denario"</note>. But in truth, they named them Perfect because, whether placed by themselves or accompanied by other consonances, they have the power—at the first moment the sense perceives them—to quiet and fully satisfy the ear when it is moved by them. For while one hears any of them placed in the low or high register, contained in its true form, it strengthens the Hearing and ensures it desires nothing further to complete its perfection or make it more sweet and pleasing. No other difference is found between the said consonances placed in the low register than is found when they are placed in the high, except that those placed in the high register strike the Hearing more swiftly than those in the low, for the reasons stated in Chapter 11 of the Second Part; for they are contained by one and the same proportion. But the others they called Imperfect because they take their form from proportions whose terms are contained by numbers found beyond the Quaternary, which are 6, 5, 4. Whence the **Ditone** <note>The Major Third</note> arises from the **Sesquiquarta** proportion <note>The ratio 5:4</note>, and the **Semiditone** <note>The Minor Third</note> from the propor—

However, they do satisfy the ear when accompanied by other intervals in such a way that the outer limits of the composition form a perfect consonance, or one of the replicated imperfect ones, as we shall see elsewhere. And although those thinkers made such a distinction, nonetheless all of them can be called perfect when they are contained in their true and natural form—that is, in their own proper proportion.

### That the Fourth and the Fifth are intermediate between the perfect and the imperfect consonances. Chapter 7.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial E, featuring a figure sitting or standing amidst vines and foliage.</image-desc>
AND ALTHOUGH the **Octave**, the **Fifth**, the **Fourth**, and their repetitions are called **perfect consonances**; nonetheless the Octave (as I have said above) is uniquely perfect; the Fifth is less perfect than the Octave; and the Fourth is less perfect than the Fifth. For just as a thing which is closer to its origin, or to its cause, retains more of that nature and is more perfect in that genus than those things which are distant from it—as is seen with light, where the part closest to its origin and cause, which is the **Sun**, has more clarity and shines more excellently, and is more perfect than that which is more remote or distant—so that consonance which is closer to its origin, which is the **Unison** <note>original: "Vniſono"</note> (contained in the proportion of Equality and in voices of the same pitch), is more perfect than any other consonance. And this is the **Octave**, which takes its form from the **Double** <note>The ratio 2:1</note>, which is closest to the proportions of Equality; it is contained between <term>equisonant</term> voices <note>Voices that sound so similar they almost blend into one</note> which are closest to Unisons, as we have seen above. Hence we can call it simpler and more perfect than any other consonance. I say simpler and more perfect because whenever a condition is found that allows for "more" or "less," and formally names both the cause and the effect, and such a thing applies to the effect because of the cause, the cause will always be named simply first, and then the effect will be named or called such in a certain manner; and this holds in all types of causes. Therefore I say: **That thing which, by means of another, is such-and-such, the thing which is the cause of it is said to be even more such-and-such.** Thus, just as we say that if a hand is hot because of a fire, the fire is "more hot"; so we say that if the Octave is "simple" because of the Unison, then the Unison is "more simple." But because the Unison is not considered by the Musician as a consonance, but rather as the principle of Consonance, when speaking of consonances we say that the Octave is simply simple: the first and most perfect of every other consonance. And in fact it is so, for from it every other interval has its being. We call the other consonances "perfect," not simply, but rather in a certain manner. Hence, the Fifth being closer to the Octave than the Fourth is, we say that the Fourth is less perfect than the Fifth; for its proportion is further from the **Double** proportion, which is the principle of Inequality and the cause of every other proportion. Similarly, we say that the Fourth is more perfect than the **Major Third** <note>original: "Ditono"</note>, and this more perfect than the **Minor Third** <note>original: "Semiditono"</note>. This is because the <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>The ratio 3:2</note>, which is the form of the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, is contained between 3 and 2, and is closer to the **Double**, which is the form of the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note> contained between these terms 2 and 1; which can also be said of the others. But if the principle of any thing is more perfect than those things which follow after, it is not reasonable for us to say that the Fifth or the Fourth are equal in perfection to the Octave, for they depend upon that Octave. And although I have said that the Fourth and the Fifth, with their repetitions, are perfect consonances in the manner shown, nonetheless the Octave alone and its repetitions are *simply* perfect. This is because nothing can be added to or taken away from them—that is, they cannot be increased or diminished in interval outside of their true and legitimate proportions in any way without great offense to the Ear. Since the Fourth, the Fifth, and their repetitions are subject to such <term>passion</term> <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the capacity of an interval to be slightly altered or "tempered" in tuning to fit a scale</note>, as I showed in Chapter 42 of the Second Part, I say that they are intermediate between the perfect and the imperfect consonances, or truly intermediate between perfection and imperfection. And because those called Imperfect are also subject to this, therefore they...

### Which consonances are fuller, and which are more charming. Chapter 8.

Musicians are often accustomed to using two terms: **Full Consonance** and **Charming Consonance**. Therefore, it seems to me, before proceeding further, that I should explain what these mean and which consonances they refer to. However, it should be noted that musicians rarely use these two terms without adding one of these two qualifiers: *More* or *Less*. Thus, they have said "more full" or "more charming" consonance, and "less full" or "less charming" consonance, always in comparison to another consonance. They call those consonances **fuller** which have a greater power to occupy the sense of hearing with diverse sounds. For this reason, one could say that the **Fifth** is fuller than the **Octave**, because its outer limits occupy the hearing more deeply and with greater delight through diverse sounds than the outer limits of the **Octave** do. The notes of the **Octave** are <term>equisonant</term> <note>original: "equisonanti"; sounds that are so similar they seem like the same pitch, as in the relationship between two 'C's an octave apart</note> and resemble one another. Therefore, setting the **Octave** aside, all others are said to be fuller than one another in proportion to their ability to satisfy the hearing, just as those that are closer to their source have greater perfection than all others. Thus, one can derive a rule: all those intervals of a larger proportion are fuller—setting aside, as I said, the **Octave** and its repetitions. They then call those **more charming** which are contained by smaller proportions, especially when placed in their proper positions. This is because those consonances whose proportions are closer to the <term>Dupla</term> <note>original: "Dupla"; the 2:1 ratio which defines the Octave</note> naturally prefer the <term>grave</term> <note>The lower or deeper register of sound</note> part as their proper place and become fuller than those whose proportions are further from the **Dupla**. Indeed, these latter ones are of smaller proportion than the former and naturally prefer the <term>acute</term> <note>The higher or sharper register of sound</note>. Thus, when placed in their proper positions, they become less full and more charming than others; for being in the high register, due to the speed of their movements, they penetrate the hearing more swiftly and are heard with greater delight. And they are all the more charming as they depart from simplicity—in which our senses do not greatly rejoice—and are accompanied by other consonances, since the senses prefer composite things to simple ones. For this reason, what happens to the Hearing regarding sounds is similar to what happens to Sight regarding the primary colors from which every other middle color is composed. Just as **White** and **Black** provide less delight than certain other middle and mixed colors, so the principal consonances provide less delight than others that are less perfect. And just as **Green**, **Red**, **Azure**, and other similar colors delight the eye more and appear more charming because they are far from the principals, more so than the color called <term>Roanno</term> <note>A reddish-gray or speckled color</note> or <term>Beretino</term> <note>A dull, ashy gray or charcoal color</note> (of which one is closer to Black and the other to White), so the Hearing delights more in consonances that are further from the simplicity of sounds. They are much more charming than those closer to it. And the Hearing delights in the composition of sounds in almost the same way the Sight delights in the composition of colors: because the composition of colors either cannot exist without some harmony, or it has some agreement with harmony, because both are composed of diverse things. Hence we can say that just as the larger consonances are fuller than the smaller ones, so the smaller ones are more charming than the larger ones; and they become all the more sonorous and pleasing to the ear when they are placed in their proper locations, as we shall say in the appropriate place. One could also say that among the perfect consonances themselves, the **Fifth** is more charming than the **Octave**, and the **Fourth** more charming than the **Fifth**, as is manifest: because they are further from equality, since even perfect consonances are not devoid of such charm; but let this suffice.

### Of the difference found between the Imperfect consonances. Chapter 9.

The **Imperfect Consonances** are divided into two parts, and this difference is placed between them: some are major, and some are minor. The **major** ones are those whose outer limits are contained by larger proportions and larger intervals; these are the <term>Ditone</term> <note>The Major Third</note> and the **Major Hexachord**, of which the first is called the **Third** and the second the **Sixth**, both major. And the **minor** ones are those that are of a smaller proportion and have a smaller interval;

and these are the <term>Semiditono</term> <note>original: "Semiditono"; literally "half-ditone," known today as the Minor Third</note>, which they call the **Minor Third**; and the **Minor Sixth** <note>original: "Essachordo minore"</note>. And although above I named the said consonances with the simple name of **Third** and **Sixth** without making any mention of **Major** or **Minor**, and now I add such differences; I have done so to follow the method used by the **Practitioners** <note>original: "Prattici"; refers to performing musicians and composers rather than theoretical scientists</note>; and to be able to first reduce them under one **Genus**, and then show their **Species** and their **Differences**; so that they might be recognized by the Practitioners (whom I wish to satisfy as much as I can in these two parts): because they are not named otherwise by them. It is quite true that they place the difference of major and minor among them, as was said above, and as they are noted here below.

| **Ditone**, or **Major Third**. | **Semiditone**, or **Minor Third**. |
| **Hexachord**, or **Major Sixth**. | **Hexachord**, or **Minor Sixth**. |

And although the difference of major and minor is placed only in the imperfect consonances; nonetheless, the species or dissonant intervals can also have such a difference; even if they are not considered by the Musician except insofar as they have the nature of an **Interval**; as we shall see elsewhere: because the **Second** is of two types according to the Practitioners; namely the **Tone** <note>Major Second</note> and the **Semitone** <note>Minor Second</note>: wherefore one can say **Major Second** and **Minor Second**. And the **Fourth** is of three types: namely the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>the Perfect Fourth consonance</note>; the <term>Tritone</term>, which is a composition of three Tones; and the <term>Semidiatessaron</term>, which is a composition of one Tone and two Semitones <note>a diminished fourth</note>; which intervals are dissonant at their extremes. This same thing could also be said of the **Fifth**, the **Octave**, and their replicates, which are left aside so as not to be long-winded.

## On the property, or nature, of Imperfect Consonances. Chapter 10.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter "I" illustrating two human figures (likely putti or classical figures) in a landscape with trees and foliage.</image-desc>

The **PROPERTY**, or Nature of imperfect consonances is that some of them are lively and cheerful, accompanied by much sonority; and some, although they are sweet and smooth, decline somewhat toward the sad or languid. The first are the **Major Thirds** and **Sixths**, and their replicates; and the others are the **Minor** ones. All these have the power to change any song <note>original: "cantilena"</note> and make it sad or cheerful according to their nature. We can see this from the fact that there are some songs which are lively and full of joy; and some others, on the contrary, are somewhat sad or languid. The reason is that in the first type, one often hears the major imperfect consonances above the extreme final or middle notes of the **Modes** or **Tones**; which are the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Eleventh, and Twelfth; as we shall see in its place. These Modes are very cheerful and lively because in them the consonances are often heard arranged according to the nature of the <term>Sonorous Number</term> <note>original: "numero sonoro"; Zarlino’s term for the numbers 1–6 (the senario) which determine musical proportions</note>; that is, the **Fifth** mediated or divided **harmonically** into a Major Third and a Minor Third; which greatly delights the ear. I say the Consonances are placed in them according to the nature of the sonorous number because then the consonances are placed in their natural places; thus the Mode is more cheerful and offers much pleasure to the sense, which greatly enjoys and delights in proportioned objects; and on the contrary, hates and abhors the disproportionate ones. In the other Modes then—which are the First, Second, Third, Fourth, Ninth, and Tenth—the Fifth is placed the opposite way; that is, mediated **arithmetically** by a middle note; so that many times the consonances are heard placed against the nature of the Sonorous Number. For which reason, just as in the first group the Major Third is often placed below the Minor; so in the second group the opposite is frequently heard, and one hears a "certain something" of sadness or languidness that makes the whole song soft; this is heard more often the more frequently they are placed in such a way, following the nature and property of the Mode in which the song is composed. Beyond this, imperfect consonances have such a nature that their extremes more conveniently and in a better way extend toward that part which is closer to its perfection than toward that which is further from it: because everything naturally desires to make itself perfect in the shortest and best way it can. Wherefore the Major imperfects desire to become larger; and the Minor ones have a contrary nature: since the **Ditone** and the **Major Hexachord** de—

Because all the movements that the parts make come to be made with the movement of some interval in which the Semitone is contained, which is truly the Salt (so to speak), the seasoning, and the cause of every good Modulation and every good Harmony; which modulations, without its help, would be almost unbearable to hear. But we shall see this more clearly when we discuss the method to be used in placing consonances and other intervals in Counterpoints.

### Particular Discussion Concerning the Unison. Chapter 11.

We can now say (if we wish to consider what we have seen above) that the simple elements, or simple species of <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>The art of combining different melodic lines</note>, both consonant and also dissonant, are Twelve; namely the Unison, the Semitone, the Tone, the <term>Semiditone</term> <note>Minor Third</note>, the <term>Ditone</term> <note>Major Third</note>, the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>Fourth</note>, the <term>Diapente</term> <note>Fifth</note>, the minor Hexachord, the major [Hexachord], the minor <term>Heptachord</term> <note>Minor Seventh</note>, the major [Heptachord] <note>Major Seventh</note>, and the <term>Diapason</term> <note>Octave</note>; each of which species shall be discussed individually at present. For although Counterpoint is composed principally of consonances, nonetheless, by accident, it is also composed of dissonances, so that it may be more cheerful and more beautiful. Desiring then to speak of such species, I will keep this order: that after I have spoken of the Unison (as duty requires, since it is the Principle from which consonances are born, and without it every other interval would not have its being), I will come to speak of the other species; not according to the order proposed by the Practitioners <note>Performing musicians</note>, but according to how one is found to be more perfect than the other; and according to how they are placed by order in the natural progression of sonorous numbers, or rather of proportions; starting first with those contained in the Multiple genus; then those whose forms are in the Superparticular genus; and having finished those, I will speak of those that have their being in the other genera. We shall take the beginning of our discussion from the definition of the Unison, saying that the Unison is a gathering of two or more equal sounds or voices that do not make any interval, but are contained in one and the same point and in one and the same place. And it is found in the proportion of Equality between 1 and 1, or between 2 and 2, and other similar ones; which proportion (as I have said elsewhere) is the principle of Inequality. This is not placed among the consonances or among the intervals: because the Unison is to the Musician as the Point is to the Geometer. Hence, just as the Point is the principle of the Line, but is not however a line, nor is the Line composed of points (because the Point has no length, nor width, nor height that can be continued or joined with another point), so the Unison is only the principle of the consonance or the interval; but it is not a consonance, nor an interval: being that it cannot be continued, just as the point cannot be continued. And because every consonance is found between two sounds distant by the low and the high, which make an interval, and is (as we see in the Second Part) a mixture or composition of low and high sound; therefore, the Unison having none of these qualities, we cannot call it by any means either a Consonance or an Interval. Which thing is proven by the words of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>; who, in criticizing the placement of property in common in a city in his *Politics* <note>original: "Politica"</note>, and making such a thing impossible, confirms his opinion with a musical example, saying that it would be no different than if one wanted to make a single unison voice out of a Consonance, or a single foot out of a Verse. From this one sees that the consonance is taken by him as distinct from the Unison. Justly, therefore, is it called "Unison," as if from one single sound; hence, when we find in a part of a song two or more figures on the same letter or string <note>original: "chorda"; refers to the pitch location on the staff</note>, whether placed on a line or in a space, we say that those will be unisons and of one single sound; and that the passage found from one to the other is a Unison: as seen in the example.

### On the First Consonance, namely the Diapason, or Octave. Chapter 12.

Since it is reasonable that in every action we begin with the simplest things, which by their nature are more easily grasped by our senses and are more manifest and intelligible, so that from these we may more easily pass to the less simple; we shall therefore begin our discussion of consonances with the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Greek term for an Octave</note>, or Octave. For indeed, no other consonance can be found that is simpler or more greatly recognized by our senses. But because I greatly desire that practitioners should not only know musical intervals insofar as they are consonant or dissonant, and their species, or whether they are perfect or less perfect, but also by what proportion they are contained; therefore, beginning with the Diapason itself, which is the first consonance, to maintain the proposed order, I say: that it is contained by the <term>Double Proportion</term> <note>original: proportion Dupla; the ratio 2:1</note> in the <term>Multiple Genus</term> <note>A mathematical category where the larger number is a multiple of the smaller</note> between these radical terms, 2 and 1; and it is first among those sounds that derive their form from the proportions of <term>Inequality</term> <note>Ratios where the two numbers are not equal</note>. Thus, I believe it was called by musicians by such a name because (as I have said elsewhere) it has jurisdiction over every consonance and every interval, whether greater or smaller than itself. This is manifest from its name, for it is composed of <note>original: Διὰ</note> *Dia*, which is a Greek word meaning "Through," and from <note>original: πᾶσα</note> *pasa*, which means "Universe" or "Each." Hence it is called <note>original: διὰ πασῶν</note> *dia pason*, that is, the "Universe of Harmony." Justly, then, and not without purpose, musicians have called it the Progenitress, Mother, Source, Origin, Principle, Place, Receptacle, and universal Subject of every consonance and every interval, however small.

This interval, when considered by the musician simply and in general—that is, when its outer notes are without any middle voice or other sound and form a single interval—is found to have only one species. For an Octave placed in the high range is contained by the same Double Proportion in its extremes as another placed in the low range. But when it is considered particularly—that is, according to how it is divided diatonically into Tones and Semitones, or mediated by other intervals—then I say that its <term>species</term> <note>Variations of the scale based on the arrangement of whole and half steps</note> are seven, according to how the intervals of the middle sounds can be differently ordered in seven ways, following the nature of the <term>Diatonic Genus</term> <note>The standard scale of tones and semitones</note>. For every consonance (as <term>Boethius</term> <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on music were foundational for the Renaissance</note> says) produces one species fewer than the number of its strings <note>In an eight-note scale, there are seven possible ways to arrange the internal steps</note>. And this variety of species arises from the variety of positions that contain the <term>Semitone</term> <note>A half-step, the smallest interval in this system</note>. For in the first species, which is found from A to a (as seen in the <term>Introductory of Guido</term> <note>Refers to the pedagogical system of Guido of Arezzo, the 11th-century monk who invented modern staff notation</note>), the Semitone, which is the cause of the distinction between species, is contained in the second and fifth intervals of the Octave, proceeding from low to high. But in the second species, which is placed between B and b, such a Semitone is found in the first and fourth places; and so on, according to the order of the seven letters shown. Thus, being mediated in such a manner, musicians say that the Diapason is a composition of eight sounds, arranged and ordered diatonically according to the nature of <term>sonorous number</term> <note>The mathematical ratios that produce pleasing sounds</note>; from which they also named it the "Octave." It contains within itself five Tones—namely three major and two minor—and two major Semitones, as seen in the examples below.

### On the Diapente, or Fifth. Chapter 13.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'B' featuring two figures (possibly putti or mythological figures) entwined with ornate foliage and vines.</image-desc>

**It is necessary** *now to remember what I said in chapter 13 of the* First Part: *that is, that every consonance, or any other interval however small, that is smaller than the* <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Greek term for an Octave</note>, *arises not by adding multiple proportions together, but by the division of the* <term>Double Proportion</term> <note>original: Dupla; the ratio 2:1</note>, *which contains the Diapason. This we have been able to see, not only from the numbers and the proportions set down in chapter 15 of the* First Part: *but by way of the* <term>Harmonic Division</term> <note>A mathematical method used to divide a string length or ratio into harmonious segments</note> *explained in chapter 39 of the* Second Part: *for from the division of the Diapason, contained by the Double proportion, was born the* <term>Diapente</term> <note>The Greek term for a Fifth</note>, *and the* <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>The Greek term for a Fourth</note>. *The Diapente (I say) is contained between these radical terms 3 and 2; and the Diatessaron between 4 and 3. And because the proportion found between 3 and 2 follows immediately after the Double proportion; therefore, having first discussed the Diapason, it seems proper to me to discuss the Diapente, and then the Diatessaron. Just as the proportion of the Diapason is the first in the* <term>Multiple Genus</term> <note>Ratios like 2:1 or 3:1, where the larger number is a direct multiple of the smaller</note>, *so that of the Diapente is the first in the* <term>Superparticular Genus</term> <note>Ratios like 3:2 or 4:3, where the larger number is the smaller number plus one part</note>. *Thus, it is not without reason that we begin from these principles, as it is necessary that they be known before anything else. Returning then to the Diapente, I say that when it is considered simply, in the manner in which it is contained within its extreme terms without any middle [notes], one can say that such a consonance is of only one species: for no Diapente is found to be larger than another, or smaller in proportion; nor are the extremes of one more distant or more narrow in proportion than those of another. But when we consider it divided within its extremes by other strings* <note>original: chorde; referring to the notes or pitches as represented on a stringed instrument like the monochord</note> *and by other proportions in the* <term>Diatonic Order</term> <note>The standard arrangement of whole steps and half steps in a scale</note>; *then we shall sa—*
<meta>catchword: —y,</meta>

<summary>Zarlino explains that intervals smaller than an octave, specifically the Fifth (Diapente) and Fourth (Diatessaron), are derived by mathematically dividing the octave's 2:1 ratio. He establishes the Fifth as the primary consonance of the Superparticular Genus, existing in only one form when considered as a simple ratio.</summary>

<header>Part Three</header>

...we say that there are four species: because when these outer notes are divided by other strings diatonically, the <term>major semitone</term> <note>The larger of the two types of half-steps used in this tuning system</note> is placed among them in four different ways (setting aside, however, any consideration of <term>major or minor tones</term> <note>In the tuning system Zarlino uses, not all "whole steps" are the same size</note> both in this and in every other consonance), for they would otherwise generate even more different species if one were to minutely consider such intervals placed between them. Of those, then, which differ from each other by the transposition of the semitone: the **First species** is that which has the semitone in the second interval; the **Second** is that which has it in the first; the **Third** in the last; and the **Fourth** in the third: as seen below.

<image-desc>Two rows of musical staves. The top row contains two examples labeled "First species" and "Second species," each showing five notes on a staff representing a musical fifth. The bottom row contains two examples labeled "Third species" and "Fourth species," similarly showing five-note sequences on staves.</image-desc>

And each of them contains within itself five voices, or sounds, and four intervals; which have among them two major tones, one minor, and one major semitone. And for this reason, from the number of strings it contains, it is called a **Fifth** by practitioners: but the Greeks called it <term>Diapente</term> <note>The Greek term for the interval of a Fifth</note>, from these two words, *dia* <note>original: διὰ</note>, which means "Through"; and *pente* <note>original: πέντε</note>, which means "Five"; as if wanting to say a consonance that proceeds through five voices or sounds. When, therefore, two parts are distant from one another in such a way that one holds the low part of each of the said species and the other the high part, then we shall say they are distant from one another by a Diapente, or by a Fifth: as seen here.

<image-desc>A small musical staff positioned to the left of the following paragraph, showing two notes, B-natural and F, illustrating a diminished fifth interval.</image-desc>

And although I placed the examples of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>The Octave</note> in the previous chapter on the low strings, one cannot do the same for those of the Diapente one after the other, as was done with those of the Diapason without interrupting the order: for if I had placed them on the strings A, B-natural <note>indicated by the symbol ♮</note>, C, and D: even though the first, third, and fourth strings would have given perfect species of the Diapente, nevertheless the second could not have given it. This is because from the string B-natural to the string F one finds a Diapente diminished by a semitone <note>A "tritone" or diminished fifth, which was considered dissonant</note>; as is manifest to everyone skilled in music. This is true even though **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works were the foundation of medieval music theory</note> did not guard against such a thing when, in chapter 13 of the fourth book of *The Fundamentals of Music*, he placed the second species of this consonance between the strings *Hypate hypaton* and *Parhypate meson* <note>Greek names for specific notes in the ancient musical system</note>, which is a diminished fifth and contains two tones and two semitones. But I believe that he did not care to state the exact truth of the matter, provided that he showed with the example of the strings what he intended to mean.

### On the Diatessaron, or Fourth. Chapter 14.

THE **Diatessaron**, which is the smaller principal part of the Diapason, and whose form is contained in the second place of the <term>Superparticular genus</term> <note>A mathematical ratio where the numerator is the denominator plus one (n+1)/n</note>, between these terms 4 and 3; being considered without any middle [notes], one finds only a single species of it, for the reasons said above regarding the Diapason and the Diapente. But when it is considered divided diatonically by other sounds or voices, then one finds three species, which arise from the variety of the semitone's position—leaving aside (as I have also said) the consideration of the [major or minor] tones. This semitone is differently placed among them in their middle strings, just as I said of the Diapason and the Diapente: for while the first species has the tone in the lowest place, it then has the major semitone in the second, and the tone in the third. But the second species has the semitone in the first place, and the third species has it in the third place, with the tones then arranged in order; as can be seen in the example placed below.
