->Third species.<-

This (as I have said elsewhere) is called the **First Symphony** <note>original: "prima Sinfonia"</note> by the Greeks, or (as Philo Judaeus <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who wrote on the harmony of the spheres</note> names it) the **First Harmony**; and Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works were the foundation of medieval music theory</note> calls it the **Minimum Consonance**. From this, we can see that they did not consider the Ditone <term>Ditone</term> <note>A major third, literally "two tones"</note> or the Semiditone <term>Semiditone</term> <note>A minor third, literally "a tone and a half"</note> to be consonances. They also called it the **Diatessaron** <note>The Greek term for the interval of a Fourth</note> from the number of strings or voices that it contains; for every Diatessaron proceeds in the manner shown through four voices. Indeed, it is named from *dia* <note>original: διὰ</note>, which means **Through**, and *tessara* <note>original: τέσσαρα</note>, which means **Four**—that is, a consonance of four voices or sounds. From this number, our modern musicians call it the **Fourth**. When, therefore, we wish to create two parts in our compositions that are distant from each other by a Diatessaron, we place the low voice on one of the outer strings of one of the examples above and the high voice on the other, as seen in the example. Because two parts are found in songs arranged with one another in this way, we can say that one is distant from the other by a Diatessaron, or rather, by a Fourth.

<image-desc>A musical system showing two voices on separate staves illustrating a harmonic Diatessaron (fourth).</image-desc>

# On the Ditone, or Major Third. Ch. 15.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'S' containing a woodcut illustration of a landscape with a tower and buildings.</image-desc>

FOLLOWING immediately after the Diatessaron is the consonance named the **Ditone**, which is contained within the terms 5 and 4. It occupies the third place in the **Superparticular** genus <term>Superparticular ratio</term> <note>A mathematical ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3/2, 4/3, 5/4)</note>, specifically the **Sesquiquarta** proportion <note>The Latin name for the 5:4 ratio, which produces the pure major third</note>. It is truly marvelous how Nature has ordered one consonance after another in such a way. Among the parts of the **Senario** <term>Senario</term> <note>Zarlino's "six-fold" number system (1-2-3-4-5-6), which he argued contained all the natural proportions of music</note>, the form of the **Diapente** <note>The Fifth</note> is found, divided arithmetically into two parts between the terms 6, 5, and 4. The musician finds these parts in reverse order within the same Diapente when it is divided harmonically into two parts between the terms 15, 12, and 10. If we consider the Ditone on its own, according to its simple radical terms, we can say what was said of the other consonances: that only one species of it is found. This is because the extremes of a Ditone placed in the high register are just as distant in proportion as those of one placed in the low register. But considering it when divided diatonically into two **Tones**, I say that its species are two, as they appear here below.

<image-desc>A musical staff labeled "First species." showing a major third (C to E) divided into two tones.</image-desc>

->First species.<-

->Or<- ->Second species.<-

<image-desc>A single line of musical notation containing two examples. On the left, an alternative example of the first species of major third; on the right, the second species of major third.</image-desc>

This difference arises from the variety of its intervals: for in the first interval of the first species one finds the **Major Tone**, and in the second the **Minor Tone** <note>In Zarlino’s tuning system (Just Intonation), not all whole steps are the same size; a "Major Third" is composed of one larger and one smaller whole step</note>; and in the second species the opposite is found—that is, the minor in the first and the major in the second. We shall say, then, that the parts of the counterpoints are distant...

### On the Semiditone, or Minor Third. Chapter 16.

The smaller part of the **Diapente** <term>Diapente</term> <note>The Greek term for the interval of a Perfect Fifth</note> is called the **Semiditone**, the mathematical form of which is contained in the Superparticular genus by the **Sesquiquinta** ratio <note>The ratio 6:5, which defines the minor third in the just intonation system</note>, in the fourth place. This is also called the **Minor Third** by practitioners, and its species are two, considering it divided diatonically into a **Major Tone** and a **Major Semitone**. For the first contains such a semitone in its second interval, and the second contains it in the first; as is seen here.

<image-desc>A line of musical notation showing two examples of the minor third divided into two intervals. The first example, labeled "First species.", shows a diamond-shaped note G followed by A, then B-flat. The second example, labeled "Second species.", shows G followed by A-flat, then B-flat.</image-desc>

->First species.<- ->Second species.<-

But considering it without any middle sound—that is, in its outer limits only—it is of only one species: since (as has been said of the other consonances) the outer strings of one placed in the low register, and those of one placed in the high register, are contained by the very same ratio. Practitioners say that when the parts of their compositions are distant from one another in such a way that one part occupies any low string one wishes, and the other occupies any high string from one of the examples shown above, they are distant by a **Semiditone**, or **Minor Third**; such as the two placed below.

<image-desc>Musical notation on two five-line staves connected by a brace. The top staff has a C-clef and a diamond-shaped note (D). The bottom staff has an F-clef and a diamond-shaped note (F).</image-desc>

This interval is called a **Semiditone**, not from the Latin word *semis* <note>meaning "half"</note>, as if it were exactly half a Ditone; but rather from *semus*: for (as Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), the primary authority on music theory for the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> maintains) that thing which does not reach a full half is called by such a name. Hence, a **semitone** is called that interval which is not a full half of a Tone, but is an **imperfect Tone**. The Semiditone is therefore called an **imperfect Ditone**: since it is diminished by a minor semitone, contained by the **Sesquiquintesima quarta** ratio <note>The ratio 25:24, representing the difference between a major third and a minor third</note>. They also name it a **Third**, from the number of strings, and they add **Minor**: because its outer limits are more narrow, and of a smaller ratio, than those of the Ditone. But let this be said sufficiently concerning those intervals which are truly consonant.

---

### On the utility that Dissonant Intervals bring to Music. Chapter 17.

And although Consonances are principally considered by the Musician, and not Dissonances—for he composes his songs principally from the former—nonetheless it appears (as Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and philosopher; Zarlino refers here to his "Life of Cicero"</note> says in the *Life of Marcus Tullius*) that he also considers those voices which are dissonant—that is, those intervals that do not create a Consonance—so that he may know how to choose those things that bring him utility and convenience, and flee from those that serve his purpose little. This is because those intervals which are dissonant generate a sound ungrateful to the ear, and make the melody harsh and without any sweetness. But because it is impossible that in singing one can go from one consonance to another, proceeding from the low to the high, or vice versa, except by means of and with the help of

such intervals; however, it is necessary that the **Musician** <note>Theorists of this era used "Musician" to mean someone who understands the science of music, not just a performer.</note> not only knows them so as not to place them in the stead of those which are consonant, but also needs to have knowledge of them in order to use them between the parts of the **composition** <note>original: "cantilena," referring to a polyphonic song or melody</note>, in the manner that I will show elsewhere. Since they are useful, and even necessary, it is appropriate that something be said specifically about them: for although they do not have the nature of consonance, they at least have the nature of an interval. Not all intervals, however, are necessary to the Musician: but only those that serve **diatonic movements** <term>modulationi diatoniche</term>, which are smaller than the **Minor Third** <term>Semiditono</term> and larger than the **minor Semitone**, and without any doubt are contained within the **Eight strings** <note>The notes of a standard octave scale</note> of each **Octave** <term>Diapason</term>: since they are separated from one another harmonically, and by diatonic division. Since they are thus useful and even necessary for the use of harmonies, it is required that they be known, and that their ratio, their number, and their utility be understood. And because everything will be recounted in its proper place, we will now only see their number. Therefore, I say that there are truly no more and no fewer than **Three**, namely the **Major Tone**, the **Minor**, and the **Major Semitone**, which are true and legitimate intervals of the **Diatonic genus**, in which they are used. And they are called true and legitimate for such a genus because they are born from **sonorous numbers** <note>The "senario" or numbers 1 through 6, which Zarlino believed governed all musical beauty</note> and are contained within its **Tetrachord**, as we have seen in Chapter 31 of the Second Part. There are also other intervals found that are dissonant, as can be seen in the division and composition of the **Monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical proportions of pitch</note> shown in the other part, and in any other that could be made with the help of harmonic numbers. But because they are smaller than the three named above, the Musician has no need of them; and these are the **minor Semitone**, which is found between strings **S B** and **K B**, and the **Comma**, which is placed between strings **R B** and **M B** of the aforementioned division. And although one sees in it that at times it is impossible to proceed from low to high, or vice-versa, and from one consonance to another without the help of one of these intervals, this matters little: for in such instruments, such additions are necessary. However, it is not necessary that these intervals be heard in a diatonic progression, nor is the interval of the **Comma** useful: for it would generate great annoyance to whoever heard it; all the more so since in the **Voices** such an interval is not heard: as they can be made sharp or flat as best suits them, and by their means any song can be brought to perfection without any inconvenience. This does not happen in artificial instruments <note>Keyboards or fretted instruments</note>: for **Art can never equal Nature in anything**. But because we see that the voices mostly approach the nature of instruments reduced to the number of **Pythagorean strings** <note>Tuning based on pure fifths (3:2), which Zarlino is critiquing in favor of his own system</note>, in which these small details are not found, rather than the nature of those tuned perfectly according to the forms of the harmonic numbers, one could say that **Participation** <term>Partecipazione</term> <note>A Renaissance term for "temperament," or slightly adjusting intervals so they sound good in all keys</note> was more useful to the Musician than perfect tuning. Wherefore it should be noted that as far as the **Science** is concerned, this [perfect tuning] is more useful: because from it one can extract the true ratio of every interval that is perfectly accommodated to its true proportion; especially because the Voices (as I have said elsewhere) follow the perfection of the intervals. But as for use and **Practice**, the other is more convenient. It is quite true that both can be called perfect in their kind, in the way I have elsewhere said and shown. Such utility, then, do the named intervals bring to Music; for wanting to pass from a **Fourth** <term>Diatessaron</term> to a **Fifth** <term>Diapente</term>, or vice-versa, one cannot arrive by any other means than with the **Major Tone**. And proceeding from the **Minor Third** <term>Semiditono</term> to the **Fourth**, or from the latter to the former, and from the **Fifth** to the **Major Sixth** <term>Essachordo maggiore</term>, or vice-versa, one only arrives by means of the **Minor Tone**. Then the utility drawn from the **Major Semitone** is this: that from the **Major Third** <term>Ditono</term> one can arrive by its means at the **Fourth**, and vice-versa; and from the **Fifth** to the **Minor Sixth** <term>Essachordo minore</term>, or from the latter to the former. Since such a convenience is had from them, it is not out of place for us to discuss them individually, leaving aside those contained in artificial instruments: since not only are they not used, but it is also impossible to have the rational proportion of those which are increased or diminished by some part of a **Comma**, as I have shown elsewhere.

## On the Major Hexachord, or Major Sixth. Chapter 20.

COMING NOW to those intervals which have their forms among the proportions of the Superbipartient genus <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number once, plus two remaining parts (e.g., 5:3 contains 3 once, with 2 left over)</note>, I say that the **Major Hexachord** <term>Effachordo maggiore</term> takes its form from the **Superbipartient Third** proportion, which is the first proportion of this genus, between these radical terms 5 and 3. And although this interval cannot be called "Simple" in an absolute sense—except in a certain manner—because the extremes of its proportion can be mediated by the number four in this way: 3, 4, 5; we can thus say it is composed of the form of the **Fourth** <term>Diatessaron</term> and the form of the **Major Third** <term>Ditono</term>. Nevertheless, we shall call it "Simple" in a certain way; not because it is composed of two intervals, but because it is not composed of the **Octave** <term>Diapason</term>, which is the "Whole," plus any of its parts. When, therefore, we consider this interval only in its extremes and without any middle term, we find that it is of only one species, whether it is placed in the low register or the high. But when we consider it divided diatonically, there will be as many Species of it as there are variations in the placement of the **Semitone** contained within it, according to the ways the divisions are made by its middle strings <note>pitches</note>, which will be three; as is seen here.

<image-desc>Three musical staves displaying sequences of notes on a staff with C-clefs and F-clefs, labeled as follows:</image-desc>

->First species.<-

->Second species.<-

->Third species.<-

Musicians call this interval a **Hexachord** because of the number of strings <note>notes</note> it contains, which is six. For among the Greeks, *Hex* <note>original Greek: Ἕξ</note> means the same as **Six** does among us; and similarly, *Chorde* <note>original Greek: Χορδὴ</note> means the same to them as **String** does to us. Hence it is called an Interval that contains six strings, or a Consonance of six voices, because it is comprised of that number of strings. Therefore, practitioners <note>performing musicians</note> call it the **Major Sixth**, to distinguish it from the minor, which is comprised of a smaller proportion. They say that the Major Sixth, or the Major Hexachord, is a composition of six voices or sounds, containing four Tones and one **Major Semitone**. Thus, when there are two parts in our counterpoints distant from one another in the low and high registers according to the ratio of the extremes of any of the above examples, we shall say then that such parts are distant from one another by a Hexachord, or Major Sixth; as is seen here in the example.

# On the Minor Hexachord, or Minor Sixth. Chapter 21.

The **Minor Hexachord**, which is contained within the *supertripartient-fifth* proportion <note>An 8:5 ratio, where 8 contains 5 once, with 3/5 remaining</note>, is (according to the definition of **practical musicians**) a composition of six voices or sounds, from which it takes the name of **Sixth**. It contains three whole Tones and two major Semitones, when considering the way it is divided diatonically by four intermediate strings <term>chorde: the notes or "strings" of the scale</term>. And because it is divided in only three ways by these aforementioned strings—as can be understood by the varying positions of the Semitones—there are only three species of it, which are shown in the example below.

<image-desc>Musical notation showing the three species of the minor hexachord on staves with C and F clefs. The first and second species are shown on the first staff, separated by a double barline, while the third species is on a separate staff below.</image-desc>

->First species. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Second species.<-

->Third species.<-

But if it were considered solely by its outer extremes, without being divided by any middle notes, one would find only a single species of it, for the reasons already stated regarding the other intervals. Furthermore, it cannot strictly be called **Simple**, because its radical terms are divided by the number **Six** <term>Senario: Zarlino’s "number of six," the integers 1 through 6 which he believed governed all musical harmony</term> in this manner: 5:6:8; as can be seen among the harmonic numbers placed in Chapter 17 of the First Part. Thus, we can call it a composite of the **Perfect Fourth** <term>Diateſſaron</term> and the **Minor Third** <term>Semiditono</term>. Nevertheless, for the reasons given regarding the **Major Hexachord**, we shall also call this one **Simple** in a certain manner. Therefore, when two parts of our counterpoints are distant from one another in the bass and the soprano according to the ratio of the outer notes of any of the shown examples, we can then say that they are distant by one **Hexachord**, or **Minor Sixth**, as found here in the example.

<image-desc>A small musical notation fragment placed to the left of the following paragraph, displaying a vertical interval of two notes on a system of two staves with C and F clefs.</image-desc>

This is also called a **Hexachord** for the reasons given for the **Major Hexachord**, wherefore, to distinguish it, they added "**Minor**." Neither the one nor the other were counted by the **Ancients** <note>Referring to ancient Greek music theorists like Pythagoras or Ptolemy</note> among the consonances, because their outer notes are drawn under the ratios of the aforementioned proportions, which are found to be numbered among those of the **Superpartient** genus <note>A category of ratios where the larger number contains the smaller number once, plus two or more parts (like 5:3 or 8:5). Ancient theorists generally only accepted "Multiple" (2:1, 3:1) or "Superparticular" (3:2, 4:3) ratios as consonant</note>. But because modern **musicians** place them in such an order, and because they are composed (if we wish to consider them so) of the **Perfect Fourth** and the **Major Third** <term>Ditono</term>, or **Minor Third**; which, when placed together, cannot be anything but consonant when they are situated in their proper places; I have therefore wished to make particular mention of them and show their species. Thus, ending now my discussion of those intervals whose proportions are contained in the **Multiple** and **Superparticular** genera, and those whose forms are in the **Superpartient** genus and are accepted by every **musician** as consonant, I shall come to discuss those that have their forms in this same genus but are entirely **Dissonant**.

# On the Fifth with the Major Third; or the Major Seventh. Chapter 22.

The outer sounds of the **Fifth with the Major Third** <term>Diapente col Ditono</term> take their form, then, from the *super-septipartient-eighth* proportion <note>A 15:8 ratio, where 15 contains 8 once with 7/8 remaining</note>. I said the "outer sounds," because although this interval can be called **Composite**—since its radical terms, which are 15 and 8, can be divided in this manner: 15, 12, 10, 9, 8, as seen in Chapter 16 of the First Part—nevertheless, for the reasons stated above, we shall call it **Incomposite** <note>original: "Incomposto," meaning treated as a single unit rather than a sequence of smaller intervals</note>.

<summary>Zarlino defines the Minor Hexachord (Minor Sixth), explaining its three species, its mathematical ratio (8:5), and why modern musicians accept it as a consonance despite ancient theory. He also introduces the Major Seventh (15:8) as the first of the dissonant intervals within the superpartient genus.</summary>

And this interval is placed in the order of dissonant intervals: because its proportion has no place among the **harmonic numbers** <note>original: "numeri harmonici"; Zarlino refers to the integers 1 through 6 (the Senario), which he believed produced all natural musical consonances. Since the ratio for a major seventh involves higher numbers, he considers it dissonant.</note>. Practical musicians name it the **Seventh** after the number of voices or sounds contained within it; they also call it the **Heptachord**, from <note>original: Ἑπτά</note> *Hepta*, which means Seven, and from <note>original: Χορδή</note> *Chorde*, which means String; and to distinguish it from the minor, they add the descriptor **Major**. ### On the Fifth with the Minor Third, or Minor Seventh. Chapter 23.

The **Fifth with the Minor Third** <term>Diapente col Semiditono: an interval spanning seven scale degrees, composed of a perfect fifth and a minor third</term> is contained within the *superquadripartient* proportion <note>A 9:5 ratio, where 9 contains 5 once, plus 4/5ths of 5 remaining (4)</note> between its outer strings. And although it could be called "composite"—seeing as its radical terms, 9 and 5, are bridged in the natural order of harmonic numbers by 8 and 6, as can be seen in Chapter 16 of the First Part—nevertheless, because it is an interval smaller than the **Octave** <term>Diapason</term>, we shall call it **Uncomposite** <note>original: "Incomposto"; Zarlino classifies intervals smaller than an octave as "simple" or "uncomposite" in their basic form, even if they can be mathematically subdivided.</note>. This interval, considered without any bridge (for the reasons cited other times), is found in only one species; but considered as bridged according to the nature of the **Diatonic genus**, Practical musicians say it is a composite of seven voices or sounds containing six intervals, among which are found four Tones and two major Semitones. Its species are **Five**, which arise from the different positions that the Semitones occupy, as seen here.

### Fifth species.

Practical musicians named it the **Seventh** based on the number of notes <note>original: "chorde", literally "strings," referring to the notes of a scale</note> it spans; it is true that they added the word **Minor** to distinguish it from the major. They also called it the **Minor Heptachord**, from those two Greek words mentioned in the previous chapter <note>original: "Hepta" (seven) and "Chorde" (string)</note>. Therefore, when two parts are distant from one another, as are the outer notes of the examples placed above, we shall say that they are separated by a **Minor Seventh**, like those placed below. Here I will conclude the discussion of Consonances and simple Intervals; leaving aside

<image-desc>Two musical staves with examples of the minor seventh interval in different clefs and vocal ranges.</image-desc>

for the sake of brevity, any discussion of **Compound Intervals** <note>intervals larger than an octave</note>. This is because any other interval, whatever it may be, that is larger than the **Diapason** <term>Diapason: the Greek term for an Octave</term>, is considered to be composed of that Octave and one of its parts. It will not be very difficult when one wishes to know their mathematical ratio; we can always find this by adding the other interval we wish to place next to the Octave, summing together the radical terms that contain such intervals. I will say this much: that the outer sounds of the **Twelfth** <note>original: "Diapasondiapente", an octave plus a fifth</note> are contained in a **Triple** ratio; those of the **Fifteenth** <note>original: "Disdiapason", a double octave</note> in a **Quadruple** ratio; those of the **Seventeenth** <note>original: "Disdiapason col Ditono", a double octave plus a major third</note> in a **Quintuple** ratio; and those of the **Nineteenth** <note>original: "Disdiapafondiapente", a double octave plus a fifth</note> in a **Septuple** ratio <note>Zarlino is listing the ratios of the harmonic series: 3:1, 4:1, 5:1, and 7:1</note>. The others can easily be investigated through reason.

## In what manner such intervals are sometimes placed by practical musicians as augmented or diminished, either naturally or by accident.
### Chap. 24.

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'E' depicting a figure in scholarly robes seated at a desk with an open book on a lectern, representing the author or a scholar.</image-desc>

And although every Consonance and every Interval divided into many parts can be named by the number of notes it spans, one must nevertheless be careful not to fall into an error into which some practical musicians have often fallen. These musicians, considering an arrangement of sounds solely by the number of notes and placing little value on the actual intervals contained within them, have sometimes placed in their compositions one of the aforementioned consonances in an **augmented** <note>original: "superflua"</note> or **diminished** form, in place of the true and legitimate species. They have done this because the outer notes of any arrangement of sounds, when considered only by the number of notes, can be found in two ways: that is, **Consonant** and **Dissonant**. The first are those placed between their true notes and comprised of their true ratios; these are the true and legitimate intervals of which we spoke above. But the second are those not contained between their proper notes and which fall outside their true ratios, even though their order and intervals remain diatonic. These are found in two sorts: either the interval is **diminished**, because it contains a smaller interval in place of a larger one (such as a Major Semitone in place of a Whole Tone); or it is **augmented**, because it contains a larger interval in place of a smaller one (such as a Whole Tone in place of a Semitone). Thus, that **Fifth** which is naturally found from <image-desc>musical flat symbol</image-desc> B-flat to F, spanning five notes, is without any doubt diminished by a Minor Semitone. This is because, in place of three Whole Tones and one Major Semitone, it contains two Whole Tones and two Semitones. It is dissonant in its outer notes because it is contained by the ratio of 45 to 19 <note>original: "Super 19 partiente 45"</note>, which has no place among the **harmonic numbers** <note>The "Senario," or numbers 1-6, which Zarlino believed governed all pure musical intervals</note>. For this reason, they call it the **Semidiapente**, the **Imperfect Fifth**, or the **Diminished Fifth**. We can say the same of the **Fourth** contained within four notes between F and <image-desc>musical natural symbol</image-desc> B-natural. Because three Whole Tones are found within it, it is called the **Tritone**, and it is augmented by a Minor Semitone. Since its outer notes are not contained within the ratios of the harmonic numbers—its form being contained by the ratio of 32 to 13—it is exceedingly dissonant. These intervals are shown below. This error can occur not only in the Fifth and the Fourth, but also in the Octave:

Similar errors can also be committed between diatonic and chromatic notes. For if we place a sharp <note>original: "♯"</note> in the high register between C and D as one of the outer notes of the Octave, and the low C as the other outer note, we will have a most dissonant Octave, contained by the ratio of 25 to 12 <note>original: "Dupla sesquiduodecima"</note>; this will be an <term>Augmented Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason superflua," literally "superfluous"</note> by a <term>Minor Semitone</term>. <image-desc>Two systems of musical notation. The first system has two sections labeled "Augmented Octave" and "Augmented Fifth." The second system is labeled "Tritone."</image-desc>

In that case, such an Octave will be diminished by a <term>Minor Semitone</term> and contained by the ratio of 23 parts over 25, which is less than a double ratio <note>the 2:1 ratio of a perfect octave</note>; for this reason, it is called a <term>Semidiapason</term> <note>Diminished Octave</note>. Similarly, such a note paired with G will give us a <term>Semidiapente</term> <note>Diminished Fifth</note>, contained by the ratio of 11 parts over 25; and paired with F it will give us the <term>Semidiatessaron</term> <note>Diminished Fourth</note>, comprised under the form of the ratio 21 parts over 75 <note>likely a typographical error in the original for 25</note>. These, along with the others, are contained in the example below and are entirely dissonant.

These and all the other intervals shown above are extremely dissonant and must not be placed in <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>the art of combining different melodic lines</note>, because they would generate discomfort for the listener. ### On the effects made by these signs: ♮, ♭, and ♯. Chapter 25.

The effect of these characters or signs (as we have been able to see) is to add or to take away the <term>Minor Semitone</term> from a whole Tone, and to make some major consonance become minor, or on the contrary, to make a minor one major. This Semitone, although it is not employed in the melodies of the <term>Diatonic genus</term> <note>the standard scale consisting of whole tones and major semitones</note>, is nevertheless found to have been used at times by composers in their songs; and especially between the melodic lines made by two parts ascending or descending together with the movement of a Third; as can be seen by examining many compositions, as much by the Ancient as well as the Modern composers. But <term>Cipriano de Rore</term> <note>c. 1515–1565, a highly influential Flemish composer of madrigals</note> used it in a single part, in that four-voice song which begins *Hélas comment* <note>original: "Hellas coment," a French chanson</note>, both in the lowest part and also in the highest part. And such a Semitone is found naturally between the note <term>Trite synemennon</term> <note>the B-flat in the ancient Greek system</note> and the <term>Paramese</term> <note>the B-natural in the ancient Greek system</note>, as I showed above in Chapter 19. Practical musicians say that such a Semitone is described between these two syllables, *Fa* and *Mi*, placing the *Mi* above the *Fa*; these are different in shape, being the ♭ and the ♮ seen in the example below: for the voice or note marked with the ♮ is higher than the one marked with the ♭. Therefore, <term>Guido of Arezzo</term> <note>an 11th-century monk and music theorist</note>, so as not to confuse singers, placed these two different characters in his *Introductory* but did not change their location on the staff; he intended that by one of them the note *Trite synemennon* should be understood, and by the other the note *Paramese*.

<image-desc>A short musical staff showing two notes on the same line, the first preceded by a flat (♭) and the second by a natural (♮).</image-desc>

Seeing this difference, musicians thereafter ordained two sorts of song: one of which they called "of Nature and of the natural-B" [square-B]; this is the one that proceeds through the notes of the <term>Meson Tetrachord</term> and those of the <term>Diezeugmenon Tetrachord</term> <note>specific four-note segments of the traditional scale</note>; and one does not place any of the shown characters at the beginning of the parts of the song. The other they named "of Nature and of the flat-B" [soft-B]; this occurs when the parts touch the notes of the <term>Synemennon Tetrachord</term> and those of the *Meson Tetrachord*, leaving aside those of the *Diezeugmenon Tetrachord*. In this sort of song, one places the character or sign of the flat at the beginning of the musical parts, before the signs of <term>Mensuration</term> <note>original: "Tempo," referring to time signatures</note>. And although the character of the natural (♮) is not placed in songs proceeding through the *Meson* and *Diezeugmenon* tetrachords, it is nonetheless understood to be there. This character is found very often in ecclesiastical books, namely in <term>Plainchant</term> <note>original: "Canti fermi"</note>, even though it has been and still is little used in <term>polyphony</term> <note>original: "Canti figurati," literally "figured songs"</note>. This is because Moderns, when they sometimes want to use the note *Paramese* instead of *Trite synemennon*, place the sharp (♯) character in place of the natural (♮); even though such a thing is done against all propriety. For one ought to use the proper character of the thing they mean to indicate, and not another foreign sign. However, this matters little, because by now everyone knows which note must be used in place of the *Trite synemennon* when they see the sharp sign (♯). But in truth, I would highly praise it if the proper sign were used. To return then to the effects that such characters make, I say that they take away or add the Minor Semitone: In...

We must, however, take care—so that the parts of the <term>cantilena</term> <note>a vocal melody or song</note> turn out to be easier and more comfortable to sing—that when one wishes to place the sign of the ♭, the singable note which is placed before the one to be marked with such a sign should proceed from the low register to the high; and when one wishes to place the ♮ or the ♯, one should do the opposite, that is, proceed from the high register to the low. This is because (as I have said) the parts are then easier to sing, and such intervals are more comfortable to pronounce, as experience demonstrates; although it would not be a great error if it were done otherwise.

### ->What is required in every composition, and first of the Subject. Chap. 26.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'V' depicting two figures, possibly classical or mythological, flanking a central vase or pedestal within a framed border.</image-desc>

I SHALL now come to reason about <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>The art of combining different melodic lines</note>: but before I begin such reasoning, it is necessary to know that in every good Counterpoint, or in every other good composition, many things are required, and if one of these were missing, it could be said to be imperfect. The first is the <term>Subject</term> <note>original: "Soggetto," the primary musical theme or melody upon which a piece is built</note>, without which nothing could be made. For just as the Agent in all his operations always has regard for the goal, and founds his work upon some Matter, which is called the Subject; so the Musician in his operations, having regard for the goal that moves him to work, finds the Matter, or the Subject, upon which he comes to found his composition, and thus comes to lead his work to perfection according to the proposed goal. Wherefore, just as the Poet, who is moved by this goal—namely, to be useful and to delight—as Horace clearly demonstrates in his *Poetics* saying;

<meta>This page continues the discussion of musical composition principles from the previous section, moving from the technical measurements of intervals to the foundational rules of creating a complete work. It establishes the "Subject" as the core element of any musical piece.</meta>

<page-num>172</page-num>

->Poets wish either to be useful or to delight;<-
->Or to say things both pleasant and suitable for life;<-
<note>original: "Aut prodesse volunt, aut delectare poetæ: / Aut simul et iucunda, et idonea dicere vitæ;" from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*</note>

In his poem, the poet takes as his <term>Subject</term><note>The "Soggetto" or Subject: the basic musical idea or theme upon which a composition is built</note> either a History or a Fable—whether he invented it himself or took it from others. He adorns and polishes it with various customs in such a manner as best pleases him, leaving out nothing worthy or praiseworthy that might delight the minds of his listeners, aiming for the magnificent and the marvelous. In the same way, the Musician is moved by the same goal: that is, to be useful and to delight the minds of the listeners with harmonic accents. He has his Subject upon which his <term>cantilena</term><note>A general term for a musical line, song, or composition</note> is founded, which he adorns with various <term>modulations</term><note>In this context, melodic movements or the "turning" of a musical line</note> and various harmonies in a way that provides pleasing enjoyment to the listeners. 

The **Second** condition is that the composition be composed principally of consonances, and then secondarily contain many dissonances by accident, placed within it in the proper ways according to the Rules, which I wish to show further below. The **Third** is that the parts of the song proceed well; that is, that the modulations proceed by true and legitimate intervals born from musical numbers, so that through them we may acquire the use of good harmonies. The **Fourth** condition required is that the modulations and the <term>concento</term><note>The overall effect of voices singing together in harmony</note> be varied; for harmony is born from nothing other than the diversity of modulations and the diversity of consonances joined together with variation. The **Fifth** is that the song be ordered under a prescribed and determined Harmony, or <term>Mode</term><note>Also referred to as a "Tone"; the scale system or "key" that governs the piece</note>, or Tone, as we might call it, and that it not be disorganized. And the **Sixth** and last (besides others that could be added) is that the harmony contained within it be so accommodated to the <term>Oration</term><note>The "Oratione": the text or lyrics being set to music</note>—that is, to the words—that in cheerful matters the harmony is not mournful, and conversely, in mournful matters the harmony is not cheerful. Therefore, so that one may have perfect knowledge of all this, I shall come to discuss all these things separately as they occur to me and as needed. 

Beginning then with the **First**, I say that the **Subject** of any musical composition is called that part upon which the Composer draws the invention to create the other parts of the song, however many there may be. And such a Subject can exist in many ways: first, it can be his own invention—that is, the Composer found it with his own genius. Then, it may be that he took it from the compositions of others, fitting it to his own song and adorning it with various parts and various modulations as most pleases him, according to the greatness of his genius. Such a Subject can be found in several forms: it can be a <term>Tenor</term><note>Historically, the "holding" part that carries the main melody</note> or another part of any song of <term>Canto fermo</term><note>Plainsong or Gregorian chant</note> or of <term>Canto figurato</term><note>Figural or polyphonic music with complex rhythms</note>; or it could be two or more parts where one follows the other in <term>Fugue</term><note>A technique where voices enter successively with the same theme</note> or <term>Consequence</term>, or in any other way; for the various types of such Subjects are infinite. 

Once the Composer has found his Subject, he then makes the other parts in the manner we shall see further on. When this is done, such a manner of composing is called, according to the <term>Practitioners</term><note>The "Prattici": professional musicians and composers who focus on the practice rather than just the theory</note>, **Doing counterpoint**. But when he has not first found a Subject, then that part which is first put into action—or that with which the Composer begins his song, whatever it may be and starting in whatever way he likes, whether low, high, or in the middle—that shall always be the Subject. Upon this, he then fits the other parts in Fugue, or Consequence, or in another way as he pleases, matching the harmonies to the words as required by the matter contained within them. But when the Composer goes about drawing the Subject from the parts of the song—that is, when he draws one part from another, creating the Subject and the composition together, as we shall see elsewhere—that little portion which he draws out from the others, upon which he then composes the parts of his work, shall always be called the Subject. This manner of composing is called by practitioners **Composing from fantasy** <note>Improvisatory or free composition without a pre-existing melody</note>, although it can also be called "Counterpointing" or "Doing counterpoint," as one wishes.

***

### That Compositions must be composed primarily of Consonances, and then by accident of Dissonances. Chap. 27.

Although (as has been said elsewhere) every Composition and every Counterpoint—and to say it in a single word, every Harmony—is composed principally of Consonances; nonetheless, for greater beauty and grace, Dissonances are also used in it secondarily, by accident. Although these are not very pleasing to the ear when heard alone, nonetheless, when they are placed in the manner they regularly ought to be, and according to...

according to the precepts that we shall demonstrate; the sense of Hearing supports them in such a way that they not only do not offend, but actually provide great pleasure and delight. From these, the Musician derives two benefits (among many others of no small value): The First has been mentioned above—that is, that with their help one can pass from one <term>consonance</term><note>A combination of notes that sounds stable and pleasant to the ear.</note> to another. The Second is that <term>Dissonance</term><note>A combination of notes that sounds tense or "clashing," which Zarlino argues makes the following stable chord sound even better by comparison.</note> makes the Consonance that immediately follows it seem more delightful; it is perceived and recognized by the ear with greater pleasure, just as light is more grateful and pleasing to the sight after darkness, and as a sweet thing is more savory and gentle after something bitter. We prove this by experience every day in sounds: if for some time the hearing is offended by a dissonance, the consonance that follows it becomes sweeter and more delightful. 

For this reason, the Ancient Musicians judged that in compositions there should be a place not only for the Consonances they call Perfect and those they call Imperfect, but for Dissonances as well. They recognized that compositions could result in more beauty and grace with them than they would have without them. Indeed, if they were composed of consonances alone, even though they would create a beautiful sound and produce good effects, such compositions (not having the Consonances mixed with Dissonances) would be almost imperfect, both in terms of the singing and the structure of the composition; for they would lack the great elegance that arises from these things. 

And although I have said that one primarily uses Consonances in compositions, and then Dissonances as an incidental feature, it should not be understood that they are to be placed in <term>Counterpoints</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines to play simultaneously.</note> or Compositions at random, without any rule or order, for confusion would follow. Rather, one must take care to place them with order and rule so that everything turns out well. Above all, one must have regard (among other things) for two matters in which, in my judgment, consists all the beauty, grace, and goodness of every composition: that is, the **Movements** made by the parts of the <term>cantilena</term><note>A general term for the musical song or melodic line.</note> as they ascend and descend through similar or contrary motions; and the **Placement** of the consonances in their proper places within the harmonies. 

Of these things, with God’s help, I intend to speak as the subject arises, for this has always been my primary intention. As an introduction to this discussion, I intend to explain some Rules given by the Ancients, who recognized the necessity of such things. By teaching the method for regularly placing Consonances and Dissonances one after another in compositions, they also gave some Rules for these Movements, even if they did so imperfectly. I will therefore set down these Rules in order and provide their explanation, showing what must be done. I will demonstrate with evident reasons how they are to be understood, adding some others that will be not only useful but very necessary for all those who desire to bring themselves to a regulated way and good order of composing learnedly and elegantly, with sound reasons and solid foundations. In this way, everyone will be able to know in which part they must place the Consonances and Dissonances, and in which place they can put the Major and Minor intervals in their songs.

### That one should begin compositions with one of the perfect consonances. Chapter 28.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'V' featuring a seated figure in a landscape with a classical building and trees.</image-desc>

**THE ANCIENT** Musicians desired—a practice observed even by the best Moderns—that in beginning Counterpoints or other musical Compositions, one should place one of the named <term>perfect consonances</term><note>Intervals considered perfectly stable: the Unison, the Fifth, and the Octave.</note>; that is, the Unison, or the Fifth, or the Octave, or one of their replicates. They did not intend for this rule to be so absolute that it could not be done otherwise—that is, that one could not also begin with one of the imperfect consonances—since perfection is always attributed to the end, and not to the beginning of things. 

However, we should not understand this rule so simply. When the part of the Counterpoint begins to sing at the same time as the part of the <term>Subject</term><note>The core musical theme or melody upon which the piece is built.</note>, then one may begin with one of the aforementioned perfect consonances. But when, for the greater beauty and grace of the Counterpoint, and also for greater convenience, the musicians arrange it so that the parts do not begin to sing together, but one after the other with the same progression of figures or notes—which is called a **Fugue** or **Consequence**—this makes the Counterpoint not only delightful but also ingenious. In that case, they may begin on whichever consonance they wish, whether perfect or imperfect.

For one begins on the note F, and the other on the note C, and they are distant by a fourth in respect to the beginning of each. Yet we shall observe the given rule of starting with one of the perfect consonances by having the parts begin to sing together on a <term>major third</term><note>original: "Terza maggiore" or "Ditono".</note>; because one begins on the note E and the other on the note C, as seen in the fourth example. Thus, such a beginning truly demonstrates that such a precept is not mandatory or necessary, but rather a matter of choice. Nor can these two parts generate anything unpleasant to the ear; for although the beginnings of the parts correspond by a fourth, as I have said, nevertheless when they begin to sing together, the <term>ditone</term><note>An interval of two whole tones, equivalent to a major third.</note> or major third is heard.

One must also take care (which is a matter of no small importance) to arrange the parts in compositions and <term>counterpoints</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines so they sound harmonious together.</note> for multiple voices in such a way that their beginnings correspond to one another. They should have a relationship based on one of the perfect or imperfect <term>consonances</term><note>Intervals that sound stable and pleasant to the ear, such as thirds, fifths, sixths, and octaves.</note>; so that when the singers wish to begin, no <term>dissonance</term><note>Intervals that sound harsh or unstable, like seconds or sevenths.</note> is heard while they are finding their notes. And this is not only because it causes annoyance to those who wish to sing, but at times it is the reason they make mistakes more easily, taking one note for another, especially when they are not very confident. 

It is indeed true that it is permissible to place the beginning of two parts in the low range a <term>fourth</term><note>An interval spanning four scale degrees.</note> apart, provided there is no other part lower than them, and that the other voices relate to them by an <term>octave</term>. This is especially common in the <term>Plagal modes</term><note>original: "Modi placali"; also called the "even" modes, these versions of the church scales have a lower range than their "Authentic" counterparts.</note>, or "Odd" modes as some call them, when the parts of the song begin to sing upon the principal notes of the <term>modes</term> in which the piece is composed. Truly, to wish to take away this freedom from the composer—to be able to place two parts in such a manner—is not a fair thing, especially since it can be done in two-voice writing. To do so would make the composer a subject, bound to a rule that serves no purpose. Indeed, beginning in such a way has been put into use by many skilled practitioners; such as <term>Josquin</term><note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), one of the most famous composers of the Renaissance.</note>, <term>Mouton</term><note>Jean Mouton (c. 1459–1522), a celebrated French composer and teacher of Adrian Willaert.</note>, and other ancient and modern musicians. We can see an example of this in the motet composed by <term>Adrian</term><note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), Zarlino's own teacher and the maestro di cappella at St. Mark's in Venice.</note> for five voices, *Praise to thee, sacred red [blood]* <note>original: "Laus tibi sacra rubens"</note>, leaving aside infinite other examples from modern and ancient composers. 

I also took such liberty in those three motets: *Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth* <note>original: "Osculetur me osculis oris sui"</note>; *I am the rose of Sharon* <note>original: "Ego rosa Saron"</note>; and *Catch for us the little foxes* <note>original: "Capite nobis vulpes parvulas"</note>, which I previously composed for five voices. As anyone can see, these serve as examples for the things said above. This is therefore granted to all composers. 

However, it is not to be praised when two parts are distant in their beginnings from the <term>Subject</term>—whether in the high or low range—one by a fourth and the other by a <term>fifth</term>. This is because those two parts would then end up being a <term>second</term><note>A highly dissonant interval of just two scale steps.</note> apart from each other, and in taking their starting notes, they would create a dissonance. Furthermore, it might be that one of these parts would begin on a note that does not belong to the <term>mode</term> upon which the composition or song is founded. 

Even though such a warning is good, it is nevertheless not strictly necessary when the principal subject of the composition is composed with such artifice that one part sings above the other in <term>Fuga</term> or <term>Consequence</term><note>original: "Fuga, o Conseguenza"; types of strict imitation where voices follow each other with the same melody.</note>. In such cases, two voices might sing over the principal part of the subject, in the high or low range, one distant from the other by a fifth or a fourth; or perhaps one is distant from the subject by a fourth and the other by a fifth, or some other interval. 

This can be seen in the motet *God, Father of Heaven* <note>original: "Pater de celis deus"</note> composed by <term>P. della Rue</term><note>Pierre de la Rue (c. 1452–1518), a leading composer of the Franco-Flemish school.</note> for six voices, and in the motet *Most prudent Virgin* <note>original: "Virgo prudentissima"</note> which I previously composed for six voices. In that piece, three parts sing in <term>fuga</term> or imitation—two toward the high range and one toward the low range using the same intervals—and in taking the voices, such an inconvenience is heard. 

But one must note that I call the "part of the <term>Subject</term>" that one upon which the other parts are arranged in imitation; it is the principal part and the guide for all the others. I do not necessarily mean the one that is the very first to begin singing; rather, I mean the one that observes and maintains the <term>Mode</term>, upon which the other parts are arranged at whatever interval. This can be seen in the Lord’s Prayer *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noster"</note> and in the Angelic Salutation *Hail Mary* <note>original: "Ave maria"</note> which I composed in the past for seven voices. There, the principal subject of those three parts singing in imitation is not the part that is first to begin singing, but rather the second. In such cases, therefore, it will be permissible to place in a composition...

## That one must not place two Consonances, contained under the same proportion, one after the other while ascending or descending without any intermediary. Chapter 29.

The Ancient composers then forbade the placing of two <term>perfect Consonances</term><note>Intervals like the unison, octave, and fifth, which were considered "perfect" because of their simple mathematical ratios.</note> of the same genus or species—contained in their extremes by the same <term>proportion</term><note>The mathematical ratio of the string lengths or frequencies; for example, an octave is always 2:1.</note>—one after the other, whether the <term>melodic lines</term><note>Original: "modulationi." Refers to the movement of the voice from one note to the next.</note> move by one or by multiple steps. This includes placing two or more <term>Unisons</term>, or two or more <term>Octaves</term>, or two or more <term>Fifths</term>, and other similar combinations, as seen in the examples below.

<image-desc>A series of musical notation examples on five-line staves, illustrating forbidden parallel intervals. The first set is labeled "Unisons," showing diamond-shaped notes on the same pitch level in two voices. The second set is labeled "Octaves," showing two voices moving in parallel at the distance of an octave. The third set is labeled "Fifths," showing two voices moving in parallel at the distance of a fifth.</image-desc>

For they knew very well that <term>Harmony</term> cannot be born except from things that are diverse, discordant, and contrary among themselves, and not from those that agree in every respect. Therefore, if Harmony is born from such variety, it will be necessary in Music that the parts of the song are not only distant from one another in <term>low</term> and <term>high pitch</term><note>Original: "graue" and "acuto."</note>, but also that their movements are different in their motions, and that they contain various consonances held by different proportions. 

And we can judge a song to be all the more harmonious when there is found in the composition of its parts more diverse distances between one and the other in the low and high ranges, diverse movements, and diverse proportions. Perhaps the Ancients saw that Consonances placed together in a way other than what I have said—even though they were at times varied in their extremes by being low or high—were similar in their proceeding and similar in the form of their proportions. Therefore, knowing that such similarity generated no variety of <term>concord</term><note>Original: "concento." The pleasant blending of sounds.</note>, and judging (as was the truth) that perfect harmony consists in variety—not so much in the positions or distances of the parts of the song, but in the variety of the movements, the melodic lines, and the proportions—they judged that placing two Consonances of similar proportion one after the other varied nothing but their location from low to high (or vice-versa), without making any good harmony, even though their outer notes were varied from one another. 

Therefore, they did not want two or more perfect Consonances, held by the same proportion, with the parts ascending or descending together, to be placed in compositions one after the other without any other intervening interval. And they especially forbade Unisons, which have no distance in their sounds, nor are they different in position, nor distant from each other, nor do they make any variation in their proceeding, but are similar in everything and in every way. Nor is any difference between low or high found in them while singing, as no interval falls between one sound and the other; for the notes of one part are found in the very same place as the notes of the other, as can be seen in the example placed above and in the definition of the Unison in Chapter 11. Nor is any diversity of movement found, because one part sings by the very same intervals through which the other proceeds. 

The same could also be said of two or more Octaves, were it not that their extremes are different from each other in the low and the high—a thing that brings somewhat more delight to the ear than do Unisons, because the Octave is somewhat varied in its extremes. The same can be said of two or more Fifths; for because of the way they proceed by steps and similar proportions, some of the Ancients held the opinion that they produced a certain kind of dissonance rather than...

harmony or consonance. Thus they held it as a truth that whenever one arrived at a perfect consonance, one had reached the goal and the perfection toward which Music tends. They did not wish for this perfection to be repeated many times, so as not to generate satiety in the listener. This beautiful and useful warning is confirmed as true and good by the operations of marvelous Nature, which, in bringing the individuals of each species into being, never produces them in such a way that they resemble each other in everything; rather, they are varied by some difference, and this difference or variety brings great pleasure to our senses. Every composer, therefore, ought to imitate such a great and beautiful order: for his works will be deemed better the more they resemble those of Nature. 

We are invited to this observance by Numbers and <term>Proportions</term><note>The mathematical ratios that define musical intervals.</note>: for among them, in the natural order, one does not find two proportions immediately following one another that are identical. For example, a progression like 1. 1. 1. or 2. 2. 2. and other similar ones would form the shapes of two <term>Unisons</term>; nor does one find a progression like 1. 2. 4. 8., which is not <term>Harmonic</term> but <term>Geometric</term>, containing the forms of three continuous <term>Octaves</term>; nor even an order like 4. 6. 9., which contains the forms of two continuous <term>Fifths</term>. We must not, therefore, in any way place two Unisons immediately after one another, nor two Octaves, nor two Fifths; since the natural cause of consonances, which is the <term>Harmonic Number</term><note>Original: "Numero harmonico." This refers to the "Senario," the numbers 1 through 6, which Zarlino believed contained all the ratios of the basic musical consonances.</note>, does not contain in its progress or natural order two identical proportions one after the other without any intermediary, as can be seen in Chapter 15 of the First Part. For even if these consonances, when placed in such a manner, did not evidently create a dissonance between the parts, they would nonetheless cause one to hear something somewhat dull <note>original: "tristo"</note> that would be displeasing. 

For so many reasons, then, we must not go against this Rule at any cost; that is, we must not place consonances one after the other in the manner shown above. Instead, we must seek to always vary the sounds, the consonances, the movements, and the intervals; in this way, we will achieve a good and perfect harmony. And we should not pay mind to the fact that some have wished to do the opposite—more out of presumption than for any reason they might have had—as we see in their compositions. For we should not imitate those who shamelessly act against the good customs and good precepts of an Art and a Science without giving any reason for it; but we should imitate those who have been observers of the good precepts, and draw near to them and embrace them as good masters, always leaving behind the bad and taking up the good. Just as looking at a painting depicted with various colors delights the eye more than if it were painted with a single color, so the Hearing is more greatly delighted and takes pleasure in varied consonances and <term>modulations</term><note>The movement of melodic lines.</note> placed by a diligent composer in his works, rather than in simple and unvaried ones. 

The most diligent ancient musicians, to whom we are much indebted, wished for this to be observed. We shall add to this that, for the reasons already stated, one should also not place two or more <term>imperfect consonances</term> one after the other without any intermediary—such as two major thirds, two minor thirds, two major sixths, or two minor sixths—as seen here in the example.

Part ### Third

...that when <term>Consonances</term><note>Intervals that sound pleasing and stable to the ear.</note> are placed one after another, they should be of different species; for example, after a major **Third** or **Sixth**, a minor one should follow, or vice versa. Likewise, after a major Third, one might place a minor Sixth, or after a minor Third, a major Sixth. Similarly, after a major Sixth, a minor Third may follow. 

There is no greater reason to forbid the placing of two Perfect consonances together than there is for two Imperfect ones: for although the former are <term>Perfect consonances</term><note>Unisons, octaves, and fifths.</note>, each of the <term>Imperfect</term> ones is nonetheless perfect within its own mathematical proportion. Just as it cannot be truly said that one Man is "more" of a Man than another, so it cannot be said that a major Third (or minor), or either of the two Sixths placed in the low register, is more or less "Third" or "Sixth" than another placed in the high register. Thus, just as it is forbidden to place two perfect Consonances of the exact same species one after the other, we should even more strictly avoid placing two imperfect ones of the same proportion, as they are not as consonant as the perfect ones.

It is true, however, that two minor Thirds placed one after another—moving upward or downward together by a single step—may be tolerated. We call this a <term>Conjunct Movement</term><note>Movement where the notes follow each other in alphabetical order, like C to D.</note> or **Continuous Movement**. Similarly, two major Sixths can be permitted in this way. Even though the ear does not hear the <term>major Semitone</term><note>The larger of the two types of half-steps used in Renaissance tuning.</note> in their melodies, and though Thirds are by nature somewhat sad and Sixths somewhat harsh, the slight difference in the movements of the parts creates a degree of variety. This is because the lower part always ascends or descends by a <term>minor Tone</term>, while the higher part moves by a <term>major Tone</term> (or vice versa). This creates a pleasing effect on the ear, especially since the voices remain distant from each other in an <term>harmonic relation</term><note>The vertical mathematical relationship between two notes.</note>. 

But when the parts move by more than one step, we shall call such a movement **Without Conjunction**, or **Separate Movement**. In this case, we must never place two or more similar intervals one after the other. Beyond failing to observe the conditions mentioned above, the voices would not maintain a proper harmonic relation, as can be seen below.

<image-desc>Two sets of musical staves in two voices (soprano/alto and bass clefs). The left example demonstrates harmonic thirds between the parts in a sequence. The right example demonstrates harmonic sixths. The notation uses diamond-shaped notes (semibreves/minims) typical of 16th-17th century printing.</image-desc>

->Example of Thirds.<- ->Example of Sixths.<-

---

To avoid the errors that can occur when it is necessary to place two Thirds or two Sixths one after another, we should observe the rule of placing the major first and then the minor, or vice versa. They may then be placed in whatever manner one wishes, whether with Conjunct Movements or Separate Movements, and everything will turn out well. 

However, one must be careful when placing a Third after a Sixth, or a Sixth after a Third, to ensure that if one is major, the other is minor. This applies when each of the parts is moving either up or down. But when one of the parts does not move at all, this rule cannot be observed without departing from other rules that we will give later for the <term>well-being of the melody</term><note>Original: "bene essere della cantilena." This refers to the overall musical quality and flow of the composition.</note>. In that case, after a major Third, it will be necessary to provide a major Sixth, and after a minor, a minor Sixth—or vice versa—as seen in the example below.

## When the parts of a song have a Harmonic relation between them, and in what way we can use the Diminished Fifth and the Tritone in compositions. Chapter 30.

BEFORE I proceed any further, I wish to clarify what I said above regarding the parts of a song; that is, when the voices sometimes have and sometimes do not have a **Harmonic relation** <note>original: "Harmonica relatione"; this refers to the relationship between notes in different voices that occur in succession.</note> between them. Thus, one should know that saying the parts of a song do not have a harmonic relation between their voices is the same as saying that the parts are near or far from one another by an <term>Augmented Octave</term><note>original: "Diapason superflua".</note>, or by a <term>Diminished Octave</term><note>original: "Semidiapason".</note>, or perhaps by a **Diminished Fifth** or a **Tritone**, and other similar intervals. I do not mean that this relation is found only between two notes, or two parts where one is distant from the other in the low and high registers; rather, I say it is found among four notes contained within two parts which form two consonances, as seen here:

<image-desc>Musical notation for two voices on two five-line staves. Underneath the lower staff, labels align with vertical pairs of notes to identify intervals: Augmented Octave, Diminished Octave, Diminished Octave, Tritone, Tritone, Tritone, Tritone, Tritone.</image-desc>

Among these is found the **Augmented Octave**, the **Diminished Octave**, the **Diminished Fifth** <note>original: "Semidiapente".</note>, and the **Tritone**, through the relation of the notes of one part to the notes of the other. Therefore, so that our compositions may be purged of every error and may be correct, we shall seek to avoid such relations, especially when we compose for two voices. This is because they cause a certain amount of annoyance to refined ears; for such intervals are not found to be placed among the <term>sonorous numbers</term><note>The "Senario" or the numbers 1 through 6, which Zarlino believed were the basis of all musical harmony.</note>, and they are not sung in any genre whatsoever. Although some have held a contrary opinion, be that as it may, they are very difficult to sing and produce a poor effect. And I marvel greatly at those who have not shied away at all from making any of the parts of their songs sing one of these intervals; nor can I imagine for what reason they have done so. Even though it is a lesser evil to find it by relation between two parts and between two melodies than to hear it within the melody of a single part, nevertheless, that same evil which is heard in one part is found divided between two, and it is that same offense to the hearing. For it matters little or not at all whether one is offended by the same blow from one source or from many, when the harm is no less. These intervals, then, which are not admitted in melodic movement, must be avoided in songs so that they are not heard through relations between the parts. This will be achieved when the parts can be exchanged with one another using proportioned harmonic intervals contained in the <term>diatonic genus</term><note>The standard musical scale of the time, consisting of whole steps and half steps.</note>; that is, when from one voice of the part—

### What regard one should have for related intervals in compositions for several voices. Chapter 31.

However, it should be noted that the displayed relations—the <term>tritones</term>, the <term>diminished fifths</term><note>original: "Semidiapente"</note>, the <term>diminished octaves</term><note>original: "Semidiapason"</note>, and others like them—when found placed in <term>counterpoints</term> alone, without being accompanied by other intervals, are counted among those things in music that can give little delight. Hence, we must strive not to place them in simple compositions, which are those for two voices, as I have said; or when two parts of any other <term>song</term><note>original: "cantilena"; here referring to a polyphonic vocal work.</note> sing alone. For then such things are heard clearly, because that harmony which we call **Proper** is not present—in which one hears a body full of consonances and harmony, by having the outer sounds mediated by other middle sounds. Instead, only that which is called **Improper** is heard, in which only two parts are heard singing together without being mediated by any other sound. These [two-part harmonies] are more easily grasped by the senses than three or four parts. Therefore, between two parts, we must vary the harmony as much as we can and observe not to place such relations, a thing that can be done without any difficulty. But in compositions of several voices, it seems to me that such regard is not so necessary; both because one could not always observe such regard (as I said above) except with great inconvenience, and also because variety consists not only in the change of consonances, but also of harmonies and of positions—which does not happen in compositions written for two voices.

And I say this because, just as many things are sometimes found that are unpleasant and harmful on their own, yet when accompanied by certain others they are good and healthful—as is seen with some ingredients that go into medicines and other <term>electuaries</term><note>A medicinal paste or syrup mixed with honey or sugar, often containing potent or bitter herbs.</note> which by themselves are deadly, but accompanied by other things in such mixtures, they undoubtedly give health—so too these relations in music, and certain other intervals, exist which by themselves give little pleasure, but accompanied by others produce wonderful effects. It seems to me, then, that we must have a different consideration of them when we want to use them simply [unaccompanied], than we do when we want to use them accompanied. For the variety of harmony in such accompaniments does not consist only in the variety of consonances found between two parts, but also in the variety of the harmonies, which consists in the position of a middle string [note] placed within the <term>fifth</term><note>original: "Quinta"</note> in the composition; or it consists in the position of the string that makes the <term>third</term><note>original: "Terza"</note> or the <term>tenth</term><note>original: "Decima"</note> above the low part of the song. 

Hence, either they are minor, and the resulting harmony is ordered by or resembles **arithmetic proportionality** or mediation; or they are major, and such harmony is ordered by or resembles **harmonic mediation**<note>Zarlino is describing the difference between what we now call major and minor chords. A "harmonic mediation" places the larger third on the bottom (a major triad), while "arithmetic" places the smaller third on the bottom (a minor triad).</note>. Upon this variety depends all the diversity and perfection of harmonies. For it is necessary (as I shall say elsewhere) that in a perfect composition the <term>fifth</term> and the <term>third</term> (or their <term>replicates</term><note>Intervals expanded by an octave, such as a tenth.</note>) are always present in act. Since beyond these two consonances, the ear cannot desire any sound that falls in the middle or outside their extremes that is entirely different and varied from those at the extremes of these two consonances placed together; for all those different sounds that can make diverse harmonies are found there. 

But because the extremes of the fifth are invariable and are always placed contained under the same proportion (leaving aside certain cases in which it is made imperfect, that is, under another form, as I have shown), the extremes of the thirds are placed differently within that fifth. I do not say different in proportion, but I mean different in position. For (as I have said elsewhere), when the **major third** is placed in the low part, the harmony becomes cheerful; and when it is placed in the high part, it becomes sad. Thus, from the diverse positioning of the thirds—placed in counterpoint between the extremes of the fifth, or placed above the octave—the variety of harmony is born. If, then, we wish to vary the harmony and observe as much as possible the Rule set down above in Chapter 29 (even though in compositions of several voices it is not as necessary as it is in those for two), it is necessary that we place the thirds differently in this manner: having first placed the major third, which makes the harmonic mediation, we can then place the minor, which will make the arithmeti-

[...thing]; <note>The syllable "ca" likely completes the word "cosa" (thing) from the previous page.</note> This could not be observed so easily if one considers these relations; for while one tries to avoid them, one would continue the harmony for quite some time in one of the aforementioned divisions without any mediation. This would cause the <term>composition</term><note>original: "cantilena"; a general term for a musical work or melody.</note> to sometimes sound sad during words that suggest joy, or sound happy during those that treat sad matters, without any purpose. I am not saying that the composer cannot place two <term>arithmetic divisions</term><note>The arithmetic division of the fifth results in what we now call a minor triad, which Zarlino associated with a "sad" or "melancholy" sound.</note> one after the other; but I say that one should not continue in such a division for a long time, because it would make the harmony very melancholy.
