In that case, the harmony has its parts placed according to their proper degrees; it reaches its ultimate goal and produces an excellent effect. It is certainly true that when two parts ascend or descend by one or two degrees, the mediation must be placed differently, especially when the <term>tritone</term> or the <term>diminished fifth</term><note>original: "Semidiapente"</note> can occur by relation between the two parts making such movements. This happens when one places two <term>major thirds</term><note>original: "Terze maggiori" or "Ditoni"</note> one after the other in the first mode, or two minor thirds in the second. But when the relation is a <term>diminished fourth</term><note>original: "Semidiatessaron"</note> and occurs between accidental signs—such as the flat (♭) and the sharp (#)—or even when only one of these signs is involved, we should not avoid it at all. Since these are two harmonic mediations, they produce a good effect, as is evident, even if they are not varied. No one should wonder at this; for when one examines the consonances placed in such orders with diligence, he will find that the <term>arithmetic order</term>—or that which resembles arithmetic proportionality—strays slightly from the perfection of harmony, because its parts are placed outside their natural locations. Conversely, he will find that the harmony arising from the <term>harmonic division</term> (or that which resembles it) will sound perfectly, because the parts of such a division are placed and ordered according to the proper degrees of that proportionality, and according to the order held by the <term>sonorous numbers</term><note>Zarlino’s "sonorous numbers" (the senario, or numbers 1 to 6) were the mathematical basis for all pure musical intervals.</note> in their natural sequence, as can be seen in Chapter 15 of the First Part. Let this be said sufficiently for now; perhaps another time, for a greater understanding of what I have said, I will touch upon it again.

### In what manner two or more perfect or imperfect consonances of the same form may be placed immediately one after the other. Chapter 32.

And although, for the reasons stated above, one cannot place two consonances of the same proportion in <term>counterpoint</term> that both ascend or descend together, it is nonetheless permitted to place two consonances contained by the same form—whether perfect or imperfect, such as two <term>octaves</term>, two <term>fifths</term>, two <term>major thirds</term><note>original: "Ditoni"</note>, two <term>minor thirds</term><note>original: "Semiditoni"</note>, and other similar intervals—one after the other without any intermediate consonance, when the low voice of one part of the song is swapped with the high voice of the other through contrary motion, as seen here:

<image-desc>A musical notation example on a staff showing voice exchange. Two voices are illustrated with notes connected by diagonal lines in an "X" pattern, demonstrating the movement of parts as they swap pitches while maintaining the same harmonic interval. The diagram is framed within the text column.</image-desc>

For in shifting or changing these notes between them, the consonance is not transported from high to low or from low to high; rather, it remains on its original pitches, changing neither location nor sounds. Therefore, no variety of low or high is heard. Since such variation is not heard, one cannot say that they are two consonances of the same form placed one after the other in the manner understood above. Instead, it is a single consonance replicated on the same notes, as is clear to the senses. And although the parts change places, ascending and descending, and one takes the place of the other and their melodic movements are varied by the contrary motions they make, their sounds are not varied. One might hear some variety when the part that was in the low range is heard more in the high range, and vice versa. But such a thing would not absolutely create variety in the sense we mean, but only in a certain way; as can be understood from the example below, for if the parts did not change place, the melodies of each would necessarily become a <term>unison</term>.

## That two or more perfect or imperfect consonances contained under different forms, placed one immediately after the other, are permitted. Chapter 33.

The observance of the aforementioned rules was indeed very necessary so that from the variety of <term>consonances</term><note>Intervals that sound "stable" or "pleasant" to the ear, such as octaves, fifths, and thirds.</note> placed in compositions with such beautiful order, sweet and delightful harmony might be born. Therefore, observing all these things, musicians later took such liberty that in their <term>counterpoints</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines to play simultaneously.</note> they placed consonances as they best saw fit; and they did not avoid placing two perfect or imperfect consonances one after the other, varying the pitch, without being separated by any other middle consonance; provided they were contained under different <term>forms</term><note>original: "forme"; in Zarlino's theory, this refers to the mathematical ratios that define an interval, such as 2:1 for an octave or 3:2 for a fifth. He is allowing a fifth to be followed by an octave, but not two fifths in a row.</note>. We, therefore, to follow such use—since it is very convenient and reasonable—will place the consonances in our counterpoints in the manner described; placing (when it is convenient) the <term>Octave</term> immediately after the <term>Fifth</term>, or vice versa; and after each of these, the <term>major Third</term> or the <term>minor</term>. Similarly, we can place the <term>Sixth</term><note>original: "Essachordo"</note> after the <term>Third</term>, and the <term>Third</term> after the <term>Sixth</term>, as it serves best, always varying the consonances, as can be seen here.

Observing, however, that the parts proceed in their <term>melodic movements</term><note>original: "modulationi"; the way a single voice moves from one note to the next.</note> through singable intervals and with graceful motion, so that good and delightful harmony results.

## That it is good to place an imperfect consonance after a perfect one, or vice versa. Chapter 34.

Although in the natural order of <term>harmonic numbers</term><note>The "Senario" or the numbers 1 through 6, which Zarlino believed were the mathematical foundation of all musical beauty.</note> the forms of perfect consonances are found one after the other without any imperfect form being interposed (as can be seen in Chapter 15 of the First Part), and then the forms of the imperfect ones follow in order without being separated by any perfect form, we should not believe—even if we must always be guided by such numbers—that the Ancients held to such an order in placing consonances in their counterpoints. For they knew very well that continuing in perfect consonances, or in imperfect ones, besides bringing a certain tediousness, would also have added difficulty. And truly it would have been almost impossible for the melodic movements of the parts to have in themselves a certain perfection, which is sought after: since it would have been difficult to accommodate them with that charm that is necessary in the <term>composition</term><note>original: "cantilena"; a general term for a musical work or melody.</note>. Therefore, so that this difficulty may be removed, we shall observe what was also observed by them: that is, to place and arrange in counter-

Because from such variety can only be born a good, charming, delightful, and perfect harmony. ### That the parts of the Composition should proceed by contrary motion. Chapter 35.

It was said above that Harmony is composed of opposites or contraries; therefore, this also applies to the <term>Motions</term> made by the parts singing together. One must observe as much as possible (which will not be outside the practices of the Ancients) that when the part upon which the <term>Counterpoint</term> is made—that is, the <term>Subject</term>—ascends, the Counterpoint should descend; and likewise, conversely, when the Subject descends, the Counterpoint should ascend. However, it will not be an error if at times they ascend or descend together, in order to accommodate the parts of the composition so they proceed with graceful movements. Thus, if we observe that when one of the parts (as I have said) ascends, the other descends, there is no doubt that the <term>modulations</term><note>The movement of the melodic lines relative to each other.</note> the parts make together will proceed by contrary motions and produce a good effect; as can be seen from the example placed below.

### In what manner the parts of the Composition may ascend or descend together. Chapter 36.

One should not believe (even though musicians urge the observance of this rule) that it is so fatal and necessary that one cannot sometimes do the opposite. For that would be to want to bind the musician without purpose to something not strictly necessary, and to take away their way of proceeding with grace and elegance, as well as the practice of singing with harmony. Furthermore, if it were necessary to always observe this, one could not (when the occasion arises) use the technique of <term>Fugue</term><note>original: "Fuga"; a technique where one voice mimics the melody of another after a short delay.</note> or <term>Consequence</term><note>original: "Consequenza"; a stricter form of imitation, similar to a canon.</note>, which is very localizable and praiseworthy in a Composer, and is used when one part of the music follows the other, in the manner we shall see elsewhere. Observing the aforementioned rule as much as possible, then, when it occurs that the parts of the composition must ascend or descend together, we shall try to repeat their movements such that they do not generate a harsh effect for the ear. It is indeed true, that it is much more laudable when the parts descend together into the lower range: because then their <term>Motions</term> necessarily become slow; and it is even more laudable the lower they are; because through the slowness, the diversity of the species <note>The "species" refers to the specific type of interval, such as a perfect fifth versus an octave.</note> is easily understood. ### That one should avoid <term>separate movements</term><note>Movement by leaps of more than a single step (disjunct motion).</note> as much as possible, and similarly the distances that can occur between the parts of a <term>composition</term><note>original: "cantilena" — a general term for a musical work or melody.</note>. Chapter 37.

Above all other things, we must take care that the parts of the compositions—not only when they ascend or descend together, but also when they move in opposite directions—should proceed by <term>conjunct movements</term><note>Movement by a single step (a second).</note> as much as possible. One must ensure that one part does not distance itself too far from the other with Leaps and separate movements; such as when one part proceeds by a leap of an <term>Octave</term> and the other by a leap of a <term>Fifth</term>, or a <term>Fourth</term>, or other similar movements, like those in the example placed below.

<image-desc>A musical score printed on two five-line staves using white mensural notation. The diamond-shaped notes on both staves illustrate disjointed or separated melodic movements (salti) as described in the text, showing wide intervals between consecutive notes.</image-desc>

*Since such distances—besides being more difficult to sing (as the voices cannot be formed so easily, nor the intervals and <term>consonances</term><note>Harmonious intervals like thirds, fifths, or octaves.</note> proportioned in those melodies that proceed in such a way, compared to those where one part moves by a step and the other by a leap)—they also generate certain effects that are sometimes not very pleasing to the ear. Hence, it is to be noted that movements are undoubtedly more "singable" the more they are united—that is, not very far apart, like those that move by a single step. They allow the <term>harmony</term> that arises between the parts to be heard with greater delight than those that are separated. This happens because the more conjunct they are, the more natural they are; for one proceeds naturally when moving from one extreme of a thing to another through the proper intermediaries. Thus, such proximity is much to be praised and commended, as it stays closer to nature. This was also greatly praised by **Augustine** in chapter 10 of the second book of "On Music" <note>original: "De Musica"</note>, saying:* <note>original: "La vicinità delle parti, tanto era più degna di essere approuata, quanto era più vicina alla equalità"</note> *that the proximity of the parts was so much more worthy of approval the closer it was to equality; even though he was reasoning on another matter. And although these distances are not dissonant in themselves, they nonetheless generate (as I have said) a certain unpleasantness to the ear that cannot be heard with delight. We shall therefore avoid these distances so that our <term>counterpoints</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines.</note> may be pleasing, sweet, sonorous, harmonious, and full of every good melody.*

### In what manner one should proceed from one Consonance to another. Chapter 38.

Many believe that for no other reason than to avoid the disorders that could occur against the given Rule, some Musicians ordained that when one proceeds from one consonance to another, one should go to the nearest one; such as from the <term>Unison</term> to the <term>Third</term>, from the Third to the <term>Fifth</term>, from the Fifth to the <term>Sixth</term>, and from the Sixth to the <term>Octave</term>, and vice versa, so as not to come to distant movements. This Rule, even though at first encounter it seems easy to understand, nonetheless requires some consideration, because it contains some things that are not only useful but also necessary for all those who wish to follow the use of the

<meta>catchword: good (buone)</meta>

<summary>Zarlino argues that musical parts should move primarily by step (conjunct motion) rather than by large leaps, as stepwise motion is more natural, easier to sing, and more pleasing to the ear. He also introduces the principle of moving to the nearest possible consonance when transitioning between intervals.</summary>

<header>Third Part</header>

...good harmonies, and lead their works to perfection; which not only Art or Science seeks, but are even observed naturally by many. When, therefore, they say that one should proceed from one consonance to another by the nearest interval, it must also be understood in this way: that when the Composer departs from an <term>Imperfect consonance</term><note>Intervals like thirds and sixths, which were considered "incomplete" and requiring resolution to a more stable sound.</note> and wishes to arrive at a <term>Perfect</term><note>The most stable intervals: the unison, fifth, and octave.</note> one, he must ensure that the preceding Imperfect one is truly the closest to it. By doing otherwise, he would not observe this rule, which is highly necessary. 

Therefore, it should be noted that when we wish to move from a <term>Sixth</term> to an <term>Octave</term>, that Sixth must be major, as it is closer to it; and we must not use a minor one, because (as we shall see further on) it is further away. And this we must observe not only when the parts of the <term>composition</term><note>original: "cantilena"</note> move in opposite directions, but even when one of them does not move from its own place, and the other ascends or descends by two steps. Similarly, when we wish to move from a Sixth to a <term>Fifth</term>, that Sixth must be minor, because it is nearer to it, and not major, because it is further away; especially when one of the parts of the composition makes no movement at all, and the other ascends or descends by one step—that is, moves with <term>conjunct movement</term><note>Stepwise motion to the adjacent note.</note>. 

Furthermore, when we wish to move from a <term>Third</term> to an Octave, the Third must be major, as the one closer to the Octave, and not minor. And it is necessary that the parts move by contrary movements—that is, one by Conjunct movement and the other by <term>separate movement</term><note>A leap (disjunct motion).</note>. But when we wish to move from a Third to a Fifth, and one of the parts makes no movement, it will be necessary for the Third to be major. But the Third will then be minor, especially in compositions for two voices, when the parts proceed by contrary conjunct movements; or when one of them descends by conjunct movement and the other likewise descends by separate movement; also, in those parts that proceed by contrary movements, the minor Third is used to avoid the <term>Relation of the Tritone</term><note>original: "Relation del Tritono" — a harsh, unstable interval of three whole tones (an augmented fourth) that was strictly regulated in Renaissance music.</note> between the parts, which is not closer to it, but further away. 

Then, when we wish to move from a Third to the <term>Unison</term> (even though it is not placed among the number of consonances, except insofar as it is their beginning), the Third will always be minor, as it is closer; but the parts must move by contrary movements, and such movements must be conjunct. For when the parts ascend together, one by conjunct movement and the other by separate movement, then the Third will be major. And if one of the parts does not move, and the other ascends or descends by separate movement, then the Third will always be minor. And I say this always having regard for the places or terms of the perfect consonance, which will be the <term>strings</term><note>original: "chorde" — the specific notes or pitches, often visualized as strings on a musical instrument like the monochord.</note> upon which that consonance must terminate, as seen in the examples placed below.

When one goes from a Perfect consonance to an Imperfect one, then it is not necessary to have this consideration, provided that the movements made by the parts are regulated according to the manner shown above. I say from Perfect to Imperfect for this reason: because everything naturally desires its own perfection, which it desires to reach as soon as possible and in the best and shortest way it can; which perfection, in this genre, is attributed to the Perfect Consonances. Therefore, everything can easily pass (as is manifest to everyone) from perfection to imperfection, but not the contrary; for it is easier to make a thing than it is to destroy and ruin it. 

Thus, if one were to work otherwise than I have said, it would be to act against the order and nature of things. For Imperfect things participate in perfection more when they approach their neighboring Perfect consonance, and they even render themselves much sweeter and more pleasant to the ear. Someone might now say to me: "If the major Sixth is closer to the Fifth than it is to the Octave (as is manifest), for what reason should we place it before the Octave rather than before the Fifth, since we must..."

<page-num>189</page-num>
<header>Part</header>

...should we go from an <term>Imperfect Consonance</term><note>Intervals like thirds and sixths, which require resolution to feel "complete."</note> to a <term>Perfect</term><note>The most stable intervals, like the fifth and octave.</note> one by the nearest path? I say that although the <term>Major Sixth</term> is physically closer to the Fifth than to the Octave, it is not true that the Minor Sixth is not closer to the Fifth than the Major one is. Wherefore we must know that, since among the Perfect intervals the Octave is greater than the Fifth, and among the Sixths the Major is of a greater quantity than the Minor, we must pair the larger of the Perfect ones with the larger of the Imperfect ones. This is due to that "symbol" (if I may call it so) or "agreement" that exists between them; for it is an easy thing to pass from one thing to another without much effort when such a similarity or agreement is found between them. 

Thus, we should move to the <term>Fifth</term> from a Minor Sixth, because it has such an agreement with it and is closer to it. Similarly, we shall move to the <term>Octave</term> from a Major Sixth, since it has such an agreement with it and is nearer to it. Nor can I see any reason to show why a thing to which one has only one relationship should be suited to two different and almost contrary things. It seems to me that using them in any other way would be like that physician whom <term>Galen</term><note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for centuries.</note> calls an "Empiricist," who wishes to cure different ailments with the same medicine, taking no account of whether the illness proceeds more from a <term>hot humor</term> than a <term>cold</term> one, because he does not recognize the <term>offending humor</term><note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that governed health; an imbalance caused disease.</note>.

Truly, the Major Sixth is suited to the Octave and not the Minor; and the Minor is best paired with the Fifth, as can be proven by reason, authority, and example. First, it is proven by reason, as I have shown above; and also because if we consider the <term>Harmonic Number</term><note>The mathematical ratios that define musical intervals.</note>, from which every musical consonance derives its form, we find that the Major Sixth has its form from the <term>superbipartient-third</term><note>The ratio 5:3, which defines a major sixth.</note> proportion, contained (as I have said elsewhere) between the terms 5 and 3, which are the root of such a proportion. Now, if we proceed further in the natural order of the aforementioned numbers, we find that after 5, the number 6 follows immediately, which with 5 contains the form of the <term>Minor Third</term>. If we pair this with the said Sixth, we arrive exactly at the Octave. 

For this reason, if we place the 3 so that it has two relations—namely to 5 and to 6—proceeding by natural order in this way: 6 : 5 : 3, it is almost in the manner of two <term>parts</term><note>Musical voices or lines.</note> where one moves from high to low and the other does not move. Or, if we place the same order between 10 : 6 : 5, it is almost like two parts where one moves from the low toward the high by a <term>minor third</term><note>original: "Semiditono"</note> and arrives at the Octave, while the other does not move; we shall see how necessary the observation of the aforementioned Rule is. We find this same observation in the order between 15 and 9, which contain the form of the Major Sixth outside its radical terms. Just as two parts—one of which ascends by a <term>Major Tone</term> and the other descends by a <term>Major Semitone</term>—reach the Octave in a wonderful way, so by placing 9 over 8 and adding 16 under 15, we find the form of the <term>Octave</term><note>original: "Diapason"</note> outside its radical terms between 16 and 8, in this natural order: 16 : 15 : 9 : 8. 

And just as one does not find in such an order that from the form of the Major Sixth one can come to the form of the Fifth except with the help of a Tone, so one can never proceed from the Minor Sixth to the Fifth except with the help of a Semitone. This can be understood from these four terms 50 : 45 : 30 : 27, between which the form of the Fifth is conveniently found between 45 and 30, and that of the <term>Minor Tone</term> on each side. And between 24 : 16 : 15 : 10, the form of the <term>Major Semitone</term> is in the middle, and that of the Fifth is on each side between 24 and 16, and between 15 and 10; in the manner of one part proceeding from low to high (or vice versa) while the other, placed in the low or high, makes no movement at all. These terms cannot be found in any other way in the natural order of the said Harmonic Numbers except with great difficulty, and they would not be placed in the natural order, but rather an accidental one. 

Those reasons I have stated regarding the Major Sixth with the Octave can be applied to the Minor with the Fifth, and to other consonances as well, which I omit for brevity. There is yet another reason to demonstrate this: of any two proposed Imperfect consonances, whichever they may be, provided they are named by the same number of strings, the larger is always more suited to take on growth in the low or the high than the smaller, which has a nature to restrict itself and become even smaller; this is because the larger has more of the "continuous" than the smaller. 

From this it follows that, since everything naturally desires and seeks its like, the Major Sixth—having more perfection than the Minor—greatly desires to approach the Octave, which by its nature is more perfect than the Fifth (indeed, it is the most perfect of all, as I have said at other times). And the Minor Sixth, as less perfect, from whichever side it may be (low or high), seeks that which is more conforming to its nature, which is the Fifth. This same observation is confirmed by the authority of <term>Franchino Gaffurio</term><note>A famous Italian music theorist of the late 15th century.</note>, who maintains that the proper nature of the...

He compares a musician who ignores these natural tendencies to an incompetent doctor who treats all patients with the same remedy without understanding their unique humors.</summary>

...[the nature of the] <term>Major Sixth</term> is to move toward the <term>Octave</term>; and the property of the <term>Minor Sixth</term> is to move toward the <term>Fifth</term>. Since such is the nature of these <term>consonances</term><note>Intervals that sound harmonious together.</note>, it must be said that they always possess this nature and inclination; and when they are placed otherwise in compositions, they are placed against their own nature. Therefore, if things placed in a work against their nature cannot produce a good effect—because they are withdrawn from their own proper purpose—we can say that whenever such Consonances are placed in <term>Counterpoint</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines.</note> against their nature, they cannot bring anything to the ear that greatly delights it. We can now see this to be true with experience in hand, and come to the promised example: for they produce a better effect when placed in Counterpoint in the manner shown above than in any other way. Wherefore Nature, which has jurisdiction over all things, has ensured that not only those who are skilled in Music, but even the unlearned and the peasants who sing in their own way without any formal reason, use the transition from the Major Sixth to the Octave, as they are taught by nature. This is heard most clearly in <term>Cadences</term><note>The concluding sequence of notes or chords that brings a musical phrase to a rest.</note> than in any other part of their songs, as is manifest to everyone skilled in Music. And perhaps the said <term>Franchino</term><note>Franchino Gaffurio (1451–1522), a famous music theorist whose writings were standard before Zarlino’s time.</note> took courage from this to say that the movement from the Major Sixth to the Octave should only be observed in Cadences, because the endings of melodies occur in them. But in my judgment, it seems to me (as can be understood from his words placed above) that this was not said with good reason, if we wish to attend to the Nature of both the one and the other. It will therefore not be permitted, if one wishes to observe this Rule, to pass from the Major Sixth to the Fifth, nor from the Minor to the Octave, without the depravation of the nature of the aforementioned consonances. Therefore, one must take care—so that this Rule may be easily observed—that whenever one wishes to proceed from an Imperfect to a Perfect consonance, at least one of the parts moves with a motion containing a <term>Major Semitone</term><note>The larger of two types of half-steps recognized in Renaissance theory; in modern terms, moving from a sharp/flat to a natural note or vice versa.</note>, whether silent or expressed. And to achieve such a thing, the use of <term>Chromatic and Enharmonic strings</term><note>References to the ancient Greek scale systems; here, Zarlino refers to the use of accidentals (sharps and flats).</note> will be very helpful, employing them in the manner that I shall demonstrate elsewhere. But because it is not always convenient for the Composer to pass from the Major Sixth to the Octave, nor from the Minor to the Fifth—just as it is sometimes not convenient to proceed from the <term>Minor Third</term> to the <term>Unison</term> in the manner I have shown above—therefore, so that everyone may know how to proceed in such cases, I will provide the example below. In it, one can see in how many ways one can pass from one or the other Sixth, and likewise from the Major and Minor Third, and other similar intervals, to another consonance.

<image-desc>A musical example consisting of two staves with diamond-shaped (lozenge) notes. The top staff uses a C-clef (Soprano/Alto) and the bottom staff uses an F-clef (Bass). The notation illustrates various two-part contrapuntal movements and interval progressions discussed in the text, primarily transitions between sixths and octaves or fifths.</image-desc>

Lastly, this is to be noted: that what has been said of simple Consonances must also be understood for <term>Replicated Consonances</term><note>Compound intervals that are larger than an octave, such as a tenth (a third plus an octave).</note>. Similarly, it should be noted that when two parts of the melody descend together, and from a Major Sixth they come to a <term>Third</term> that is Major, it will land better and produce a better effect than if it landed on a Minor Third, even though both ways are good. For it will undoubtedly land upon a consonance that is closer to perfection than the Minor Third is, as can be heard and examined in these two examples placed here to the side.

<image-desc>Two short musical examples placed side-by-side. Each example consists of two staves showing a two-note progression in two voices. Part Three.

### In what manner each Song should be finished. Chapter 39.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'V' featuring a woman holding a stringed instrument (lute or viol) with a child standing beside her.</image-desc>
Musicians have ultimately willed that <term>Songs</term><note>original: "Cantilene"; refers to any polyphonic musical composition.</note> should finish with one of the perfect <term>consonances</term><note>Intervals that sound stable and complete, such as the unison, fifth, or octave.</note>. This is because they truly saw that, by every right, the perfection of a thing is attributed to its end, by which it is then judged. And because they saw that no greater perfection could be found in consonances than that which is found in the <term>Octave</term>—it being more perfect than any other—they willed that this rule should be absolute. They mandated that songs must finish on the Octave, or indeed on the <term>Unison</term>, and that under no circumstances should one do otherwise, even though this rule has been poorly observed by some of little judgment. 

Therefore, if we desire to follow all those who have been the founders and observers of good rules, when we come to conclude any of our <term>Counterpoints</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines.</note>, we shall end them with one of the named consonances, for they are the most perfect of all others. This rule was truly very well established; for if songs ended otherwise, the ears of the listeners would remain in suspense and would long for their perfection. In this, that would happen which usually happens to those who hear a speech being recited: while they listen with an attentive mind, they simultaneously desire and expect its epilogue and conclusion, in which the speech is brought to its perfection. 

Another inconvenience would also arise if the song were ended otherwise. Since the judgment of which <term>Mode</term><note>A system of scales used before the modern major/minor system.</note> a piece is composed in is attributed to the last note of each song—that is, whether the harmony arising from it belongs to the First, Third, or another Mode, as we shall see in the Fourth Part—one could then take the final note of whichever part one wished, even if it were not the proper final note of the Mode (be it the low or the high note). One would then judge a Mode by one that is not its own, and thus a false judgment would be made. This would truly happen if said Counterpoints finished on a <term>Fifth</term>, or a <term>Third</term>, or one of their <term>replicates</term><note>Intervals expanded by an octave, such as a tenth (a replicate of a third).</note>. In such cases, one would not know so easily which note should be taken, the high or the low, to judge the song—though one could judge such a thing in the middle of it by seeing its form, that is, the way it proceeds. 

With great judgment, therefore, the ancient Musicians ordained this and the other rules given above, which are very useful and greatly necessary to anyone who desires to correctly compose any song. Therefore, everyone should strive to put them into use, so that from their labors they may draw some benefit, and principally acquire honor. But let this be said sufficiently concerning the essential rules of composing simple counterpoints for two voices, which are called <term>Note-against-note</term><note>original: "Nota contra nota"; a style where each note in one voice is matched by a single note of equal duration in the other.</note>. These are not only useful and necessary for these compositions, but they also serve every other way of composing, whatever it may be—whether the counterpoint is simple or <term>diminished</term><note>original: "diminuito"; florid counterpoint where one voice moves more quickly with smaller note values.</note>—as can be clearly seen.

### The method to be followed in making simple counterpoints for two voices, called Note-against-note. Chapter 40.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar, at a desk with books.</image-desc>
To now come to the use of the given rules, I will show the method that must be followed in making counterpoints, beginning with those composed simply for two voices, Note-against-note, so that from them one may pass to the Diminished ones and to the use of other compositions. Desiring then to observe that which has been observed by all good writers and composers of any other subject, we shall reasonably begin with the easiest things, so that the reader may more easily become learned and so that confusion does not follow. 

First, then, having regard for what was said above in Chapter 26, it is necessary to find a <term>Tenor</term> of any <term>Plainchant</term><note>original: "Canto fermo"; a pre-existing sacred melody used as the foundation for the counterpoint.</note> you wish, which shall be the **Subject** of the composition—that is, of the Counterpoint. Then it must be examined with all diligence to see under which Mode it is composed, in order to be able to make the <term>Cadences</term><note>The points of rest or conclusion in a musical phrase.</note> in their proper places with purpose, and to know the nature of the composition from them. For if they were made inadvertently out of place and purpose, mixing those of one Mode with those of another, the end would not be in harmony with the beginning and the middle of the song. 

But let us suppose that the Subject found is the Tenor of the plainchant placed below, contained in the First Mode. One must notice before all other things what was said above in Chapter 28 regarding the way to begin the song;

Part Three.

Therefore, we shall place the first figure, or note, of the <term>Counterpoint</term><note>The new melody being composed against an existing one.</note> at a distance from the first note of the <term>Subject</term><note>original: "Soggetto"; the pre-existing melody, often called the cantus firmus, which serves as the foundation for the composition.</note> such that they are separated by one of the perfect <term>consonances</term><note>Stable intervals like the unison, fifth, or octave.</note>. Once this is done, we will accompany the second note of the counterpoint with the second note of the subject in such a way that they are a consonance apart, whether perfect or imperfect; provided that it is different from the first, so as not to go against what was determined in Chapter 29. We must always keep an eye on what was said in Chapter 38, ensuring that the parts of the song stay as closely united as possible, and that neither part makes movements of large intervals, so that the parts are not very far from each other, according to what I said in Chapter 27.

After this is done, one may proceed to the third figure, or note, of the counterpoint and accompany it with the third of the subject, varying not only the <term>pitches</term><note>original: "chorde"; literally "strings," referring to the specific notes on the scale.</note> or positions, but also the consonance—placing a perfect consonance after an imperfect one, and vice versa; or alternatively, placing two different species of perfect or imperfect consonances one after the other, according to the rules given above in Chapters 33 and 34. We shall do the same for the fourth note of the counterpoint with the fourth of the subject, and so for the fifth, the sixth, and the others in order, until reaching the very last. According to the rule given in the preceding chapter, we will finish the counterpoint with a perfect consonance from those named in the aforementioned chapter.

But above all else, one must seek to ensure that the counterpoint part is varied, not only through different movements—touching different pitches, now in the low range, now in the high, and now in the middle—but also that it is varied in its consonances against the subject. And most of all, one must ensure that the counterpoint part "sings well" and proceeds as much as possible by <term>conjunct movements</term><note>Stepwise motion, where the notes move to their immediate neighbors in the scale, rather than jumping.</note>. For in this consists a part of the beauty of counterpoint, which, added to the many other qualities required (as we shall see), brings it to its perfection.

Thus, anyone who first practices this simple way of composing will afterward be able to easily and quickly arrive at greater things. By trying to create various compositions and counterpoints over a subject—now in the low range, now in the high—they will become well-practiced in the pitches and the distances of each consonance. Afterward, according to the precepts I am about to show, they can proceed to the <term>diminution</term><note>original: "diminutione"; the practice of breaking down long notes into shorter, faster decorative notes.</note> of the figures—that is, to "diminished counterpoint"—sometimes making the counterpoint parts flee from those of the subject <note>an early reference to fugal or imitative writing</note>, sometimes imitating them, and using other methods, as we shall see. After these, they can come to compositions for more voices; so that, aided by our warnings and their own ingenuity, they will in a short period become a good and learned composer.

But it must be noted that I do not set down a specific rule here for the exact path one must take in creating the counterpoint part over a subject; rather, I only provide a universal one. Thus, from those rules placed above, the composer must use their own intellect to derive the counterpoint part, working with judgment. To the acquisition of such judgment, rules and precepts are of little value if one is not aided by nature. Nor should anyone wonder at this, as it is common to every Art and every Doctrine. For all those who have wished to provide knowledge of and teach any Art or Science have always proposed the Universal; because Science does not deal with particulars, which are infinite, but rather with Universals.

We see that the precepts of Poetry and of the Oratorical art written by Plato, Aristotle, Hermogenes, Cicero, Quintilian, Horace, and still others are concerned with the Universal and not the Particular. And to give an example, I recall what Horace writes <note>original: *Ars Poetica*, lines 42-44</note> when speaking universally of the order that poets must maintain in arranging their subject—which is the history or the fable in their narrations—where he says:

> This will be the virtue and grace of order, or I am mistaken, <note>original: "Ordinis haec virtus erit, & Venus, aut ego fallor,"</note>
> That the poet says now what ought to be said now, <note>original: "Ut iam nunc dicat: iam nunc debentia dici"</note>
> And defers most things, omitting them for the present time. <note>original: "Pleraq; differat, & praesens in tempus omittat."</note>

The most learned Virgil knew this rule very well, as can be understood; for having taken a specific subject—which was to write of the ruin and burning of Troy and the navigation of Aeneas—he began first with the navigation, interrupting the chronological order, even though the navigation happened afterward. But he understood that his poem would turn out with greater artistry and majesty if he had the history recited in order by Aeneas in the presence of Dido, as he did, taking the opportunity from the fortune Aeneas had in being brought to Carthage. Poets are accustomed to do this, and not only poets, but also painters—for painting is nothing other than a "silent poetry." They adapt histories or fables as best suits their purpose. Hence, having decided to paint a history or fable, the painter arranges the figures and accompanies them together according to what seems to him to look best and produce the best effects; nor does he mind placing one figure more in a mo-

All these things must be observed by he who desires to enter well into the art of counterpoint. But above all else, he must exercise himself with all study, primarily for many days, in this sort of composition; so that he may afterward come with greater ease to the use of **Diminished Counterpoint** <term>Contrapunto diminuito: A more complex style where one note in the subject is set against multiple faster notes in the counterpoint.</term>, in which he may use many other techniques, as we shall see in the appropriate places. Once these are examined, one may then easily understand those things I will show elsewhere, and be able to work with less labor.

Everyone should be warned that making note-against-note counterpoint seems, and truly is, somewhat more difficult than making diminished counterpoint. This is because there is not the same liberty found in the diminished style; for in the first, it is necessary that every note or singable figure have only one **consonance** <note>An interval that sounds stable and harmonious to the ear.</note>, whereas in the second, many notes are placed, mixed with many **dissonances** <note>Intervals that sound unstable or "clashing," which require resolution to a consonance.</note>, according to the will and good judgment of the composer. Hence, in the first method, one cannot always order the parts as well as one might wish so that they are without leaps and easy to sing—especially when one wishes to compose many counterpoints over the same subject that are varied in every part. ### That in Counterpoint, Unisons Should Be Avoided as Much as Possible, and Octaves Should Not Be Frequently Repeated for Too Long. Chapter 41.

And so that we may compose our <term>melodies</term> <note>original: *cantilene*; a general term for polyphonic vocal compositions</note> so that they give pleasing enjoyment and delight to the ear; before I go any further, I will give several very useful warnings for the beauty and grace of **Counterpoint**. The first of these shall be that the Composer must, as much as possible, avoid placing **Unisons** in his counterpoints, and he should not use **Octaves** very often. This is because unisons are not (as I have said elsewhere) placed among the number of consonances <note>In Renaissance theory, the unison was considered the "source" of consonances rather than a consonance itself, much like the number one was the source of numbers but not a "multitude."</note>; and octaves, because of a certain similarity they have with the Unison, are not as charming to the ear as the others are. 

And this [rule] is not without purpose: for if the Ancients, by means of Music, moderated and regulated not only the Arts but also many Sciences—regarding Sounds as well as Numbers and Proportions, as can be seen in Grammar, Rhetoric, and similarly in Poetry and many others—then whatever they possess that is good and beautiful, they have it (I shall say) through Music. For music is truly that science (as Augustine demonstrates) <note>Likely referring to St. Augustine's treatise *De Musica*, which explores the relationship between musical rhythm and poetry.</note> from which all these things are learned; it would not be unfitting, then, for music to be ordered just as the other Arts and Sciences are. Indeed, it would be (in my judgment) a very blameworthy thing if music were disordered and without any rule in those very matters through which the other Sciences and Arts have been ordered and well-regulated. 

Wherefore, if the Grammarian, the Rhetorician, and the Poet have gained this knowledge from Music—that the continuation of a sound, that is, the repeating of a single syllable or letter many times in a clause of an Oration, generates a certain unpleasantness to the ear which the Greeks call <term>cacophoton</term> <note>original: *κακόφατον*; literally "bad-sounding." In rhetoric, this refers to harsh sounds or awkward repetitions.</note>, that is, "bad speech" or "bad consonance"—it is heard in that verse: *O fortunate Rome, born when I was consul* <note>original: *O fortunatam natam me consule Romam*; a line by Cicero famously criticized by ancient stylists for the repetitive "natam natam" sound.</note>; because of the doubling of the syllable *natam*, and because of the ending of the verse in the syllable *mam*, which give little pleasure to the ear. It is also heard in the beginning of that Epistle which Cicero writes to Lentulus the Proconsul: *In all my duty* <note>original: *Ego omni officio*; from Cicero's *Ad Familiares* 1.1. Critics noted the repetitive "o" sounds (*eg**o** **o**mni **o**ffici**o***) were ungraceful.</note>; where in three words one reads the letter *O* four times, and in almost infinite other places where something unpleasant is heard that "purged ears" <note>A common Renaissance expression for ears trained in refined taste and harmony.</note> cannot bear to hear. 

The Musician would truly be worthy of blame if he allowed a similar disorder in his compositions. For if all these others, by common opinion, have concluded with universal laws that it is not permitted in either Prose or Verse (unless such a thing were placed there artfully to show some specific effect) to use these strange modes of speech, then even more so must the Musician banish from his compositions every "bad sound" and anything else that might offend the ear. The Musician must therefore take care not to commit similar errors in his melodies; rather, he must regulate his harmonies in such a way that everything heard in them is good. 

And truly, Counterpoint would not be so well-purified if such disorders were heard in it very often and without any purpose. This would happen if one made many Unisons or many Octaves heard one after the other, separated only by a single other consonance—especially when they were placed upon the same pitch, even if the parts proceeded with separate movements. How pleasing such consonances would be to anyone of sound judgment, when placed in such a manner, can be recognized from the example below.

I do not say, however, that they should never be used; but I say that they should not be used too often. For when it happens that the Composer cannot accommodate a good and convenient <term>modulation</term> <note>original: *modulatione*; in this period, it refers to the graceful movement or "inflection" of a melodic line rather than a change of key.</note>—that is, a beautiful and elegant progression with a lovely and graceful way of singing—he must by all means use them. They should, however, be interspersed with other consonances. One should also always prefer to place the **Octave** rather than the **Unison** when it is convenient, because the Unison (as we have seen) is not in any way a **Consonance**, whereas the Octave truly is.

## Of Diminished Counterpoints for Two Voices, and in What Manner Dissonances May Be Used. Chapter 42.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated woodcut initial 'Q' containing two figures, possibly a child and an adult figure, amidst classical foliage and scrolls within a square border.</image-desc>WHEN one has used every diligence in making **Counterpoint** of note-against-note—which is highly necessary for all beginners to practice recognizing the placement and distances of Consonances—and has learned to do it well and correctly, then one may pass to **Diminished Counterpoint**. <note>original: *Contrapunto diminuito*; also known as "florid" counterpoint, where the notes are "diminished" or broken down into smaller rhythmic values.</note> First, one must find the **Subject**, just as we did in simple counterpoints. And because only equal figures of the same kind were placed in those, you must take note that in this type, different figures will occur. Thus, just as Simple Counterpoint was composed of Consonances alone, without any **Dissonance** being mixed in, so the Diminished will be capable of receiving not only Consonances but also Dissonances—and this "by accident," as we shall see. These are not to be placed in the music without consideration or order, but thoughtfully, with purpose, and with reason, so that confusion does not follow. While confusion should be avoided in all things, it must be most strictly forbidden in Music. 

Therefore, it should be noted that, just as in the simple counterpoints shown above, every figure of the Subject had a corresponding figure in the counterpoint part; so now, over any figure of such a Subject, it will be permitted to place as many and whichever figures serve the purpose, provided that those placed in the counterpoint part are equivalent in value to those in the Subject. Hence, over every <term>Semibreve</term> <note>equivalent to a modern whole note</note> contained in the Subject, we may place two <term>Minims</term> <note>half notes</note>, or four <term>Crotchets</term> <note>original: *Semiminime*; quarter notes</note>, and likewise one Minim and two Crotchets, and other similar combinations as best fits. 

This must follow this order, however: if placing two Minims in the counterpoint over one Semibreve in the Subject, each of them must be consonant. This is because these two parts of the Semibreve are heavily perceived by the senses in relation to the **Beat** <note>original: *Battuta*; the basic pulse or measure, traditionally marked by a downward and upward motion of the hand.</note>, which is considered in two ways: the downbeat and the upbeat, as we shall see elsewhere. Of these parts, one Minim is given to the first [downbeat] and the other to the second [upbeat], which together equal the Semibreve in the Subject. 

When one then wishes to place four Crotchets equivalent to such a Semibreve in the counterpoint, it will follow that those Crotchets which fall upon the downbeat and the upbeat of the Beat must be accompanied by consonance. For this reason, it will be necessary for the **First** and **Third** Crotchets to be consonant; the others (the Second and Fourth) need not be, although it would be better if they were. And everything I have said should be understood as applying when the counterpoint proceeds by **Conjunct Motion** <note>original: *Mouimenti congiunti*; movement by step (e.g., C to D).</note>. For when proceeding by **Disjunct Motion** <note>original: *Mouimenti separati*; movement by leaps (e.g., C to E).</note>, it is necessary that those figures containing such movements be consonant with the Subject part. 

But because sometimes, for greater grace, a tied Minim is used—that is, a Minim followed by a **Dot**—one must take care to place the Dot so that it is consonant. For if it were placed otherwise, anyone could hear for themselves how unpleasant it would be to the ear. And although the Minim tied in this way can be placed in two manners in counterpoints—first on the downbeat (at the start of the Beat) and then on the upbeat—the first manner should only be used at the beginning of counterpoints and not in the middle (and I say this regarding counterpoints for two voices). But the second manner can be used not only at the beginning but also in the middle, as seen in the example. 

The counterpunter may also sometimes alternately place two minims, one of which is consonant and the other dissonant, provided that the consonant one falls on the downbeat and the dissonant on the upbeat. However, they must proceed toward the bass or the treble by many continuous steps without any leaps. And when such a progression begins at the start of the counterpoint, one may use the dotted Semibreve before anything else, provided it fits well; but not in the middle of the counterpoint. This is because a simple Semibreve is not used in such a place, nor a dotted Minim unless it is syncopated. On the contrary (outside of that case), every figure of the Subject that is <term>Cantus Firmus</term> <note>original: *Canto fermo*; a fixed, pre-existing melody used as the basis of a polyphonic composition.</note> must have at least two consonances over it, one on the downbeat and the other on the...

At times, it should proceed with figures of somewhat greater value than those contained in the Subject: for it is necessary that at least one part be heard making movement, both on the downbeat and on the upbeat of the Measure.

For although the **Dissonance** is placed on the second minim in conjunct motion, such movement and the slight speed found in pronouncing such figures do not let anything be heard that displeases. But this is not so in <term>disjunct motions</term> <note>original: *Mouimenti separati*; melodic movement by leap rather than by step.</note>: for through such separation, the Dissonance becomes so manifest that it can hardly be tolerated; as is clear to all those who have judgment in such matters.

<meta>catchword: the Fourth</meta>

One may nonetheless place the first part of the <term>Measure</term> <note>original: *battuta*; the basic unit of musical time marked by a downbeat and upbeat.</note> as a dissonance when it is the second <term>Minim</term> <note>original: *minima*; a rhythmic value half the length of a semibreve.</note> of a syncopated <term>Semibreve</term> <note>original: *Semibreue*; the fundamental whole-note in this period's notation.</note> in the Counterpoint. This is because the first part of such a figure will undoubtedly be placed on the upbeat, and the second on the downbeat, making such a dissonance tolerable. In singing a syncopated Semibreve, the voice is held steady and one hears a kind of suspension or silence found in the middle of the "strike" from which sounds are born. It is through this strike that sounds are discerned from one another in time; therefore, the sense of hearing hardly notices the dissonance because it is not moved by it in a way that it can fully comprehend it. The ear is not "struck" by it anew, and the movement perceived in it is weak because it lacks the percussive start that moves the senses. Thus, as the voice perseveres through the <term>Syncopation</term> <note>original: *Sincopa*; a rhythmic displacement where a note begins on a weak beat and is held across a strong beat.</note>, it loses that vivacity it had at the first strike. Being thus weakened, and being struck against the second part of the syncopation—where the dissonance is hidden—by the more vigorous movement of another strong voice moving from one place to another with more power, such a dissonance is barely heard, especially since it passes by quickly. And if the sense of hearing is somewhat offended, it is immediately compensated by the <term>Consonance</term> <note>original: *Consonanza*; a harmonious interval pleasant to the ear.</note> that follows without any delay. Not only does such a dissonance not displease the ear, but it actually provides great pleasure, for it makes the following consonance sound with greater sweetness and smoothness. This perhaps happens because **every contrary is more clearly revealed and made better known to the senses by comparison with its opposite.**

But one must never place the first part of the Semibreve as a dissonance, whether it is syncopated or not. Two things must be observed in every way: first, that after the dissonance, the <term>Consonance</term> nearest to it must follow; second, that the movement made by the syncopated part must always **descend**, and be **conjunct** <note>original: *congiunto*; moving by step to the very next note in the scale rather than leaping.</note>, and not ascend. Thus, this rule may be useful: when the dissonance placed in the second part of the syncopated Semibreve is a **Second**, we shall then perfectly accommodate the **Third**, which is nearest to it. Likewise, when a **Fourth** is placed in that syncopation, one shall do the same <note>The 4th resolves down to a 3rd.</note>. A **Seventh** will be accompanied by a **Sixth**, as it is its nearest neighbor. One could say the same for compound intervals: such as the **Ninth**, which is accompanied by the **Tenth**, and the **Eleventh**, after which one must similarly place the **Tenth**, as can be seen in the examples.

Regarding Quarter notes <note>original: *Semiminime*; in this period, these are four to a whole note, similar to modern quarter notes.</note> that follow the beat of a Half note <note>original: *Minima battuta*</note>, or a <term>Whole note</term> <note>original: *Semibreue*</note> that is dotted or syncopated <note>original: *sincopata*; a note shifted so it begins on a weak beat and carries over to a strong beat.</note>, when their progression moves through <term>stepwise motion</term> <note>original: *Mouimenti congiunti*; moving to the very next note in the scale rather than leaping.</note> toward the lower part: in order that no confusion is created in the mind of the Composer, we shall now determine which of the two Quarter notes should be placed as the consonant one. Wherefore I say that, by all means, one must make the second note consonant, and not the first. This has been commonly used not only by good and learned Musicians, but by others as well, even though the first note falls on the "up" of the beat <note>original: *leuar la battuta*</note> (that is, in the second part of the beat). Truly, such a progression is nothing other than a tolerable <term>diminution</term> <note>original: *diminutione*; the breaking down of a long note into several faster notes.</note> of two Half notes a <term>Third</term> <note>original: *Terza*; an interval spanning three scale degrees.</note> apart, done for the sake of making the parts easy to sing, or for the convenience of fitting the harmonies to the words, which arise from the pronunciation of the figures or notes of the melody <note>original: *cantilena*</note>. When placed in such a manner, they are tolerable and pass well, because the slowness and delay of the first figure (the preceding note) and the speed of the following Quarter note—where the time, the sound, and the voice pass quickly together—ensure that the dissonance placed upon the said Quarter note is not easily perceived by the ear. Therefore, it is not held in any particular consideration by Musicians; and even if it is perceived, the immediately following note, which is consonant, fully settles the whole matter. When, therefore, after a Half note or a Whole note (with or without a dot) two Quarter notes follow one after the other in the manner described above, we shall always make the second one consonant, even if the first is dissonant. But when there are more than two, we may do otherwise; that is, we may make the first one consonant and the others afterward, as has been said above. Though in some cases the said first Quarter note, which is placed as a dissonance, can be placed as a consonance—especially when moving from an Octave to a Fifth, or vice-versa, proceeding by contrary motions in <term>diminished counterpoint</term> <note>original: *Contrapunti diminuiti*; florid counterpoint where one voice moves faster than the primary melody.</note>, as can be seen. I have said all this to remove confusion from the mind of the Composer: for it is not right that in this Science, which ordains and gives rules to every other, anything disordered should fall into the realm of Sounds; especially since it is not right that these Quarter notes should be placed one way by one group of Musicians and another way by others in the same passage. If, therefore, it happens that we must make such passages for ornament or necessity, we shall be careful to place them according to the determined method and in the manner seen in the example placed below.

## The Way the Composer Must Proceed in Making Counterpoints
## Over a Part, or a Diminished Subject. Chapter 43.

It will happen, besides this, that the counterpoint student—after having practiced for many days in making <term>counterpoint</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines according to established rules of harmony.</note> over a <term>plainchant subject</term><note>original: *Canto fermo*; a pre-existing, slow-moving melody, usually from the Gregorian tradition, used as a foundation.</note>, and knowing how to do so without any error—will wish to go further and come to another type of composition, also for two voices. Therefore, to become accustomed to <term>invention</term><note>The creative process of discovering or creating new musical themes.</note>, I say that it will not be out of place if he first takes as a **Subject** a part from any melody of <term>figured song</term><note>original: *Canto figurato*; music that uses varied rhythmic values (polyphony) rather than the equal notes of plainchant.</note>. If he does not wish to do that, he may compose it himself, according to what seems most suitable to him. This being done, I say that he may then, according to his own wit, compose another part in the **low range**, or, as it may better suit him, in the **high range**. It is certainly true that if he wishes to compose the **Subject** himself, he may compose both parts together, so that at the same time he creates the **Subject** and brings the melody to its end. This is because (as I have said elsewhere) I call the **Subject** that part which is placed before the other parts in the composition, or rather that part which the Composer first imagined. 

In this way, he will be able to compose with much greater ease the more he observes those **Rules** which he followed in making counterpoints over plainchant. It is true, however, that this method of composing is freer and more expeditious, because one can <term>diminish</term><note>original: *diminuire*; the technique of breaking down long notes into shorter, faster notes to create a more active melody.</note> whichever part one wishes, whether high or low; one may leave one of these parts with notes of somewhat longer value, or place similar or different rhythmic figures in both parts against each other—something that could not be done in the first method. The Composer may therefore do whatever is most convenient, taking care, however, always to arrange the parts of the melody so that they sing well and have a beautiful and elegant progression, with a certain something mixed with solemnity <note>original: *gravità*; a sense of dignity or weightiness appropriate for serious music.</note>.

And so that one may see the method to be held in composing such counterpoints or compositions (since one cannot give a particular **Rule** for everything, as individual cases are infinite), I will provide two examples. One of these will be founded upon a pre-existing **Subject**, which begins *We know we have deserved this crime of ours* <note>original Latin: *Scimus hoc nostrum meruisse crimen*</note>, which is the high part of a graceful two-voice composition by **Adrian** <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the influential Flemish composer and maestro di cappella at St. Mark's in Venice, who was Zarlino's teacher.</note>. The other will be composed entirely from the imagination. Thus, by seeing and examining these two and other similar compositions, one may easily and well come to the practice of composing.

## That it is not necessary for the Subject and Counterpoint parts to begin together. Chapter 44.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a bearded man sitting at a desk with a book, possibly a scholar or monk, framed by foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

**I WOULD NOT** want anyone to believe that there was so much (so to speak) **superstition** in Music that everyone was bound by an unbreakable law to begin their <term>Counterpoints</term><note>Counterpoint: the art of combining different melodic lines according to established rules.</note> in only one way; always making the <term>Subject</term><note>Subject (Soggetto): the primary melody upon which a composition is built.</note> part begin to sing together with the Counterpoint part, and that it was not permitted to use <term>Rests</term> at the beginning of whichever part one chooses. In truth, the use of Rests was not only invented for the decoration of the melody, but also out of necessity, as I shall discuss elsewhere. Therefore, when it is convenient to place them at the beginning of any part of the melody, one may do so without any error. One may place not only the Rests of a <term>Breve</term> or <term>Semibreve</term>, but those of a <term>Minim</term> as well. And doing so will not be without the precedent of Ancient and Modern composers, who took such liberty, seeing that it was very convenient for them.

Wishing, then, to begin Counterpoints in this manner, one must first have one of the two parts sing, starting at the beginning of the <term>Beat</term><note>original: *Battuta*; the basic unit of time or tactus in Renaissance music.</note>; the other part may then be made to sing by placing a Minim Rest—commonly called a **Sigh** (*Sospiro*)—at the beginning before the first singable note. After this rest, one may place whatever note value is convenient, provided its value does not exceed that of a Semibreve. This Semibreve, when placed after a Minim Rest, will necessarily become <term>syncopated</term><note>Syncopation occurs here because the note starts on an off-beat (after the minim rest) and continues across the next strong pulse.</note>. 

However, one must avoid starting both the Counterpoint and the Subject at the beginning of the Beat with notes of a value smaller than a <term>Semiminim</term><note>Semiminim: equivalent to a modern quarter note or crotchet.</note>, for this would cause the melody to begin with a very fast movement—indeed, an extremely fast one. When starting with a Semiminim, we should always place a Minim Rest before it. 

In this, as in all other things, we must truly imitate **Nature**, whose process is seen to be very regular. For if we observe natural movements, we will find that they are somewhat slower at their beginning than they are in the middle and at the end. This can be seen in a stone dropped from a height to the ground; its movement is undoubtedly faster at the end than it is at the beginning. We shall therefore imitate Nature and proceed in such a way that the movements made by the parts of the Counterpoint are not very fast at the beginning. We should observe this also in the middle and at the end of each part: when they begin to sing after Rests, their start should be with a note of some value, such as a Semibreve or another larger value. 

If we wish to proceed with somewhat faster movements, we should ensure that after that first note, another follows that is "closer" to it and of lesser value, such as a Minim, and after that, a Semiminim. I do not mean to say that after a Minim one cannot place two or more similar notes one after the other—for after one Semiminim one can place another, or even more, and likewise after a Minim—but I say that when wishing to move from a larger note to a smaller one, propriety demands that the following note be the one closest in value to the preceding one. 

Nor do I wish anyone to think that I set such a Rule as so strictly necessary that one cannot do otherwise; rather, what I have shown is to give a little light and judgment to the Composer. And because I said above that one should proceed from one singable note to another using its closest neighbor, it should be noted that some musicians skilled in a certain branch of theirs called <term>Quantitative</term> <note>Quantitative: refers to the system of proportions and relationships between different note values (mensuration).</note> divide singable notes into four differences. They call some **Proximate Parts** of another note, some **Remote Parts**, some **More Remote**, and some others **Most Remote**. 

Thus they say that a note is the **Proximate Part** (*Parte propinqua*) of another if it follows it directly in the order established above in Chapter 2. Therefore, it can be said that the Breve is the proximate part of the Long; the Semibreve is the proximate part of the Breve; the Minim of the Semibreve, and so on with the others that follow (though in this consideration they did not go beyond the Minim, as it is the last figure among those that undergo <term>alteration</term><note>Alteration: a rule in mensural notation where a note's value is doubled to fill out a rhythmic grouping.</note>, as I may show elsewhere). But when they skipped one intermediate note and took the next one, they called that note the **Remote Part** (*Parte remota*) of the first. Thus, it can truly be said that the Semibreve is the Remote Part of the Long, and the Minim is the remote part of the Breve, and so on in order. When they then skipped two intermediate notes, the one that followed the two skipped*

<meta>catchword: lassate, (skipped)</meta>

<summary>This chapter discusses the rhythmic flexibility of starting a composition, arguing that voices need not begin simultaneously and should follow the "natural" principle of starting with slower note values before accelerating.</summary>

omitted, they called it the **More Remote Part** of the first; as we might say of the <term>Minim</term><note>original: *Minima*; a note value half the length of a semibreve.</note> relative to the <term>Long</term>, and others as well. But when they omitted three, they called the following one the **Most Remote Part**; like the Minim relative to the <term>Maxima</term>. Returning now to our first point, I say that it is permitted for anyone to place two <term>Crotchets</term><note>original: *Semiminime*; note values half the length of a minim.</note> and even more after a <term>Minim Rest</term><note>original: *Sospiro*; literally a 'sigh', representing a rest equal to a minim.</note>; just as they can be placed after a Minim, because the rest is equal in value to the Minim, and each of these is its **near part**<note>original: *parte propinqua*; an immediate subdivision in the hierarchy of note values.</note>, even though such a rest or pause is not sung. But these Crotchets will not be so well suited after a <term>Semibreve rest</term> or after another larger rest, since they are **Remote Parts**. Nor will it be good to place many <term>Quavers</term><note>original: *Chrome*; note values half the length of a crotchet.</note> after a Minim rest. Placing two Crotchets after a dotted <term>Semibreve</term><note>A whole note.</note> or after a syncopated Semibreve will be lawful: because that part upon which the **Beat**<note>original: *Battuta*; the basic unit of time or "tactus" used to keep the singers together.</note> falls—which is upon the dot, or upon the second part of the syncopation—is considered separate from the other by the Beat; that is, it is taken as a separate Minim upon which the said Beat falls. It is not, however, praiseworthy (though few take care to avoid it) to place figures in such an order that after a Semibreve that is beaten without a dot, two or more Crotchets follow. This is because they are **Remote Parts** and not near parts of the Semibreve; anyone can understand for themselves how pleasant and convenient these are to singers when they hear the music proceed from one singable note to another with a sudden change from slow to fast time, without any other middle transition.

## That the Melodic Lines should be well-regulated, and what the Singer should observe in singing. Cap. 45.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'S' featuring scrolling floral and foliate motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

**IT WOULD BE** too difficult a task if I wished to discuss every minute thing that can occur in composing, and it would bring no small annoyance to the readers. Therefore, setting aside those things that are not so necessary, I will come to those of some importance, some of which pertain to the Composer and some to the Singer. Those that pertain to the Composer are these: First, he must compose his songs according to the rules given above, not departing from the precepts I am about to demonstrate further on. Then, he must apply all his study so that the <term>Counterpoint</term><note>The art of combining melodic lines according to established rules.</note>—that is, the parts of his song—are ordered and regulated in such a way that they can be sung easily and are without any difficulty. For if Harmony is born (as we saw in the Second Part) from the singing that the parts of the song do together without any offense to the ear, it can never be born from things that are without any proportion to each other. He shall therefore be careful to make the parts singable and ensure they proceed by true and legitimate intervals contained within the <term>Harmonic Numbers</term><note>original: *Numeri harmonici*; the numbers 1 through 6, which Zarlino believed were the source of all pure musical intervals.</note>, whether they be consonant or dissonant. Consonant, I say, such as the Octave, Fifth, Fourth, Third, and other similar ones; as are those of the Tenth as well, which will be done without any error, since the master of the ancient musicians, <term>Josquin</term><note>original: *Iosquino*; referring to Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), a highly influential composer of the Renaissance.</note>, not only used such an interval but even used that of the Twelfth, as can be seen in the <term>Motet</term><note>A polyphonic vocal composition.</note> for five voices, *Inviolata, integra, et casta es Maria*<note>original Latin: "Unviolated, whole, and chaste are you, Mary," a well-known hymn to the Virgin Mary.</note>. Dissonant as well, such as those of the Major Semitone and those of the Tone, which are the differences by which one consonance exceeds another, as I showed in Chapter 39 of the Second Part. It is true that sometimes the Seventh and Ninth are placed, although rarely, as some good composers have used and still use. But those of the <term>Tritone</term><note>An interval of three whole tones, considered very harsh (the "devil in music").</note>, the <term>Semidiapente</term><note>A diminished fifth.</note>, and other similar intervals should not be used, as some Moderns have done, wishing to attribute this to the progression of <term>Chromatic</term> modulations. Truly, these intervals do not have their forms contained within the Harmonic Numbers. Therefore, it is not possible for them to produce any good effect in the melodic lines; rather, they can greatly offend the senses, as experience shows us. And if Music (as <term>Augustine</term><note>St. Augustine of Hippo, who wrote an influential treatise on music in the 4th century.</note> defines it) is the "Science of singing well or modulating well," and attends to nothing else but this, in what manner can a song be placed among the number of those that observe and tend toward this goal, if it
