<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 45 of the Third Part, transitioning from the duties of the composer to the responsibilities of the singer in performing a musical work accurately and gracefully.</meta>

<page-num>204</page-num>
<header>Third</header>

will have its <term>modulations</term><note>In this context, the melodic movement or "turning" of the musical lines.</note> full of similar errors, and will be so disordered that one could hardly bear to see it, let alone sing it? Regarding this, one should also seek what was said in Chapter 37: namely, that the parts should proceed, as much as possible, through <term>conjunct movements</term><note>Moving by step to the next adjacent note in the scale, rather than leaping.</note>, for these are more natural than those that are separated by leaps. The composer shall therefore strive to make the parts of his <term>cantilena</term><note>A general term for a vocal melody or musical composition.</note> singable, good, and easy, proceeding with beautiful, graceful, and elegant movements, so that the listeners may take delight in such melodies and not be offended in any way.

Those things that pertain to the singer are as follows: First, he must provide every diligence in his singing to deliver the melody in the way it was composed by the composer. He must not do as some ill-advised people do, who, to make themselves appear more capable and wiser than the others, sometimes devise wild <term>diminutions</term><note>original: *diminutioni*; the practice of breaking a long note into many fast, decorative notes; also known as "divisions."</note> (if I may call them that) of their own head. These are so out of place that they not only annoy those who listen to them but also commit a thousand errors in singing. At times, they produce many <term>discords</term> along with two or more <term>unisons</term>, two <term>octaves</term>, or even two <term>fifths</term>, and other similar things that are undoubtedly not tolerated in compositions.

Then there are some who, in their singing, sometimes make a voice higher or lower than it ought to be—something the composer never intended—such as singing a <term>tone</term><note>A whole step.</note> instead of a <term>semitone</term><note>A half step.</note>, or the reverse, and other similar things. From this follows infinite errors, besides the offense to the senses. Singers must, therefore, be careful to sing correctly those things that are written according to the mind of the composer, intoning the voices well and placing them in their proper locations, seeking to accommodate them to the <term>consonance</term><note>A combination of notes that sounds pleasant and stable.</note>. They must sing according to the nature of the words contained in the composition: when the words contain cheerful matters, they must sing cheerfully and with vigorous movements; and when they contain sad matters, they must change their approach.

But above all (so that the words of the melody may be understood), they must guard against an error found among many: that is, not changing the vowel letters of the words, such as uttering A in place of E, or I in place of O, or U in place of one of the others. They must instead utter them according to their true pronunciation. It is truly a shameful thing, worthy of a thousand reprimands, to sometimes hear some clumsy people singing in choirs and public chapels, as well as in private chambers, and uttering corrupted words when they ought to utter them clearly, expeditiously, and without any error.

I say that if (for the sake of example) we sometimes hear some people screeching (I will not say singing) with very graceless voices and with such counterfeited acts and manners that they truly seem like monkeys, performing some song and saying: "Harsh face, and savage, and crude value"<note>original: "Aspra cara, e saluaggia e croda uaglia"; a garbled mispronunciation.</note>, when they should say: "Harsh heart, and savage, and cruel desire"<note>original: "Aspro core, e seluaggio, e cruda voglia"; a famous line by the poet Petrarch.</note>—who would not laugh? Or rather (to put it better), who would not fly into a rage, hearing a thing so distorted, so ugly, and so horrid?

The singer, therefore, must not send out his voice with impetus and fury like a beast, but must sing with a moderate voice and proportion it with those of the other singers, in such a way that he does not overpower the others or prevent their voices from being heard. In such cases, one hears a noise rather than <term>harmony</term>, for harmony is born of nothing other than the tempering of many things placed together in such a way that one does not overpower the other.

Singers shall also take this advice: one sings in one way in churches and public chapels, and in another way in private chambers. In the former, one sings with a full voice (though only in the manner described above), but in chambers, one sings with a more subdued and sweet voice, without making any noise. Therefore, when they sing in such places, they should proceed with judgment, lest they be deservedly blamed for doing otherwise. Besides this, they must observe not to sing with movements of the body, nor with such acts or gestures that incite laughter in those who see and hear them, as some do who move in such a fashion—even some instrumentalists do this—that they truly seem to be dancing.

But leaving that matter aside for now, I say that if the composer and the singers together observe those things that pertain to their office, there is no doubt that every <term>cantilena</term> will be delightful, sweet, suave, and full of good harmony, and will bring grateful and sweet pleasure to the listeners.

### That one should not continue for too long in the low or the high register in melodic movements. Chapter 46.

And because it sometimes happens that continuing a part of the <term>cantilena</term><note>A general term for a vocal melody or musical composition.</note> for some time in the **low** register, or in the **high**, is the reason that the **singer** tires; especially when they have a **low** voice and remain long in the **high** register, or when they have a **high** voice and are forced to stay in the **low**. For as the voice becomes weak and begins to drop if it is in the **high** register, or to rise if it is found in the **low**, it ends up creating much dissonance. Therefore, I would wish (to remove such inconvenience and disorder) that the **contrapuntist** take heed of this matter, and that he arrange the melody in such a way that the parts do not sing for a long time in the **low** register, nor stay very long in the **high**. But every time they ascend or descend, they should not be placed in such a manner without a purpose, and should not dwell for long in these two extremes. I have said "not without purpose" because modern **composers** have the custom (which is not to be blamed) that when the words denote **grave**, **low**, **deep** things, **descent**, **fear**, **weeping**, **tears**, and other similar things, they make their <term>modulations</term><note>The melodic movement or "turning" of the musical lines.</note> continue somewhat in the **low** register. But when they signify **height**, **sharpness**, **ascent**, **joy**, **laughter**, and other such things, they make them modulate in the **high** register. It is indeed true that they must not make the harmony continue for long in such extremes; rather, they must ensure that the modulations touch the **low** <term>strings</term><note>original: *chorde*; here referring to the specific pitches or notes of the musical scale.</note>, and also the **high** ones, along with the middle notes of the parts of the melody, always varying the movements. Nor should he allow the extremities of the parts to pass into the **low** or **high** registers beyond their boundaries, against their nature and against the nature of the **Mode** upon which the melody is founded; that is, he must not let the **Soprano** take the place of the **Tenor**, nor the latter the place of the **Soprano**. Instead, he must ensure that each part stays within its limits, as we shall see in the Fourth Part when we speak about the method to be held in arranging the parts. Although in some cases this is permitted for a short space of time, by ordering them so they do not exceed their boundaries, nothing can follow but great convenience for the singer and the birth of good and perfect harmonies.

### That placing a Dissonance or a Minim Rest between two perfect Consonances of the same species, which ascend or descend together, does not mean that such consonances are not repeated. Chapter 47.

Some **usually** consider it no inconvenience to place two **perfect consonances** of one and the same species one after the other in their compositions, which ascend or descend together without any other consonance placed between them; for they believe that placing a ***Dissonance*** or a ***Minim Rest***<note>A short silence equal to a half-note in modern notation.</note> between them causes the species to vary, and that because of this, they do not go against the Rule set down above in Chapter 29. But in truth, how much these men deceive themselves anyone can know through experience itself, after they have heard what is contained in the examples below. For they will realize that the ***Dissonance*** placed between two perfect consonances makes no variation in the harmony; nor does it prevent such consonances from being placed one after the other without any [real] mediation, since consonances are considered by the musician for their own sake, and dissonances only by accident, as I have said elsewhere. And if the ***Dissonance***, which is a sound, placed between the said consonances has no power to make any variation, even less will the ***Minim Rest*** have such power, as it represents no sound, but rather silence and privation. It shall therefore not be permitted to place two ***Octaves*** one after the other, separated only by a ***Seventh*** or a ***Ninth***; nor two ***Unisons*** separated by a ***Second***. And although the ***Fourth*** and the ***Sixth*** are consonances (as was determined) and one might say that one or the other placed between two ***Fifths*** makes some variation in the harmony, nevertheless they should not be used except in compositions of many voices. For in simple [two-voice] compositions they generate I know not what kind of "sadness" [or poor quality], as can be heard in the examples below.

*Composers also occasionally tend, in a small section of the composition—after an **Octave** placed above a <term>Semibreve</term><note>The primary unit of time in Renaissance notation, roughly equivalent to a whole note.</note> that descends and has a <term>Minim</term><note>Equivalent to a half note.</note> above or below it—to immediately place two **Semiminims** <note>Equivalent to quarter notes.</note> which descend by <term>conjunct movements</term><note>Stepwise motion, such as moving from C to B.</note>. The first of these was stated above in chapter 42; and the second is that because of the swift change made by the **Sixth** or the **Tenth** placed between them, or because of the fast movement they make, they are **almost not heard**. This is especially true since, in the two semiminims that follow the minim or the <term>syncopated</term><note>A rhythmic technique where a note is held over from a weak beat to a strong beat, often creating a suspension.</note> **Semibreve**, the first is placed among the **Dissonances** and the second among the **Consonances**. Thus, such **Octaves** are heard more prominently, and one ends up acting against what was determined above in chapter 41: that they should not be used very often when arranged in such a manner in **Counterpoint**. ## On the Beat. Chapter 48.

Having used these terms **Beat**, **Syncopation**, and **Rest** several times, it is reasonable, before we go further, that we see what they are; so that we do not proceed using unknown terms, which truly cannot bring any knowledge. Therefore we must know that musicians, seeing that due to the diversity of movements that the parts of the <term>composition</term> <note>original: "cantilena"</note> make while singing together—one being faster or slower than the other—ordered a certain **Sign** by which each singer would be guided in uttering the voice with a measure of fast or slow time, according to what is shown by the various singable figures placed above in Chapter 2. And they imagined that it would be good if such a sign were made with the hand, so that every singer could see it and be regulated in its movement in the manner of the human **Pulse**. Hence, after giving such an order, some called this sign **Beat** <note>original: "Battuta"</note>, others **Sounding Time** <note>original: "Tempo sonoro"</note>; and others, such as the most holy doctor **Augustine** in Chapter 10 of the second book of *Music*, names it with the Latin word **Rhythmic Clapping** <note>original: "Plauso", from "Plaudo", meaning the clapping of hands or feet to mark time.</note>. And truly it seems to me that they thought well: for I do not see what movement we could find made naturally that could give them a rule and proportion besides this one. For if we consider the qualities found in both—that is, in the **Beat** and in the **Pulse**, which by the Greeks is called **sphygmos** <note>original: "σφυγμός"</note>—we will find many similarities between them: since the **Pulse** (as defined by **Galen** and **Paul of Aegina**) is a certain expansion and contraction, or let us say rising and falling of the heart and arteries, it comes to be composed (as **Avicenna** holds in the second *Fen* of Book 1) of two movements and two rests. The **Beat** is similarly composed of these things; and first of two movements, which are the **Downward Placement** <note>original: "Positione"</note> and the **Raising** <note>original: "Leuatione"</note> made with the hand, in which are found the expansion and contraction, or the rising and falling mentioned, which are two contrary movements; and then two rests: for (according to the mind of **Aristotle**) between these movements (as I also mentioned in Chapter 42 above) they are always found, especially because it is impossible that similar movements could be continued one with the other. And just as **Medicine** calls the first movement **systole** <note>original: "συστολή", meaning contraction.</note> and the second **diastole** <note>original: "διαστολή", meaning expansion.</note>, so **Music** names the **Downward Placement**, or the **Beat**, **thesis** <note>original: "θέσις"</note>, and the **Raising**, **arsis** <note>original: "ἄρσις"</note>. Similarly, just as the **Pulse** is found in two ways, according to the authority of the mentioned princes of Medicine—that is, **Equal** and **Unequal**—taking only that equality and inequality that arises from speed and slowness, from which **Rhythm**,

<meta>This page continues the discussion on musical proportions, moving from the avoidance of parallel intervals to a formal definition of the "Beat" (Tactus) and how it relates to both modern musical notation and ancient poetic meters.</meta>

# Third Part

From **Rhythm**, which gives rise to many proportioned movements contained within the <term>Multiple</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number is a multiple of the smaller, such as 2:1 or 3:1.</note> and <term>Superparticular</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one part, such as 3:2 or 4:3.</note> genres—aside from others that are omitted because they do not fall under these categories—we can say that the **Beat** is found in two manners: **Equal** and **Unequal**, to which every proportioned movement made with the voice is reduced. I say this because the ancient musicians, and the poets as well (who were once, as I have said elsewhere, considered one and the same), by a certain natural instinct of theirs, divided voices into two parts. They attributed a **Short Time** to some and a **Long Time** to others; and to the **Long Time** they applied two **Short Times**. They placed the syllables or voices of Short Time, which are of lesser quantity, in the first position, and those of Long Time, which are of greater quantity, in the second position, as is proper; for just as Unity among numbers comes before the Binary (which contains two units), so the Short Time should hold the first place and the Long the second. But it must be noted that they considered the **Beat** in two parts, and they attributed the measure of either a Short or Long time to both the first and second parts, as it was most convenient for them.

It is true that the Moderns primarily applied to the Beat sometimes the <term>imperfect Breve</term> and sometimes the <term>imperfect Semibreve</term> <note>These are standard rhythmic units of the 16th century; the Breve is the longer, the Semibreve the shorter.</note>, making them equal to the timing of the **human pulse**, divided into two equal movements. Thus, such a Beat can truly be called **Equal**, since one finds the proportion of Equality between the **Downbeat** <note>original: *Positione*</note> and the **Upbeat** <note>original: *Leuatione*</note>; for the Long Time, or indeed the Short, is attributed equally to both the lowering and the raising of the hand.

Later, they applied sometimes the Breve with the Semibreve, and sometimes the Semibreve with the <term>Minim</term>, and divided it into two unequal movements, applying the Long Time to the **Downbeat** and the Short Time to the **Upbeat**, placing them in a <term>Duple proportion</term> <note>A 2:1 ratio.</note>. And because the proportion of Inequality falls between the Downbeat and the Upbeat, such a Beat can truthfully be called **Unequal**.

Having this regard, when these musicians intended an **Equal Beat**, they marked their compositions at the beginning with these signs <note>original symbols: a circle ○ and a semicircle C</note>, or with these <note>original symbols: a circle with a vertical line and a semicircle with a vertical line 𝇉</note>. And when they intended the **Unequal Beat**, they marked them with these <note>original symbols: a dotted circle and a dotted semicircle</note>, or indeed with these <note>original symbols: a dotted circle and dotted semicircle with vertical lines</note>. And if at times they did not wish to mark the Unequal Beat with these, they placed the numeral for three over the numeral for two in this manner: $\frac{3}{2}$, accompanying them with the Sign of Time placed before them. They called such numbers **Sesquialtera** <note>Latin: "one and a half," representing a 3:2 ratio.</note>, and perhaps not without reason. 

For these can be considered in four ways: 
1. First, when they are placed at the beginning of all the parts of the song; and then the **Unequal Beat** is used. 
2. Second, when they are likewise placed at the beginning, but not in all the parts; whereby each part is regulated under the **Equal Beat**. 
3. Third, when they are placed in the middle of the song in every part, and the **Unequal Beat** is likewise used. 
4. And fourth, when they are placed in the middle of only some parts, and the parts are similarly regulated by the **Equal Beat**. 

Thus, such numerals can signify two things: first (as is the opinion of the Moderns), that by having regard to the Sign of Time, one places the **Unequal Measure** against the **Equal**, that is, three Long or Short times against two. Furthermore, they signify that within the entire Beat are contained three Long or Short times (whichever they may be), of which two are placed on the **Downbeat** and one on the **Upbeat**, especially when no other numerical figures occur that denote some proportion in the figures or notes of the song, as some musicians used to do. Once the Beat is understood in this manner, it removes many difficulties that can occur for composers and singers alike.

We can now see from what has been said that the **Beat** is nothing other than a sign made by the musician, either equally or unequally according to some proportion, with the lowering and the raising of the hand, in imitation of the **human pulse**. Since the Beat is therefore of two kinds, as we have seen, both the Musician and the Poet can accommodate the measure of time for each foot of a verse within them. 

For in the **Equal Beat**, they can accommodate the **Pyrrhic** <note>A poetic foot of two short syllables ($ \smile \smile $).</note>, which is a foot composed of two short syllables, which poets usually mark with these signs $\smile \smile$. Thus, musicians usually mark their times, which are two short times, with two equal figures like these: <note>musical staff with two brevis notes under a horizontal bracket</note>, or others similar. For the Poet considers only whether the syllable is **Long**, which he marks with this sign <note>horizontal line segment —</note>, or whether it is **Short**, which he notes with this other one <note>curved breve symbol ◡</note>; and the Musician considers the Long or Short time, and marks it with one of the eight singable figures, as best suits him. They can also accommodate the **Spondee** <note>A poetic foot of two long syllables ($ - - $).</note>, which they mark with these two <note>two horizontal line segments — —</note> denoting two long syllables, or with these <note>musical staff with two long notes under horizontal brackets</note> which signify the two long times of which it is composed. They can similarly accommodate the **Dactyl** <note>A poetic foot of one long and two short syllables ($ - \smile \smile $).</note>, which contains one long syllable and two short ones, in this manner $- \smile \smile$; or it contains one long time and two short ones, in this manner <note>musical staff with one long note and two shorter notes under brackets</note>. Similarly, they can accommodate the **Anapest** <note>A poetic foot of two short syllables and one long ($ \smile \smile - $).</note> in this way $\smile \smile -$, or indeed <note>musical staff with two short notes and one long note under brackets</note>.

But let this be said sufficiently regarding the Beat.

## On Syncopation. Chapter 49.

<image-desc>Large woodcut ornamental initial 'L' depicting a landscape within a square frame.</image-desc> **SYNCopation** truly cannot be understood by the Musician without knowledge of the Beat, wherefore it was appropriate that we first discussed the beat, as it is very necessary for its understanding, and then declare what this name "Syncopation" signifies. But it must be known that Syncopation is not considered by the Musician as the Grammarian considers it, who maintains that it is a figure of diction, or of a word—as we might say—which occurs when a letter or syllable is cut or removed from the middle; as is done when, for the sake of the verse's meter, in place of putting **boldly** <note>original: "Audaciter"</note>, one puts **boldly** <note>original: "Audacter" - a shortened form.</note>; or needing to say **he sold** <note>original: "Vendidit"</note>, one says **he sells** <note>original: "Vendit"</note> <note>The author is comparing the grammatical shortening of words to the rhythmic displacement in music.</note>: but [the musician] considers it as the **transportation** or **reduction** of some figure, or minor singable note, beyond one or more larger notes to its similar; where it can conveniently be applied and counted to complete the number of the measure of its Time. And this happens not only in <term>Perfect Time</term> <note>original: "Tempo perfetto" - triple meter.</note>, understood by the full circle $\bigcirc$, or the cut circle <image-desc>Musical time signature: a circle with a vertical slash.</image-desc>, which is completed by the number three; but also in the <term>Imperfect Time</term> <note>original: "imperfetto" - duple meter.</note>, which is understood by the full half-circle $\text{C}$, or the cut half-circle <image-desc>Musical time signature: a capital C with a vertical slash.</image-desc>, completed in the number two: because Time (as we shall see in its place) is of two sorts among Musicians. Hence that figure or note is called **Syncopated**, or is said to make a **Syncopation**, when it begins on the "elevation" of the beat <note>The upbeat.</note>, and is also subjected to the "position" <note>The downbeat.</note>; nor can it ever fall, as its nature dictates, on the position, until it finds a smaller figure, or other figures that are equal to it in value, with which it may be joined and return to where the beat had its beginning. For which it should be noted (to give an example) that the proper nature of the **Semibreve** is to fall and be sung together in Perfect Time, and in Imperfect Time also at the start of the beat—that is, under these two signs $\bigcirc$ and $\text{C}$—and the **Breve** under this other <image-desc>Musical time signature: a capital C with a vertical slash.</image-desc>: But if it happens that one or the other is sung or uttered on the rising of the beat, such a figure or note is called a **Syncopation**, or **Syncopated**; as is seen in the two examples placed here below.

*Because this breaks the <term>Measure</term><note>original: "Misura" — the regular pulse or tactus that governs the music.</note> and the Time, which naturally falls upon the beginning of each note under their proper signs, as I will show elsewhere; it also creates inconvenience for the Singers. These inconveniences, therefore, must be avoided in every way: because they were never tolerated by good and discerning Musicians; as can be seen in the compositions of <term>Ockeghem</term><note>Johannes Ockeghem (c. 1410–1497), a highly influential Franco-Flemish composer.</note>, of <term>Josquin</term><note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), perhaps the most famous composer of the High Renaissance.</note>, of <term>Mouton</term><note>original: "Morone" — likely referring to Jean Mouton (c. 1459–1522), a master of polyphony.</note>, and others more Ancient than they; provided they have not been corrupted by some ignorant scribe. ## Of Rests. Chapter 50.

Just as the notes of a <term>song</term><note>original: "cantilena" — a general term for a musical composition or melody.</note> are positive figures or signs, because they represent the voices or sounds from which harmonies are born, and their variety represents the fast or slow movement of the <term>Time</term><note>In this context, "Time" refers to the rhythmic duration or measurement of the music.</note> that the voice is held; so too are Rests called "privative" figures. This is because they are an indication of quiet or silence, representing the time one must remain silent, which is discerned by their different shapes. These are signs made by the Musician with certain lines that fall perpendicularly across one or more of the five shown parallel lines, drawn differently according to the will of the Composer. And there are as many types as there are singable figures, minus two, beginning from the <term>Lunga</term><note>The "Long," a very large note value in Renaissance notation.</note> and leaving out the <term>Maxima</term><note>The largest possible note value; its rest was usually indicated by doubling the Lunga rest.</note>; for in its place, one uses a doubled Lunga rest. The <term>Semichroma</term><note>A very short note value, equivalent to a modern sixteenth note.</note> rest is also left out, because being of such minimal value, it is not used. Rests have the same value and are called by the same name as the figure or note they represent. These Rests, when placed under the sign of <term>Perfect Time</term><note>Triple meter, often symbolized by a circle.</note> or <term>Imperfect Time</term><note>Duple meter, often symbolized by a half-circle.</note>, whichever it may be, never span more than three of the aforementioned lines, as can be seen here below.

->Of the Lunga. Of the Breve. Of the Semibreve. Of the Minim. Of the Crotchet. Of the Quaver.<-

<image-desc>A musical staff with five horizontal lines showing different vertical bars representing musical rests (pause). The "Di Lunga" rest spans three spaces; "Di Breue" spans two; "Di Semibreue" hangs from a line into one space; "Di Minima" sits on a line; "Di Semiminima" and "Di Chroma" are represented by vertical strokes with flags/hooks at the top.</image-desc>

It is quite true that sometimes they reach the fourth line, but such Rests are called "Rests of <term>Mode</term><note>A higher level of rhythmic organization in mensural notation concerning the relationship between the largest note values.</note>," as we shall see in the proper place. Rests were invented to the great benefit of both the Composer and the Singer for two reasons: one for Necessity, and the other for the Ornamentation of songs. First, for necessity: because it was impossible for Singers to reach the end of a song from the beginning without ever resting, except with great discomfort; indeed, they truly could not have endured it. Therefore, perhaps remembering what is said by Ovid in his *Heroides* <note>original: "amorose Epistole"</note>:

> *That which lacks alternate rest is not durable;* <note>original: "Quod caret alterna requie, durabile non est"</note>

they found the opportune remedy. Thus, one can truly say of the Rest that which follows:

> *This restores strength and relieves weary limbs.* <note>original: "Haec reparat vires, fessáque membra leuat"</note>

Rests were also invented for ornamentation: because by means of them, the parts can be placed one after the other in <term>fugue</term><note>The technique of one voice imitating another, entering at different times.</note> or consequence, as we shall see. This method makes the song not only ingenious but also delightful. For singing continuously, as when all the parts of a song perform together, generates boredom not only for the singers but also induces satiety in the listeners. Making the parts fall silent at certain times with a specific purpose—that is, having now two, now three, now four voices sing, and sometimes (if the composition is for many voices) all <unclear>together</unclear>, <unclear>especially</unclear> at the end, since it is necessary that all parts sing together and finish together—ensures that compositions, through such variety, turn out more charming and delightful. Thus they found a sign to represent this quiet or silence, used it for the thing it signifies, and named it a Rest. Which, because of its function, they said was a certain "artful intermission of the voice." And they rightly said "artful intermission," wanting to warn us that we should not place Rests in songs without purpose or without skill, but should arrange them in such a way that it is clear that necessity and art required them. For just as it is a faulty thing for someone to speak always and not know how to put an end or limit to their speaking, so it is a faulty thing for the Musician who does not know how to give rest to the parts of their composition at the right time and place. Thus, just as there is virtue in knowing how to reason and how to be silent with purpose, so too it is not without virtue for a Musician to know how to make the parts of their song silent or sing at the right time and place. But one must note that where it happens that many Rests are placed which exceed the value of the Lunga, then this must be doubled, as would happen when one wishes to mark the Rest of the Maxima. But when one wishes to double the Rests representing the Maxima itself, or place them near other smaller rests, then one may place those that are added across the other lines, as seen in this example placed below.

<header>Third Part</header>

<image-desc>Musical notation showing rests of various durations on a five-line staff: a four-space long rest, a two-space breve rest, a semibreve rest (hanging), a minim rest (sitting), a crotchet rest (hooked), and a quaver rest (double hooked).</image-desc>

There have been various opinions regarding this name, **Rest** <note>original: "Pausa"</note>: for some have held the opinion that the **Rest** was named from the Greek word "to cease" <note>original: "παῦσαι" (pausai)</note>, which means to stop, to settle, or to leave off. Others have wanted it to be so named from the clapping of hands, which by the Latins is called **clapping** <note>original: "Plauso"</note>: since it is measured by the downbeat and the upbeat of the <term>tactus</term><note>The "beat" or steady hand motion used to keep time in Renaissance music.</note>, which is known by the sign formed by the hand, as we have seen above. And perhaps it was not called by either of these two ways in the beginning; but rather (as it seems to some) from the French word **pose** <note>original: "Posa"</note>, which means a "rested position." Thus one usually says one rest, two rests, and so on; that is, one pose, two poses, and so forth. But let it be named from whatever you like, this matters little; provided that one knows that when the composer places **Rests** in the <term>song</term><note>original: "cantilena" — a general term for a musical composition.</note>, he intends for the singer to be silent for as much space of time as the value of the **Rests** signifies. Churchmen also place **Rests** in their chants, not indeed for ornament, but out of necessity: because it is impossible to reach the end of such songs without taking some rest; therefore, being aware of this, they devised a sign by which every singer is warned that, upon arriving there, he must stop and take **breath** <note>original: "Spirito"</note>. For such an effect, they called it **breath** <note>original: "πνεῦμα" (pneuma)</note>, which means spirit. They also placed such a sign so that all the singers might stop together in harmony, wherefore they called it a **nod** <note>original: "νεῦμα" (neuma)</note>, which means a sign or consensus. It is quite true that they do not place such **Rests** in the manner shown above: for they place them in a way that they gird and embrace all the lines of the song; sometimes placing them single, and sometimes doubled; as they are seen here.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing a single vertical bar line and a double vertical bar line, both spanning the entire height of the staff from the first to the fifth line.</image-desc>

And one must by all means observe what many of the Ancients have already observed; that is, not to place such **Rests** except at the end of **clauses** <note>original: "Clauſule" — musical cadences or grammatical phrases.</note>, or the points of the **sentence** <note>original: "Oratione"</note> upon which the song is composed, and similarly at the end of every period. This is something that Composers must also be mindful of; so that the members of the sentence are divided, and the meaning of the words may be heard and understood entirely: for by doing so in this way, one can then say that the **Rests** have been placed in the parts of the song with some purpose, and not by chance. Nor should they be placed in any way before the sentence is finished, that is, in the middle of a **clause**: for he who would place them in such a way would truly show himself to be a sheep, a dunce, and an ignoramus. Therefore, the Musician shall strive not to fall into such errors, so as not to give the learned a bad opinion of himself—a thing which ought to be highly prized and preferred above all else.

### Of Fugues, or Consequences, or "Reditte," as we wish to call them. Chapter 51.

And although, by observing the rules given above, nothing would be found in the compositions worthy of reproach—being purged of every error and polished, and hearing in them nothing but good and sweet harmony—there would nonetheless be lacking a "certain something" of beauty, grace, and elegance, if one did not hear that which is now known by everyone, being much used and frequented by Musicians in their compositions; namely, that proceeding which the parts sometimes make one after the other, called a **Fugue** <note>original: "Fuga" — literally "flight," where one voice "flees" and the other chases.</note> or **Consequence**, which some also call a **Reditta** <note>original: "Reditta" — a return or repetition.</note>, which signify the same thing. And it is a certain **Repetition** of several notes in the song, or the repetition of the entire melody contained in one part, made by another after some time, singing and proceeding through the same singable figures; or through different ones, and through the same intervals of whole tones and semitones, and other similar ones. This **Consequence** is made in many ways; for either one part responds to, or (to put it better) follows the other at the **Unison**, that is, singing in that same voice; or else at a **Fourth**, or a **Fifth**, or an **Octave**. And this manner of singing is not only delightful, but in itself contains elegance and artifice; all the more so when it proceeds with a beautiful and regulated order.

<header>Third Part</header>

…and regulated <term>counterpoint</term><note>A style of composition where two or more independent melodic lines are combined according to specific rules.</note>. In this manner of composing, it is customary to have one part follow the other, sometimes making a <term>Minim</term> rest <note>The equivalent of a half note in modern notation.</note>, sometimes a <term>Semibreve</term> <note>The equivalent of a whole note.</note>, and occasionally a Semibreve and a Minim together; and likewise those of a <term>Breve</term> <note>A double whole note.</note>, and of three Semibreves, and sometimes one of a <term>Long</term> <note>A very long note value, typically equal to two or three Breves.</note>, according to the will of the composer. This manner is used not only in counterpoints made over the <term>cantus firmus</term><note>original: "Canto fermo" — a pre-existing melody, usually from plainchant, used as the foundation for a polyphonic work.</note>, but it is also used in each part of the <term>diminished</term> ones <note>Counterpoint that uses faster, decorative notes (diminutions) against a slower melody.</note>; and it is used more in these than in those, because the composer finds himself freer and has a greater and wider field to work in. There are, however, two types of <term>Fugues</term> or <term>Consequences</term><note>General terms for musical imitation; in this era, "Fugue" referred to any imitation, while "Consequence" often implied a strict canon.</note>; that is, **Bound** <note>original: "Legate"</note> and **Free** <note>original: "Sciolte"</note>.

The first are those found ordered in such a way that the same <term>melody</term><note>original: "modulatione"</note> performed by one part of the <term>harmony</term><note>original: "concento"</note> is also sung by another; hence composers are accustomed to write the parts in a single line <note>This refers to a canon where two voices read from the same written melody but start at different times.</note>. It is necessary, however, to observe that in those parts which sing in this way, one must place not only the musical notes in a single way, but the rests as well, when they occur, and every other accidental; even if one of the parts should double the melody or the figures while singing, as is sometimes customary.

But **Free Fugues** or **Consequences** are found among those parts that do not sing with such obligations, but only one of them proceeds in Fugue or Consequence for a certain number of notes found in another part; the rest of the notes are then not subject to such a law. And in this mode of composing, the composer is not obliged to observe the equality of the figures, or to place similar rests, nor to observe other similar accidents; but he can do what most pleases him, such as having one part proceed by Minims and the other proceed by other figures, namely by Semibreves, and similarly by Minims and <term>Semiminims</term><note>The equivalent of a modern quarter note.</note> mixed together, as is observed in counterpoints made over the cantus firmus. 

It should be noted, however, that the part which begins the Fugue—whether bound or free—is called the **Guide** <note>original: "Guida"</note>, and the one that follows is called the **Follower** <note>original: "Consequente"</note>. And because those Fugues that are distant from one another by the space or time of a Minim rest, or a Semibreve, and some others as well, are more intelligible due to their proximity—because they are easily understood by the senses—musicians therefore strove to make the parts of their <term>songs</term><note>original: "cantilene" — a general term for a musical composition.</note> as close in the Fugue or Consequence as possible. But the excessive continuation of such proximity caused a fall into a certain common way of composing, so that at present there is almost no Fugue found that has not been used a thousand thousands of times by various composers. Therefore, so that some variety may be heard in our songs, we shall strive to use more than...

->SUBJECT.<-

...rarely [use] **Fugues** so close and joined; and we will distance ourselves somewhat from those **Consequences** that are so common. We will seek with all our power to create Fugues that are more original: for when we make the **Guide** and the **Consequent** <note>The "Guide" (Guida) is the leading voice, and the "Consequent" (Consequente) is the following voice in a canon.</note> somewhat distant from each other—by three **Minim** rests, or five, or other similar intervals—we will undoubtedly come to create some new variation. I do not mean to say that Consequences separated by a single Minim rest or a **Semibreve** <note>A Semibreve is equivalent to a modern whole note; a Minim is a half note.</note> should never be used, but I say they should not be used very often; this is to avoid falling into those Fugues which are so common that one cannot find a book in which they are not replicated many, many times. I omit showing these to avoid being tedious and to avoid offending anyone. 

But so that some fruit may be gathered from what I have said, I have first placed above the example of those called **Free** <note>original: "Sciolte" — these are imitative passages where the following voice does not have to follow the leader exactly until the end.</note>, which are made over the **plainchants** <note>original: "canti fermi"</note> in imitation of them. Regarding the Free fugues found between two diminished parts, one can find two suitable examples placed above in Chapter 43. In those Fugues then, which are called **Bound** <note>original: "Legate" — today known as strict canons, where the imitation must be exact.</note>, one must observe this: that they be placed with one another in Consequence at the **Unison**, or at the **Fourth**, or at the **Fifth**, or indeed at the **Octave**; starting from whichever part one wishes, whether the low or the high, for this matters little. 

And that part which one begins to compose first shall be the **Guide**; and that which is composed afterward with the same figures and every other property shall be the **Consequent**. Whereupon, when the whole is finished, as is seen here, one will take the part that begins to sing—that is, the Guide—and write it out in full; 

<image-desc>Musical notation in white mensural style. Two staves are shown. The first staff is labeled 'GUIDE.' and contains a melody starting with several semi-breves and minims. The second staff is labeled 'CONSEQUENT.' and contains the same melody shifted in time and pitch.</image-desc>

and where the Consequent is to begin singing—that is, over the note placed in the Guide—one will place a sign like this: <insert>$\dot{\int}$</insert> <note>Signum congruentiae or Presa</note>, which is called by musicians the **Presa** <note>A "catch" or starting mark indicating where the second voice enters.</note>. And at the end, where it is to stop, the Guide's part is marked with the said sign, or with this <insert>$\dot{\cap}$</insert> <note>Coronata or fermata</note>, placing it over the final note where the Consequent must stop; and such a sign they call the **Coronata** <note>Crowned sign, commonly known today as a fermata.</note>. 

This being done, to give notice of the manner in which the parts are to be sung, a **Rule** is placed over the Guide's part. This rule was called a **Canon** <note>original: "Kanon"</note> by the Greeks; however, some less-intelligent musicians use the name **Canon** for what they ought to call a **Fugue**, a **Consequence**, or a **Repetition** <note>original: "Reditta"</note>. This Rule is written in this way: *Fugue, or Consequence at the Octave* <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. If the Consequent is higher than the Guide, one adds "in the high [register]"; adding to this, moreover, the **Time** <note>The number of measures or beats.</note> that the Consequent part must wait before it begins to sing, even if the location is already marked with the sign <insert>$\dot{\int}$</insert>. Whereupon one writes:

->Fugue, or Consequence of two Measures, at the high Octave.<-

But if the **Consequent** <note>The "Consequent" (Consequente) is the following voice in a canon.</note> were to sing in the low register, instead of saying "High," one would say "Low." Indeed, the methods are almost infinite, and it would be a long task to recount them one by one; but I have set down only these so that they may be a light and a guide to everyone who wishes to undertake this beautiful, ingenious, and honorable labor.

### On Imitations, and what they are. Chapter 52.
---

**Imitation** is of no small use to Composers; for besides the ornament that it brings to the song, it is the work of an ingenious mind and is highly praiseworthy. It is of two sorts, just as the Fugue is: namely, **Strict** and **Free**. It is also called Fugue by practitioners; but in truth, there is this difference between the **Fugue** and **Imitation**: that the Fugue (whether strict or free) is found between many parts of the song which—either by similar or contrary movements—contain those same intervals contained in their **Guide**, as I have shown. But **Imitation** (free or strict, as you like), although it is found among many parts (as we shall show) and proceeds in the same manner, nevertheless does not travel by those same intervals in the consequent parts that are found in the **Guide**. Wherefore, just as the Fugue can be made at the Unison, the Fourth, the Fifth, the Octave, or other intervals, so **Imitation** can be adapted to every interval *except* for the Unison and the others just named. Because of this, it can be placed at the Second, the Third, the Sixth, the Seventh, and other similar intervals. We shall say, then, that **Imitation** is that which is found between two or more parts; in which the **Consequent**, imitating the movements of the **Guide**, proceeds only by the same degrees <note>The melodic shape or "steps" on the staff.</note> without having any other consideration for the [exact size of the] intervals. Knowledge of both the strict and free types can be easily gained once one understands what Strict Fugue and Free Fugue mean. But for greater clarity, I will come to a specific example from which one can understand what I have intended to say in general.

<image-desc>Musical notation examples on four staves. The first two staves use soprano clefs and are labeled "High part" in the space between them. The next two staves use bass clefs and are labeled "Low part" in the space between them. The notation represents two-part musical imitation in white mensural notation.</image-desc>

->High part.<-

->Low part.<-

Those **Imitations**, then, which are made by contrary movements <note>Inversion, where an upward step in the first voice becomes a downward step in the second.</note> have a **Guide** and a **Consequent** in the same way that Fugues do. Hence, in writing out the **Guide** at length, one also uses the same methods that were used in Fugues.

For this is commonly called a **Fugue** <note>original: "Fuga" — literally "flight," where one voice seems to chase the other.</note>; and it is used very often in compositions for multiple voices, as can be seen in many **songs** <note>original: "cantilene" — a general term for vocal polyphonic pieces.</note>. ### On the Cadence: what it is, its types, and its use. Chapter 53.

Several times above I have mentioned the **Cadence** <note>original: "Cadenza" — from the Latin 'cadere,' meaning 'to fall'; the conclusion of a musical phrase.</note>, and now I will say what it is, show the different kinds of Cadence, and teach how they are used. The Cadence, then, is a certain action that the parts of a **song** <note>original: "cantilena" — refers to a polyphonic musical composition.</note> perform while singing together, which denotes either a general rest in the harmony or the completion of the sense of the words upon which the song is composed. Or rather, we might say that it is a certain termination of a part of the whole **harmonic ensemble** <note>original: "concento"</note>, acting as a middle or final conclusion or distinction in the context of the **text** <note>original: "Oratione" — literally 'oration' or 'speech,' referring to the prose or verse being set to music.</note>. And although the Cadence is very necessary in harmonies—because when they lack one, they miss a great and necessary ornament, both for the distinction of the musical parts and those of the text—it should not be used except when arriving at the **Clause** <note>original: "Claufula"</note> or the **Period** contained in the prose or verse; that is, in that part which ends a member of the sentence or one of its parts. 

Hence, the Cadence is of as much value in Music as the **Period** <note>original: "Punto" — a full stop or punctuation mark</note> is in Speech; and it can truly be called the Period of the Song. It is true that it is also placed where one rests—that is, where the termination of a part of the harmony is found—in the same way that we pause in the context of speech, when we find not only a middle distinction but also a final one. Nor should we always place it in the same spot, but rather in various places, so that from this variety a more pleasing and delightful harmony follows. And the Period of the text and the Cadence should end together; not just upon any pitch, but on the proper regular pitches of the **Modes** <note>original: "Modi" — the historical scales or tonal systems used in the Renaissance.</note> in which the song is composed. I will show these pitches in the Fourth Part when I speak separately of each of them. 

But it should be noted that Cadences in **plainchant** <note>original: "Canti fermi" — monophonic, traditional church chant.</note> are made in a single part, but in **polyphony** <note>original: "figurati" — music with varied rhythmic 'figures' or note values.</note> other parts are added. In plainchant, they are placed when the sentence of the words is finished; in polyphony, however, they are not only made when the perfect Clause is heard in the speech, but they are sometimes used out of necessity, or to follow a certain order in the **Counterpoint** <note>original: "Contrapunto"</note> started by the Composer. It is also true that those of polyphonic music are of two sorts: those that terminate between two parts in a **Unison**, and those that end in an **Octave**. And although there are some others that end in a **Fifth**, and some others in a **Third**, and some by various other consonances, they are not to be called Cadences absolutely, except in a certain way and with an addition—namely, **imperfect cadences**. 

All types of Cadences are found in two modes: they are either **Simple**, or they are **Diminished** <note>original: "Diminuite" — refers to 'division' or breaking long notes into smaller, more decorative rhythmic values.</note>. The simple ones are those whose parts proceed in similar figures or notes and contain no dissonance; the Diminished ones are those that contain various figures and some **Dissonances** between the parts of the song. Each of them is comprised of at least three notes, whether in the low part or the high part of the song; and they are made between at least two parts proceeding in contrary motion. The first sort of Cadence, then, terminating in a **Unison**, is that which contains a progression made by two parts of a song against each other; of which one, ascending and then descending (or descending only) with its notes by **steps** <note>original: "gradi, o mouimenti congiunti" — moving to the very next note in the scale without leaping.</note>, and the other descending and then ascending by similar steps; the second note of the low part being a **Minor Third** apart from the second note of the high part, the third notes of each part come to end and join together on the same pitch; that is, in the same sound. This Cadence can also be made in various other ways, but let it be done in whatever manner one wishes, for it matters little, provided that its final notes and those preceding them are placed in the manner described, as can be seen in the example below.

*The **Diminished Cadences** <term>Diminution (Diminuite): The practice of decorating a simple musical line by breaking long notes into many smaller, faster notes.</term> ending in a **Unison** <note>original: "Vnisono" — the interval where two voices sing the exact same pitch.</note> are those that proceed in a similar fashion; but they are created with various rhythmic figures, among which one finds the **Syncopation** <term>Syncopation (Sincopa): In this context, it refers to a suspension, where a note is held over into a beat where it does not belong, creating a momentary clash (dissonance) before resolving.</term>. The second part of this syncopation, which is the part struck by the **Downbeat** <note>original: "Battuta" — the primary rhythmic pulse or stroke used to keep time.</note>, is found to be dissonant—specifically a **Second**. From there, by immediately following with a **Minor Third**, one arrives at the conclusion in a **Unison**.*

*And because practical musicians usually **diminish** (ornament) that part of the Cadence containing the syncopation—so that they may, as it suits them, accommodate the harmonies to the **Words**—before I go any further, I wish to provide such Diminutions so they may be seen. These are set out below and can be used to great advantage, as we shall see in the*

### Fourth Part.
Here, every Composer must be careful not to fall into error: although the Cadences are placed only in the locations shown, they can nevertheless be made in any other place where it is convenient, provided that the Rule given above in **Chapter 38** is observed—namely, to move from an **Imperfect Consonance** to a **Perfect** one via the closest neighbor. Therefore, it is necessary that in the penultimate (second-to-last) notes of these Cadences there be a **Minor Third**. This will always be heard when the movement goes to a Unison in such a way that one voice descends by a **whole tone** <note>original: "Tuono"</note> and the other by a **major semitone** <note>original: "Semituono maggiore"</note>, or vice versa.

*This can always be done in any place without placing the sign of the **chromatic string** <term>Chromatic string (chorda chromatica): An early term for a musical accidental, such as a sharp or flat.</term> to turn the interval of a whole tone into a semitone. This is because in the part where the movement ascends between the penultimate and final notes, it is always understood that a semitone is located there, provided the other part does not descend by a similar interval. In that case, the semitone could not be placed in both parts (that is, in both the low and the high part), because one would hear an interval smaller than a **Minor Third** <note>original: "Semidituono"</note>, which would be dissonant. But Nature has provided for such things: for not only the experts of Music, but even the **peasants** <note>A famous observation by Zarlino: he argues that the "leading tone" (raising the note to create a semitone at a cadence) is so natural to the human ear that even uneducated singers do it instinctively.</note> who sing without any art, proceed by the interval of the semitone. And these are properly called Cadences; even if their first notes are a **Fifth** apart, their second notes a **Minor Third** apart, and the last notes end in a **Unison** (as seen below), they could still be called Cadences, though one might say they are called Cadences "improperly."*

*The Cadence ending in an **Octave** <note>original: "Ottava"</note> is of such a sort that its notes must be ordered in this way: the first, second, and third notes of the high part, and the first, second, and third of the low part, move in **contrary** and stepwise motion against one another. The second notes of the parts should be a **Major Sixth** <note>original: "Sesta maggiore"</note> apart, and the final notes should be an **Octave** apart. And although there might be some difference in...*

...movements between the first and the second notes: because the notes of the **High** <note>original: "parte acuta" — the soprano or upper voice.</note> part always move by **Step** <note>original: "mouimenti congiunti" — conjunct motion, or moving to the next adjacent note in the scale.</note>, those of the **Low** <note>original: "parte graue" — the bass or lower voice.</note> part can sometimes proceed by **Leap** <note>original: "mouimenti separati" — disjunct motion, or moving by an interval larger than a second.</note>, at times descending together. However they are arranged, the second-to-last notes of the **Cadence** will always be separated from one another by the interval of a **Major Sixth**, and the final notes will resolve into an **Octave**. 

This will always result in a good harmony when one part moves by a **Semitone** <term>Semitone (Semituono): The smallest interval in traditional Western music, such as the distance between B and C.</term>—whether in the low or the high voice—and the other moves by a **Whole Tone** <term>Whole Tone (Tuono): An interval consisting of two semitones, such as the distance between C and D.</term>. This rule applies to these and all other types of Cadences, whether they are **Simple** <note>A cadence where the notes are of equal length and lack decoration.</note> or **Diminished** <note>A cadence where the melody is broken into smaller, faster notes for ornamentation.</note>. It is certainly true that diminished cadences contain a **Syncopation** <term>Syncopation (Sincopa): A rhythmic device where a note is held across a beat, creating a dissonance (clash) that then resolves.</term>, in which one hears a **Seventh** during its second part—that is, on the downbeat. But the simple cadence is entirely **Consonant** <note>Meaning it contains only "sweet" sounding intervals without intentional clashes.</note> because its notes are of equal value, as can be seen in the examples provided below.

<image-desc>Six musical examples in two-part counterpoint using mensural notation. The staves show various ways two voices can move from a major sixth to an octave. In some, the upper voice moves up a semitone while the lower moves down a tone; in others, the roles are reversed.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Two short musical staves on the left showing a simple two-note transition in two voices.</image-desc>

One can also see how the parts of the Cadence can often be swapped with one another, placing the melodic passage usually found in the low part into the high part; and conversely, taking the passage from the high part and placing it in the low part, so that they correspond by an **Octave**. Such variations are very convenient for Composers. 

Besides these two types of Cadence, there is another that ends in an **Octave** or a **Unison**. This occurs when the second-to-last notes of the low and high parts are separated by a **Ditone** <term>Ditone (Ditono): A major third, an interval spanning two whole tones.</term>. In this case, the low part descends by the interval of a **Fifth** or ascends by a **Fourth**, while the high part ascends by **Step**, as is shown here:

# Part Three

And these **Cadences** <term>Cadence (Cadenza): A melodic or harmonic configuration that creates a sense of resolution or repose.</term> are likewise of two types; that is, **Simple** and **Diminished**; as can be seen. Those that are Simple have similar note shapes; and the Diminished have diverse note shapes; and among them one finds **Syncopation** <term>Syncopation (Sincopa): A rhythmic technique where a note is held from a weak beat into a strong beat, often creating a temporary clash or dissonance.</term>, which has in its second part a **Fourth**, after which immediately follows a **Major Third**; as I have shown. But because these Cadences are not used very often in compositions for two voices—since ascending by the illustrated disjunct movements, and descending also, is characteristic of the lowest part of a composition made for many voices, in which they are used—we should therefore be careful not to place them too frequently. And when we wish to use them, we should always place them in the middle, and not at the end of the **Cantilena** <note>original: "cantilena" — a song or vocal melody.</note>; except when necessity compels us to do so; that is, when we wish to set the parts of the composition in **Canon** <term>Canon (Consequenza): A contrapuntal technique where one voice strictly follows the melody of another at a set distance.</term>, or in **Imitation** <term>Imitation (Imitatione): A technique where a melody in one voice is repeated shortly after in another voice, though not necessarily exactly.</term>; according to the methods shown above; and when a passage convenient for singing and a pleasing melody cannot be obtained in any other way. It is certainly true that I want this to be advice rather than a strict precept: because if they were also placed at the beginning and at the end, it would not be a great error.

Beyond this, one finds the Cadence ending on a **Fifth**, or on a **Third**, or on another consonance, which is called an **Improper Cadence** <note>original: "Cadenza impropiamente" — a cadence that does not resolve to the most stable intervals of the unison or octave.</note>; and it is similarly contained by a similar number of note shapes; and it is ordered in such a way that, the second notes of both parts being a Third apart, the final notes come to fall into one of the named consonances; and this happens when the high part moves by **Step** <term>Step (mouimento congiunto): Moving to the next adjacent note in the scale.</term> while ascending. And it is of two types, that is, Simple and Diminished; each of which, by so many examples given above, I believe is now known by everyone. Therefore it will suffice to say only that in the Diminished form, one hears the **Fourth** in the second part of the Syncopation, and no other dissonance; just as can be heard in each one found in the examples placed below.

[The first musical example displays two-part counterpoint illustrating simple and diminished cadences with syncopated resolutions.]

[The second musical example illustrates further variations of cadences, showing how voices interact through steps and leaps to reach stable intervals.]

Nor in these (when they are made for two voices) is it necessary that one always hears the movement of a **Major Semitone** <note>The larger of two types of half-steps recognized in Renaissance theory.</note> in one part, whether it be the low or high voice: because one would sometimes hear a relationship between the parts that would not be harmonious; as I have declared in Chapter 30. It would be a very tedious thing if I wanted to give a particular example of every **Proper** and **Improper Cadence**: since they are almost infinite; wherefore it is necessary that the **Contrapuntist** <term>Contrapuntist (Contrapuntista): A composer or student of counterpoint, the art of combining different melodic lines.</term> strives to always find new ones, continually investigating new methods; and let him take care not to commit errors. And so that he may see in what way Cadences can be ordered in diverse ways, and in what manner they can be used, in order not to be long-winded, I will provide many examples, from which one can perceive what must be done in the invention of others.

I also do not wish to omit mentioning that **practitioners** <note>original: "Prattici" — those who compose and perform by experience rather than theoretical study.</note> are sometimes accustomed to using, in **Cadences** and even in other places, a **dotted semibreve** <term>Semibreve: In this period, the standard unit of time, equivalent to a modern whole note. The "dot" increases its value by half.</term> placed as a dissonance, instead of a **syncopated semibreve**. They then use those movements that are appropriate for the Cadence and for the **Syncopation** <term>Syncopation (Sincopa): A rhythmic technique where a note is held across a beat, creating a temporary clash or "suspension" that then resolves.</term> placed in such a manner. And although this practice is tolerated, it nevertheless does not fully satisfy the ear. For this reason, I would urge the composer not to make such passages very often in his compositions, even though they are in use; because (in my judgment) it seems to me that they should not be placed among the number of Cadences; especially since they do not observe everything that a Cadence requires, as everyone will be able to judge after they have heard and examined the examples placed below.

<image-desc>Musical notation in mensural style on four five-line staves, arranged in two systems of two parts each. These examples show cadences resolving to imperfect consonances. The word "Acuto." is placed below the first staff of the first system, and "Graue." is placed below the first staff of the second system.</image-desc>

Therefore, concluding for now, I say that if Cadences were invented both for the perfection of the parts of the entire harmony and also so that through them the perfect sense of the words could be finished, it is proper that when one wishes to end the text with them, the music should finish on one of the **most perfect consonances**—that is, the **Octave** or at least the **Unison**—so that the "Perfect" is appropriately finished with the "Perfect." But when one wish to make some middle distinction in the harmony and the words together, where they have not perfectly finished their thought, we can use those Cadences that end on a **Third**, a **Fifth**, a **Sixth**, or other similar consonances. Finishing in this way is not a perfect end to a Cadence, but is called **evading the cadence** <term>Evading the Cadence (Fuggir la Cadenza): A technique where the music suggests a final resolution is coming, but the composer diverts it to a different interval to keep the music moving.</term>, as musicians call it today. 

And it was a good thing to discover that Cadences could also end in such a manner, because it often happens to a Composer that a beautiful passage comes to his hands in which a Cadence would fit perfectly, but because he has not yet reached the end of the **Period** <note>original: "Periodo" — a complete musical or textual sentence.</note> in the words, it would not be proper for the music to finish there. He therefore seeks to evade it, not only in the way shown, but in the manner that I will show in the following chapter. And although from what I have said, one could conclude that whenever any Cadence does not end in the Octave or the Unison, it could be called **Imperfect** (because it evades the perfect end); nevertheless, because evading the cadence is done in many other ways, I want us to see now in what guise it can be evaded, and the method that can be held when one part of the **Counterpoint** <term>Counterpoint (Contrapunto): The art of combining different melodic lines to sound together harmoniously.</term> makes a separate movement; that is, when it moves by two or more steps, as happens many times in compositions.

### Part Three

### The Way to Evade the Cadences; and What One Must Observe When the Subject Moves by Two or More Degrees. Chapter 54.

IT SEEMS TO ME that we need not linger long on this point; for I believe that, from what has been said and shown thus far, everyone may now be quite well instructed in this matter, as well as in those things which are useful and necessary to the art of **Counterpoint** <term>Counterpoint (Contrapunto): The art of combining different melodic lines according to specific rules of harmony and rhythm.</term>. Therefore (as I see it), it will suffice only to say that **Evading the Cadence** <note>original: "fuggir la Cadenza" — a technique where the listener expects a resolution to a stable chord, but the composer diverts the voices elsewhere to maintain musical momentum.</note> is (as we have seen) a certain action performed by the voices, suggesting that they intend to reach a **perfect termination** <note>A final resolution to a unison or octave.</note> according to one of the methods shown above, but then turning elsewhere. It will be enough to provide an example from which one can understand the many ways we might evade it when the opportunity arises. One will also be able to see what must be observed when the **Subject** <term>Subject (Soggetto): The principal melodic theme or musical idea upon which a composition is based.</term> makes certain movements of a **Third**, a **Fourth**, or other similar separated intervals <note>In this context, "separated intervals" refers to melodic leaps rather than stepwise motion.</note>. Thus, when someone is well-instructed in this, they will know what to do when they happen to use such passages.

Part Three.

## When it is permissible to use a passage two or more times in one part of the Composition, and when it is not. Chapter 55.

*JUST AS variety in things brings pleasure and delight, so too the same thing used too often sometimes generates boredom and annoyance. Therefore we must strive above all else, to avoid falling into common errors, so that our **Counterpoints** <term>Counterpoint (Contrapunto): The art of combining different melodic lines according to specific rules of harmony and rhythm.</term> are varied in such a way that one does not hear the same passage or the same harmony twice or more, repeated with the same consonances, the same movements, and on the same strings <note>original: "chorde" — in this era, "strings" refers to specific pitches or notes on the musical scale.</note>. And although it is impossible for anything dissonant or unpleasant to the ear to be heard in these counterpoints when they are well-ordered, nevertheless, repeating the same harmony so many times does not give the pleasure that it would if it were varied. Furthermore, the **Composer** would be judged very poor in invention by those who are knowledgeable in the Art; for they would think (having used the same passage more than once) that he had no other counterpoint at hand. Therefore, everyone should be warned not to commit such a thing as is found in the example placed below; for such a thing may be attributed to him as a vice.*

<image-desc>Musical notation example in white mensural notation. The example consists of two staves. The top staff is labeled "SOGGETTO" (Subject) and contains a simple melodic line. The bottom staff is labeled "Contrapunto" (Counterpoint) and shows a counterpoint line that repeats a specific melodic figure and the same intervals against the subject several times, illustrating the "vice" of repetitive writing.</image-desc>

*I have said that one should not use a passage many times, meaning the **Counterpoint** repeated with the same consonances, the same movements, and on the same strings. For it is not only permissible, but very praiseworthy to repeat a certain **melodic phrase** <note>original: "modulatione"</note> and the same passage as many times as one wishes or is able, provided that the Counterpoint is always different and varied. Such repetitions have something ingenious about them; wherefore everyone should strive to make such repetitions whenever the opportunity arises to do so well, without any error. Indeed, he will be regarded by the knowledgeable as a man of rare <note>original: "pellegrino" — literally "pilgrim," but in this context meaning rare, exotic, or remarkably fine</note> genius and abundant invention. I said he "should strive" because the **Counterpoint writer** <term>Counterpoint writer (Contrapuntiſta): The composer or student specialized in the rules of vocal polyphony.</term> is not so bound that he cannot change and alter such passages according to his will. Furthermore, repeated in that way, they could not be used for too long without great inconvenience to the parts—that is, without resulting in awkward melodic progressions <note>original: "sinistre modulationi"</note>. But when such inconveniences do not occur, they may be repeated, for they create a good effect, as can be heard in the examples below.*

<image-desc>A second musical notation example in two staves. The top staff, labeled "SOGGETTO.", displays a series of long notes. The bottom staff, labeled "Contrapunto.", provides a more complex and praiseworthy counterpoint that utilizes imitation and repetition of a specific motif, but varies the harmonic relationship to the subject each time.</image-desc>

Lower part.

And because sometimes **Musicians** are accustomed to obligating themselves to create a **counterpoint** <term>Counterpoint (Contrapunto): The technique of combining two or more melodic lines so they are harmonically interdependent yet independent in rhythm and contour.</term> by always using a specific passage, though varying the harmony; this method is called **Writing counterpoint with a constraint** <term>Obligo: A self-imposed rule or "obligation" where a composer restricts themselves to using a specific musical idea throughout a piece.</term>. Such repetitions or passages are called **Obstinacies** <term>Pertinacie: Literally "stubbornness"; in music, this refers to the persistent repetition of a short melodic figure, similar to what we might today call an ostinato.</term>. Therefore, when someone wishes to obligate themselves to such a thing, they will take a **Theme** or passage and begin to compose the counterpoint over the proposed **Subject**. 

But because this manner of composing counterpoint is very difficult, the **Composer** <term>Contrapuntista: A specialist in writing counterpoint.</term> may take certain liberties; such as occasionally using certain **melodic motions** <note>original: "modulationi" — in this period, this refers to the movement of the voice from one pitch to another rather than shifting between keys.</note> that might not be as easy to sing as they ought to be if the counterpoint were written without any such constraint. He may also use whichever note values are most convenient for him, varying the harmony by using now **Breves**, now **Semibreves**, now **Minims**, or other figures <note>In the 16th century, a Breve was a long note, a Semibreve was half its length (equivalent to a modern whole note), and a Minim was half of that (a half note).</note>. These he may place sometimes with **syncopation** <term>Sincopa: A rhythmic technique where a note is started on a weak beat and held over a strong beat, often creating a suspension or "clash" that resolves.</term> and sometimes without, in order to satisfy his obligation. 

Nevertheless, he must always keep an eye on observing what has been discussed and demonstrated above, avoiding errors as much as possible so that his counterpoint is praised rather than blamed. For a task that is performed well despite being difficult is much more worthy of praise than one that is performed well without any difficulty. Therefore, so that one may have full knowledge of this matter, I will provide two examples from which one may learn what can be done in other similar cases.
