## Of Double Counterpoints, and what they are. Cap. 56.

HAVING seen in what manner one can compose every sort of **Counterpoint** for two voices; I wish for us to see now in what way one can also make some sorts of **artful Counterpoint** <term>Contrapunto arteficioso: Counterpoint constructed using specific mathematical or structural rules, such as inversion or canon.</term> for two voices likewise, over whatever **Subject** one wishes; this is called **Double Counterpoint** <term>Contrapunto doppio: A type of counterpoint designed so that the voices can be swapped (the high part becomes the low part and vice versa) and still sound correct.</term>. This is nothing other than a composition made ingeniously so that it can be sung in multiple ways by changing its parts, in such a manner that when it is repeated, a different **harmony** <note>original: "concento" — the overall sonic effect of the voices combined.</note> is heard from that which was first heard in the same parts. Therefore, we should know that such counterpoint is found to be of two sorts. 

The first is when the **Principal** <term>Principale: The original version of the counterpoint before any parts are swapped.</term> (that is, the first part that is composed) and the **Replica** <term>Replica: The second version, created by inverting or swapping the voices of the Principal.</term> (that is, that which is heard after the first) are sung by changing the parts in this way: that the **higher part** <note>original: "acuta"</note> becomes the **lower** <note>original: "grave"</note> and the lower becomes the higher, without any variation of movement. This sort is also of two kinds: for when the parts are changed, one proceeds either by the same intervals or by varied ones. If by the same intervals, the replicated counterpoint is sung at the **Twelfth** <note>Inversion at the twelfth means that if you move the lower voice up an octave and a fifth, the intervals remain largely consistent.</note>; and if one proceeds by varied intervals, it is sung at the **Tenth**. 

The second sort is when, after the Principal, the Replica is sung proceeding by **contrary motions** <term>Movimenti contrarij: When one voice moves up while the other moves down.</term>, having first changed the parts as was said—that is, the lower into the higher and the higher into the lower. 

When, therefore, one wishes to compose in the first way (which proceeds by the same movements and intervals), we shall observe never to place the **Sixth** in the Principal: because in the Replica, it cannot form a **consonance** <note>In double counterpoint at the twelfth, a sixth inverts to become a seventh, which is a dissonance.</note>. Nor shall we ever place the parts of the song so far apart from each other that they exceed the span of a **Twelfth**; nor shall we ever place the higher part in the place of the lower, nor conversely the lower in the place of the higher. For not only do the figures that exceed the Twelfth cause problems, but also those by which one part comes to occupy the place of the other, resulting in **dissonance** in the Replica. 

We shall also not use the **Syncopation** <term>Sincopa: A suspension or tied note that creates a temporary dissonance before resolving.</term> containing a **Seventh**, because it does not turn out well in the Replica. We may well use the Syncopation containing the **Second** and the **Fourth**, since these create very good effects in the Replica, especially when resolved according to the ways shown elsewhere. And so that no **unharmonic relation** <term>Relatione non harmonica: A discordant relationship between notes, such as a tritone, that makes the melody sound "harsh" or "wrong" to the ears of the period.</term> is heard between the parts of the Replica, one must take care not to place the **minor Tenth** in the Principal in any way if it is followed by an **Octave** or a **Twelfth**; nor a **minor Third** before a **Unison** or a **Fifth** when the parts proceed by contrary movements. For when placed in such a way, a **Tritone** <note>The interval of an augmented fourth, famously known as "the devil in music" for its instability.</note> or other inconvenience follows between the parts. 

Beyond this, one should note that every Twelfth in the Principal becomes a **Unison** in the Replica, and every Fifth becomes an **Octave**. Furthermore, one must observe that every rule shown above is entirely followed in the Principal; for then the Replica will turn out to be without any error. It is true, however, that if one wishes to end the Counterpoint with a **Cadence**, it will be necessary for the Principal or the Replica to have the Cadence end on a Fifth or a Twelfth; this also happens in middle cadences, and the relation of the Tritone will be heard between the parts. But this will be of little importance when the rest is ordered regularly, as is seen here in the Principal. We shall then sing the Replica in this way, making the lower part high...

[...the twelfth] and the low part in the high register distant by a **Twelfth**: But because it provides no variation of harmony <note>original: "concento"</note> different from that heard in the **Replica**, I will not set it down otherwise, so as not to multiply things without purpose. Wanting then to compose that which holds the second place in the first manner—that is, the version where the **Replica** proceeds by the same movements but with different intervals than those in the **Principal**—we will observe not to place, in any way, two similar consonances in the **Principal**. This includes two **Thirds**, or two **Sixths**, or other similar intervals, one after the other without anything in between, even if one were major and the other minor. We must also place **Syncopations** <term>Sincope: In Renaissance theory, these are usually suspensions—notes held over from a previous beat to create a temporary tension before resolving.</term> so that they are consonant in all their parts. I said that one does not use two **Sixths**, because in these and similar **Counterpoints**, the **Sixth** can be used to good effect; and one can have the low part take the place of the high, and the high take the place of the low, as is most convenient. This is on the condition, however, that when they are placed in such a manner, one is not distant from the other by more than a **Third**; whereas if each remains within its own bounds, they can then be placed a **Twelfth** apart from each other. It is true that one could go further, but if one does, the **Thirteenth** must not be used under any circumstances, because it would turn out very inconvenient <note>In this context, "inconvenient" means it would create a dissonance when transposed.</note>. We shall not, therefore, exceed the **Twelfth**, and we shall observe the rules given, ensuring that the parts of the song <term>cantilena: A general term for a melodic line or a piece of vocal music.</term> sing comfortably with **conjunct movements** <term>mouimenti congiunti: Melodic motion by step (e.g., C to D) rather than by leap (e.g., C to G).</term> as much as possible; for leaps of a **Fourth** or **Fifth** can generate some difficulty in certain places of the **Replica**. Having observed this, we may have a **Counterpoint** purged of every error, similar to this one:

One could also make the high part lower by an **Octave** and the low part higher by a **Tenth**; and this would please me more, because the **Mode** would be heard more within its proper limits, as would a different harmony. However, the **Counterpoint** would not turn out as well-observed as the one seen in the **Replica**. These **Counterpoints** could also be sung with three voices, by having another part sing a **Tenth** above the low part of the **Principal**, and in the **Replica**, a **Seventeenth** below the high part. It is true, however, that the **Counterpoint** would not be as well-purged of many errors as it ought to be. But because making this sort of **Counterpoint** is very difficult if one wants it to be error-free in the **Replica**, I wish to set down some general rules. ### What the Contrapuntist must observe beyond the rules given, and some licenses he may take. Chapter 57.

I will now condense several things into one chapter, giving a particular example through which the **Composer** may understand the universal principle; so that by observing them, his **song** <note>original: "cantilena"</note> might be full of sweet **harmony**, and the **concord** <note>original: "concento," referring to the harmonious sounding of multiple voices together.</note> might bring delight to all who hear it. # Third Part

<header>Part.</header>

If the **Counterpoint** <term>Contrapunto: The art of combining different melodic lines according to specific rules.</term> moves [quickly], it will sometimes be impossible to maintain a variety of **Consonances** <term>Consonanze: Combinations of notes that sound harmonious and stable, such as thirds, fifths, and sixths.</term> for very long without great difficulty. In such a case, one may use many syncopated figures, such as the **Semibreve** <term>Semibreue: A rhythmic value equivalent to a whole note in modern notation.</term> and the **Minim** <term>Minima: A rhythmic value equivalent to a half note.</term> with a dot, always varying the pitches and the sounds. Figures placed in this manner will make the **Counterpoint** pass with much grace and will provide great convenience to the composer, because it will be "tied" in such a way that it creates a very good effect. But one should know that the **Counterpoint** can be called "tied" [syncopated] when it is syncopated in such a way that the **Semibreve** of the **Subject** <term>Soggetto: The primary melody or "cantus firmus" upon which the counterpoint is built.</term> does not fall entirely on the beat against the **Semibreve** of the **Counterpoint**, but rather against its half. This occurs when it is placed as a syncopation, or when it falls on the dot of the **Minim**. It shall also be called "tied" when the part of the **Subject** remains still—that is, it does not move from one pitch to another—while the **Counterpoint** moves and modulates through various pitches. Similarly, it will be called "tied" when the **Counterpoint** remains still and the **Subject** passes through various pitches; this happens when it is "diminished" <note>Diminution is the breaking down of long notes into shorter, faster notes.</note>. When it then becomes necessary to use **Unisons** <term>Vnisoni: Two parts singing the exact same pitch.</term>, either by necessity or for some other reason, they may be placed on the second part of the **Semibreve**, provided that the part of the **Subject** and the **Counterpoint** do not meet to perform the **Unison** at the same time on the downbeat or the upbeat. This is because when placed on the second part of any figure, it is almost unheard, whereas it would be heard if they met together on the first part. For this reason, it can also be placed when it falls on the dot of a **Semibreve** or a **Minim**, in whichever part one wishes, provided that such a part is diminished. This works well in compositions for several voices, as that **Unison** takes the place of that **Minim** (of which the dot holds the place) which is not only almost unheard, but sometimes singers even remain silent on such a dot. This is often the reason why the harmony is left deprived of one of its parts—that is, the **Fifth** or the **Third**—as we shall see elsewhere, and in this way, it remains imperfect. But because the observance of the shown rules sometimes binds the composer in such a way that he cannot only fail to acquire a beautiful and charming modulation that delights, but he also cannot place the parts of the **Song** <term>Cantilena: A general term for a vocal melody or musical composition.</term> in "fuga" [imitation] or consequence as he would desire; therefore, just as poets are sometimes allowed to go against the rules of meter and to use one expression for another, or a long syllable in place of a short one or vice versa, so too shall it be permitted to the musician at times to put things on paper that go against the given rules. However, he will not be allowed to continue them too long, just as the poet is not permitted to use such licenses frequently. The musician may therefore, when it is convenient and he cannot do otherwise due to some circumstance, place a **Fifth** after a **Major Sixth**, contrary to the rule given above in Chapter 38, when the **Sixth** is placed in the second part of a syncopated **Semibreve**, as is seen here: for if the **Second** and the **Seventh**, which are **Dissonances** <term>Dissonanze: Intervals that sound unstable or "clashing" and typically require resolution.</term>, are tolerated in syncopations, how much

more should the **Sixth** be tolerated, which is not only not **Dissonant**, but is accepted by everyone as a **Consonance**? Perhaps someone might say here that with this same license and in the same manner, one could also move from the **Minor Sixth** to the **Octave**. I respond that this would be done against all 
<column-break/>

reason. For although the Major [Sixth] has the nature of moving to the **Octave** as its neighbor, it is nonetheless closer to the **Fifth** than the Minor [Sixth] is to the **Octave**. Thus one sees that, since one must (as is proper) go from an imperfect **Consonance** to a perfect one using the closest interval, under this license, the **Major Sixth** is more suited to the **Fifth** than the minor is to the **Octave**. There is, then, no reason that excuses us, or offends us, should one wish to commit such a disorder. He may also move from the **Minor Sixth** to the **Octave** with a sin-

Thus, if a Second, or a Seventh, or any other dissonance placed in such a way is tolerated, how much more can a Sixth placed in this manner be tolerated? And it is even more to be tolerated because it is frequently made major by skilled singers, whose hearing cannot endure even the slightest discomfort. But when any of the **chromatic strings** enter (even if placed to achieve a consonance), they should not be used [in this way]: because such notes were not discovered for the destruction of good harmonies and good musical practices, but rather for their construction and well-being. Therefore, it will not be permitted to make any passage similar to those shown here in the examples: because the chromatic notes will always have a corresponding diatonic note in the melody at the interval of a **Semidiapente**, a **Tritone** <term>Tritono: An augmented fourth interval consisting of three whole tones, considered very harsh.</term>, or a **Semiditono** <term>Semiditono: A minor third.</term>, according to the composition; these are intervals or movements without harmony. It will also be permitted to use chromatic notes occasionally when one wishes to move from a Sixth (made major by such notes) to a Tenth or a major Third, with a movement of a Fourth or a Fifth, in order to arrive from there at the **Octave** or the **Unison**; as seen here. This is for two reasons: first, because the progression is diatonic within the chromatic notes; and second, because the movements of the parts proceed by **harmonic intervals** and are regulated according to the rules shown above.

These notes should be marked with the sharp sign **X** for many reasons; and especially for the sake of less-attentive singers, so that they do not occasionally commit some error by placing one note in place of another—that is, the Diatonic in place of the Chromatic—causing a dissonance to be heard.

It is quite true that in melodic phrases <term>modulationi: The movement of voice from one interval to another in a composition.</term> there are certain intervals—such as the Fourth, the Fifth, and the Octave—where the singer must place the chromatic note <note>original: "chorda chromatica"; a note altered by a sharp or flat.</note>, even if it has not been marked by the Composer, so that the movement of the parts is correctly ordered. Were the composition to require it <note>Usually implying that the meaning of the lyrics justifies extreme chromaticism.</note>, this would be bearable. This is because by continuing in them for a long time, the song comes to change its Mode, passing from one into another—which is a particular vice of some. And above all, one must beware of placing such notes at the beginning without purpose; as some do, who not only mark the second figure of the melody with the ♯ Chromatic sign, but even mark the first. They often do this believing they are starting a melody in the First Mode (to give an example) while, without realizing it, they begin a song in the Seventh; as

*...by the practical musicians <note>original: "Prattici"; referring to performing musicians or those who compose by ear rather than theory.</note>; however, I wanted to make mention of it, and leave such a matter to the sound judgment of good and excellent Composers, so that they may see in what manner they ought to be used. Then let the Minim follow in whatever way one likes, whether consonant or dissonant, provided that it proceeds by stepwise motion, as is seen here.*

*Beyond this, the composer must observe that whenever he wishes to make the Counterpoint somewhat languid or sad, or similarly sweet or smooth, he must also proceed by sweet and smooth movements, such as those that proceed by the <term>Semitone: The smallest interval in this system, often associated with mourning or sweetness.</term>, by the <term>Semiditono: A minor third.</term>, and other similar intervals. He should use the minor imperfect consonances, which are the minor third, the minor <term>Hexachord: An interval of a sixth.</term>, and their octaves <note>original: "Replicate"; intervals expanded by an octave, like a tenth or a thirteenth.</note>; these consonances by their nature (as I said in chapter 10) are suited to such things. Conversely, wishing to make it cheerful, the movement will be that of the Whole Tone, that of the <term>Ditono: A major third.</term>, and other similar intervals. And wishing to make it so that it sometimes has a bit of harshness, he may use the major intervals, which are the Major Third, the Major Sixth, and their octaves, in the lower parts of the song. It will be all the more harsh the more it contains the said Major Sixth in notes of significant value in the lower part of the harmony. It is truly a difficult thing to try to teach specifically in what manner and at what time such things ought to be used; but because what I have said can be of great help when one wishes at times to use such styles, this shall suffice for now, because perhaps another time I will speak of it more extensively.*

## The manner to be held in composing Songs for more than two voices; and the names of the parts. Chapter 58.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop-cap 'N' (translated from the Italian 'H') showing a scene with several figures in a landscape, possibly representing the Muses or a musical assembly.</image-desc>

*Now I perceive that I have reasoned sufficiently regarding the giving of Rules and teaching the manner that must be held in composing Songs for two voices. Therefore, it seems to me to be time to leave all other things that might occur regarding this to the good and judicious Reader; for by seeing and examining the learned compositions of good and excellent Composers, he will be able to be clear on everything that may happen to him. And it seems to me to be time to come to show the manner he must hold when wishing to compose those works that are made for many voices. Therefore, before we pass further, it should be noted that Musicians in their songs usually place Four parts, in which they say the whole perfection of harmony is contained. And because they are principally composed of such parts, they called them "Elemental," in the fashion of the four Elements. For just as every mixed Body is composed of them, so every perfect song is composed of these. Thus, the lowest part they name the **Bass**, which we will attribute to the Element of **Earth**; for just as the Earth holds the lowest place among the other elements, so the Bass occupies the lowest place of the song. To this, proceeding somewhat further upwards toward the high notes, they accommodated another part and call it the **Tenor**, which we will liken to **Water**. For just as Water immediately follows Earth in the order of the Elements and is embraced by it, so in the order of the said parts, the Tenor follows the Bass without any intermediary, and its lower notes are in no way different from those of the Bass when placed in the high range. Similarly, they accommodated the Third part above the Tenor, which some call*

# Part Three

The **Countertenor**, which some call **Contralto** and others name **Alto**, was placed in the third position, which is the middle of the musical composition <note>original: "cantilena"; a general term for a polyphonic vocal work.</note>. This part can truly be compared to the **Air**; for just as Air shares certain qualities with Water and Fire, so too do the low notes of the Alto harmonize with the high notes of the Tenor, and the high notes of the Alto harmonize with the low notes of the fourth part placed in the highest range, called the **Canto** <note>The "Canto" is the highest part, now commonly known as the Soprano.</note>. This was set in the supreme position of the composition; hence, because of the place it holds, some also call it the **Soprano**. We might compare it to **Fire**, which follows immediately after the Air in the highest level of this order.

And this comparison is not made without reason. Since the low part holds the bottom position of the composition and proceeds with slow and rare movements—from which low sounds are born, which by their nature are close to silence (as I said in Chapter 11 of the Second Part)—it has a great affinity with the **Earth**, which by its nature is immobile and cannot produce any sound on its own. And if I compared the highest part of all to Fire, I did not do so without cause: for high sounds, which are born from fast and frequent movements, have such a nature that they make themselves heard through their sudden and swift striking of the air. Presenting themselves to the sense of hearing with such speed, they come to possess almost the nature of Fire, which is not only sharp and rare, but also swift and active by its very self. The other middle parts, because of the temperament of their movements and the similarity of their placement, I have compared to the other two middle Elements <note>Water and Air</note>, because they hold their specific nature according to their different positions. In what manner these parts are then to be ordered and arranged, and how far one ought to be from the other, we shall see in the Part that follows.

If we now wish to examine the property of these parts from what has been said, we will find that the **Soprano**, as the one that is higher than any other part and more penetrating to the ear, makes itself heard before all others. Therefore, just as Fire nourishes and is the cause of producing every natural thing found for the adornment and preservation of the World, so the Composer shall strive to ensure that the highest part of his composition has a beautiful, ornate, and elegant progression, in such a way that it nourishes and feeds the souls of those who listen. And just as the Earth is placed as the foundation of the other Elements, so the **Bass** has the property of sustaining, stabilizing, fortifying, and giving growth to the other parts; it is placed as the base and foundation of the harmony. Hence it is called "Bass," as if it were the "Base" and support of the other parts. But just as it would happen if the Element of Earth were missing (if such a thing were possible) that such a beautiful order of things would collapse and both worldly and human harmony would be destroyed, so if the Bass were missing, the entire composition would be filled with confusion and dissonance, and everything would fall into ruin.

Therefore, when the Composer writes the Bass of his composition, he shall proceed with movements that are somewhat slow and somewhat separated—or rather, further apart than those placed in the other parts—so that the middle parts can proceed with elegant and stepwise movements <note>original: "movimenti congiunti"; movement to the adjacent note in the scale.</note>, and especially the Soprano, for this is its proper nature. The Bass, then, should not have many rapid notes <note>original: "diminuito"; referring to "division" or "diminution," the breaking of long notes into many fast ones.</note>; rather, it should proceed for the most part with note values of somewhat greater length than those in the other parts. It must be ordered in such a way that it produces good effects and is not difficult to sing; thus, the other parts can be perfectly placed in their proper locations within the composition.

The **Tenor** follows immediately after the Bass toward the high range. This is the part that rules and governs the composition, and it is the one that maintains the <term>Mode: The scale or melodic framework upon which a piece is built, similar to a modern musical key.</term> upon which the work is founded. It should be composed with elegant movements and in such an order that it observes the nature of the Mode in which it is composed—whether it be the first, second, third, or any other—taking care to make the <term>Cadences: Musical points of rest or arrival, similar to punctuation in a sentence.</term> in the proper places and with purpose.

But just as every thing clears up and everything below is seen to laugh and be full of joy when the Air is illuminated by the rays of the Sun, so when the **Alto** is well-ordered and well-composed, adorned with beautiful and elegant passages, it always embellishes and makes the composition charming. Therefore, the Composer must take care to compose the Alto part in such a way that it produces good effects. The duty and nature of these parts were expressed playfully and with great artifice by that witty Mantuan poet <note>Teofilo Folengo (1491–1544), also known by the pseudonym Merlin Cocai, famous for his "Macaronic" poetry blending Latin and Italian.</note> in his coarse verses, saying:

> *The Soprano catches the ears of the listeners more.* <note>original Latin: "Plus ascoltantum Sopranus captat orecchias."</note>
> *But the Tenor is the ruler of the voices, or the Guide of the Tones.* <note>original Latin: "Sed Tenor est vocum rector, vel Guida Tonorum."</note>
> *The Alto paints and adorns the Apollonian song.* <note>original Latin: "Altus Apollineum carmen depingit & ornat."</note>
> *The Bass nourishes the voices, fattens, founds, and increases them.* <note>original Latin: "Bassus alit voces, ingrassat, fundat, & auget."</note>

I wanted to include these so that the Composer, by remembering them, may know what he must do when composing these parts. These are, then, the principal and elementary parts of every perfect composition; and although the Alto is the last

# Part Three

...to be composed: because once the other parts are composed, the Bass comes to supply and make perfect the harmony, which among the others could not be made perfect. Nonetheless, it is not a fatal law that it must always be placed last in the composition; likewise, there is nothing that constrains us to compose one part before another. It should be noted, however, that when musicians wish to compose any song for ***Three voices***, they most often leave out the Contralto or the Soprano and take the other parts. And if they wish to proceed beyond the four named voices, they do not add any new part; instead, they double them, placing two Sopranos, or two Altos, or two Tenors, and likewise two Basses, and thus achieve their purpose. 

Whenever one wishes to compose any harmony upon a discovered Subject <note>original: "Soggetto"; the primary musical theme or melody upon which a piece is built.</note>—be it <term>cantus firmus</term> <note>original: "Canto fermo"; the traditional, slow-moving plainchant of the Church.</note> or figurate music <note>original: "figurato"; polyphonic music with varied rhythmic values.</note>—or if one wishes to compose a Song, Madrigal, or Motet, and it is necessary for the Composer to be the inventor of the Subject, he must first observe which <term>Mode</term> <note>The predecessor to our modern "keys"; specific scales that determined the emotional character and structure of the music.</note> the Subject belongs to. Or rather, he must decide upon which Mode he wishes to compose his song, so that he knows the pitches upon which the <term>Cadences</term> <note>original: "Cadenze"; the musical "punctuation marks" or points of arrival that define a section's end.</note> must be made, in order to compose the harmony in such a way that the end is not dissonant from the middle and the beginning. 

Once these things are considered, one may begin from whichever part is most convenient; always beginning, however, on a pitch that is regular to the Mode upon which the song is to be founded, observing what is contained in the many rules set down above. But because musicians are accustomed to starting their compositions most of the time with the Tenor, and then placing the Soprano, to which they add the Bass, and finally the Alto—and having shown many examples above contained between these two parts (that is, between the Soprano and the Tenor)—it is only necessary to provide the table below. In this table, one can understand without much effort all the chords that the added parts can make together with the two named ones, however many voices there may be. 

And I have maintained this order: first, placing the chords that the Soprano and Tenor make together; then, how far the Bass can be from the Tenor in the low register so that everything harmonizes; and finally, given those named parts, what is required for the Alto to be above the Bass so that the harmony becomes perfect. But it should be noted that one will sometimes find more than one chord in the Alto; therefore, such chords can serve not only for the Alto itself but also for the other parts that might be added to the song beyond the four named. Nor will the Contralto be found placed with the other parts in <term>Unison</term> <note>When two voices sing the exact same pitch.</note> or in the <term>Octave</term>, except in four places. For when the other parts have the Fifth and the Third between them (or their replicates), then the parts added to these—however many they may be—will necessarily come to be in an Octave or Unison with one of the three named parts. 

But so that there is a full understanding of what has been said, I will provide an example. Let us suppose that in the composition the Soprano is placed in Unison with the Tenor; that is, upon the same pitch. I say that if one wishes to add a third part to these two, it will be necessary to place the Bass at the distance of one of these consonances—that is, a Third, Fifth, Sixth, or Octave, or any other (as seen in the Table)—below the Tenor. Thus, if the Bass is a Third away, the Alto can be a Fifth or a Sixth above the Bass in the high register. The other parts (if there were more than four) could be in Unison or an Octave away from one of these four. But if the Bass were a Fifth below the Tenor in the low register, the Alto could be placed a Third or a Tenth above the Bass; and the other parts added would be in Unison or an Octave away from one of these four. And if the Bass were also a Sixth away, by looking at the third example in the Table one will find what the Contralto can be; which can also be seen for the others in order, just as they are placed systematically, as can be seen clearly and distinctly in order here below.

<header>Part Three</header>

FROM these arrangements, anyone can see for themselves that when the Soprano is distant from the Tenor by another <term>consonance</term> <note>A combination of notes that sounds pleasant and stable together.</note>, and the Bass is at some other interval below the Tenor, what would necessarily be required for the Contralto’s distance in the <term>high register</term> <note>original: "acuto"; the higher range of pitches.</note> from the Bass. This is left to the judgment of the discreet Composer, so as not to go on at too much length. One must, however, notice that at times (according to the will of the one composing) the Bass part is placed in the location of the Tenor, although this happens rarely; and conversely, that of the Tenor in the location of the Bass. So too the Soprano is sometimes placed in the location of the Alto, and the latter in that of the Soprano. Or the Tenor is placed in the location of the Contralto, and vice versa. However, let everyone be warned that in this Table the Soprano is always taken as the highest part, and the Bass as the part that is the <term>lowest</term> <note>original: "grave"; the deep or low range of pitches.</note>; even though sometimes the parts designated by these names exchange their assigned and proper places by accident. One should also understand the Tenor to be that part which immediately follows the Bass toward the high register; and then the Contralto to be that which is composed after the three named parts. Indeed, by understanding the matter in such a way, anyone can exchange the parts with one another as it becomes convenient, without any error.

### On <term>Musical Compositions</term> <note>original: "Cantilene"; a general term for vocal musical works or songs.</note> that are composed for Three voices; and on what must be
### observed in composing them. Chapter 59.

PASSING now to the method that must be held when composing works for Three voices—so that from these one may easily come to the composition of those for Four, and even more voices—I say that it is necessary to know that, beyond the observance of the Rules already given, it is necessary to also observe certain other things, which I will show step by step as the need arises. And to begin, let us suppose that one had to make a <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>The art of combining different melodic lines to play simultaneously.</note> for Three voices over a <term>Subject</term> <note>original: "Soggetto"; the primary melody or theme upon which a composition is built.</note>, which would be the Tenor placed lowest in the example. I say that after one has arranged and ordered the parts that enter into the composition one under the other—placing the Subject on top first, and then the others in order, making sure the low part always holds the lowest place and the high part the highest—one may (according to the given Rules) compose the other two parts in imitation of it before beginning to let the Subject part sing. Then, making it enter into the song with grace, and maintaining that order in the <term>diminution</term> <note>original: "diminutione"; the practice of breaking down long notes into many shorter, decorative notes.</note> of the added part that was held in two-voice compositions, aided by the Table placed above, one may continue in such a way that one will have the composition placed here below as an example.

But one should take care that when the parts of the <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>The art of composing one or more melodies to be played simultaneously with a pre-existing one.</note> begin the melody, they start upon that <term>string</term> <note>original: "chorda"; used here to mean a specific pitch or note, as if on a stringed instrument.</note> which begins the first note of the <term>Cantus Firmus</term> <note>original: "Canto fermo"; the "fixed song" or plainchant melody that serves as the foundation of the composition.</note>; as is only right, imitating it as much as possible; placing the parts of the counterpoint in <term>Consequence</term> <note>original: "Consequenza"; a technique where one voice follows another in imitation, similar to a canon.</note> with one another. And if they are also placed in imitation with the Cantus Firmus, it will do no harm. It is quite true that to place them in this second way is not a new manner, nor a new invention; for nothing can be done that has not already been done thousands of times. But I will say that the first way, if it is not entirely new, will at least be nearly new and little used. 

One may also, with great convenience (which is also praiseworthy), place the parts in Consequence with each other, not with that same order and arrangement used in <term>strict canons</term> <note>original: "Fughe legate"; literally "tied fugues," referring to strict imitative compositions where the voices are bound to follow each other exactly.</note>, but with an interrupted order; placing some of the figures ascending and some descending; and using only the same number of notes of the same value. One might sometimes use an imitation of figures in reverse—that is, placing the <term>Guide</term> <note>original: "Guida"; the leading voice in an imitative passage.</note> or Principal voice so that it proceeds through a number of ascending notes, and the <term>Consequent</term> <note>original: "Consequente"; the following voice that mimics the Guide.</note> voice so that it descends with that same number of notes; as can be understood from the example placed below.

<image-desc>Musical notation printed on three sets of dual staves. The notation is in white mensural style, featuring diamond and oval-shaped notes. It illustrates a two-part contrapuntal exercise with various intervals and rhythmic figures, demonstrating the imitative techniques discussed in the text. Clefs include C-clefs and F-clefs.</image-desc>

In this example, I wanted to provide only one part for two reasons: First, because there is no lack of learned compositions by many excellent Musicians which are full of these things, from which one can understand the method to be held in the composition of other melodies; second, so as not to increase the volume of the book with so many examples. From this single part, one can understand what I wished to say, and in what manner one may proceed, drawing the invention of one part from the progression of the other, in order to fill the Counterpoint with beautiful fantasies and graceful inventions. 

But it should be noted that although the Bass (as I have said elsewhere) can sometimes take the place of the Tenor, and likewise one of the other parts take the place of another; nonetheless, one must ensure that the Bass always finishes upon the regular and <term>final string</term> <note>The "tonic" or home note of the musical mode being used.</note> of the <term>Mode</term> <note>The specific scale or melodic system upon which the piece is built.</note> upon which the melody is composed; and likewise the other parts in their proper places: because we must judge the Mode by that final note. And even if the Tenor should happen to finish on a note other than the final, this would not be of much importance, provided that it has proceeded in its <term>modulation</term> <note>original: "modulatione"; here meaning the melodic movement and phrasing, rather than a change of key.</note> according to the nature of the melody's Mode; which should also be understood for each of the other parts. 

Beyond this, it should be noted that a composition can be called **Perfect** if, at every change of note—whether toward the <term>low</term> <note>original: "grave"; deep or low-pitched sounds.</note> or toward the <term>high</term> <note>original: "acuto"; high-pitched sounds.</note>—one always hears all those <term>Consonances</term> <note>Intervals that sound stable and pleasant.</note> that create a variety of sound in their outer notes. And that is truly **Perfect Harmony** which allows such consonances to be heard. But the Sounds, or Consonances, that can create diversity for the senses are two: namely the **Fifth** and the **Third**, or the octaves of one and the other. This is because their outer notes have no similarity to each other, as those of the **Octave** do; nor do the outer notes of one resemble the outer notes of the other. The outer notes of the Fifth do not move the hearing in the same way that those of the Third do, nor vice versa. 

When the <term>Ditone</term> <note>original: "Ditono"; a Major Third.</note> is added to the <term>Semiditone</term> <note>original: "Semiditono"; a Minor Third.</note>, they generate the **Fifth**, which is contained within outer notes that are very different from the sounds heard in the extremes of the Ditone or the Semiditone; for the outer notes of the Ditone are also very different from those of the Semiditone. This is not found in the **Octave**, for its outer notes have such a similarity that they seem like a single sound; they resemble the <term>Unison</term> <note>Two voices playing the exact same pitch.</note> in such a way that, by adding whatever consonance you wish to it, it seems to be joined (as I have also said elsewhere) almost to a single sound. Since variety is found only between the extremes of the Fifth and those of the Third, and since Harmony is composed of things that are diverse from one another, we must by all means (so that we may have such perfect harmony) seek with all our power to make these two Consonances heard in our Compositions as much as possible, or their octaves. It is quite true that many times practical musicians place the...

# Third Part

A **Sixth** in place of the **Fifth**, and it is well done: But one must take care that when the said Sixth is placed in one of the parts above the **Bass**, one should not place any other part that is a **Fifth** above it [the Bass]: because these two parts would end up being a **Tone** or a **Semitone** apart from each other; such that a dissonance would be heard. <note>If one voice has a 6th above the bass (e.g., an A over a C) and another has a 5th (a G over a C), the interval between the two upper voices is a second (G to A), which is dissonant.</note> I have said that we must do everything in our power to always place these two **Consonances** <note>Referring to the Third and the Fifth (or Sixth), which together create a complete chord.</note> in compositions: though they cannot always be placed; especially in compositions for **Three voices**: because in place of one of them, the **Octave** is often used, so as not to spoil the beautiful, elegant, and easy singing of the parts: hence, wanting to observe the rule of always placing such Consonances in such compositions would be nearly impossible. But in **Compositions for Four voices**, it would be a greater error to leave out one of the two named [intervals] than in those composed for Three voices: for where one cannot observe such a **Rule** with three parts, the **Fourth part** permits us to do so. And we are all the more obliged to the observance of this **Law** the more the number of the parts increases.

It is truly a great shame for some who not only make their four-voice compositions poor by lacking one of the said consonances, but do even worse, placing the parts in such a way that they are in **Unison** with one another, or distant from each other by only an **Octave**: whereby the harmony is heard to be much dismembered and poor: because the parts are distant from one another by such Octaves, which are called **Doubled**. But this would be of little consequence if the same error were not found in compositions for **Five, Six, Seven**, and more voices; in which there are some places so dismembered and poor that they are heard with little satisfaction by the ear. Therefore, the **Counterpuntee** <note>original: "Contrapuntista"; a composer skilled in the art of counterpoint.</note> must guard against committing such failings, which are truly worthy of correction; and he must know that such errors are committed not only in the notes that are performed on the **downbeat** or the **upbeat** <note>original: "nel battere, o nel leuare della battuta"; the downward and upward motions used by a conductor to keep time.</note>, but also in every singable note that is placed among the consonances. 

The Composer shall therefore observe this, so that his **composition** <note>original: "cantilena"; here referring to the musical work as a whole.</note> may be sonorous and full, and so that it may contain within itself every perfection of harmony. But this is not to be understood to mean that he must observe such a law from the beginning of the composition until the end: because one must also take care in every piece to give some rest to the parts, and not make them sing always together: but to ensure that now two are heard, now three, now four, according to their total number, and sometimes all together, especially at the end: because such variation will bring with it convenience for the composer and the singer, beauty to the piece, and delight and pleasure to the ear.

->TENORE.<-

->BASSO.<-

Therefore, by proceeding in this way, it is impossible to always observe such a law; especially because, when occasionally writing for few parts, wanting to achieve the aforementioned consonances might lead to movements so awkward that they would ruin any good and sonorous composition. Then, as the number of parts increases, if one does not observe what has been said, it will be revealed how well one has imitated **Nature**, which (when not corrupted) reduces all things to their perfection. Beyond this, one should know that once three parts of any composition have been arranged—containing among them the already mentioned consonances, or the **Sixth** in place of the **Fifth**—all the other parts added to these would necessarily be **Unisons** or at the **Octave** with one of the three named parts, no matter how many additions there are; as can be understood in many places in the example above. Therefore, the Composer may arrange them in the melody as best suits his convenience. It is certainly true that one should choose the **Octave** rather than the **Unison**; because (as we have said elsewhere) the Unison is not a consonance. <note>In Zarlino's theory, a consonance requires a "mixture" of different pitches; since the Unison is the same pitch, he considers it the "source" of consonance rather than a consonance itself.</note>

## How the Fourth may be placed in compositions. Chapter 60.

Although in compositions for two voices the **Fourth** is not placed unless it is syncopated; <note>In two-part writing, the perfect fourth was treated as a dissonance and allowed only as a suspension (syncopation).</note> and in these [multi-voice] works it can be placed even without syncopation, as best suits the need: because its use is not only useful, but also necessary. Nevertheless, one must know that since the **Fourth** is a consonance, as I have proved elsewhere, it can be arranged in compositions in two ways, as modern Musicians are accustomed to do. First, by placing the **Bass** and the **Tenor** a **Fifth** apart from each other, and adding to these two parts a third part distant from the Bass by an **Octave**; in such a way that the pitch of the Tenor comes to divide, or mediate, such an Octave in **harmonic proportionality**. <note>The "harmonic" division of an octave (2:1) results in a fifth (3:2) on the bottom and a fourth (4:3) on the top. For example, C2-G2-C3.</note> When the parts are positioned in such a manner, a delightful and sweet harmony is born; nor did Musicians ever place it otherwise when they accompanied it with the Fifth. Next, we accompany it with the **Third**; and this we shall do in two ways: for we will either accompany it with the Third placed in the low range, or with the Third placed in the high range. Each of these two accompaniments can be done in two modes: since when one accompanies it with the Third in the low range, one either places the **major [third]** or adds the **minor [third]**. We should know that the **Fourth** accompanied in such a way will always produce a better effect when accompanied by the **minor Third** <note>original: "Terza minore" or "Semiditono"</note> than it would if it had the major one below it. This is because, when placed in that way, it is situated naturally according to the degrees of the consonances, as can be seen in Chapter 15 of the First Part; in which it is seen that after the **minor Third** <note>original: "Semiditono"</note> contained between the terms 6 & 5, there follows immediately the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note> placed between the terms 8 & 6. <note>Zarlino refers to the "Senario," the numbers 1 through 6, and their extensions. The ratio 5:6:8 represents a minor third with a fourth on top, forming a major triad in second inversion (like E-G-C).</note> But when it is arranged with the **major Third** <note>original: "Ditono"</note>, it cannot produce a good effect: because they are not placed together according to the natural order of such consonances; rather, they are joined together in an accidental order. This is because in the named [natural] order, one does not find the major Third placed without any intermediary before the Fourth. Therefore, these two consonances being arranged one after the other against their nature—placing in the high range that which should be placed in the low, and in the low range that which should hold the high—it follows that the sounds born from strings ordered in such a way are less pleasing to the ear than those born from strings stretched according to their natural degrees. For this reason, anyone can know for themselves through experience, and evidently understand from the examples placed below, which of the two accompaniments is truly the good one.

<image-desc>Two musical examples on four-line staves illustrating harmonic intervals. The first stave is labeled "Good." and the second "Less good." showing vertical note alignments (chords) in white mensural notation.</image-desc>

Furthermore, when one accompanies the **Fourth** with the **Third** placed in the high range, this can similarly be done in two ways: for one either adds the **major Third**, or accompanies it with the **minor**. When it is accompanied by the major, it produces a good effect. But when it is accompanied by the minor, it sounds almost like a dissonance. And this is not without reason: for, besides what can be understood from the two examples placed here below when the voices or sounds are performed, the natural order of the **Harmonic Numbers** shows it to us; in which, the proportion of the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note> being found between the terms 4 & 3 (as can be seen in the said place), there follows without any intermediary the propor-

<meta>This page continues Part Three of Zarlino’s treatise, specifically Chapter 60 regarding the placement of the Fourth. The text begins mid-word, completing a discussion on the mathematical ratios (proportions) of intervals within the "harmonic numbers" (the sequence 1 to 6).</meta>

<header>Part Three</header>
<page-num>246</page-num>

...position of the **Major Third** <note>original: "Ditono"</note>, placed between 3 & 4. But in such an order one does not find that, after the proportion or form of the **Fourth** <note>The ratio 4:3</note>, there immediately follows the form of the **Minor Third** <note>The ratio 6:5; original: "Terza minore"</note> by proceeding in said order; as everyone can see. Because of this, it happens that those **Consonances** which are outside of their natural places, and are not ordered according to how their forms lie among the **harmonic numbers** <note>The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, which Zarlino calls the *Senario*</note>, undoubtedly create some dissonance. Therefore, I say that the **Fourth** accompanied by the **Minor Third** placed in the **bass** <note>original: "graue"</note> may always be used; as well as that which has the **Major Third** in the **treble** <note>original: "acuto"</note>; for these cannot produce anything but good effects. 

But when it has the **Major Third** in the bass, or the **Minor Third** in the treble, one will always hear a certain sad effect. Nor should this seem strange to anyone: for what happens to Sight regarding visible things also happens to Hearing regarding audible things. Just as it is a strange thing to see in a building some part placed in the place of another—as if to say the Foundations in the place of the Roof, or the Windows in the place of the Doors, and everything placed contrary to its natural place and without any proportion—so it is a strange thing to hear a mass of sounds, or consonances placed together without proportion and outside of their natural places. 

One will also find, by investigating further, that the **Fourth** which has the **Major Third** <note>original: "Ditono"</note> in the treble is more pleasing to the ear than that which has it in the bass; just as that which has the **Minor Third** <note>original: "Semiditono"</note> in the bass is more pleasing than that which has it in the treble. Of these two compositions, that **Fourth** which is accompanied by the **Minor Third** in the bass will produce a better effect than any other accompaniment; as can be understood from these examples.

->Good. Not good.<-

For although the **Sixths** <note>original: "Seste"</note> which contain the outer limits of these parts placed together are not different from one another in their proportion, and do not make a variation of sounds and consonances, nonetheless the variety of the **pitches** <note>original: "chorde," literally "strings"</note> that they receive in their middle is the reason why one accompaniment is heard as better than the other; it makes the difference between two accompaniments that are both good, distinguishing the "good" from the "better."

->Good. Better.<-

Truly, so great is the power of consonances when they are placed in their own natural places, that not only are those which are arranged in such a manner according to the nature of the harmonic numbers more pleasing to the ear than those placed to the contrary, but they also make every composition in which they are placed more cheerful and more sonorous. This, then, we shall gather from what has been said: that **Fourths** may be placed excellently in compositions when they are located in such a way that they have the **Fifth** or the **Third** beneath them in the bass, as I have shown above. Furthermore, one may sometimes place the **Third** in the treble, especially when it is the **Major Third**; even though this has been little considered by the majority of **practical musicians** <note>original: "Musici prattici"; Zarlino often distinguishes between the "theorist" and the "practitioner"</note> until now. For if the accompaniment of the Fourth with the Major Third placed in the bass—which is truly not very consonant—is tolerated, I see no reason why the accompaniment of the Major Third placed in the treble should not be tolerated; given that this accompaniment is truly better, as experience will always show us.

---

# General Rules. Chapter 61.

There is no doubt that, since the **Fourth** is a consonance, and having shown in the previous Chapter how it must be composed with the **Fifth** and with the **Third**, whenever it is accompanied in the manners I have shown, it will always produce a good effect in the composition. Whenever we wish to use it, we may—without placing the Fifth or the Third in the bass—place the **Major Third** in the treble part, especially when the parts proceed by natural order in this way; for it will bring great convenience to the Composer, aiding him in the beauty of the melodic lines <note>original: "modulationi"</note> and in avoiding the **Tritone** <note>An interval of three whole tones, considered the "devil in music" for its harshness</note>, which could...

<meta>Catchword: could (potrebbe)</meta>

<summary>Zarlino explains that the Fourth sounds best when its internal arrangement mirrors the natural order of the harmonic series, preferring a Third below it or a Major Third above it. He uses an architectural analogy to argue that intervals placed "out of order" create a "sad" or "strange" effect, even if the individual intervals are consonant.</summary>

[which] <note>The sentence completes a thought from the previous page.</note> might arise at times between the parts of the song <term>cantilena; a polyphonic vocal composition</term>; as can be understood in the second example. One can also use the **Eleventh**; as seen further below; which is composed of the **Octave** and the **Fourth**. This is justified because **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, 2nd-century Greek astronomer and music theorist.</note> in the Fifth Chapter of the First book of the *Harmonics* <note>original: "Harmonica"</note>, and **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard textbook for a millennium.</note> in Chapter 10 of the First book of the *Music* place it among the **consonances**. From these examples, one can recognize their nature and how pleasing they might be to the ear; though the usage of modern and ancient composers, who have often accompanied it in such a manner, might be sufficient for us.

<image-desc>A polyphonic musical score with three voices (Treble, Tenor, Bass) illustrating the use of the Eleventh and various distributions of voices.</image-desc>

->Treble. Tenor. Bass.<-

Some composers are in the habit of placing the **high part** <note>Canto</note> at the distance of a **Fourth** from the **middle part** <note>Tenore</note>, and the middle part at the distance of a **Third** from the **low part** <note>Basso</note>. In this arrangement, the **Bass** is a **Sixth** away from the **Soprano**, with a major or minor **Third** in between. When parts are composed in this way, they usually move them up or down several steps together; this way of proceeding is called **Fauxbourdon** <term>Falso bordone; a style of composition using parallel chords in first inversion</term>. But in truth, although such a manner is very much in use and would be very difficult to eliminate, I say that it is not praiseworthy. Aside from the fact that the **Fourth** is a perfect consonance (as I have shown elsewhere) and that we should not violate the Rule given in Chapter 29, it sometimes generates certain relations between the parts that are not harmonic. Therefore, they bring little delight to the ear, as anyone can recognize by the example provided below. The error of such a thing...

<image-desc>A three-part musical example illustrating the "incorrect" or "less delightful" parallel motion of Fauxbourdon.</image-desc>

->Treble. Tenor. Bass.<-

...is manifest from this: if we wish to place the **Thirds** in their natural positions where they reasonably belong, or at least above the **Octave**, one can see how much more reason there is for doing so. Just as in the previous example one heard many **Fourths**, in the example below we can hear just as many **Fifths**. I know well that for many people, the authority of those who have usurped such a license will carry more weight than the reasons I have given above.

<image-desc>A three-part musical example showing Zarlino’s preferred "natural" distribution of intervals, resulting in parallel Fifths (to demonstrate the structural shift) or better spacing.</image-desc>

->Treble. Tenor. Bass.<-

But let those who say "this thing has been used by many" do the worst they can; I care little for them, since they are not—nor do they wish to be—capable of reason. And although the **Third** is a consonance and can be placed wherever it is convenient, nevertheless its true place is not in the **low register** <term>graue</term>, but in the **high register** <term>acuto</term>, above the **Double Octave** <term>Disdiapason</term> or **Fifteenth** <term>Quintadecima</term>. Naturally, an **Octave** placed in the bass cannot be mediated by any other sound; it must be placed simply, without any middle note. This is shown by the **harmonic numbers** <note>The integers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6</note> listed in Chapter 15 of the First Part. Among these, we see the first **Double ratio** <term>Dupla; the 2:1 ratio of the Octave</term> contained within the **Six** <term>Senario</term> between 2 and 1. This is its form, and it is not divided by any middle term. However, the second Octave, placed between 4 and 2, is indeed divided by the number 3 into a **Sesquialtera** <note>The 3:2 ratio, which forms a Fifth</note> found between 3 and 2, and a **Sesquiterza** <note>The 4:3 ratio, which forms a Fourth</note> found between 4 and 3. These are the forms of the **Fifth** <term>Diapente</term> and **Fourth** <term>Diatessaron</term> consonances. Hence, the Fifth in that second Octave remains undivided and whole. But beyond the **Quadruple ratio** <note>The 4:1 ratio, representing two octaves</note>, which is the form of the **Double Octave**, the space is found divided into two parts: a **Sesquiquarta** <note>The 5:4 ratio, which forms a Major Third</note>, which is the for[m]...

He defends the status of the Eleventh as a consonance, citing ancient authorities like Ptolemy and Boethius.</summary>

# Part Three

but the true form of the **Major Third** <term>Ditono; the interval of a major third, with the ratio 5:4</term>, and in a **ratio of 6:5** <term>Sesquiquinta</term>, which is the form of the **Minor Third** <term>Semiditono; the interval of a minor third</term>; the first of which is located between 5 & 4, and the other between 6 & 5. It can be seen, therefore, that the first **Octave** is naturally placed among the **Sonorous Numbers** <note>The "Sonorous Numbers" or *Senario* (1–6) are the basis of Zarlino's harmonic theory, representing the ratios of all "perfect" consonances.</note> without any other middle number; and the **Fifth** follows it without any intermediary; then follows the **Fourth**; and from these two larger parts the second **Octave** <term>Diapason</term> is composed, from which arises the **Double Octave** <term>Disdiapason</term>, that is, the **Fifteenth**. After these comes the **Major Third**, and immediately after it follows the **Minor Third**: in such a way that, if such consonances were placed in **counterpoint** (if this could always be done conveniently) in their proper and natural places, there is no doubt that a harmony would arise as harmonious as man could imagine. And of this we can always see the experience in artificial instruments, especially on the **Organ**, where, having placed the named consonances in order one after the other as I have shown, one cannot describe the good effect they produce. But if by chance the first Octave is divided in the low register by the Fifth, then the harmony becomes somewhat sad; and if such a Fifth were divided into two Thirds, one could hardly bear to hear such a combination, especially if the Minor Third held the place of the Major—that is, if it were placed in the low register. Nevertheless, the first Octave divided in **harmonic proportionality** by the Fifth is bearable; and when the Third is placed above it, it does not produce a sad effect, even though such consonances are not placed in their proper places; and this occurs because they occupy the middle register of the instrument where such an order is contained. One should, therefore, place the Third immediately after the Fifteenth, or at least after the Octave in order; and it should be the **Major Third**, so that the harmony is more cheerful and full; but if it happens to be the Minor, as often occurs, then the harmony will be more mournful. These things are truly little considered by **practical musicians** <term>Prattici; working composers and performers who focus on practice rather than mathematical theory</term>, for without any regard they place the Fifth among the low strings, and also the Third, as it is most convenient for them; how much delight these bring to the ear, I will leave to the judgment of those who possess it. Hence I wish to say only this: that when needing to place the Third in a composition, it is better to always place it above the Octave than within it; I mean to imply that the **Tenth** <note>An Octave plus a Third.</note> will always produce a better effect than the Third. And although one could say that it would also be better to place the Fifth above the Octave in the low part of the **song** <term>cantilena</term>—as it is a closer thing, according to the nature of **harmonic numbers**—than the Third, which is further away; nevertheless, however it is placed, it will always turn out well. But how much better an effect the Tenth makes than the Third can be known by anyone of judgment from these two examples.

This is because that small amount of dissonance heard in the **Tritone** <term>Tritono; an interval of three whole tones, considered the most unstable dissonance</term> and in the **Diminished Fifth** <term>Semidiapente; an interval slightly smaller than a perfect fifth</term> passes quickly and adds sweetness to the following consonance, more than would be heard if it were not there. One may also pass from a **Major Third** to a **Unison**, when the Soprano

proceeds from the high register to the low with the movement of a **Major Third** <term>Ditono</term>; and the Bass and Soprano are arranged according to the precepts given above, while the Tenor remains without changing its position, as is seen. Because the extreme parts—which are perceived by the senses more than the others—are well-regulated, if something should occasionally occur in the other parts that is not so well-regulated, it can be tolerated. Therefore, it is granted to the composer that he may sometimes take some license outside the rule given above in Chapter 38. It shall also be lawful for him to pass from a **Minor Third** to an **Octave** by contrary motions, when the parts are arranged in such a way that the part found at a distance by a similar consonance, which then passes to the Octave, has a **Major Third** in the low register; so that the high part is a **Fifth** distant from the low part, as is seen here.

<image-desc>Three musical staves labeled CANTO, TENORE, and BASSO showing a polyphonic passage. The Tenore part includes a sharp sign (♯) for a leading tone resolution.</image-desc>

Indeed, it is necessary that the parts stay in such a manner: for if they were placed otherwise, making that Third (which is minor) major with the **sharp sign** <note>original: "segno ♯"</note> so that (according to the given rules) one arrives at the perfect interval from the nearest imperfect one, such a thing could not be done in any way without great offense to the hearing. This is because one would end up making a **Fifth** that would have two Major Thirds. But let it be said once and for all: the obligation lies in possible things, and not in the impossible, to which no one is bound. We must, besides this, observe that in the principal **Cadences** of the composition, the parts are arranged and accommodated in such a way that the second part of the suspended note, which is placed as a dissonance, is always distant from the lower part by a **Fourth**, or rather by an **Eleventh**; and with the other part it is always distant by a **Second** or a **Seventh**. This must be observed also in every suspended figure where there is a dissonance, as seen in these examples, from which one may understand the method to be held in other similar cases when they occur. But if we wish to add a fourth part to these, it can always be placed an Octave away from one of the two parts that are a Fifth or **Twelfth** apart, arranging it now in one place and now in another, as it turns out best.

Therefore, the **composer of counterpoint** <term>Contrapuntista; a musician skilled in the art of combining independent melodic lines</term> shall be careful when using them; and he must altogether avoid having any part of the composition perform the **Cadence** <term>Cadenza; a musical conclusion or arrival point</term> when the other parts are arranged in such a way that whichever of the lower voices forms a **Fifth** <term>Quinta; an interval spanning five scale degrees</term> with the middle note of the cadence placed in the high voice, making a **stepwise movement** <term>mouimento congiunto; moving to the very next note in the scale</term> of a **Semitone** <term>Semituono; the smallest interval in this system</term>, when such a note can be marked with the **chromatic sharp sign** <term>cifra ♯ Chromatica</term>. For (as I have said elsewhere) since that part of the cadence naturally produces a semitone, it would be difficult for the singer in such a case to be careful not to perform it in the way it is naturally sung. Consequently, he would then commit an error and place a dissonance where there should be a consonance; that is, he would end up placing an **augmented fifth** <note>original: "Diapente superflua"</note> in place of a true one, as seen here:

<image-desc>Musical notation for four voices (Canto, Alto, Tenore, Basso) showing a musical error related to the use of a chromatic sharp (♯) in a cadence.</image-desc>

The **Soprano** <note>original: "Soprano"</note> will then make the Cadence at the distance of a Fifth from the low part toward the high; as seen in this example. For this reason, composers must be alert to such a thing and not allow the parts to exchange places with one another in this manner: because such an inconvenience would bring something to the ear that it would not much like; even though such Fifths might not be heard when the parts are sung. And because many practitioners do not pay much attention to this, I wanted to say a word about it. Leaving off, then, speaking further on this matter, I shall come to discuss the **counterpoints** composed for three voices that are called **Double**, and those that are made with some **restriction** <term>obbligo; a structural constraint or rule the composer imposes on himself, such as a canon</term>.

## On the various types of Counterpoints, and first on those called Double. Chapter 62.

**Double counterpoint** <term>Contrapunto doppio; a style of writing where voices can be swapped or inverted while maintaining harmony</term> for three voices is almost the same as the double counterpoint for two voices, which I explained and showed above in Chapter 56. However, such a difference is found between the two: while the former cannot be sung by more than two voices—or three if adding a part that sings in the high or low range, above or below one of the principal parts by a **Tenth** <term>Decima; an interval of an octave plus a third</term>—the latter cannot be sung except with those parts that are principally composed, that is, for three voices, with great variety of **harmony** in the **Repeat** <term>Replica; the inversion or restatement of the musical section</term>, and very different from that heard in the principal version. Therefore, remembering what double counterpoint for two voices is, it is...

**Third**

It would be redundant to repeat what **double counterpoint for three voices** <term>Contrapunto doppio a tre voci; a technique where three independent musical lines are written so they can be rearranged or swapped while still sounding harmonious</term> is; for by understanding the nature of the first [two-voice version], one can easily grasp the essence of the second. In discussing these double counterpoints composed for three voices, I say that they take many forms. They can be composed in various ways by following certain rules, so that when the **Principal** <term>Principale; the original version of a polyphonic composition</term> is sung and one kind of harmony is heard, the same notes and intervals are then sung differently in the **Reply** <term>Replica; the version of the music where the voice parts have been swapped or transposed</term>, producing a great diversity of sound.

Although there are many ways to compose such counterpoints, I will present only those that seem the most challenging and refined, so as not to weary the reader. From these examples, any clever student will be able to understand how to manage any other style of similar composition.

The first method will be this: once the three principal parts have been composed as shown—following certain necessary precautions—and we wish to create the Reply, we shall place the **Bass** of the Principal in the position of the **Soprano**, transposed a **Fifth** <term>Quinta; a musical interval spanning five scale degrees</term> higher; the Soprano in the position of the **Tenor**, transposed an **Octave** <term>Ottaua; the interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency</term> lower; and the Tenor in the position of the Bass, likewise transposed an Octave lower. It is done in this manner. It would truly be impossible for this to turn out well if one did not

# [Part] Three

<page-num>253</page-num>
**Part 253**

<image-desc>Musical notation for a bass part (BASSO) on two staves using white mensural notation and a bass clef (F-clef).</image-desc>

->BASS.<-

...one should observe never to place the **Bass** in the **Principal** <term>Principale; the original version of a polyphonic composition</term> at the distance of a **Sixth** <term>Sesta; a musical interval spanning six scale degrees</term> from the other parts, even though the other two parts may be so placed. Similarly, one must never place the Bass with the **Tenor** in a **Third** <term>Terza; a three-note interval</term> followed by a **Fifth** <term>Quinta; a five-note interval</term>; nor the Bass with the **Soprano** in a **Tenth** <term>Decima; an interval of an octave plus a third</term> followed by a **Twelfth** <term>Duodecima; an interval of an octave plus a fifth</term> when the parts descend together. This is because the Twelfth, which is placed in the Principal between the Bass and the Soprano, becomes a **Unison** <term>Vnisono; two voices sounding the same pitch</term> between the Tenor and the Soprano in the **Reply** <term>Replica; the version where voices are swapped or transposed</term>; and the Fifth, likewise, becomes an **Octave** <term>Ottaua; an eight-note interval</term>. 

We can now see that in this kind of counterpoint or composition, one cannot use a **Seventh Suspension** <term>Sincopa di Settima; a rhythmic device where a note is held to create a dissonance that must resolve</term> in the Principal, since it cannot resolve to a Sixth. Nor can one use a Tenth followed by a Fifth when proceeding by **contrary motion** <term>mouimenti contrarij; when one voice moves up while the other moves down</term>. 

However, when the Bass is at an Octave with the Tenor, then the Soprano may be a Third below the Tenor; and similarly, when they are at the distance of a Tenth from one another, which is not permitted in any other way. The Tenor may likewise descend below the Bass by any interval desired, but one must be careful not to exceed the Sixth, because the parts would then become separated by too great a distance. One could also place the Soprano below the Bass if necessary, but it should not exceed a Fifth, because parts placed in such a way become very distant from each other in the Reply. One may also use a Seventh placed in the Soprano within a suspension when the Bass is placed a Fifth above the Tenor. Likewise, it can be used in the Bass, but only when it is placed above the Tenor. 

Many other things would need to be shown that must be observed to have an easy way of composing; these, to avoid being long-winded and because they are not strictly necessary, are left out. Indeed, I have been moved to omit them for this reason: that if anyone desires to make something excellent, they must create the Principal and the Reply together; and thus they will be able to see all the inconveniences that might occur. Finally, one must know that if the Principal is composed according to the observance of our rules shown above, the Reply will likewise be observed; if it is done otherwise, the opposite will follow. 

And let this be said sufficiently regarding the **First Type** of double counterpoint for three voices, whose Reply proceeds with similar movements to those contained in the Principal.

The **Second Type** is that in which the Reply proceeds by contrary motion to those movements found in the parts of the Principal, as can be seen in the examples below. But the Reply could never turn out well unless certain things were observed, such as: ensuring that all parts of the **Suspensions** <term>Sincope</term> placed in the Principal are **consonant** <term>consonanti; intervals that sound stable and pleasant</term>; and never placing the Tenor at the distance of a **Fourth** <term>Quarta; a four-note interval</term> from the Soprano. These things must be principally observed in every way; other things that might occur will not be difficult when...

The **Reply** <term>Replica; the version of the music where the original voices are swapped or transposed</term> will be composed together with the **Principal** <term>Principale; the primary or original version of a polyphonic composition</term>. In this kind of **Counterpoint** <term>Contrapunto; the art of combining different melodic lines</term>, one may use **Sixths** <term>Seste; an interval spanning six scale degrees</term> and place the parts as far from one another as one wishes. The **Tenor** can take the place of the **Bass**, and the **Soprano** can take the place of the Tenor, or even that of the Bass. 

To create the Reply, one places the Bass of the Principal in the position of the Soprano, higher by a **Sixth**; the Soprano in the position of the Bass, lower by a **Tenth** <term>Decima; an interval of an octave plus a third</term>; and the Tenor, lower by a **Whole Tone** <term>Tuono; a standard whole step in the musical scale</term>. In doing this, ensure that the parts proceed by **contrary motions** <term>mouimenti contrarij; one voice moving up while the other moves down</term> compared to those found in the Principal. In this way, we will have a different harmony, just as the placements and the movements of the voices are varied and different. 

If we observe the rules in the composition of the Principal that have been declared in many places, there is no doubt that the Reply (if not in its entirety, at least in many parts) will also be correctly observed. One can also compose another type of similar **double counterpoint** <term>Contrapunto doppio; a composition designed so that its parts can be transposed and still sound harmonious</term>, which will share the qualities of both types of these counterpoints. This is achieved when one observes all those rules used in their composition, which are **negative rules**—that is, they forbid doing certain things. Once this is done, we will have a counterpoint that can have a Reply similar to the first and second modes shown here, as can be seen:
