# Part 255

The Third species of the said counterpoint is created when the *Principal* <term>Principale; the primary version of a musical composition</term> is composed in such a way that the *Bass* remains on its original pitches <note>original: "chorde principali", literally "principal strings," referring to the notes of the scale</note> without any change; and the *Soprano* becomes the *Bass* in the *Reply* <term>Replica; the inverted or transposed version of the music</term>, transposed a *Twelfth* <term>Duodecima; an interval spanning an octave plus a fifth</term> lower; and the *Tenor* by a *Fifth* <term>Quinta; an interval spanning five scale degrees</term> lower, in the manner seen here.

<image-desc>A musical score featuring five staves of white mensural notation. The staves represent different voices categorized as 'Principal' and 'Reply'. ->*Principal, &* SOPRANO.<-

->TENOR *of the Principal.*<-

->BASS *of the Principal; &* SOPRANO <note>original: "Canto", referring to the highest voice</note> *of the Reply.*<-

->BASS *of the Reply.*<-

It is certainly true that this method is more difficult than any of those shown; therefore, if one wishes to use it, many things must be observed so that the *Reply* turns out well. First: When the *Tenor* sings with the *Bass* in two voices, the parts must not be separated by an *Octave* <term>Ottaua; an interval of eight scale degrees</term> nor by a *Sixth* <term>Sesta; an interval of six scale degrees</term>, especially when the *Tenor* is placed above the *Bass*. But when it is placed below the *Bass*, it must not be distant from the *Bass* by a *Third* <term>Terza; an interval of three scale degrees</term> nor a *Fifth*; rather, it should be a *Sixth* or an *Octave*, and even a *Fifth*—on the condition, however, that such a *Fifth* occurs on the second part of a *syncopation* <term>sincopa; a suspension or rhythmic displacement</term>, immediately followed by a *Sixth*. This is because when these two parts are placed in their proper positions, they cannot be further apart than a *Fifth*; and such a *Fifth* becomes a *Unison* <term>Vnisono; two voices sounding the same pitch</term> in the *Reply*. One should also not use a syncopation of a *Seventh* <term>Settima; an interval of seven scale degrees</term>, but only that of a *Second* <term>Seconda; an interval of two scale degrees</term> or a *Fourth* <term>Quarta; an interval of four scale degrees</term>.

Similarly, when the *Soprano* and the *Bass* sing alone, one must take care that the *Soprano* does not pass below the *Bass*; nor should one use a syncopation of a *Seventh*, although that of a *Second* and *Fourth* can be used excellently in the *Soprano*. Nor should these parts be separated by a *Sixth*, nor should they be further apart than a *Twelfth*. Do not use a *Third* followed by a *Fifth*, or a *Tenth* <term>Decima; an interval of an octave plus a third</term> followed by a *Twelfth* when the parts are descending.

When the *Tenor* and the *Soprano* sing together, one should not use a *Fifth* unless the *Tenor* makes a *Syncopation*, in the second part of which the *Fifth* is contained; this must be followed immediately by a *Sixth*, and after that a *Third* or another *Sixth*. Do not use a *Sixth* followed by an *Octave* when the parts are descending; instead, place the *Sixth* in another way that sounds well. The *Soprano* can descend below the *Tenor* by up to an *octave* when it is convenient. And when one wishes to use a syncopation of a *Fourth* in either of these two parts, it will work very well. One must be careful not to dwell for a long time on a *Third*, because in the *Reply* this becomes a *Sixth* with the *Bass*. Nor should we rest the parts upon an *Octave*, as this turns into a *Unison*. 

All these things must be observed so that one may reach the desired end with some ease. Because by observing these rules, it will be easy to compose these *Three-voice Counterpoints*; all the more so because one should compose the *Principal* and the *Reply* at the same time, so that the composer can see the difficulties that may occur in such compositions. However, as a final conclusion, it should be noted that even if the *Principal* were purged

### On Three-Voice Counterpoint Composed with Certain Constraints. Chapter 63.

There is also another way of making Three-voice Counterpoint which some practitioners use when writing over a Plainchant <term>Canto fermo; a pre-existing, steady melody, usually from liturgical chant</term>, or over any other Subject <term>Soggetto; the main musical theme or melody used as a foundation</term>, with a certain constraint <term>obligo; a self-imposed rule or structural requirement, such as a canon</term>. An example of this would be making two parts sing one after the other in Succession <term>Conseguenza; a musical sequence where one voice follows another, often called a canon</term>, or in Imitation, for a certain duration. This method is certainly not to be looked down upon, because it is beautiful and ingenious, and proves very useful, especially when composed with the proper techniques. And although the types of constraints are infinite, I will nonetheless show only a few so as not to weary the reader, so that from them one may learn the method to follow in other similar cases.

The first way, then, is when the counterpoint parts are composed with such a constraint that one follows the other in the aforementioned manner, through the same steps or movements, after the duration of a Minim <term>Minima; a musical note value equivalent to a half note</term>. This can be done in two ways: namely, when the parts sing in the low register <term>grave; the lower range of voices</term> below the Subject part, and when they sing above in the high register <term>acuto; the higher range of voices</term>. In these two ways, one must observe that the principal part—that is, the Guide <term>Guida; the leading voice that begins a canon</term>—does not move by a single step, which is to say a Second <term>Seconda; the distance between two adjacent notes on a scale</term>. For the Follower <term>Consequente; the voice that mirrors the melody of the Guide</term> would necessarily end up being a dissonant interval away from it; namely, a Second. Therefore, once this has been observed, by ensuring the parts sing with graceful movements, these and other similar Counterpoints will then arise.

The second way is when two parts of the Counterpoint <term>Contrapunto; the art of combining different melodic lines</term> follow one another at the distance of a **Fifth**, after a **Minim Rest** <gloss>Pausa di Minima</gloss>. And this can likewise be done in two ways: either the Leader <gloss>Guida</gloss> will be the higher of the two counterpoint parts and the Follower <gloss>Consequente</gloss> the lower; or conversely, the Leader will be the lower and the Follower the higher. It must be noted, however, that it is characteristic of both methods to modulate—or sing, if we prefer—by leaps or movements of the **Octave**, the **Sixth**, and the **Third**; it very rarely happens that one can sing by leaps of a **Fifth**. And when they proceed by many conjunct degrees <term>gradi congiunti; moving from one note to the very next in the scale</term>, it is characteristic of the first method that the Leader proceeds from high to low; in the second method, it is the opposite—that is, from low to high—as can be seen in both of these two examples.

And the composer, while crafting counterpoint in any of the demonstrated ways—whether writing it down or improvising <term>alla sprovveduta; literally "unprepared," referring to the practice of composing music mentally or at the keyboard without prior notation</term>—must always have regard for what the Follower part is capable of doing, so as not to commit an error. These things, then, must be primarily observed in such counterpoints; for even if some other observation were required, it would be of little consequence. But one must know that it is impossible in all these types of double counterpoints, and those made with similar constraints <term>oblighi; strict rules or formal patterns the composer must follow</term>, to fully observe the Rules given above; especially when such constraints increase. This is because one cannot always maintain the beauty and decorum of the Counterpoint, both in terms of the modulation and the invention <gloss>inuentione</gloss>, and the manner of placing the

I say this so that the diligent observer of our Rules <term>Precetti; the foundational principles of music theory being taught here</term>, seeing some things that are not so well corrected, will not be surprised. And if at times I have shown things that do not turn out so well, I have wanted in this to imitate the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle, often called simply "The Philosopher" in the Renaissance.</note>, who, having shown the goodness of Logic and Philosophy and the true way of arguing, after having written many things in both faculties, also wrote the books of fallacious or Sophistical Syllogisms, which he called *Refutations* <note>original: "Elenchi," referring to Aristotle's *Sophistici Elenchi* (On Sophistical Refutations).</note>. He did this not so they would be used, but so that (should the occasion arise) everyone would know how to guard against the entanglements of the Sophists, who wish to be held as learned even though they are not. It is truly a good and excellent thing to know such Counterpoints and use them when convenient, but I do not highly praise frequenting them. This is because it is impossible—when the Counterpustist is bound to the observance of so many constraints—for the Counterpoint to be so elegant and sonorous that it brings pleasing delight to the Ear.

### What must be observed when one wishes to improvise a Third part over two others already provided. Chapter 64.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure (possibly a satyr or Pan) sitting in a landscape with floral flourishes.</image-desc>
SKILLED Counterpustists are sometimes accustomed, when a song <gloss>cantilena</gloss> for two voices is sung, to elegantly add a Third part spontaneously <term>alla sprovveduta; literally "unprepared," referring to the practice of improvising a new melodic line over existing music without prior notation</term>, in such a way that they make the harmony <gloss>concento</gloss> heard in Three voices. Therefore, I—in order not to leave behind anything useful or honorable in this Art—have decided (besides having shown the method to be held in composing three-voice counterpoint of various types) to show the method one must hold when wishing to practice singing such a part in this manner. And I have taken up this task willingly, since I have sometimes heard some—I will not say foolish, but altogether presumptuous and arrogant men—who, to make it understood that they are very brave and capable in this, set out to go even further. For they are not only content to want to make a Third part over such songs, but moreover, over any other song, even if it were for Twelve voices, they want to add a Thirteenth part. This part they make by only performing counterpoint over the Bass, without seeing any of the other parts; and they often make use of a Rule of theirs, which they hold as a great secret: to place the part they are adding at the distance of a Third or a Tenth from the Bass. In such a way, they lead the fools who are like them, and who understand nothing more, to believe that they are performing miracles. But how well this is done, I will let everyone of judgment decide. For when these added parts of theirs are seen written down in the manner they sing them—besides the fact that those skilled in Music hear the things they do against the Art—even if they are not in writing, a thousand errors they commit against the common Rules would be discovered, and they would be seen to be full of infinite dissonances. Now, to come to my first intention, I say that after everyone has practiced excellently in the composition of the demonstrated Counterpoints and wishes to add such a part spontaneously, it will be necessary for him to work separately for a few days on such a thing in this manner: Having proposed some song composed for two voices to which he wishes to add the Third part, he must diligently keep in mind the passages and the melodic movements <gloss>modulationi</gloss> that the two proposed parts make together, so that he can understand in what manner their counterpoint is ordered, and can then add without any error the part he desires. And he must by all means keep this order: because a single part is not sufficient (as many who are ignorant advise) to show the Counterpoint that must be added in the Third part, especially since varied Counterpoints can be placed over the same Subject <term>Soggetto; the main musical theme or cantus firmus</term>.

Part. 260

catchword: Quo <note>The catchword refers to the beginning of a Latin quotation from Horace likely appearing on the next page.</note>

*Therefore, having such regard, the counterpoint composer <note>original: "Contrapuntista"</note> will be able to perfectly arrange his counterpoint in the manner that seems best and most convenient to him; whether he wishes to add a high part <note>original: "parte acuta"</note> above the low part of the two proposed voices, or whether he wishes to place a low part <note>original: "parte graue"</note> beneath them. It is quite true that sometimes placing the added part at the distance of a tenth <term>tenth; an interval spanning an octave plus a third</term> or a third <term>third; an interval spanning three scale degrees</term> from one of the two parts is very convenient. But one must be careful: when the proposed voices are a third apart and the added part sings a tenth away from the lower of the two (when adding a high part) or the higher of the two (when adding a low part), the octave <note>original: "Ottaua"</note> will always be heard. I say the same when they are a tenth apart and the added part sings a third away. Thus, if the two proposed voices have many thirds or tenths in succession—as is sometimes done—the added part would create just as many consecutive octaves without any intervening interval, which would be an error. Therefore, it is a good and even necessary thing to examine the counterpoint of the two proposed voices to avoid errors that might occur. If one were to do otherwise, it would be impossible to produce good work, unless one had every part perfectly memorized.*

*And because it may happen that one accommodates or adds such a part in two ways—namely, to some songs <note>original: "cantilene"</note> that are not composed according to the warnings or rules given, and likewise to those ordered according to the methods shown above—the counterpoint composer shall not be so strictly bound to observe the aforementioned precepts when making a third part over those composed without said warnings. Nevertheless, it will always be praiseworthy, when possible, for such an added part to meet the conditions required in every good composition. But when the song is composed regularly, he must by all means adhere to the shown precepts as much as he can, as is proper. To better understand the method to be held in such a business, I have chosen to add two different versions of a third part; added, I say, to a two-voice composition by Josquin <note>original: "Iosquino"</note> found in the motet *Blessed are you, Queen of the Heavens* <note>original: "Benedicta es coelorum regina"</note> for six voices. Once these have been seen and examined, one can see the method to be held when wishing to add such a part to any other two-voice composition. But it should be noted that added parts sometimes proceed by movements that are somewhat distant [leaps], and this is tolerable due to the difficulty found in accommodating such a part to the continuous melody of the song. For it is one thing to compose all parts together, and another to add a third to two existing parts—which is a very difficult thing, requiring a man highly accomplished in music, and a very praiseworthy thing when the addition is well-made.*

## What must be observed regarding Compositions of Four or more voices. Chapter 65.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'V' containing a scene of a man in a landscape standing near a tree.</image-desc>

*HAVING SEEN sufficiently what is required in the composition of songs for three voices, it is fitting that we now show those things that coincide in songs composed for four, and even more voices. Therefore, it should be noted that in these compositions, one must observe all those things that were observed in the aforementioned compositions. The greatest difficulty that may occur is in arranging the parts of the song in such a way that one gives way to the other, that they are easy to sing, and that they have a beautiful, regulated, and elegant progression. These things cannot be so easily taught on paper; therefore, they are left to the discretion and judgment of the composer. I will say that what happens to the musician is what also happens to the physician: just as the latter cannot have perfect knowledge of medicine simply by having studied Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, and many other excellent doctors—unless he has practiced with other physicians, frequently reasoned and discussed many things belonging to that art, felt many pulses, viewed excrement, and made a thousand experiments—so the musician cannot be perfect simply by having read and re-read many books. In the end, to well understand what I have shown above and many other things I am about to show, he will need at times to discuss with someone who has knowledge of the practice (that is, of counterpoint), so that if he has picked up any vice or understood something incorrectly, he may be corrected. For a vice taken from the beginning turns into a habit when continued for long, and such a habit is difficult to leave behind; just as Horace <note>original: "Horatio"</note> demonstrates to us, saying:*

Header: Part

> *A jar will long preserve the scent of what it was once steeped in when new.* <note>original: "Quo semel imbuta recens, seruabit odorem Testa diu." A quote from the Roman poet Horace, suggesting that early lessons or habits are the most enduring.</note> And if Theory <term>Speculativa; the mathematical and philosophical study of music</term> without Practice <term>Prattica; the application of music through performance and composition</term> (as I have said at other times) is worth little—considering that Music does not consist solely in Theory—so too is Practice truly imperfect without the former. And this is obvious: because certain Theorists, wanting to treat musical matters without having a good knowledge of Practice, have spoken a thousand bits of nonsense and committed a thousand errors. Similarly, some who have wanted to govern themselves by Practice alone, without knowing any underlying reason, have committed thousands upon thousands of follies in their compositions, without even noticing a thing. But returning to our purpose, I say that when wanting to begin the types of Compositions mentioned above, one must first find the Subject <term>Soggetto; the primary melodic theme or "subject" upon which a polyphonic work is built</term>. Once found, one can begin the Counterpoint from whichever part is most convenient. Thus, let us suppose one wishes to begin the song with the Bass part; immediately the Composer will be able to recognize the placement of the Alto, the Soprano, and the Tenor. Likewise, if starting with any other part, such as the Tenor or the Bass, he will know the positions of the other parts in order, guiding himself according to the method shown above in the Table <note>Likely referring to a table of voice-leading intervals provided earlier in Zarlino's treatise.</note>; also observing those Rules that I have shown in many places above when discussing the method of composing for Two and Three voices. By observing all this, he will be able to reach the desired goal and acquire honor, which often results in great profit as well. But so that one may see the method to be held and the procedure in such compositions—although there are infinite examples for Four voices composed by many excellent composers—I will provide only two compositions based on the Plainchant <term>Canto fermo; a pre-existing, "fixed" melody, usually from the Gregorian chant tradition</term>. Once these have been examined, one may gain some light to follow further from good to better, and undertake greater tasks; and to compose other songs from one's imagination <note>original: "di fantasia"</note>, such as Motets <note>Sacred choral works.</note>, Madrigals <note>Secular vocal compositions for several voices.</note>, and other beautiful Songs; preparing the Subject either by taking some other Plainchant or any other part, as seems best to the Composer.

And although in every perfect composition four parts alone are sufficient—namely the Soprano, the Alto, the Tenor, and the Bass—nevertheless, when one wishes to go further and have a greater number of parts, it will suffice simply to double (as I have said elsewhere) one of the four named parts. Such an added part will likewise be called Soprano, or Tenor, or indeed Alto, or Bass, according to which part has been doubled; one adds to them the designation "Second" or "Third" according to the number of those parts found in such a song <term>cantilena; a general term for a polyphonic musical work</term>. Furthermore, the extreme pitches <term>chorde; literally "strings," referring here to the outer notes or the vocal range</term> of the added part are made equal to those of the part being doubled. However, it would not be an error if they were not equal, and the pitches of the added part extended further toward the low <term>grave; the lower register</term> or toward the high <term>acuto; the higher register</term> than those of the doubled part (that is, the principal part). # Part Three

...habitual to compose the song <term>cantilena; a general term for a polyphonic musical work</term> without the Soprano; in whose place one puts a Contralto, somewhat higher than the main one by a Third more or less, which matters little. The same is done when leaving out both the Soprano and the Alto: composing with three Tenors and a Bass; or with three Basses and one Tenor; and sometimes with four Basses, and in other ways as well, as it turns out most convenient. This way of composing is called for **Changed Voices** <note>original: "a Voci mutate"; voices moved out of their standard ranges</note>, or for **Equal Voices** <note>original: "a Voci pari"</note>. One also composes with two Sopranos and a Contralto, or a Tenor and the Bass; sometimes with three Sopranos and a Bass; sometimes with four Sopranos, both in four voices as well as in five and more; always adding those parts that are necessary, as is seen every day in modern compositions.

But this manner of composing—even though the parts come to multiply and be arranged differently than is done in others—makes no variety of harmony; that is, it does not give birth to a variation of chords beyond those I showed in Chapter 58 above. It is very true that such a difference is found between the first [standard] and these second [equal voice] compositions: that while in those the field is wider—that is, the low part is further from the high part of the entire harmony—in these the space is more restricted. For the extremes of the low and high parts together are enclosed quite conveniently between fifteen strings <term>chorde; notes or pitches</term> at most, and even less if necessary; whereas in the others they are enclosed within twenty, as we shall see in the Fourth Part.

## Some Warnings Concerning Compositions Made
## for More than Three Voices. Chapter 66.

THE Counterpunter <term>Contrapuntiſta; the composer of counterpoint</term> must furthermore take note that, although I have said elsewhere that he should strive to place the parts of the song so that they proceed by contrary movements, in compositions for many voices this Rule shall be understood to be observed when at least one of the named parts ascends or descends by contrary movements. For if one wished to observe such a rule in all parts, this, if it were not impossible, would at least be difficult.

He must also take note that in every composition for many voices, when any syncopated figure <note>a suspension</note> is used in which a dissonance is found in its second part, all the other parts of the composition—be they as many as you like—must accord among themselves. For (as was said elsewhere) the Dissonance placed in the syncopation is almost not perceived by the senses for many reasons. And even if the ear is offended in some part by the Dissonance placed in such a manner, the other parts must not be dissonant among themselves, so as not to doubly offend the Ear. Hence, when the second part of the syncopated figure is dissonant, those parts that strike together over that dissonant part must be consonant among themselves. Therefore, when the Dissonance is found placed in such a manner, we can then place four parts distant from one another by a Third, among which the Octave will not be heard, as is seen here:

And because it will sometimes happen that one composes upon words which require a somewhat harsh and rough harmony, so that the effects come to imitate the subject contained in the speech <term>Oratione; the text or lyrics</term>; when it is necessary to use such harshness, then one may use Sixths in which the notes are of some value, such as Breves and Semibreves mixed together. Or, one can use Dissonances among themselves that are ordered according to the Rules and modes shown above, and the purpose will be achieved; as would happen by placing the Fourth or the Eleventh in the Syncopation, as can be seen in the following examples.

...found likewise distant by an Octave; provided that they ascend or descend one after the other; and that the voice which is first to touch the second pitch <term>chorda; literally 'string', referring to a specific note or pitch</term> does not wait for the other part, but immediately changes place. If the second part has first made a Pause <term>Pausa; a rest</term> of the same value as the note <term>figura; the visual shape of the note indicating its duration</term> placed on that second pitch, even if both parts touch that same pitch, it can never truly be said that two Unisons <term>Vnisoni; two voices on the exact same pitch</term> or two Octaves have been made between them. And although I have already said in Chapter 47 that a Rest or a Dissonance placed between two perfect consonances is not enough to create a variation in the harmony <term>concento; the overall harmonic effect</term>, I say now that I showed there that the notes making up the Counterpoint <term>Contrapunto</term> were arranged differently than they are in these types of counterpoint. This is because two Unisons or two Octaves are truly made when the parts ascend or descend together without being separated by any Rest; or when, after the Rest, one of the parts falls upon the other without any middle ground. Therefore, when Rests are interposed and one part flees before the other arrives at the pitch already touched, they are not understood to be, nor are they, nor can it ever be said in any way that they are placed against any of the given Rules; as is seen below in the example. such a manner, they can always be used in every composition, whether for Four, Five, or whatever other number of voices one desires. Regarding these and other similar cases that may occur, everyone can find a full resolution from what has been said; therefore, I will not extend myself further, so as not to lose time. Whenever it also happens that one wishes to compose a Song <term>Cantilena</term> for Five, Six, or even more voices, one can observe what has been practiced by many most celebrated Musicians: they would sometimes take for a Subject a Tenor of Plainchant <term>Canto fermo; a pre-existing melody used as the foundation of a polyphonic work</term>, and then accommodate it with various note values as it turned out most convenient for them. They founded the Composition upon such a Tenor and made the parts sing in the way that suited them best, so that they created a good harmony, using Imitation <term>Fuga; literally 'flight', the technique of voices following one another with the same melody</term> with one another, or making one imitate the other in the manner I have shown above. If one desires an example of this, it can be seen in several Motets <term>Motetti; sacred polyphonic choral works</term> already composed by Adriano <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), Zarlino's teacher and the maestro di cappella at St. Mark's in Venice</note>, such as the one for six voices that begins *Nothing after the sacred* <note>original: "Nil postquam sacrum"</note>; and in those for five voices, *Victory, hail!* <note>original: "Victor io salve"</note> and *Renowned of the Sforzas* <note>original: "Inclite sforciadum"</note>; and in many others by other Composers. They also took a Tenor of plainchant over which they arranged (as they still do today) two or three parts in Canon <term>Consequenza; 'consequence', where one or more voices strictly follow a leading voice</term>; and then they built the other parts over those. An example of this can be found in the Motets *The Word from on high* <note>original: "Verbum supernum"</note> over the chant *O saving victim* <note>original: "O salutaris hostia"</note>; and in the one that begins *Beyond the course of things* <note>original: "Præter rerum seriem"</note>, composed by Adriano for seven voices; and in the one by Iachetto <note>likely Jacquet of Mantua (1483–1559), a prolific composer of motets</note> for six voices that begins *I went down into my garden* <note>original: "Descendi in ortum meum"</note>. Furthermore, one will find composed in the same manner the motet *Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me* <note>original: "Miserere mei Deus, miserere mei"</note> over the Antiphon *Remember not, O Lord* <note>original: "Ne reminiscaris Domine"</note>; and the Lord’s Prayer *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noster"</note> with the Angelic Salutation *Hail Mary* <note>original: "Ave Maria"</note>, which were composed one for six and the others for seven voices. However, the Composer must be careful that in those Imitations made over such Tenors, the parts can be distant from each other by a Third, a Fourth, a Fifth, a Sixth, or other similar Consonances <term>Consonanze</term>; but rarely is the Fourth used followed immediately by the Sixth, or vice versa. 265 [Third] Part.

...sometimes two Sixths <note>Sixths are intervals that can be difficult to manage in counterpoint when many voices are moving together.</note> are placed: because they are difficult to accompany with the other parts. Such Consequences <term>Consequenze; here referring to the "follower" voice in a canon or fugue</term> should, and indeed truly must, be composed before the other parts are composed: but in composing them, one must always consider how the parts that are to be added can be accommodated in the song <term>cantilena; a general term for a musical composition or melody</term>; so that one does not have double the labor in composing the whole body of the work, should something go wrong in such Consequences. And if, in adding the other parts, some inconvenience were found; or, if by changing the parts of the Fixed Song <term>Canto fermo; a pre-existing melody, often from plainchant, used as the basis for a polyphonic work</term> placed in such Consequences, a better effect were made; then the Composer should not spare any effort; but must change his mind, adding to or taking away from the said parts whatever is necessary. This will be easy when the parts have been well-ordered from the beginning. 

But it should be noted that the parts that sing in Fugue <term>Fuga; at this time, this usually referred to a strict canon where one voice mimics another exactly</term> cannot always be arranged in such a way that the Follower <term>Consequente</term> sings everything that the Guide <term>Guida; the leading voice in a canon</term> sings; therefore it is necessary that, as the Guide continues singing until the end, the Follower comes to a stop a short distance away; as can be seen in many songs composed in such a manner; and especially in those Motets *Come Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Veni sancte Spiritus"</note> by Adrian <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), a highly influential Flemish composer and maestro di cappella at St. Mark’s in Venice.</note> composed for Six voices; and *O blessed pontiff* <note>original: "O beatum pontificem"</note>, which I once composed by imitating the fixed song, for Five voices. 

One should also use such discretion in arranging the parts; so that the one that sings the Fixed Song in its proper place; after having sung all that is necessary, whether it be the Fixed Song or an Imitation; that which it might sing further than what the Follower must sing, should at least be almost a repetition. The Follower then must be arranged in such a way that it sings and finishes the entire Fixed Song, and not out of its order. Of these, many suitable examples can be found, such as the Motet, *Hail Queen of Mercy* <note>original: "Salue regina misericordiæ"</note>; and the one that begins, *The Jews were arguing* <note>original: "Litigabant Iudæi"</note>, over the fixed song, *Eat the fat* <note>original: "Comedite pinguia"</note>, which I composed many years ago for Six voices. 

One can also take a Fixed Song and arrange many parts over it; placing two or more against each other in continuous Fugue, or "tied" <term>legata; a strict, continuous canon</term>, as we might say; as Jachet <note>Jachet de Mantua (1483–1559), a prominent composer of the post-Josquin generation.</note> did in the motet *Your wall* <note>original: "Murus tuus"</note>; and Adrian in the motet *Hail holy mother* <note>original: "Salue sancta parens"</note> for Six voices. We could similarly take any Tenor, arranging it with another part in Fugue in such a manner that, by repeating the parts, they make a second section, so that the one which was first the Guide becomes the Follower; and likewise the one that was the Follower becomes the Guide. Many compositions are found in this manner, among which is the motet by Adrian, *The hunter of hares* <note>original: "Venator lepores"</note>, over the Fixed Song, *Silver and gold have I none* <note>original: "Argentum, & aurum non est mihi"</note>; and the motet *In the beginning God, before He made the earth* <note>original: "In principio Deus antequàm terram faceret"</note>, over that fixed song, *All wisdom* <note>original: "Omnis sapientia"</note>, which I once composed to be sung by Six voices, just as the aforementioned is also sung. 

Practitioners <note>The "Prattici," or practical composers, as opposed to pure theorists.</note> also sometimes use the technique of imitating two or more Tenors from various church chants to compose certain songs for many voices, in such a way that one of the parts comes to imitate one chant, and another part the other; as did Josquin <note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), perhaps the most famous composer of the High Renaissance.</note>, who in such a manner in a composition for Six voices imitated Four, namely: *Loving mother of the Redeemer* <note>original: "Alma redemptoris mater"</note>, *Hail Queen of the Heavens* <note>original: "Aue regina cœlorum"</note>, *Inviolate, whole, and chaste* <note>original: "Inuiolata, integra, & casta"</note>, and *Queen of Heaven* <note>original: "Regina cœli"</note>; as Gombert <note>Nicolas Gombert (c. 1495–c. 1560), known for his dense polyphonic style.</note> also did in a Song for Four voices, which begins *Hail Queen. Loving mother of the Redeemer. Inviolate. Hail Queen of the Heavens*, imitating many of them, as can be seen there; which anyone else could also do, imitating various others: because truly such a thing is very praiseworthy, being ingenious. 

One can also take two Tenors of a fixed song, and arrange them as best suits the song, and compose the other parts over them; as Costanzo Festa <note>Costanzo Festa (c. 1485–1545), an early master of the Italian madrigal and sacred music.</note> did in the motet *I will exalt You, Lord* <note>original: "Exaltabo te Domine"</note> for Six voices, in which he arranged the Antiphon *With joy* <note>original: "Cum iucunditatem"</note>, and the first verse of the Song of Zechariah, *Blessed be the Lord God of Israel* <note>original: "Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel"</note>. We could also (as others have done) place two parts of the song—leaving the fixed song aside—in Consequence; or else place them tied together with Imitation; of which one can find an example in the motet *Behold, you are beautiful* <note>original: "Ecce tu pulchra es"</note>, which I once composed for Five voices. 

One could also compose Songs by making the parts doubled, that is, placing the parts two by two in Consequence, or in Imitation; as Mouton <note>Jean Mouton (c. 1459–1522), teacher of Adrian Willaert.</note> did in the motet *The mother knowing not [a man]* <note>original: "Nesciens mater"</note>; and Gombert in the motet *Inviolate, whole, and chaste* <note>original: "Inuiolata, integra, & casta"</note>; both composed for Eight voices; and Adrian the named motet *Hail holy mother* <note>original: "Salue sancta parens"</note>, and the song *Upon the dark grass* <note>original: "Sur l'herbe brunette"</note>, both of which are sung by Six voices. 

Beyond this, one can compose for Four, Five, and more voices in a thousand ways (so to speak), placing the parts sometimes in Consequence, sometimes in Imitation; where there will be as many Followers as there are Guides; as can be seen in that motet by Adrian, *Holy and immaculate virginity* <note>original: "Sancta, & imaculata virginitas"</note>; and in one of his songs *Little snub-nosed girl* <note>original: "Petite camusete"</note>, for Four voices. It will also be praiseworthy to compose Four parts over one, placing some in Fugue, and some in Imitation; as P. della Rue <note>Pierre de la Rue (c. 1452–1518), a leading composer of the Franco-Flemish school.</note> did in the mass *O saving victim* <note>original: "O salutaris hostia"</note>; and Adrian also, with much skill...

...grace, in the mass *Mente tota* <note>Latin: "With all [my] mind." This likely refers to a Mass setting based on the motet of the same name by Josquin des Prez or Antoine de Févin.</note>; both of which are found for four voices. There are infinite ways to compose in such manners, and it would be difficult, indeed impossible, to try to recount one by one the arrangements of the parts and the order maintained. But to avoid being tedious, I will conclude; especially because every day many other compositions are seen, composed by the most excellent Adrian Willaert <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562) was a Flemish composer who became the maestro di cappella at St Mark's in Venice, exerting a massive influence on music theory and practice.</note>, which, besides being full of a thousand beautiful and graceful inventions, are also learnedly and elegantly composed. There are also infinite others composed by other most excellent musicians, many of which can be found in a small book that was previously printed in Venice <note>original: "Vinegia"</note> by Andrea Antico <note>An early 16th-century music printer known for his beautiful woodcut editions.</note> in octavo format <note>A book size where each printed sheet is folded to create eight leaves, resulting in a portable "pocket-sized" book.</note>. Once these have been seen, they can be of great help in discovering other similar inventions; for from them one will gain such enlightenment that anyone thereafter will be able to set themselves to greater, more difficult, and more honorable undertakings. Truly, besides these, there would be no shortage of a thousand graceful inventions that could be made; such as wanting to compose three parts over a Tenor <term>Tenore; the voice part that "holds" the melody, often the foundation of the composition</term> of Plainchant <term>Canto fermo; a pre-existing melody, usually from church liturgy, used as the basis for a polyphonic work</term> in this manner: where two parts follow each other by contrary motions <term>mouimenti contrarij; a technique where one voice moves up in pitch while the other moves down</term>, and the other part is composed according to the composer's wish, as seen here in the example.

One may also compose four parts in such a way that the Soprano with the Bass, and the Contralto <term>the voice part between the Tenor and Soprano</term> with the Tenor, sing in Consequence <term>in canon; where one voice follows another strictly</term> by contrary motions, as seen in the example placed below. *And because the ancient musicians observed—and the moderns still observe at present—the practice of not composing any Mass unless it is based upon some <term>Subject</term> <note>original: "Soggetto." In this context, a pre-existing melody or a specific musical idea used as the foundation for a polyphonic composition.</note>, the same shall be done in the future. But one must know that such a Subject can be created by the Composer himself, just as Josquin <note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), one of the most famous and influential composers of the Renaissance.</note> created the Tenor of *La, sol, fa, re, mi* <note>A Mass by Josquin where the main theme is based on these five solfège syllables.</note>; and the Tenor of the Mass *Hercules, Duke of Ferrara* <note>original: "Hercules Dux Ferrariæ." This is a famous example of a "soggetto cavato" (a carved subject), where Josquin derived the musical notes from the vowels of the Duke's name: Her-cu-les Dux Fer-ra-ri-e (re-ut-re-ut-re-fa-mi-re).</note>, which was carved from the vowels of those words, upon which he composed two Masses for four voices that are worthy of being heard.*

*Alternatively, the composer may take such a Subject from others; for instance, by taking a <term>Plainchant</term> <note>original: "Canto fermo." The traditional, monophonic chant of the Church used as a structural basis for a complex work.</note> Tenor, as the same Josquin did when he wrote the Mass *Sing, my tongue* <note>original: "Pange lingua."</note>, the Mass *Let us rejoice* <note>original: "Gaudeamus."</note>, and that of *Hail, star of the sea* <note>original: "Ave maris stella."</note>. Likewise, Brumel <note>Antoine Brumel (c. 1460–1512/1513), a student of Josquin known for his complex polyphony.</note> wrote the Mass for the Dead <note>original: "de i Defunti" or Requiem.</note>, all for four voices. Indeed, they took great delight in composing over plainchants, and one can see infinite other examples of this, so many that it would be impossible to count them. Therefore, when we wish to compose a Mass, we should first find the Subject, whether it be a Plainchant, or some Motet as is common, or something similar. Afterward, we shall seek to arrange it in various ways, finding new inventions and beautiful fantasies, imitating the Ancients.*

*We may take our example from that Mass composed by P. Moulu <note>Pierre Moulu (c. 1484–c. 1550), a Franco-Flemish composer. The work mentioned is likely his "Missa Alma Redemptoris Mater."</note>, which he wrote in such a manner that it can be sung both with the rests and without them, and it works very well; and also from the work of Ockeghem <note>Johannes Ockeghem (c. 1410–1497), a master of complex counterpoint and the teacher of Josquin.</note>, who was the master of Josquin, which...*

*...which he composed in such a way that it could be sung in whatever <term>Time</term> <note>Tempo</note> or <term>Prolation</term> <note>Prolatione; these terms refer to the relationship between different note values in Renaissance notation.</note> one wished, which produced a fine effect. It will happen at times that some Psalms are composed in a manner called <term>split choir</term> <note>original: "a Choro spezzato," a polychoral technique where two or more choirs alternate.</note>, which are very often sung in Venice during Vespers and other hours of solemn feasts. These are arranged and divided into two choirs, or sometimes three, in which four voices sing in each. The choirs sing now one, then the other in turn; and sometimes (according to the composer's purpose) all together, especially at the end, which sounds very well. And because such choirs are placed somewhat distant from one another, the composer shall take care—so that no dissonance is heard among the parts in any of them—to write the composition in such a way that each choir is consonant on its own. That is, the parts of one choir should be arranged just as if they were composed for four simple voices, without considering the other choirs. However, one must still ensure that when all parts play together, they accord with one another and there is no dissonance. For when the choirs are composed in this manner, each can be sung separately without hearing anything that offends the ear. This advice is not to be despised, for it is of great convenience, and it was devised by the most excellent Adrian <note>Adrian Willaert.</note>. Although it is somewhat difficult, one should not avoid the labor, for it is a very laudable and virtuous thing. Such difficulty will become easier once one has examined the learned compositions of this same Adrian, such as those Psalms: "I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous" <note>original: "Confitebor tibi domine in toto corde meo in consilio iustorum."</note>; "Praise the Lord, ye children" <note>original: "Laudate pueri dominum."</note>; "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem" <note>original: "Lauda Ierusalem dominum."</note>; "Out of the depths" <note>original: "De profundis."</note>; "Lord, remember David" <note>original: "Memento domine Dauid."</note>; and many others. Among these is the Canticle of the Blessed Virgin, "My soul doth magnify the Lord" <note>original: "Magnificat anima mea Dominum."</note>, which I composed many years ago for three choirs. These compositions, once seen and examined, will be of great benefit to all those who delight in composing in this manner. For one will find that the Basses of the choirs are always placed in Unisons or Octaves with each other, though sometimes they are placed in Thirds; but they are not placed in Fifths, because that becomes very inconvenient, and besides the difficulty that arises, it is impossible to make it work well for the intended purpose. This rule is very helpful to composers, for it removes the difficulty of making the parts of the choirs sing without finding dissonance between them. Now, to conclude this discussion, I say that once the composer has understood all these things, he must also be careful to determine the number of note shapes <note>original: "figure"</note> for each of his compositions, according to what is required by the Time, the Mode, and the Prolation—the frameworks under which he will compose the song. And because such frameworks were once of great importance, and are still in use by some, I will discuss the most necessary aspects of them so that everyone may have knowledge of such things. I will leave aside those parts that are superstitious or irrelevant, and I will begin with Time, as it is (in my opinion) the most universal and the first among all these accidents.*

### Of Time, Mode, and Prolation; and in what quantity
### the Songs should be finished or numbered. Chapter 67.

*Indeed, I had determined when I began to write about music not to discuss anything beyond what is necessary for the knowledge of Proportions, Sounds, Voices, and all those things that contribute to the creation of good Harmony and the knowledge belonging to this Science. But because I realize that sometimes ancient songs come into the hands of the modern musician which are composed under certain rules of <term>Mode</term> and <term>Prolation</term>, and not being able to explain them, he remains in shame over something of such little importance, I have changed my purpose. Since it is necessary for me to speak of <term>Time</term> <note>Tempo</note>, I shall also discuss the most important aspects of Mode and Prolation. I say, then, that since the <term>Breve</term> <note>A note value in mensural notation, usually shaped like a square.</note> is (as I have said elsewhere) the mother and source of every other singable figure, it is first necessary to discuss all those accidents that can occur concerning her, and then the others that occur regarding the other figures subject to change. Therefore, I say that in this place I do not call "Time" that which signifies the good state or good fortune of a person, as when it is said, "Francis is a man of good time"—meaning he leads a tranquil and happy life. Nor do I mean the good temperature of the air, as one usually says, "Today is good time"—meaning today is a serene, clear, and happy day. Nor even do I name "Time" that which the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> defines as the number or measure of movement or of any other successive thing. Rather, I say that Time is a certain and determined quantity of smaller figures, con-*

# Part [Three]

...contained, or considered within one <term>Breve</term> <note>A square-shaped note that served as the primary unit for measuring musical time in this period.</note>. This <term>Time</term> is of two kinds: *Perfect* and *Imperfect*. *Perfect Time* is found in compositions marked at their beginning with the circle **O**, which denotes that every *Breve* throughout the song is "perfect"—that is, it takes the place of three <term>Semibreves</term> <note>The note value directly below the Breve; in Perfect Time, the ratio is 3:1.</note>; or conversely, three *Semibreves* in the place of one *Breve*. But *Imperfect Time* is found when the semicircle **C** is placed at the beginning instead of the circle; by this, it is understood that the *Breve* is "imperfect"—that is, it takes the place of two *Semibreves*, or conversely, two *Semibreves* in place of one *Breve*. Therefore, when a composition is written under the sign of *Perfect Time* (the Circle), which denotes the number three—considered by some to be a "Perfect" number—it will be counted in perfect *Breves*, meaning three *Semibreves* for every unit of *Time*. But when it is composed under the sign of *Imperfect Time* (the Semicircle), it will be counted in imperfect *Breves*, meaning two *Semibreves* for every unit of *Time*; for in this case, one considers the number two, which some call an "Imperfect" number. One must note, however, that the final Figure or Note of every song is not included in this count: since it is the finale, the harmony and the *Time* both end there. Each of these ends upon that figure in which they began, which is the first *Semibreve*.

Leaving aside the definition discussed in the Third Part, the Ancients <note>Referring to earlier medieval and early Renaissance music theorists.</note> said that <term>Mode</term> <note>Modo; the mensural relationship governing the largest note values.</note> was a quantity of <term>Longs</term> or *Breves* considered within the <term>Maxima</term> or the <term>Long</term>, according to binary or ternary division. They divided this into two parts: *Major* and *Minor*; and each of these could be either *Perfect* or *Imperfect*. They understood it to be *Major* when they placed two or three <term>Long rests</term> together, which spanned two or three spaces and three or four of the five staff lines shown here:

<image-desc>A five-line musical staff containing two long rests (pause di lunga), each spanning three spaces and touching four lines.</image-desc>

But they considered it *Minor* when they placed a single *Rest* that spanned three or four of the aforementioned lines.

<image-desc>A five-line musical staff containing a single long rest spanning three spaces.</image-desc>

They understood *Major Perfect Mode* when they placed three of these shown rests together; and *Major Imperfect* when there were only two. For *Minor Perfect Mode*, they used one rest that spanned four lines and three of the named spaces; and *Minor Imperfect* when the said rest, placed in such a manner, spanned only three lines and two spaces. Thus, in *Major Perfect Mode*, they made the *Maxima* worth three *Longs*, and in the *Imperfect*, two. Similarly, in *Minor Perfect Mode*, they made the *Long* worth three *Breves*, and in the *Imperfect*, two. 

Therefore, when they composed, they arranged their songs in such a way that in *Major Perfect Mode*, they counted by groups of three *Longs* (whether perfect or imperfect); and under *Major Imperfect Mode*, by groups of two *Longs*. Likewise, in *Minor Perfect Mode*, they counted by groups of three *Breves*, and in the *Imperfect*, by twos. Thus, one can see that if a composer wrote under any of these *Modes* and did not count the song according to the required number, it could truly be said that he was careless and had no knowledge of such matters. The Ancients placed these *Rests* in two ways: some before the signs of *Time*, and some after. The first they called <term>Indicative Rests</term> <note>original: "Pause Inditiali"</note> only: because they were not counted as silences in the composition, but were placed there only to show whether the song was composed in *Major* or *Minor* *Mode*. The second they called *Indicative* and <term>Essential Rests</term> <note>original: "Pause Essentiali"</note>: because they served not only to show the *Mode*, but were also used as actual silences in the song, as can be understood in the example below.

<image-desc>A musical staff showing different configurations of rests and mensuration signs. On the left are groups of two and three long vertical lines (rests). In the center are signs like O and C. On the right are more rests intermingled with the signs.</image-desc>

->*Indicative Rests only.* <- -> *Indicative and Essential Rests.*<-

They also had <term>Prolation</term> <note>Prolatione; the relationship between the Semibreve and the Minim.</note>, which (besides the many other things this word can mean) they said was a quantity of <term>Minims</term> considered or applied to a *Semibreve*. They showed this with the circular or semicircular sign. They made two types of it: the first they called *Perfect*,

...perfect, and the other Imperfect. They understood **Perfect Prolation** <note>In early music theory, "Prolation" describes the relationship between the Semibreve and the Minim.</note> to be in effect when they placed the signs with dots in the music, in this manner: <image-desc>a circle with a central dot and a semicircle with a central dot</image-desc>; and **Imperfect Prolation** when the signs were placed without dots. They made the <term>Semibreve</term> <note>A diamond-shaped note value.</note> worth three <term>Minims</term> <note>The note value directly below the Semibreve.</note> under the first two dotted signs, and two under those that were not dotted. 

They then counted the songs in this way: those placed under **Perfect Prolation** proceeded and were numbered in groups of three Minims; and those composed under the **Imperfect**, in groups of two. They numbered the song by <term>Longs</term>, or <term>Breves</term>, or <term>Semibreves</term> <note>These represent the hierarchy of note durations from longest to shortest.</note>: because each Long, Breve, or Semibreve can be perfect or imperfect. And because these two degrees—the Perfect and the Imperfect—were often joined together, they took care in such a conjunction: if the **Major Mode** <note>The relationship between the Maxima and the Long.</note> was joined with the **Minor Mode** <note>The relationship between the Long and the Breve.</note>, and both were Perfect, then they numbered the song in groups of three perfect Longs. But if the Mode was Minor Perfect, they numbered it with three imperfect Longs. 

They proceeded with similar considerations for the other degrees, such as **Time** and **Prolation**, whether perfect or imperfect. We can now see that through the signs—that is, the Circle and the Semicircle—they had knowledge of **Perfect** or **Imperfect Time**. Through the **Pauses** <note>Rest markings of specific lengths.</note>, they had knowledge of the Mode, whether Major or Minor, Perfect or Imperfect; and through the dotted or undotted signs of Time, they knew the **Perfect** or **Imperfect Prolation**. 

In this way, we can also see that they attributed:
*   The **Major Perfect Mode** to the <term>Maxima</term> <note>The largest note value.</note> when it was worth three Longs; and the **Major Imperfect Mode** to the Maxima when it was worth two.
*   Similarly, they attributed the **Minor Perfect Mode** to the **Long** when it was worth three Breves, and the **Minor Imperfect Mode** to the Long when it was worth two.
*   They attributed **Perfect Time** to the **Breve** when it was worth three Semibreves, and **Imperfect Time** to the Breve when it was worth two.
*   They also gave **Perfect Prolation** to the **Semibreve** when it was worth three Minims, and **Imperfect Prolation** to the Semibreve when it was worth two.

The Ancients were also accustomed to "cutting" or slashing the signs of Time in this manner: <image-desc>four symbols representing musical time signatures: a slashed circle, a slashed semicircle, a slashed circle containing a dot, and a slashed semicircle containing a dot</image-desc>. They did this when they wanted the figures subject to perfection, imperfection, and also <term>Alteration</term> <note>A rule where a note's value is doubled to fill out a triple meter.</note> in Perfect and Imperfect Time to be faster. 

These figures (as we shall see) are five: **Maxima**, **Long**, **Breve**, **Semibreve**, and **Minim**. It is quite true that they made the **Minims black** to make them fast; in this way, neither the slashing of the signs nor the darkening of the figures changed their names, but they retained them just as if the signs had been whole. Nor did the slashing of said signs remove imperfection, perfection, or Alteration; they were just as subject to these "accidents" and "passions" <note>Technical terms for the ways note values are modified by their context.</note> as if the signs had remained whole. 

At present, we have another reason for the **black Minim**, as (I have shown elsewhere) it is called a <term>Semiminim</term> <note>Equivalent to a modern quarter note.</note>, which is divided into two **Chromas** <note>Eighth notes.</note>, and the **Chroma** into two **Semichromas** <note>Sixteenth notes.</note>. Under the sign of **Perfect Time (slashed)**, they also had a double consideration in numbering when composing songs: for they numbered by threes, and also by twos—that is, in groups of two perfect Breves, or in groups of three Semibreves. Thus, the numbering of the Semibreves ended in the **Senary number** <note>The number six; original: "numero Senario".</note>; for if they measured otherwise, they would not find the measure of the Breve in their songs. 

We shall likewise seek to observe this, not only in **Perfect Time**, but also in **Imperfect Cut Time**; proceeding in groups of two imperfect Breves, so that the song ends in the **Quaternary number** <note>The number four; original: "numero Quaternario".</note>. What shall we say now of certain modern Composers, who not only fail to observe the measure of the Senary or Quaternary numbers in their songs, but furthermore do not observe the **Ternary number** <note>The number three; original: "numero Ternario".</note> in Perfect Time, nor the **Binary number** <note>The number two; original: "numero Binario".</note> in Imperfect Time, whether they are slashed or not? This is truly a great shame for them, for they come to break the Time and the measure—things which the Ancients observed with great diligence—and in such a manner, they ruin and confound everything.

### On the Perfection of Singable Figures. Chapter 68.

From what has been said, it can now be understood that in every composition one finds **Time**, **Mode**, and **Prolation**, under which each of the five named figures varies its value according to the different "accidents" that accompany them. 

Wherefore, it should be known that the Ancients also observed the naming of these figures by their effects: some as **Agents** and some as **Patients**. They named the **Minim** an "Agent," because they established it as immutable—that is, it could not receive any "perfection" <note>Meaning it cannot be lengthened by context.</note>, but it could cause "imperfection" in larger notes. I say "immutable" because it cannot be divided into any of the other named figures, being the smallest of all...

### Part.

than any other in value; even though it is divisible into two <term>Semiminims</term> <note>Equivalent to modern quarter notes.</note>, and into four <term>Chromas</term> <note>Equivalent to modern eighth notes.</note>; as has been said elsewhere. They then called the <term>Maxima</term> the **Patient**: because, being the greatest of all others, it can "suffer" <note>In the philosophical sense of *passio*, meaning to be acted upon or changed.</note> imperfection. But the **Long**, the **Breve**, and the **Semibreve** they called both **Agents** and **Patients**: because they not only can be made perfect, but they also suffer imperfection. 

Hence, it should be noted that they named as **perfect** that figure which is worth as much as three of the figures that are its "proximate parts"; such as the Maxima, which is called Perfect when it is worth three Longs; and the Long, when it is worth three Breves; and the Breve, when it is worth three Semibreves; and the Semibreve, when it is of the value of three Minims. Similarly, they called such figures **imperfect** when they were worth two; such as the Maxima being two Longs; the Long two Breves; the Breve two Semibreves; and the Semibreve two Minims. 

Besides this, they considered these figures in many other ways; as proximate parts, or remote, or more remote, or even most remote from one another; as I have shown in Chapter 44. Wherefore the Long has no "most remote" part; nor does the Breve have a "more remote" or "most remote" part; and the Semibreve has neither the remote, nor the more remote, nor even the most remote. And because some might doubt whether figures subject to Time, Mode, and Prolation can always be perfect; it is therefore necessary to know (so as not to depart from the authority of the Ancients) that they truly can be perfect, and also imperfect, according to the will of the Composer. 

Wherefore it should be noted that the Ancients intended that any Figure placed before another similar figure, whether white or black, should always be perfect; such as in the **Major Mode Perfect**, a Maxima before another Maxima, whether it be white or black. The Long in the **Major Mode Imperfect**, and **Minor Perfect**. The Breve in **Perfect Time**; and the Semibreve in **Perfect Prolation**. And they did this with good reason: because "like does not suffer any imperfection from its like"; as is understood in two things that are equal in virtue and power, where one cannot overcome, nor can it be overcome by the other. 

But the "similarity" in these figures is understood with respect to their **form**, and not their color: because the Form is that which truly gives being to a thing. Thus, being black does not take away its form; just as the color black does not take away from an Ethiopian the state of being a Man, and being Rational: since Color is nothing other than an accident, even though at times it is inseparable from the Subject. <note>Zarlino is using Aristotelian logic here: the "substance" or "form" of the note is its shape, which dictates its base value, while the "accident" is the color (black or white), which is secondary.</note> Hence, no Figure can be made imperfect by one larger than itself, but indeed by one smaller than itself: since the larger, with respect to the smaller, is always the "patient"; and conversely, the smaller, with respect to the larger, is always the "agent." 

Every Figure is also perfect when it is placed before the **Rests** of its own denomination; such as the Maxima before three rests that denote the Major Mode Perfect; whether they be rests of three times or two; because said rests represent the quantity and value of a Maxima. Likewise the Long of the Minor Mode Perfect before a Rest of three times, or of two; and the Breve, and the Semibreve of Perfect Time and Perfect Prolation, before their rests; as seen here.

<image-desc>Two musical staves demonstrating rhythmic notation and rests. The first staff shows Maximas, Longas, and Breves followed by vertical line rests of different heights spanning multiple staff lines. The second staff shows Breves, Semibreves, and Minims (including diamond-shaped notes) followed by smaller vertical rests and diamond-shaped rests on the lines.</image-desc>

The Maxima is also always perfect when placed before a **Ligature** <note>A group of notes joined together in a single symbol, common in medieval and Renaissance notation.</note> of the value of two Longs; and the Long before one of two Breves; and the Breve before one of two Semibreves, or two Semibreve rests placed upon the same line; for such Ligatures or Rests placed in this manner have the virtue of unity. This also happens to the Semibreve when it is placed before two Minim rests placed in the same way. But if such Rests were separated, this Rule would not hold. And if anyone wished to say that a Figure placed before a Ligature cannot be perfect; whatever reason they might bring, one could respond: that if the Breve is perfect when placed before two Semibreve rests on the same line under the sign of Perfect Time; it must be even more perfect before a Ligature; since Rests denote nothing other than the privation of sound or voice, whereas the Ligature puts it into being; as seen here.

Sometimes any of the shown figures will be perfect when it is followed by the <term>Dot of perfection</term> <note>original: "Punto di perfettione"; a small mark that ensures a note is counted as three units instead of two.</note>; such as the <term>Maxima</term> in <term>Greater Perfect Mode</term>; the <term>Long</term> in <term>Lesser Perfect Mode</term>; the <term>Breve</term> in <term>Perfect Time</term>; and the <term>Semibreve</term> in <term>Perfect Prolation</term>; as can be seen here in the example.

When two or three smaller proximate figures are placed between two larger ones, the first larger one will always be perfect. For example, in <term>Greater Perfect Mode</term>, two or three <term>Longs</term> placed between two <term>Maximas</term> cause the first Maxima to be perfect; in <term>Lesser Perfect Mode</term>, two or three <term>Breves</term> placed between two Longs cause the first Long to be perfect. The same occurs with two or three <term>Semibreves</term> placed between two Breves in <term>Perfect Time</term>; and in <term>Greater Prolation</term>, two or three <term>Minims</term> placed between two Semibreves: because the first Breve and the first Semibreve become perfect. Figures and <term>Rests</term> <note>original: "Pause"</note> of the same value placed together in the same manner will do the same: but it must be noted that when a single smaller figure and its corresponding Rest are placed between two larger ones, the Rest is placed first, and then the figure. But when two smaller figures and one Rest are placed, then the Rest may be placed wherever it is most convenient; as can be seen in the example below.

<image-desc>A large musical example consisting of three systems of five-line staves. It features various combinations of Breves, Semibreves, and Minims along with rests (pauses) of different durations, demonstrating the placement rules described in the text.</image-desc>

When five or six Semibreves are placed between two Breves in <term>Perfect Time</term>, then the first Breve will be perfect, and the last of the five Semibreves will be <term>altered</term> <note>original: "alterata"; in this context, the note's duration is doubled to fill the triple meter.</note>; that is, doubled. But the first Breve placed before six Semibreves will always be perfect, without the <term>alteration</term> of any of the Semibreves: because the six Semibreves are placed to represent two whole <term>Times</term> <note>original: "Tempi"; referring to the "tempus," the basic unit of measurement equivalent to a Breve.</note>; as they are seen here.

<image-desc>A single staff of musical notation showing a Breve followed by a series of Semibreves and another Breve, illustrating the text concerning five or six semibreves.</image-desc>

<vocab>
**mensural notation**: the musical system used from the 13th to 16th centuries where the shape of the note defines its exact duration.
**dot of perfection**: a mark used to make a note "perfect" (triple value).
**Greater Perfect Mode**: a rhythmic structure where the Maxima equals three Longs.
**Lesser Perfect Mode**: a rhythmic structure where the Long equals three Breves.
**Perfect Time**: a rhythmic structure where the Breve equals three Semibreves (similar to modern 3/4 or 3/2 time).
**Perfect Prolation**: a rhythmic structure where the Semibreve equals three Minims.
**Maxima**: the largest note value.
**Long**: a large note value, usually half or a third of a Maxima.
**Breve**: a standard unit of time, originally the "short" note.
**Semibreve**: a division of the Breve.
**Minim**: a smaller division of the Semibreve.
**Rests**: marks indicating silence of a specific duration.
**alteration**: the doubling of a note's value to complete a triple measurement.
</vocab>

## On the Imperfection of Singable Figures. Chapter 69.

AND because every Imperfect thing has its origin in the Perfect; having made mention of the Perfection of singable figures, it remains for us to see the ways by which each of them can be made imperfect; or when they may be called imperfect. Hence, if it is true what the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>original: "Filosofo"; referring to Aristotle, whose principle was that the study of one thing includes the study of its opposite (e.g., health and sickness).</note> says, that the discipline of opposites is one and the same, I say: that having seen what is required for Perfection, it will be an easy thing to know what is required regarding their Imperfection. They will be found to be imperfect when they are not accompanied by the accidental features shown above. But before we go further, we will look at some general matters regarding this subject; and then we will descend to specifics. I say then that the Figures that can be made imperfect are Four; and these are all the <term>Patients</term> <note>original: "Patienti"; those notes that "suffer" or receive the action of being reduced in value.</note> shown above; that is, the <term>Maxima</term>, the <term>Long</term>, the <term>Breve</term>, and the <term>Semibreve</term>. And that which suffers the imperfection is always greater than that which causes the imperfection: conversely, that which is the cause of the imperfection is always smaller. And that Figure which is the cause of such imperfection must be considered in terms of <term>perfect quantity</term>; that is, regarding those figures that are subject to the <term>Ternary number</term> <note>a count of three</note>, and not to those subject to the <term>Binary</term> <note>a count of two</note>; just as the Maxima in <term>Greater Perfect Mode</term>; the Long in <term>Lesser Perfect Mode</term>; the Breve in <term>Perfect Time</term>; and the Semibreve in <term>Perfect Prolation</term>. And because the Maxima (as I have said) is only a "patient," it does not cause, but only suffers imperfection. Likewise, the <term>Minim</term>, being only an <term>Agent</term> <note>original: "Agente"; the note that performs the action of reducing another's value</note>, does not suffer imperfection, but is the cause of it. Therefore, the Long, the Breve, and the Semibreve are those which, being not only agents but also patients, both cause and suffer imperfection. 

But it must be noted that being Perfect is considered in two ways: first, in regard to the Whole; then, in regard to the Parts. In regard to the Whole, a Figure is understood as imperfect when it is made imperfect by its <term>proximate part</term> <note>the next note value down in the hierarchy, such as a Long being the proximate part of a Maxima</note>; and this is the greatest imperfection that can be given to it. But in regard to the Part, it is understood when it is made imperfect by a <term>remote part</term>, or more remote, or most remote <note>notes two or more levels down in the hierarchy, such as a Breve or Semibreve relative to a Maxima</note>. And the Figure that can be made imperfect can be made so not only regarding the Whole with the proximate part, but with the remote parts and the others as well; provided that the quantity is equal to the Third part of its Whole: because Imperfection in Figures is nothing other than a certain diminution of a Third part, reducible to the figure in the perfection of the Ternary number. 

The Figures that cause imperfection are placed in three ways: they are placed after the one being made perfect; or before it; or both before and after: since every figure can be made imperfect in only one of these three ways. And as much is taken away from each figure that is made imperfect as is the value of the figures that cause such imperfection. And although the Minim is an "agent" figure, it cannot make any figure imperfect that is not subject to <term>Perfect Prolation</term>. Nor should it be believed that such imperfections are made only with such figures in the way I have said: for <term>Rests</term>, <term>Color</term> <note>blackening the note head</note>, and even <term>Dots</term> have the same power. It is indeed true that Rests are not subject to imperfection: because they are only "agents" and not "patients"; that is, they cause perfection and imperfection, but they themselves, by whatever accident, are not made imperfect. Color always takes away a Third part of the Whole from figures subject to perfection; but in imperfection (as the Moderns use it) it always takes away a Fourth part. The Imperfection of figures, then, is the taking away of a Third part of their value, which is their proximate part; and this is imperfection regarding the Whole. Each of the said figures is therefore imperfect regarding its Whole when its proximate part follows it without any intermediary; such as the Long after the Maxima; the Breve after the Long; the Semibreve after the Breve; and the Minim after the Semibreve, under their signs of perfection; as can be seen in the example placed below.

<image-desc>A single line of musical notation on a staff, displaying pairs of mensural notes and rests (Maximas, Longs, Breves, Semibreves, and Minims) to illustrate how a larger note is made imperfect by a following smaller note of its own species under signs of perfection.</image-desc>

The same can also happen to the aforementioned <term>Figures</term> <note>original: "Figure"; the shapes used to represent note values.</note> when they are immediately followed by a <term>Rest</term> <note>original: "Pausa."</note> equal in value to their <term>constituent part</term> <note>original: "parte propinqua"; the next smaller note value in the hierarchy (e.g., a semibreve is the constituent part of a breve).</note>. Similarly, <term>Coloration</term> <note>original: "Colore"; the practice of filling in the body of a note (usually in red or black) to indicate a change in rhythmic value.</note> is a cause of such imperfection; and such im-

perfections are called "From the part after" <note>original: "Dalla parte dopo"; also known in Latin as "a parte post."</note>. On the other hand, imperfections "From the part before" <note>original: "Dalla parte inanti"; or "a parte ante."</note> occur when

the figures are placed in the opposite way; such as when the rests or the smaller figures are placed before the larger ones. These figures will also be imperfect both "from the part after" and "from the part before"—that is, by both the following and the preceding part—by means of the <term>Dot</term>; this happens when two smaller constituent figures are placed between two larger figures, with a Dot placed between the smaller ones, as seen here:

For the first and the last [larger notes] will remain imperfect in their constituent part by virtue of the Dot placed between the smaller ones, which is called the <term>Dot of Division</term>; as we shall see further on. These figures will also be imperfect when, between two larger ones, a figure that is its constituent part is placed on the left side, followed immediately and without any intermediary by a Rest of the same value, as seen here. Figures are also made imperfect in many other ways regarding their <term>Whole</term> <note>original: "Tutto"; the total duration of the note.</note>; but because these ways are somewhat <term>superstitious</term> <note>original: "superstitiosi"; here meaning overly complex, pedantic, or archaic.</note>, it will suffice only to have said what I have regarding the imperfection of singable figures in their Whole—that is, regarding the constituent part. For as for the imperfection of their other parts, after one has considered everything I have said above, we will find that such imperfection occurs when they are made imperfect by a smaller quantity than those shown, whether they are imperfect from the part before, or from the part after, or even from both of the named sides.
