## On the Dot, its species, and its effects. Chapter 70.

THE Dot is not considered by the Musician in the same way that the <term>Geometer</term> considers it; the latter maintains (as <term>Euclid</term> demonstrates) that it has no parts and is indivisible. Nor does he consider it as <term>Unity</term> having a position, as the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>original: "Filosofo"; referring to Aristotle.</note> defines it. Instead, the Musician says that the Dot is a minimal particle, or a certain indivisible quantity; or rather a minimal sign that is added to singable figures by accident—sometimes after, sometimes above, and sometimes placed between them. He considers it in four ways: in how it makes perfect, how it increases, how it divides, and how it alters or doubles the said figures. Whence musicians, having considered its functions, say that it is found in four kinds (leaving aside the others that are of little relevance to the subject): that is, of <term>Perfection</term>, of <term>Augmentation</term>, of <term>Division</term>, and of <term>Alteration</term> (or Doubling). They call the <term>Dot of Perfection</term> that which is placed immediately after a figure that can be made, or can be, perfect, only within the <term>Signs of Perfection</term> <note>Meter signatures indicating triple time.</note>, in order to preserve the perfection of such a figure; as seen here below.

### Part Three.

<image-desc>Two musical staves showing mensural notation with C-clefs and various note values (Longas, Breves, Semibreves, and Minims) featuring dots in different rhythmic contexts.</image-desc>

The **Dot of Addition** <note>original: "Punto di Accrescimento"; similar to the modern dot, it adds value to a note.</note> is that which is placed without any space after a <term>figure</term> <note>the shape or symbol representing a note's duration.</note> that cannot be made "perfect" in any way. This includes any figure placed under <term>Signs of Imperfection</term> <note>musical meters where notes are naturally divided into two parts (duple time), rather than three.</note>, as well as figures under Signs of Perfection that are smaller in value than a <term>Semibreve</term>; as can be seen here:

<image-desc>Two musical staves illustrating the use of the "Dot of Addition" on various note shapes under different mensuration signs.</image-desc>

Thus, it should be noted that the aforementioned Dots are written (as I have shown) in the middle of the right side of the figure, whether it be perfect or imperfect. They make the imperfect figure larger by half its value—that is, by half of its "Whole." For example, a <term>Long</term> <note>a very long note value, often worth 4 or 9 semibreves depending on the meter.</note> that is worth four Semibreves will be worth six when a Dot is added. However, when a Dot is added to figures that *can* be made perfect <note>in triple meter systems, where a note naturally contains three smaller beats.</note>, the Dot always equals the **third part** of the perfect figure to which it is attached, which is also half of the imperfect figure. 

By this, one sees the difference between the **Dot of Perfection** and the **Dot of Addition**: the first is only placed next to those figures that can be made perfect, under the Signs of Perfection; the other is placed next to those that cannot be made perfect. Such Dots function the same way in <term>ligatures</term> <note>groups of notes tied together in a single symbol.</note> as they do in single notes. 

The **Dot of Division** <note>original: "Punto di diuisione."</note> is that which is placed between two similar smaller figures that are themselves placed between two larger ones, under the Signs of Perfection. Its function is to divide the figures and to make both of the larger figures <term>imperfect</term> <note>reducing their value from three beats to two.</note>; the first from the part after, and the second from the part before. It is written above such figures in the middle of them, and this Dot is **not sung** <note>it is a visual marker for the singer to understand the rhythm, not a note itself.</note>. Because it separates one of the two smaller figures from the other and groups them with the larger ones, it is called "of Division." But because it creates imperfection in the larger notes, it can also be called the **Dot of Imperfection**. By all rights, it must always be placed at the end of the "Time" <note>the measure or tactus.</note> that has passed, and at the beginning of the one that is present. It is also placed between a <term>Rest</term> that holds the first place and a Figure that holds the second, provided they are of the same value, as seen in the example below.

<columns>2</columns>
<image-desc>Two short musical staves on the left illustrating the "Dot of Division" or "Dot of Imperfection" within a sequence of notes.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

The **Dot of Alteration** is that which is placed before two smaller figures that precede a larger nearby figure. Its function is to **double** the second smaller figure that follows the dot and precedes the larger one, so that between these two smaller ones, a "Perfect Time" <note>a complete unit of three beats.</note> is fulfilled. One must take care to place this Dot in such a way that it stands at the end of the preceding Time and the beginning of the following one, as the learned ancient musicians observed. This dot (like the Dot of Division) is **not sung**. 

"Alteration" means nothing other than **Doubling** <note>original: "Raddoppiamento."</note>, which occurs in the constituent parts of the notes or figures being sung which can be made perfect under their signs. This always happens (as I said) to the second figure placed after the dot. Because the first note has the nature of "Unity" <note>representing 1 beat.</note> and the second has the nature of "Binary" <note>representing 2 beats.</note>, it is proper that the Binary follows the Unity <note>1 + 2 = 3, completing the perfect triple group.</note>. Thus, the Dot is placed in this manner:

<image-desc>A full-width musical staff showing a specific example of alteration in mensural notation across different note groupings.</image-desc>

However, this Alteration or Doubling was considered by the ancient musicians not only in figures placed in this specific manner, but also in many other ways, such as when they placed two smaller figures...

However, **Blackness**, or **Color** <note>the practice of filling in a note head to change its value or rhythm.</note>, and often the **Dot of Division**, drives away such Alteration, as I have shown. It must furthermore be noted that the **Perfection** of figures can be considered in three ways: first, by virtue of the Rests; then, by virtue of the Sign (such as the Circle or the Semicircle); finally, by virtue of the Dot placed within said Circle or Semicircle. However, the Maxima and the Long will always be perfect by virtue of the Rests, regardless of which sign they are placed under. The Breve is made perfect by virtue of the Circle; and the Semibreve by virtue of the dotted Sign. Wherefore it should be noted that **no figure is perfect by virtue of the sign except the Breve and the Semibreve**; the others, which are the Maxima and the Long, are perfect (as has been said) by virtue of the Rests. # Part [Three]

...all-black figures, without any additional cipher; but then they call it <term>Hemiola</term> <note>original: "Hemiolia," from the Greek ἡμιόλιος (hēmiolios), meaning "one and a half."</note>, a Greek word which means the same as what we call <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>A musical ratio of 3:2, where three notes are played in the time of two.</note>. <image-desc>A musical staff with black diamond-shaped notes (breves and semibreves).</image-desc>

->Greater Hemiola.<-

for the color removes all these things, as can be understood below. Such a <term>Beat</term> <note>original: "Battuta," the down-and-up motion of the hand used to keep time, often called the tactus.</note> is used not only in the signs for Perfect or Imperfect Time, whether they are dotted or "cut" <note>Musical signs like a circle or half-circle, sometimes with a vertical line through them (cut) or a dot in the center.</note>; but also in simple signs placed without dots or cuts. <image-desc>Two musical notation staves displayed side-by-side. The left staff shows white notes with a 3/2 time signature. The right staff shows black notes without a time signature.</image-desc>

->Lesser Sesquialtera. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Lesser Hemiola.<-

When practical musicians place the Breve and the Semibreve in the Beat, they call such a beat or <term>Prolation</term> <note>The relationship between the semibreve and the minim.</note> the Greater Sesquialtera or Greater Hemiola. When they place the Semibreve and the Minim, they call it the Lesser. But one must be careful when composing songs to calculate the composition—both in the Greater and Lesser Sesquialteras or Hemiolas—according to what is required by the <term>Mood</term>, <term>Time</term>, and <term>Prolation</term> <note>The three levels of the rhythmic system governing how longs, breves, and semibreves are divided.</note>, just as I showed in Chapter 67. One should set the Breve and Semibreve contained in the Greater Sesquialtera or Hemiola as a single "Time" <note>The duration of one full measure or cycle of the beat.</note>; likewise the Semibreve with the Minim in the Lesser version, regardless of whether the song is governed by a Perfect or Imperfect sign. And because musicians sometimes set aside not only the "Indicative Rests" in the Greater and Lesser Moods, but sometimes even omit the "Essential Rests," the singer should be advised that Perfections and Imperfections are sometimes recognized by certain signs called "Intrinsic." These include Colors and Dots. Such signs are of two types: those just named, and "Extrinsic" signs, which are the Rests, the signs of Time, and those of Prolation. Therefore, when such Intrinsic signs are found, one can easily judge under which Mood or Prolation the song was composed. As one can see in the <term>Tenor</term> <note>The structural "holding" voice of a polyphonic composition.</note> below, it is composed under the Greater and Lesser Perfect Mood, because among the figures subject to perfection in the aforementioned Moods, one finds the Dot of Division, the Dot of Alteration, and Color, as seen therein.

<image-desc>A musical staff labeled 'Tenore' at the beginning, containing various note values including white and black breves and semibreves with dots.</image-desc>

Besides these, the Ancients had many other accidents and ciphers of various kinds in their compositions. But because they are hardly used anymore and are of no use to good and sonorous harmonies, we shall leave further discussion of such things to those who are idle and who delight in such ciphers more than we do.

## On the Utility that the shown Accidents bring to good harmonies. Chapter 71.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' depicting a male figure sitting beneath a tree in a landscape.</image-desc>

Before we proceed further, we must see how useful the shown "Accidents" are to good and sonorous harmonies. But for greater understanding (taking our discussion to a somewhat higher level), it is necessary to know that since the true object of Sensation is the Body that moves it through the sense organ; insofar as such a Body is considered according to different reasons of movement, it necessarily places different powers in the Sensation...

# Third [Part]

<meta>catchword: another</meta>

...since that which is considered insofar as it can be seen is called **Visible**, and it cannot be perceived by any other sense than **Sight**. And this Object is truly of two kinds: for it is either **Principal**—such as **Color**, which is seen before anything else—or it is **Adequate** (or, we might say, **Proportionate**); and this is not Color, and is found in many things that are not colored, such as Fire, the Moon, the Sun, the Stars, and other similar things. This Object, for this reason, does not truly have a name of its own, but is simply called **Visible**; and under it are contained all those things that are seen by means of Light, such as all the luminous Bodies, which are the Stars, the Sun, the Moon, and other such things. Insofar as such an Object can be heard, such as Voices and Sounds, it is called **Audible**, and it cannot be perceived by any other sense than **Hearing**; which could also be said of the others. These Objects are called **Proper Sensibles** <note>original: "Proprij sensibili." In Aristotelian philosophy, these are qualities that can only be perceived by one specific sense (e.g., color by sight, sound by hearing).</note>, because any one of them can be understood by only one of the named senses. It is quite true that there are some Objects called **Common** [Sensibles], which can be understood by many senses; such as **Movement**, **Rest**, **Number**, **Figure** <note>Shape or form.</note>, and every **Magnitude** <note>Size or dimension.</note>, which can be seen, heard, and touched, as is manifest. There are also some other **Sensible Objects by accident** <note>original: "sensibili per accidente." Things perceived indirectly through their qualities, like recognizing a person because of their color or shape.</note>, which are those that cannot be felt except by means of another thing; such as sounding Bodies, which cannot be heard except through the Sound made in the Air, as I showed in the second part. These Objects are more pleasing to their own sense, and more sweet, the more they are proportionate to it. And so, conversely, as is seen with our Eye, which is offended when looking at the Sun because such an Object is not proportionate to it; and what the **Philosophers** <note>A common reference to Aristotle and his commentators.</note> say is true: that an **Excellent Sensible** <note>An overwhelming sensory stimulus.</note>, if it does not corrupt the Sense itself, at least corrupts its Instrument. If, therefore, the Proper Sensible objects cannot be perceived or judged by any other sense than their own—as Sound by Hearing, Color by Sight, and so on for the others—tell me now, pray, those who labor so hard and take such care to place so many entanglements in their <term>melodies</term> <note>original: "cantilene." While often meaning a simple song, here it refers to complex polyphonic compositions.</note>: what and how much delight and utility can they provide to the sense [of hearing]? And are they more lovely and more sonorous than those that do not have such things, which are nothing but visible, and do not fall under any sense except that of Sight, nor can they in any way be heard? For they are not Common Objects, like those mentioned, which can be understood by many senses. I know they will answer, if they have judgment, that they provide no utility in this; for when they are reduced to a simple and common way, without such ciphers, the harmony heard in them will be exactly the same as that heard in these [complex ones]. If, therefore, they are of no use for the achievement of good harmonies, nor do they bring any utility to the sense, for what purpose should one add such obligations and increase the burden on the **Singer** with such things, without purpose? For when he ought to be intent on singing those melodies proposed to him cheerfully, he must instead be attentive to considering such chimeras, which fall (according to various accidents) under <term>Mode</term>, <term>Time</term>, and <term>Prolation</term> <note>These are the three levels of rhythmic measurement in Renaissance notation (mensural theory).</note>; and he must not let anything pass that is depicted without giving it great consideration; since if he did otherwise, he would be reputed (I shall say it thus) a dolt and an ignorant person. And if they provide no utility (as they truly do not), it seems to me truly a great madness that anyone of elevated genius should halt his study, spend his time, and weary himself around such impertinent things. Therefore, I would advise everyone to cast these ciphers aside and attend to those things by means of which one can acquire good and sweet harmonies. Perhaps someone will say: is it not a beautiful thing to see a **Tenor** arranged under the signs of Mode, Time, and Prolation, as those ancient Musicians did, who attended to almost nothing else? Yes, truly, it is a very beautiful thing; especially when it is written, or painted and even illuminated by the hands of an excellent scribe and illuminator, with the best inks, fine colors, and proportionate measurements; and perhaps a Shield will be added (as I have already seen) with a Miter or a Hat, with some other beautiful thing nearby. But what does this matter, if that melody which has a Tenor written simply and without any entanglement, reduced to an easy way, will be just as sonorous (or just as lacking in grace) as if it were full of these things? Thus, one can truly say that such a way of composing is nothing other than a multiplying of difficulties without any necessity, and not a multiplying of harmony; and that such a thing is done without any utility, since things are multiplied in vain without any necessity, as the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle; a reference to the principle of parsimony (Ockham's Razor avant la lettre).</note> holds. For Music being a science that deals with Sounds and Voices, which are the Proper Objects of Hearing, it goes about speculating only on the <term>concord</term> <note>original: "concento." The harmonious sounding together of voices.</note> (as **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Hermiae (c. 440–520 AD), a Greek philosopher who wrote commentaries on Aristotle's works on logic and physics.</note> says) that arises from strings and voices, and does not consider so many other things. Whence it seems to me that everything in Music that is speculated upon and not directed toward such an end is vain and useless; since Music was truly discovered for nothing else...

<summary>Zarlino argues that music is fundamentally for the ears, and complex visual notation (ciphers, Mode, Time, Prolation) adds unnecessary difficulty for singers without improving the actual sound of the harmony. He uses Aristotelian sensory theory to distinguish between visible and audible objects, concluding that visual "chimeras" in scores are a waste of a composer's genius.</summary>

# Part 279

<meta>catchword: in the days</meta>

...no other purpose than to delight and to benefit; nothing else has power except for the **Voices** and the **Sounds** that arise from strings. These strings—as **Aurelius Cassiodorus** <note>A 6th-century Roman statesman and scholar whose writings on the liberal arts influenced medieval music theory.</note> imagined—are named in such a way because they move the **Hearts**; as he demonstrates with great grace using these two Latin words *Chordæ* and *Corda* <note>original: "Chordæ, et Corda." A play on words: *chordae* means strings, and *corda* means hearts.</note>. By this means, we feel the pleasure and the benefit that we take in hearing **Harmonies** and **Melodies**. We shall conclude, therefore, from what has been said, that the method of composing in such a [complex] manner is not only useless, but even harmful, due to the loss of time—which is more precious than anything else. 

Furthermore, the **Points**, the **Lines**, the **Circles**, the **Semicircles**, and other similar things that are painted on paper are subject to the sense of **Sight**, and not to that of **Hearing**; these are things considered by the **Geometer**. But **Sounds** and **Voices**—as those which are truly the proper Object of Hearing, from which every good Consonance and every Harmony is born—are principally considered by the **Musician**, even if he may occasionally consider many other things by accident. 

Perhaps someone here will wish to reprove and blame me, seeing that many learned and most celebrated ancient Musicians (whose names still live among us) have applied themselves to such a way of composing. To this I say: if such detractors consider the matter, they will find no greater utility in those compositions entangled in such bonds than they would find if the compositions were naked and pure, without any difficulty. They will see that they complain with great injustice and will understand that they themselves are worthy of reproach, as those who oppose the truth. 

For even if the **Ancients** followed such a method, they knew very well that such "accidents" <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to visual notation features like coloration or complex proportions that do not change the fundamental pitch or interval.</note> could not bring any increase or decrease to the harmony; rather, they worked on such things to show they were not ignorant of that **Theory** which had been put into use by certain idle **Speculative thinkers** of those times. By then, the matter had already been reduced to such a point that the Speculative part of the science consisted more in the contemplation of such accidents than in the consideration of Sounds, Voices, and the other things shown in the First and Second parts of these my labors. 

Evidence of this is found in many books composed by various authors that treat nothing but **Circles** and **Semicircles**; dotted and undotted; whole and cut <note>Refers to "mensuration signs," the ancestors of modern time signatures.</note> not only once, but even twice; in which one sees so many Points, so many Rests, so many Colors, so many Ciphers, so many Signs, so many Numbers against numbers, and so many other strange things that they sometimes look like the ledgers of a confused merchant. Nor can anything else be read in those books of theirs that could lead a man to the understanding of anything falling under the judgment of the sense of Hearing—such as the Voices or the Sounds from which Harmonies and Melodies are born—other than the things named. 

And even if the names of some Musicians still live honorably among us, they did not acquire their reputation through such chimeras, but through good harmonies and harmonious concerts heard in their compositions. Although they mixed in those entanglements, they also strove—if not through theory, then at least aided by their own judgment—to reduce their Harmonies to that ultimate perfection they could give them, even though by many others it was poorly understood and badly used (as evidenced by many errors committed by practical composers in their works). 

As for the **Reasoning**—that is, the **Speculative** side—few are seen to have held the right path. For, besides what **Boethius** <note>Annius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524), whose *De institutione musica* was the standard music theory textbook for a millennium.</note> wrote in the Latin language regarding this science (which is also found to be imperfect), one finds no one—leaving aside the learned **Franchino** <note>Franchino Gaffurio (1451–1522), a major Italian theorist.</note> and **Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples** <note>original: "Fabro Stapulense," a French humanist and mathematician.</note> on one hand, who were, one might say, commentators on Boethius—who proceeded further in speculating about things pertaining to Music, rediscovering the true **Proportions** of musical intervals, except for **Lodovico Fogliano of Modena**. Having perhaps considered what **Ptolemy** left written regarding the **Syntonic Diatonic** <note>A tuning system proposed by Claudius Ptolemy that uses "just" or pure major thirds, which Zarlino championed.</note>, Fogliano labored in writing a Latin volume on that faculty to show with all truth the real Proportions of the named intervals. 

The rest of the Theoretical Musicians, standing by what Boethius wrote on such matters, did not wish or were not able to go any further. Instead, they gave themselves to writing about the things shown which they called the **Quantitative genre**—which are contained in **Mood**, **Time**, and **Prolation** <note>The complex system of rhythmic levels in Renaissance notation.</note>—as can be seen in the *Recaneto of Music*, the *Toscanello*, the *Scintille* <note>Specific contemporary music manuals: *Recanetum de musica* (1533) by Stephano Vanneo; *Toscanello in musica* (1523) by Pietro Aaron; and *Scintille di musica* (1533) by Giovanni Maria Lanfranco.</note>, and in a thousand other similar books. 

Moreover, one also finds various opinions and very long disputes on such matters that never come to an end. One also finds many Treatises and many Apologies written by some Musicians against others, in which (even if they were read a thousand times) after being read, re-read, and examined, one finds nothing but infinite insults, slanders, and little of anything good; so much so that it is a cause for wonder. But truly, these men are also excusable: for just as in the time of **Socrates** and **Plato** there were the **Sophists**, so too were these men found in those times, and they were esteemed as much as the Sophists were in their own age. And this Quantitative genre was practiced so much then that it can truly be called the **Sophistic Art in Music**, and such musicians **Sophist Musicians**; just as the Sophists in the days...

<summary>Zarlino critiques the obsession with complex visual notation and "quantitative" theory, arguing that music should serve the ear rather than provide visual puzzles. He praises Lodovico Fogliano for returning to the study of true proportions (Ptolemy's Syntonic Diatonic) while dismissing many contemporary manuals as "sophistry."</summary>

# On the Common and Particular Strings of Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic songs. Chapter 72.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' containing a scene with a small building or chapel in a landscape with trees and hills.</image-desc>

HAVING reasoned until now regarding those things that belong to the composition of songs in the <term>Diatonic (The most natural musical genus, primarily using whole tones and semitones)</term> genus, it is reasonable (so as not to leave behind anything worthy of consideration) that I should reason a little regarding the other genera, which are the <term>Chromatic (A genus using semitones and minor thirds)</term> and the <term>Enharmonic (The most complex genus, using microtones or quarter-tones)</term>; especially because today some practitioners work very hard and place all their care into wanting to put them into use. But before I come to reason upon anything, it seems to me that it will be well done to reduce the <term>Strings (Chorde: used here to mean both the physical strings of an instrument and the specific notes/pitches of the scale)</term> of each of these three genera to their proper places in order between the usual lines and spaces, according to the method these men follow; and to show all those which are **Common** and serve each genus, and also the **Particular** ones; so that what I have to say may be more easily understood. 

Wherefore, one must know that within the <term>Greatest System (The 'Greater Perfect System' of Greek music theory, covering a two-octave range)</term> of each genus—from the <term>Proslabanomenos (The lowest note, literally 'the acquired string')</term> to the <term>Netehyperboleon (The highest note of the highest group)</term>—there are eighteen strings, divided and ordered into five <term>Tetrachords (A grouping of four notes spanning the interval of a fourth)</term>; as **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), the Roman scholar whose work transmitted Greek music theory to the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> also shows. Some of these are called **Natural** and **Essential** to the genus, and some are **Accidental**. The Natural ones are those contained within the four tetrachords: <term>Hypaton (Lowest group)</term>, <term>Meson (Middle group)</term>, <term>Diezeugmenon (Disjunct or separated group)</term>, and <term>Hyperboleon (Highest group)</term>; and the Accidental ones are those contained in the <term>Synemennon (Conjunct group, used to introduce the 'B-flat')</term> tetrachord. These are called Accidental because they are placed among the first ones by happenstance, as can be understood; since few of them are found to correspond with any other string placed between the <term>Proslabanomenos</term> and the <term>Mese (The central 'middle' note of the system)</term> by a <term>Diapason (The interval of an octave)</term>, as do those of the other tetrachords, the <term>Diezeugmenon</term> and <term>Hyperboleon</term>. Indeed, many of them are different from some strings of these two tetrachords in everything but name. 

In this manner, the natural and essential strings of each genus come to be fifteen, and three are found to be accidental; for the string <term>Mese</term> is the end of the <term>Meson tetrachord</term> and the beginning of the <term>Synemennon</term>, as can be seen in many places. And although such strings have been named according to the order shown in Chapter 28 of the Second Part—so that in terms of their naming, one finds no difference between the <term>Parhypate (The 'next to the lowest' note in a tetrachord)</term> and the <term>Lychanos (The 'index finger' note)</term> of the Diatonic from those of the Chromatic and the Enharmonic—nonetheless, when each of them is placed on an instrument, they are different in terms of position or site. That is to say, one may be more toward the low or toward the high than the other; as can be seen in the **Enharmonic Parhypate**, which is lower than the **Parhypate** of the other two genera; and similarly in the **Diatonic Lychanos**, which is higher than the **Chromatic Lychanos** and the Enharmonic one, as can be understood in Chapter 38 of the Second Part. 

Therefore, so that it may clearly appear which are the **Proper** and **Natural** strings, and which are the **Accidental** and the **Common** strings of any of the three named genera, I will set out three orders of strings. The first of these will contain only those that serve the **Diatonic**, without placing any other string that is (so to speak) "foreign"; and I will reduce them to the common order used by practitioners. The second will contain those that serve the **Chromatic**; although we shall find many among them that will be common to each genus, they will not, however, be particular Diatonic or particular Enharmonic strings. In this order, we can distinguish the particular Chromatic strings from the particular ones of the other two genera, for they will all be marked with an **X**, and the common ones will be without it. And even if the strings ♭ and ♮ <note>The 'soft' B (flat) and 'square' B (natural).</note> make up the **Synemennon Tetrachord** in this genus, they will not be particular, but common to every genus, because such a tetrachord is joined to the first four by accident, as I have said. The third order will then contain those strings that serve the **Enharmonic**, in which we will find the particular strings of this genus, which will be marked with this sign **X**, to distinguish them from those that are particular and also common to the other two genera, as can be seen in the orders placed below. Wherefore, the particular strings of these genera will be these: first, the third string of every tetrachord of the first order, proceeding from the low to the high, will be **Diatonic-particular**. Next, the third of every tetrachord placed in the second order marked with this sign **X** will be particular...

## Whether the last two Genera can be used simply in their natural strings, without employing the particular strings of the Genera shown. Chapter 73.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop-cap 'I' containing an illustration of a landscape with trees and a building.</image-desc>

I believe I have reasoned enough until now regarding the Diatonic genus that everyone can understand whether such a Genus can be used perfectly in its natural <gloss>notes</gloss> strings, or not. Passing then further along, we shall see if the same can be done in the other two Genera, without using the particular strings of another, and without the loss of many consonances <note>Harmonious intervals like thirds and fifths</note> that contribute to the generation of perfect harmonies. order <note>The "Third order" refers to the Enharmonic genus, which uses quarter-tones.</note>—we will find many figures that cannot be accompanied in such a way that, once accompanied, one hears a perfect harmony, as good, sonorous, and perfect compositions require. Indeed, we will find many notes that cannot have those consonances that are desired. And even if they do have them in some places, it will be necessary for the parts to sing in such a way that they render an unpleasant and ungentle sound to the ears of the listeners, as experience will always show us. We can therefore conclude that it is impossible to use these last two genera simply and by themselves in such a way that there is perfect harmony without the use of particular strings from some other genus.

### That Music can be used in two manners, and that the songs composed by some moderns do not belong to any of the named Genera. Chapter 74.

Music being used in two manners—that is, in the way the Ancients used it, as I have shown in the Second Part and am about to demonstrate again, and in the way the Moderns use it—it should be noted that if anyone wished to use it in the first way, it would not be impossible for him to observe everything the Ancients observed in their melodies. But when one wishes to use it according to the way of the Moderns, with the multiplication of many parts, and to ensure that perfect harmony is heard within it: whenever he took up this task and wished to put the two aforementioned Genera into use, he would labor in vain. This can be understood from what was said in the previous chapter, especially if he does not wish to depart from the precepts given by the ancient Practitioners and shown by me above regarding the composition of songs.

And although some are of the opinion that they compose the ancient Chromatic and Enharmonic harmonies in our day, it is not actually so. For truly, they exceed the boundaries and do not use those things that contribute to their composition, which are Harmony, Rhythm, and the Words joined together. Nor do they only use the strings proper to that genus to which they say the composition belongs; but they also use those that are proper to and serve the other genera particularly, as well as some others that are entirely foreign. They also use many diatonic intervals and modulations as strange as can be said, such as intervals of <term>Tritones (An interval of three whole tones, traditionally considered dissonant and difficult to sing)</term>, <term>Semidiapentes (A diminished fifth, slightly smaller than a perfect fifth)</term>, and other similar ones, which were greatly avoided by the Ancients. For these not only offend the senses but also contradict reason;

...as can be heard and seen together in their compositions. ## That the Diatonic genus can proceed through the intervals of the major or minor Third in its melodies; and that this does not cause any change of genus. Chapter 75.

And although they realize they have no firm reason by which they can show that their compositions are purely **Chromatic** or **Enharmonic**, they nevertheless strive to prove that it is so in practice. They say that the **Diatonic** proceeds by two Tones and one Semitone in each of its tetrachords; the **Chromatic** by two Semitones and one Trihemitone <note>A Trihemitone literally means "three half-tones," which we now call a minor third.</note>, which is the minor Third; and the **Enharmonic** by two Diesis and one Ditone <note>A Ditone literally means "two tones," which we now call a major third.</note>, which is the major Third. They argue that since the Diatonic cannot proceed by the Ditone, nor even by the Semiditone <note>Another term for the minor third.</note>, it follows that when such intervals are used, the song changes its Genus. This argument of theirs would truly be conclusive if what they say were true; but in my judgment, it seems to me that they are mistaken. Since all these intervals are found in the Diatonic, as we have seen in many places in the Second Part, it is not improper that they can sometimes be used in such a genus without being divided; nor does the song become Chromatic or Enharmonic because of this, as they imagine. This is because when they are used in such a way, they are not used as **Elements** or **Simple parts** of that genus, but as **Mixed** or **Composite** parts made of the primary intervals, which are the true Elements. 

And that this is true can be understood from what **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works were the foundation of medieval and Renaissance music theory.</note> says in Chapter 23 of the First Book of *Music*. Speaking on this subject, he says that one can also call the Tone and the Semitone a "Trihemitone" in the Diatonic genus, but it is not **Incomposite** <note>Incomposite (Incomposto) refers to a basic, indivisible building block of a scale. Zarlino argues that while a minor third is a "block" in the Chromatic scale, it is a "compound" of a tone and semitone in the Diatonic scale.</note>, because it is made of two intervals. In this way, one can see (as I have also shown in the Second Part) that Boethius takes the incomposite Trihemitone as an **Element** of the Chromatic genus, while in the Diatonic he takes it as a **Mixed** or **Composite** of two elements: the Tone and the Semitone. The same can also be said of the Ditone in the Diatonic, which is Composite and not simple, whereas in the Enharmonic it is Incomposite—that is, an Element of that genus. 

But it is even better understood by this: when he speaks of such intervals, he always says, "They are called so," and never says that they are Incomposite; for he knew very well that the latter two genera borrowed their intervals (as they say) from the Diatonic, as could be seen in many places in the Second Part. Nor can it be improper to pass from the **Simple** to the **Composite**, for such is the order of things. But it would indeed be impossible if one wanted to pass from the Simple elements to something even simpler within the same genus. We see this, for example, with **Letters**, from which all **Words** are composed; if one wished to pass to things simpler than the letters themselves, it would be impossible, because nothing simpler is found within their kind. 

Indeed, it is not impossible for a thing that is **Composite** in one genus to be **Simple** or **Elemental** in another; for in one genus it may be considered in one way, and in another genus in another manner. Therefore, it is no error that the Trihemitone and the Ditone, which are found as composites in the Diatonic, are placed as Elements in the other two genera. And even if these two intervals are not found as "incomposite" in the Diatonic genus in practice, they are nonetheless there in potential; since they can be reduced to such a form easily, otherwise such potential would be useless. 

And this should not seem strange: for just as Man is an "animal capable of laughter" <note>Original: "animal risibile." A classic philosophical definition: humans are the only animals with the capacity for laughter, even if they aren't laughing at every moment.</note>, and yet he does not always laugh in practice; so in the Diatonic genus, one does not always proceed by Tone, Tone, and Semitone for every Tetrachord. Therefore, I say that "passing from one genus to another" cannot be understood as when one uses the Composites (which serve as Elements for another genus), but rather when one uses the **Simple intervals** that are unique and used specifically in that genus—intervals that cannot be found as either simple or composite in another. Therefore, the conclusion these people make does not hold when they say: "In this song the interval of the Ditone and the Semiditone are found without any middle note; therefore it is Chromatic or Enharmonic." But it *would* be valid to say: "This song proceeds by the **minor Semitone**; therefore it is Chromatic," and "This song proceeds by the **Diesis** <note>In Zarlino's time, the "diesis" referred specifically to the microtonal interval or "quarter-tone" characteristic of the Enharmonic genus.</note>; therefore it is..."

<summary>Zarlino argues that the Diatonic genus naturally includes major and minor thirds as composite intervals, refuting critics who claim their use automatically makes music Chromatic or Enharmonic. He distinguishes between "elements" (simple building blocks) and "composites" (combinations of elements) to explain how the three musical genera overlap.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 75, where Zarlino is refuting the idea that using a major or minor third automatically changes the musical genus from Diatonic to Enharmonic or Chromatic. He is using formal logic to show that these intervals are properties of the Diatonic system.</meta>

...[this skip] is Enharmonic; just as if one were to say, *“This is a rational and mortal animal; or, This is capable of laughter; therefore it is a Man;”* <note>Zarlino is using a classic example from Aristotelian logic: a "difference" (like the ability to laugh) defines the "species" (Man).</note> seeing as it is the difference that constitutes the Species: *just as these ultimate differences of the Semitone and the Diesis <note>The Diesis here refers to the tiny quarter-tone interval used in the Enharmonic genus.</note> are proper to these two genera.* From this, it should be known that the intervals found in the **Diatonic tetrachords** can be considered in two ways: that is, **Simple**, such as those just mentioned; and **Composite**, such as the **major Third** and the **minor Third**. Because when they are considered alongside an intermediate sound, they can be called, along with the Greeks, **Systems** <note>original: *Sistemi*. In Greek music theory, a "system" is a group of intervals or a scale structure.</note>, as if they were complexes or ordered compositions; but when they are considered without any middle [note], they can be called **Diastems** <note>original: *Diastemati*. This refers to a "space" or a leap between two notes without sounding the steps in between.</note>, which is to say, spaces or intervals. 

It would truly be great madness to believe that we today—and the Ancients before us, before the other two genera were in use—could not use any sort of interval smaller than those contained in the Systems; and that they could not be Systems; and not those [intervals] which are larger and can also be Systems. For if there had not been, and were not now, such freedom, I do not see in what manner Harmonies could succeed well; considering that it would have been (and would still be) necessary that whenever one began to sing, starting in the low range, we would have to ascend to the high range by small intervals only; and to climb so much that one ended in the high range, and never returned to the low by taking up any of the previous notes; and likewise the opposite. 

But I ask these men, for mercy's sake: what sweetness, or what smoothness of harmony could this be? It seems to me that understanding it in this way is the same as saying that if we began to speak with any letter of the Alphabet we wished, it would be necessary to follow all the letters in order as they are placed, until the end, without skipping any. But in what manner could one express concepts? 

Perhaps someone will say that repeating notes is permitted when one takes the note by an Octave, or a Fifth, or a Fourth. If that was permitted, then **Diastems** (or larger Intervals) were also permitted. And if it was permitted to use not only these in repetitions, but even the Tritones (as these men do), which are dissonant intervals, I do not see for what reason it was not also permitted in every part of the melody to use both these and those smaller than these—which are the **Ditone** <note>A major third.</note> and the **Semiditono** <note>A minor third.</note>—since they have their mathematical forms contained within the **Sonorous Numbers** <note>Zarlino’s "Senario" or the numbers 1 through 6, which he believed governed all consonant intervals.</note> and are consonant. 

Therefore, since there are no other reasons, we can say that since larger Diastems were permitted in the Diatonic genus, these others we have shown were also permitted. For this reason, they did not prevent such a genus from being Diatonic; and not only Diatonic, but **Pure** <note>original: *Semplice*.</note> as well, without any mixture of any other genus. This did not happen in the other two [genera]: for whenever they proceeded by the Major Tone, they were receiving an interval that is proper to the Diatonic; and in such a manner, those genera could be called **Mixed**. 

And what I have said of one Genus, I also mean for the others regarding proceeding by Diastems, or larger Intervals. For when a melody of the minor Semitone or the Diesis is heard in Diatonic songs, that melody could be called mixed; which could also be said of the Chromatic ones. But we must note that although the Diatonic melody is properly that which moves from low to high by one Semitone and two Tones in each tetrachord; and the Chromatic by one major Semitone, one minor, and one **Trihemitone** <note>A minor third (literally "three half-tones").</note>; and the Enharmonic by two Diesis and one **Ditone**; and likewise the opposite, proceeding from high to low; nonetheless, when singing larger Diastems, many of these come to be common [to all]. 

Thus, what remains proper only to the Diatonic genus is the melody of the **Major Tone**; to the Chromatic, that of the **minor Semitone**; and to the Enharmonic, that of the **Diesis**; as anyone can know by experience. Concluding, then, we will say that if the following argument were valid: *“In this song, the major Third is sung without any middle [note], therefore it is Enharmonic; or the minor is sung, therefore it is Chromatic,”* such an argument would have been valid even before such genera were discovered—when simply the Diatonic was used, and the Chromatic Semitone and the Diesis were not otherwise in use—since (as can truly be held for certain, for the reasons given above) the Ancients sang such intervals without any intermediate sound. How far this [opposing view] is from reason, I will leave to be considered by anyone who has even a little judgment in matters of Music.

<summary>Zarlino concludes his defense of the Diatonic genus by arguing that leaps of major and minor thirds are inherent to it, using an analogy to the alphabet to show that music must be allowed to skip steps to be expressive. He defines the specific intervals that truly distinguish the three genera: the Major Tone for Diatonic, the minor Semitone for Chromatic, and the Diesis for Enharmonic.</summary>

### That where no variety of Harmony is heard in compositions, there can be no variety of Genus. Chap. 76.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring floral patterns and a landscape scene with a building inside a square frame.</image-desc>

WE HAVE seen above that the change of Genus does not consist in placing the **major Third** or the **minor [Third]** <note>In the original Italian, these are called the Ditono and Semiditono.</note>—whether filled with intermediate sounds or not—but rather in the modulation of the intervals proper to those Genera. It remains now to say that the change of one genus into another similarly consists in the change of the **Harmonies**; just as the change of one **Mode** into another consists in the change of the modulations from one species of **System** <note>original: *Sistema*. Here, Zarlino refers to the underlying scale structure.</note> to another, and in the change of the **Cadences**. For if I hear that same Harmony in a song where the parts proceed through a System of a major Third or a minor Third that I hear in a song where the parts proceed through their own **Diastema** <note>original: *Diastema*. A leap or space between two notes without sounding the steps between them.</note>; and if the one moves my hearing in the same manner as the other, I cannot see what great difference there can be between these two songs. Therefore, I say that there can be no difference of Genus in those compositions where no difference of harmony is heard; just as there can be no difference of Mode where there is no difference of modulation and cadences. And I add that one can only say there is a difference and variety of genus in compositions when one hears a variety of harmony that is **numerous** <note>original: *numerosa*. In Renaissance theory, this refers to being governed by "number," meaning rhythm and poetic meter.</note>, with appropriate words accommodated to it. I do not mean, however, that the variety is like the harmonies of one Mode compared to another (such as from the first Mode to the third Mode), because this variety is undoubtedly found in Diatonic songs; but I mean a variety of harmony that is, in every way and in every part, different from the harmony that arises from Diatonic compositions. I mean a harmony which, used in the manner of the **Ancients** and accompanied by Rhythm, moves the hearing in another, unusual way compared to common harmonies heard continuously, and makes one hear a diversity of Modes. Whether this diversity is actually heard or not, I will refrain from saying, and leave the judgment to those who are experts in the Art and the <term>Science of Music</term> <note>Zarlino distinguishes between the "Art" (practice) and "Science" (theory/mathematical laws) of music.</note>.

---

### On the utility provided by the aforementioned two Genera, and in what manner they can be used to produce good effects. Chap. 77.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring scrolling floral patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>

IF I said above that the last two genera <note>The Chromatic and Enharmonic genera.</note> cannot be used simply, without the mixture of the **Diatonic** genus, it seems to me I have not spoken without reason. For I have not found any writer, Greek or Latin, who truly says that they were used, or could be used, separately and "purely," except for the Diatonic, as I have shown. And in confirmation of this, **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works transmitted Greek music theory to the Middle Ages.</note>, in Chapter 4 of the 4th book of *Music*, places the division of the **Lydian mode** within the simple Diatonic genus, even though he does not show the division of the other Modes. And at the beginning of Chapter 5, he calls it not only "Simpler," but also "Prince of all the others." In which division (to also confirm with an example what I said above), he places the interval of the minor Third four times without placing any string <note>meaning any note or pitch</note> in the middle. In Chapter 3, he then places the symbols of the said Mode for all three Genera reduced into one, reserving the symbols of the other Modes for another, more convenient time and place; yet I have found no example of the other Genera in their simple form. For although **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and music theorist.</note> in Chapter 15 of the second book of *Music* provides examples of the Modes in the other Genera, he nevertheless does not present them without mixture, as anyone can see. I wanted to say this because it is one thing to place the intervals of a genus in an order of Sounds, and quite another to say that they can be used simply in their own Genus to produce a good effect. For many things are found that are simple in their existence and are of little good on their own; but when accompanied by other things and used with the proper means, they are good and produce a wonderful effect. We see this with **Flour**, among other things; for by itself, I truly cannot imagine how delightful and good it could be to eat. But accompanied by other things and put to use with the proper means, we have **Bread** and other compositions that bring great comfort to the human race. Thus, the same can be said of these last two Genera, which by themselves cannot be sufficient...

<summary>Zarlino argues that a change in musical Genus requires a fundamental change in the emotional and sonic character of the harmony, not just a change in intervals. He also likens the Chromatic and Enharmonic genera to flour, which is useless on its own but essential when mixed with the "Diatonic" genus to create beautiful music.</summary>

# Third [Part]

...sufficient to give delight to the ear; but when accompanied by the Diatonic, they are of great utility and much convenience, using and accompanying them with one another in those ways required in composition. And this can be understood from what I am about to say. Primarily, we can have this benefit from them: that by means of their notes <note>original: *chorde*. In this context, Zarlino uses the word for "strings" to mean specific musical pitches or notes.</note> accommodated among the diatonic notes, we can move toward the use of perfect harmonies, making use of them to acquire many major or minor imperfect consonances <note>Imperfect consonances refer to thirds and sixths, which provide the "color" or sweetness of the harmony.</note>; which in many places cannot be had within the order of diatonic notes, as is manifest to anyone practiced in the Art of composition. These notes are sometimes useful for making the harmony correspond—whether cheerful or sad—to the nature of the words. We can then, by means of the notes of these genera, perform the **Transpositions** of the Modes toward the high <note>original: *acuto*</note> or toward the low <note>original: *graue*</note>. These transpositions are very necessary to the Organists who serve in the Chapels <note>Referring to church choirs or "cappelle."</note>; for it is necessary that they sometimes transpose the Mode, now from the high to the low, and sometimes from the low to the high, according to what the nature of the Voices found there requires; for without their help, it would be impossible to do so. And although such notes are used frequently on such occasions, one nevertheless proceeds through them only diatonically, according to the modes shown above; in such a way that the greatest pleasure and delight is born in all who listen. On the contrary, they greatly annoy the listeners and greatly offend the sense when they are used inappropriately, without rule, and without any order. Hence, when one note is played frequently in place of another, there arises that which **Horace** says on this subject; for then

->*The lyre-player is laughed at, who always blunders on the same string.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Citharœdus Ridetur, chorda qui semper oberrat eadem.* From Horace’s *Ars Poetica*.</note>

And let no one marvel that I have said we use the notes of the [other] genera and proceed according to the modes shown above. For we truly use the notes of these genera, but not the genus itself; that is, we use the Parts, but not the Whole. This is because (as we shall see further on) the entire use of the genus cannot produce a good effect; but the use of the Parts can—namely, the notes marked with these accidental signs ♮, ♭, and ♯, and also with this ×—using them in the manner I have shown above. And if we sometimes find a song entirely free from these symbols, we can say (as is true) that it proceeds by diatonic notes only. But when we find one that has within it such characters as ♭ and ♯, then we shall say that it proceeds by Chromatic notes mixed with Diatonic ones. And if we find one which has some note not found numbered among the Diatonic or the Chromatic ones, we can name it **Enharmonic**, provided that such a note can be marked with the sign of the enharmonic note, which is this ×, and can divide the major Semitone into two parts. For such a note will be one of those found in the third order shown above; and we could say that such a song proceeds by the notes of each of the three named genera. But it must be noted that such a mixture can be made in several ways, according to the will of the Composers or the Players, transposing the Modes lower or higher outside of their natural notes contained in the notes of the Diatonic genus; and the composition (as they say) is sung as <term>Feigned Music</term> <note>original: *Musica finta*, also known as *musica ficta*. This refers to the practice of using accidentals to adjust pitches for harmonic or melodic reasons outside the "natural" scale.</note>. The First of these (leaving aside those that are not so much in use) is when the songs proceed by the notes marked with the **round b** <note>The flat sign (♭), used to indicate the "soft" B.</note> from their beginning, transposed toward the low by a Whole Tone; such as the Motet *Verbum iniquum, & dolosum* by the Spaniard **Morales** for five voices, and the most beautiful and artful motet *Aspice Domine* by **Adrian** <note>Adrian Willaert, the influential Flemish composer and Zarlino's teacher.</note> for six voices. The Second way is that in which one proceeds by the notes marked from the beginning of the song with the ♯ sign, and the Mode is transposed by a Whole Tone toward the high. And in both types of these songs, the enharmonic notes are sometimes touched to have the major and minor imperfect consonances as required, though they are touched rarely. In this manner, we come to use the two said genera, which produce most wonderful effects. I do not say (as I have also said) that we use the entire genus, but rather some part of the genus—that is, some notes—adapting them to the Diatonic genus and proceeding, according to the nature of this genus, by whole Tones and major Semitones, as is evident to everyone.

He introduces the concept of "Musica finta" (fictional music) and cites works by Morales and Willaert as examples of these practices.</summary>

# For what reason the Compositions that some Moderns compose as Chromatic produce poor effects.
## Chapter 78.

**I**T SEEMS TO ME *(from what has been said) that we have sufficiently responded to those who wish for us to use the Chromatic and the Enharmonic in compositions whenever we use the notes <note>original: *chorde*. Literally "strings," referring to the specific pitches of the scale.</note> of the aforementioned genera. But truly, it is one thing to use the Genus, and another to accommodate some Notes of such a genus; or even to accommodate some of its intervals; just as the use of the Whole is one thing, and that of the Parts is another.*
*Therefore, the use of the notes, and even of a single Interval that is sonorous, can be allowed, because it produces a good effect; and such is the use of the Parts. But the use of the Whole—that is, of all the notes of a genus and all its intervals—is not permitted, since it produces a poor <note>original: *tristo*. While it can mean "sad," in this musical context it refers to a "bad" or "unpleasant" aesthetic result.</note> effect. For this reason, the use of the Genus is to use all its notes and all those intervals considered by the Musician in that genus, and no other; and I say this regarding the melodic lines <note>original: *modulationi*</note> that form the parts of the vocal piece <note>original: *cantilena*</note>. But the use of the Notes is nothing other than accommodating them within the melodies of diatonic songs, proceeding through those intervals found—or that could be found—in the Diatonic genus; just as they have been, and still are, successfully used by many. This involves setting aside those intervals that are specific to the chromatic and enharmonic notes we use, namely the minor Semitone and the Diesis <note>The *diesis* here refers to the small melodic interval characteristic of the Enharmonic genus, often translated as a "quarter-tone" in modern terms.</note>. And because there are some who say that if the use of chromatic notes (even if the genus itself is not used) produces wonderful effects in songs, then if one heard the pure genus, the Melody would be multiplied; to this I say that although the response given above—that the simple Chromatic and Enharmonic genera cannot be used—would suffice for them, one can also say (supposing the Genus could be used) that the logical consequence does not always hold: "the use of the Parts is beneficial, therefore the use of the Whole is even more so." For it is found in practice that this is not true, as anyone of sound judgment can be certain. And this is verified not only in Music, but also in the other Arts, as we see in the Art of Sculpture <note>original: *Scultoria*</note>: not all the Marble that the Sculptor takes to make a Statue serves his purpose, but only some parts. First he chooses it, then he accommodates those parts that best suit his purpose, removing the superfluous, and conducts the work to the desired end. The Sculptor, therefore, does not take all that stone he had placed before him, but only that part he sees as necessary for his needs. Hence Musicians also, knowing that the use of chromatic notes was very purposeful for them, and that the use of the [pure] genera was very inconvenient, took that part which served them to make the Diatonic more beautiful and more graceful, and by such means reduced it to its perfection. For within it (according to one's aims) every manner of harmony <note>original: *concento*</note> can be heard, whether sweet, or harsh, or however one wishes, especially when the consonances are employed with purpose by a Composer who possesses judgment.*
*The use of the Parts is therefore useful—indeed, I would say necessary—and not that of the Whole. For with the help of a chromatic note, we can arrive at the use of good and sonorous harmonies, and avoid within the Diatonic genus certain inconvenient relations of Tritones, Diminished Fifths <note>original: *Semidiapenti*</note>, and other similar intervals that the parts make while singing together, as I have shown elsewhere. Without such help, one could often hear not only many harshnesses, but also some awkward melodic movements. And although all these inconveniences could be avoided using only diatonic notes, it would nevertheless be done with much greater difficulty, especially when wishing (as is one's duty) to seek variety in the harmony. Thus it happens that through the use of such a note, the Modes become sweeter and more suave. I am inclined to believe that the Ancients called the Diatonic "harder" and "more natural" than the other two genera for no other reason than that they saw the harmony was multiplied and made more lascivious by chromatic notes; whereas staying within its own notes, it was somewhat more manly and possessed more of the fierce. And I believe also that the Chromatic took its name of "lascivious," "soft," and "effeminate" from the effect produced by its notes when placed among those of the Diatonic. Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose works on music were foundational for Renaissance theory.</note> makes me believe this when he says that a single note added by Timothy <note>Timothy of Miletus, a Greek musician known for his innovations.</note> to the ancient instrument—which was arranged in an order of sounds divided diatonically—produced such an effect. The same was true of the addition made by Terpander <note>An early Greek poet and musician.</note> (as one reads) to the same instrument; whereby one can also underst-*

<meta>catchword: ...and,</meta>

<summary>Zarlino argues that while the pure Chromatic and Enharmonic systems are aesthetically displeasing, integrating individual notes from them into the Diatonic system is essential for creating beautiful, varied, and technically correct harmonies.</summary>
<keywords>Diatonic, Chromatic, Enharmonic, musical genera, harmony, sculpture analogy, Boethius, Timothy of Miletus, Terpander, music theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Zarlino's critique of the modern "Chromaticists." He argues that while individual notes from the Chromatic or Enharmonic scales can be used as ornaments, the wholesale adoption of these systems leads to music that is naturally unpleasant to the human ear due to a lack of mathematical proportion.</meta>

...to understand that they did not use the simple Chromatic, and also that they only used such a note <note>original: *chorda*. Literally "string," referring to the pitch produced by a string on a monochord.</note> for the ornamentation of the Diatonic genus. And because I see that moving through the Enharmonic notes placed on our modern instruments is somewhat more difficult, and requires a somewhat more expert player than is needed when passing through the Diatonic and Chromatic notes together; this leads me to think that the Ancients, having respect for such things, called the Enharmonic genus "difficult." This is true even though the difficulty lay in many other things, as I intend to demonstrate further on.

Returning then to our purpose, we shall say that the use of the **Parts** is good and becomes very convenient for the Composer; but the use of the **Whole** (besides being inconvenient) makes the song <note>original: *cantilena*</note> without any charm. This is because in its composition, certain things enter which are undoubtedly very disproportionate and outside of all harmony, and they cannot create any good ensemble sound <note>original: *concento*</note>. 

And if anyone should say that such things are displeasing not because they are bad <note>original: *triste*</note> in themselves, but because the Hearing is not accustomed to hearing them, it seems to me that this person wants to say that a bad and tasteless food must become pleasing after the taste has been used to it for a long time. But let it be as it will, I do not believe that just as someone who has accustomed his taste to bad food (unless he were entirely out of his mind) would not recognize—after tasting another that is good and perfect—and truly confess that such food is good, delightful, and sweet, and that what he ate before was bad and without any sweetness; so I do not believe that anyone who has accustomed his Hearing to such songs, after hearing a well-ordered Diatonic one, would not truly confess that the latter is good and the others are bad. 

And so that it does not seem that what I have said is said without any reason, I want us to investigate now the cause of why these songs cannot be good. Wherefore it is to be known that, just as it is impossible that a thing which has its parts in a certain corresponding proportion (which by the Greeks is called <term>symmetry</term> <note>original: *συμμετρία*</note>) should not truly delight the sense—given that the sense greatly delights in proportioned Objects—so it is impossible that a thing which has its parts outside of such proportion can delight. 

Wherefore I say that, since the Diatonic genus has in itself such proportion (as I am about to declare), it cannot fail to truly delight, and the sense cannot fail to take the highest pleasure from it. Conversely, the **Parts** of the Chromatic and those of the Enharmonic being disproportionate with the **Whole**, it is impossible that they can delight. However, it should be noted that I call the **Whole** in this place the entire body of the song—that is, all the parts together; and I name the **Parte** truly the melodic movement <note>original: *modulatione*</note> of one of its voices. Similarly, I call a consonance the **Whole**, and the **Part** is each interval contained within the <term>System</term> <note>original: *Sistema*</note> of such consonance. 

Now, having understood this, I say that it is impossible that the Diatonic should not delight, having its Parts in proportion with the Whole. This is because one does not find in its parts any singable interval that is not similar to a consonance used in counterpoint <note>original: *Contrapunto*</note>. Just as we can see, for example, that the <term>Diastema</term> <note>the distance or interval</note> of the Octave sung in the parts is similar to the interval of the Octave found placed in counterpoint between one voice and another. Similarly, the interval of the Fifth when sung is similar to that of the Fifth placed in the counterpoint; the same can also be said of the interval of the Fourth, of the two Thirds, the two Sixths, and of those of the Tones and the Major Semitone. These are placed in the counterpoint with that same proportion by which they are found to be sung in the parts of the song. 

Hence it is no wonder if I have said that the Diatonic genus cannot produce anything but a good effect; and on the contrary, that the Chromatic genus produces a bad effect, and similarly the Enharmonic. This is because the Intervals of the one and the other placed in the Counterpoint are not proportioned with those that are sung in the parts, nor vice versa. For the interval of the minor semitone, which is sung in the Chromatic, is not proportioned with any of those placed in the counterpoint. Nor indeed is such an interval placed in counterpoint, because it would produce a bad effect, as is manifest; even if it were placed in a syncopation, it is not contained by such a proportion that, added to any other interval, it could make a consonance. For it is numbered among those called <term>Ecmeli</term> <note>original: *Ecmeli*. From the Greek *ekmelis*, meaning "out of tune" or "unsuitable for melody."</note>, which I showed in Chapter 4. 

Among these is also placed the Enharmonic <term>Diesis</term> <note>In this context, a quarter-tone interval</note>, which is entirely outside of all proportion with the intervals placed in the counterpoint; for it resembles none of them, and is much further from such proportion than is the minor semitone. From this it follows that the Enharmonic is less harmonious in Counterpoint than the Chromatic, since the more a genus departs from such proportion, the more it offends the feeling. And although the Enharmonic is called "Harmonic" by many from the common harmony, and they want it to be an excellent genus—because (in the manner I have declared) when it enters into the melody of other genera it can produce a good effect—nevertheless, as Psellus <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar whose works on music were influential in the Renaissance.</note> says, <note>original: *Δυσμελωδικώτατον μέντοι τὸ ἀρ...* [catchword: *μονικὸν*]. "The enharmonic, however, is most unmelodic..."</note>

<summary>Zarlino argues that the Diatonic genus is naturally superior because its intervals match the mathematical proportions of musical consonances, whereas the Chromatic and Enharmonic systems use "Ecmelic" intervals that offend the ear.</summary>
<keywords>proportion, symmetry, Diatonic, Chromatic, Enharmonic, counterpoint, Ecmeli, Psellus, musical aesthetics, intervals</keywords>

He previously argued that these systems are mathematically disproportionate and therefore naturally unpleasant to the ear. Parte.
<sig>Q</sig>
<meta>catchword: they sang</meta>

"...the Enharmonic genus of melody exists," <note>original: *μονικὸν γένος τῆς μελῳδίας ἐσὶ* — likely a fragment of a Greek definition of the Enharmonic genus.</note> that is, the **Enharmonic genus** has a most unpleasant melody within the melody itself; even though some understand this to mean that its harmony can only be practiced with great difficulty. And it is true that it has a most unpleasant melody: for when one comes to its **Counterpoint**, it produces a most dismal effect; not having (as I have said) the sung intervals similar in proportion to those that are placed in Counterpoints. For this reason, then, I say that the Counterpoint, or rather the Harmony, of these last two genres <note>The Chromatic and the Enharmonic.</note> cannot in any way be good. It is quite true that the harmony is as much less unpleasant as it more closely approaches the corresponding proportion already mentioned.

## Of the things that concurred in the composition of the Genres. Chap. 79.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring floral motifs and a landscape background.</image-desc>
And although in the Second Part I showed the manner the Ancients held in reciting Music, and those things that concurred in the composition of their Melodies; and this might suffice for the Reader to recognize the difference regarding the use and composition of modern Music from the ancient; nevertheless, I wish (so as not to leave out anything worthy of consideration) that we now see some things the Ancients observed in the composition of the Melodies of these genres; so that it may be clearly known if the modern **Chromaticists** <note>A group of 16th-century composers and theorists, such as Nicola Vicentino, who sought to revive ancient Greek musical practices.</note> approach the truth, or if they are entirely off the right path. We must therefore remember that I said the Ancients, in their songs <note>original: *cantilene*</note>, considered a composition of **Number**, **Harmony**, and **Words**; which composition they named **Melody**. But it should be noted that in the composition of the Genres, they had not only different harmonies, but also the **Number**, or **Meter** <note>original: *Metro*</note>, as we might call it, which was determined and diverse: because those poetic feet contained in a Verse that they used in one genre, they did not use in another. 

And this can be understood by reading the *Music* of **Plutarch**, where, speaking clearly of the **Feet** <note>The rhythmic units of poetry, such as the dactyl or spondee.</note> that were placed in the Enharmonic pieces, among many other words that demonstrate this, he says that in the first place the **Spondee** <note>A metrical foot consisting of two long syllables.</note> was placed. And further down, speaking of the Enharmonic works of **Olympus**, one sees that he most clearly makes commemoration of the **Paeon** <note>A metrical foot of four syllables, one long and three short.</note> and the **Trochee** <note>A foot consisting of one long syllable followed by one short one.</note> which enter into the composition of such a genre. And they did not only use such things in the Enharmonic, but also in the others; as can be understood from the words of **Boethius**, placed in Chapter 3 of the Fourth Book of *Music*; which say briefly: that the Ancients, so as not to always write the full names of the strings <note>Referring to the names of the notes on the Greek scale, like *Proslambanomenos*.</note> in their songs, invented certain **ciphers** <note>original: *cifere* — musical notation symbols.</note> with which they noted such names, and they divided them by the Genres and by the Modes. And they sought to act with brevity when they wished to write any of their songs over a composition made in verse by placing these ciphers; whereby they came not only to explain the words contained in such verses, but also the melody itself. 

**Plutarch** also says further on that the first **Laws** <note>original: *Leggi*, referring to the Greek *Nomoi*, or traditional melodic formulas.</note> of the songs that were sung with stringed instruments were mixed with Verses, in which the **Dithyrambic Word** was sung. And this word was composed of several words, such as this one: **Selanneoana** <note>original: *Σελαννεοάνα*</note>, placed by **Plato** in the *Cratylus*, which is composed of three words; that is, of **Selas** <note>original: *Σέλας*</note>, which means Light; of **Neon** <note>original: *νέον*</note>, which signifies New; and of **Ennon** <note>original: *Ἔννον*</note>, which implies Old; by which name he says the Moon should be called, since it is continually changing its light and renewing itself. Of these words **Aristophanes** is most abundant in his Comedies; and they are perhaps those which **Horace** calls **Sesquipedalia** <note>Words "a foot and a half long."</note>. 

Then the Dithyrambic word was contained under certain poetic feet faster than any other foot; and from such feet, which were placed in the Verses, they took the **Measure** of the movements of the Harmony. This Harmony was bounded and established under a certain **Mode**, or **Air**, as we might call it, for singing; just as those modes of singing are upon which we currently sing the Sonnets or Songs of **Petrarch**, or the Rhymes of **Ariosto**. And such Modes cannot be changed or altered in any part outside of their determined Number or Meter without offending the hearing; just as we see in the harmony of **Dances**, which offends greatly when it is altered by even a tiny foot. From this it is clearly seen that in the composition of the genres, there entered the **Number**, or **Meter**, contained in the feet of the Verses. And not only Number speaking absolutely, but this or that number—that is, this or that foot: either **Dactyl**, **Spondee**, **Trochee**, or whatever other similar one it might be. For which reason it is only too clear that the Ancients used in such genres a determined sort of Verse; even though it cannot be known with certainty what manner of Verses they were, just as we can have no knowledge of the Mode or Air of their singing: since by no one (as far as can be seen) has anything been left in writing. Nor is it found that the Ancients had many parts sung, as we do, in a single ensemble <note>original: *concento* — polyphony.</note>; but...

<summary>Zarlino explains that ancient Greek musical genres were strictly tied to specific poetic meters and rhythmic "feet," unlike the experimental works of modern "Chromaticists." He argues that ancient melody was a unified composition of words, harmony, and rhythm (Number), often following traditional melodic formulas or "Laws."</summary>
<keywords>Enharmonic genre, Counterpoint, Plutarch, Boethius, poetic feet, Spondee, Trochee, Dithyrambic word, Plato's Cratylus, Petrarch, Ariosto, musical meter</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how ancient musicians composed and performed, contrasting their simpler methods with the complex counterpoint of the 16th century. Zarlino is arguing that the Ancients used instruments primarily to support a single vocal line.</meta>
