<header>Third Part</header>

they sang alone, accompanying their voices with the sound of an instrument; the Hebrews also did this, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> and the Divine Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> testify: they say that in ancient times the sacred Psalms were sung with the voice joined to the organ. And I hold for certain that some of the strings of their instruments were tuned (as I have seen and heard many) by the Octave, by the Fifth, and by the Fourth; and the harmony that came from these strings was always heard as a continuous sound, without any rest while they played; and then above these, they would perform a part in their own manner with the other higher-pitched strings. And what makes me believe this is that I see, even to this day, some very ancient instruments which are made and played as I have said: among which is found that which the Tuscans call a *Symphony* <note>original: "Sinfonia" — here referring to the hurdy-gurdy or organistrum, which uses a crank-turned wheel to create a continuous drone.</note>; which some claim was the ancient Lyre. And perhaps Ottmar Luscinius <note>A German humanist and music theorist.</note> in the first book of his *Musurgia*, holding such an opinion, named it the Lyre. And it could easily be that which Horace commemorates, saying:

<margin>As a discordant symphony amidst pleasant tables. <note>original: "Ut gratas inter mensas Symphonia discors." — from Horace's *Ars Poetica*.</note></margin>
There is also found another sort of instrument, about a cubit long, the name of which in Venice is called the *Altobasso* <note>A rectangular stringed instrument played with a stick while the performer simultaneously plays a small flute.</note>; it is square and hollow, over which are stretched several strings tuned to one of the named consonances. It is used in this manner: while the player of this instrument strikes the strings with a stick in one hand to a certain rhythm or time, with the other hand he plays a flute, making a melody in his own style. And not only are such stringed instruments found, but there is also found among the wind instruments one called the Bagpipe <term>Cornamusa: a traditional wind instrument using a reservoir of air to sustain drones.</term> in Tuscany; in which one used to hear two or three continuous sounds tuned together in consonance, which arose from two or three bass pipes <note>original: "Pifferi gravi" — the drone pipes.</note>; although at present only one is heard, and then a melody is heard performed by a high pipe <note>original: "piffero acuto" — the chanter.</note>, which, even if it does not harmonize with the sound of those pipes in every part, at least agrees at the end and in certain cadences: as is also done in each of the aforementioned instruments. This same thing is also found in the Trumpets used in armies and naval fleets: for while many of them sound with a continuous tone, some others make their sound vary according to the purpose; now giving the signal to fight, and now regrouping the army. Therefore, I think that those pipes that the Ancients called "Right" and "Left," <note>original: "Destri & Sinistri" — refers to the *tibia*, ancient double pipes where one played high and the other low.</note> which they used (as I have said elsewhere) in Comedies, were tuned in such a manner. Ancient Organs also approached this manner: for they were not made as modern ones are; and of this, the most excellent maker of such instruments, Master Vincenzo Colombi of Casalmaggiore <note>A famous 16th-century Italian organ builder.</note>, gave me proof. He told me in Venice that while in Turin in Piedmont many years ago, he found a very ancient one that was without pipes and completely decayed; it had a keyboard <note>original: "Tastame"</note> of such a kind that on the left side, that is in the bass, the keys were so wide that even for a large hand, one could barely reach the fifth key; and this keyboard, the more one went toward the right side, that is toward the treble, the smaller it became. And (from what he saw) he holds for certain that it must have also been tuned in a different manner than our modern ones are tuned. Many other instruments, both stringed and wind, are also found made to be played in such a way; which I will leave out so as not to be long-winded. Their Genres were thus composed of Harmony, Rhythm <note>original: "Numero" — referring to poetic meter or musical time.</note>, and Speech <note>original: "Oratione"</note>; nor did all sorts of verses or feet enter into their compositions, but only this or that one; that is, a set number. In this way, the ancient musicians practiced music in their genres; nor was this difficult for them, nor impossible: because by using it in this way, they could make whatever interval they wished heard in their melodies, which could not generate such annoyance that it could not be tolerated: since they did not use the **Counterpoints** <term>Counterpoint: the technique of combining two or more melodic lines to sound simultaneously.</term> that we use in our compositions; rather, they used a simple mode of harmony, as has been seen.

## Refutation of the Chromaticists' Opinions. Chap. 80.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'H' featuring two figures in a room with a window.</image-desc>
FINALLY, the **Chromaticists** <note>Music theorists of Zarlino's time, like Nicola Vicentino, who sought to revive ancient chromatic and enharmonic systems.</note> hold the opinion that in songs one can use any interval whatsoever while singing, even if it does not have its form or proportion located among the **Harmonic Numbers** <term>Harmonic Numbers: the ratios (1 to 6) that Zarlino believed defined all pure musical consonances.</term>. And they are moved by this reason: that since the voice can form every interval, and since it is necessary to imitate familiar speech in pronouncing words—as Orators do, and as is proper—it is not inconvenient that one can use all those intervals that serve the purpose of expressing the concepts contained in the words, with those accents and other things, in the way we pronounce them when speaking, so that they may move the passions. To

<meta>catchword: which</meta>

<summary>Zarlino describes various ancient and folk instruments (like the hurdy-gurdy, bagpipe, and early organs) to illustrate that the Ancients used simple harmonies and drones rather than modern complex counterpoint. He then begins to challenge the "Chromaticists" who argue that music should use any interval possible to mimic the emotional inflections of human speech.</summary>

<keywords>Ancient instruments, Sinfonia, Altobasso, Cornamusa, Organ history, Vincenzo Colombi, Counterpoint, Chromaticists, Musical imitation of speech, Harmonic Numbers</keywords>

--- Page 309 ---
<meta>This page continues Zarlino's critique of "modern" composers who attempt to revive ancient musical practices (like the chromatic and enharmonic genera) without understanding the underlying principles of harmony or the rhetorical goals of the Ancients. He argues for a rational, purposeful use of musical intervals.</meta>

<page-num>291</page-num>
<header>Part.</header>

to which one responds that it is truly a great inconvenience: for it is one thing to speak familiarly, and another to speak modulating or singing. *Nor have I ever heard an Orator (since they say it is necessary to imitate Orators, so that Music may move the affects <note>original: "affetti" — the emotional states or passions of the soul.</note>) who uses in his speech those strange and clumsy intervals that these men use: because if he were to use them, I do not see how he could sway the mind of the Judge, and persuade him to do his will—as is his goal—unless he achieved the opposite effect. For although everything could be done conveniently in one part of the musical composition <note>original: "cantilena"</note>, and such accents were heard to be made with purpose and to produce good effects; nevertheless, in the accompaniments one would hear such "thievish" <note>original: "ladre" — likely meaning "dishonest" or "vile" sounds that steal away the harmony.</note> things that it would be necessary to plug one's ears.* Nor is their conclusion valid: *The voice can produce every interval, therefore every interval can and should be used:* because this would be the same as saying that, since a man can do both good and evil, it would be lawful for him to commit every crime and use every illicit way against good customs, against all duty, and against all justice.

But truly the Ancients never held such a malicious opinion; nor did they take such a presumptuous license as to want to spoil anything good in Music; rather they sought to fix the bad, to increase the good, and to make it even better. *For which reason, how laudable such licenses were among them can be understood from what was written by the prince of Ancient Musicians, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose work "Harmonics" was a primary source for Zarlino.</note>, against Aristoxenus, Didymus, and Eratosthenes; for he did not wish to praise, but rather blamed some of their Divisions of Tetrachords <note>term: <term>Tetrachord</term> (the basic four-note building block of ancient Greek musical scales).</note>, made in such a way that their intervals were not contained by the proportions of the Superparticular <note>term: <term>Superparticular</term> (a mathematical ratio where the numerator is one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 4:3. Zarlino believed these were the only "natural" musical ratios).</note> genus. And if for the modulation of one Tetrachord, which did not involve Counterpoint <note>term: <term>Counterpoint</term> (the art of combining multiple independent melodic lines simultaneously).</note>, those men were so blamed and so rebuked; how much would these moderns have been rebuked, if he had seen their compositions? Which not only in one of the parts, but sometimes in all, proceed together through awkward and disproportionate intervals. Truly, as a man of great authority and as a good teacher, he would not have wasted many words, but would have given them such punishment as would be worthy of such presumption.* 

They say also that all those strings that are on an instrument should be used, so that they are not placed in it in vain. And truly they speak the truth: for when they are not used, they would be placed there without purpose: but it is necessary to use them with reason and purpose: since without reason and without purpose they are not used well, but are used badly. And if it were necessary to use all the intervals on an instrument—which at times are a great number—by saying they are in such-and-such an order, one could say the same if these intervals were divided into two parts, and others into two more, and so proceeding to infinity, multiplying the orders of sounds to have (as they say) every sort of voice to express every sort of accent. How ridiculous this is, I shall leave to be judged by all those who are capable of reason. *And even if there are many strings on an instrument, among which are found many and varied intervals, they should not be used except with purpose, and when the composition and the Mode <note>term: <term>Mode</term> (the specific scale or "key" that governs the emotional character of a piece).</note> require it: since using anything without necessity and without purpose is truly a vain thing and denotes little prudence; besides which it generates great annoyance in the very sensation of such an object. It is quite true that many do not feel such boredom, provided they hear new and fantastic things; whether they be good or bad as they please, they care little for it: But those who delight in rare and good things cannot suffer anything bad.* 

There are, however, some who are deceived by the opinion of many, and not having much judgment of their own, they hold to the words of some who have more authority than they, and say, "this is good," and "this is bad." But if the truth were shown to these people, they would change their mind immediately and be of another opinion. These can be compared to those who have no judgment of Jewels: when shown a counterfeit and false one that happens to be beautiful, and they are told it is of great value, they prize it much because they do not know it, and because of their belief that Jewels must be worth a lot of money; and that which is good, but not so beautiful, they prize little. But when they are told that the first is false and the second is good, they immediately change their mind and hold a different opinion. *I wanted to say all this for those who believe that a Flea is an Elephant <note>A proverbial expression for making a mountain out of a molehill, or exaggerating the value of something small.</note>; so that they can see and hear that they will never have anything good outside of our genus <note>Zarlino refers to the Diatonic genus as the foundation of modern music.</note>; using the Chromatic and Enharmonic <note>term: <term>Chromatic/Enharmonic</term> (ancient Greek tunings that used sharps, flats, and quarter-tones, which some of Zarlino's contemporaries were trying to revive incorrectly).</note> strings with purpose as we do; unless one were to return to joining together (as the Ancients did) Number, Harmony, and Words, in which were contained the things shown in Chapter 7 of the second part: For if any good thing could have been found besides our usage, there is no doubt that in all these many years that Music has existed, after having been dismissed*

O 2
<meta>catchword: the two</meta>

<summary>Zarlino argues against the use of "clumsy" and irrational intervals in modern music, comparing the composer's duty to that of an orator and warning that novelty without mathematical reason is merely a "false jewel." He emphasizes that while all strings of an instrument can be used, they must be used with specific purpose and according to the natural proportions defined by ancient authorities like Ptolemy.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Part Three of Zarlino's treatise. Having criticized the modern misuse of ancient Greek musical genera (the chromatic and enharmonic) on the previous page, Zarlino here reflects on why these styles were abandoned and expresses his hope for a future "noble spirit" to perfect the science of music beyond mere commercial interests.</meta>

<page-num>292</page-num>
<header>Third</header>

concerning these two last genera <note>The chromatic and enharmonic, which Zarlino views as largely lost or misunderstood by moderns.</note>; there would not have been any person of excellent talent who would not have put at least one of them into use, since truly there have been many who for many years (as I hear from many) have toiled over this matter; yet they could never find anything that gave them delight. Truly it would have been a very unfortunate thing if the good and the beautiful in Music had been cast aside, and the less good retained. But this is not credible; because just as in other Arts and Sciences—those involving great speculation but little practical utility—the good has always been preserved, and the bad, as a useless thing, has been allowed to fade away; so I believe it has been in Music. Although I hope one day to see labor devoted to this Science in such a manner, and to see it brought to such perfection, that nothing more could be desired in it beyond what is put into practice. And I say this because I do not see it yet in that state of perfection which it could attain—a perfection I hold in my mind, yet which truly cannot be expressed. This will happen when it is embraced by some noble spirit <note>original: "spirito gentile"</note> whose ultimate goal is not profit—which is the way of the common laborer <note>original: "meccanico" — Zarlino distinguishes between the "mechanical" act of performing for money and the "liberal" science of understanding harmony.</note>—but rather honor and immortal glory. This glory he shall acquire after having labored within this Science and raised it to that ultimate degree of which I have spoken.

# THE FOURTH AND FINAL PART
## *Of the Harmonic Institutions*
### BY M. GIOSEFFO ZARLINO
### OF CHIOGGIA.

#### What a Mode is. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'V' featuring a figure in classical or religious attire seated at a table, within a rectangular frame decorated with floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>*HAVING SEEN in the previous Part, and sufficiently shown the method that must be kept in composing musical pieces; and in what manner, and with what beautiful and regulated order the Consonances are linked with one another, and even with the Dissonances; I shall now come to speak of the Modes. And although such an undertaking is not a little difficult (especially as I wish to discuss certain things regarding them according to the use of the Ancients), both because at present (as I have said at other times) modern Music is practiced differently from Ancient music; and also because no example or vestige of them remains that could lead us to a true and perfect knowledge; nevertheless, I do not wish to refrain from discussing certain things. I will do so in the best way I can, speaking in general and also in particular, touching upon some of the most notable points as they occur to my memory and as they become relevant to my purpose. From these, students will be able to arrive at the resolution of any doubt that might occur to them on this subject. This done, I shall then show in what manner modern Musicians use them; and I will speak of how many sorts are found, their order, and in what manner the Harmonies <note>In this context, Zarlino uses "Harmony" to refer to the overall musical effect or specific tonal character of a mode.</note> that arise from them are accommodated to Speech—that is, to the Words. Since I must begin such a discussion, we shall first see what a Mode <term>Mode: In Renaissance music theory, a "mode" is a system of organizing pitches, similar to a modern "key," but with specific melodic behaviors and emotional associations.</term> is, so that we may know what it is we intend to discuss. Nor will this be done out of place, since the Mode is the principal Subject of this, our final discussion. It should therefore be noted that this word "Mode," besides all its other meanings, which are many, properly signifies Reason—that is, that measure or form which we use in doing anything, which then constrains us not to go further, making us perform all things with a certain moderation or restraint. And truly so, because (as Pindar says) measure follows upon everything <note>original: "ἔπεται δ' ἐν ἑκάστω μέτρον"</note>. In each thing there is a Mode, or measure; which Horace also said after him:*

> There is a measure in things, there are fixed limits at last;
> Beyond and short of which the right cannot consist <note>original Latin: "Est modus in rebus, sunt certi denique fines; Quos vltra citraque nequit consistere rectum"</note>:

*For such moderation or restraint is nothing other than a certain manner, or a determined and firm order in proceeding, by which a thing is preserved in its being, by virtue of the proportion found within it; which not only delights us, but also brings us great benefit. From this it follows that if, by chance or by design, such an order departs from that proportion, one cannot say how much it offends, and how much the sense abhors such an order. Having therefore considered such a thing, the ancient Musicians and Poets—because the one and the other were the same thing (as I have said elsewhere)—called their compositions Modes; in which, under various subjects, by way of Speech, they expressed different Numbers or Meters, and different Harmonies, accompanied one to another with proportion. From this it arose later that they established three Genres of Modes, having no regard for the Sound or the Harmony that was produced, but only for the other parts joined together; one of which they called Dithyrambic, the other Tragic, and the third Nomic <note>These terms refer to ancient Greek poetic/musical forms: Dithyrambs were choral hymns to Dionysus; Tragic refers to the music of drama; Nomic refers to a traditional, structured melodic type.</note>; of which their species were many, such as Epithalamia <note>Wedding songs.</note>, Comic, Encomiastic <note>Songs of praise.</note>, and other similar ones. Considering then the Harmonies by themselves that issued from such combinations, because they retained in them a certain, proper, and determined form, they likewise named them Modes; adding to them Dorian, or Phrygian, or another name according to the name of the peoples who were the inventors of that harmony, or from those who*

they delighted more in one kind of harmony than another: because the Dorian harmony was named after the Dorians, who were its inventors; the Phrygian from the people who inhabited Phrygia; and the Lydian from those of Lydia, and so on for the others in order. It is certainly true that each of these had something unique in its song, and being accompanied by different <term>Numbers<note>In this context, "Numbers" (*Numeri*) refers to the rhythmic proportions and poetic meters that governed the movement of the music.</note></term>, they called some of them grave and severe; some bacchanalic and furious; some decent and religious; and others they named lascivious and warlike. Therefore, in this respect, they took great care in matching such Harmonies to the rhythmic Numbers, and this together with a purpose suited to the subject matter they expressed in Oratory or Speech, according to their nature. Taking all these things into consideration, they named their compositions according to the nature of the compound, such as, for example, the **Mournful Modes**, which are the Elegies: for they contain sad and mournful matters. This can be seen expressly in those two volumes (besides the almost infinite others by other authors) which Ovid wrote after he was sent into exile by Augustus; and also from what he writes in the *Epistle of Sappho to Phaon*, wanting to show that amorous things are mournful matters and that they suit the Elegy, saying:

> Perhaps you ask why my verses are in alternating meters,
> when I am better suited to lyric modes.
> My love is to be wept for. Elegy is a mournful song.
> No lyre is made for my tears.
> <note>Original Latin: *Forsitan & quare mea sint alterna requiris / Carmina, cùm lyricis sim magis apta modis. / Flendus amor meus est. Elegia flebile carmen. / Non facit ad lacrymas barbitos ulla meos.*</note>

Horace made mention of these Modes, saying:

> You always pursue with mournful modes
> the loss of Mystes.
> <note>Original Latin: *Tu semper urges flebilibus modis / Mysten ademptum.*</note>

And also Boethius in the third book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> Once the Thracian bard <note>Referring to Orpheus.</note>,
> mourning his wife's death,
> after he had compelled the forests to run,
> and the swift rivers to stand still with mournful modes;
> <note>Original Latin: *Quondam funera coniugis / Vates thraicius gemens, / Postquàm flebilibus modis, / Syluas currere, mobiles / Amnes stare coegerat;*</note>

Just as Cicero also commemorated them in the *Tusculan Disputations*, when (mentioning the humble and low ones together) he said: *These things, when sung with low and mournful modes, bring sadness to entire theaters.* <note>Original Latin: *Hæc cum pressis & flebilibus modis, qui totis theatris moestitiam inferant, concinuntur.*</note> And in another place, mentioning the slow ones: *The same Roscius used to say that as he aged, he would make the modes of the flute player slower and the songs more relaxed.* <note>Original Latin: *Solet idem Roscius dicere, se quo plus ætatis sibi accederet, eo tardiores tibicinis modos, & cantus remissiores esse facturum.*</note>

Others named them **Lamenting Modes**, as can be seen in Apuleius, when he says: *And the sound of the wedding flute changes into the complaining Lydian mode.* <note>Original Latin: *Et sonus Tibiæ Zigiæ mutatur in quærulum Lydij modum.*</note> Some then called them **Sweet Modes**, as the same Horace shows us in another place, when he says:

> Now Thracian Chloe rules me,
> learned in sweet modes, and 
> skilled with the lyre.
> <note>Original Latin: *Me nunc Tressa Chloe regit, / Dulces docta modos, & / Citharæ sciens.*</note>

And Seneca also: *Let the flute pour out sweet modes for the sacrifice.* <note>Original Latin: *Sacrificas dulces tibia effundat modos.*</note> They also named some others **Sad Modes**, as can be seen from the authority of Boethius:

> I who once composed songs with flourishing zeal, 
> am now forced, alas, to enter into mournful modes of sadness;
> <note>Original Latin: *Carmina qui quondam studio florente peregi, / Flebilis heu mæstos cogor inire modos;*</note>

And some **Immodest Modes**, which Quintilian commemorates saying: *I think it must be stated more openly that I am not teaching this [music] which is now effeminate on stages and broken by immodest modes.* <note>Original Latin: *Apertius tamen profitendum puto, non hanc a me præcipi, quæ nunc in scenis effæminata, & impu dicis modis fracta.*</note> Others called them **Crude** or **Coarse Modes**, which Ovid demonstrates:

> And while the Tuscan flute player provides a crude mode,
> the Lydian strikes the leveled ground three times with his foot;
> <note>Original Latin: *Dumq; rudem præbente modum tibicine Tusco, / Lydius æquatam ter pede pulsat humum;*</note>

And others **Discordant Modes**; and of these Statius makes mention:

> I attempt discordant modes,
> and sobbing words.
> <note>Original Latin: *Discordesq; modos, & singultantia uerba / Molior.*</note>

Finally (leaving out many others for brevity), they universally called some compositions **Lyric Modes**, as can be understood from the authority of Ovid cited above. Such matters were not expressed by the voice alone, but were accompanied by the Harmony that arose from some instrument, whether it be the <term>Cittern<note>A wire-strung fretted instrument, popular in the Renaissance.</note></term>, or the Lyre, or the <term>Pipe<note>The "Piffero" or flute.</note></term>, or of any other sort. There was nonetheless a great difference between these Modes: since the people of one province used one manner of Verse and one Instrument, and those of another used another Instrument and another manner. And they were not different in these alone, but in the Harmonies as well: for one kind of harmony was used by one people and another by another; in such a way that they were also different in the rhythmic Numbers found in the verses. From this it arose later that the Modes were named after those peoples (as I have said above) who most

delighted in that style, or had been its inventors. From this, one can understand that if a people, such as those of Phrygia, heard a certain foreign style, they would say it was the Mode of that province where it was most used, or where it had been discovered. In this way, they called the *Aeolian Mode* after the people of *Aeolia*, its inventors; it was contained within a certain *Hymn*, composed in the *Lyric mode* according to certain <term>Numbers<note>In Renaissance theory, "Numbers" (*Numeri*) refers to the rhythmic proportions and poetic meters that govern the movement of music and verse.</note></term>. For these people took great delight in the *Lyre*, or *Cithara*, which according to the opinion of some (which I consider false) were the same thing in those times; to its sound, they sang the aforementioned *Hymn*. The *Dorians* used a similar instrument, although they perhaps sang a different kind of *Verse* and used a very different *Harmony*. *Pindar* bears witness to this when he names such an instrument *Δωρίαν φόρμιγγα* <note>original Greek: "Dorian cithara"</note>, that is, the *Dorian cithara*; and *Horace* says:

> A song sounding from a lyre mixed with pipes,
> This one Dorian, those Barbarian.
> <note>Original Latin: *Sonantem mistum tibijs carmen lyra, / Hac Dorium, illis Barbarum.*</note>

From that word *Barbarian*, one can see that he intends the *Phrygian mode*, for the people of *Phrygia* also used *Pipes* <note>Zarlino uses *Pifferi*, referring to woodwind instruments like the ancient *tibia* or the Renaissance shawm.</note>. And they truly used to play such a *Mode* with similar instruments, as I could show with many examples, which I leave out for the sake of brevity; one from *Virgil* will suffice, who speaks in this manner:

> *O you truly Phrygian women (for you are not Phrygian men), go through high*
> *Dindymus, where the pipe gives its two-holed song to those accustomed to it;*
> <note>Original Latin: *O vere phrygiæ (neq; enim phryges) ite per alta / Dyndima, vbi assuetis biforem dat tibia cantum;*</note>

And one from *Ovid*:

> *The pipe gives Phrygian modes, as it did before;*
> <note>Original Latin: *Tibia dat phrygios, vt dedit ante modos;*</note>

From these, one can understand that what I have said is true. With this instrument, the people who inhabited *Lydia* likewise made their harmonies, and of this *Horace* is a witness, saying:

> *We shall sing of leaders who performed with valor in the manner of our fathers,*
> *with a song mixed with Lydian pipes,*
> *of Troy, and Anchises, and the kindly*
> *progeny of Venus;*
> <note>Original Latin: *Virtute functos more patrum duces, / Lydis remisto carmine tibijs, / Troiamq;, & Anchisen, & alma / Progeniem Veneris canemus;*</note>

And *Pindar*, who, before him, supplicating *Jupiter* for *Psaumis of Camarina*, winner in the Olympic games, says: *I come to you as a suppliant, O Jupiter, Λυδίοις αὐλοῖς* <note>original Greek: "with Lydian pipes"</note>, that is, with *Lydian Pipes*. To demonstrate this, there is also the testimony of *Apuleius*, with the authority cited above, and many others; but these shall suffice. From this, therefore, we can understand that the *Modes* in ancient times consisted of the *Harmonies* and the *Numbers* expressed by a certain kind of instrument; and that their diversity lay in the variation of the *Harmonies*, in the diversity of the *Numbers*, and in the manner of expression—that is, the *Instrument*.

And even if some peoples agreed with others in their *Harmonies* or *Instruments*, they were then different in their *Numbers*; and if they were in accord in these, they disagreed in the *Harmonies* and the *Instruments*. Thus, if they were alike in one or two things, they varied in the rest. We see this very same thing today in different nations: for the *Italian* uses the *Number*—that is, the *Verse of feet* or *syllables*—in common with the *French* and the *Spanish*, such as the verse of *Eleven syllables*; nevertheless, when one hears one or the other sing, a different *Harmony* is perceived, and another manner of proceeding. For the *Italian* sings differently than the *French*, and the *Spanish* sings in another manner than the *German*—to say nothing of the manifest differences of the barbarian nations of the infidels. The *Italian* and also the *French* greatly use the *Lute*, and the *Spanish* use the *Ceterone* <note>A large, wire-strung instrument of the cittern family.</note>, though it varies little from the *Lute*; and other peoples use the *Pipe*. 

Regarding the *Numbers* or *verses*, one can see how much difference there is between peoples, and how much one people has a different manner from another, starting from this point: although outside of *Italy*, the *linked* or *loose* verse of *Eleven syllables* (made in the likeness of the *Latin hendecasyllable*) is not used in some parts, it is nevertheless used much in *Italy*, *France*, and *Spain*. And what is called *Rhyme* (*Rima*) in *Italy*, I believe is derived from the Greek word *ρυθμός* (*rhythmos*), which signifies (as I have said elsewhere) *Number* or *Consonance*. Because from those correspondences and links found at the end of *Verses*, which they call *Cadences*, arises the *Consonance* or *Harmony* found within them. *Italians* use such *Cadences* not only in those types of *Verses* found in <term>Ottava rima<note>A stanza of eight lines with an ABABABCC rhyme scheme.</note></term> or *Stanzas*, in <term>Sonnets</term>, in <term>Capitoli<note>A poem in terza rima, often used for instructional or satirical subjects.</note></term>, and other similar forms that require *Whole verses*; but also in <term>Canzoni</term> and <term>Madrigals</term>, where many types of *Verses* are placed, such as those of *Seven syllables* and other similar ones called *Broken verses*. For in *Italy*, mother of good and rare intellects, various manners of composing are used, as can be understood from the aforementioned *Ottava rima*, or *Stanzas* if we wish to call them so, from <term>Terzetti<note>Three-line stanzas, as used in Dante's Divine Comedy.</note></term>, from <term>Sestine</term>, from *Sonnets*, and from *Capitoli*, in which only one kind of *Verse* is employed: the *Whole* verses. And in the *Canzoni*, and in the...

### Part Four

->**Madrigals**<- and other similar forms, in which various kinds of <term>Numbers<note>In Renaissance theory, "Numbers" (*Numeri*) refers to the rhythmic proportions and poetic meters that govern the movement of music and verse.</note></term> are placed in imitation of the Odes of **Horace**; although the Horatian Numbers are without the aforementioned <term>cadences<note>Here, Zarlino uses "cadences" (*cadenze*) to refer to rhyming line-endings, which were absent in classical Latin poetry but central to Italian verse.</note></term>, and the Italian ones are bound by these cadences in that manner; as can be seen in the learned and graceful *Canzoni* of **Petrarch**, and of many other most excellent men. I hold for certain that the learned Italian spirits were the inventors of these: for I do not remember ever having found among any other poet, neither Greek nor Latin, a similar way of composing with such cadences; even though the most learned **Horace** sang many Odes in many styles. It is quite true that the Latin poets (though not very often) used similar cadences, or correspondences, in the middle syllables and the last syllables of some of their verses, which they call **canine** <note>original: "Canini." Zarlino likely refers to what are more commonly known as Leonine verses—hexameters where the middle rhymes with the end—but he uses the term "canine."</note>; as the Poet <note>Likely referring to Virgil, often called "The Poet" by Renaissance authors.</note> has done in each of these:

> *They sent them to the earth, or gave the sick ones to the fires.* <note>original Latin: *Ad terram misêre, aut ignibus ægra dedêre.*</note>
> *We turned the horns of the veiled sail-yards.* <note>original Latin: *Cornua vellatarum obuertimus antennarum.*</note>
> *One like a man indignant; and like a man threatening.* <note>original Latin: *Illum indignanti similem; similemq; minanti.*</note>
> *Then the head of the one praying in vain, and begging much.* <note>original Latin: *Tum caput orantis nequicquàm, & multa precantis.*</note>
<margin>And **Ovid** also observed this law in this line.</margin>
> *His right hand twisted the mouths of the swift horses;* <note>original Latin: *Ora citatorum dextra contorsit equorum;*</note>

And in many others, which are not included so as not to increase the volume. Whence **Petrarch** (as I believe), imitating such a manner of composing, placed them in another way, matching the end of the preceding verse with the middle of the following one in this guise:

> *I no longer wish to sing as I used to:*
> *For others did not understand me: whence I had shame.* <note>original Italian: *Mai non vò più cantar com' io soleua: / Ch'altri non m'intendeua: onde hebbi scorno.*</note>
<margin>He also observed this in the Song that begins *Beautiful Virgin*.</margin>
> *And in a beautiful dwelling one can be troubled;* <note>original Italian: *E puossi in bel soggiorno esser molesto;*</note>

And so with the rest of that song. He also observed this in the Song that begins *Beautiful Virgin* <note>Petrarch's *Vergine bella*, the final poem of his *Canzoniere*.</note>. But even if such a manner of composing with similar cadences were found among the Greek or Latin poets, it would matter little, since the first inventor of such an Italian manner of composing could boast just as much—even if he had taken the invention from some Greek or Latin poet—as **Horace** boasted of being the first who found the way to compose lyric verses in Latin in the manner of the Greeks; as can be understood from his words, when he says:

> *I shall be spoken of where the violent Aufidus roars,*
> *and where Daunus, poor in water, ruled over*
> *rustic peoples; having risen from humble power*
> *to be the first to have brought Aeolian song*
> *to Italian measures.* <note>original Latin: *Dicar, quà violens obstrepit Aufidus, / Et qua pauper aquæ Daunus agrestium / Regnator populorum, ex humili potens / Princeps Aeolium carmen ad Italos / Deduxisse modos.* (Horace, Odes 3.30)</note>

For this, **Tolomei** <note>Claudio Tolomei (1492–1556), who attempted to adapt classical quantitative meters to Italian poetry.</note> can also boast of being the first who expressed the **Heroic verse**, the **Hexameter**, and the **Pentameter** in the Italian muses. Some maintain that the most learned **Dante Alighieri**, the Florentine poet, was the first inventor of <term>Terzetti<note>More commonly known today as *terza rima*, the interlocking three-line rhyme scheme of the *Divine Comedy*.</note></term>, and **Boccaccio** of <term>Ottava rima<note>An eight-line stanza form used later by Ariosto and Tasso.</note></term>: for which reason, if one wished to give a particular name to such manners of composing, wanting to name them from the region in which they were found: both manners would be called (as Horace invites us with the authority cited above) **Italian Modes**; or wanting to name them from their homeland, they would be called **Tuscan Modes**. But if one wanted to name them after their own inventors, the first manner would be named (so to speak) the **Dantean Mode**, and the second manner the **Boccaccian Mode**; just as the *citharistic* and *tibial* laws <note>The rules for playing the cithara (lyre) and the tibia (pipes).</note> (as we saw in the Second Part) were named partly after nations and partly after their inventors. And although in Italy one finds not only one manner of verse, but even many particular manners, as I have shown; nevertheless, the Greeks in our day, besides their other manners, have the **Verse of Fifteen Syllables**; as are these, which are by **Constantine Manasses**, the great philosopher:

> *The starless heaven he brought forth from the beginning;* <note>original Greek: Τὸν οὐρανὸν τὸν ἄνασρον παρήγαγεν ἀρχῆθεν;</note> and they mean: *The Word of God, all-perfect in everything; and*
> *He who built all the things of the world, from the beginning built the starless heaven;* <note>original Greek: Ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παντέλειος, καὶ παντοκτίσωρ λόγος. Zarlino is quoting from Manasses's *Hexaemeron* (a poetic account of the six days of creation).</note> *of which verses his entire Hexaemeron is full; and they sing them under a particular Mode, according to their custom; which is not used in Italy.*

Therefore (leaving aside the other peoples), from these two we can see the difference that could exist in the Numbers and the Harmonies in the Modes of those peoples, at the time when Music was in its flower in Greece. For just as we see these two peoples in our times having a particular manner of verse and a particular manner of singing; we must believe the same was true anciently among those peoples. And although in our day some peoples of different nations agree in the Number or in the Feet of the Verse, and in the composition of their songs; nonetheless they are then different regarding the manner **of...**

<meta>This page continues Zarlino’s exploration of the "Modes" (musical scales and styles). On the previous page, he discussed how Italian poetic forms like the Madrigal might be named after their inventors, just as ancient musical modes were named after specific peoples or regions. Here, he begins to define more technically what a "Mode" is, distinguishing it from the terms "Trope" and "Tone," and explaining why rhythm (Number) is as essential to a Mode as the melody itself.</meta>

<sig>P</sig>

of singing. And not only are such differences found among different nations, but also within the same nation and the same homeland, as can be seen in *Italy*. For the songs called *Villotte* <note>original: "Villote." These were light, often rustic polyphonic songs popular in 16th-century Italy.</note> are sung in one way in the places near *Venice*, and in another way in *Tuscany*, and in the Kingdom of *Naples*. It was much the same among the *Ancients*: for although the people of *Doria* and those of *Aeolia* used the same quality or sort of *Verse* and the same *Instrument*, their *Harmonies* <note>In this context, "Harmonies" refers to the specific arrangements of intervals or scales.</note> were nonetheless different in some part. From this one can understand the diversity of names among the *Modes*; just as in one *Mode* the <term>Number<note>The "Number" (*Numero*) refers to the rhythmic proportions or poetic meter.</note></term>, the *Instrument*, and the *Harmony* were found to be different from another *Mode*, so too arose the diversity of names. 

Therefore, I believe that the *Dorian Mode* was different from the *Aeolian*, just as the *Phrygian* was different from the *Lydian*. This was true not only in the *Harmonies*, but also in the *Numbers*, as can be understood from the various effects that were born from one and the other, as we shall see in the proper place. Thus, when we read of **Philoxenus** <note>A famous Greek dithyrambic poet (c. 435–380 BC).</note>—who, having attempted to compose a <term>Dithyrambic poem<note>A wild, rhythmic hymn sung in honor of Dionysus.</note></term> in the *Dorian mode*, was never able to bring it to the desired conclusion because he was pulled back by the nature of the *Mode* into the *Phrygian harmony* suited to such a poem—we should not be surprised. This is because its *Feet* <note>Rhythmic units in poetry.</note> and its *Number* are faster than any other poem, while on the contrary, the *Numbers* of the *Dorian mode* are slower and more relaxed. Because there were certain *Numbers* in the *Dorian* and others in the *Phrygian harmony* (as has been said), it was impossible for **Philoxenus** to produce anything good. 

In the same way, it would be impossible to take the *Numbers* of a *Sapphic Verse*—which is composed of a <term>Trochee<note>A long syllable followed by a short one.</note></term>, a <term>Spondee<note>Two long syllables.</note></term>, a <term>Dactyl<note>One long syllable followed by two short ones.</note></term>, and finally two *Trochees* (or a *Trochee* and a *Spondee*)—as are these two lines from **Horace**:

> Eloquent Mercury, grandson of Atlas; and <note>original: "Mercuri facunde nepos Atlantis"</note>
> Boy, I detest Persian displays; <note>original: "Persicos odi puer apparatus"</note>

and try to sing them or stretch them into an *Heroic verse*, which is composed of six feet varied with *Dactyls* and *Spondees*, as can be seen in each of these two lines from **Virgil**:

> But meanwhile it flees, time flees irretrievably. <note>original: "Sed fugit interea, fugit irreparabile tempus."</note>
> To spare the conquered, and to crush the proud. <note>original: "Parcere subiectis, & debellare superbos."</note>

I have chosen to make this discourse perhaps longer than was necessary for no other purpose than that one might more easily understand what a *Mode* was in *Music*. Thus, we can truly say that in ancient times, the *Mode* was a certain and determined form of *Melody*, crafted with reason and artifice, contained under a determined and proportioned order of *Numbers* and *Harmony*, suited to the subject matter contained in the speech. 

And although *modern Musicians* do not consider anything in their compositions except a certain order of singing and a certain species of harmony—leaving aside the consideration of the specific *Number* or *Meter*, for they say this belongs to the *Poets* (especially since *Music* in our times is separated from *Poetry*)—they nevertheless consider such an order insofar as it is contained within one of the *Seven* species of the <term>Diapason<note>The Greek term for the octave.</note></term> shown previously, mediated harmonically or arithmetically, as we shall see further on. Among these, one finds a certain way of singing in one that is varied in another. This order of singing with a different manner or melody they call a *Mode*; some call it a *Trope*; and some a *Tone*. Nor should we wonder at this, since <note>original: "Τρόπος"</note> *Tropos* is a Greek word signifying *Mode* or *Reason*, from which they claim they are so named. And if they were also named from <note>original: "Τροπή"</note> *Tropē*, which means *Conversion* or *Mutation*, it would be equally fitting, since one is converted and changed into the other, as we shall see. 

They also name it *Tone*, and this is not poorly said: for by *Tone* (as **Euclid** shows in his *Introduction*) four things can be understood. First, that which the Greeks call <note>original: "φθόγγος"</note> *phthongos*, which signifies any *Sound* or unarticulated *Voice* that does not extend toward the low or the high. Second, one of those two intervals shown in Chapter 18 of the *Third Part* <note>i.e., the musical interval of a whole step.</note>. Third, a strong and sonorous voice; as when we say, "*Francesco* has a good tone, sonorous and vigorous"—that is, a good, sonorous, and vigorous voice. Lastly, it can be understood as what we have named above: as when one says the *Dorian Tone*, the *Phrygian*, and the others—that is, the *Dorian Mode*, the *Phrygian*, and those following in order. And because this name *Tone* extends to many things, as we have seen, I have chosen to call them *Modes* and not *Tones* as much as possible to avoid *Ambiguity*. 

Wishing then to declare what a *Mode* is, we shall say with **Boethius** that a *Mode* is a certain constitution in all orders of voices, differing by the low and the high; and such a *Constitution* is like a body full of modulation, which has its being from the conjunction of *Consonances*, such as the *Diapason* [octave], the *Diapasondiapente* [twelfth], or the *Disdiapason* [double octave]. In such a way that from the <term>Proslambanomenos<note>The lowest note in the ancient Greek musical system.</note></term> to the <term>Mese<note>The middle note of the ancient Greek system, acting as a functional center.</note></term> there comes to be a constitution, counting the middle strings or voices; and likewise from the *Mese* to the <term>Nete hyperboleon<note>The highest note of the ancient Greek musical system.</note></term>, always including its middle sounds. But

because these arrangements are truly the various species of the <term>Octave<note>original: "Diapason." In Renaissance music theory, the octave was divided into different patterns of whole tones and semitones to create scales.</note></term> that are found from one letter to another; just as we saw in Chapter 12 of the Third Part, by numbering their middle strings. Therefore, we shall say that the **Mode** is a certain form, or quality of harmony, found in each of the named seven species of the Octave. When these are divided **harmonically**—as they are considered for now—they give us seven principal and **authentic** modes; from these, their collateral modes are born through **arithmetic** division, which are called (as we shall see) **Plagal**, or *Placali*.

## That the Modes have been named differently by many, and for what reason. Chapter 2.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' featuring leafy flourishes and scrollwork within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

AND although I have named such manners of singing "Modes," there have nonetheless been some who have also called them **Harmonies**, some **Tropes**, some **Tones**, and some **Systems**, or **Entire Constitutions**. Those who called them Harmonies were many, among whom were **Plato**, **Pliny**, and **Julius Pollux**. It is quite true that Pollux (in my opinion) places a difference between the Harmony and the Mode; for he takes "Harmony" to mean only the blend of sounds <note>original: "concento." A harmonious sounding together of voices.</note> arising from sounds or voices added to <term>Number<note>original: "Numero." In this context, it refers to rhythm, meter, or poetic proportion.</note></term>. He then takes "Mode" to be the composite of Harmony, Number, and <term>Speech<note>original: "Oratione." Referring to the text or lyrics of a song.</note></term>, which Plato calls **Melody**; and he shows how much the Mode differs from Harmony. Now, since in our times the use of Music is very different from that of the Ancients (as I have shown elsewhere), and since no attention is paid to "Number" in it (leaving aside those Harmonies heard in Dances, because they must necessarily be joined to such rhythm), according to his opinion we should sooner call them Harmonies than Modes. But this was done because the name "Mode" is more common among Musicians for such things than "Harmony" is. Therefore, when Pollux calls them Harmonies, he does not disagree at all with Plato, meaning that blend of sounds arising from voices joined to rhythm. But when he names them Modes, he then means Melody—that is, the composite of the three things named above. Nor should we wonder that a single thing is named in so many ways; for it is not inappropriate that the same thing, when considered differently, is also named differently. 

However, when Plato and the others name them Harmonies, it may be that they gave them such a name for the concordance of many dissimilar sounds or voices, and from the joining of many consonances united together, which is found among many parts and even in a single one. For **Harmony**, according to the opinion of **Quintilian**, is the name for that concordance born from the joining of several things dissimilar to one another. And if some others called them **Tropes** <note>original: "Tropi," from the Greek "tropos," meaning a turn or direction.</note>, it was also well said, since they change one into another in the low or in the high pitch. From this, they are different from one another by these qualities: for all the strings of one Mode are lower or higher by the interval of a **Tone** or a **Semitone** than the strings of the Mode closest to it. Considering, then, the passage they make into one another by ascending or descending with the strings of one order into the strings of another, they were named in such a way—as if to say, "turned from the low to the high," or vice versa. 

But if we were to consider them according to modern use—that is, regarding the conversion of their <term>Fourths<note>original: "Diatessaron." An interval of a perfect fourth.</note></term>, which are placed (as we shall see) sometimes below and sometimes above the common <term>Fifth<note>original: "Diapente." An interval of a perfect fifth.</note></term>—they could also be called **Tropes**. Thus, it seems to me not out of place that some have called these two species (the Fifth and the Fourth) the **Sides** or **Members** of the Octave, and the Octave itself the **Body**; since from this follows such a great variation that it produces a wonderful effect. From this it came that some called part of these Modes "lateral," such as the **Plagal** modes, named after the one side of theirs that changes, which is the Fourth. 

And those who named them **Tones** did not do so without reason, one of whom was **Ptolemy**, who says that perhaps they were called in such a way from the space of the **Tone**, by which the three principal Modes—**Dorian**, **Phrygian**, and **Lydian** (as he shows in Chapter 7 and 10 of the second book of the *Harmonics*)—are distant from one another. Still others want them to be named in such a way from a certain abundance of intervals, such as from the five Tones found in every Octave, besides the two major Semitones. Or alternatively, from the last sound or **Final Voice** of each (as some others wish), by means of which they derive a rule for knowing and judging from the ascent and descent of their <term>Melodic Lines<note>original: "Modulationi."</note></term> under which Mode any song is composed. But this last opinion does not please me, because it has no reason in itself that satisfies the intellect. They are also called **Modes** from this Latin word *Modus*, which derives from the verb *Modulari*, which means:

Singing: or rather they are called **Modes** from the *moderate order* perceived in them: for it is not permitted, without offending the ear, to pass beyond their boundaries, nor to fail to observe the property and nature of each. Those who called them **Systems**, or **Entire Constitutions**—among whom is **Ptolemy**—were moved by this reason: because "System" signifies a congregation of voices or sounds that contains within itself a certain ordered and complete modulation, or conjunction of <term>consonances<note>A "consonance" is a combination of notes that sounds pleasing and stable to the ear.</note></term>, such as those of the <term>Fifth<note>original: "Diapente."</note></term>, the <term>Fourth<note>original: "Diatessaron."</note></term>, and others besides. In this way, every Mode is situated entirely within one of the seven species of the <term>Octave<note>original: "Diapason."</note></term>, which is the most perfect of any other constitution whatsoever.

## On the Name and Number of the Modes. Chapter 3.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial letter 'S', featuring a central capital letter S surrounded by ornate foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>

JUST AS one sees great variety among all those who have made mention of the Modes regarding their name in general, as we have seen, so too does the same occur regarding certain particular names and their number. For if we wish to consider what **Plato** writes on this matter, we will find that he sets down only six Modes, calling some of them "Mixed Lydian" harmonies, some "High Lydian," others "Ionian," and others simply "Lydian," without adding anything further. He then adds to these the **Dorian** and the **Phrygian**, praising and approving only these last two above all others as being very useful to a well-ordered Republic. In another place, he commemorates only the Dorian, Ionian, Phrygian, and Lydian; and among these, he seems to praise only the Dorian as more severe and better than any other. 

**Aristoxenus** as well (according to **Martianus Capella**) sets down fifteen modes: that is, five principal ones—Lydian, Iastian, Aeolian, Phrygian, and Dorian—with ten collaterals, adding to each of them these two Greek particles: <note>original: "ὑπὲρ" (hyper)</note> **Above** and <note>original: "ὑπὸ" (hypo)</note> **Below**. From these he gives birth to two other Modes, one of which he calls **Hyperlydian** and the other **Hypolydian**, and he does the same for the others in order. **Cassiodorus** sets down the same number with similar names in his *Compendium of Music*; yet writing to **Boethius**, he sets down five: the Dorian, Phrygian, Aeolian, Iastian, and Lydian. He says that every Mode has a High and a Low, and these two are so called in respect to the middle; meaning to imply that each of those named has two collateral Modes, as he demonstrates later when he says that the "artificial music" is contained by fifteen modes, and in this he agrees with Martianus.

But **Euclid**, who also followed Aristoxenus, sets down only thirteen; **Censorinus** does the same. Thus one sees two followers of the same author being very discordant and varied in number. **Ptolemy**, when he reasons on such things, sets down seven: the Hypodorian, Hypophrygian, Hypolydian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian. To these he adds an eighth, calling it **Hypermixolydian** (called **Hyperphrygian** by Euclid). He did this so that the <term>Great System<note>The "Great System" or "Greater Perfect System" was the foundational theoretical framework of Greek music, spanning two octaves.</note></term>—that is, the fifteen strings from the *Proslambanomenos* to the *Netehyperboleon*—would be comprised by the strings of these Modes. And although he knew very well that besides these seven Modes and his added one, many others were found (as can be seen when he commemorates the Iastian and Aeolian, calling them "Harmonies"), he nevertheless did not wish to exceed that number. This was perhaps because he intended to accommodate—according to his purpose—one of the named eight Modes to each circle of the **celestial sphere**, as can be seen in Chapter 9 of the Third Book of his *Music*, in the manner that the Ancients had also designated for each Sphere, as **Pliny** shows in his *Natural History*. 

**Julius Pollux** agrees with Plato in number but disagrees in name, for he sets down the Dorian, Ionian, and Aeolian, and names them "First Harmonies," to which he adds the Phrygian, Lydian, Ionian, and one he names "Continuous," as one of those harmonies that served the sound of the pipes. **Aristides Quintilianus**, in the first book of his *Music*, sets down six Modes which he calls **Tones**: the Lydian, Dorian, Phrygian, Iastian, Mixolydian, and Syntonolydian (which we can call "Taut Lydian" or "High Lydian"). But **Gaudentius** the philosopher, having mentioned in his *Introduction* the Mixolydian, Lydian, Phrygian, Dorian, Hypolydian, Hypophrygian, and that which he calls "Common" (naming it later **Locrian** and **Hypodorian**), adds in the examples he provides the example of the Aeolian and that of the Hypoaeolian. **Apuleius**, besides these, sets down five Modes: Aeolian, Iastian, Lydian, Phrygian, and Dorian. And **Lucian** four: Phrygian, Lydian, Dorian, and Ionian. I will omit what **Boethius** does, since in Chapters 14 and 15 of his fourth book, he does not disagree in any way with the Modes set down by Ptolemy. And although **Plutarch** maintains that the Modes are only three—Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian—he mentions these as the principals, for he adds later that every other mode depends upon and derives from these. He said this because he saw that there were no more than three types of... <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> [fourth]... as in Chapter 14 of the...

<header>Fourth Part</header>

In the third part I have shown; from which the variety of the **Modes** arises. There are those who (leaving aside the counting of their names, which are almost infinite) have mentioned only the **Dorian**, the **Aeolian**, and the **Ionian**, as those that were truly Greek Modes; because (as **Cicero** shows) **Greece** was divided into three parts, namely **Doria**, **Aeolia**, and **Ionia**; as **Pliny** also demonstrates in the sixth book, Chapter 2, of his *Natural History*. Others have mentioned some of them incidentally; such as **Pindar**, who named the **Dorian** under the name of the *Dorian Lyre*, and likewise the **Aeolian**. And **Horace** in various places names the **Ionian**, the **Aeolian**, the **Dorian**, and the **Lydian**. So it follows that from the diversity of the order, from the variety of the number, and from the difference in their names found in all these authors, one can extract nothing but confusion of the mind.

But however they may be placed or ordered; however many they may be in number, and whatever name they may have, this matters little to us; it being enough for us to know this for now: that the **Ancients** used their Modes in the manner I have shown above; and that considering them according to the use of modern Musicians—placed in one of the seven species of the <term>Octave<note>original: "Diapason"</note></term> <term>harmonically or arithmetically divided<note>These are mathematical methods for determining the "middle" note of a scale to create different types of modes.</note></term>—there are **Twelve**. For in twelve ways only, and no more, can they be conveniently divided; of which six are the **principal** <note>Also known as "Authentic" modes.</note> and six are their **collaterals** <note>Also known as "Plagal" modes.</note>, as we shall see; regardless of how many Modes the Ancients might have had.

From what truly arises such great discord among writers—both concerning the number and also concerning the names and their order—is a difficult thing to judge; unless we wish to say that this happened because either in the time of some of them all the Modes were not yet known, or they made mention only of those that suited their purpose at a convenient time and place. We can therefore gather from what has been said that the principal Modes among the Ancients were six: **Dorian**, **Phrygian**, **Lydian**, **Mixolydian**, **Aeolian**, and **Ionian**. And even if **Ptolemy** with **Apuleius** and many others also call the **Ionian** mode the **Iastian** mode, this matters little or not at all; for considering them both in the Greek language, one means as much as the other; just as the **Mixolydian** mode is called **Locrian** or **Locrensian** by **Julius Pollux**; and **Athenaeus** held it as a certain thing that the **Hypodorian** was the **Aeolian**.

It is truly a very difficult thing to wish to have clear and perfect knowledge of this if one wants to follow the use of the Ancients; because this cannot be demonstrated by any path, their usage being totally extinct, so that we can find no trace of them. Nor should we wonder at this, since Time consumes every created thing; but rather we should wonder at some who, believing they are putting into use the <term>Chromatic<note>A style of music using sharps and flats to create smaller intervals than a standard scale.</note></term> and <term>Enharmonic<note>The most complex ancient Greek scale system, using "quarter-tones" that were long lost by Zarlino's time.</note></term> genera—already abandoned for so very long; and knowing neither their manner nor any trace of them—do not realize that we do not yet have full knowledge even of the <term>Diatonic<note>The standard musical scale consisting of whole tones and semitones.</note></term>. For truly they do not know in what manner such Modes were put into use according to the custom of the Ancients. Wherefore I believe that if they wish to examine the matter well, they will find without any doubt—after having wracked their brains for a long time with much labor and hardship—that they have thrown away time, more precious than anything else; and have been deceived in the manner of the **Alchemists**, concerning the desire to find that which they can never find: that which I call the <term>Fifth Essence<note>original: "Quinta essentia." A reference to the elusive "Philosopher's Stone" or ultimate substance sought by alchemists; here used to mock music theorists chasing impossible ancient secrets.</note></term>.

## On the Inventors of the Modes. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' depicting a landscape with buildings under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>

It would not be out of place (if it were possible) to narrate who was the first inventor of the **modern Modes**; for until now I have not found anyone who says so; although it is manifest to all those who read **Platina**, that **Pope Gregory I**, a man of most holy life, was the one who ordered that the **Introits**, the <term>Lord have mercy<note>original Greek: "Κύριε ἐλέησον" (Kyrie eleison).</note></term> nine times, the **Alleluia**, and the other things sung in the sacrifice <note>The Mass.</note> should be sung. Similarly, that **Vitalian** (the first of this name) ordered the Chant, and added together the **Organs** (as some maintain) for consonance. But **Leo II**, a man skilled in Music, composed the chant of the **Psalms**; that is, he discovered their **Intonations** and the way they are sung; and he reduced the **Hymns** to better consonance; **Damasus I** having previously ordered that such Psalms be sung in church one verse per Choir <note>Antiphonal singing.</note>, and at their end the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria patri"</note> should be added with the rest. All this has been said concerning **Ecclesiastical Chant**, even if the first inventor of it cannot be found. But as for the invention of those Modes that are in **Figured Song** <note>Polyphony, or music with written rhythms.</note>, and the invention of composing in the manner that we do at present; there is no doubt that we cannot have any certainty of this; although (from what can be seen) it has not been a long time since such a way of composing in

<summary>Zarlino critiques scholars who attempt to revive lost ancient Greek musical systems, arguing instead for a logical twelve-mode system. He also attributes various liturgical and musical innovations to early Popes, including Gregory I and Leo II.</summary>

--- Page 319 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 300, where Zarlino analyzed the confusion among ancient authors regarding the number and names of the musical modes. Here, he explores the legendary inventors of these modes and their emotional effects.</meta>

<page-num>301</page-num>
<header>Part</header>

<term>figured song<note>original: "canto figurato"; this refers to polyphonic music where different voices have different rhythmic patterns, as opposed to plainchant.</note></term> was discovered. And although almost the same difficulty arises regarding the inventors of the **Ancient Modes**, we can nevertheless have some knowledge of the inventors of many of them. For **Pliny** claims that **Amphion**, son of **Jove** (or of **Mercury**, as some prefer) and of **Antiopa**, was the inventor of the **Lydian** harmony. With this harmony (according to what **Aristoxenus** relates in the first book of *Music*), **Olympus** was the one who played the pipe at the funeral during the burial of the serpent **Python**. This harmony was also used in the funeral procession of the virgin **Psyche**, as was mentioned above. It is indeed true that **Clement of Alexandria** attributes the invention of the **Lydian** harmonies to **Olympus of Mysia**, who was perhaps the one named above; and others claim that the **Lydian** melody was discovered for no other purpose than to use it for such a task as mentioned above. They also say that the rustics used such melody at the crossroads and junctions in honor of **Diana**, in imitation of **Ceres**, who with great cries sought the abducted **Proserpina**; as the Poet hints when he says:

> Were you not used, you unskilled one, to destroy a miserable song on a screeching straw in the crossroads? <note>original: "Non tu in triuijs indocte solebas / Stridenti miserum stipula disperdere carmen?" — Virgil, *Eclogues* 3.26-27.</note>

Where it is seen that they did not perform such a task with many instruments, but with a single pipe; of which (as **Apuleius** holds) **Hyagnis the Phrygian**—who was the father of that **Marsyas** who was severely punished by **Apollo** for his arrogance—was the inventor. They did this same thing also with the <term>shepherd’s pipe<note>original: "Zuffolo"; a small flute or whistle-pipe.</note></term>, of which (as some hold, and especially **Virgil**) **Pan**, the god of shepherds, was the inventor, because, as he says:

> Pan first taught how to join several reeds with wax. <note>original: "Pan primus calamos cera coniungere plures / Instituit." — Virgil, *Eclogues* 2.32.</note>

But the **Dorian** melodies, according to the same **Clement** (with whom **Pliny** also agreed), were discovered by **Thamyris**, who was from Thrace. The **Phrygian**, the **Mixed Lydian**, and the **Mixed Phrygian** (as the named **Clement** holds) were discovered by the aforementioned **Marsyas**, who was from Phrygia; although some wish that **Sappho of Lesbos**, the ancient poetess, was the inventress of the **Mixed Lydian**; and others attribute such invention to **Thersander**; and others to a trumpeter called **Pythoclides**. But **Plutarch**, taking the testimony of one **Lysias**, holds that **Lamprocles of Athens** was the inventor of such melodies; and some hold that **Damon the Pythagorean** was the inventor of the **Hypophrygian**, and **Polymnestus** of the **Hypolydian**. I have not found the inventors of the other Modes. But if the authority of **Aristotle** placed in the second book of the *Metaphysics* were valid in this regard, one could say that **Timothy** was the inventor of the rest; even though **Phrynis**, a perfect musician of those times, had come before him; for (as he says) if it had not been for **Timothy**, we would not have many melodies. But in truth, it seems to me that they are older than **Timothy**, as can be seen by reading many authors and examining them regarding the time. Which of them was the first to be discovered is—I will not say most difficult, but rather impossible to know; even though some wish that the **Lydian** was the first Mode discovered. To this opinion we might lean if the order of the Modes set by **Plato**, **Pliny**, **Martianus**, and many others were set according to which one was discovered before the other. But truly it is a weak argument, for we could say the same of any other Mode that was placed first in any other order, such as the **Phrygian**, which is placed first in order by **Lucian**, and the **Aeolian**, which is placed in the first spot by **Apuleius**. We shall now leave off reasoning further of such things and come to speak of their nature, for we shall speak of the property of the modern Modes another time.

## On the Nature or Property of the Modes. Cap. 5.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'E' featuring a classical figure, possibly a scholar or musician, framed by elaborate foliage and architectural scrollwork.</image-desc>
SINCE the ancient Modes were already, as we have seen elsewhere, a composition of several things put together, from their variety arose a certain difference between Modes, from which it could be understood that each of them retained within itself a certain "something" of variation; especially when all the things that entered into the composition were put together proportionately. Hence it was powerful enough to induce various passions in the minds of the listeners, inducing in them new and diverse habits and customs. From this it then followed that all those who have written anything about them attributed to each its own property, based on the effects they saw arising from them. Thus some called the **Dorian** a stable mode, and held that it was by its nature very suitable to the customs of the minds of civilized men, as **Aristotle** demonstrates in the *Politics*; although **Lucian** calls it severe, because it preserves within itself a certain severity, and **Apuleius** names it warlike. But **Athenaeus** attributes to it severity, majesty, and

<header>Fourth Part</header>

steadfastness and vehemence; and **Cassiodorus** says that it is a giver of modesty and a preserver of chastity. They also say that it is a **Mode** <note>In ancient and Renaissance music, a "mode" is a type of scale or melodic pattern believed to possess specific emotional qualities.</note> that contains gravity within itself. For this reason, **Laches**, in the works of **Plato**, used to compare those who reasoned or disputed about grave and severe matters—such as **Virtue**, **Wisdom**, and other similar things—to a musician who sang to the sound of the **Cithara** or **Lyre**, not using the **Ionian**, **Phrygian**, or **Lydian** melodies, but rather the **Dorian**. He esteemed this as the only truly Greek harmony, especially when the men were worthy of such words, creating a certain consonance between the men and the words spoken. And because the **Dorians** used a **Harmony** <term>Harmony<note>original: "Harmonia"; here referring to a specific melodic mode or tuning system rather than modern chordal harmony.</note></term> that was somewhat grave and severe, with rhythms that were not very fast, it contained severe and grave matters when joined with speech. Therefore, the **Ancients** intended that through the **Dorian mode**, one might acquire **prudence**, and that it might induce a chaste and virtuous mind in us.

And this was not said without reason, as can be understood from historical events. For (as **Strabo** recounts) **King Agamemnon**, before departing his homeland to go to the **Trojan War**, gave his wife **Clytemnestra** into the keeping of a **Dorian musician**. He knew that while the musician was near her, she could not be corrupted by anyone. When the wicked **Aegisthus** realized this, he removed the musician from his sight and thus gave fulfillment to his unbridled desires. But because this might seem a strange thing to some, if they consider what I said in the second part, they will find that it is not impossible. Indeed, it is to be believed that the good musician was such that he continually stimulated her with learned narrations, accompanied by appropriate harmonies, toward virtuous deeds and the contempt of vice. He would have proposed many examples of most chaste and well-mannered matrons for her to imitate, teaching her the way she should maintain her chastity, and entertaining her also with philosophical narrations and most sweet songs, as was fitting for a chaste and modest woman.

In such a manner, **Dido** also, in the works of **Virgil**, was entertained with severe and grave songs by the good musician **Iopas**. This is the custom among honest and chaste women, but certainly not among the lascivious and less than honest, as we read in the same **Virgil** regarding the **Nymphs**:

> Among whom Clymene was telling of Vulcan’s wasted care, and the deceits of Mars, and his sweet thefts. <note>original: "Inter quas curam Clymene narrabat inanem / Vulcani, Martisq; dolos, & dulcia furta." — Virgil, *Georgics* 4.345-46.</note>

For such effects, therefore, the **Ancients** attributed the narrated properties to the **Dorian mode**, and applied to it matters that were severe, grave, and full of wisdom. And when they departed from these and passed to pleasant, joyful, and light things, they used the **Phrygian mode**, as its rhythms were faster than those of any other **Mode**, and its harmony higher in pitch than that of the **Dorian**. From this, I believe, came that proverb which says, ***From the Dorian to the Phrygian***. This can be applied when one passes from a discussion of most high and grave things to one containing light, low, and not very ingenious matters—similarly, things that are joyful, festive, and even not very honest.

**Clement of Alexandria**, following the opinion of **Aristoxenus**, maintains that the **Enharmonic Genus** <term>Enharmonic Genus<note>A type of scale in ancient Greek music involving very small intervals called quarter-tones, considered very elegant and difficult.</note></term> greatly suits the **Dorian Harmonies** as an ornate and elegant genus, and the **Diatonic** suits the **Phrygian** as more vehement and sharp. The **Dorian** was once held in such veneration that no other, except for this and the **Phrygian**, was approved and admitted by those two most wise philosophers, **Plato** and **Aristotle**. They recognized the great utility they brought to a well-instituted **Republic**, esteeming the others of little use and value. Hence, they wished for children to be instructed in music from their tender age.

The **Ancients** also intended for the **Hypodorian** to have a nature entirely different from that of the **Dorian**. For just as the **Dorian** disposed one toward a certain manly constancy and modesty, the **Hypodorian**, through the gravity of its movements, induced a certain sluggishness and rest. Wherefore (as **Ptolemy** and **Quintilian** recount) the **Pythagoreans** had such a custom that they used the **Hypodorian** during the day and when they went to sleep to mitigate the labors and cares of the mind from the past day; and in the night, having been awakened from sleep, they would return to their interrupted studies with the **Dorian**. **Athenaeus** (as I have said elsewhere) thought that this was the **Aeolian**, and attributed to it that it induced a certain swelling and pomp in minds, being of a somewhat soft nature.

The **Ancients** also attributed to the **Phrygian** (as **Plutarch** manifests to us) the nature of igniting the soul and inflaming it to anger and choler, and of provoking lust and lechery. For they esteemed it a somewhat vehement and furious **Mode**, and also of a most severe and cruel nature, which would leave a man stunned. Wherefore (in my opinion) **Lucian** touched upon its nature very well with these words: "Just as those," he says, "who hear the **Phrygian pipe** do not all go mad, but only those who are touched by **Rhea**; and these, having heard the Verse, remember their first affection, or primary passion..."
