> In holiness let us serve the Lord, and he will deliver us from our enemies. <note>original: "In sanctitate serviamus Domino, & liberabit nos ab inimicis nostris."</note>

I say that if in such a Tenor, or in another similar to it, the pitch B-flat <note>original: "♭"</note> were changed to B-natural <note>original: "♮"</note> only once or twice, this would not cause the Mode to be transformed, except in that small part where it was placed; it would not have the power to make such a Mode anything other than the Seventh. For although such a pitch placed in this way is necessary to regulate the melody, nevertheless, being accidental, it does not change the form of the Mode in such a way that it should not be recognized as the Seventh, as can be seen from this example:

> Wash me yet more, O Lord, from my injustice. <note>original: "Amplius lava me Domine ab iniustitia mea."</note>

But if we place the sign B-flat at the beginning of such Tenors, which shows that throughout the entire song we must proceed through the pitches of the <term>Synemmenon tetrachord: A four-note grouping in the ancient Greek system that includes the B-flat (Tetrachordo fynemennon).</term>, I say that then such a pitch will be natural and not accidental; it will have the power to change the Seventh Mode into the First. This is because it varies the species of the <term>Fifth: The interval of five notes (Diapente).</term>, which was previously the fourth species between G and d; and it brings into being the first species between those same pitches, as seen here:

<image-desc>Musical notation with a flat signature at the beginning of the staff. The text underneath is in Latin: "In sanctitate serviamus Domino, & liberabit nos ab inimicis nostris."</image-desc>

> In holiness let us serve the Lord, and he will deliver us from our enemies. <note>original: "In sanctitate serviamus Domino, & liberabit nos ab inimicis nostris."</note>

It is certainly true that the Mode is not found in its natural pitches, because it is transposed a <term>Fourth: The interval of four notes (Diatessaron).</term> higher. Therefore, if one wished to place it in its [proper] place, it would be found arranged in this manner:

<image-desc>Musical notation illustrating the transposition of the previous melody. The text underneath is in Latin: "In sanctitate serviamus Domino, & liberabit nos ab inimicis nostris."</image-desc>

> In holiness let us serve the Lord, and he will deliver us from our enemies. <note>original: "In sanctitate serviamus Domino, & liberabit nos ab inimicis nostris."</note>

It is not, therefore, absolutely true that placing the *synemmenon* tetrachord in a song in place of the <term>diezeugmenon: The "disjunct" tetrachord in the Greek system that includes B-natural.</term> lacks the power to change that Mode into another; rather, it is true when it is placed according to the manner shown. We shall say, then, that if a variation of the Mode follows from the variation of the Octave, and from the variation of the Octave follows the variation of the Mode; then, proceeding from the first to the last, we say that such a tetrachord, placed in the second manner shown, has the power to change one Mode into another. In this manner, Jean Mouton <note>original: "Gioan Motone" (c. 1459–1522), a famous French Renaissance composer.</note> varied the Mode in the Mass he composed on the Antiphon *Silver and gold have I none* <note>original: "Argentum, & au rum non eft mihi"</note>, which is in the Seventh Mode; nonetheless, by transposing the tetrachord, or rather changing it, he made it in the Eleventh Mode <note>In the 12-mode system used by the author, the Eleventh Mode corresponds to the Ionian or C-major scale.</note>. We shall conclude, then, that whenever we place the pitch B-flat in a song in place of B-natural, that pitch will always cause the Mode to vary; and likewise to the contrary, placing B-natural in place of B-flat, as experience shows us.

# On the Transposition of the Modes.

If it is possible, then (as has been shown), that by changing one note for another—that is, by placing the note **b** <note>B-flat</note> in place of the **♮** <note>B-natural</note>, or more accurately, by transposing the <term>semitone: The smallest interval in this system of music, roughly half of a whole tone.</term>—one can vary one Mode into another, turning the First into the Seventh, and the Seventh into the First; then there is no doubt that any Mode, whether it be the First, Second, Third, Fourth, or any other, can be transposed. With the help of certain notes that change one <term>Diapason: An octave; the interval of eight notes.</term> into another, we can transpose any Mode we wish toward the high <note>original: "acuto"</note> or toward the low <note>original: "grave"</note> at our pleasure.

I will let anyone with good judgment decide how convenient this can be at times. Such transpositions are useful and highly necessary for every skilled organist who serves <term>choir music: "Musiche choriste," referring to polyphonic or plainchant music performed by a church choir.</term>, and similarly for other players of different instruments. It allows them to accommodate the sound of the instruments to the voices, which sometimes cannot ascend or descend as far as the natural positions of the Modes, as set on those instruments, would require. Such transpositions are now in use among modern musicians, just as they were among the ancients—<note>Johannes Ockeghem (c. 1410–1497), a celebrated master of the Franco-Flemish school.</note>Ockeghem and his disciple <note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), perhaps the most famous composer of the High Renaissance.</note>Josquin, and countless others, as can be seen in their compositions.

When, therefore, it happens that out of necessity or any other circumstance it becomes necessary to transpose the Mode contained in a <term>melody: "Cantilena," a general term for a vocal or instrumental musical line.</term>, one must take care above all else to arrange it in such a manner and in such a place that, in ascending and descending, one has all those notes necessary to the constitution of that Mode. That is, they must provide the tones and semitones necessary to its essential nature. 

Composers must observe this most strictly when they wish to compose such melodies to be played on an instrument. However, when they compose them to be sung only, it would not be a great error if they marked certain notes with an accidental sign that might not be found on the instrument—especially on the <term>Harpsichord: "Clavocembalo," a keyboard instrument where strings are plucked.</term>—such as the <term>Enharmonic: In this period, these were microtonal divisions or "split keys" on certain keyboard instruments, which were quite rare.</term> intervals found on few artificial instruments. I say this because the voice can be made high or low, or used in any other way according to the will of the singer, which cannot be done so freely with such instruments.

Now, to show how any melody can be conveniently transposed away from its natural notes, we will take no other example than the Third and Fourth examples placed in the preceding chapter. These will perfectly show how every melody that proceeds through the note **♮** <note>B-natural</note> can be transposed a <term>fourth: "Diatessaron," the interval of four notes.</term> higher with the help of the note **b** <note>B-flat</note>. Conversely, when the song proceeds through the note **b**, it can be transposed lower by the same interval with the help of the **♮**.

But because musicians sometimes transpose Modes—not out of necessity, but rather as a joke or a whim, or perhaps to "entangle the brains" (so to speak) of the singers—they often move them higher or lower by a whole tone or another interval. In doing so, they use not only <term>chromatic: Notes outside the standard seven-note scale, often marked with sharps or flats.</term> notes, but even Enharmonic ones, so they can correctly place the tones and semitones according to the Mode's proper form. Therefore, I wish to show how they are usually transposed. Although musicians use many ways to transpose the Modes, I will provide here only the two most common transpositions made in the First Mode, from which anyone can understand the method for the others. These are shown below: one is made with the help of notes marked with the flat (**b**), and the other with the help of those marked with the sharp (**♯**). It should be noted that the Moderns...

They call these transpositions "feigned music" <note>original: "Musica finta," often called *musica ficta*. This refers to music that uses notes outside the standard medieval "hand" or scale, such as sharps and flats, to allow for transposition.</note>, which (according to their explanation) they say is a transposition of the musical figures—meaning the entire order found in each Mode—from their own proper seat to another. I now leave it to every person skilled in music to judge how useful such knowledge can be to any organist who is not as well-instructed in music. For from the examples shown, he will be able to see and know what he must do when he happens to transpose any song while serving in chapels where various songs belonging to the choirs are sung, not only in the Masses and Vespers, but also in the other Hours, both of the day and of the night. But this must be known above all else: that although I have provided examples only of the First Mode, such transpositions can be made in the songs of the other Modes as well; I have declined to show them only for the sake of brevity.

## A particular discussion regarding the First Mode: its nature, its beginnings, and its cadences.
### Chapter 18.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' with ornate floral and foliage patterns in a square frame.</image-desc>
I WILL now begin the discussion of each Mode separately, starting with the First so that we may proceed in order. I will first show that it is in use not only among church musicians but also among the entire school of musicians. Then I will show where one may regularly begin this Mode, and where (both in this and in every other Mode) one may make the <term>Cadences: Musical points of rest or arrival, similar to punctuation in a sentence.</term>. This being done, I will speak a little concerning its Nature. I say, then, that the First Mode is that which, as I have shown, is contained within the fourth species of the <term>Diapason: An octave; the interval of eight notes.</term> divided harmonically; it is found between these two extreme strings <note>notes</note> **D** and **d**. From this division, the practical musicians say that such a Mode is composed of the first species of the <term>Diapente: A perfect fifth.</term> (**D** and **a**) and the first species of the <term>Diatessaron: A perfect fourth.</term> (**a** and **d**), placed above the fifth. Within this mode, one finds infinite church songs, such as Introits, Graduals, Antiphons, Responsories, and other similar things. And among other musicians, the compositions written in this Mode are almost infinite, such as Masses, Motets, Hymns, Madrigals, and other songs. Among these are found the motets *Come, Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Veni sancte Spiritus"</note> and *The Paschal Victim* <note>original: "Victimae paschali"</note>, composed for six voices; and the madrigal *Love has joined me* <note>original: "Giunt'om'hà Amor"</note>, composed for five voices by Adrian <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), Zarlino's teacher and the maestro di cappella at St. Mark's in Venice.</note>. I also composed many songs in this Mode, among which are two motets for five voices: *O blessed bishop* <note>original: "O beatum pontificem"</note> and *I am black but beautiful* <note>original: "Nigra sum sed formosa"</note>. Many other compositions by many excellent musicians are also found, which I will refrain from naming so as not to be long-winded. 

And although the true and natural beginnings, not only of this but of every other Mode, are on the extreme notes of their Fifth and Fourth, and on the middle note that divides the Fifth into a <term>Ditone: A major third.</term> and a <term>Semiditone: A minor third.</term>, nonetheless many songs are found that have their beginning on other notes. I will not stop to commemorate these so as not to be long-winded. In their chants, the church musicians observed certain middle-endings at the conclusion of every musical clause or period and of every perfect sentence. Some called these cadences; they are very necessary for the distinction of the words, which creates the perfect sense in the sentence. And whoever wishes to know what they are may read Chapter 53 of the Third Part, for I have discussed that matter sufficiently there, and one may have full knowledge of them. Therefore, it will suffice in this place only to say now and forever that cadences are of two sorts: Regular and Irregular. The Regular ones are those that are always made on the extreme sounds or notes of the Modes, and where the Octave in each Mode is mediated or divided harmonically or arithmetically by the middle note; these will be on the extreme notes of the Fifth and the Fourth. Similarly, they are where the Fifth is divided by a middle note into a major third and a minor third; or to put it better, where the true and natural beginnings of each Mode are. The others, made wherever one wishes, are called Irregular. The regular cadences of the First Mode, therefore, are those made on these notes: **D**, **F**, **a**, and **d**; and the Irregular ones are those made on the other notes. But so that what has been said may be more easily perceived, I will provide a two-voice example from which one may recognize the proper places for the regular cadences and see the method one must hold in their melodies. This we shall observe not only in this First Mode, but in the others as well, as we shall see; and it shall be the one placed below.

One must notice, however, that the cadences <note>A cadence marks the conclusion of a musical phrase.</note> of the Psalmody <note>The practice of singing psalms to specific melodic formulas.</note> are always made where the conclusion of the mediation <note>In a psalm tone, the 'mediation' is the melodic formula used for the pause in the middle of a verse.</note> of their Intonation falls. Therefore, the cadences of the mediation, or middle point of the Psalmody of the First, Fourth, and Sixth modes, shall be made on *a*; those of the Second on *F*; those of the Third, Fifth, and Eighth on *c*; and those of the Seventh on *e*. This is because such mediations, or middle points, end there; as can be seen in the *Recanetto*, the *Thoscanello* <note>Two influential 16th-century music treatises: Stefano Vanneo’s *Recanetum de musica aurea* (1533) and Pietro Aaron’s *Toscanello de la musica* (1523).</note>, and in many other books that contain such Psalmody, or Intonations, as we might call them. The finals <note>The concluding note of a melody.</note> are then always made in the place where each verse of such Psalmody, or each Psalm itself, is made to end.

We must also always observe to make the cadences primarily in the Tenor: since this part is the principal guide of the Modes in which the song <note>original: "cantilena"</note> is composed; and from it, the composer must take the invention of the other parts. But such cadences are made in the other parts of the song when they fit well.

<header>Fourth [Part]</header>

...from the natural <note>original: "♮"</note>, and by placing the flat <note>original: "b"</note> there; as the Spanish composer Morales <note>Cristóbal de Morales (c. 1500–1553), the most influential Spanish composer of the Renaissance.</note> did in the motet *Holy and Immaculate Virginity* <note>original: "Sancta, & immaculata virginitas"</note>, for four voices. And because the *First mode* has a certain intermediate effect between the sad and the cheerful, owing to the minor third <term>Semiditono: A minor third, consisting of a tone and a semitone</term> that is heard in the harmony above the outer strings of the fifth <term>Diapente: The interval of a perfect fifth</term> and the fourth <term>Diatessaron: The interval of a perfect fourth</term>; not having a major third <term>Ditono: A major third, consisting of two whole tones</term> in the lower part, it is by its nature somewhat sad. Therefore, we can excellently adapt to it those words which are full of gravity and which treat of lofty and sententious matters, so that the harmony agrees with the subject matter contained within them.

## On the Second Mode. Chapter 19.

Some held that the *Second mode* contained within itself a certain severe gravity, not flattering; and that its nature was tearful and humble; so that, moved by this opinion, they called it the *Tearful, humble, and deprecatory mode*. Hence it is seen that the Church authorities, holding this as certain, have used it in sad and tearful matters, such as those of the season of Lent <term>Quadragesimali: The forty days of fasting before Easter</term> and other days of fast-

Its principal and regular Cadences (since this Mode differs little from the First, because both are composed of the same species) are placed on the notes named above, which are A, F, D, and A, as seen in the example; the others that are placed in other locations are all Irregular. Practical musicians <note>original: "Prattici"</note> say that this Mode is composed of the first species of the Fifth <term>Diapente: The interval of a perfect fifth</term>, A and D, placed in the high range, and of the first species of the Fourth <term>Diatessaron: The interval of a perfect fourth</term>, D and A, placed in the low range; they call it the Collateral or Plagal <note>A plagal mode is a "side" mode that shares the same final note as its "authentic" counterpart but has a lower melodic range.</note> of the First mode. I also composed in this Mode the *Lord’s Prayer* <note>original: "Oratione Dominicale"</note>, *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>; with the *Angelic Salutation* <note>original: "Salutatione angelica"</note>, *Hail Mary* <note>original: "Aue maria"</note>, for seven voices; and the motets, *I am the Rose of Sharon* <note>original: "Ego rosa Saron"</note>, and *Catch for us the little foxes* <note>original: "Capite nobis vulpes paruulas"</note> for five voices. One also finds many other compositions made by various composers, which, being almost infinite, are left out. This Mode is rarely found in figured music <note>Polyphonic music with written rhythms, as opposed to plainchant.</note> on its proper notes, but is most often found transposed by a Fourth; as can be seen in the motets named; and this is because it can be transposed, just as the First mode can also be transposed toward the high range with the help of the note *B-flat* <term>Trite synemennon: The term from the ancient Greek system for the note B-flat.</term>. And just as the First has much in common with the Ninth, so this one truly has much in common with the Tenth.

### On the Third Mode. Chapter 20.

They say the Third mode is born from the fifth species of the Octave <term>Diapason: The interval of an octave.</term> divided harmonically by the note B-natural <note>original: "♮"</note>; or rather from the union of the second species of the Fifth <term>Diapente</term>, E and B-natural, placed in the low range, with the second species of the Fourth <term>Diatessaron</term>, B-natural and E, placed in the high range. This Mode has its final note E in common with the Fourth mode; and the Church authorities have infinite chants in this Mode, as can be seen in their books. Its Cadences

The principal [cadences] are made on the notes of its regular starting points, which are the notes shown as **E**, **G**, **B-natural** <note>original: ♮</note>, and **e**; these are the extremes of its <term>Diapente: An interval of a perfect fifth</term>, and of its <term>Diatessaron: An interval of a perfect fourth</term>, and the middle note of the fifth. The others, which are Irregular, can be made on the other notes. But because the Regular ones are known, one can easily recognize the Irregular ones; therefore we will give an example of the first, so that we may come to know the second. It should be noted, however, that both in this mode and in the Fourth, Seventh, and Eighth modes, cadences are regularly made on the note **B-natural** <note>original: ♮</note>. But because this note has no correspondence by a Fifth in the high range, nor by a Fourth in the low range <note>The note B-natural forms a "tritone" or diminished fifth with F, making it technically unstable in Renaissance theory.</note>, it is somewhat harsh; however, such harshness is tolerated in compositions for more than two voices because they follow an order that produces a good effect, as can be seen among the Cadences placed in Chapter 61 of the Third Part. Many compositions are found written in this Mode, among which is the motet *O Mary Mother of Christ* <note>original: "O Maria mater Christi"</note> for four voices by Isaac <note>Heinrich Isaac (c. 1450–1517), a Flemish composer.</note>; and the motets of Adrian <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), Zarlino’s mentor.</note>, *Thee, God the Father* <note>original: "Te Deum patrem"</note>; *Hither to me from the starry heights* <note>original: "Huc me sydereo"</note>; and *This is the house of the Lord* <note>original: "Hæc est domus domini"</note>, composed for seven voices; and the Madrigal *I turn back* <note>original: "I mi riuolgo indietro"</note>, likewise composed by Adrian for five voices. To these we will add *King Solomon made himself a litter* <note>original: "Ferculum fecit sibi rex Salomon"</note>, which I previously composed along with many others in this Mode for five voices. If this Mode were not mixed with the Ninth, and were heard in its simple form, its harmony would be somewhat harsh; but because it is tempered by the Fifth of the Ninth Mode, and by the Cadence made on **A**, which is used greatly within it, some have been of the opinion that it has a nature suited to moving one to tears. Therefore, they willingly applied to it those words that are tearful and full of lamentation. It has great compatibility with the said Ninth Mode because they share the same second species of Fourth between them; and modern musicians often transpose it out of its natural notes up a Fourth, with the help of the **B-flat** <note>original: ♭</note> note, even though it is most often found placed in its proper and natural location.

->### Of the Fourth Mode. Chapter 21.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'S' at the beginning of the chapter, featuring floral and foliate motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

FOLLOWING THIS is the Fourth [Mode], contained within the second species of the <term>Diapason: An interval of a full octave</term> from **B-natural** to **B-natural**, mediated arithmetically by its final note **E**. This (as the practitioners say) is composed of the second species of the Fifth from **B-natural** to **E**, placed in the high range; and of the second species of the Fourth from **E** to **B-natural**, joined to the Fifth in the low range. This mode likewise, according to their opinion, is marvelously suited to words or subjects that are lamenting, containing sadness or supplicating lamentation; such as amorous subjects, and those that signify leisure, quiet, tranquility, flattery, fraud, and detraction; which is why, because of its effect, some called it the "Flattery Mode." This is somewhat more mournful than its principal [the Third Mode], especially when it proceeds by contrary movements—that is, from high to low—with slow movements. I believe that if it were used simply, without mixing in the Fifth and the Cadence placed on **A** (which serves the Tenth Mode), it would have somewhat more virility than it does when so mixed. But accompanied in such a manner, it is used extensively, so much so that many songs are found composed in this Mode, among which is the motet *Out of the depths I have cried to Thee, O Lord* <note>original: "Deprofundis clamaui ad te Domine"</note> for four voices by Josquin <note>Josquin des Prez.</note>; and the motet *My sins, O Lord* <note>original: "Peccata mea Domine"</note>, along with the Madrigal *Break the hard rock of the wicked heart* <note>original: "Rompi dell'empio cor' il duro scoglio"</note> by Adrian, both composed for six voices; and the madrigal *My sacred Laura* <note>original: "Laura mia sacra"</note> composed for five voices. I also composed many songs, among which is the motet for six voices *Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me* <note>original: "Miserere mei Deus miserere mei"</note>, and a Mass, without using the observances shown in the Third Part; and I did this for no other reason than to show that anyone who wishes to compose without departing from the given Rules can also compose easily without these strict observances, and much better than those who do not know them when they wish to do so. One finds almost infinite ecclesiastical chants in this Mode, in which very rarely (indeed, if I said never, I would not be wrong) does one see the note **B-natural** <note>original: ♮</note> touched. It is quite true that it passes in the high range to the note **C**, so that when the <term>Semitone: The smallest interval in traditional music</term> should be heard in the low range, it is heard in the high range; and thus the extremes of this Mode come to be the notes **C** and **c**. Its irregular Starting Points among the Church musicians are found in many places, but the regular ones are on the notes **B-natural**, **E**, **G**, and **B-natural** only; just as its regular Cadences are also found, which are those placed below; although many are Irregular. Most of the time, practitioners transpose it up a Fourth, placing the **B-flat** <note>original: ♭</note> note in place of the **B-natural**, as can be seen in infinite songs; which they also do (as I have said) in the other Modes.

### Of the Fifth Mode. Chapter 22.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "I" depicting two figures in an outdoor setting with architectural elements in the background.</image-desc>The Fifth mode is contained within the sixth species of the <term>Diapason: An interval of an octave</term> from **F** to **f**, divided harmonically by the note **c**. Practitioners of music say that it is composed of the third species of the <term>Diapente: An interval of a perfect fifth</term> from **F** to **c**, and the third species of the <term>Diatessaron: An interval of a perfect fourth</term> from **c** to **f**, which is placed in the higher part of the fifth. The note **F** is its common final note, shared with the Sixth mode, which is its <term>collateral: Also known as a "plagal" mode, which shares the same final note but has a different range</term>. From this species of octave, we derive only this single Mode, because it does not allow for any division other than the harmonic one. Some maintain that when sung, this Mode brings modesty, joy, and a lifting of the spirit from tedious cares. Therefore, the Ancients used to adapt it to words or subjects that contained some victory; for this reason, some called it the Joyful, Modest, and Delightful Mode. 

And although its natural starting points are placed on the notes **F**, **a**, **c**, and **f**, as these are the regular notes; nonetheless, among church musicians, other starting points are found on various other notes, as can be seen in their books. The regular <term>Cadences: Musical points of rest or arrival</term> of this Mode are made on the four named notes, as seen in the example; and the Irregular ones, when one wishes to use them, are made on the others. Many compositions are found in the church books in this Mode, even though it is not much in use among modern composers. This is because it seems to them to be a harsher and more unpleasant Mode than any other. Nonetheless, many compositions are found written in it, such as the *Hymn of Saint Francis*; *The Egyptians Despoiled* <note>original: "Spoliatis ægyptijs"</note> by Adrian <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), a Flemish composer who was Zarlino's teacher.</note>; and two madrigals by Cipriano de Rore <note>A highly influential Flemish composer of madrigals.</note>, *From time to time it becomes less harsh to me* <note>original: "Di tempo in tempo mi si fà men dura"</note> and *Lady, you who are adorned* <note>original: "Donna che ornata sete"</note>; along with Francesco Viola’s *Among all those whom love* <note>original: "Fra quanti amor"</note>; all composed for four voices; and many others besides,

### Of the Sixth Mode. Chapter 23.

After the Fifth follows the Sixth mode, contained within the third species of the <term>Diapason: An octave</term> between **c** and **C**, divided harmonically. <note>In the system Zarlino is describing here, the Sixth mode occupies the octave from C to c, but is centered around its final note, F.</note> Practitioners say that this Mode is formed and born from the conjunction of the third species of the <term>Diapente: A perfect fifth</term> from **c** to **F**, placed in the high register, with the third species of the <term>Diatessaron: A perfect fourth</term> from **F** to **C**, accompanying it in the low register; and that the note **F** is its final note. This mode has been much frequented by the <term>Ecclesiastics: Church musicians and composers of plainchant</term>, just as its <term>Principal Mode: The authentic version of the mode, which is the Fifth mode</term> was also much used. For many songs are found in their books composed in this Mode, which they say is not very cheerful nor very elegant; and therefore they used it in grave and devout songs that contain compassion, and they matched it to those subjects that contain tears. So much so that they called it the <term>Devout Mode</term> and the "tearful" mode, in contrast to the Second, which is more funeral and calamitous than anything else. The regular beginnings of this Mode, and its regular cadences...

## Of the Seventh Mode. Cap. 24.

The Seventh mode is contained within the seventh species of the <term>Diapason: An octave</term> between **G** and **g**, divided harmonically. This mode (as the Moderns say) is born from the conjunction of the first species of the <term>Diatessaron: A perfect fourth</term> from **d** to **g**, with the fourth species of the <term>Diapente: A perfect fifth</term> from **G** to **d**; the latter placed in the low register, and the former in the high. To this mode (according to what they say) are suited words or subjects that are lascivious <note>In the 16th century, "lascivious" often referred to playful, light, or secular dance-like qualities rather than purely the modern sexual connotation</note>, or that treat of playful matters; those that are cheerful, spoken with modesty; and those that signify threats, disturbances, and anger. Its regular starting points, and its principal and regular cadences, are placed on the notes **G**, **b**, **d**, and **g**, as seen here.

### Of the Eighth Mode. Chapter 25.

Following the Seventh comes the Eighth mode, contained within the fourth species of the octave <term>Diapason</term> between **d** and **D**, divided arithmetically by the note **G**; and (as they say) it is born from the joining of the fourth species of the fifth <term>Diapente</term> between **d** and **G**, placed in the upper register, with the first species of the fourth <term>Diatessaron</term> between **D** and **G**, placed in the lower register. This mode shares the common final note **G** with the Seventh; and the practitioners <note>referring to practical musicians or performers as opposed to theorists</note> say that this Mode has a nature containing a certain natural sweetness and abundant softness, which fills the souls of listeners with joy, mixed with the utmost playfulness and sweetness; they maintain that it is entirely distant from lasciviousness and from every vice. For this reason, they accompanied it with words or subjects that are gentle, well-mannered, and grave, containing profound, speculative, and divine matters, such as those suited to implore grace from God. Many songs are found in the church books in this Mode, which has its regular starting points on the notes **d**, **b**, **G**, and **D**; but the irregular ones are found on other notes; and its regular cadences are similarly placed on the four notes shown, as can be seen in the example placed below.

## Of the Ninth Mode. Chapter 26.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop-cap initial 'I' set within a square frame. The illustration inside the letter depicts a group of four figures in classical or Renaissance academic dress standing in a landscape with hills and a small building in the background.</image-desc>

THE NINTH mode (as the practical musicians say) arises from the joining of the first species of the fifth <term>Diapente</term> **A** and **e**, or **a** and **e** (as you prefer) with the second species of the fourth <term>Diatessaron</term> **E** and **a**, or **e** and **aa**; and to put it better, it is contained within the first species of the octave <term>Diapason</term> **A** and **a**, or **a** and **aa**, divided harmonically by the note **E**, or by **e**. One can never truly say that this is a new Mode: rather, it is very ancient; even though until now it has been deprived of its name and its proper place. This is because some have placed it among those Modes they call Irregular; as if it were not subject to that same Rule to which the others are subject; and as if its octave <term>Diapason</term> were not divided harmonically like that of the other Modes, but in some other strange manner. It is quite true (as I have said elsewhere) that to the...

<header>Part Four</header>

Regarding the Psalm Intonations <note>The melodic formulas used for singing psalms</note>, church authorities have only designated the first eight Modes, as can be seen in their books. However, one cannot say because of this that the other modes are irregular. This is because the Intonation of the Psalms is one thing, and the melodies found in various Modes—both in plainchant <note>unaccompanied church chant</note> and in figured music <note>polyphonic music with rhythmic notation</note>—are quite another. Nor do I wish to believe for any reason that whenever an Antiphon <note>a short chant sung before or after a psalm</note> is found composed in one of these last four Modes [Modes 9 through 12], one could not apply one of the eight named Intonations to it. This is especially true since each of them has various endings, as is obvious to all those who are experienced in such matters. This Mode has been called "open" and "clear" by some, and is most fit for lyrical verses. Therefore, one can accommodate it to words containing cheerful, sweet, pleasant, and resonant subjects. This is because (as they say) it possesses a graceful severity mixed with a certain cheerfulness and an exceeding sweetness. It is well known to all experts in music that this Mode and the First Mode are very similar to each other, because the first species of the fifth <term>Diapente: an interval of a perfect fifth</term> is common to both, and one can easily transition from one to the other. The same can also be said of the Third and Eleventh modes. Many ecclesiastical songs are in this Mode, which would take too long to list; among them is found the chant for the Lord's Prayer <note>original Latin: "Pater noster"</note>, which ends on the note A in this manner, as can be seen in some corrected ancient copies.

Also found in this Mode is the Nicene Creed <note>The "Symbolo Niceno" or profession of faith</note>, *I believe in one God* <note>original Latin: "Credo in unum Deum"</note>. Its intonation begins on the note D and comes to an end (as seen in corrected copies) on the note A likewise—not on the note <term>♮</term> <note>B-natural or "Hard B"</note>, nor on the note E transposed up a fourth <term>Diatessaron: an interval of a perfect fourth</term> with the help of the note B-flat <term>b: the "Soft B" or flat sign</term>, as some do. Such a transposed chant ought to end on the note D, as is proper; but it has been spoiled and corrupted by the ignorance of scribes, as happens in other matters

<columns>1</columns>

of greater importance. And it is not only the endings of the shown chants that are found outside their proper and natural note; many others are found spoiled and corrupted in such a way that it would be too long to show if one wanted to give a particular example of each. But how easy it is in Church Chants to change one Mode into another, simply by varying the final note, or by transposing it from high to low, or low to high, without any help from the B-flat—this is easy to see for all those who are practiced in Music, if they will minutely examine their melodies and their progression. This would not be very difficult to show if one wanted to spend a little time on it. In this Mode, one finds the Antiphon *Hail Mary, full of grace* <note>original Latin: "Ave Maria gratia plena"</note> composed; in ancient books, it is found ending on its natural notes in this way, though in modern books it is found

written a fifth <term>Diapente: an interval of a perfect fifth</term> lower. To prove that this is true, we can understand that Pierre de la Rue <note>P. della Rue (c. 1452–1518), a famous Franco-Flemish composer</note> composed a Mass for four voices based on this Antiphon using the true and essential notes of this Mode. In

<columns>1</columns>

this same mode, one also finds the Introit *Let us all rejoice in the Lord* <note>original Latin: "Gaudeamus omnes in Domino"</note>. Nor should anyone wonder at this, especially seeing that the Psalmody of the Psalm that follows is in the First Mode; for (as I have said before) it is not improper that each of the last four Modes can be reduced to the Intonation of one of the eight named Psalm-tones. And if the note B-flat <term>b</term> placed in the position of the B-natural <term>♮</term> has the power to change one Mode into another...

However, the beginnings and likewise the irregular cadences are placed on other strings <note>Zarlino uses "strings" to refer to the specific notes or pitches of the scale</note>. But this Mode can be transposed a <term>Diapente: a perfect fifth</term> lower, with the help of the string $b$ <note>original: "chorda b"; referring to the use of B-flat</note>, just as the others can also be transposed.

### Of the Tenth Mode. Chapter 27.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'S' depicting a landscape with classical architecture and foliage.</image-desc>
IT WOULD BE a very long affair if one wished to show all the songs found in the Ecclesiastical books composed under the Ninth mode, and also under the Tenth, and under the other two that follow. These are for the most part Graduals, Offertories, Postcommunions, and the like; they are not as easy to recognize for those who are not well-instructed in Music as are those that are followed by certain intonations of Psalm verses, or the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original Latin: "Gloria patri"</note>. Such works include Antiphons, Responsories, and Introits, which can be easily identified by their ending and by the beginning of certain figures placed over the word **SEVOEAE** <note>a mnemonic using the vowels of "SAECULORUM AMEN," the closing of the Lesser Doxology</note>, which are the vowels of *world without end, Amen* <note>original Latin: "Seculorum amen"</note>. By these, they easily know under which Mode they are composed. They hold this Rule: when the end of the song finishes on $D$, and the beginning of their *Seuouae* starts on $a$, they know that such a song is in the First mode. When the end of one is placed on $D$, and the beginning of the other is placed on $F$, they know it is composed under the Second mode. But when the end of one is placed on $E$, and the beginning of the other on $c$, they say it is of the Third mode; similarly, they say the song is of the Fourth mode when it finishes on $E$ and the *Seuouae* begins on $a$. They also recognize that a work is composed under the Fifth mode when it ends on the string $F$ and the *Seuouae* begins on the string $c$; just as they know it to be of the Sixth when one ends on the string $F$ and the other begins on that same string, or on $a$. They then say that a song which ends on the string $G$ and has its *Seuouae* beginning on the string $d$ is of the Seventh mode; and that which ends on $G$ and has the beginning of the termination of the Psalm verse (for the said *Seuouae* is nothing else) on $c$ is of the Eighth. In this manner, through such Rules, they can easily come to the knowledge of the Modes, and then know in what way they ought to intone the said Verse or Psalm that follows such an Antiphon. These songs are composed under the first Eight Modes. But those that do not have such Intonations are free, and can be composed under whichever Mode most pleases [the composer], and they are not as easy to recognize as the ones already named. Therefore, it is no wonder if some have not had perfect knowledge of these last four Modes, since they cannot be known by that route. Wishing then to have perfect knowledge of them, one will note (returning to the discussion of the Tenth mode) that this Mode is contained within the strings of the Fifth species of the <term>Diapason: an octave</term>, $E$ and $e$, divided arithmetically by the string $a$. Because of this, some say that the said Mode is composed of the First species of the <term>Diapente: a perfect fifth</term>, $e$ and $a$, placed in the high range, and the Second species of the <term>Diatessaron: a perfect fourth</term>, $a$ and $E$, placed in the low range, joined at the string $a$, which is the final note of this Mode. We can say that the nature of this Mode is not very far from that of the Second and the Fourth, if such a judgment can be made from the harmony that arises from it; for it makes use of the Fifth which is common to the Second, and the Fourth which also serves the Fourth mode. Its regular Beginnings are on the strings $e$, $c$, $a$, and $E$; likewise its Cadences. But because having knowledge of the regular Cadences makes it easy to know on which strings the Irregular ones are made, I will give an example only of the former, which shall be placed below. Many compositions are found in this Mode, such as *The archangel Gabriel spoke to Zechariah* <note>original Latin: "Gabriel archangelus locutus est Zachariæ"</note> by Verdeloto <note>Philippe Verdelot (c. 1480–1530), a pioneer of the Italian madrigal</note>; similarly *Weep, eyes; bedew, cheeks* <note>original Latin: "Flete oculi, rorate genas"</note> by Adriano <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), Zarlino's teacher and maestro di cappella at St. Mark's</note>, both for four voices, and many others. This Mode is transposed a Fifth lower with the help of the string $b$ <note>B-flat</note>, without which little could be done that would be good.

->Of the Eleventh Mode. Chapter 28.<-

FROM THE third species of the <term>Diapason: the octave</term> **C** and **c**, which is harmonically divided by the string **G**, the Eleventh Mode is born. Practical musicians maintain that this Mode is composed of the fourth species of the <term>Diapente: the perfect fifth</term> **C** and **G**, placed in the lower register, and the third species of the <term>Diatessaron: the perfect fourth</term> **G** and **c**, placed in the higher register. This mode is by its very nature very well-suited to dances and balls; because of this, we see that the majority of dances heard in Italy are played in this Mode; from this, it arose that some called it the "Lascivious Mode" <note>This refers to the Ionian mode, which Zarlino views as light and cheerful, unlike the more "serious" or "austere" church modes</note>. Many songs are found in this mode in the Church books, such as the Mass they call the *Mass of the Angels*, and the Antiphons *Nourishing Mother of the Redeemer* <note>original Latin: "Alma redemptoris mater"</note> and *Queen of Heaven, Rejoice, Hallelujah* <note>original Latin: "Regina Cœli lætare Haleluiah"</note>. This Mode is so much in use and so beloved by the Moderns that many songs composed in the Fifth Mode <note>The Lydian mode, based on F</note>, by adding the string **b** <note>B-flat</note> in place of **♮** <note>B-natural</note>, have changed into the Eleventh; led by its sweetness and its beauty. Its regular beginnings are placed on the strings **C**, **E**, **G**, and **c**, and its cadences are placed there as well. Its irregular beginnings and cadences are placed upon other strings. Musicians have composed many songs in this Mode, among which is *The grieving mother stood* <note>original Latin: "Stabat mater dolorosa"</note> by **Josquin** <note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), arguably the most famous composer of the High Renaissance</note> for five voices; *O saving victim* <note>original Latin: "O salutaris hostia"</note>, *Nourishing Mother of the Redeemer* <note>original Latin: "Alma redemptoris mater"</note>, and *Full of a lovely thought* <note>original Italian: "Pien d'un vago pensier"</note> by **Adrian** <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the influential chapel master at St. Mark’s in Venice and Zarlino's teacher</note>; and *I went down into my garden* <note>original Latin: "Descendi in ortum meum"</note> by **Giachetto** <note>Jacquet of Mantua (1483–1559)</note>, all composed for six voices. Likewise the motet, *Hear, daughter, and see* <note>original Latin: "Audi filia, & vide"</note> by **Gombert** <note>Nicolas Gombert (c. 1495–c. 1560)</note>, along with *I have come into my garden* <note>original Latin: "Ego veni in hortum meum"</note>, which I composed many years ago, which are for five voices; and infinite others that would be tedious to number. This Mode is transposed away from its natural strings by a fourth into the higher register, or by a fifth into the lower register, with the help of the string **b** <note>B-flat</note>; passing through the strings of the <term>Tetrachord synemennon: the "connected" or B-flat tetrachord in ancient Greek theory</term>.

## Of the Twelfth Mode. Chapter 29.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring a seated figure in a landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

THE LAST of the Twelve Modes is the Twelfth, contained within the seventh species of the <term>Diapason: the octave</term> from **G** to **g**, divided arithmetically by its final note, **c**. This mode (as they say) is born from the conjunction of the fourth species of the <term>Diapente: the perfect fifth</term> **g** and **c**, placed in the high register, with the third species of the <term>Diatessaron: the perfect fourth</term> **c** and **G**, placed in the lower part. <note>Zarlino is describing the Hypoionian mode, which uses the same notes as the Ionian (C major) but ranges from G to G, with C as the 'final' or home note.</note>

This Mode was little used by the ancient Church musicians; but more modern composers, with the help of the <term>Tetrachordo synemennon: the "joined" tetrachord</term>—that is, using the note **B-flat**—have fashioned the majority of their melodies (which were originally in the sixth mode) into the Twelfth Mode. These moderns have also composed many new melodies in this Mode; among which is found the Antiphon *Hail, Queen of Heaven* <note>original Latin: "Ave regina coelorum"</note>, and many others. This Mode is well-suited to amorous matters containing lamentations, because in Plainchant it is a mournful Mode and possesses a certain sadness, according to their opinion. Nevertheless, any composer who desires to create a melody that is cheerful cannot help but depart from it. Its regular starting points are placed together with its regular cadences, as seen in the example, on the notes **g**, **e**, **c**, and **G**; the irregular starts and cadences are then placed upon other notes. One finds innumerable melodies in this Mode composed by many practical musicians, among which is the motet *Untouched, whole, and chaste are you, Mary* <note>original Latin: "Inviolata integra, & casta es Maria"</note> by Josquin <note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), one of the most famous composers of the Renaissance.</note> for five voices, and another by Adrian <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), Zarlino's teacher and maestro di cappella at St. Mark's in Venice.</note> for seven voices; the motet *He sends to the virgin* <note>original Latin: "Mittit ad virginem"</note> for six voices, and the madrigals *When you were born, Love* <note>original Italian: "Quando nascesti Amor"</note> for seven voices, *I saw on earth angelic manners* <note>original Italian: "I vidi in terra angelici costumi"</note> for six voices, and *When among other women* <note>original Italian: "Quando fra l'altre donne"</note> for five voices, all composed by Adrian. To these is added the motet by Jacquet <note>Jacquet of Mantua (1483–1559), a prominent composer of the mid-16th century.</note> for five voices, *The people sang out* <note>original Latin: "Decantabat populus"</note>, and the motets...

*No one comes to me* <note>original Latin: "Nemo venit ad me"</note> for five voices, and *O how glorious is the kingdom* <note>original Latin: "O quàm gloriosum est regnum"</note>—the former of which I composed long ago for five voices, and the latter for six—and many others. And although the natural <term>chords: pitches or notes</term> of this Mode are those shown above, nevertheless musicians, with the help of the <term>note b: B-flat</term>, transpose it downward by a <term>Diatessaron: a perfect fourth</term>. <note>By adding a B-flat, composers could shift the entire mode to a different pitch level while keeping the same intervals.</note> But let this be said sufficiently concerning the Nature and the Property of the Modes, and regarding the use, the Beginnings, and the <term>Cadences</term> of each one. <header>Part Four</header>

# What the Composer Must Observe in Composing, and in What Manner the Modes Should Be Judged.
## Chapter 30.

First, it must be noted that although the songs of each of the shown Modes are nearly infinite in number, many of them are not composed in their simple Modes, but in "Mixed" ones. For we will find the Third mode mixed with the Tenth, the Eighth with the Eleventh, and so on, moving through the others one by one, as can be understood by examining these songs. This is seen especially in those of the Third mode, which, instead of having the second species of the <term>Diapente: a perfect fifth</term> (E to B-natural) placed in the lower part, have the second species of the <term>Diatessaron: a perfect fourth</term> (E to A); and instead of the second species of the Diatessaron (B-natural to e), one finds the first species of the Diapente (A to e) in the upper part. Thus, even though these species are contained within the same <term>Diapason: an octave</term> (the span from E to e), in one Mode it is divided <term>harmonically</term> <note>Harmonic division places the smaller interval—the fourth—on top, creating the characteristic sound of "authentic" modes.</note> and holds the form of the Third mode, and in the other it is divided <term>arithmetically</term> <note>Arithmetic division places the smaller interval on the bottom, creating the "plagal" or collateral modes.</note> and holds the form of the Tenth. When such species are heard repeated so many times, not only does the greater part of the composition lack any character of the Third mode, but the entire song comes to be composed under the Tenth mode. 

The truth of this can be understood by the fact that if we add these two species together—that is, the Diatessaron E to A and the Diapente A to e—placing the latter in the high range and the former in the low, there is no doubt that we will have the form of the Tenth mode, contained within the fifth species of the Diapason, arithmetically mediated. In this way, a composition that we judge to be in the Third mode may have nothing by which we can judge it to be so, except for the end, because it finishes on the <term>chord: the pitch or note</term> E. 

However, even if the final note of the Mode is that by which we must judge the song (as the goal), and not before—as some wish, since everything is rightly judged by its end—we must not assume that we can recognize the Mode simply by that note alone. We should not believe that the judgment must be made from the note itself, but rather we must wait until the song is brought to its conclusion and judge there according to what is right. For it is then that the song is perfect and has its true form, which provides the opportunity to make such a judgment. 

But it should be noted that such an opportunity can be taken from two things: first, from the form of the entire song, and then from its end, that is, from its final note. Since the form is what gives "being" to a thing, I would judge it reasonable that this judgment should be made not from the final note simply, as some have wanted, but from the entire form contained in the song. Therefore, I say that if I had to judge any song by such a form—that is, by its progression, as is proper—I would not find it inconvenient for a principal Mode to end on the middle note of its harmonically divided octave, or for a collateral Mode to end on the outer notes of its arithmetically divided octave, leaving the "final" note to one side. 

How elegantly this can be done can be understood from the <term>motet</term> *If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord* <note>original Latin: "Si bona suscepimus de manu Domini"</note> for five voices, composed by Verdelot <note>Philippe Verdelot, a French composer active in Italy, considered a father of the Italian madrigal.</note>, and from the madrigal *O envy, enemy of virtue* <note>original Italian: "O inuidia nemica di virtute"</note> by Adrian <note>Adrian Willaert, Zarlino's teacher and the maestro di cappella at St. Mark's in Venice.</note>, also composed for five voices. From one end to the other, one has the progression of the Ninth mode and the other has the progression of the Second; yet they do not end on their true final note, but on the middle one. 

And what I say of the Third and Tenth modes could also be shown in the others, which I leave aside for brevity. For this reason, it is not surprising if one often hears no difference between a Mode that ends on the note E and another that ends on A, since they are composed as mixtures in the manner described. But if they were composed simply, without any mixing, there is no doubt that one would hear a great variety of harmony between one and the other. When, therefore, we have to judge any song whatever, we must consider it well from the beginning to the end, and see under what form it is composed—whether under the form of the First, the Second, or any other Mode—having regard for the <term>Cadences</term>, which give great light in such a matter. Then we can judge in which Mode it is composed, even if it does not have its end on its own final note, but rather on the middle one, or any other that suits the purpose. And if we

if we use such a manner of ending, it will not be out of place: since the Clergy also used such a method in their chants; as can be seen in the <term>Kyrie eleison: Lord have mercy</term> <note>original: "κύριε ἐλέησον"</note>, which they call of the Minor Double, or of the Apostles. The form of these (as is evident) is of the First mode; nonetheless, the last of them ends on the note *a*, which they call the *Confinal* <note>The confinal is a secondary ending note, usually a perfect fifth above the main final of the mode.</note>, and is the middle of the <term>Diapason: octave</term> between *D* and *d*, containing the form of the First mode. Furthermore, one finds the *Offertory* sung in the Mass of the Wednesday of the Third Sunday of Lent, *Lord, deal with me according to your mercy* <note>original: "Domine fac meum secundum misericordiam tuam"</note>, contained between its extreme notes *F* and *e*. And two other chants; the first of which is, *Bring offerings* <note>original: "Tollite hostias"</note>, contained between the aforementioned extreme notes, which is sung after the Communion of the Mass of the Eighteenth Sunday after Pentecost; the second is, *By the sign of the Cross* <note>original: "Per signum Crucis"</note>, which is sung on the solemn days of the Finding and the Exaltation of the Holy Cross; and it is contained between the extreme notes *F* and *g*. These chants hold within them the form of the Seventh mode: because in them one finds the modulation of its <term>Diapente: perfect fifth</term> *G* and *d*, and of its <term>Diatessaron: perfect fourth</term> *d* and *g*; and they end on the note *♮* <note>The note B-natural.</note>, which is the middle of the said Diapente. It is quite true that some moderns attribute such songs to the *Fourteenth* mode, as they say; but of this I shall let everyone who has understanding be the judge. Such songs, in some modern books, are found transposed into the bass by a Diapente, without the help of the note *b* <note>The note B-flat.</note>, outside of their natural notes; whether this was the ignorance or the laziness of the scribes, or perhaps the presumption of others with little understanding. But in good and corrected copies—of which I have an ancient one near me, written by hand, which can still be seen and examined—they are found among the notes named above. But it must be noted that I name the form of the Mode as the Octave divided into the Fifth and the Fourth; and also these two parts, which arise from the <term>harmonic and arithmetic divisions</term> <note>Harmonic division creates the "authentic" modes (fifth below the fourth), while arithmetic division creates "plagal" modes (fourth below the fifth).</note>, which are heard repeated many times in their proper Modes. When, therefore, we have to compose, we can know from what has been said the manner we must maintain in making the parts of the song; and in placing the *Cadences* in suitable places for the distinction of the words. And similarly, we can know what we must do in judging every other composition, in whatever manner it may be composed, as much in <term>Canto fermo: plainsong</term> as in <term>Canto figurato: polyphony</term>.

# Of the manner to be maintained in arranging the parts of the song; and of their extremities; and how far the highest notes of each part placed in the high range may be from the lowest note placed in the bass of the harmony.
## Chap. 31.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'M' showing a landscape with a figure and foliage.</image-desc>BUT BECAUSE there are sometimes some so indiscreet and of such little judgment in composing and in arranging the parts in a song, making them pass at times beyond measure into the *deep bass* or the *high treble*, so that they can hardly be sung; therefore, so that all the inconveniences that could occur in this Art may be removed, and that one may compose in such a way that every song can be sung comfortably, I will now show in what way the parts should be arranged among themselves; and how much they may similarly ascend or descend; and how distant the extreme notes of each song should be from one another. I say then, that whenever the Musician has proposed to compose any *Motet* or *Madrigal*, or any other sort of song; having first considered the matter—that is, the subject Words—he must then choose the Mode suitable to their nature. This being done, he shall observe that his *Tenor* proceeds regularly, modulating through the notes of that Mode, making its *Cadences* according as the perfection of the *Oration* <note>The text or speech being set to music.</note> and the end of its periods require. And above all, he must seek with every diligence to make such a *Tenor* as regular, beautiful, graceful, and full of sweetness as possible; for the song is usually founded upon it, so that it becomes the nerve and the bond of all its parts; which must be united together in such a manner and joined in such a way that the Tenor occupying the notes of some Mo-

<page-num>338</page-num>
<header>Part Four</header>

either authentic or plagal; the Bass should be the one that embraces the notes of its companion mode. And even if the Tenor should pass beyond the notes of the <term>Diapason: octave</term> containing the Mode in the low or high registers by one or two notes, this would matter little. For musicians do not care whether the Tenors and the other parts of their Modes are perfect, imperfect, or superfluous, provided that the parts are well-suited to the melody in a way that creates good harmony. It would indeed be proper that each of them did not exceed eight notes and remained gathered within the notes of its octave; but because they often go beyond this, and it sometimes proves greatly convenient for Composers, we shall attribute this more to a certain license they take than to the perfection of the thing itself. Truly, however, the parts must be ordered in such a way that the Mode upon which the <term>cantilena: song or composition</term> is based is founded in the Tenor. If the Mode occupies the notes of the Authentic in that part, as I have said, the Bass should contain the collateral or plagal Mode within its own notes. Conversely, if the Tenor occupies the plagal Mode in its notes, the Bass should come to contain the Authentic. In this way, when they are arranged in such a manner, the other parts will then be accommodated excellently without any inconvenience to the composition. One must therefore take care to ensure that the extreme notes of the Bass are not more distant from the extreme notes of the Tenor than by a <term>Diatessaron: perfect fourth</term> or a <term>Diapente: perfect fifth</term>; although it would not be an error if they passed even one note further. Being placed in such a manner, they will come to be as was said above: one occupying the notes of the Authentic mode and the other of its Plagal. 

With the Bass and Tenor thus linked, it will be an easy thing to put the other parts in their place and arrange them in the composition. The extreme notes of the soprano should be placed at the distance of an octave from the extremes of the Tenor; thus both the Tenor and the Soprano will come to sing in the notes of the authentic Mode. Similarly, those of the Alto should be placed at the distance of an octave from those of the Bass, and these parts will then be situated in such a way that they occupy the notes of the plagal Mode. With all these parts arranged in this fashion, the Soprano will hold the highest place in the composition, and the Bass the lowest. The Tenor and the Alto will then form the middle parts, with this difference: the notes of the Alto will be higher than those of the Tenor by about a perfect fourth, more or words. And the extreme notes of the Soprano will be as far from those of the Alto as those of the Tenor are from those of the Bass. 

And although (as I have said) such parts can sometimes extend by one note in the low register, and also in the high, and even by two or more if necessary beyond their octaves, one must nevertheless strive to ensure that the parts sing comfortably and that they do not exceed the tenth or eleventh note in their extremes. Otherwise, they would become strained, tiring, and difficult to sing due to their excessive ascent and descent. Beyond this, one must take care that the Bass does not extend much beyond the notes of its octave containing the Mode in the low register, nor the Soprano likewise in the high; for this would cause the composition to become extreme, which would result in great discomfort for the singers. The Composer should therefore ensure that, measuring from the lowest note of the Bass to the highest note of the Soprano, the range does not exceed the nineteenth note, though it would not be a great inconvenience if it reached the twentieth, but no further. By observing this, the parts will remain within their boundaries and will be singable without any effort. 

And because sometimes one is accustomed to composing without the Soprano—a style of composing that practitioners call <term>Comporre a voci mutate: composing for changed voices</term> <note>This refers to compositions for an all-male ensemble where the soprano part is absent or performed by lower voices.</note>—or composing only for multiple Tenors and the Bass, which they call <term>Comporre a voci pari: composing for equal voices</term>, I want it to be known that in the first type of composition, the Contralto is taken in place of the Soprano, and the other part comes to be contained within the same notes as the Contralto or within the notes of the Tenor. In this way, such a composition comes to be composed with two Contraltos or with three Tenors. It is true that respect is given to the part taken for the Soprano, for it is always somewhat higher than the one taken for the Alto, as the latter proceeds in a somewhat more relaxed manner. But be that as it may, one must compose the parts of the song in such a way that their extremes do not pass beyond the fifteenth note, counting the lowest and the highest. 

Other parts that might be added beyond the four named could not be added in any other way except by doubling one of them; they would be called Second Tenor or Second Bass, and I say the same of the others. Always, that part which continues to stay more in the high register than the low and reaches higher than the others may truly be called the Soprano. But one must note that the clefs of the Sopranos and Tenors in all the Modes are written as shown in the examples of each Mode, and those of the Basses are accommodated so that their notes can be (as I have said) distant from those of the Tenors by a fourth or a fifth; which I also say regarding the Sopranos

from those of the Contraltos. And it should be noted that at the beginning of the Second parts of <term>cantilene: songs or compositions</term>, the parts that begin to sing alone should resume their melodies upon a <term>chorda: note</term> that is a regular starting point of the Mode upon which the song is founded; or upon any other note, provided it is a natural note of that Mode. For it is not praiseworthy if, at the end of a first part, the Contralto, Tenor, or Soprano ends on one note, such as <note>original: "♮"</note> B-natural, and in the Second part begins on the note <note>original: "♭"</note> B-flat; or the reverse. The Composer will therefore be warned of such a thing, so that his composition may be purged of every error and every inconvenience, and he may be reputed a good and perfect Musician.

## In what manner Harmonies are accommodated to the subject Words. Chapter 32.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'R' featuring a seated figure in a scholarly or musical setting, surrounded by an ornate frame.</image-desc>

It remains now to be seen (since the time and place require it) in what manner one ought to accompany the Harmonies to the subject Words. I say "accompany the Harmonies to the Words" for this reason: because although in the Second Part (declaring according to the mind of Plato what Melody was), it was said that it is a compound of <term>Oratione: Speech or Text</term>, of Harmony, and of <term>Numero: Rhythm or Meter</term>; and it seems that in such a composition one of these things is not prior to the other; nevertheless, he places Speech before the other parts as the principal thing, and the other two parts as those that serve it. For after he has manifested the whole by means of the parts, he says that Harmony and Rhythm must follow Speech, and not Speech follow Rhythm or Harmony. And this is as it should be: because if in Speech—either by way of narration or imitation (things found within it)—one can treat matters that are happy or sad, or grave and even without any gravity, similarly matters that are honest or lascivious, it is necessary that we also make a choice of Harmony and a Rhythm similar to the nature of the matters contained in the Speech. Thus, from the composition of these things put together with proportion, the Melody may result according to the purpose. And truly we must heed what Horace says in his *Epistle on the Art of Poetry* <note>The Ars Poetica</note> when he says:

> <note>original: "Versibus exponi Tragicis res Comica non vult"</note> A comic matter does not wish to be set in tragic verses.

For just as it is not permitted among Poets to compose a Comedy with Tragic verses, so it will not be permitted to the Musician to accompany these two things—that is, the Harmony and the Words—together in an inappropriate way. It would not be suitable, therefore, to use sad Harmony and grave Rhythms for a happy subject; nor where funeral matters full of tears are treated is it permitted to use a happy Harmony and light or fast Rhythms (however we wish to call them). On the contrary, one must use happy harmonies and fast rhythms for happy matters, and sad harmonies and grave rhythms for sad matters, so that everything is done with proportion. I think everyone will know how to do this excellently when they have regard for what I have written in the Third Part and considered the nature of the Mode upon which they wish to compose the song. 

And one must take care to accompany every word in such a way that where it denotes harshness, hardness, cruelty, bitterness, and other similar things, the harmony is similar to it—that is, somewhat hard and harsh, yet in a way that does not offend. Similarly, when any of the words demonstrate weeping, pain, heartbreak, sighs, tears, and other similar things, the harmony should be full of sadness. This will be done excellently, when wanting to express the first effects, by using movements for the parts of the song that proceed without the <term>Semituono: semitone or half-step</term>, such as those of the <term>Tuono: whole tone</term> and those of the <term>Ditono: major third</term>, letting the <term>Sesta maggiore: major sixth</term> or the <term>Terzadecima maggiore: major thirteenth</term> be heard (which by their nature are somewhat harsh) above the lowest note of the harmony. These can also be accompanied by the <term>sincopa: syncopation</term> of the Fourth or the Eleventh above that part, with somewhat slow movements, among which one can even use the syncopation of the Seventh. 

But when one wishes to express the second effects <note>i.e., sadness or weeping</note>, then one shall use (according to the observance of the given Rules) movements that proceed by the Semitone, those of the <term>Semiditono: minor third</term>, and other similar ones; frequently using <term>Seste minori: minor sixths</term> or <term>Terzedecime minori: minor thirteenths</term> above the lowest note of the song, which are by their nature sweet and smooth—especially when accompanied in the proper ways and with discretion and judgment. But it must be noted that the cause of expressing such effects is not attributed solely to the aforementioned consonances placed in such a manner; it is also attributed to the Movements made by the parts while singing. These movements are of two sorts: Natural and Accidental. Natural movements are those made between the natural notes of the song, where no sign or accidental note intervenes; and these movements have more of the virile <note>meaning strong or vigorous</note> than those made by means of...

accidental notes, marked with such signs <note>flats and sharps</note>, which are truly accidental and have something of the languid about them; from these, a sort of interval is similarly born, called Accidental. But from the first ones <note>natural notes</note> are born those intervals called Natural. Wherefore we must note that the first movements make the <term>cantilena: song or melody</term> somewhat more sonorous and virile, and the second ones make it sweeter and somewhat more languid. For this reason, the first can serve to express the first effects <note>stronger emotions</note>, and the second movements can serve the others; so that by accompanying the intervals of the major and minor consonances with the natural and accidental movements made by the parts with some judgment, one will come to imitate the words with well-understood harmony. As for the observance of the <term>Numbers: the rhythmic and metrical proportions of the music</term>, having first considered the matter contained in the <term>Oratione: the speech or text</term>, if it is cheerful, one must proceed with vigorous and fast movements—that is, with figures that carry speed of time with them, such as <term>Minims: half notes</term> and <term>Semiminims: quarter notes</term>. But when the matter is mournful, one must proceed with tardy and slow movements. In this, <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the maestro di cappella at St. Mark’s in Venice and Zarlino's teacher, famous for his careful text setting.</note> Adriano has taught us how to express both modes in many songs, among which are found these: *I saw on earth angelic customs* <note>original: "I vidi in terra angeli costumi"</note>; *Harsh heart and savage* <note>original: "Aspro core e seluaggio"</note>; *Where I turned my eyes* <note>original: "Ove chi' posi gli occhi"</note>; all composed for six voices; and *When among the other women* <note>original: "Quando fra l'altre donne"</note>; *Love has reached me* <note>original: "Giunto m'ha Amor"</note>, for five voices; and infinite others, with infinite <term>motets: sacred choral compositions</term> which I do not name, so as not to be long-winded. And this must be observed not only regarding the Numbers—even though the Ancients understood such things in a different manner than the Moderns do, as is clearly seen in many places in Plato—but we must also take care to accommodate the words of the Text to the singable figures in such a way, and with such Numbers, that no <term>Barbarism: a grammatical or rhythmic error in text setting</term> is heard. This occurs when a long syllable is made to be uttered as short in the singing, or conversely, a short one is made to be uttered as long, as is heard every day in infinite songs; which truly is a shameful thing. Nor is this vice found only in <term>Canti figurati: polyphonic music</term>, but also in <term>Canti fermi: plainchant</term>, as is manifest to all those who have judgment. For there are few that are not full of such barbarisms, and in which one does not hear, infinite times, the penultimate syllables of these words—"Lord" <note>original: "Dominus"</note>, "Angel" <note>original: "Angelus"</note>, "Son" <note>original: "Filius"</note>, "Miracle" <note>original: "Miraculum"</note>, "Glory" <note>original: "Gloria"</note>, and many others that pass quickly—being uttered with great length of time. This would be a very praiseworthy thing and so easy to correct; by changing them just a little bit, the song would be accommodated without changing its primary form. This is because the error consists only in the <term>Ligature: a group of notes tied together</term> of many figures or notes placed under said short syllables, which make them long without any purpose, when a single figure would be sufficient. One must similarly be careful not to separate any part of the Text from another with Pauses <note>rests</note>, as some poorly-informed people do, until its <term>Clausula: a musical phrase or clause</term> or any of its parts are finished, so that the meaning of the words is perfect. Do not make the <term>Cadence</term>—especially one of the principal ones—or place Pauses larger than that of a minim if the Period or the perfect sentence of the Text is not finished; use the minim pause only at middle points. Indeed, it is a faulty thing; how much it is observed by some poorly-advised practitioners, anyone who wants to pay attention to such a thing can easily see and know. The Composer must, therefore, in such things, open his eyes and not keep them closed, for it is of great importance. This is so that he is not considered ignorant of such a necessary thing. He must be careful to place the Pause of a minim or a semiminim, as it suits him, at the head of the middle points of the Text, for they will serve as commas; but at the end of Periods, he must place whatever quantity of pauses suits him. For it seems to me that, placed in such a manner, the members of the Period can be perfectly discerned from one another, and the perfect sense of the words can be heard without any inconvenience.

## The method to be held in placing the singable Figures under the Words. Chapter 33.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' containing a circular scene with two figures in a hilly landscape with buildings in the distance.</image-desc>

Who could ever recount the bad order and the bad grace held by many practitioners, and how much confusion they have made in accommodating the singable figures to the words of the proposed Text? Certainly, this could be done, but with great difficulty. However, when I consider that a Science which has given laws and good order to other sciences is sometimes so confused in certain things that it can hardly be tolerated, I cannot help but be saddened. It is truly a wonder to hear and see the songs that are found, in which—besides hearing the periods confused in the delivery of the words—one hears imperfect clauses, cadences out of place, singing without order, infinite errors in applying the harmonies to the words, the...

He insists that musical rests must align with grammatical pauses like commas and periods to preserve the meaning of the words.</summary>
