# Part Four

...the few observations of the <term>Modes: the melodic scales used in Renaissance music</term>, the poorly fitted parts, the passages without charm, the <term>Numbers: the rhythmic proportions</term> without proportion, and the movements without purpose; one also finds in these compositions the <term>singable figures: musical notes</term> fitted to the words in such a way that the singer does not know how to decide, nor find a comfortable way to pronounce them. Now he sees many notes contained under two syllables, and now many syllables under two notes. Now he hears a part that, while singing in some place, makes an <term>apostrophe: the elision or "collision" of two vowel sounds into one</term>, as the words require; yet when he wishes to do the same while singing his own part, he loses the beauty and the elegant way of singing because a note carrying a long duration is placed under a short syllable, and vice versa. Wherefore he sometimes hears that long syllable pronounced in the other parts, while in his own he is necessarily required to pronounce it short; so that hearing such diversity, he knows not what to do, but remains entirely astonished and confused.

And because everything consists in fitting the singable figures to the underlying words—and in songs it is required that the strings <note>the musical pitches</note> be described and noted with them so that the sounds and voices can be uttered in every melody—it is through these figures that one expresses the "Number," that is, the length and brevity of the syllables contained in the <term>Oratione: the text or speech</term>. Under these syllables, one often places not just one, but two, three, or more of the aforementioned notes. Therefore, so that no confusion occurs in fitting them to the syllables of the underlying words, and wishing to remove such disorder if I can—besides the many rules given in various places fitted to the subject matter according to the purpose—I will now set down these rules, which will serve not only the composer but also the singer.

*The First Rule* shall be to always place a suitable note under a long or short syllable so that no <term>barbarism: an error in linguistic pronunciation or accent</term> is heard. For in <term>canto figurato: polyphonic or "measured" music</term>, every singable note that is distinct and not tied (excepting the <term>Semiminim: a quarter note</term> and all those smaller than it) carries its own syllable; this is also observed in <term>canto fermo: plainchant</term>. In chant, every square note is fitted to its own syllable, except sometimes the middle notes which are treated like minims or even semiminims, as is understood in many melodies and especially in the <note>original: "Credo in vnum Deum"</note> *I believe in one God*, which they call the "Cardinal's" <note>A specific, well-known plainchant melody for the Credo.</note>.

*The Second Rule* is that for every <term>Ligature: a group of notes written as a single connected symbol</term> of several figures or notes, whether in polyphony or plainchant, only one syllable is placed at the beginning.

*The Third Rule* is that no syllable is fitted to the <term>Dot: a point of addition that increases a note's value</term> placed near notes in polyphony, even though the dot itself is sung.

*The Fourth Rule* is that it is rarely the custom to place a syllable above any Semiminim, nor above those notes smaller than it, nor on the note that immediately follows it.

*The Fifth Rule* is that no syllable is customarily paired with notes that immediately follow the dots of a <term>Semibreve: a whole note</term> or a <term>Minim: a half note</term> when those notes are of lesser value than the dots—such as a Semiminim after a dotted Semibreve, or a <term>Chroma: an eighth note</term> after a dotted Minim. The same applies to notes immediately following those smaller figures.

*The Sixth Rule* is that when a syllable is placed above a Semiminim, another syllable may also be placed above the following note.

*The Seventh Rule* is that any note, whatever it may be, that is placed at the beginning of a song or in the middle after any rest, necessarily carries with it the pronunciation of a syllable.

*The Eighth Rule* is that in plainchant, one never repeats a word or syllable, even though one sometimes hears those who do so (a truly blameworthy thing). But in polyphony, such repetitions are tolerated—I do not mean of a single syllable or word, but of some part of the text when the meaning is complete. This may be done when there is a sufficient quantity of notes that they can be repeated conveniently; although repeating the same thing so many times is not (in my judgment) very good, unless it were done to better express words that contain some grave sentiment worthy of consideration.

*The Ninth Rule* is that after having fitted all the syllables found in a <term>Period: a complete sentence or musical phrase</term> or part of the text to the singable notes, when only the penultimate and the last syllables remain, that penultimate syllable may have several of the smaller notes under it—such as two, three, or another quantity—provided that the said penultimate syllable is long and not short. For if it were short, a barbarism would be committed; by singing in this way, one does what many call the <term>Neuma: a melisma, or a long passage of notes on a single syllable</term>, which occurs when many notes are uttered under one syllable, even though placing notes in such a manner goes against the first rule given.

*The Tenth and final rule* is that the last syllable of the text must end, according to the observance of the given rules, on the last note of the song.

But because one can find infinite examples in this matter by examining the learned compositions of <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562)</note> Adriano and those who have truly been and are his disciples, I shall move on to discuss Ligatures, which are made with certain singable figures and serve such a purpose, without showing any further example.

### Fourth Part: On Ligatures. Chapter 34.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' depicting a putto sitting in a landscape with a tree and distant hills.</image-desc>**S**urely <term>Ligatures: groups of two or more notes joined together into a single symbol</term> are necessary in <term>figured song: polyphonic music where notes have specific rhythmic values</term> for many reasons. They are convenient not only for composers when fitting the singable figures (or notes) to the syllables of the chosen text, but also because composers sometimes take a subject from a <term>plainchant antiphon: a traditional, unmeasured church melody</term> that contains many linked figures. In wanting to base their composition upon such a chant and wanting to imitate it, they find it necessary to use these same ligatures in the same manner. However, they do not use all of them, as it is sometimes inconvenient, but rather select a few—and not always with those exact figures, but with different ones, as the composer sees fit. Therefore, so that one may have full knowledge of such things and know in what manner they are to be made, which figures are to be linked, and what their value is, we shall treat them now; but first, we must see what a Ligature actually is. 

Practical musicians say that a Ligature is a certain binding or joining of simple figures made with appropriate strokes or lines, in which each figure that can be linked is formed with either a square or an <term>oblique: a slanted, diamond-like shape representing two notes</term> body. Such Ligatures are made with three types of figures: the Maxima, the Long, and the Breve. Of these, the two extremes—the Maxima and the Breve—vary their value depending on how they are linked. The Maxima is a "passive" figure, meaning it is subject to a reduction of its value and can never be increased; the Breve is similarly passive, as it can be increased or decreased according to how it is placed and the position it holds within the Ligature. The Long, however, is not subject to such things, as it receives no increase or decrease; this is because it is always placed in the Ligature without any variation to its form, regardless of where it is positioned. 

Every Ligature is considered in two ways: first, when the following figure is placed higher than the preceding one; second, conversely, when the preceding figure is placed higher than the following one. When figures are placed in the first way, the Ligature is called **Ascending**; when they are placed in the second way, it is called **Descending**. It is true that one often makes a Ligature where the figures are linked both ascending and descending, as we shall see. One must note that the Maxima is placed in the Ligature in two ways: first, according to its true form, which is a straight, long body; second, with an oblique or "twisted" body, if we wish to call it that. When it is placed without the oblique shape, it appears in two ways: either with a "tail" (or "leg," as we might call it) on the right side, or without one. When placed in these ways—whether linked with other figures or not, and whether at the beginning, middle, or end of the Ligature—it always retains its value: that is, it is worth four Breves. 

When it is placed as an oblique, it appears in two ways: either it ascends from the "low" part (the left side) to the "high" part (the right side), or it descends from the high left side to the low right side. This happens in two manners: either having a leg on the left side or being without one. If it has a leg, it is either turned downward or upward. When it has a downward leg and is oblique toward the low notes, both its first and second parts are worth one Breve; the same applies when it is oblique moving upward, though this form is no longer in use today. But when it has the leg turned upward and is similarly oblique (whether toward the low or the high, though this is also not used), both the first and second parts individually are worth a <term>Semibreve: a note value half as long as a Breve</term>. 

When such oblique shapes do not have a leg: if the second part goes toward the low notes, the first part is worth a Long and the second a Breve. But when it goes toward the high notes (which musicians no longer practice), both the first and second parts individually are worth one Breve. This is understood when they are not accompanied or linked with other figures; when they are linked, other considerations apply. Regarding the Breve, I say it is found in these Ligatures in two ways: with a leg and without a leg. When it has a leg, it appears in two manners: with the leg on the left side turned downward, and with the leg turned upward. When placed in a Ligature in this way, different rules apply. Every figure that can be linked is placed in the Ligature in three ways: at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end; and from these positions, one recognizes the value of the parts of each Ligature. Therefore, to have perfect knowledge of the value of each, many Rules are given, the first of which is: *That every figure placed at the beginning of the Ligature which is without a leg, whether it be square or oblique,*

*here, except for the <term>Maxima: the longest note value in this system</term> placed with or without a stem (provided it is not an <term>oblique: a slanted shape representing two notes</term> where the second note descends); such a figure, or the first part of any figure, will always have the value of a <term>Long: a note value usually equal to two or three Breves</term>. These rules concern the first figures; but regarding the middle figures, there is a different consideration:*

But two things must be noted: first, that the discussion of such figures has focused on the **Form** of their bodies and not on anything else; second, that any figure placed in the aforementioned Ligatures is subject to those same <term>accidents: rhythmic alterations like perfection or imperfection</term> that <term>simple notes: individual, unlinked notes</term> are subject to, even though some have held the contrary. And because such Ligatures (as I believe) were ordered in this manner by the first inventor and assigned a certain quantity according to the different styles of the figures placed in them, and according to different positions as it seemed fit to him; therefore, everyone may be content with what I have said about them, not seeking for what reason he wished to value one more than another, or to order such Ligatures more in one way than another: for such a search is a vain thing.*

## What everyone must have who desires to reach any
## perfection in Music.
### Cap. 35.

NOW that I realize I have, by divine favor, finally arrived at the desired end of these labors of mine; before I conclude this discussion, I want us to see two things. One of these will be that we show those things required of one who desires to reach the highest level of this Science. The other is that we say that, in making a judgment of the things of Music, we must not give it entirely over to the senses (because they are fallible) but rather accompany them with reason. For since these two parts, joined together, are in agreement, there is no doubt that one cannot commit any error, and the judgment will be perfect. Beginning then from the first point, I say that he who desires to reach that perfection in the matters of Music which can be attained, and to see all that is permitted in such a Science, needs to have many things within himself so that he may easily come into knowledge of those things which are hidden to many in this faculty, without the help of others. If even one of these things were lacking, one could not hope to reach that mark which he had designed. Therefore, it should be known that Music is a science <term>subalternated to Arithmetic: a science that derives its principles from a higher science (in this case, the math of ratios)</term>, as I declared in Chapter 20 of the First Part; because the forms of the con- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "consonances."</note>

consonances are contained under certain determined proportions, which are understood through Numbers; to have a full understanding of all the occurrences relating to them, it is necessary to be well-instructed in the matters of **Arithmetic** <note>original: "Arithmetica"</note> in the handling of Numbers and Proportions; or rather, if one wishes to learn from these labors of mine only those things which are necessary for such business, he should at least know the handling of **mercantile numbers**; so that when he comes to the use of Proportions, he may easily obtain what he desires. And because the ratios of Sounds cannot be known except by means of **Sonorous Bodies**—which are quantities that can be divided and are truly those which provide the Matter of consonances—it is therefore necessary to be instructed in the matters of **Geometry**; or at least, to know how to use the **Compass** <note>original: "Compasso, o Sesto"</note> well in dividing a line, and to know the significance of a Point, a Line (whether curved or straight), a Surface, a Body, and other similar things belonging to **continuous Quantity**; so that in his speculations, he may more easily have the help of this Science in dividing any sonorous Quantity whatever. He must also, if not perfectly, then at least passably know how to play the **Monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used for demonstrating musical intervals</note> or the **Harpsichord** <note>original: "Arpichordo"</note>; and this because it is the most stable and the most perfect in its tuning of all other instruments; so that from it, he may have knowledge of sonorous and dissonant intervals, and may at times put into practice and test those things that he finds anew each day, in order to investigate the properties of sonorous Numbers with proof in hand. 

But this presupposes that he knows how to tune such an instrument perfectly and that he has perfect hearing; so that when he wishes to investigate (as happens at times) many differences of intervals, he may make a perfect judgment without committing an error; and if he wishes to tune any other instrument, he will know what needs to be done. It is also necessary that he be instructed primarily in the **Art of Singing**, and in the art of **Counterpoint** <note>The technique of combining different melodic lines</note> (or Composition), and that he has a good understanding of it; so that he may know how to put into action all that occurs in Music, and may know how to judge if it is achievable or not: for bringing the things of Music into being is truly nothing other than leading them to their ultimate end and their perfection; just as happens also in the other Arts and Sciences that contain these two parts within them—that is, the **Speculative** <note>The theoretical or contemplative side</note> and the **Practical** <note>The applied or performative side</note>—as is the case with Medicine. 

I will now omit, for the sake of brevity, how much benefit the knowledge of other Sciences may be to him: first, **Grammar**, through which one has perfect knowledge of languages to be able to clearly understand the authors who treat of Music, and for wishing to write anything about it; and also because sometimes one reads certain Histories in which many things are found that are of great help and provide great light when one wishes to have exact knowledge of the matters of this science. **Dialectic** <note>The art of logical argument</note> is then of great benefit for being able to reason and discourse upon good foundations. As for how useful **Rhetoric** can be to students of this Science for being able to express their concepts in an orderly fashion, and for being instructed in matters of **Natural Science** <note>original: "Scienza naturale," referring to Physics/Natural Philosophy</note>, I will leave that to be judged by anyone who has even a grain of sense: since Music is not only subject to Mathematical science, but also to **Natural Philosophy**, as I have declared elsewhere; and in other sciences as well, for truly they can only be of help. And although its end consists in operation—that is, in being reduced to action—and although the Hearing, when it is purified, cannot easily be defrauded by sound; nevertheless, things can sometimes occur where a man (being deprived of any of the aforementioned things which are of great use in knowing their causes) remains greatly deceived. Wishing therefore to acquire perfect knowledge of Music, it is necessary to be endowed with all these things; for whenever he has need of any of them, he will be that much less able to arrive at that degree which he desires; and he will arrive there with as much greater difficulty as the ignorance of the named things, which are of greater importance and more necessary, is greater.

## On the fallacy of the senses; and that judgment should not be made
## solely by their means: but reason must
## accompany them. Chapter 36.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter E featuring a landscape with a classical building and trees.</image-desc>

**E**ven if this proposition is very famous among Philosophers—that the **Sense** never errs regarding its own sensible object—nevertheless, if such a proposition were understood simply as the words sound, it would sometimes be false: Because the proper object is taken in two ways. First, for that which is not understood by any other sense, and by itself changes the sense, and contains under itself all those things that by themselves are understood...

understood only by that sense; like *Color*, or the *Visible thing*, which is the proper object of *Seeing*; and *Sound*, which is the proper object of *Hearing*; and so on for the others; as I declared in Chapter 71 of the Third Part. Next, for that which by itself moves the sense, and cannot be felt or understood by another sense. In such a way that the species contained under the proper object taken in the first way is called the *Proper sensible* <term>Proper sensible: A technical term in Aristotelian philosophy for a quality, like color or smell, that is perceived by one specific sense alone.</term>; just as whiteness and blackness: since they move the vision, imprinting their image into it, and are not understood by themselves except by vision; and the same is understood of the species of *Sounds*, and of other things. Hence, although the Sense does not err concerning the Proper Object in the first way; it may very well err in the second: especially when those conditions that are required are not found; that is, that the Sense be properly near the Object; that the Organ be properly disposed; and that the Medium be pure and not corrupted. And even if it did not err (as the *Philosopher* <note>original: "Filosofo"; referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in Renaissance texts.</note> intends) concerning the proper object in the second way, given the conditions already mentioned, it can nonetheless err concerning the *Subject* of the proper sensible objects, that is, concerning the place and where it is positioned: because this does not belong to the external feeling, but to the internal, such as the cogitative virtue or power <term>Cogitative power: An internal faculty that was believed to process and judge the data collected by the external senses.</term>, which is the noblest among the sensitive powers; for being closer than any other to the intellect.

And I have wished to say this: because many believe that since the Sciences had their origin from the feelings, we should give greater faith to them than to any other thing: since they cannot be deceived regarding their own proper objects. But truly these people are greatly distant from the truth, believing that one cannot err: For while it is true that every science had its beginning from them; nevertheless, they have not acquired the name of science from them, and from them one has not had the certainty of what is sought in science: but rather from the reasons and from the demonstrations made by way of the internal feelings; that is, by the work of the intellect, which is discourse <note>In this context, "discourse" refers to the step-by-step process of logical reasoning.</note>. And if the intellect can err at times while reasoning, as it truly does err; how much more might the sense err? Therefore I say, that neither the Sense without reason, nor Reason without the sense, will be able to give good judgment of any scientific object: but rather when these two parts are joined together.

And that this is true, we can easily know from this; that if we wish to divide (to give an example) any thing into two parts which are equal by means of the Sense alone, we can never divide it perfectly. And even if it happened that after the division was made they were equal; this would be done by chance, and we could never be certain of such a thing, if another test were not made. And every division made in such a way will be even more difficult the more parts we wish to make of the thing that is to be divided. And even if (as I have said) such divisions were made according to the purpose; nevertheless the intellect can never be at peace, until reason shows it that it has been well done; and this happens because the Sense cannot know the minute differences that are found between things: since it remains confused by too much or too little, and is even corrupted; as is understood of the sense of *Hearing* regarding *Sounds*, which is offended by greatness, that is, by some great noise; and is not capable of smallness, or a minimum quantity.

Therefore it will be necessary to have a thoughtful reason to find such differences; as one sees that if from a large mountain of grain one were to remove twenty-five or fifty grains, *Vision* would not be capable of perceiving such a quantity, which is almost insensible compared to the mountain; just as it could not make any judgment if the aforementioned number of grains were added to such a mountain; hence, wanting to know such a thing, it would be necessary to proceed otherwise than by way of the sense. The same truly happens regarding *Sounds*, for although Hearing cannot err in the first way shown, in judging consonant intervals from dissonant ones; nevertheless its office is not to judge how far one is from the other according to the low and the high pitch; and by what quantity one exceeds or is exceeded by the other: since if it could not err regarding such things; truly the discovered measures, and the discovered weights, and other similar things would be used in vain. But truly they were not discovered in vain; because the ancient Philosophers knew very well that the feeling regarding this could be deceived.

We say then, that although the science of Music had its origin from the sense of hearing; as was said in the First Chapter of the First Part; and its ultimate perfection and final end is to put it into action and to practice it; even though *Sound* is the proper sensible, or rather the object of *Hearing*; it is not for this reason that we should give this office of judging to feeling alone in matters of *Sounds* and *Voices*: but we must always accompany it with reason. Nor should such judgment be given entirely to reason, leaving aside the sense: because one without the other can always be a cause of error. Therefore, having to have perfect knowledge of the matters of Music, it will not be enough to rely on the sense; even if someone were of excellent

judgment: but one must seek to investigate, and to know the whole, in such a way that reason is not discordant from sense, nor sense from reason, and then everything will be well. But just as to make this judgment in matters of **Science** <term>Science: In this context, "science" (scienza) refers to a structured body of theoretical knowledge or a philosophical system.</term> it is necessary that these two things coincide together; so it is necessary that he who wishes to judge anything belonging to **Art** <term>Art: Referring to the practical application of skill or craft, as opposed to pure theory.</term> should have two parts; first, that he be expert in matters of science, that is, of the **speculative** <term>Speculative: The theoretical or contemplative study of music, often involving mathematics and philosophy.</term>; and then also in those of Art, which consists in **practice**; and he must know how to compose. For no one will ever be able to judge rightly that which he does not know; rather, it is inevitable that, not knowing it, he will judge it poorly. Wherefore, just as one who is only learned in that part of Medicine called **Theory** will never be able to make a perfect judgment of an illness if he has not put his hand to **Practice**; or he will always be liable to err, trusting only in Science; so the practical Musician without the speculative, or the speculative without the practice, will always be liable to error, and to make a bad judgment of the matters of Music. Hence, just as it would be a crazy thing to trust a Doctor who did not have both of the named things joined together; so he would truly be foolish and crazy who would want to trust the judgment of one who was only a practitioner, or had given his work only to Theory. I have wanted to say this because some are found of such little judgment, and so reckless and presumptuous, that although they possess neither of these parts, they wish to make judgment of that which they do not know. And there are some others who, by their own wretched nature, to show they are not ignorant, blame the good as much as the wretched labors of everyone. There are some others who, having neither judgment nor knowledge, follow that which pleases the ignorant common people; and at times they wish to judge the competence of someone by their name, nation, homeland, the service they hold with others, or their person. If being excellent and rare in a profession consisted in the name, the nation, the country, the service, the person, and other such things, I believe for certain that many years would not pass before a man could not be found who was ignorant. For every father would open his eyes to such a thing and would do everything possible to have children distinguished in any profession; since there is not found (as I think) a father who does not have this natural desire: that their children be superior to everyone in any science and in any profession. But in truth the opposite is seen; for where great and famous men of any profession have been born—who have been few in respect to the total number—there have been born thousands and thousands of obscure, ignorant, clumsy, and crazy men, as one can see by looking around. I have wanted to say this because sometimes a public cry and a public fame carry such weight, not only among men of some judgment, that such a thing makes it so that no one dares to speak against the common opinion (even though they perceive it at times to be most evidently false); rather, it makes them keep silent, and stay suspended and mute. And to give some appropriate example of this, I remember that reading once in the second book of *The Courtier* by Count Baldassare Castiglione, I found that when some verses were presented in the court of the Lady Duchess of Urbino under the name of **Sannazaro** <note>Jacopo Sannazaro (1458–1530) was a famous Italian poet of the Renaissance.</note>, everyone judged them to be very excellent and praised them most highly; later, when it was known for certain that they had been composed by another, they immediately lost their reputation and were judged less than mediocre. Similarly, I found that when a **motet** <term>Motet: A short piece of sacred choral music, typically polyphonic and unaccompanied.</term> was sung in the presence of the named Lady, it did not please, nor was it reckoned among the good ones, until it was known that the composition was by **Josquin** <note>Josquin des Prez (c. 1450–1521), widely considered the greatest composer of the high Renaissance.</note>. But to show also how much malice and ignorance together in men can sometimes do, there comes to my memory now that which I have many times heard said by the most excellent **Adrian Willaert** <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the influential Flemish composer and maestro di cappella at St. Mark’s in Venice; Zarlino was his student.</note>: that while that six-voice motet, *A good and sweet word* <note>original: "*Verbum bonum, & suaue*"; a famous sequence for the Virgin Mary.</note>, was sung in Rome in the Pope's chapel almost every feast of Our Lady under the name of Josquin, it was held to be one of the most beautiful compositions sung in those times. He, having come from Flanders to Italy in the time of **Leo X** <note>Pope Leo X, reigned 1513–1521, a great patron of the arts.</note>, and finding himself in the place where this motet was being sung, saw that it was attributed to Josquin; and when he said it was his own, as it truly was, the malice or (I shall say more modestly) the ignorance of those people was so great that they never wanted to sing it again. Of those who are without any judgment, Count Baldassare adds in that same place another example of one who, drinking of the very same wine, said at one time that it was most perfect, and at another time most insipid, because he was persuaded that they were of two different sorts of wine. Now let everyone see that judgment is not given to all; and from this let them learn not to be precipitous in praising or blaming anything, in Music as also in every other Science or Art; since for so many reasons—such as many impediments that can occur, and many things of which the causes cannot be known—judging is a very difficult thing.

<summary>Zarlino argues that true musical judgment requires a balance of theoretical knowledge and practical skill, warning that fame and prejudice often cloud the perception of even the most experienced listeners.</summary>

difficult and dangerous; all the more so, because different tastes <note>Original: "appetiti." In this period, the word refers to sensory inclinations or personal preferences.</note> are found, in such a way that what pleases one does not please another; and while one person delights in a **sweet and suave harmony** <term>Harmony: In the Renaissance, this referred to the pleasing relationship between different musical parts or intervals.</term>, another will want it to be somewhat harsher and sharper. Nor, upon hearing such judgments, should **Musicians** despair, even if they were to hear these people blame and speak every ill of their compositions; instead, they should take heart and be comforted, since the number of those who lack judgment is almost infinite. Indeed, there are few who do not judge themselves worthy of being counted among prudent and judicious men.

<header>Part.</header>

<warning>The text on this page consists of mirrored bleed-through from the reverse side of the leaf. It is transcribed here as it was intended to be read.</warning>

...the danger to which you expose yourself: all the more so, because those who speak these [languages] do not understand you, nor do they understand those languages that they do not know; but the **Demons** <note>In the context of Renaissance treatises, "Demons" often refers to spiritual entities believed to be the source of occult or forbidden knowledge.</note> understand them well, for they are their authors. In this, and in every other thing you do, flee from **pride**, because God watches over the humble: flee from **vainglory**, because its reward is empty smoke: flee from **obstinacy**: because the obstinate man is one of the children of **perdition** <term>Perdition: A state of eternal punishment or spiritual ruin.</term>. Love the Lord God with all your heart, and keep yourself in **humility**, so that God does not abandon you: because man by himself cannot do any good. And finally I tell you, that if anyone else should tell you otherwise: do not believe them, because the truth is this, which I tell you out of charity, for the good I wish for you, and for the salvation of your soul: may God give us all His holy grace. Amen.

### END.
